title: Battles loom over social care, but this fight must be won. At last, we have a PM who believes that | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Burnham seems ready to use his power and influence. He understands the depth of this crisis: the task is persuading all those still in denial, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Burnham seems ready to use his power and influence. He understands the depth of this crisis: the task is persuading all those still in denial, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Illustration: Bill Bragg/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Bill Bragg/The GuardianOpinionSocial careBattles loom over social care, but this fight must be won. At last, we have a PM who believes thatPolly ToynbeeBurnham seems ready to use his power and influence. He understands the depth of this crisis: the task is persuading all those still in denialWed 29 Jul 2026 13.48 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 14.30 EDTShare“People pleaser!” That’s the insult Andy Burnham’s enemies sneer at him. And yes, he will need all his mightiest people-pleasing talents to win over voters to contribute to a new national care service. Choosing this forever failed policy (22 major reviews over three decades) as his first great challenge is a remarkable act of bravery. No mere people pleaser would dare step on this political live rail.It will use up vast amounts of political capital to get a national care service off the ground. He hardly neededTuesday’s Mail front page(“Burnham’s £18bn ‘death tax’ nightmare”) to remind him. But he has already fought on the battleground that is social care reform. “I do have some of the scars,”he said. How good to also hear him take a firm swipe at media attackers, who will now redouble their efforts. “You can’t create scare stories when people are already scared by what they’re seeing anyway through their own eyes in their own homes or in care homes,” he said. This is no grasp at low-hanging fruit, no search for a quick win. It’s a cause of deep conviction.In his speech from a north London care home, the prime minister told of his father with dementia, and of the struggle for families to get any help, the poor quality of much of it, the astronomical costs for some and the profiteering of private equity firms buying up care homes. That will have resonated with many, but his challenge now is to win the attention, hearts and minds of those who know nothing of social care. Making people care about care is the first vital step.Asurvey last yearfound 33% of people in England believed care was generally free at the point of need, like the NHS, and another 18% didn’t know whether it was. Many get a nasty shock when they need it for their family and find they must pay if they have savings above £23,250. Only 4% listed social care as a top priority for the country; its political salience is low because at any one time, few people are using it – and they put it out their minds afterwards. In England, this unseen serviceuses up a phenomenal 78% of local council funds: no wonder people think they get bad value for their council tax, as visible services keep shrinking to pay for it. Everything about it is broken.People need to wake up to what confronts us. They need to know that the roulette wheel of fate decides which families are stricken by dementia:one in three people alive today will get this most dreaded of diseases. Some may live for years in a nursing home:one in seven will pay over £100,000and some will have to sell the family home.But still, this nation of gamblers shrugs. People bet that it will never happen to them; that when their time comes, they will just drop dead. Burnham rightly described the UK’s social care system as equally unfair as the US health system: it bankrupts some. Would people rather pay a defined amount or risk losing everything? It’s an insurance offer to protect against the risk of catastrophic loss.Researchby the Health Foundation has found public support for funding reform, but – here’s the catch – “once people understand the current system”. As Louise Casey embarks on herBig Conversationon care, educating people about the system will be her primary task: only then can we discuss which other payment options are least unacceptable.This is about better care, too. For-profit care is lower quality than voluntary, non-profit or local authority-run care services,the Blavatnik School of Governmenthas found. This chaotic system includes16,500 care homes: 85% for profit, many small family-run businesses and some private equity big chains that will not be part of the new care service.Why do we endure this barely regulated, barely inspected patchwork of confusion? This was another disastrous Margaret Thatcher privatisation, of the kind Burnham intents to repair. After a 1988 report by the supermarket executive Roy Griffiths, Thatcher effectively ordered councils to close their own homes and services, outsourcing them to the private sector, and closedNHSgeriatric care wards. Crafting a new national care service out of all this would be the hardest of all in-sourcing tasks.This week, the prime minister warned the NHS could collapse unless social care is repaired. Last month, about 13,600 beds were occupied by people who were there only for lack of social care elsewhere, and delayed dischargescost the NHS £2.7bn last year. Burnham talks of integrating NHS and social care, with a workforce eventually on the same pay and with the same career progression. Currently, a starter NHS healthcare assistant is paid more than a care assistant.Will people agree to pay up? There are signs they will: when Boris Johnsonproposed a care levy, it was surprisingly popular. But it wasabolished by Kwasi Kwartengbefore it could be implemented. Which was just as well, because the plan added 1.25 percentage points to employee and employer national insurance. That meant workers, not pensioners, would pay. No extra tax would fall on dividends or other unearned income that doesn’t attract NI contributions. What’s more, the highest paid pay the lowest marginal NI rates.Whatever system emerges from these consultations, one principle must be that not a penny more is paid by the young for the old. Pensioners in the UK are theleast likely group to be in poverty(though, of course, some are). They generally have the most wealth and property, alongside final salary and triple-locked pensions. They are the overwhelming beneficiaries of the NHS. It’s no cliche to say the young are the future, so they must come first, in better early-years education, holiday childcare and schools with a wider technical, arts, drama, sports and design curriculum, while further education gets the funding and status it needs. The old must pay for the old, in one way or another.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis is a minefield. The politics of social care are fraught beyond all the other great problems Burnham could have chosen at the start. But the tone of his speech suggests the new prime minister really may lift this as a national priority. The wreckers in the Tory and Reform parties may find themselves wrong-footed; the Mail, yet again, out of tune with the public mood.When Burnham says we need “a different kind of politics: problem-solving, not point-scoring”, some old hands sigh and say: “Good luck with that!” But Burnham may strike a chord. A public grown hostile to politics may see through Kemi Badenoch’s deliberately impossible conditions for consensus agreement, asshe cynically and childishly demandsno borrowing, no taxes and no taking from “those who have made provisions and saved up over the course of their lives”. They know someone must pay, and that includes those lucky enough to have “made provisions”.It has never been the right time to brave social care reform. But it may be now, with a leader driven by personal belief, in his early stages, when he still has substantial amounts of political capital. He has grasped the nettle: will society, politics and the media? If not now, when?Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Jared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret review – the tales of abuse are utterly disturbing | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Four women speak out about their underage experiences with the movie star and musician. Are the floodgates finally about to open?
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: Four women speak out about their underage experiences with the movie star and musician. Are the floodgates finally about to open?
Content: ‘No longer a box office draw’ … Jared Leto: Hollywood's Dark Secret.Photograph: BBC/Pete DaddsView image in fullscreen‘No longer a box office draw’ … Jared Leto: Hollywood's Dark Secret.Photograph: BBC/Pete DaddsTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewJared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret review – the tales of abuse are utterly disturbingFour women speak out about their underage experiences with the movie star and musician. Are the floodgates finally about to open?Stuart HeritageWed 29 Jul 2026 08.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 13.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJared Leto has long been a person with something of a reputational issue. The public-facing side of this was bad enough – while playing The Joker in 2016’s Suicide Squad, he reportedly sent rats, dead pigs and used condoms to his cast mates – but for years there have been upsetting rumours about what he does in private. After a lengthy investigation, the BBC documentary Jared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret has finally brought at least some of them to light.This is, as you might imagine, not a fun thing to watch. The film documents allegations of what are said to be decades of systematic criminal misconduct against teenage girls. The women interviewed here allege sexual assault, threatened sexual assault, sexualised grooming and statutory rape. They are backed up by anonymous male former co-workers who claim to have witnessed the machinery that Leto set up to procure underage girls from concerts.What is particularly galling about Hollywood’s Dark Secret is that this is not the first time someone has tried to investigate these claims. As far back as 2005, the New York Post was runninggossip columnsthat claimed he was “aggressively pursuing” what were described as “underage objects of desire” at a New York hotel. By 2018, actor Dylan Sprouse and director James Gunn weretrading jokesabout Leto’s interest in teenage girls online. Last year,Air Mail’s Elena Clavarino spoke to nine womenwho variously claimed that Leto pursued them, engaged in sexually explicit telephone conversations with them, exposed himself to them and masturbated in front of them – all while they were underage.View image in fullscreenLet the testimonies speak for themselves … Alex on Jared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret.Photograph: BBC Studios/Theo TennantWhen that report was published, Leto’s representatives issued a denial. It seemed that everything continued as normal. He promoted his movie. He toured with his band. For a while it seemed that the world had blinked and moved on.However, something with the heft of Hollywood’s Dark Secret will be harder to ignore. Released on YouTube as well as the BBC to ensure maximum impact, it is a disturbing look at what is alleged to be a skin-crawling pattern of behaviour. Jessica Sartenaer and her team have put together a case that bears the unmistakable smell of shoe leather. Clearly, it often takes a long time for allegations like this to see the light because of a culture of silence. People are often scared to go public for fear of shame or reprisal, and it is in the financial interests of many people to keep the Jared Leto machine running as long as possible.That Sartenaer was able to find four women, and allay their concerns enough to let them show their faces onscreen, speaks volumes. We should let their testimonies speak for themselves (this really is a documentary that deserves to be seen, rather than simply read about), but their bravery deserves to be commended.View image in fullscreenIncredible bravery … Isabel on Jared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret.Photograph: BBC Studios/Theo TennantAlthough historical – these women are now all in their 20s, 30s and 40s – it is difficult to watch them recount what they experienced while they were underage. Some of their stories are straight from the Hollywood predator playbook, with them being procured by Leto’s team and led to dingy hotel rooms. Others are more baffling, like the woman who found herself receiving sexually explicit calls from Leto as a 16-year-old girl, only to then receive further calls of a similar nature from a man she believes was Leto in character as somebody else.Cumulatively, when these stories have been added to archive footage of concerts where Leto has his arms draped around young girls, and talkshow appearances where he brags about sleeping with fans, and one particularly unnerving clip where he quotes the old Dazed and Confused line about high school girls – “I keep getting older but they stay the same age” – the effect is completely disturbing.So far, Leto has been bulletproof against allegations like these, but you can’t help feeling that this film will land a blow. Of course, it should be noted that the timing of the documentary might help. Leto is no longer the box office draw he once was. Last year’s Tron: Ares reportedly lost somewhere in the region of $130m, and his latest film – Masters of the Universe – is among the biggest flops of the year so far. It isn’t the best reflection of Hollywood that it will only choose to round on alleged sexual predators once the bottom line has been weakened, but better late than never.Leto declined to comment to Sartenaer and her team, unlike the robust denial he gave after the Air Mail investigation. Maybe it’s a sign that the floodgates will finally open?Jared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret is on BBC iPlayer and YouTube nowSupport for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 inScotland, or 0800 0246 991 inNorthern Ireland. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionJared LetoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Braiding used to be low maintenance and budget-friendly. What happened? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Every time I get my hair done, I find myself confronted with rising costs, and dizzyingly long maintenance regimes
Author: Micha Frazer-Carroll
Headline: Every time I get my hair done, I find myself confronted with rising costs, and dizzyingly long maintenance regimes
Content: Getting a braiding appointment has proven to be a labyrinthine task for me.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGetting a braiding appointment has proven to be a labyrinthine task for me.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianThe Long WaveLife and styleBraiding used to be low maintenance and budget-friendly. What happened?Every time I get my hair done, I find myself confronted with rising costs, and dizzyingly long maintenance regimesDon’t already get The Long Wave in your inbox? Sign up hereMicha Frazer-CarrollWed 29 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 11.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis week, I tried to book in for some knotless braids at the last minute. I knew I was going to be writing about how the simple pleasure of getting a head of box braids is starting to feel increasingly complicated, and thought that it would be good to get some pictures of the process. Then, I found myself getting wound up as the subject of this newsletter began to play out on a sort of meta-level.View image in fullscreenMicha Frazer-Carroll having her braids done at Ama Hair Salon in South Tottenham. Hair stylists: Belinda Parker (in black, behind Micha) and Mary Agyei (in white).Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianWhen I decided to get my hair done for this piece, I knew that booking a next-day braiding slot would prove to be a kafkaesque task. My usual place asks that you schedule around a month in advance. My second option says that we’d need a “private room” to bring a photographer, bumping the bill up to £600. While trying to write an immersive report on the difficulties that come with getting braids, I suddenly realise that I am livingthe report.None of the salons seem to care about my journalistic endeavour. They don’t need the publicity, or have time for it. As one salon tells me: “We have a high demand for braids, which is why it is hard to be super flexible.”The lack of supply is causing tension. Braided divas frequently bemoan the power stylists have to set increasingly high prices. New Yorkers can payaround $450(£339) for knotless braids, a more expensive style that has become the standard in the city in the past five or so years. In London, I’ll pay between £150 and £250 for the same. It wasn’t always like this.Navigating an elaborate affairView image in fullscreen‘Having your hair done isn’t much of a choice, with one in five Black American women aged 25-34 having been sent home from work for their hair.’Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianWith braiding you’re paying for every inch of labour – with waist length costing £20 more than bra length, small braids costing about £40 more than medium, and so on. If your hair isn’t pre-stretched, add another £20. Want your hair washed and blow dried? That’ll be an extra £20-35. For boho or goddess braids, a newer trend where wispy tendrils cascade out of your plaits, that could be, say, £50 more. If you’re using synthetic hair, it’s going to matt over the one to two months that you wear the style, so it’s better to use human hair bundles. But these can cost upwards of £250. Each of these decisions fills me with a moment of micro-dread.When The Long Wave’s lead writer, Nesrine Malik, tells me that the Dutch braids she just got in Nairobi were the equivalent of £2, and that a full head of knotless only costs £20, I get a bit hot and itchy.Obviously, London is its own economy. But I can’t simply opt out of the dizzyingly expensive process. Having your hair done isn’t exactly a choice, with one in five Black American women aged 25-34having been sent home from work for their hair. To make matters worse, shifting beauty standards have completely normalised (if not mandated) these boho, knotless and butt-length styles, which take at least five hours to install.“Braiding used to be a matter of convenience and low maintenance,” Nesrine tells me. “Branded as a ‘protective style’, it felt like something that could deliver you from the hamster wheel of washing and drying and curling or straightening. Now it is its own elaborate stressful affair.” And even once they’re done, the pressure doesn’t end. “Many of us are told that we’re doing it wrong: not washing them enough, keeping them in too long, getting braided too tight, too heavy.”Anna Gifty Opoku-Agyeman, economist, Harvard PhD student and author ofThe Double Tax: How Women of Color Are Overcharged and Underpaid, agrees. “This is a topic that’s significantly understudied,” she tells me. “But we do know that the cost of beauty has gone up over time. That’s due, in part, to inflation, but also to ever-growing beauty standards.”Victimised by similar forcesView image in fullscreenAma Hair Salon in South Tottenham.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianStill, Opoku-Agyeman believes that it’s shortsighted to solely focus on the experience of the consumer. “[Black hair stylists] are expected to know how to do everybody’s hair, and you get penalised if you can’t,” she says. “So you might have to just get more products, in order to accommodate all the different hair types that might come through your door.”Opoku-Agyeman, who is Ghanaian-American, says you also need to factor in the spiralling rent in places like the US, and that shipping synthetic hair from China is no longer as cheap as it was. “When tariffs entered the picture, I was telling folks that this was actually going to hit black women very hard.”Other specialised products like conditioners and gels made by Black-owned businesses may be more expensive, because they can struggle to gain investment, leading to low levels of supply. Opoku-Agyeman believes that the costs customers complain about aren’t resulting in massive profits for braiders. I still feel a little uncertain about the extra costs: I’ve heard stories of customers being charged extra for being a new client, or for having long or thick hair. Opoku-Agyeman gently checks me on these annoyances. “You have your sort of corner case type people, who will charge you just for parting your hair, right?” she says. “I think [this] is preposterous, but I don’t know how frequent they are.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd I don’t want to undervalue Black women’s labour for, not only a specialised skill, but an art form. Perhaps as consumers we’re directing our ire towards victims of the same forces. “The folks who own the means of production around hair braiding are not the folks who are typically using hair-braiding services,” Opoku-Agyeman says. Most braiding products are not sourced from Black-owned businesses.“Back in the day, people used to braid outside, braid in their houses, but now people are trying to build out a business.” They also are tending to you for the five to eight hours that you’re in the chair, often without a lunch break. Braiders need to be trained, which can be expensive. It’s hard work.Paying the societal costView image in fullscreen‘People are willing to spend $500 to get their hair done, because if I don’t, I’m not going to get the job,’ says Opoku-Agyeman.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianWhat Opoku-Agyeman, Nesrine and I agree on is that Black women feel an intense pressure to be “presentable”, which comes from within and outside Black communities. “There is a real societal cost, and literal cost, to not getting your hair done,” Opoku-Agyeman tells me. “People are willing to spend $500 to get their hair done, because if I don’t, I’m not going to get the job … you could getsuspended. You could get expelled.” Maybe when we get angry at add-ons, we’re really feeling anger at a lifetime of having to pay luxury prices for something that feels like a necessity.This doesn’t only apply to braids. You could say the same for “wash and go” routines, the “straight natural” movement, locs, relaxers, fades and other Black hairstyles that have been subject to similar creeping policing and commercialisation. No matter what style you choose, the restrictions are tight and only seem to get tighter: with numerous steps, products and services deemed “essential” to keep you looking neat and professional.Thehair discriminationthat forms part of this pressure is something that we can address in our own schools and workplaces. But it is also only one symptom of a longer, knotty history in which Black women’s hair has simultaneously beena site of expression and oppression. For many of us, going to the salon can feel like both of these things at the same time.So what are we to do? As I admire my French curl braids, topped off with scalp-slick canerows, all I can think about is where I might channel my resentment at these rising prices. After six hours in the chair, it’s not toward my braiders. The beauty industry that profits from our social and economic anxieties? That’s a different question.To receive the complete version of The Long Wave in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Tap inCan you keep up with the increasing stress, and cost, of braids? Share your experience by emailing us atthelongwave@theguardian.comand we may include your response in our next issue.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Long WaveWomen's hairBeautyHair carenewslettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘Saltburn are the Argentina of local cricket’: victims and neighbours on the ‘Clicky Ponting’ scandal | North Yorkshire | The Guardian
description: Laughter, disbelief and outrage over video appearing to show Saltburn player tricking umpire into giving batters out
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: Laughter, disbelief and outrage over video appearing to show Saltburn player tricking umpire into giving batters out
Content: Vic Makins and the Saltburn ukulele club on Wednesday. Their reaction to the alleged cheating was one of laughter.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenVic Makins and the Saltburn ukulele club on Wednesday. Their reaction to the alleged cheating was one of laughter.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianNorth Yorkshire‘Saltburn are the Argentina of local cricket’: victims and neighbours on the ‘Clicky Ponting’ scandalLaughter, disbelief and outrage over video appearing to show Saltburn player tricking umpire into giving batters outMark BrownNorth of England correspondent; photographs byGary CaltonWed 29 Jul 2026 10.41 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the Saltburn over-60s ukulele club there was a unanimous reaction to news that the town’s cricket club were being compared to the Argentina football team: laughter. Then a spirited rendition of I Love to Boogie.Saltburn over-60s ukulele perform rendition of I Love to Boogie – videoOn the seafront, a litter-picking volunteer was looking forward to the Wednesday night quiz just to get the gossip. But she had her own view. “All I would say is it’s just not cricket, is it?”Bill Peters, a retired steelworker on a day out from Middlesbrough with his wife, Janet, reflected on what would have happened in St Lucia where he played cricket growing up. “There would have been a big fight,” he said slowly and purposefully.Cricket player seems to show fielder tricking umpire by clicking to imitate edgesSaltburn-by-the-Sea is a lovely Victorian town in north-eastEnglandwhose usual claim to fame is the cliff lift, the oldest water-balanced funicular still in operation in Great Britain, although currently out of operation.This week it has becomethe centre of a cheating storythat has made headlines all over the world.It began after a video was posted online of Saturday’s game between Saltburn second XI and Norton second XI.The video appeared to show a fielder clicking his fingers as the batter swings for the ball. The fielder has been accused of trying to trick the umpire into thinking the ball clipped the edge of the bat before being caught.Thebemused batter can be seen protesting to the umpireas Saltburn players celebrate.It has been called ‘Clickgate’ and the fielder dubbed ‘Clicky Ponting’, although his name is Brian.Ponting, a former Australian cricket captain, is, it should be emphasised, entirely blameless and not a character in the affair beyond his name Ricky rhyming with Clicky.View image in fullscreenBill Peters with his wife, Janet. He said cheating at cricket on his home island of St Lucia would have led to a fight.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianThe clip has been viewed more than 7m times and has made headlines around the world including, as would be expected, in Australia. One wit on Facebook remarked: “It’s official, Saltburn are the Argentina of local cricket.”Neither Saltburn nor Norton have commented on the affair, which is being investigated by theNorth Yorkshireand South Durham Cricket League.When the Guardian visited the cricket club no one wanted to talk. Tennis players arriving for games on the adjacent courts just burst out laughing.In town, Pete Welsh, part of the litter-picking posse, was struggling to get his head round it. “It must have been a very loud click,” said the retired teacher. “If he was doing it and cricket is a gentleman’s game, it wasn’t very gentleman-like. I reckon if the lad has anything about him he will come forward and say yes, it was me.”Just how someone managed to click his fingers so loudly that the umpire heard it is baffling a lot of people. Thecommentator Jonathan Agnew, told BBC Breakfast: “I can’t wrap my head round it. Can I hear someone click his fingers from 30 yards away? That umpire … must have incredible hearing. They call it a gentleman’s game, but it’s not really.”View image in fullscreenPete Welsh, a retired teacher, said the apparent cheating was ungentlemanly.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianThe story has prompted many jokes but if you play cricket in the league then it is less of a laughing matter.In Saltburn’s previous match, against Shildon Railway second XI, the wicketkeeper made an incredible eight catches in his team’s 22-run victory. The men’s Test record for catches by a keeper in an innings is seven.Shane Rowley was playing for Shildon Railway and is sure he was a victim of clicking. When he was judged out, he said to the umpire: “Come on, please. You know I haven’t hit that one. I was miles away from it. I wish I was somewhere near it!”He didn’t hear the ball hit his bat – “but everyone else did,” Rowley told the Guardian. Or did they?View image in fullscreenNo one wanted to talk at Saltburn Cricket Club.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianAfter the game and the eight catches behind, Rowley said they raised complaints about poor umpiring. After Clickgate footage emerged on social media, Rowley said he rang an umpiring official to apologise.“I said, can I just retract what I said earlier in the week and apologise and please extend apologies to the umpires.”Rowley said three players did get a nick on the ball before they were caught. The others were adamant they did not and were “absolutely fuming”. Including him, his team’s last man out.“It is absolutely unbelievable,” said Rowley. “I’ve never been involved in a game where I’ve seen anything like it and I’ve been playing for 30 years, since I was eight.”To say other clubs are annoyed might be an understatement. Ian Palmer, chair of Newton AycliffeCricketClub, said, if true, it was “scandalous”.View image in fullscreenSaltburn Cricket Club has not commented on the incident, which has been seen 7m times on social media.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianHe added: “These are lads giving up all of their Saturday to play a game of cricket and if they are being cheated it is just not on really.”The “Clicky Ponting” player has been identified as Brian Devine, a 38-year-old company secretary who has lost sponsorship from a local Indian restaurant. Unconfirmed reports suggest he has been suspended by his club. Devine did not respond to an approach for comment.For Neal Toulson, a former chair of Thornaby Cricket Club and someone involved in the game for more than 50 years, the allegations are a reflection of a wider malaise.“I think cricket in general has gone down the pan a little bit with regards to gamesmanship,” he said. “When I was a lad – and it’s a while ago now – you never even appealed unless you thought it was genuinely out. Now everybody’s shouting for everything. And then there’s the sledging.”Sledging, the dark art of trying to put off a batter with insults or teasing, goes on all the time in lower league cricket, Toulson said.He added: “You’d think they were playing for money. It’s crazy, right? I always took cricket seriously, I competed as hard as I could but at the same time – you play fair.”Toulson said he hoped there would be a full investigation and if cheating was found then a ban should be the consequence.“It has come across as a bit of a joke but it’s not. It’s cheating. If the guy is found guilty he should be punished. I’ve seen players banned for swearing to themselves and it is a lot worse than that.”Explore more on these topicsNorth YorkshireCricketEnglandNorth of EnglandnewsShareReuse this content
