title: Tony review – knives out in tasty reheat of Anthony Bourdain’s memoir | Movies | The Guardian
description: Dominic Sessa stars as a conceited yet vulnerable young chef alongside Antonio Banderas – but the feelgood factor is compromised by what we know of the author
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Dominic Sessa stars as a conceited yet vulnerable young chef alongside Antonio Banderas – but the feelgood factor is compromised by what we know of the author
Content: Kitchen confidential … Antonio Banderas and Dominic Sessa in Tony.Photograph: A24View image in fullscreenKitchen confidential … Antonio Banderas and Dominic Sessa in Tony.Photograph: A24MoviesReviewTony review – knives out in tasty reheat of Anthony Bourdain’s memoirDominic Sessa stars as a conceited yet vulnerable young chef alongside Antonio Banderas – but the feelgood factor is compromised by what we know of the authorPeter BradshawWed 29 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor all the drugs and punch-ups, this is an unexpectedly sentimental coming-of-age story – or maybe origin myth – about the formative youthful kitchen experiences of legendary badass chefAnthony Bourdain. It is taken from the opening chapters in his bestselling memoir Kitchen Confidential; Canadian film-maker Matt Johnson directs and Dominic Sessa (the callow kid from Alexander Payne’s The Holdovers) plays the conceited, smug yet lonely and vulnerable young college student Tony. “Anthony” is in the future.It is the mid-1970s and Tony effectively runs away from home after failing to get a residential summer writing scholarship that he had assured everyone was in the bag. He shows up nearly penniless in the seaside vacation resort of Provincetown, Massachusetts – a place that is pretty similar to Amity Island in Jaws, which is showing at every drive-in. The reason is that he has a desperate crush on Nancy (Emilia Jones) who is there for the summer too and whom he desperately wants to impress with his smouldering intellectualism.Then, having got drunkenly thrown out of a bar serving seafood, pathetic Tony gets hired there as a humble dishwasher by its kindly-stern chef (Antonio Banderas). He finds he kinda likes the heat in the kitchen, and gets to know louche, coke-addled womanising chef Sal (Leo Woodall) who shows Tony the ropes of being a tough guy and a player, but who is, in the time-honoured manner of films like this, Tony’s sacrificial mentor: inspirational figure and awful warning.This is a strange film in some ways. It is watchable and entertaining, but its feelgood trajectory is compromised by what we know of the author. In 2000, when the book came out and Bourdain was approaching the height of his celebrity, these anecdotes would have felt simply warm, wry and funny. If he was still alive now, Bourdain would assuredly have an ironic cameo, perhaps as one of the greybeard authority figures that obstruct the rake’s progress. But we are watching the film in the knowledge thatBourdain took his own life in 2018after a painful breakup, having suffered from instability and depression. All the sadness, all the emotional danger that this film gestures at, all the crises that the drama suggests are just obstacles to be surmounted … they are all very real.How exactly, for example, do we take the moment in this movie when Banderas’s character tells Tony aboutFrançois Vatel, chef to Louis XIV, who killed himself in shame when the key ingredients didn’t arrive for a banquet? (It’s not in the book, though Bourdain spoke about it in interviews as an example of extreme perfectionism.) The scene is presumably there tacitly to acknowledge Bourdain’s heartbreaking fate. It sits oddly.As for Sessa himself, Johnson gives him plenty of shots looking silently stricken, or hungover, often sporting a black eye. In a way, Tony is the author, the narrator who just bleakly sees it all, but for a writer he sometimes doesn’t have much to say about the situation in which he finds himself. There’s some nice support from Rich Sommer and Dagmara Dominczyk as Pierre and Gladys, Tony’s parents, and Banderas always has gentleness and charm. A bittersweet dish.Tony is out on 7 August in the US, 14 August in the UK, and 20 August in Australia.Explore more on these topicsFilmBiopicsAnthony BourdainFoodreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Revealed: George Cottrell transferred $2m to his mother days before her donations to Reform UK | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Sources say Fiona Cottrell told bankers the transfers, received 24-72 hours before her donations to Reform, came from her son
Author: Anna Isaac
Headline: Exclusive: Sources say Fiona Cottrell told bankers the transfers, received 24-72 hours before her donations to Reform, came from her son
Content: George Cottrell with Nigel Farage in 2019. Sources say the Reform UK leader’s aide deposited several tranches of hundreds of thousands of dollars into his mother Fiona’s account shortly before she donated to the party.Photograph: Mark Kerrison/AlamyView image in fullscreenGeorge Cottrell with Nigel Farage in 2019. Sources say the Reform UK leader’s aide deposited several tranches of hundreds of thousands of dollars into his mother Fiona’s account shortly before she donated to the party.Photograph: Mark Kerrison/AlamyReform UKRevealed: George Cottrell transferred $2m to his mother days before her donations to Reform UKExclusive: Sources say Fiona Cottrell told bankers the transfers, received 24-72 hours before her donations to Reform, came from her sonAnna IsaacCity editorWed 29 Jul 2026 12.34 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe convicted fraudster George Cottrell transferred a total of more than $2m to his mother, Fiona Cottrell, in the days before her 2024 donations toReform UK, the Guardian understands.Financial industry sources told the Guardian that Fiona received one deposit of $1.4m and two tranches of more than $300,000 each – money she attributed to having come from her son, George, when bankers asked about the deposits.On each occasion, the Guardian understands transfers were made 24-72 hours before Fiona made a donation either directly to Reform, or via Britain Means Business, a fundraising vehicle for the political party.According to sources, the lump sums went through US-based cryptocurrency exchanges before entering Fiona’s account. These platforms allow crypto-assets to be changed for hard currency, such as US dollars or British pounds. Some were routed to Fiona via money exchange services.The Metropolitan police areinvestigatingthe funding of Reform UK, with a focus on scrutinising whether there were attempts to disguise the ultimate source of donations.The new disclosures will add to the questions facing Reform and its leader, Nigel Farage, whose finances have been under the spotlight since the Guardianrevealed he received a £5m giftfrom the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne.Fiona was one of the most important donors to the party in 2024, making secret as well as public donations. She gave two lots of £250,000 in May 2024, which were disclosed transparently to the Electoral Commission. It can be revealed that these donations were preceded by transfers of $318,878 and $328,815 from her son.As first revealed by the Guardian, she also gave more than £1m to Britain Means Business, a company controlled by the party’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, in June 2024. That cash transfer was not declared officially at the time, and was routed via the bank account of Oneify, an Australian money exchange service. Half that sum was transferred directly to the party days later by Tice, with no declaration that it originated from Fiona Cottrell.It can now be revealed that sources have told the Guardian that $1,400,000 was deposited into Fiona Cottrell’s account by her son before she gave the £1,075,000 to Britain Means Business on 10 June 2024, just weeks before the general election.In total, George Cottrell deposited $2,047,693 into his mother’s account, the Guardian has been told. Taking into account her 2024 donations to Britain Means Business and Reform UK, Fiona gave a total of £1.5m that year. These amounts are roughly equivalent, based on exchange rate data from May and June 2024.Two Reform UK sources who were involved in party fundraising before the 2024 vote told the Guardian that George had assured senior party figures that some money would be on its way into the party’s coffers in the weeks leading up to the vote.“He was acting as a sort of shadow treasurer, saying he would find a way to get more money in,” one of the sources said.Asked about the transfers, lawyers for George Cottrell said their client had no further comment.In previous legal correspondence, George has not denied giving his mother – who is understood to be of relatively modest means – large sums of money. Instead, he said via lawyers that “any political donations his mother has made have been entirely her own decision, and are a matter for her”.Fiona Cottrell has not responded to several attempts by the Guardian to contact her.Get in touchContact Anna Isaac about this storyIf you have something to share about this story you can contact Anna using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.To send a message to Anna Isaac please choose the ‘Business (UK and Global)’ team.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can email: anna.isaac@theguardian.comMessaging appsYou can message Anna using the Signal Messenger app: 07341998403SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreGeorge Cottrell, a convicted fraudster whom Farage has described as being “like a son to me”, lives in Montenegro and has said he is resident there for tax purposes. He has been described as Farage’s chief of staff by Reform insiders, even though the party maintains that he is only a volunteer.His lawyers have said he is a permissible donor, despite living abroad, but have not explained how he meets the criteria or when he first met them. The only declared donation George Cottrell made to Reform in 2024 was£15,000 to part-fund Farage’s trip to Floridathat December, where he met Elon Musk.It comes as pressure mounts on Reform’s leadership to explain the lack of transparency, and apparent overlap, between personal funders and political backers.The Guardian revealed in recent weeks that Tice had received an undisclosed loan of £80,000 from George Cottrell, who has also donated to Reform UK.In April, this newspaper revealed thatNigel Farage received an undisclosed gift of £5mfrom the party’s most important donor, Harborne.Several of these transactions caused bankers to raise potential money-laundering concerns with the UK’s National Crime Agency, via suspicious activity reports (SARs), according to financial industry sources.After the Clacton byelection, Farage faces investigations by the parliamentary standards commissioner into whether he should have declared the £5m and also over benefits in kind given by George Cottrell.In an interview with the Telegraph last week, Farage appeared for the first time to acknowledge that he should have declared the £5m on the register of MPs’ interests: “All right, perhaps I should have filled in a piece of paper. If that’s the worst thing I’ve done in life – not filling in a form – I would say that’s not too bad.”Tice has failed to engage with questions about his loan from George Cottrell and decision to transfer £500,000 to Reform UK from Britain Means Business despite bankers raising concerns with him about the origin of the funds. He has accused the Metropolitan police of being involved in a smear campaign against him and briefing the media.He posted on X: “The Establishment are playing dirtier than ever to try to smear & discredit Reform leaders.”The Met investigation into Fiona Cottrell’s four donations in 2024 has been continuing for more than a year.The Met issued this statement on its investigation in recent weeks: “An investigation was launched in February 2025 after a referral was made to theMetropolitan policeby the Electoral Commission relating to donations made to a political party ahead of the 2024 UK general election.“Detectives from the Met’s special inquiry team are investigating alleged offences under section 61 of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000. Early investigative advice has been sought from the Crown Prosecution Service and two people have so far been interviewed under caution. No arrests have been made.“An offence under this section is not one that the Electoral Commission can investigate and, as such, it is a matter for the police.”Asked whether Reform had been assured that George Cottrell would find a way to provide funds, and was regarded as a shadow treasurer, a spokesperson said: “We deny this completely. Reform takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations and always ensures that the Electoral Commission guidelines on donations, as set out in the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000, are strictly followed, as has been the case with all donations.”Explore more on these topicsReform UKParty fundingNigel FarageRichard TicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Three firefighters killed on Crete and in mainland Greece as Europe battles wildfires | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Repeated heatwaves and strong winds alarm experts, who warn blazes are becoming harder to quell
Author: Ajit Niranjan
Headline: Repeated heatwaves and strong winds alarm experts, who warn blazes are becoming harder to quell
Content: Low-lying vegetation ablaze in Krya Vrysi, Rethymno, Crete on Wednesday.Photograph: Nikos Chalkiadakis/EPAView image in fullscreenLow-lying vegetation ablaze in Krya Vrysi, Rethymno, Crete on Wednesday.Photograph: Nikos Chalkiadakis/EPAWildfiresThree firefighters killed on Crete and in mainland Greece as Europe battles wildfiresRepeated heatwaves and strong winds alarm experts, who warn blazes are becoming harder to quellAjit NiranjanandJennifer RankinWed 29 Jul 2026 14.30 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 10.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree Greek firefighters have died while tackling wildfires on the island of Crete and in the south of the mainland, the Greek fire department has said, as extreme heat hinders efforts to control blazes ravaging southernEurope.The arc of brutal fires, which runs from the Atlantic coast to the eastern Mediterranean, and from the Scottish Highlands to the south ofSpain, has alarmed experts because many of the fires have been out of control and burning close to towns and cities.Temperatures exacerbated by the climate crisis reached 38C on Wednesday in Bordeaux in France, where firefighters kept ahuge blazein nearby pine forests from reaching the suburbs, and 37C in Madrid, west of which Spain’s largest wildfire on recordhad been “technically stabilised”, according to the interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska.Dozens of ground crews had managed to contain the Madrid fire overnight, emergency services for the region said on Wednesday morning, but a separate fire near València, where temperatures will peak at a cooler 32C, is still out of control.View image in fullscreenMembers of the Emergency Military Unit utilise controlled burns to halt the spread of wildfires in the Madrid border region in Cebreros, Ávila province, on Tuesday night.Photograph: Pablo Blázquez Domínguez/Getty ImagesIn televised comments from the Navalcarnero command centre on Wednesday morning, the Spanish prime minister,Pedro Sánchez, said the situation near the capital was improving but stressed it was the first time in Spanish history that a wildfire had been raised to “operational level 3”, with the national government taking over the disaster response.“I believe the next 12 hours will be very important,” he said. “They are going to be decisive in consolidating the work done by the national civil protection system.”Accompanied by strong winds, the fourth heatwave of western Europe’s scorching summer hasalarmed firefighters, who warn it makes blazes harder to quell and raises the risk of fires restarting in areas that have been stabilised. New fires also prompted evacuations in Greece and Turkey.View image in fullscreenWildfires in Crete, where authorities say two firefighters ‘fell heroically in the line of duty’.Photograph: ERT GRView image in fullscreenThe remains of a firefighting vehicle seen south of Rethymno in Crete on Wednesday.Photograph: Costas Metaxakis/AFP/Getty ImagesFrench authorities benefited from a calm night on Tuesday that allowed flare-ups to be swiftly extinguished but warned of “unfavourable” developing weather conditions that could hamper progress. The prefecture of Gironde said 126 firefighters had been injured since the start of the fire but the total burned area remained stable at 42,000 hectares (104,000 acres) on Wednesday morning.Wildfires have burned a record-breaking area of France, data from the European Forest Fire Information System shows, while France and Spain have experienced record-breaking numbers of fires for this time of year. More than 330,000 people in southern Europe have been forced to flee their homes and hotels.Officials began to lift evacuation orders on Tuesday as fires were brought under control, allowing tens of thousands of people living in towns near Bordeaux, Madrid and València to go back to their homes.Some of them returnedto find burnt-out buildings and charred belongings.View image in fullscreenA house which remained untouched by wildfires despite nearby land being scorched, in La Vilavella, Castellón province, in Spain.Photograph: Nacho Doce/ReutersJosé Fernández, a 74-year-old pensioner, told AFP he had “no money, no documents, no home” after he came back to the remains of what used to be his house in Pelayos de la Presa, in the Community of Madrid. “This place has been reduced to a total ruin.”Europe’s wildfire season is growing hotter and longer as carbon pollution heats the continent twice as fast as the global average. Repeated heatwaves this year have dried vegetation and turned forests and shrubland into tinderboxes, alarming EU officials, who have said wildfires could still be burning in November.Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, thanked firefighters for their “courage and commitment” on Wednesday.“As the fires in France and Spain continue to ravage, European solidarity knows no limit,” she said in a social media post. “Romania andGreecehave decided to extend their missions, continuing their support to the affected regions. And from Saturday, Poland will join the fray.”View image in fullscreenA volunteer carries a water bucket to help battling the fire in Lanton, west of Bordeaux.Photograph: Romain Perrocheau/AFP/Getty ImagesEarlier this week, the European Commission said it had sentFranceseven planes and four helicopters from countries as far away as Sweden and Turkey, while in Spain, it said it had mobilised six planes from Greece, Italy and Turkey, along with 134 personnel and 41 vehicles from Portugal. A Super Puma helicopter from Serbia was expected to arrive in Madrid on Wednesday, according to Spain’s interior ministry, with 40 personnel and 18 vehicles to shortly follow.The European Union’s crisis management team said on Wednesday it expected difficult weeks ahead, fearing a further outbreak of wildfires in Italy and Greece later in the summer.View image in fullscreenA firefighting plane makes a drop amid efforts to battle a wildfire in Artana, Spain on Wednesday.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersMaria Zuber, a senior official at the EU’s emergency response coordination centre (ERCC) in Brussels, which coordinates the dispatch of firefighting planes, equipment and teams to countries that have asked for help, said the next few days would be “very difficult” for France and that “now we see it will go to Greece”.Moisés Galán Santano, a wildfire expert at the ERCC, said more needed to be done to prevent wildfires and that it would be a task for many years. “The [emergency] response is not only the answer. It’s the last answer. But it’s not all the answer. We need to focus on prevention.”mapEarlier this year, a policy paper from the European Commission set out how countries could better prevent and recover from wildfires that are expected to become bigger and more damaging across the continent. It promoted measures such as more extensive grazing, the restoration of wetlands, rivers and floodplains, better data on forest fires and raising public awareness of risky behaviour and safe evacuation.Scientists say western Europe’s scorching summer has been deadly, costly and exacerbated by fossil fuel pollution. Rapid analyses have found June’s heatwave would have been “virtually impossible”in a world without climate breakdown, while the recent level of soil dryness in western Europe – a driver of bigger blazes – was madefive times more likely. The heatwaves are estimated to have claimed at least 10,000 lives andcost grain farmers€2bn in lost crops.View image in fullscreenPeople try to extinguish a fire in the town of Plomari on the Greek island of Lesbos on Wednesday.Photograph: Manolis Lagoutaris/AFP/Getty ImagesVula Tsetsi, a co-chair of the European Green party, called on European institutions to take action on Wednesday and noted the European Commission had not yet published its heating and cooling plan, which was expected in April.“Climate-driven heatwaves and wildfires are already claiming lives, destroying homes and ravaging forests at a record pace,” she said. “There is a widening gap between the scale of Europe’s heatwaves – literally hitting every EU country – and the absence of decisive European action.”Explore more on these topicsWildfiresFranceSpainGreeceExtreme heatPedro SánchezEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Trident renewal central to defence spending, says Andy Burnham | Politics | The Guardian
description: Prime minister to highlight investment in communities as he launches next phase of nuclear submarine replacement
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Prime minister to highlight investment in communities as he launches next phase of nuclear submarine replacement
Content: Andy Burnham’s visit to Barrow-in-Furness shipyard, owned by BAE Systems, offers an opportunity to reinforce his pro-Trident credentials.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham’s visit to Barrow-in-Furness shipyard, owned by BAE Systems, offers an opportunity to reinforce his pro-Trident credentials.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianPoliticsTrident renewal central to defence spending, says Andy BurnhamPrime minister to highlight investment in communities as he launches next phase of nuclear submarine replacementDan SabbaghDefence and security editorWed 29 Jul 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will place the renewal of Trident at the heart of his vision of a reindustrialised Britain on Thursday when he travels to Barrow-in-Furness to launch the next phase of the nuclear submarine replacement programme.The new prime minister intends to emphasise that defence spending on projects such as the £31bn Dreadnought-class boats built in the Cumbrian town is a case study of taxpayer investment revitalising communities around the UK.“Keeping this country safe is the first responsibility of any government – but security is not only about what we build; it is about who builds it, and who benefits from it,” Burnham said ahead of his visit to England’s north-west.A new phase of contracts worth £8.4bn, part of the already agreed Dreadnought programme, will help support 18,000 extra jobs in nuclear defence by 2030 and 22,000 additional apprentices by 2035, Downing Street said.“To every young person across the country, I want you to know that there is a path for you into a reindustrialised Britain, and it starts with the apprenticeships we are funding through this investment today,” the prime minister added.The visit also presents an opportunity to reinforce Burnham’s pro-Trident credentials. The prime minister voted to build the new submarines in 2016, when theLabourparty split over the issue and its then leader, Jeremy Corbyn, voted against.Wes Streeting, the new defence secretary, and John Healey, the chancellor, were also among the MPs who voted in favour, though other another key figure in Burnham’s team, Louise Haigh, who runs the newoffice of the prime minister, voted no.View image in fullscreenLabour has previously been split over the issue of Trident, with Jeremy Corbyn voting against new submarines in 2016.Photograph: Anthony Devlin/PA Archive/PA ImagesThe UK’s military nuclear activities currently support 47,000 jobs, including 13,500 in the Barrow shipyard. Its surrounding constituency historically switched from Labour to Conservative, and was retaken by Labour at the last election in 2024.Burnham, who has had limited previous engagement with foreign and defence policy, entered office just over a week ago and immediately lent into a Nato commitment to increase defence spending by over £25bn a year to reach 3.5% of GDP by 2035.A row over whether his predecessor, Keir Starmer, was serious about the pledge led to the shock resignation of Healey as defence secretary last month. Starmer was so seriously undermined it precipitated his own departure.When Healey quit, he also called for military budgets to hit 3% of GDP by 2030 as an interim target to show the UK was committed to the Nato goal. Starmer had only been willing to offer an increase to 2.68% of GDP.But on Wednesday, at a press conference, Burnham declined to commit to hitting 3% by 2030. Instead he referred to the UK pledge to meet the Nato target to increase it to 3.5% of GDP by 2035, reiterating comments already made by Streeting and Healey.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“When it comes to defence, obviously those commitments … relate to the parliament after this one,” Burnham said. “In terms of our Nato commitments, I have been very clear that we will honour those commitments. It does mean being prepared to look at challenging issues,” he added.The new Dreadnought submarines are intended to replace the ageing Vanguard-class submarines, one of which is always at sea carrying Britain’s nuclear deterrent. Each of the existing submarines can carry 40 nuclear warheads, with enough destructive power to destroy Moscow and several other major Russian cities.The largest share of the latest phase of work in the Dreadnought programme is being awarded to BAE Systems, the owner of the Barrow shipyard. The British defence giant has been awarded a new £5.9bn contract to complete the build of the first four new boats, HMS Dreadnought, so it can be ready for service in early 2030s.The work is part of the overall £31bn Dreadnought programme, which is so complex it includes a £10bn contingency to cover overspends. Concern about the scale of the programme has meant it has already been placed on amber alert by government procurement monitors.Trident warheads are designed and built at AWE in Aldermaston and Burghfield in Berkshire, which employ 9,000, while a further 4,000 at Rolls-Royce in Derby help build the nuclear reactors that power the Dreadnought and other submarines used by the Royal Navy.Explore more on these topicsPoliticsDefence policyAndy BurnhamLabourCumbrianewsShareReuse this content

title: Man who stabbed Salman Rushdie in 2022 convicted of federal terrorism charges | Salman Rushdie | The Guardian
description: Jury finds Hadi Matar, who is already serving a 25-year New York state prison sentence, guilty of all charges against him
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Jury finds Hadi Matar, who is already serving a 25-year New York state prison sentence, guilty of all charges against him
Content: A courtroom sketch of Salman Rushdie testifying in federal court on 23 July.Photograph: Alexandra Newbould/APView image in fullscreenA courtroom sketch of Salman Rushdie testifying in federal court on 23 July.Photograph: Alexandra Newbould/APSalman RushdieMan who stabbed Salman Rushdie in 2022 convicted of federal terrorism chargesJury finds Hadi Matar, who is already serving a 25-year New York state prison sentence, guilty of all charges against himMaya Yangand agenciesWed 29 Jul 2026 17.38 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 17.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man was convicted on Wednesday of federal terrorism charges in the 2022 stabbing ofSalman Rushdie, the author who has faced a decades-old death threat over his novel The Satanic Verses.A jury found Hadi Matar guilty of all the charges against him, including engaging in an act of transnational terrorism.Matar declined to take the stand, with his attorney Nathaniel Baronesayingearlier this week: “At this time, the defense rests.”Matar, 28, is already serving a 25-year New York state prison sentence on an attempted murder conviction in the August 2022 attack on an amphitheater stage. The federal conviction carries a potential life sentence.ProsecutorsallegeMatar shared propaganda videos before the attack and communicated with an Iran-based contact who claimed to know “where to find Rushdie”. They also say Matar asked whether the fatwa against Rushdie was still active.Rushdie, who had been about to speak on writers’ safety, was slashed 15 times in front of a stunned audience. He was gravely wounded.Speakingfrom the stand last February, Rushdie said: “I became aware of a great quantity of blood I was lying in. My sense of time was quite cloudy, I was in pain from my eye and hand, and it occurred to me quite clearly I was dying.”Following the attack, which also wounded Ralph Henry Reese, the moderator at Rushdie’s planned lecture, Rushdie lost the sight in his right eye.According toa federal indictment, Matar’s motivation for trying to kill Rushdie stemmed from a 2006 speech delivered by Hezbollah’s chief at the time, Hassan Nasrallah. In the speech, Nasrallah had endorsed a decades-old fatwa, or death warrant, placed on Rushdie by Iranian religious leaders more than 35 years ago as a result of his novel,The Satanic Verses, which won Rushdie the Booker prize in 1981.In 2022, following Rushdie’s stabbing, Mataradmittedto having read only “a couple pages” of the book that Iranian religious leaders denounced as blasphemous.In April 2024, Rushdie, who was born in India and moved to Britain as a teenager, wrote a memoir on his attempted assassination, which he titled Knife.“After I finished writing the memoir, almost immediately, it’s like a door in my head opened and the stories came back,” Rushdiesaidat Tulane University’s New Orleans book festival in March.“I’d been really worried that I wouldn’t be able to write fiction any more … because of trauma and the shocking impact of what happened,” he added.Rushdie also said he was tired of being everyone’s “free speech Barbie”, adding: “It’s a subject I’m anxious to change.”“I don’t feel symbolic … I feel actual. I feel like I’m a working writer trying to make his work,” he said.The Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsSalman RushdieLaw (US)US crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: US-Saudi strikes in Iraq push region into ‘uncharted territory’, analysts warn | Iraq | The Guardian
description: Riyadh’s decision to join US in strikes on Iran-backed militia further complicates widening and ‘unpredictable’ war
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Riyadh’s decision to join US in strikes on Iran-backed militia further complicates widening and ‘unpredictable’ war
Content: Mourners in Mosul, Iraq, carry coffins draped in Iranian and Iraqi flags during a group funeral for Popular Mobilisation Forces fighters killed in US-Saudi airstrikes on Wednesday.Photograph: Hadi Mizban/APView image in fullscreenMourners in Mosul, Iraq, carry coffins draped in Iranian and Iraqi flags during a group funeral for Popular Mobilisation Forces fighters killed in US-Saudi airstrikes on Wednesday.Photograph: Hadi Mizban/APIraqUS-Saudi strikes in Iraq push region into ‘uncharted territory’, analysts warnRiyadh’s decision to join US in strikes on Iran-backed militia further complicates widening and ‘unpredictable’ warMiddle East crisis – live updatesPeter BeaumontSenior international correspondentWed 29 Jul 2026 13.55 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 11.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS-Saudi strikes on Iran-backed militia in Iraq have pushed the region into “uncharted territory”, analysts have warned.Amid stark warnings of a widening and increasingly “unpredictable” conflict,Riyadh’s decision to publicly join the USin striking sites associated with Iraq’s Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), killing at least 20 fighters, has added another complicating dimension to the war.The strikes on Wednesday came after a brief lull in direct US attacks on targets in Iran, but Tehran’s allies in Yemen and beyond have become increasingly drawn in.Iran, meanwhile, launched missiles at US military installations in Jordan in its first attack in the region since the pause in fighting with the US.33:00Is Iran a ‘forever war’? – Stateside with Kai and CarterThose tit-for-tat strikes seemed to indicate the pause in fighting was at an end The US president,Donald Trump, said the US would be “be hitting [Iran] hard”, even as he claimed the strikes in Iraq were coordinated with the government, despite Baghdad’s condemnation.Also on Wednesday, explosions ⁠hit a natural gas loading port on the Mediterranean Sea in Damietta, Egypt, reportedly involving a drone strike, the first reported strike on Egypt in the war. The source of the drone was unclear.The British maritime security company Ambrey said a US-owned floating storage tanker there had been hit by a drone, in another potential spread of the Middle East war.View image in fullscreenThe group funeral for militia fighters killed in US-Saudi airstrikes.Photograph: Hadi Mizban/APIn Baghdad, the Iraqi presidency called the air raids on the PMF, also known as al-Hashd al-Shaabi – an armed alliance that includes powerful pro-Iran factions – “a blatant violation of Iraq’s sovereignty, targeting its official institutions”.The PMF is a network of Shia-majority factions that was established in 2014 to fight the Islamic State group. Their efforts were overseen by the Iranian general, Qassem Suleimani, the former head of the al-Quds force, the foreign operations arm of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Suleimaniwas killed by a US missile strike in Baghdadduring Trump’s first term.The Iraqi ⁠prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, who recently met Trump, ⁠called off ​a planned meeting ⁠with Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin ⁠Salman ​in ‌Jeddah on ‌Thursday in the wake of the strikes.Iraq’s Harakat ⁠Hezbollah ⁠al-Nujaba, ​an Iran-backed ⁠militia, added that ‌Washington’s and ‌Riyadh’s interests ‌and security would face ‌consequences. Mourners shouted Shia ⁠sectarian slogans and “Death to America!” as they carried the bodies of slain fighters in body bags out of a hospital in Mosul, northern Iraq.Iraq, heavily affected by the closure of the strait of Hormuz, through which most of its oil is exported, has struggled to prevent the war between the US and Iran spilling over its borders.Its governments have tried to maintain a delicate balance between the US, which invaded the Shia-majority country in 2003, and Iran, which has long sought to exert influence there and has backed powerful militias that played a leading role in the fight against IS.View image in fullscreenPeople carry bodies on Wednesday after members of Iraq’s Popular Mobilisation Forces were killed in strikes by the US.Photograph: Al Ahad/ReutersWhile Saudi Arabia has reportedly been involved in a handful of secretive strikes on Iran as part of the war, Riyadh’s overt involvement marks a new turning point in the conflict. Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels announced a blockade of Saudi ports and cargoes at the entrance to the Red Sea barely a week ago.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe latest serious flare-up in fighting follows days in which Tehran and its proxies have targeted bases and facilities of the US and its allies, including in Saudi Arabia, despite the brief US pause.The sense of growing chaos in the Middle East was summed up by Sanam Vakil, the director of theMiddle East and north Africaprogramme at the Chatham House thinktank.“Everyone is trying make sense of something that is increasingly senseless,” she said. “One view is that the informal [US] pause in direct strikes on Iran saw a shift from Tehran to its proxies to maintain pressure [on Washington]. But there is no longer any plausible deniability because everyone knows how the relationships are intertwined.”On the Iranian side, suggested Vakil, the unpredictability of Tehran’s tactics appeared to be a deliberate strategy to pressure Trump “either into confrontation or concession” with the aim of maintaining “a stranglehold on the strait of Hormuz”.View image in fullscreenThe site of an airstrike on a Popular Mobilisation Forces base in Mosul, Iraq, on Wednesday.Photograph: Farid Abdulwahed/APVakil also said countries in the region were interpreting the chaotic context of the conflict as a historic opportunity, including to weaken Iran. And on the Saudi side, she said there was a similar desire to be unpredictable. “No one wants to stay in the status quo.”“I think from the point of view of the Saudis,” said HA Hellyer, a senior associate fellow in Middle East studies at the Royal United Services Institute, “there is a feeling that the Iranians are doing what they are doing because they feel that the Gulf Arab states won’t move up the escalatory ladder. The Saudis want to make it clear that assessment is wrong and that if Tehran thinks the Gulf states are easy prey, they are wrong.”The problem, Hellyer said, was that while the Saudis may have rationalised the attack on the PMF as a precisely calculated act, it may be impossible to anticipate the response.“Because we don’t know that, we are in uncharted territory not just because of the context of the war this year, but the wider issues in the region,” he said. “And it is risky because Tehran sees itself as having been targeted by the US and Israel in a war of existential survival. They see everything through a prism that they have to reset the rules of the game in the region dramatically even if they are wrong and overplaying their hand.”Explore more on these topicsIraqIranStrait of HormuzSaudi ArabiaDonald TrumpMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Hackers steal sensitive data from UK Department for Education and police | Cybercrime | The Guardian
description: Details of parents and staff, including email addresses and phone numbers, are among data taken by cybercriminals
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Details of parents and staff, including email addresses and phone numbers, are among data taken by cybercriminals
Content: The police national legal database hack includes the theft of passwords used to access the site.Photograph: Dave Hunt/AAPView image in fullscreenThe police national legal database hack includes the theft of passwords used to access the site.Photograph: Dave Hunt/AAPCybercrimeHackers steal sensitive data from UK Department for Education and policeDetails of parents and staff, including email addresses and phone numbers, are among data taken by cybercriminalsDan MilmoandVikram DoddWed 29 Jul 2026 15.10 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 16.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheDepartment for Educationand a police database have been targeted by a cyber-attack, exposing more than 740,000 pieces of data.Details of government officials, senior school leaders, university staff, police officers and members of the public have been taken by hackers.Just over 600,000 lines of data have been stolen from the DfE’s help-desk portal. They show parent and staff contacts including full names, email addresses, phone numbers and job titles, according to a “leak” website set up by the hackers.A smaller package of similar data has been taken from the department’s Turing portal, which manages a scheme for students studying abroad.The hackers have also breached the police national legal database (PNLD), which provides legal assistance to UK police forces. The cybercriminals claimed to have taken 135,000 pieces of data.The PNLD said the details taken related to “police officers and those working in criminal justice including their name, the force or organisation they work for and their work email address”.Some names and addresses of members of the public who had previously submitted a question to the Ask thePoliceservice had also been taken. It said the database did not hold confidential victim, witness or offender information.While embarrassing, the breach of the police legal database is not thought to be serious.A previously unknown hacking gang calling itself ExfilSquad claimed it had carried out the attack and posted samples of the data on its leak site, a typical gambit for cybercriminals seeking money for the information they have stolen.The hackers are demanding a payment from the DfE and PNLD in exchange for not posting all the data, according to screen grabs seen by the Guardian.The message states that only a small sample of data has been posted for now but indicates that all of it will be uploaded if the DfE, PNLD and other hacking victims do not make an unspecified payment.“The payment we request of you is simply a rounding error compared to the litigation costs of your data leaking. Be smart and just pay,” said the gang.The message is apparently directed at 14 hacking victims including the DfE. The list of alleged victims includes a UK university that has been contacted by the Guardian.Sophos, a cybersecurity company that provided the screenshots, said the data samples appeared to be legitimate. It added that an account on the social media platform X apparently belonging to the group had been suspended but had been illustrated by a picture of a cybersecurity researcher who had been targeted before by members ofthe Com, a sprawling ecosystem of native English-speaking hackers.However, it is understood that the DfE has not seen evidence that ransomware – a type ofmalicious softwarethat locks up a victim’s IT systems – had been deployed in the hack.The Times, which first reported the DfE hack, said the data included details of government officials, senior school leaders and university staff. The DfE is responsible for early years, schools, higher and further education in England.The PNLD hack includes the theft of passwords used to access the site.One senior source briefed on the PNLD leak said: “The risk is low. The question is, if you use your password for the PNLD, do you use it for more sensitive systems?”The database is hosted by West Yorkshire police and is open for forces across England and Wales to view.The source added that it was “early days in our understanding of what has happened.”Any hack of two other police databases – the police national database and the police national computer – would have been deemed far more serious. It is not believed that any direct information about officers in sensitive postings could be gleaned from the data leaked.The government said it was working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and the NationalCrimeAgency on the DfE hack. The DfE and PNLD have also reported the incident to the Information Commissioner’s Office, the data watchdog.The DfE said “swift action” had been taken to contain the incident.“The information involved is limited to customer service contact details relating to individuals and organisations,” it said. “No other data has been accessed.”It is understood the help-desk data includes different sets of data that cannot be connected to each other easily.Explore more on these topicsCybercrimeDepartment for EducationData and computer securityData protectionPoliceCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Children’s animation series Wolfoo found guilty of copying Peppa Pig | Peppa Pig | The Guardian
description: Judge orders removal of all Wolfoo videos from online platforms after finding ‘prolific’ copyright infringement
Author: Sinéad Campbell
Headline: Judge orders removal of all Wolfoo videos from online platforms after finding ‘prolific’ copyright infringement
Content: A still from an episode of Wolfoo, including Mrs Wolf and Piggy.Photograph: Wolfoo YoutubeView image in fullscreenA still from an episode of Wolfoo, including Mrs Wolf and Piggy.Photograph: Wolfoo YoutubePeppa PigChildren’s animation series Wolfoo found guilty of copying Peppa PigJudge orders removal of all Wolfoo videos from online platforms after finding ‘prolific’ copyright infringementSinéad CampbellWed 29 Jul 2026 18.24 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 17.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe corporate owners ofPeppa Pighave won a copyright battle against the copycat animation Wolfoo after a judge ruled the latter had illegally used audio from the famous cartoon pig.The US-headquartered entertainment company Hasbro, which owns the rights to Peppa Pig, sued SConnect – the Vietnamese makers of Wolfoo – for copyright infringement regarding videos which used short audio clips of Peppa and her family saying words such as “Hooray!”A high court judge in London has ordered all videos featuring the animated character Wolfoo to be removed from online platforms includingYouTube, stating that the copying had been “prolific”, “longstanding” and that the evidence of “copying of the audio clips is compelling”.The judge ordered the Wolfoo videos to be removed before 4pm BST on Monday.Wolfoo is an animated series starring a young wolf who lives with his family. It has hundreds of millions of views online across channels including YouTube, YouTube Kids and the official Wolfoo World website.Wolfoo’s makers denied the claims of copyright infringement. They said videos made before mid-2020 contained audio from Peppa Pig because an independent third-party contractor had used these sounds without their knowledge, and that all videos made after this period had used original sounds that were created in-house.SConnect said that all videos that infringed upon copyright laws have been removed.However, the high court judge said sound clips from Peppa Pig were found in all of the 92 English-language Wolfoo videos that were examined, and in 75% of the foreign-language videos.The judge said putting the blame on third-party contractors was “irrelevant” and the claim that videos made after mid-2020 used sound recorded in-house “can be disproved”.The court action began in 2022, when Hasbro and Peppa Pig’s creators, the London-based Astley Baker Davies studio, claimed that SConnect had attempted “to deceive the young Wolfoo viewership, most aged between two and five, into believing that Wolfoo is the same character as Peppa Pig”.They also claimed that Wolfoo’s appearance and artwork were similar to Peppa Pig’s design. The legal case was focused on the audio because it was believed that this area would be where it was easiest to prove that copyright infringement had taken place.SConnect argued that the ruling to remove the Wolfoo videos should only apply to those examined in the sample. It also argued that the ruling to remove Wolfoo videos in the UK, EU and all 166 World Trade Organization member states – including the US and Vietnam – was “too broad”.The judge said the copying was “extensive, seemingly endemic at least so far as the English-language Wolfoo videos are concerned”.The Wolfoo animation was released in 2018. It is available in English and has been dubbed into languages including Arabic, Chinese, French and Spanish. Like Peppa Pig, it is aimed at children aged two to seven.SConnect and Hasbro have been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsPeppa PigChildren's TVYouTubeIntellectual propertynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The breath just went out of us’: people return to their homes after wildfires near Madrid | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Residents struggle to take in the devastation five days after El Morro was evacuated as fires burned across countryside west of Spanish capital
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Residents struggle to take in the devastation five days after El Morro was evacuated as fires burned across countryside west of Spanish capital
Content: A man walks past burnt-out cars after the wildfire in Navas del Rey, about 50km (30 miles) west of Madrid.Photograph: Pablo Blázquez Domínguez/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA man walks past burnt-out cars after the wildfire in Navas del Rey, about 50km (30 miles) west of Madrid.Photograph: Pablo Blázquez Domínguez/Getty ImagesWildfires‘The breath just went out of us’: people return to their homes after wildfires near MadridResidents struggle to take in the devastation five days after El Morro was evacuated as fires burned across countryside west of Spanish capitalSam Jonesin Navas del ReyWed 29 Jul 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe handwritten sign taped to the front gate of a house in the mountains an hour west of Madrid offered as succinct a summary of recent events as you will find.“EMPTY,” it said. “No people or animals here.”The quiet streets of El Morro, a hamlet on the outskirts of the town of Navas del Rey, held further evidence: two burnt-out cars barely identifiable as an Audi and a Seat; blackened gnomes atop a gatepost; charred hedges whose leaves had crumbled to a fine ash; and, everywhere, the smell of burnt, or still smouldering, wood.View image in fullscreenConcepción García enters her home for the first time after it was destroyed by a raging wildfire that swept through areas of the town of Navas del Rey, south-west of Madrid.Photograph: Miguel Riopa/AFP/Getty ImagesOn Wednesday, almost a week after the area was one of many evacuated as firefighters rushed to contain the blazes that haveconsumed tens of thousands of hectaresof land west of the Spanish capital, the returning residents of El Morro were trying to process what had happened. Some phoned their insurance companies, some swept up the debris in and around their homes, and some were still too deep in shock.A man led his elderly father out of a house that had been gutted by fire, telling him it was time to go and get a change of clothes. “We’re all doing so-so,” said the son, which seemed brave but unlikely.Towards the outskirts of El Morro, a couple in late middle-age walked around what had been their garden. The house had survived bar some smoke staining, but the garden and the patio furniture had been chewed up by the fire.“We came back to the village, saw what had happened and the breath just went out of us,” said the woman.View image in fullscreenMercedes Merino, 70, in her burnt garden in El Morro, a hamlet on the outskirts of Navas del Rey.Photograph: Sam Jones/The GuardianMercedes Merino, who has lived in El Morro for 35 of her 70 years, apologised for being able to offer visitors nothing but lukewarm water – the electricity was still off – as she pointed to her blackened garden, with its flame-twisted cypress, dying loquat and sooty swimming pool. Still, at least her house had been spared.“We’ve had fires here before, but nothing like this,” she said. “I knew what we were coming back to because lots of videos of the village have been going round. We’re all feeling really low. Some people are crying and some people have lost their houses, like the guy next door.”Like the burnt-out cars, next door bore little resemblance to what it had once been. Rather than a house, it was a tangle of warped and burnt building materials, its roof collapsed into ripples of tile and its chimney absurdly horizontal.View image in fullscreenThe house next door to Mercedes Merino in El Morro.Photograph: Sam Jones/The Guardian“The firefighters have been amazing,” said Merino. “But how do you stop fires like these when you live in mountains covered with pine trees? We must have a guardian angel who was watching over us and protecting our house.”Across the road, Javier Herraiz and his family, who had just returned to El Morro after fleeing south-west to Cáceres, were sitting down to a tortilla and counting their blessings.The smoke that rose over the mountains towards the end of last week, combined with a visit from the Guardia Civil to warn them that an evacuation order was imminent, had persuaded them to leave sooner rather than later.Although the damage that greeted them when they returned home on Wednesday morning was minimal, the state of the mountains and the hamlet had shaken them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenUME personnel fighting a wildfire near Navas del Rey, southwest of Madrid, on 23 July.Photograph: UME/AFP/Getty Images“What we saw when we got here was just Dantesque,” said Herraiz, 68. “It’s such a beautiful place but all of a sudden, it had come to look like hell.”The damage to the family home amounted to little more than a warped pipe and the loss of a rainwater tank, which had probably helped protect the property as it melted and disgorged its contents over the terrace beneath.“We’ve been so lucky,” said Herraiz. “Some people have lost their houses and some of them still have mortgages to pay.”A ​decade on the Iberian ​frontline​ has shown me that Europe’s ​climate ​emergency​ is ​impossible to ​denyRead moreEva Manso, whose home backs on to steep, wooded hillside, credited a sturdy brick wall – and probably a large measure of luck – with protecting her house from the flames. The wall had certainly done its job; the hills on the other side were black, its trees naked and clawed by the heat of the flames.“We’ve never been through anything like this,” said Manso. “Yes, we had the Covid lockdown and Storm Filomena, but they were nothing like this. I don’t think anyone thought this would happen.”View image in fullscreenMoha Haddad puts out a fire at his house after being allowed to return after the wildfires in Navas del Rey.Photograph: Pablo Blázquez Domínguez/Getty ImagesThat sense of bafflement, shock and fear was as evident in El Morro as it must be across the swathes ofSpainthat have been affected by another year of wildfires, from Madrid and the neighbouring province of Ávila to the eastern region of Valencia.“I never cry over life’s difficult moments, but I sometimes cry over silly little things like a mosquito being squashed,” said Merino as she sat on her porch and looked over her ruined garden.“Maybe I’ll find myself crying in a week’s time and I won’t be able to stop.”Explore more on these topicsWildfiresSpainEuropeClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Brave New World or Groundhog Day? Burnham revisits old ground in speech on social care | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Rightwing media hostility helped sink his reform plans in 2010, but the new PM’s passionate speech suggests there is now clear political will for change
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: Rightwing media hostility helped sink his reform plans in 2010, but the new PM’s passionate speech suggests there is now clear political will for change
Content: Andy Burnham meets residents and staff at a Jewish care home in north London after his speech on reforming England’s social care system.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham meets residents and staff at a Jewish care home in north London after his speech on reforming England’s social care system.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APAndy BurnhamAnalysisBrave New World or Groundhog Day? Burnham revisits old ground in speech on social carePatrick ButlerSocial policy editorRightwing media hostility helped sink his reform plans in 2010, but the new PM’s passionate speech suggests there is now clear political will for changeWed 29 Jul 2026 14.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 15.57 EDTShareFor campaigners perpetually disappointed by the failure of England’s political classes to fix England’s creaking adult social care system, the fear was that Andy Burnham’s long-trailed speech on Wednesday would be less Brave New World, more Groundhog Day.Burnham acknowledged he had been here before. Back in 2010, as health and social care secretary, he unveiled extensive proposals to overhaul social care, only for them to collapse amid rightwing media hostility and furious political rows about “death taxes”.The new PM might talk a good game about expending political capital on an issue close to his heart, but recent history suggests that social care reform invariably ends up in what the King’s Fund thinktank calls the “Westminster graveyard of good intentions” – 22 official reviews in the past 30 years, all which have come to nothingBurnham sketched out his broad ambitions for social care reformin a brisk, partly off-the-cuff speech at a Jewish care home in north London on Wednesday. There was, as expected, little policy detail, but enough to show a clear direction of travel.He would be acceleratingLouise Casey’s review of social care, which under Keir Starmer had been slated for 2028, effectively pushing it back into a putative Labour second term. Lady Casey’s recommendations for a National Care Service would be published within 12 months. He would back Casey “100%”, he promised.He was dropping no clues as to what it might look like. It could be “fully fledged or lesser options or something in between”, he said vaguely. Casey would come up with funding options. But it wasn’t just about money: the quality of social care had to improve, work more closely with theNHS, be built around the needs of care users.There would be investment and focus on the social care workforce, boosting pay and training. He wasn’t opposed to private providers (which currently provide most care in England) but he wouldn’t put up with “profiteering” by care firms. There needed to be more support for unpaid carers, too often broken by their sacrifices.The key message, however, was about politics. Blame for the dire state of English social care lay with his generation of politicians, he said. They had serially ducked the challenge of reform, put point-scoring before fixing injustices, fomented a political culture of risk aversion and inertia.“How have we got to a position where it’s too difficult to fix the basic care that we give to each other, that fellow human beings receive?” he asked.He arrived at No 10 promising he would do politics differently, but this was a challenge to the other main political parties to do the same. He wouldn’t be drawn on whether he’d raise tax to reform social care, but it felt like he was prepared to test the very idea that a government might raise taxes to fix a glaring social injustice.“If everybody, on the NHS principle, contributed a little, it would mean everyone could protect the majority of what they’d worked for,” he said at one point. “Now I know the Mail and probably the Telegraph doesn’t support that. But I don’t know – do people support that?”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe consensus in the social care world was that this was an impressive start. “There was a sense of excitement in the room,” one veteran campaigner said. “He had every opportunity to downplay expectations but he didn’t.”Burnham showed passion, humanity, and a grasp of detail. He framed the injustices simply. He strikingly compared the inequity of social care in England with the privatised US healthcare system: “The vulnerable pay with everything and it can completely leave them with nothing.”For once, some observers said, with a flicker of amazement, there was clear political will, from the very top, to break the entrenched consensus that fixing social care is impossible. It’s early days, but for now there is the rare whiff of hope and optimism.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamSocial careNHSHealthLabouranalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘It hurts to lose a job you love’: Starmer loyalist Bridget Phillipson fights on despite cabinet demotion | Bridget Phillipson | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: The former education secretary on her new role as Labour chair and continuing as the minister for women and equalities
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Exclusive: The former education secretary on her new role as Labour chair and continuing as the minister for women and equalities
Content: Bridget Phillipson, the new chair of the Labour party, at a Rape Crisis centre in Cambridge on Tuesday.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBridget Phillipson, the new chair of the Labour party, at a Rape Crisis centre in Cambridge on Tuesday.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianBridget PhillipsonInterview‘It hurts to lose a job you love’: Starmer loyalist Bridget Phillipson fights on despite cabinet demotionAlexandra ToppingExclusive: The former education secretary on her new role as Labour chair and continuing as the minister for women and equalitiesWed 29 Jul 2026 09.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIfBridget Phillipsonis angry at losing a job – one that, in the brief honeymoon period at the start of Keir Starmer’s Labour government, she called the “honour of my life” – she is doing a good job of hiding it. “It hurts to lose a job you love,” she says. “Being education secretary was amazing … and I’m really proud of what we achieved in that time.”Phillipson was removed during the clearout of Starmer’s cabinet whenAndy Burnhamtook office last week, and was replaced by Lucy Powell, an ally of the new prime minister. But unlike some spurned colleagues, Phillipson didn’t walk away from government, instead accepting the brief of women and equalities minister – now a cabinet standalone position – which she had previously held alongside education.Her visit to a Rape Crisis centre in Cambridge this week highlighted why retaining the women and equalities brief may prove a canny move. On Monday, Burnham appointed Phillipson as the new chair of theLabourparty – an apparent olive branch to Starmer allies, and a not entirely subtle attempt to restore some sense of unity to the party.View image in fullscreenBridget Phillipson talks with Nora al-Ani at the Rape Crisis centre in Cambridge.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianThe role of Labour party chair is a nebulous one. Part election planner, administrator and party cheerleader, the chair’s importance rests heavily on the backing of the PM. On Monday, Burnham said Phillipson wouldplay a “vital role”in getting Labour “match fit for the next election”.With the subtlety of a sledgehammer, Labour’s communications stressed that the appointment showed Burnham’s commitment to building “one united team”. Phillipson echoed that it was by “uniting together” that Labour would “bring hope back to communities and strengthen British society against those working to divide us”.Unity will involve working harmoniously with Powell, who defeated her in October’s deputy leadership contest and has now replaced her as education secretary. “That contest was almost a year ago. It’s in the past, and Lucy’s a great colleague,” Phillipson says. “We’ve worked together for many years, and she has my full support in the role.”Phillipson hopes she can act as a vital bridge between bruised Starmer loyalists – many of whom are making no secret of their anger behind the scenes – and Burnham’s team.“I know how people will feel, those who’ve lost out – I know it hurts. It hurts to lose a job that you have loved and put heart and soul into,” she says. “But I know that however people feel at the moment, they want to win the next election as much as I do, and they know how high the stakes are.”Despite being a gentler character than some of her predecessors in the chair role, including Angela Rayner and Tom Watson, Phillipson insists she won’t pull her punches. She points to her record in developing the government’s fraught issue ofreforming special educational needs provisionin schools and pushing Starmer and Rachel Reeves to eventuallylift the two-child benefit cap.“I’m my own person, and I’ve always believed that there are different ways of being effective,” she says.The fight against Reform UK, whichslipped into second placebehind Labour in a voter intention poll for the first time in more than a year this week, is a message she returns to repeatedly.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We’ve got the fight of our lives on our hands to win at the next general election, our country is at a perilous moment,” she says. “We’ve got to modernise and unite our party and our movement, and take the fight to Reform. That is a huge responsibility.”She accuses Nigel Farage and his party of “shamefully” weaponising women’s pain with their focus on Pakistani grooming gangs and sexual violence committed by foreigners, and vows to keep the issue on the agenda as women and equalities minister. “We should go after whoever commits violence against women and girls, whatever their background, whatever their ethnicity,” she says.Phillipson insists that Labour’s manifesto commitment to halve violence against women and girls in a decade still stands, despite Burnham making no reference to it so far. Making her role a standalone cabinet position “demonstrates his commitment to equality and advancing women’s rights in our country”, she says, adding that ministers will be tracking VAWG crimes reported in the crime survey for England and Wales to hold themselves to account.A week and a half into Burnham’s government, after ablitz of new policies,social media videosand abounce in the polls, Phillipson says the new PM has brought “a real sense of hope, optimism and energy”. But she adds that he is building on the “good work” of the last two years under Starmer. “I am very sad at how things ended for Keir because he has achieved something that very few Labour leaders ever do, which is going from opposition into government and winning a landslide victory,” she says.But she makes it clear that her loyalties lie with the new man in No 10. “I supported Keir from opposition to government because I believe it is right that you support the leader of your party and you support your prime minister,” she says. “It is therefore now right that Andy commands that loyalty from all of us.”Explore more on these topicsBridget PhillipsonLabourAndy BurnhamKeir StarmerinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: the secret to summer layering? Sheer bravery | Women | The Guardian
description: Adding layers doesn’t have to leave you a hot mess – think sheer scarves and crochet with flashes of colour to elevate your look
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Adding layers doesn’t have to leave you a hot mess – think sheer scarves and crochet with flashes of colour to elevate your look
Content: Video: David Newby/The Guardian. Styling: Roz DonoghueJess Cartner-Morley on fashionWomenJess Cartner-Morley on fashion: the secret to summer layering? Sheer braveryAdding layers doesn’t have to leave you a hot mess – think sheer scarves and crochet with flashes of colour to elevate your lookJess Cartner-MorleyWed 29 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Perhaps I shouldn’t admit this, but I’m in two minds about summer dressing. Part of me believes summer is about joy, sunshine and good times, and clothes should embrace all of that. This woman loves Pucci and owns not one but two silver kaftans. The other part of me believes summer should be uncomplicated, laid-back and earthy. This woman never checks in luggage and has worn the same black beach cover-up for so many years it’s too threadbare to cover anything much.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The thing is, either approach looks absurd if taken to extremes. Candy swirls, cherry prints and strawberry bag charms are delightful, but pile them too high and you look like a walking knickerbocker glory. And while white linen shirts and simple black sandals are chic, you risk looking a bit like you’re on a meditation retreat where the dress code is “wealthy disciple”. Know what I mean?double quotation markWhether you go for a lace bra or sturdy vest depends on how much sauciness you are comfortable withWhich is why I want to talk about layering, even though we are bang in the middle of summer. This tactic can be the key to landing your look in the sweet spot between the two extremes. A way to give your summer wardrobe some chat, without making it shout.Summer layering isn’t about keeping warm. It’s about adding interest and hinting at skin without necessarily baring it. For a summer layering starter pack, all you need is a shirt that isn’t entirely opaque – sheer silk works, but so does fine linen – and then, crucially, something underneath that is visible on purpose. So instead of instinctively reaching for nude tones, choose a neon pink or black.Whether this just-visible under layer is a lace bra or a sturdy vest top depends on how sheer the shirt is and how much sauciness you are comfortable with. But maybe try to be a little bit brave? An odd quirk of British dressing is that we don’t bat an eyelid at wearing a tight spaghetti strap vest, with its accompanying expanse of bare skin, but we consider it risque to wear, say, a billowing sheer shirt with a peekaboo hint of bra underneath. Yet sheer coverage is the more sophisticated option, as well as the sexier one.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: David Newby/The GuardianNext: crochet. Left to its own devices, crochet has a tendency to look more beach or festival than real life. You know the look: floppy hat, enough anklets to start a percussion section. But treat crochet as a translucent top layer rather than the main event and it suddenly feels sharper. An open-knit jumper thrown over a tomato-red swimsuit gives you all the texture without the boho baggage. The flash of saturated colour makes the holes in the knit feel graphic rather than homespun, and the open weave does something clever with colour, softening a hot coral or an acid green bottom layer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJess Cartner-Morley on fashion: flip-flops are once again having a fashion moment. But please tread carefullyRead moreWhen one piece is visible under another, your outfit looks instantly less basic. Clothes that are in conversation with each other is what style is all about. A sheer skirt can look sensational over black knickers as a party look, or intriguing worn with ballet flats and over cycling shorts for daytime. I see a lot of gen Z women with sheer scarves round their waists over trousers – a DIY nod to the sheer skirt. It sounds counterintuitive to add a layer in the heat, but silk weighs almost nothing and has an old-school glamour that elevates everything.Summer layering asks you to think less about buying new clothes and more about wearing the clothes you already own differently, which is always a good thing. It’s also a way of reconciling those two women I mentioned at the start. The Pucci-loving magpie gets her colour and sparkle, but it’s softened by a sheer shirt or an open knit. The linen minimalist gets her simplicity, but with a kick that stops the whole thing becoming monastic. Why choose between maximalism and minimalism when we can spend summer in the happy, sun-dappled space in between?Styling: Roz Donoghue. Styling assistant: Charlotte Gornall. Model: Chizoba at Milk.
