title: Your worst fears about cultural collapse might be true – here’s what you can do about it | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Writer Sarah Wilson argues we’re hurtling toward the same end as ancient Rome and the Mayan civilisation – but there’s plenty to fight for
Author: Elle Hunt
Headline: Writer Sarah Wilson argues we’re hurtling toward the same end as ancient Rome and the Mayan civilisation – but there’s plenty to fight for
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesDeep diveWell actuallyYour worst fears about cultural collapse might be true – here’s what you can do about itWriter Sarah Wilson argues we’re hurtling toward the same end as ancient Rome and the Mayan civilisation – but there’s plenty to fight forElle HuntWed 29 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 16.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Sarah Wilson’s new book, one page is mostly blank. It’s intended as a reprieve, a neutral space “for you to stare at for a minute while your feelings catch up”.You will need it. InI Eat the Stars, Wilson argues that the world as we know it is in collapse – and that we are too late to avoid the worst.This is not just about the climate, but civilisation buckling under the weight of its own complexity. Given worsening inequality, political polarisation, falling fertility, resource shortages and global conflicts, Wilson argues that we are hurtling towards the same end as ancient Rome, the Mayan civilisation and every other sophisticated society before us.View image in fullscreenI Eat the Stars by Sarah WilsonPhotograph: Penguin Random HouseWilson, an Australian journalist, has often been ahead of the curve, writing bestselling books about quitting sugar, anxiety and the climate crisis before those topics were mainstream. I Eat the Stars was serialised onWilson’s Substack newsletterbefore being published by Penguin.It is an intensely sobering read, seeming to confirm all our worst fears about the future. But it also delivers clarity. Yes, things are that bad, but there is still plenty to fight for and much we can shape – if we are willing to confront reality.I spoke to Wilson, who lives nomadically, shortly after she arrived in Greece. “A life skill I’ve developed over the years is finding wifi,” she jokes. Our conversation has been edited and condensed.You’ve written about sugar, anxiety, the climate crisis and now collapse. What do you see as the common line?My first book, I Quit Sugar, was contentious back in 2009. Can you imagine, our biggest enemy being big sugar? There were headlines: “Sarah Wilson’s telling us to get rid of a food group.” It was very hard for people to understand that there could be a different framing. From there I moved on to anxiety, tackling big pharma and the hold it had on the narrative – not saying that there isn’t a place for medication, but again treading in the grey area.What I do is feel what people are thinking and wrangling with internally, but hasn’t yet been expressed as a public narrative. My dad says: “If there’s an elephant in the room, Sarah will just scream it out.” I’m not claiming to be the expert – I’m just bringing the complex science into the public realm.What’s the difference between climate crisis and collapse?We’ve been dealing with the climate as an isolated, almost linear concept, where it’s a problem with a fix. But not a single nation stuck to the Paris agreement. People are getting solar panels, but we’re all using more carbon-emitting fossil fuels as well – our habits aren’t changing. We’re still trapped in the mindset that caused the problem in the first place: believing in infinite growth, and that we don’t have to change our ways of being.We are living in a time of polycrisis. If you feel trapped – you’re not aloneRead moreA civilisation is a complex system of complex systems. Eventually all complex systems, without exception throughout history, have collapsed under the weight of their complexity. A small crisis like a heatwave can be enough to tip the whole thing over, so the climate crisis is a really powerful node in this whole thing, because it is dictating the buildup of tension of all these other complex systems – while those, of course, are also adding to the climate crisis.We’re used to glimpses of this, in headlines, reports, expert warnings – you bring them all together, and the outlook is dire. What’s actually at stake right now?I think we are in a liminal moment: we know the present set-up can’t hold, but we don’t know what’s going to come next. We are basically at the top of this very sharp bell curve, just in the moments before it tips down the other side. Everything that has been going up and up and up – population, wealth, the price of oil – are about to dip.It’s a terrifying moment, I’m not going to pretend otherwise, but it’s also a moment of stunning possibility. These periods of transition historically have been times of incredible human flourishing. Existentialism, communism and fascism were established between the two world wars. TheAxial Agewas another liminal time that produced Judaism, Buddhism, Confucianism, the market system and great art. There’s a threshold, and an opportunity.What does collapse look like?We do not know: uncertainty is the main characteristic of all this. Anyone who tries to tell you when and how collapse is going to happen, I wouldn’t believe them. We know that certain models are going to decline, but how that plays out will depend on how those things interact together, and also where you live. I would argue that there are parts of the world, such as Sudan and Gaza, that already know what collapse looks like.double quotation markI would argue that there are parts of the world, such as Sudan and Gaza, that already know what collapse looks like.What I would say is that, for anyone alive today, things are not going to keep improving. Particularly around the climate crisis, we’ve been hoping that if we just get solar panels and recycle and vote in a good government, then we can go back to the way things were – that ain’t going to happen. Collapse is going to basically look like things being shit and, instead of improving,getting shittier still. At a bare minimum, life is going to get extremely uncomfortable over the coming decades.If everything is only going to get worse, why should we try to change or care about the future at all?The reason I wrote the book is that there’s an opportunity here: what’s collapsing is the post-industrial, colonialist, extractivist, growth-based system. If we tether ourselves to that system, we will go down with it, but if we start to distance ourselves, see what’s happening and refuse to take part in its worst excesses, the better chance we have. The way it’s going, the ultra-rich and the tech bros are going to take everything anyway. The market is going to collapse, the millionaire set will suddenly be without assets, and that’s when revolution happens.Many feel angry that this is our lot, and that people in power aren’t doing enough. How can we avoid turning on each other?I go into detail explaining these complex systems concepts so that people can see there isn’t a cabal of bad dudes plotting; the government isn’t out to get us. We’re all part of this system … no one is to blame. Yes, there are people who are responsible, and opportunists who are taking advantage of this chaotic time – Trump, the technofascists and so on – but saying “They’re doing it to us” is a very binary thing. I think that by talking about the layers of crises, we can actually resolve the dissonance in our brain, relax and start thinking expansively.When I started writing about what was happening in this brutal, upfront way, the response was relief. Once you’ve absorbed all that, you want to understand more. The next layer is realising, “hey, this is what’s happened to other civilisations, because they got too complex”. This is not because people are horrible, or it’s “us versus them”. It’s all of us.You’ve said you have no hope. None?I have no hope that it’s all going to be OK if we just recycle, or that we can return to the way things were, when everything was comfortable and we didn’t have to take responsibility. But I still have hope that the natural systems of life are going to force us into being the best versions of ourselves.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSystems are crumbling – but daily life continues. The dissonance is realRead moreBasically I see what’s happening as a correction: we’ve gone in the wrong direction, we took individualism too far, capitalism no longer serves us and the centre cannot hold. Nature will recalibrate and find balance again. That’s what’s happening now. In the process, we are being forced to return to everything that makes us human.AI, for example – it’s going like a bull out of a gate, and we were not consulted. It’s terrifying, but it’s actually forcing us to ask: if it can take our jobs, and become a lover, what is left? It’s art, poetry, messiness, all that juicy human stuff.What collective action should we be prioritising?Not everyone has the capacity to comprehend all of this. Those of us who do, need to get sturdy in our nervous systems, become islands of sanity and use whatever privilege we have to fight for things we want to hang on to.The pathway into the new world will be based on ideas that exist now. I would argue that we need to be fighting for democracy, and our rights to protest, which are being eroded everywhere.Researchers have found that the two determinants of the speed and likelihood of collapse are basically levels of inequality and polarisation. We have the capacity to actually do something about those two things. That will steer how fast and how bad things are, and how much time we have to adjust.On the individual front, are there practical things we should be doing, to prepare?One way is starting to simplify your life, make consumer choices that are based on the smallest amount of trade routes and supply chains.Another is going analogue – building that muscle and normalising it with your children. There’s a whole generation who don’t know how to get across their suburb without their phone, but at a bare minimum, we’re going to be experiencing outages of power and internet.Knowing how to ride a bike, use a compass – I would go as far as saying they’re survival skills. People in Europe havealready been advisedto put together survival kits, whether for world war three or heatwaves. Having water and food for three days, a battery-operated torch, pen and paper ready to hand – it’s not so fringe.So do you think we should all be preppers?People often ask me this. I say absolutely not, because if things get so bad that you need to be off in the hills with a stockpile of tinned corn and batteries, then you’ll need to be able to defend it with weapons and violence. I myself am not prepared to do that, and I think it is absolutely the wrong direction.double quotation markWe don’t know what’s going to happen – so live beautifully regardless.We need to be going collectivist. Our strength as a species is in collaboration and communication. That’s when we flourish. Studies have shown that less than 5% of “intentional communities”, which are set up away from the usual systems in an assumed “self sustaining” fashion, last longer than five years. What does work are organically formed communities of roughly 20 to 30 families, or an apartment block. We need to be forming stronger bonds where we are now: joining food co-ops, getting together in groups, sharing tools and assets and skills whenever we can.You write that there’s joy to be found from going through this transition. How?The title of the book, I Eat the Stars, comes from a poem written by Rebecca Elson, an astronomer who was diagnosed with terminal cancer, as an antidote to fear of death. Once we’re pushed right up against the prospect of things ending, then we go: well, let’s max the hell out of this. There’s an urgency to live fully.Neoliberalism has taught us that we don’t live for the moment; instead we save up, build a nest egg, retire, play golf and then we die. What we’re talking about here puts a bomb underneath all of that. I see a lot of people putting off what really matters to them, because they’re caught up in a system that is now going down.We don’t know what’s going to happen – so live beautifully regardless. That’s what these aphorisms and parables are essentially saying: you’re still allowed to have a beautiful life. In fact there’s an imperative now.I Eat the Stars: How to Live Fully and Beautifully in a Collapsing World by Sarah Wilson is out now through Penguin LifeExplore more on these topicsWell actuallyDeep divefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Drinkflation: why British booze is getting weaker | Consumer affairs | The Guardian
description: While the sizes and prices are staying the same, brands are reducing the alcohol content in their beer
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: While the sizes and prices are staying the same, brands are reducing the alcohol content in their beer
Content: Less is more?Photograph: Posed by models; Brasileira/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLess is more?Photograph: Posed by models; Brasileira/Getty ImagesPass notesConsumer affairsDrinkflation: why British booze is getting weakerWhile the sizes and prices are staying the same, brands are reducing the alcohol content in their beerWed 29 Jul 2026 11.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 13.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Drinkflation.Age:The current round started in 2023.Appearance:To the naked eye, no appreciable change.But drinks are getting bigger?Drinks are staying the same size.Then the price of these same-sized drinks is getting higher?Prices are also staying the same.So what is happening?The drinks are getting less alcoholic.Which drinks?Specifically, beer. Even more specifically, Carling Original, which is being reduced in strength from 4.0% alcohol by volume (ABV) to 3.4%.I hadn’t noticed.You won’t have done, because the change doesn’t come into effect until October.And also because I don’t drink Carling. Or indeed beer.Good for you.Anyway, if they’re actually reducing the alcohol, why is it called drinkflation?It’s a coinage based on shrinkflation: the practice of reducing food portion sizes – putting fewer crisps in the bag, say – while keeping prices the same.Sneaky.Are any other beer brands considering doing something similar?Lots already have: Foster’s has gone from 4.0% to 3.4% ABV over the last three years; Sol went from 4.2% to 3.4% in 2025. Carlsberg, Grolsch, John Smith’s, Coors and Amstel have also reduced their alcohol levels.Is this because drinkers prefer weaker beer? Or is it a bid to curb the nation’s alcohol consumption on the sly?Neither. It’s a bid to save money and maximise profits.How much money can yousave by reducing the level of alcoholby a few measly percentage points?A lot. But it’s not the alcohol that costs money, it’s the tax.I have no idea what you’re talking about.The move could have something to do with thechanges to alcohol dutyin 2023, under which packaged beer between 3.5% and 8.4% ABV attracts a levy of £22.58 per litre of pure alcohol.I don’t know what that amounts to.For a 4.0% beer it’s about 41p a pint. Whereas a 3.4% beer is subject to a duty of just £9.96 per litre of pure alcohol, or about 19p a pint.That’s quite a difference, but what if people don’t like Carling’s new weak beer?The company claimsthe 3.4% version actually ranked “higher for overall taste” in consumer tests. It alsolaid the groundworkfor the reduction by introducing a stronger and more expensive Black Label version in February, at 4.7%, creating a “value-premium price ladder” within the brand.Do say:“Alcohol duty must strike a difficult balance between raising revenue and improving health.”Don’t say:“3.4%? My urine is stronger than that.”Explore more on these topicsConsumer affairsPass notesAlcoholFood & drink industryShoppingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham wants to fix social care. It’s personal for him and for a lot of us too | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Finally a grownup is in charge who speaks to voters as fellow adults. If he fixes this, he’ll achieve more than most other PMs
Author: John Crace
Headline: Finally a grownup is in charge who speaks to voters as fellow adults. If he fixes this, he’ll achieve more than most other PMs
Content: Andy Burnham talked unscripted, from the heart, about his own experiences of social care and met residents at a north London care home.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham talked unscripted, from the heart, about his own experiences of social care and met residents at a north London care home.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/PAThe politics sketchSocial careAndy Burnham wants to fix social care. It’s personal for him and for a lot of us tooJohn CraceFinally a grownup is in charge who speaks to voters as fellow adults. If he fixes this, he’ll achieve more than most other PMsUK politics live – latest updatesWed 29 Jul 2026 09.21 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 08.44 EDTShareIt feels like the UK has a prime minister again. Not the Maybot paralysed with indecision. Not the clown-like Boris Johnson who crumbled under the weight of his own narcissism. Not the ridiculous Liz Truss. Not the steamrollered Rishi Sunak for whom everything was impossible. Not the automaton-like Keir Starmer who was never entirely sure what he wanted to do.But a prime minister who is emotionally intelligent. Who understands the country and can connect with it. Who is prepared to expend political capital to get the things done that other politicians were too weak to go near. You can almost feel the sense of relief in a UK that has become almost accepting of decline and failure. It’s the return of hope over grievance. Where once more we have an adult prime minister prepared to speak to voters as fellow adults. It could catch on.This was Andy Burnham’s first big set piece since taking office. And he went straight for social care. An issue that previous governments over the past 30 years have done their utmost to avoid. A royal commission, 22 reviews and absolutely nothing has changed. Too difficult, too many hard choices. Far simpler to keep on with a system that’s failing. Let the next government deal with it. They can take the hits. Just concentrate on trying to win the next election.“This is personal to me,” said Andy, as he addressed a small audience of care workers and the media at Jewish Care in north London. Personal because his father has dementia and needs daily care.It’s personal for a lot of us. It’s personal for me. My mother had Alzheimer’s and needed to be in a care home for seven years before she died last year. My sisters and I had to sell her home to pay for the care she got. We didn’t resent it. It was just what needed to happen and the care she got from a mostly overseas staff was superb. We couldn’t have asked for more. But my mother would have been bitterly upset had she been aware of what we had done. Before she got dementia she had always been so proud she would be able to leave her house to us children. It was to have been her last gift to us.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham meets residents and staff at a care home in north London.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/PAHere’s the thing. No one wants to pay for social care until the point when you find you have no choice. It’s a lottery. Some people just drop dead of heart disease. Others die of cancer. By and large they have no need for a social care system. But then one day you find an elderly relative is beginning to behave differently. Their personality begins to change. They start forgetting things. You try to explain it away. Maybe they are anxious and depressed. The doctor puts them on antidepressants. Old people’s memories do fail. It’s only months later you accept it’s dementia.Then the choices become harder. You find a carer to make daily visits to their home. To get them dressed. To make sure they are still eating. Then you up the care so there’s someone with them at night. Next there comes a time when the carers say your loved one’s needs have become too much for them to be looked after at home. And all the while you are having to make the financial calculation. How can I give them the best care when I have no idea how long they are going to live. When they might die within a year or live for seven. It’s a nightmare.And Burnham gets that it’s a nightmare. That hard choices need to be made. No one wants to pay extra for social care, but how can it be fair that some families are left with next to nothing just because they can’t choose the manner of their own death? Here was Andy talking human. Talking unscripted from the heart. Accepting that some people will be cynical about his intentions as they’ve heard warm words that have come to nothing before. But putting his political career on the line. He had no idea how long the public would give him in No 10, but he would make it his mission to reform the system.Assisted dying debate should come after end-of-life care reform, says BurnhamRead moreFirst the good bits. The men and women – paid and unpaid – who deliver quality care day in, day out. But there was so much that didn’t work. The 15-minute care packages. The emergency calls. The bedblocking. The care homes that profited from others’ misfortunes. The random nature of who could afford what level of care provision. A system that was ultimately unsustainable. Every bit as unfair as the US health system, where time and again it’s the vulnerable who are left to pick up the tab.So there would be three changes. Bringing forward the review to be completed next year. Converging the social care andNHSworkforce. And, most importantly, starting cross-party talks. Kemi Badenoch and Ed Davey had written to Burnham at the weekend so he had invited them to be part of the consensus. Presumably Nigel Farage had not written, preferring to snipe from the sidelines about a death tax. One day he might discover that even Reform supporters may need social care at some point. There again, this was probably a politics that was a little too grown up for Nige.Then we got to the questions. Here, Burnham was also a revelation. Some media outlets have been moaning for the past week about how Andy was avoiding being interrogated. Running scared. Running a totalitarian socialist state. But he answered everything. No rambling. No answering questions he wished he had been asked. Just straightforward responses. Grownup to grownup.Yes, it was going to be difficult. That’s why no one had tried to do it before. Yes, he did believe in consensus. Doing the big stuff involved dropping the political point scoring for the bigger picture. He hoped Ed and Kemi would be up to the challenge. He seemed to have given up on Nige already. And, yes, though some of the costs could be met from efficiency savings, there would inevitably be some hard choices on tax to be made. Do you feel lucky that no one in your family will need social care? Maybe you do. But it’s coming for most of us.Andy left with a smile. Maybe this had been the easy bit. Starting the ball rolling. But it was better than ignoring it. And what a relief to have someone in No 10 who talks human. We should enjoy it while we can. Just think of the prize. If Andy were to do nothing in his time in office but fix social care, he would have achieved more than most other prime ministers.Explore more on these topicsSocial careThe politics sketchAndy BurnhamOlder peopleDementiaNHSAlzheimer'sLouise CaseyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Suddenly the British right feels a political chill. It’s getting cold in Andy Burnham’s shadow | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: The Tories and Reform had it easy when Keir Starmer was self-destructing – but a new PM with ideas exposes how vacant the opposition has become, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: The Tories and Reform had it easy when Keir Starmer was self-destructing – but a new PM with ideas exposes how vacant the opposition has become, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/GettyOpinionAndy BurnhamSuddenly the British right feels a political chill. It’s getting cold in Andy Burnham’s shadowRafael BehrThe Tories and Reform had it easy when Keir Starmer was self-destructing – but a new PM with ideas exposes how vacant the opposition has becomeWed 29 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 11.13 EDTShareAndy Burnham’s recollections of Britain in the 1970s must be pretty hazy. He was nine when the decade ended. Kemi Badenoch, born in 1980, can remember nothing. Lacking first-hand experience, the Conservative leader evokes the turmoil of a bygone era with cautionary zeal borrowed from an older generation. In a speech last week, sheaccused the new prime ministerof pining for “endless strikes, rubbish not being collected, bodies not being buried, inflation at 25% and a chancellor going cap-in-hand to the IMF”.This is more incantation than argument, a ritual fondling of beads on the Tory rosary. It is a symptom of a leader under stress, affirming her faith in Our Lady Margaret Thatcher and warding off socialist devils. Burnham has done nothing to support the claim that his government is a 70s tribute act, unless you count the appointment of aman named Healeyaschancellorand the imposition of price controls on buses.What the prime minister has done is trace Britain’s present malaise to choices made in the Thatcher era. From thethreshold of No 10he delivered the verdict on that legacy: “Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, large parts of the country de-industrialised, and they still haven’t recovered.” That statement has become the foundation stone for an edifice of neuralgic conservative commentary, bemoaning Britain’s capture by anti-market, pro-state fanatics.The right of British politics seems to be disoriented by the appearance of a Labour prime minister whose message isn’t crafted as a preemptive flinch at the accusation that he might come from the left, believe some leftish things and gamble on them being popular. Nigel Farage is playing it safe with the predictable but flimsy complaint that Burnham lacks a mandate. The Reform UK leader knows that isn’t how British politics works and, given that his personal ratings areon a downward drift, he doesn’t want a general election anyway.Badenoch’s reach back to the Seventies is a default setting in the absence of better ideas. It isn’t totally irrational, given the hint of nostalgia in Burnham’s tone. His ascendancy to No 10 relied on him being acceptable to a coalition of disputatiousLabourfactions. Lamentation over the death of a proletarian way of life, killed by Thatcher’s hand, is a hymn the party can sing in harmony. The new leader is a skilled choirmaster – in contrast to his predecessor, who knew the words but couldn’t carry a tune.But Burnham has also just spent nine years as mayor of Manchester, leaving it an enterprising capitalist city. He argues that its success is a function of pragmatic partnership between government and business, and that this model can be replicated on a national scale. It is hardly wild dogma to suggest that a strategically minded state can guide the hand of the market. The prime minister believes devolving power will give that hand a defter feel for local needs.Conservatives might disagree, but it takes wilful denial, or maybe intellectual laziness, to pretend that Burnham’s Manchester blueprint is retro-socialism, plain and simple. The prime minister could hardly be more explicit in rejecting the 20th-century central planner’s adage that “the gentleman in Whitehall knows best”.It is normal for oppositions to take time to get the measure of a new prime minister, and vice versa. Leaders need to make a few mistakes before their weaknesses form a pattern that can be woven into an effective political attack. Keir Starmer was a slippery target in opposition. But in government he made life easy for his enemies by shedding what modest popularity he had accrued almost immediately. Badenoch didn’t have to develop an argument against a prime minister who struggled to explain what he was trying to do and waseasily bulliedinto doing something else.The Tories were bystanders while Starmer’s government self-immolated, mostly to the benefit of Reform UK and the Greens. Badenoch’s personal ratings have picked up over the past year, reflecting perhaps growing squeamishness on the right about Farage as a prospective prime minister. But the Conservative vote share hasyet to climb as highas the giddy depths it fell to in July 2024, when the party suffered itsworst ever general election defeat.Disillusionment with Labour rule has done nothing to revive public interest in a Conservative alternative. Badenoch has done nothing to make her party interesting. She wasted her first year fretting perversely that the Tories had been too leftwing in office, thereby endorsing the case for defection toReform UK.She then switched to a focus on fiscal parsimony, hoping to occupy electoral terrain between public wariness of Labour’s tax-and-spend instincts and suspicion that Farage was a bit spivvy where money is concerned. But having scoped out a desirable patch of political real estate, Badenoch isn’t building anything. She has no theory of public service reform. Toread her speechesis to inhabit a parallel universe where the obvious causes of dissatisfaction with the state are chronic overfunding and infestation by militant leftwing civil servants.It is a vacuous analysis, coloured by excessive consumption of radical US conservative content online. British politics has always been shaped by trends across the Atlantic, but the radicalisation of the British right throughexposure to Maga influence(both cultural and financial) in recent years amounts to cognitive surrender. Political fandom has usurped judgment; craving validation from a foreign power takes precedence over loyalty to the national interest.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA Labour prime minister has the excuse of realpolitik, being obliged to show deference to a despotic US president who despises democratic allies but remains indispensable when it comes to their defence needs. Even then, Starmer found the courage to distance himself from Donald Trump’s disastrous military adventure in Iran. Not so, Badenoch. She turned squeamish only when she realised how far her initial gung-ho instincts had carried her from British mainstream opinion.What British conservatives either fail to observe or refuse to acknowledge in their mindless orbit around Planet Trump is that Maga politics contains more heresies against the sacred Thatcherite creed than anything Burnham proposes. The US president hates free trade. He admires single-party regimes where a supreme ruler directs economic activity. He imposes arbitrary tariffs. He uses his office to extort money from private companies or coerce them into givingequity stakesto his government. And he acquired the power to do all of this by skilfully manipulating economic and social grievances caused by deindustrialisation – the alienation and dislocation felt by working-class communities that felt their security and dignity washed away by cold global market tides.It is the same trend that Burnham identifies as a cause of British discontent and economic stagnation. The difference is that the UK prime minister talks about healing wounds, while Trump keeps them salted with partisan spite. It should be obvious to anyone who cares about democracy and the rule of law which model is preferable. Maybe the new prime minister’s methods will not work. Perhaps his prescriptions are flawed. At least his diagnosis belongs in 2026. It is the leader of the opposition, craving reenactment of a battle that was won before she was born, who is stuck in the wrong century.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionKemi BadenochNigel FarageLabourConservativesReform UKDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Even Maga is falling out of love with JD Vance. If only his rivals weren’t even worse … | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The US vice-president is facing a barrage of allegations and complaints from inside and outside the Republican ranks. Good news for Marco Rubio – but not for the rest of the world, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The US vice-president is facing a barrage of allegations and complaints from inside and outside the Republican ranks. Good news for Marco Rubio – but not for the rest of the world, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: ‘The president is loving Vance’s svelte new figure’ … the vice-president in Winconsin earlier this month.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The president is loving Vance’s svelte new figure’ … the vice-president in Winconsin earlier this month.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/ReutersOpinionJD VanceEven Maga is falling out of love with JD Vance. If only his rivals weren’t even worse …Arwa MahdawiThe US vice-president is facing a barrage of allegations and complaints from inside and outside the Republican ranks. Good news for Marco Rubio – but not for the rest of the worldWed 29 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTShareThere’s something a bit off about JD Vance. And I mean that literally: the vice-president has been snacking on sauerkraut and other fermented foods as part of a weight-loss regime. Health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr got a number of Trump officials, including Vance, on to the diet, and isthrilled with the results. “Within 20 days I lost 20 pounds,” Kennedy said at an event in Michigan last month. “JD Vance is also on the diet and you can see how different he looks.” Dunno about that: still looks like a naked opportunist to me.If you want to get into Donald Trump’s good books, improving your looks is a surefire way to do so.According to MS Now, the president is loving Vance’s svelte new figure; it’s helped propel him back into Trump’s good graces. Which is lucky for him because he doesn’t have many other fans. They may be full of beneficial bacteria, but everyone around Vance seems to hate his guts.That includes a member of his protective detail, who is now under investigation for revealing to the media the Vance family’s lavishtravel requests. The Hillbilly Elegy authorreportedly askedfor one of his sons to be dropped off at a golf lesson via helicopter, and demanded last-minute chopper trips to Virginia to go house-hunting. With help like that you can understand why Vance is so pronatalist. I’d be popping out kids too, if I could get the taxpayer to fund helicopter trips to their extracurriculars.It’s not just the help he has angered. On Fridaythe Washington Postreported that Vance has faced a barrage of attacks from within his party “unlike that faced by other vice-presidents in decades”. Vance’s allies told the Post that the attacks, which seem largely driven by his mild criticism of Israel and the Iran war, are a “coordinated” attempt to poison his 2028 presidential chances. Over the weekend aFox News panelcriticised Vance for a recent appearance on Joe Rogan’s podcast where (in a brief moment of good judgment) he questioned putting troops on the ground in Iran. “[Vance] seems to be going off base a lot, and contradicting the president a lot in public lately, and it’s not helpful,” Fox News contributor Marc Thiessen said.I can’t say it’s not fun to watch Maga infighting. Nevertheless, it’s hard to take too much satisfaction from Vance’s troubles considering they only really benefit his rival for the 2028 Republican nomination: the odious war hawk Marco Rubio, who is nownarrowing the gapwith Vance in the polls. A setback for one awful politician always seems to spell a career boost for someone even worse. It’s really quite the pickle.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Wildfires are raging – and the world has junked 45 climate pledges. Disaster looms, and little wonder | Bill McGuire | The Guardian
description: Five years ago, I wrote an open letter asking climate scientists to speak out. Now governments are in retreat, it is surely time to act, says climate professor Bill McGuire
Author: Bill McGuire
Headline: Five years ago, I wrote an open letter asking climate scientists to speak out. Now governments are in retreat, it is surely time to act, says climate professor Bill McGuire
Content: 0:57Spain wildfire burns 'out of extinguishing capacity' as fires engulf parts of Europe – videoOpinionClimate crisisWildfires are raging – and the world has junked 45 climate pledges. Disaster looms, and little wonderBill McGuireFive years ago, I wrote an open letter asking climate scientists to speak out against fossil fuels. Now governments are in retreat, it is surely time to actFrance and Spain race to contain huge wildfires before fresh heatwave beginsWed 29 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 13.53 EDTShareSuch is the astonishing scale of the wildfires burning at the gates ofBordeauxandMadrid, that if they had happened 20 – even 10 – years back, they may well have shocked the world into taking action on the climate crisis. But like the proverbial frog in a pot of slowly heating water, we have become inured; not only to the ever more devastating impacts of climate breakdown, but increasingly to the actions needed to bring global heating to heel.Even as more than35,000 wildfiresrage across the surface of our world, and as we continue to rewind our planet’s climate so itresembles hotter episodes from its distant past, governments and trading blocs are very deliberately turning away from climate action.The latest evidence that we are not only doing too little but actually doing less as time goes by isprovided by the climate action media platform, We Don’t Have Time. It reported last week that the 12 months to July this year saw the reversal across the world of 45 climate policies. The retreat on climate action is global, but Europe – previously seen as a leader in emissions reductions – is in the vanguard, weakening measures across the board, including in the areas of carbon pricing, methane emissions and the phasing out of petrol and diesel vehicles.This isn’t yet an apocalyptic reversal of the majority of climate commitments, as the continuity of countless other climate policies testifies. We are, however, at an especially critical period: if we don’t want backsliding on climate action to continue, we have to act now.Croatian firefighting pilots help battle wildfire in France – loopWe Don’t Have Time lays the blame squarely at the foot of lobbying by the fossil fuel sector, and other industries antagonistic to climate action, making the point that as long as the usual suspects continue to make the most noise in the meetings where decisions are made, they will get what they want. What we have to do, then, is to make even more noise – on the streets, via the ballot box and in the media – putting pressure on politicians and governments so that they don’t cave in to vested business interests.We must force those in power to join the dots between the fires raging across Europe and theEl Niño building in the Pacific, and the activities of the fossil fuel corporations and others who choose not to do so.But we need our own lobbyists too – those qualified and in positions to speak truth to power about the dire straits we are already in, who can add credence to the noisy debate. Cue the world’s climate scientists. At this critical moment, the science has a duty to out-shout and out-shine corporate weasel words and government irresponsibility. The problem is that even now, at a time when the rate of global heating has doubled, this is just not happening.Sure, there are climate scientists out there telling it like it is, making a lot of noise and often putting their livelihoods and career prospects on the line, but they remain the exception rather than the rule. Far too many individuals, for one reason or another, still keep silent, heads below the parapet, fears and frets internalised.In 2021, Iwrote an open letterto all climate scientists, reminding them that they had a duty to speak out, to come down off the fence and to force those who need to know to listen to the truth. Sadly, five years on, little has changed. For far too many, fears about funding, academic advancement, prestige, and the contempt or ridicule of colleagues, still trump speaking out.As the heat continues to ratchet up, this cannot go on. If we want to have any possibility of drowning out the bogus claptrap of those determined to prevent serious climate action, then climate scientists – all scientists for that matter – need to wake up now and make themselves heard.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionClimate science is a vast tent that incorporates aspects of geology, chemistry, physics, oceanography, meteorology, economics, social science and many other fields, so that one source putting the number of climate scientists at18,000 worldwideis almost certainly an underestimate. When it comes to scientists of every ilk, the global figurecomes out at not far short of 10 million. Just imagine how much racket the scientific community could make if it spoke with the same voice – demanding the reinstatement of climate-friendly policies, arguing for more rapid emissions cuts, and at the same time overwhelming the perfidious calls for inertia from those lobbying for business as usual.This may well be our last chance to turn things around; to help politicians grow the backbones they need to stand up to vested interests. At this crucial time every scientist needs to examine their conscience, take on board the reality that there will be no research grants on a dead planet – and act accordingly.Bill McGuire is professor emeritus of geophysical and climate hazards at University College London and author ofThe Fate of the World: a History and Future of the Climate CrisisThe Guardian’s climate forum 2026On Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington and our panel of experts – including Professor Andy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman – for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening.Book ticketshereExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionWildfiresExtreme heatFranceSpainGreenhouse gas emissionsFossil fuelscommentShareReuse this content

title: Uefa has to show backbone: concrete action can make Fifa’s World Cup plans untenable | Uefa | The Guardian
description: European football has shown an increased willingness to talk tough with Fifa but words can only be wielded so many times
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: European football has shown an increased willingness to talk tough with Fifa but words can only be wielded so many times
Content: The Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, and his Fifa counterpart, Gianni Infantino.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, and his Fifa counterpart, Gianni Infantino.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesUefaUefa has to show backbone: concrete action can make Fifa’s World Cup plans untenableNick AmesEuropean football has shown an increased willingness to talk tough with Fifa but words can only be wielded so many timesFA joins criticism of Fifa plan to sell off World Cup stakesWed 29 Jul 2026 06.22 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 15.56 EDTShareAs the World Cup neared its conclusion, one leading figure in European football pondered how Gianni Infantino might attempt to rinse away the damaging stain ofthe Folarin Balogun scandal. It all came down to money. “He will just announce more funds for everyone,” was the gist, although the tournament passed without any explanation of how Fifa would carve up its record $15bn (£11.2bn) haul.That was the tip of the iceberg. Infantino’s plan tosell chunks of the World Cup to private investors, announced on Tuesday, nine days after the final, has sent shock waves around the sport and left senior personnel scrambling. There is little time for a coordinated response given Fifa, at the height of what passes for football’s holiday period, has given FAs until 19 September to decide whether to accept the initial $20m payment that would effectively count as endorsement of the new scheme.FA joins criticism of Fifa plan to sell off World Cup stakes to private investorsRead moreThe reaction must come quickly. Perhaps, when Uefa assesses its next move, it will look back to 2021 and remember the credit it happily banked inblocking the proposed European Super League. Fifa’s plan, which could allow private investors a say in how and when its tournaments are run, is potentially more seismic and global in scale. If football’s future has been on a ticking clock under Infantino, the time is one minute to midnight.Uefa’s speed in responding to the plan was of a piece with its renewed appetite, honed over a number of run-ins over the past 15 months, to stick the boot intoFifa. “This crosses a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross,” it said, although anyone feeling a sense of deja vu needed only to scroll back three weeks. On 6 July, another Uefa statement said the shelving of Balogun’s suspension “crossed a red line”. These are strong, accurate words, but they can be wielded only so many times.Infantino can rush his proposals through by counting on votes from the overwhelming number of FAs, primarily based outside Europe, who pledge fealty to his administration. But a show of backbone from football’s most powerful continent, a sporting behemoth that has eaten up any competition on the pitch and through the financial clout of its institutions, would be a major blow to Fifa. It would only take concrete action from a few of Europe’s major nations, with their governments in lockstep, to render any plan to sell off football’s crown jewels untenable.View image in fullscreenFireworks go off at New York New Jersey Stadium as Spain’s Rodri lifts the World Cup.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersWho will put their heads above the parapet? This is a moment to remember that,as the Guardian revealed in mid-July, more than 200 of Fifa’s 211 members have already submitted letters in support of his candidacy for re-election early next year. Most of those resisting significant pressure to offer backing are from Europe, with Germany the highest-profile holdout. But England’s FA, which is hoping to rubber-stamp its hosting of the 2035 Women’s World Cup, was quick to offer its endorsement well before this summer.Then there are cases such as Finland, whose FA president, Ari Lahti, said in June that his country aimed “not to be an eyesore” by refusing to back Infantino. It is a common stance, even among federations who are vocal in private about their disgust for Fifa’s trampling over norms andproximity to the Donald Trump administration. Countries of all sizes have a duty to put the beauty contest on hold.Any talk of boycotting future World Cups, which would surely have to include the women’s edition in Brazil next year, is complicated by a section of Fifa’s statutes that says its members are obliged to take part in its competitions. The only way to avoid financially prohibitive sanctions may be to threaten the most radical step of all: a withdrawal from Fifa and the creation of a new governance model for football.Uefa’s position may be made trickier by its close relationship to the thus far taciturn European Football Clubs (EFC), which would like to set up a joint venture with Fifa to run the Club World Cup. EFC andUefaalready run a joint venture, UC3, that operates the commercial aspect of Uefa competitions, but one of the key differences from Fifa’s proposal is that it does not involve private capital.Somehow, everyone must be corralled together if Infantino is to be tackled. Another way would be to remove some wind from Infantino’s sails by putting up a serious electoral opponent. After the Balogun affair, conversations with figures at all levels of the sport speculated whether Uefa might endorse its own candidate to run for the Fifa presidency in March. Consensus suggested it would be too soon; that this will be a period of positioning for 2031 when, according to Fifa’s current rules, Infantino must stand aside.Is the World Cup for sale? Here’s what Fifa’s plans mean and what happens next | Paul MacInnesRead moreBut there is no time to play a long game when Infantino plans to carve up football’s future among private interests in rapid order. Nor is there the opportunity to wait for any European Commission response to the complaint by FifPro, the global players’ union, and the European Leagues organisation about Fifa’s grip on the international match calendar, which was lodged in October 2024. A favourable outcome could place obstacles in front of any plans by Fifa, or its friends in private investment, to expand its tournaments, but no resolution appears in sight.Uefa and Europe must take a lead and reject the status quo. Doing so might reveal friends in unexpected places. There are certainly countries in Asia, among other confederations, that would be open to clear suggestions of a better path. The fear is that a rush of nebulous statements such as that by the Danish FA, which responded to Infantino’s plan by emphasising the need to “gain a complete understanding of the proposal and the process behind it” will result in nothing bar the standard procrastination and tacit acceptance.Bravery and sturdy spines are required now, more than ever, if football is to survive in anything resembling its present form.11:17Infantino tries to cash in on World Cup: is football’s soul for sale? - The LatestExplore more on these topicsUefaFifaWorld CupFootball politicsGianni InfantinocommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump has singled out us Canadians for special treatment in his tariff war – there is no choice but to get nasty | Matt Gurney | The Guardian
description: The White House fails to understand that Mark Carney and Canada’s regional leaders can’t cave in to the US president: it’s too toxic to voters, says Toronto-based journalist Matt Gurney
Author: Matt Gurney
Headline: The White House fails to understand that Mark Carney and Canada’s regional leaders can’t cave in to the US president: it’s too toxic to voters, says Toronto-based journalist Matt Gurney
Content: Donald Trump and Mark Carney at a working lunch with G7 and Middle East leaders in Évian-les-Bains, France, 16 June 2026.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Pool Reuters/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Mark Carney at a working lunch with G7 and Middle East leaders in Évian-les-Bains, France, 16 June 2026.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Pool Reuters/APOpinionCanadaTrump has singled out us Canadians for special treatment in his tariff war – there is no choice but to get nastyMatt GurneyThe White House fails to understand that Mark Carney and Canada’s regional leaders can’t cave in to the US president: it’s too toxic to votersMatt Gurney is a journalist based in TorontoWed 29 Jul 2026 07.01 EDTShareThough many hate to admit it, Canadians have long wished for more attention from the US. Well, we’re getting it now. And it turns out that President Trump and some of his top supporters in the Maga movement don’t much like us.The first big hint was when he startedtalking about annexing us, saying we couldn’t survive without American support. But the most recent example of Trump’s dislike for Canada can be seen in his latest tariff policies. Canada was largely spared the impact of his“Liberation Day” tariffsin April 2025 by its pre-existing free trade deal with the US (and Mexico), but earlier this month, as expected, the USdeclined to extendthat deal for another 16-year term. It’s now subject to annual renegotiations. Then, last week, the White House announcedtariffs as high as 50%on a selection of Canadian products including, for the first time, items previously protected by the trade agreement. The US called it retaliation for Canadian trade practices.It’s true that the US announced tariffs against dozens more countries just days later, but there has been something odd about the lopsided attention paid to Canada, which most US presidents tend to politely ignore. Most of the tariffsTrump recently announcedwere in the range of about 10%, but Canada was hit by 50% tariffs (albeit on a narrower range of exports). The president, it seems, wanted to send a message to Canada, but without hurting US consumers too much.The tariffs also land differently here, given Trump’s stateddesire to annexCanada as a 51st state. The president has ruled out using military force to accomplish that, saying instead thathe would use “economic force”. Tariffs would meet that definition.There may have been little sign that the talk of annexation is anything more than typical Trumpian bluster, but even the suggestion, along with the tariffs, has been a shock for a Canadian political class that has long taken a friendly America as a law of nature – and has letCanadagrow shockingly dependent on the US for defence and trade. An unfriendly, potentially even hostile US is a staggeringly consequential change. It’s hard to overestimate how huge a shock this has been.And it’s having a massive effect on our domestic politics, thus far to the benefit of the Liberal party and the prime minister, Mark Carney. The return of Trump to the White Houseupset an election last yearthat the Liberals had been set to lose decisively. Canada’s Conservatives were cruising to an easy win with a campaign focused on public safety and the cost of living, but once Trump began musing about annexation, the Liberals dumped Justin Trudeau, replaced him with Carney, wrapped themselves in the flag, and won decisively. Carney remains popular, largely because Canadians see him as the right choice to deal with Trump.US pressure is complicating Canada’s increasingly fraught internal politics in other ways. Canada does not have a true national economy, but a series of regional ones. Ontario and Quebec, the most populous provinces, are heavily dependent on manufacturing. In western Canada, particularly the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, the economies depend more on exporting natural resources, including oil. Most of this goes to the US, as Canada lacks the transportation infrastructure to readily export it elsewhere (there’s that dependency).The response has therefore been more fragmented than unified. Ontario has pursued astrategy of confrontation; the western provinces havepreferred to appealto shared interestswith the US. These are obvious fissures that the US could choose to exploit. It was strange to see, when the most recent round of tariffs was announced, that most of the economic damage landed on Ontario and Quebec and the province of British Columbia – three jurisdictions that have taken stronger anti-Trump positions. The economies of Alberta and Saskatchewan were relatively spared.Trump’s administration was probably hoping to mete out some punishment to provincial leaders it finds irritating. But it would have given Canada a much more challenging problem had it targeted instead the western provinces, where scepticism of rule by “eastern elites” and separatist movements are intensely divisive issues (Albertans will vote in areferendum this fallon whether to pursue independence). Carney must consider domestic blowback from any possible retaliation, such as an export tax on oil, lest he further inflame existing regional tensions.Trump’s new tariffs aren’t due to take effect for several weeks, and Canada has not yet given any signal of how it will respond. To date, though, it has generally retaliated against US levies – Carney, whose political success rests on public belief that he will stand up to Trump, would find it very difficult not to retaliate this time.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis, more than anything else, is what the White House has failed to understand about Canada. The US has some legitimate gripes with us, including trade barriers and Canada’s chronic underinvestment in defence. It’s reasonable to be angry about those things. But the nature of Trump’s actions has made resistance the only plausible Canadian response: caving in to the US president is toxic for Canadian voters. Some provincial resistance is likely due to unpopular regional leaders seeing salvation in battling Trump – and although Carney has made some concessions since becoming prime minister, includingscrapping a planned digital taxthat angered US tech companies, he dare only go so far.Trump has often complained that dealing with Canadians is unpleasant and nasty. He should expect us to get nastier still. Whether he knows it or not, he’s left us little choice.Matt Gurney is a journalist based in Toronto, and co-editor of The Line, an online magazineExplore more on these topicsCanadaOpinionMark CarneyTariffsDonald TrumpRepublicansAmericasTrump administrationcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on funding social care: building consensus requires candour about taxes | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The prime minister is right to want to change the political culture, but aversion to honesty about the funding options runs deep in Westminster
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The prime minister is right to want to change the political culture, but aversion to honesty about the funding options runs deep in Westminster
Content: Andy Burnham visits a care home in London on Wednesday.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham visits a care home in London on Wednesday.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/PAOpinionSocial careThe Guardian view on funding social care: building consensus requires candour about taxesEditorialThe prime minister is right to want to change the political culture, but aversion to honesty about the funding options runs deep in WestminsterWed 29 Jul 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 14.30 EDTShareAndy Burnham is well qualified to speak on the subject of what can go wrong with social care policy. As health secretary in 2010, he proposed reforms to be funded by a 10% inheritance levy. This was called a “death tax” by the opposition. It was never introduced.Where Mr Burnham failed, none have subsequently succeeded. David Cameron accepted the recommendations of the 2011Dilnot commission, which proposed a cap on the amount any individual would pay for care, but the cost to the exchequer thwarted implementation. Theresa May suggested plugging the money gap with a revised means test and no individual cap. This was branded a “dementia tax” by opponents and never saw the light of day.Boris Johnson planned a “health and social care levy” alongside a means test. That fell foul of the Tories’ ideological allergy to tax rises. Labour’s 2024 election manifesto promised a “national care service”. Sir Keir Starmer then commissioned a review, led by Louise Casey, to explore reform options and report back in 2028, a timetable that made change before the next general electionunlikely.View image in fullscreenLouise Casey.Photograph: James Manning/PAMr Burnham has retrieved the Casey review from the long grass. It will now report next year. The prime minister has also called for a “national conversation” with a view to finding cross-party consensus on social care in England. He has invited the leaders of the Liberal Democrats andConservatives(but notably not Reform UK or the Greens) for talks. Dame Louise will oversee a wider consultation exercise, taking views from the public. Lessons can also be learned from Scotland and Wales, with their devolved care models. This process is intended, in the prime minister’s words, to enable “more problem solving, less point-scoring” in the politics of social care.The idea is laudable. Inhis speechon Wednesday, Mr Burnham was eloquent on the subject of what has to change in Westminster culture: the need to foster a climate where hard issues might be debated in good faith, without long-term national interests being sabotaged for short-term partisan advantage.The prime minister was also refreshingly generous in his praise for care workers, recognising the technical and emotional challenges they meet forinadequate reward. He is right to say that they deserve higher wages and to make explicit the debt that all of Britain owes to a section of the labour force that is substantially staffed by immigrants.Generosity of spirit is easier to dispense than money. Mr Burnham is new enough to Downing Street that he can afford to set out broad principles without being pinned down to specifics. That privilege will not last long. He admits that a commitment to grapple with an issue that is notoriously destructive of political capital is a gamble. Cross-party consensus will remain elusive if any revenue-raising mechanism is liable to be denounced as an unconscionable tax raid. TheConservativesandReform UK, forgoing the opportunity to appear broad-minded, have already indicated that this is their position.Mr Burnham has enoughLabourMPs to enact change without opposition support. Reforms, and the contributions that pay for them within the fiscal rules, will form the basis for a future consensus if enough voters are persuaded they are necessary and fair. There is a long road to travel before that campaign begins, but the prime minister’s first steps are the right ones.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on selling off the World Cup: a red-card offence by Gianni Infantino | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Fifa’s president hopes to sell stakes in the planet’s most watched sporting event. In the wider interests of football, he must be resisted
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Fifa’s president hopes to sell stakes in the planet’s most watched sporting event. In the wider interests of football, he must be resisted
Content: Gianni Infantino and Donald Trump with the World Cup trophy after the final match between Spain and Argentina.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino and Donald Trump with the World Cup trophy after the final match between Spain and Argentina.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoOpinionGianni InfantinoThe Guardian view on selling off the World Cup: a red-card offence by Gianni InfantinoEditorialFifa’s president hopes to sell stakes in the planet’s most watched sporting event. In the wider interests of football, he must be resistedWed 29 Jul 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 14.30 EDTShareLike a sporting Dr Pangloss, Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, would like to persuade football followers that they are living in the best of all possible worlds. Maddeningly for him, many disagree. On Monday, Mr Infantinopublisheda 15-page Instagram rant in which he bemoaned the “hate and false rumours” in circulation during the recent men’s World Cup. White Houseinterferenceover a crucial refereeing decision, prohibitive ticketprices, unnecessary but lucrativehydration breaks; it was all, as his best friend in politics, Donald Trump, would say, “fake news”.But where the president of world football’s governing body sees haters, others see lovers of the game rightly concerned over where he is taking it. On Tuesday, Fifaconfirmedthat it hopes to sell stakes in the World Cup and other tournaments to private investors who may include Joshua Kushner, the brother of Mr Trump’s son-in-law Jared. The investors would buy into a new$20bn company, Fifa Forward Enterprise, which would sell all of Fifa’s commercial rights, including ticketing, and take charge of “operational delivery” of World Cups.View image in fullscreenJoshua Kushner.Photograph: Edward Berthelot/Getty ImagesMembers of the extended Trump family do not generally contemplate business ventures out of a desire to spread “joy and happiness” in the world (which the egregious Mr Infantino presents as hismission). If the plans go ahead – sweetened by offers of a $30m windfall for national associations – investors’ desires to maximise revenues would undoubtedly accelerate the hyper-monetisation of the World Cup that is already taking place.Almost certainly there would be pressure for more frequent and bigger tournaments at both club and national level, distorting the international game’s calendar to the detriment of domestic leagues. Mr Infantino has already indicated that he would look favourably on such an expansion, despiteobjectionsfrom bodies such as Uefa, European football’s governing body. Innovations such as the widely loathed hydration breaks – which by breaking games up into four quarters, US-style, allowed extra advertising slots – would no doubt proliferate.The prospect revives fears generated by the failed European Super Leagueproposals, which were furiously opposed by football supporters in 2021. During this summer’s World Cup in the US, Mr Kushner and others will haveseenat first-hand the vast commercial possibilities of an event that unites a global audience in an age of fragmented media. As the highest-level steward of the game, Fifa’s primary job is to protect football from forces that might be interested in exploiting its appeal by selling its soul; instead, under Mr Infantino, it appears happy to do their job for them.Angry opposition to the plans from Uefa and Concacaf (the equivalent body for North and Central America) suggests that the governance of the game may be at a crossroads. Mr Infantino’s tireless self-promotion, and shameless efforts to curryfavourwith the Trump administration, have long grated. But placing the planet’s most-watched sporting competition at risk from predation by private capital is of a somewhat different order of magnitude.The visionary creator of the World Cup, Jules Rimet,hopedthat it would help foster unity and solidarity between nations. Mr Infantino routinely pays lip service to such ideals, and did so again in his Instagram screed. In reality, though, he is dragging the world’s favourite sport further and further away from its roots, as he relentlessly follows the money wherever it leads.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Shameful treatment of vulnerable families in heatwave | Extreme heat | The Guardian
description: Letters: Fernando Quintana Marrero responds to a report about children housed in a building in London becoming sick after families were denied air conditioning
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Fernando Quintana Marrero responds to a report about children housed in a building in London becoming sick after families were denied air conditioning
Content: Families placed in Britannia Point in Colliers Wood, southwest London, experienced such stifling conditions that young children became ill.Photograph: Paul Gapper/AlamyView image in fullscreenFamilies placed in Britannia Point in Colliers Wood, southwest London, experienced such stifling conditions that young children became ill.Photograph: Paul Gapper/AlamyExtreme heatLettersShameful treatment of vulnerable families in heatwaveFernando Quintana Marreroresponds to a report about children housed in a building in London becoming sick after families were denied air conditioningWed 29 Jul 2026 12.10 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 13.12 EDTShareHow did London get here (Families in London temporary housing told they cannot use in-built air conditioning, 27 July)? Your report says homeless families, including young children, were placed in a glass tower during a heatwave and told they could not use the building’s air conditioning because it had “not been offered as an amenity”. If that doesn’t make every Londoner stop in disbelief, we’ve become dangerously desensitised. This is no longer a housing crisis, it is a crisis of basic human dignity.London proudly markets itself as one of the world’s greatest cities: a global financial capital overflowing with luxury developments, billion-pound property portfolios and record-breaking real estate values. Yet, in the shadow of that wealth, children are being expected to endure dangerously hot flats where the very system designed to make the building habitable is effectively treated as a luxury.When a city reaches the point where vulnerable families are housed in buildings that become ovens, while the solution exists but is deemed off limits, something has gone profoundly wrong.This isn’t an administrative oversight. It is the triumph of bureaucracy over common sense and, ultimately, over compassion. Politicians have spent years telling us London is thriving. Thriving for whom? It certainly isn’t thriving for the record number of families trapped in temporary accommodation or the children growing up without a stable home.History teaches us that great cities are judged not by the height of their skyscrapers, but by how they treat those with the least power. On that measure, London should be deeply ashamed. A city where air conditioning exists but compassion is switched off is no longer a world-class city. It is simply a dystopia.Fernando Quintana MarreroLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The feelgood factor of Burnham’s bus fare cap | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Jonathan Freedland’s article on one of the new prime minister’s first policy announcements in office
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Jonathan Freedland’s article on one of the new prime minister’s first policy announcements in office
Content: ‘Driving change in transport with bus fare cap.’Photograph: Richard Burdon/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Driving change in transport with bus fare cap.’Photograph: Richard Burdon/AlamyAndy BurnhamLettersThe feelgood factor of Burnham’s bus fare capReaders respond to Jonathan Freedland’s article on one of the new prime minister’s first policy announcements in officeWed 29 Jul 2026 12.11 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.21 EDTShareJonathan Freedland recounts how when he was 14 years old, Greater London council, led by Ken Livingstone, reduced child fares on the buses to 5p in a scheme called Fares Fair (Scoff at cheaper bus fares and No 10 North if you like, but Andy Burnham knows what he’s doing, 24 July). In 1950s Liverpool,the corporationhad a scheme for schoolchildren in the holidays whereby they could buy a “penny return” to anywhere on the tram network. You could, for example, travel from the Pier Head by the Mersey on the number 10 tram to Prescot, almost 10 miles inland, and back again. Or you could use your ticket to transfer from your first destination to a different one rather than using it as a return. Sadly the last tram ran in 1957.I remember on one occasion being on the tram when a rather tall boy asked for a penny return. The conductor obviously suspected that he was over the age limit. He gave him his ticket, but asked him: “Why didn’t you bring the missis?” And by the way, this was of course the old penny, of which there were 240 to the pound sterling.Joe CockerLeominster, HerefordshireJonathan Freedland is admiring of leaders who make the big statement that defines their term. Those he mentions are a mixed bag. Nye Bevan was right with the NHS, as was Harold Wilson with the Open University, but was Margaret Thatcher with right to buy? All that happened was house price inflation, unfair property windfalls and many of those properties ending up in the avaricious hands of private landlords.As for Gordon Brown’s Bank of England independence, all that happened was that monetary policy and fiscal policy got separated into ghettoes with no effect on boom or bust. In the 10 years from 1997 to 2007, high Bank rates had no effect in damping down the party, while in the decade from 2010 to Covid, the Bank rate at 0.5% or lower had absolutely no effect in getting the economy anywhere near to normal levels of growth. Might it be a better idea if politicians had a longer think about their headline policies? Headlines one day, fish and chip wrappers the next.David RedshawSaltdean, East SussexAndy Burnham’s bus fare cap rang a bell for me: the South Yorkshire equivalent was reduced fares to 10p for adults and 2p for children in the early 1980s. Little things have long shadows: in Sheffield, almost half a century later, it is still mentioned every time we bemoan the parlous, life-limiting, economy-harming state of the privatised buses. Small changes to conserve small change could amount to a radical shift of gear. Hold tight, please.Robin HughesSheffieldIn the late 1940s and 50s, a return bus ticket from Thorne to Doncaster in South Yorkshire, 10 miles each way, was one shilling and 10 old pence. My dad always said we had the cheapest fares in England. This made us feel travel was affordable and encouraged us to go places. We also went to Doncaster, our nearest big town, more frequently, for shopping trips. Cheap public transport spreads the feelgood factor. Expensive transport equals stress and distrust of the provider. So well done, Andy Burnham.Jennifer KennerleyNorwichDear Andy Burnham, please provide Shropshire with a comprehensive bus service so that residents can benefit from the £2 cap on bus fares.Roz ConwayShrewsbury, ShropshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Brief letters: I’m Sorry, I’ll Read That Again | Marmite ice-cream | Obituaries | Natural causes | Vanished plate
Content: ‘As a lifelong depressive, when I heard about Bill’s own battle, I felt sympathy for him and comfort for myself.’Photograph: Ian West/PAView image in fullscreen‘As a lifelong depressive, when I heard about Bill’s own battle, I felt sympathy for him and comfort for myself.’Photograph: Ian West/PABrief lettersBill OddieLettersHow Bill Oddie was a comfort to meI’m Sorry, I’ll Read That Again | Marmite ice-cream | Obituaries | Natural causes | Vanished plateWed 29 Jul 2026 12.09 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.22 EDTShareSad to hear of Bill Oddie’s death (Report, 27 July). He first grabbed my attention in I’m Sorry, I’ll Read That Again, a 1960s radio show with fine comedic talent: John Cleese, Tim Brooke-Taylor, Graeme Garden, David Hatch, Jo Kendall. Bill’s songs were always witty. I remember going to a recording of the show and watching him grapple with the line “He battled with the rollocks”. To a 14-year-old that was hysterical. As a lifelong depressive, when I heard about Bill’s own battle, I felt sympathy for him and comfort for myself.Chris HouseHertfordRegarding the best ice-creams, Lucy Knight awards 5/10 for flavour to the Marmite on toast creation (Scoop of the year!, 28 July). Surely in the case of Marmite, the only appropriate ratings are 10 or zero?Adrian BrodkinLondonRegarding Dr Terry Scragg’s letter on obituaries (27 July), one of the most consistent words used to describe the deceased is “generous”. I long to read “stingy git” – or do they never die?Siobhán Ní ChuanaighDublin, IrelandRe the preponderance of deaths after a “short illness”, the great American clown Palfi used to conclude shows by proffering a collection box to the audience, suggesting they contribute to research into the most dangerous of ailments – “natural causes”.Antony BellekomCollingham, NottinghamshireOn the mystery of the vanished beef joint, the dog and the missing plate (Letters, 28 July), did Jeanette Hamilton check the dishwasher?Paul WrightKing’s Lynn, NorfolkHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Making proportional representation work in Britain | Proportional representation | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Guardian analysis examining what Britain would look like under an electoral system of PR
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Guardian analysis examining what Britain would look like under an electoral system of PR
Content: ‘A helpful view on how Britain’s electoral landscape could look under different voting systems.’Composite: The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘A helpful view on how Britain’s electoral landscape could look under different voting systems.’Composite: The GuardianProportional representationLettersMaking proportional representation work in BritainReaders respond to Guardian analysis examining what Britain would look like under an electoral system of PRWed 29 Jul 2026 12.09 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.12 EDTShareAntonio Voce and Ashley Kirk’s excellent article (How could Britain look under proportional representation?, 22 July) provides a helpful view on how Britain’s electoral landscape could look under different voting systems.Perhaps most striking is that whichever the proportional representation (PR) system used, when compared with first past the post they all make a good job of producing a parliament that reflects how the nation voted. There is not as much difference between them as enthusiasts of each PR system might expect, in terms of each party winning its fair proportion of seats, and in terms of voters therefore getting a fair say in who governs us.It is also important to emphasise that the numerics of the systems proposed do not have to be as they are in the article’s examples. So using the additional member system does not mean we need to increase our parliament to more than 1,000 MPs. Using a single transferable vote does not mean we have to have constituencies any bigger than, say, four to seven MPs. And party list districts do not have to be as big as the official English regions or the whole of Scotland. PR for Westminster can be designed with MPs much more localised, if that is what the people want.The much-needed new Westminster election system coming our way of course needs to be as good as we can make it. This requires both expert design and legitimacy with the public. If Andy Burnham is as good as his word to date, he will set up aNational Commission on Electoral Reform, as already proposed by theall party parliamentary group for fair elections.Michael BursillReigate, SurreyAntonio Voce and Ashley Kirk note that voters may resist replacing a system they understand. Yet, do they truly understand its absurd outcomes of first past the post? For instance, both Margaret Thatcher in 1983 and Theresa May in 2017 secured exactly 42.4% of the vote.
