Under first past the post, this gave Thatcher a landslide majority of 144, but left May with a minority, reliant on the DUP to form a government.While the additional member system is often touted as a British compromise, it introduces its own flaws. If we are to reform our democracy, the only sensible choice is the single transferable vote (STV). By providing a choice of several constituency MPs, STV forces politicians to compete for our votes, effectively eliminating safe seats and complacency. Crucially, it delivers a truly representative parliament where parties must work together in coalition to govern.Tom BeardWorcester Park, LondonExplore more on these topicsProportional representationElectoral reformFirst past the postAndy BurnhamLabourlettersShareReuse this content

title: Idi Amin’s grandson disqualified from Commonwealth Games boxing for head-butt | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: The Commonwealth Games debut of Idi Amin’s grandson ended in disgrace after Aziz Abdul was disqualified for head-butting Damar Thomas in the boxing
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The Commonwealth Games debut of Idi Amin’s grandson ended in disgrace after Aziz Abdul was disqualified for head-butting Damar Thomas in the boxing
Content: Aziz Abdul (left) was disqualified for head-butting Damar Thomas.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAziz Abdul (left) was disqualified for head-butting Damar Thomas.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026Idi Amin’s grandson disqualified from Commonwealth Games boxing for head-buttAziz Abdul disqualified for ‘Glasgow kiss’ in third roundUgandan boxer: ‘Why can’t they let this fight continue?’Sean Ingleat SEC CentreWed 29 Jul 2026 18.12 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 18.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheCommonwealth Gamesdebut of Idi Amin’s grandson ended in ignominy and disgrace as the boxer was disqualified in the third round for head-butting his English opponent – and then launched a bitter verbal assault on the referee.Things then took an even more bizarre turn as Aziz Abdul, a 25-year-old from Uganda, refused to speak to a journalist afterwards because of what he had writtenabout the tyrannical dictator.Madias Ngake’s real-life movie script ends with weightlifting silver for EnglandRead more“No, not you,” Abdul told the man from the Press Association. “I don’t like you.” A Ugandan team official quickly clarified: “It is because of the things you said about his grandad.”Amin is estimated to have killed half a million people in Uganda after coming to power in a coup d’état in 1971, and also forced the expulsion of 80,000 people of Asian descent.However, Abdul insisted before his super-heavyweight fight with the 21-year-old Damar Thomas from Kilburn that his grandfather’s achievements “had inspired me” and “I am so proud of him”.Abdul, who is alsoknown as Aziz Ringoafter his self-titled signature punch, also promised he would be “the new king of Scotland” – after his grandfather had offered to liberate the Scots from England. However, the most Scottish thing about Abdul proved to be the Glasgow kiss he planted on Thomas when he was 20-16 down on the scorecards. Afterwards he complained, without foundation, that the decision was unfair.Afterwards Abdul complained that the decision was unfair. “There were a lot of fouls,” he said. “Holding, elbowing, a lot of bullshit. The officials cannot judge them. When other countries do this they are disqualified. All I can say about this is the referee’s decision is not right and I am not happy.”View image in fullscreenAziz ‘Ringo’ was critical of the referee’s ruling in his contest.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianAbdul also criticised the referee for ruling that he had been knocked down in the first round, after taking a punch. “He took a light punch and they counted,” he said. “I landed a heavy punch on him and they deducted my points and warned me. I’m a black African, I know. It’s God’s plan. I don’t know why the officials are scared about this fight. Why can’t they let this fight continue?”He also insisted he had not deliberately head-butted his opponent. “He got me with the elbow,” he said. “It was not intentional because I was trying to come back. How can I head-butt someone? I would not head-butt someone.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“When I was still in Uganda, I said I must win by knockout. It’s an away match for me here. Next time I must end the fight in the first minute.”“Next time, I will get him,” he added. “Anytime in the future. Two years, five years, 10 years. I will show him that Aziz Ringo is a real warrior. It’s so painful.”Thomas, meanwhile, is now guaranteed a medal after a wild fight with plenty of haymakers and very little quality work. “I got the job done, not how I wanted to, but the job is done,” he said. “He was running at me with his head. There was a bit of ring rust from me but it is what it is.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026BoxingCommonwealth GamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Madias Ngake’s real-life movie script ends with weightlifting silver after sleeping rough | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Madias Nagake, who gave up elite sport for more than a decade after representing Cameroon, said: ‘I never believed that I would ever be here’
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Madias Nagake, who gave up elite sport for more than a decade after representing Cameroon, said: ‘I never believed that I would ever be here’
Content: Madias Ngake said ‘I never believed that I would ever be here’ after her silver medal in the women’s 87kg competition.Photograph: François Nel/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMadias Ngake said ‘I never believed that I would ever be here’ after her silver medal in the women’s 87kg competition.Photograph: François Nel/Getty ImagesCommonwealth Games 2026Madias Ngake’s real-life movie script ends with weightlifting silver after sleeping roughNgake left Cameroon due to homosexuality lawsShe fled from London 2012 village and slept on streetsSean Ingleat the SEC ArmadilloWed 29 Jul 2026 17.57 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 17.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirst Madias Ngake lifted the weight of an upright piano to her shoulders. Then, with another staggering act of power and defiance, she sent a 128kg barbell high above her head.And, just like that, the 34-year-old Team England weightlifter had won a silver medal and written one of the most remarkable stories of these Games.Fourteen years ago, Ngake fled the London 2012 Olympic village after finishing sixth in her competition and ended up sleeping rough for a month.Ramsay-Peaty ends Commonwealth Games career with silver for England in medley relayRead moreThe reason? She was competing for Cameroon, where homosexuality is illegal, and someone in the team had found out that she was a lesbian. And so began a journey that led to Ngake giving up elite sport for more than a decade, deciding to come back in 2023, and then transferring allegiances to Britain a year later.“When I left the Olympics in 2012 I got on a bus,” she explained. “After the last stop, they told me this is closed, so I can’t go anywhere. So I decided I will sleep outside at the bus stop. I slept rough for about a month. Nobody looked after me.“I had to leave because someone on the team knew about my situation, that I am a lesbian.”But having won a European medal earlier this year, Ngake showed her strength as she led the women’s 87kg competition after the first event, the snatch, with a powerful lift of 108kg.That put her 3kg clear of Australia’s Eileen Cikamatana. However in the clean and jerk, Cikamatana was able to thrust a barbell 140kg over her head like it was a rag doll to score a combined lift of 245kg – a new Games record – to take gold by 6kg.View image in fullscreenEileen Cikamatana with her gold medal, flanked by Madias Ngake (left) and the bronze medallist Rose Beaudoin of Canada.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPBut Ngake was not too disappointed afterwards. Asked if her life was like a movie, she replied: “Yes. And I never believed I would ever be here.”Ngake’s hair was dyed red, the colour of her home country. Afterwards she said that it had been the idea of Emily Campbell, Team GB’s double Olympic medallist, who competes on Thursday.Ngake also explained it was only after 2017 that she was legally able to work. She was an office cleaner in Leeds for nine years, earning about £2,000 a year. However she has recently moved to Nottingham to train as a full-time athlete and hopes to make the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.Amazingly, if she were to win an Olympic medal, it would be her second one. That’s because in 2019, she was awarded a bronze medal from London 2012 after three weightlifters who finished above her at the Games were disqualified for doping offences.However, as the medal was sent to Cameroon, Ngake has never seen it as she has not been back to her home country. “I would like to have it, yes,” she explained. “But I don’t think it’s going to be possible because the medal is in Cameroon and there is a situation and I don’t want to do politics.”But Ngake knows how to do medals. And her adopted country was certainly delighted on Wednesday night.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesWeightliftingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ramsay-Peaty ends his Commonwealth Games with silver for England in medley relay | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Adam Ramsay-Peaty’s Commonwealth Games ended with a silver medal as England were beaten by Australia’s swimmers in the 4x100m medley relay
Author: Yara El-Shaboury
Headline: Adam Ramsay-Peaty’s Commonwealth Games ended with a silver medal as England were beaten by Australia’s swimmers in the 4x100m medley relay
Content: England’s (from left) Jacob Mills, Oliver Morgan, Adam Ramsay-Peaty and Edward Mildred celebrate winning silver in the medley relay.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/ReutersView image in fullscreenEngland’s (from left) Jacob Mills, Oliver Morgan, Adam Ramsay-Peaty and Edward Mildred celebrate winning silver in the medley relay.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/ReutersCommonwealth Games 2026Ramsay-Peaty ends his Commonwealth Games with silver for England in medley relayEngland second behind Australia in 4x100m medleyScotland win silver in women’s 4x100m medley relayYara El-Shabouryat Tollcross International Swimming CentreWed 29 Jul 2026 18.11 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 17.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter six days of Australian dominance in the pool, the swimming programme at Glasgow 2026 came to a close in familiar fashion as the green and gold claimed one final victory after finishing with an extraordinary 37 gold, 16 silver and 23 bronze medals in the water. The closing race also produced a slice ofCommonwealth Gameshistory as South Africa’s bronze in the men’s 4x100m medley relay earned Chad le Clos a record-breaking 21st Commonwealth Games medal, making him the most decorated athlete in the competition’s history.Adam Ramsay-Peaty, meanwhile, bowed out of the Games with a silver medal after England finished runners-up to Australia in the final swimming event. Australia surged through the second half of the race to secure gold in a Games record of 3min 28.71sec, while England’s quartet of Oliver Morgan, Ramsay-Peaty, Edward Mildred and Jacob Mills claimed silver in 3:30.68 after holding off South Africa.Madias Ngake’s live movie script ends with weightlifting silver for EnglandRead moreMorgan gave England a strong start with a 53.20 opening leg before Ramsay-Peaty kept them in second with a 58.74 split. Mildred slipped briefly to third on the third leg despite clocking 51.04, before Jacob Mills produced a 47.70 anchor to haul England back into second.“To come in with the boys and get a silver medal, I can’t complain whatsoever,” said Morgan. “It’s my fifth of the week. Some of us have had tough weeks but it shows the resilience we’ve had in the team. I’ve not had the best week individually, so to come away with some silverware is really impressive. It’s about building on that, moving into next season and into LA [2028 Olympics].”In the penultimate race, Scotland rounded off their memorable night with a silver medal in the women’s 4x100m medley relay after coming out in kilts as Australia stormed to gold in another record time.“It’s absolutely amazing,” said Katie Shanahan. “I’m sure I can speak for all of us when I say there’s no better way to finish off a home meet than by getting that silver medal. It’s just been such an amazing meet, and it’s a week I’ll definitely remember for the rest of my life.”“It’s something we save for the last night,” said Evelyn Davis on walking out with kilts on. “Katie’s falling off in the walkout actually calmed my nerves a bit before the crowd got going again, so it was good fun.”View image in fullscreenAdam Ramsay-Peaty finished the Commonwealth Games with a silver in the medley relay.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/ReutersRoared on by a vocal crowd, Shanahan, Angharad Evans and Keanna MacInnes battled for the lead throughout before Davis produced a composed anchor leg to hold off South Africa and Canada to secure second place. Australia, who had qualified more than four seconds faster than the field, lived up to their billing as favourites as Iona Anderson, Sienna Toohey, Alex Perkins and Meg Harris powered to gold, while South Africa snatched bronze ahead of Canada in the closing stages.Earlier Evans had delighted the home support by winning a second breaststroke gold of the Games. The 23-year-old followed up her 100m breaststroke triumph by winning the women’s 200m breaststroke, holding off a late charge from South Africa’s Kaylene Corbett to seal victory by 0.67. Northern Ireland’s Ellie McCartney completed the podium with bronze.“It’s been absolutely unreal,” Evans said. “With the 100m I put too much pressure on myself because that’s what I see as my main event. The 200m feels even more special because afterwards I had all these doubts: did I only win the 100m because it was a fluke? Did I just get lucky? As crazy as that sounds. To back it up with not just another medal but another gold is just so surreal.”The evening had begun with another statement performance from South Africa’s Pieter Coetze, who retained his men’s 100m backstroke crown in emphatic fashion. He clocked a Commonwealth Games record of 51.77 – just 0.17 outside the world record – to collect his third gold medal in Glasgow after winning the 50m and 200m backstroke titles. England’s Morgan claimed silver, while Coetze’s compatriot Ruard van Renen secured bronze.Australia also dominated the sprint events, with clean sweeps in the women’s 50m freestyle and men’s 50m butterfly. Harris led home her teammates Perkins and Shayna Jack, taking bronze in the final race of her career, in the women’s event. The Welsh teenager Theodora Taylor was fourth. In the men’s butterfly, Kyle Chalmers and Ben Armbruster shared gold after both broke the Games record with identical times of 22.7. Cameron McEvoy took bronze.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesSwimmingAdam Ramsay-PeatynewsShareReuse this content

title: Uefa calls emergency meeting as opposition to Fifa plan hardens | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Uefa’s 55 members will meet on Thursday afternoon to discuss a coordinated response to Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Uefa’s 55 members will meet on Thursday afternoon to discuss a coordinated response to Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup
Content: Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors has drawn widespread criticism.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino’s plan to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors has drawn widespread criticism.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAFifaUefa calls emergency meeting as opposition to Fifa plan hardens55 members to meet on Thursday to coordinate response‘Uefa knows there is significant and growing opposition’Matt HughesandNick AmesWed 29 Jul 2026 15.07 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 18.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUefa has called an emergency ­meeting of its 55 members for Thursday afternoon to discuss a coordinated response to Gianni Infantino’splan to sell off stakes in the World Cupto private investors. A European boycott of Fifa tournaments is among the options under consideration.As the next major event in the Fifa calendar, a boycott of next year’s Women’sWorld Cuphas been ­mentioned in preliminary ­discussions, although there would be a reluctance in some quarters to make the women’s game suffer as a consequence of a protest against Fifa proposals that primarily revolve around ­monetising the men’s World Cup and Club World Cup.Infantino’s World Cup plan is part of a desire for expansion that was clear from the start | Paul MacInnesRead moreUefa’s initial condemnation of Fifa’s plan to “sell the soul” of ­football has received strong backing from Concacaf – the North, Central ­American and Caribbean ­confederation – and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC). If their members follow their leads there should be sufficient votes to block the proposal.Those three confederations make up 143 of the 211Fifamembers, but unanimity is not guaranteed, as was made clear when Czechia’s ­football association became the first in Europe to back the plan.Having received more than 200 ­letters of endorsement backing his re-election next year, Infantino is confident he has enough votes – although it is unclear whether the proposal requires a simple ­majority to be passed. Several sources have said that creating a new commercial entity – Fifa Forward Enterprise [FFE] – and selling a 20% stake to investors would necessitate a change of Fifa statutes, which requires a 75% majority that would be much harder to obtain.View image in fullscreenFifa’s branding was impossible to miss during the World Cup.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersOn Wednesday evening, Infantino released a video to address the ­backlash. “FFE is actually a ­proposal, an offer,” he said. “It’s part of a democratic process – a ­consultation process – and, above all, it is an opportunity but not an ­obligation. It is a golden opportunity to turbocharge the development of the game globally.”Earlier, Uefa redoubled its attack on Fifa by accusing the world ­governing body of “using our sport to enrich themselves and their friends” after it emerged that ­Infantino had ­presented members with a deadline of 19 September to decide whether to apply for an ­initial payment of $20m (£15m) from the proposed sell-off.A further $20m for each ­association would also be made available at a later date, although it is unclear whether accepting the money would equate to a formal ­endorsement and therefore remove the need for a vote.Uefa has to show backbone: concrete action can make Fifa’s World Cup plans untenable | Nick AmesRead more“Today we have learned of Fifa’s deadline to associations to support their proposals or have the one-off payout offer withdrawn,” Uefa said. “This says everything you need to know about this plan. But having held discussions with many stakeholders across the game, Uefa knows there is significant and growing opposition to Fifa’s scheme. Fifa cannot continue to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends. We can grow the game correctly. It’s time to prioritise associations, clubs, leagues, players and fans.”Uefa’s second statement of condemnation followed a similarly strong intervention from ­Concacaf, which is particularly ­significant given the confederation has just hosted the most ­lucrative World Cup and covers the region that has brought the proposed new investment from the New York-based Thrive Eternal.The Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, was instrumental in the success of the US, Mexican and Canadian bid for the tournament, but along with the seven other Fifa vice‑presidents and Fifa council members he was kept in the dark over the plans.“Concacaf was only made aware of this matter through media reports and, subsequently, via a media release,” Concacaf said. “We are deeply concerned by the lack of due process.“We share the ­disappointment of many within our region and the game that this level of detail has been designed and shared publicly before any discussion with the ­relevant governance bodies and stakeholders has taken place.“As leaders within football, we are the custodians of the game. Collectively, Fifa, the confederations and every member association have a responsibility to always act in the best interests of the sport. Every decision we make must be guided by good governance, robust processes and long-term stewardship.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino announces Saudi Arabia as the 2034 World Cup hosts. The AFC’s statement is understood to have the backing of the Saudi Arabian federation.Photograph: Fifa“This is the framework within which Concacaf operates. We trust that all within the Fifa family will act in the same manner.”The AFC issued a similar statement of disapproval, which significantly is understood to have the backing of the Saudi Arabian football federation, a close ally of Infantino and the host of the 2034 World Cup.“The AFC was not consulted on the proposal and is disappointed that a matter of such significance entered the public domain before the AFC family had been afforded the opportunity to examine and discuss it through the appropriate and established governance channels,” it said.“While the AFC recognises the importance of exploring innovative approaches that can strengthen the future of global football, initiatives of this scale and consequence must be founded upon the principles of good governance, transparency and meaningful consultation.“Decisions that may reshape the commercial and financial future of the game require comprehensive prior engagement with confederations, member associations and other relevant stakeholders before any proposal is made to the appropriate decision-making bodies.”Elite clubs also expressed their unhappiness, with the European Football Clubs organisation pointing out that Fifa had not consulted it despite the two bodies having signed a memorandum of understanding.“As an institution that represents over 850 football clubs – whose member clubs, their players and communities are fundamental participants in football worldwide, not least in Fifa’s competitions including all the international club competitions – it would be wholly appropriate for EFC to be fully consulted on a proposal of such magnitude,” it said.“EFC learned about this proposal in the same way as most global football stakeholders – without warning and through the media.”Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoWorld CupFootball politicsUefanewsShareReuse this content

title: Stephen Fleming to be appointed England Test coach after impressing ECB | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: Stephen Fleming is to be England’s new Test coach, but he will probably not start until the South Africa tour in December
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: Stephen Fleming is to be England’s new Test coach, but he will probably not start until the South Africa tour in December
Content: Stephen Fleming is a compatriot, former teammate and friend of Brendon McCullum.Photograph: Prakash Singh/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStephen Fleming is a compatriot, former teammate and friend of Brendon McCullum.Photograph: Prakash Singh/Getty ImagesEngland cricket teamStephen Fleming to be appointed England Test coach after impressing ECBNew Zealander will succeed Brendon McCullumLikely to start on South Africa tour in DecemberSimon BurntonWed 29 Jul 2026 15.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 16.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStephen Fleming is expected to be named as England’s Test coach, after impressing the England and Wales Cricket Board in a series of interviews over the past two weeks. The 53-year-old would work alongside his predecessor, compatriot, former teammate and friendBrendon McCullum, who remains in charge of the white-ball teams.Fleming stood down as head coach of the Indian Premier League franchise Chennai Super Kings – as well as their subsidiaries Joburg Super Kings in South Africa’s SA20 and Texas Super Kings in America’s Major League Cricket – this month. That announcement was made after CSK finished eighth out of 10 teams in this year’s IPL, following on from a last-place finish in 2025, but also less than 24 hours afterMcCullum was sacked by the ECBas Test coach.Justin Langer has not heard from ECB about England job but could be temptedRead moreIt is expected Fleming will be in place for the tour of South Africa starting in December, but the three-Test series against Pakistan that begins at Headingley on 19 August may still be overseen by an interim, probably Marcus Trescothick.Fleming has extensive experience of English cricket, not just from playing 10 Tests and 17 ODIs in this country between 1994 and 2004, but also from spells at Middlesex, Yorkshire and Nottinghamshire. He also coached Southern Brave in the Hundred for two years, leaving in 2024.He was approached by England in 2009, shortly after he retired as a player, only to turn them down. “I was flattered to be offered,” he said. “It came down to the fact it wasn’t my time. If I get another couple of years [as a coach] I can see if it is what I want to do and if I would be any good at it.”England ended up turning to Andy Flower, who,having been the early frontrunnerto replace McCullum, has now returned the favour byrejecting the joband opening the door for Fleming’s appointment.Fleming’s relationship with McCullum gave him an advantage over his rivals for the England job, the Australian Tom Moody, the former England batter and Afghanistan coach Jonathan Trott and Richard Dawson, the head coach at Glamorgan.View image in fullscreenNew Zealand’s Brendon McCullum (left) and Stephen Fleming celebrate the wicket of England’s Andrew Strauss in the third Test at McLean Park in Napier in March 2008.Photograph: Ross Setford/APBeyond their friendship, the pair have been business associates at two companies, the software company CricHQ and the export business Quality New Zealand. Daniel Vettori, another former New Zealand captain coaching in England, at Sunrisers Leeds, described the pair as “very good friends” with “a lot of similar traits”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMcCullum made 126 of his 432 international appearances under Fleming’s captaincy before taking over from him and has described him as a major influence. “The way Stephen Fleming led the team tactically was something that really resonated with me,” he said in 2019.“He’s one of my great mates as well now, and what I loved about Stephen Fleming is whilst on the field it looked quite instinctive there was always scores and scores of detail in behind.“The other thing I loved about him was his man management as a leader. It’s very hard to ask players to implement the plans that you have if you don’t understand those players.”Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamBrendon McCullumECBCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Charley Hull shooting for Open glory after multiple near misses at majors | Women's Open | The Guardian
description: Nelly Korda may be a safer bet, but home fans would be thrilled to see Hull triumph after five runner-up finishes
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Nelly Korda may be a safer bet, but home fans would be thrilled to see Hull triumph after five runner-up finishes
Content: Charley Hull lines up a putt. ‘She’s such a great personality,’ Nelly Korda said of the Englishwoman. ‘It would be great for her to do it on kind of home soil.’Photograph: Charlie Crowhurst/R&A/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCharley Hull lines up a putt. ‘She’s such a great personality,’ Nelly Korda said of the Englishwoman. ‘It would be great for her to do it on kind of home soil.’Photograph: Charlie Crowhurst/R&A/Getty ImagesWomen's OpenCharley Hull shooting for Open glory after multiple near misses at majorsNelly Korda may be a safer bet, but home fans would be thrilled to see Hull triumph after five runner-up finishesEwan Murrayat Royal Lytham & St AnnesWed 29 Jul 2026 11.35 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNelly Korda is the likeliest winner of the Women’s Open, but there is no question who would be the most popular. Charley Hull’s brushes with major glory – she has five runner‑up finishes – have only intensified a widespread desire for the 30‑year‑old to break through the tape. Royal Lytham & St Annes provides the latest opportunity for the flamboyant Englishwoman.Korda arrived in Lancashire with half her four major triumphs having come in 2026. Perhaps the Floridian can afford to be generous and she has endorsed Hull’s prospects. “She’s such a great personality,” Korda said. “It would be great for her to do it on home soil, too. She’s an amazing player. I enjoy playing with her. It would be great for the game.”‘Where has that time gone?’: first Women’s Open champion Jenny Lee Smith on 1976 glory, Kevin Keegan and finding her secret twinRead moreHull does not seem the type to be dispirited by close shaves. A year agoshe was pipped by Miyu Yamashita. Hull finished a shot adrift of Korda, the champion, in theUS Women’s Openlast month. “That’s sometimes how she goes,” Korda said. “It’s about putting yourself in that position. You can’t control what others are doing, but she’s doing something right to always be there and be relevant, to be in the hunt.“It’s like Sam Burns. He’s been in the hunt a lot during major championships, hasn’t got it done. Eventually he will. You can’t get discouraged, it has to be encouraging.”History is in Hull’s favour. The last time the Women’s Open visited here, in 2018,England’s Georgia Hall claimed her maiden majorvictory. A scorched links will render this a wonderful test. Korda estimates she will employ her driver five times per round at most, instead adding a four-iron to her armoury.This is also something of a trial run, with the men’s Open due to make a long-awaited return in 2028.Korda is more comfortable than ever at being the name on everyone’s lips. Early in her career, the world No 1 struggled with fame and attention. Having parents who were professional tennis players, a brother who still competes in that domain and a sister who is also on the LPGA Tour has helped with her mindset. So, too, has a frustrating 2025.View image in fullscreen‘I decided that I need to stop getting so frustrated with everything,’ said Nelly Korda. ‘It’s draining having that attitude.’Photograph: Alan Martin/Action Plus/Shutterstock“My family always make sure my batteries are recharged,” she said. “It’s a funny conversation; my dad and my mum are always telling me to take more days off. I’m like: ‘No, no, I don’t want to. I want to grind on my craft.’“There gets a point in the season where I’m really tired. It’s not just golf. It’s not just like the travel. It’s kind of a combination of everything people don’t really see behind the scenes.“My parents are people I go to all the time for advice. My sister, too. She has been at a lot of majors this year. Those are my people. I’m so comfortable and vulnerable with them. They’ve seen every side of me and know me the best.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I decided I need to stop getting so frustrated with everything. I hit a great shot, it goes in a divot and I would get frustrated. What is going on? Why am I getting these bounces? It’s draining having that attitude. I just told myself: ‘I’m not going to have this attitude.’”Lytham stardust also includesLydia Ko, who beat Korda to the Women’s Open titlein 2024. Ko has taken inspiration from her fellow New ZealanderRyan Fox after his Open gloryat nearby Royal Birkdale. Fox became the fourth player from New Zealand to win a major title, reducing Ko to tears as she watched from the west coast of the US.“He’s very humble and I would say he’s your typical Kiwi guy that happens to be a freak athlete,” Ko said. “I went to work out and everywhere I went I was like: ‘Please turn on the Open.’ It ended up not working on the TV so I had my trainer turn it on my cellphone. I can’t remember my workout at all because my whole focus was there.“I took an Uber ride back home. As soon as I got home he was on the 18th and when I saw that drive I was so relieved, but so excited, super pumped.“I screamed when his winning putt went in. I closed the door and I screamed. My husband ran out and was like: ‘What’s happening?’ Ten seconds later, I was crying.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's OpenGolfUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: WSL brings back Sunday evening kick-offs after indifferent viewing figures | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: The move is part of an overhaul of its broadcast strategy after Sunday evening kick-offs were dropped last season after negative feedback from clubs and fans
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The move is part of an overhaul of its broadcast strategy after Sunday evening kick-offs were dropped last season after negative feedback from clubs and fans
Content: The WSL will offer six different TV slots to broadcasters after releasing its fixtures for the 2026-27 campaign.Photograph: Richard Pelham/WSL/The FA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe WSL will offer six different TV slots to broadcasters after releasing its fixtures for the 2026-27 campaign.Photograph: Richard Pelham/WSL/The FA/Getty ImagesWomen's Super LeagueWSL brings back Sunday evening kick-offs after indifferent viewing figuresMove part of an overhaul of its broadcast strategySunday evening games were dropped last seasonExclusive byMatt HughesWed 29 Jul 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 19.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Women’s Super League will bring back Sunday evening kick-offs this season as part of an overhaul of its broadcast strategy after indifferent viewing figures last season.The Guardian has learned that the WSL will offer six different TV slots to broadcasters after releasing its fixtures for the 2026-27 campaign later on Thursday in a significant change from last season, when the majority of televised games took place on Saturday and Sunday lunchtimes.Why Tottenham Women have provided distraction from the gloom of watching men’s team | Mark BurtonRead moreSky Sports, which has the live rights for 163 of the WSL’s 182 games, retains the Saturday 12.45pm slot and noon on Sundays, but has also been given new regular kick-off times of 7pm on Friday and 6pm on Sunday.The BBC will broadcast 19 matches live at 12.30pm on Saturdays and 2.30pm on Sundays.The WSL’s new strategy is to spread games across the weekend after scheduling most fixtures at noon on Sundays last season, with multiple televised matches kicking off at the same time in a move that diluted the audience.The change this seasonfollows a lengthy consultationwith broadcasters, clubs and fans, with the WSL seeking a schedule that maximises its TV audience and matchday attendances.The Sunday evening kick-off was dropped last season after negative feedback from clubs and fans, as attendances were generally poor, but it was popular with broadcasters and was Sky’s best performing slot in 2024-25 with an average audience of 144,000.In an attempt to balance these competing interests, the Sunday evening game will mostly be brought forward 45 minutes to 6pm – with some changes likely to avoid clashes with the 4.30pm Premier League games – while the WSL will attempt to schedule derbies for that slot and Friday evenings where possible.The Guardian revealed last December that the WSL was considering further changes to its kick-off times this season after concern from Sky in particular at some of their viewing figures for lunchtime games.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAn average audience of 59,000 watched Sky’s live coverage of Arsenal’s home win over Liverpool that month, even fewer than the 71,000 people who watched Arsenal v Chelsea on Sky in the same noon kick-off slot the previous month.As well as struggling to attract a casual audience the decision to schedule up to four of the six weekly matches at the same time proved unpopular with the most committed WSL fans, who were unable to watch multiple matches live.Sky are paying the vast majority of the joint £65m broadcast deal with the BBC, who are believed to contribute around £8m in rights fees, so have a significant say but the WSL has consulted widely.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Police take no further action over Polanski sharing Farage guillotine image | Zack Polanski | The Guardian
description: Scotland Yard says threshold not met for criminal action against Green leader, who has refused to apologise to his Reform rival
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Scotland Yard says threshold not met for criminal action against Green leader, who has refused to apologise to his Reform rival
Content: Zack Polanski says sharing an image of a T-shirt showing a guillotine and the words ‘we’re only making plans for Nigel’ was an ‘inadvertent mistake’.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAView image in fullscreenZack Polanski says sharing an image of a T-shirt showing a guillotine and the words ‘we’re only making plans for Nigel’ was an ‘inadvertent mistake’.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAZack PolanskiPolice take no further action over Polanski sharing Farage guillotine imageScotland Yard says threshold not met for criminal action against Green leader, who has refused to apologise to his Reform rivalAletha AduPolitical correspondentWed 29 Jul 2026 15.56 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 02.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo further action will be taken by police afterZack Polanskishared a photo of a man with a T-shirt showing a guillotine and the phrase “we’re only making plans for Nigel”.The Metropolitan police’s decision comes after the Green party leader for England and Wales said he had made an “inadvertent mistake” and would not apologise toNigel Farage.Polanski told the BBC’s Newsnight programme he had accepted a request to collaborate with a photographer on Instagram, with the first photo in a set of 20 showing himself, and the fifth showing the T-shirt.The image was later removed from Polanski’s feed, with the Greens saying the T-shirt was “clearly in poor taste”. Polanski told Newsnight: “As soon as I was aware of what happened, I unaccepted it and took it down.”A Met spokesperson said: “We absolutely understand the reaction to this image being shared online, particularly in the context of increasing threats toward politicians.“While there will be people who will argue that those who shared the image in this Instagram post should be subject to criminal action, our review has concluded that on this occasion, the threshold is not met.”‘Terminally online’: why frustrated Greens want Polanski to hand over his social mediaRead morePolanski repeatedly ruled out apologising to Farage. “If I’d done it deliberately, I’d be apologising,” he said. “But because this was a mistake, I think the important thing is that I point out it’s a mistake, that I also make sure that I condemn political violence and also crucially make a commitment to be better on my social media.”Reform UK had reported Polanski to the Metropolitan police. Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, accused him of “inciting murder”. Farage called for Polanski to be arrested.But the Met said that after“conducting inquiries”it had concluded that it was unlikely that the sharing of the image online would constitute a criminal offence.However, it added that the wearing of the T-shirt should be recorded as a crime and had referred a crime report to Avon and Somerset police, which covers Bristol, where the photo was taken.Writing in the Daily Mail, Farage said Polanski must “face the consequences of his appalling decisions”, adding: “Political violence is real, it is serious, it needs dealing with.”Polanski stressed on Newsnight: “This was not my post, it was a collaboration from a photographer. It had 20 images and I just didn’t look carefully enough and I accepted it.“As soon as I was aware of what happened, I unaccepted it and took it down. I think it would be odd for the police to speak to me about that because I think it’s quite obvious that I’ve not done anything wrong other than making an inadvertent mistake. That being said, if the police do want to talk to me, of course I’m very happy to cooperate.”A Reform UK source told BBC Newsnight: “It’s truly astonishing and quite frankly sickening that Zack Polanski won’t apologise for inciting murder. He admits it was wrong. He admits it’s dangerous, but he still refuses to apologise. Mr Polanski is not fit to lead a national political party.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCriticising Farage’s messaging, Polanski said: “If Nigel Farage wants to apologise for all the times that he’s put other people in danger than I’ll be happy to make an apology.”The work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, when asked about the controversy, said all politicians had “a duty to be careful about what they post”. He said people could make mistakes and it was for the police to decide if any action was needed. “It’s not the first time Zack Polanski has done something like this,” McFadden added.In May,Polanski apologised for sharing a post on X critical of policeafter the Golders Green stabbings. Police were filmed detaining a suspect after two Jewish people were stabbed in the north-west London suburb. Footage of the arrest shared on social media showed two officers appearing to kick the man on or near his head.Polanski retweeted, without comment, a post on X alleging that officers were “repeatedly and violently kicking a mentally ill man in the head” when he was already incapacitated by a stun gun.When challenged on Newsnight over why he chose to appear on television to highlight his mistake but not apologise, Polanski replied: “They’re different mistakes. This time I’ve inadvertently accepted something and as soon as I’ve realised I’ve corrected it. They’re different things.”One national opinion poll this week showed the Greens’ score falling by three percentage points, while a second showed the party holding at 13%, well above the level before Polanski became leader last September.AGreen partyspokesperson said: “The police have examined the evidence and concluded that no crime was committed. This was obvious from the start, as was the fact that Reform were always using this as a political football for their own cynical purposes to distract from questions about their own dodgy donations.”Explore more on these topicsZack PolanskiGreen partyNigel FarageReform UKnewsShareReuse this content

title: Two people accuse Epstein of sexual conduct at Michigan fine arts school | Jeffrey Epstein | The Guardian
description: Report on Interlochen Center for the Arts details sexual allegations against 47 faculty and staff members since 1950s
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Report on Interlochen Center for the Arts details sexual allegations against 47 faculty and staff members since 1950s
Content: Jeffrey Epstein, in a 28 March 2017 photo provided by the New York State Sex Offender Registry.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenJeffrey Epstein, in a 28 March 2017 photo provided by the New York State Sex Offender Registry.Photograph: APJeffrey EpsteinTwo people accuse Epstein of sexual conduct at Michigan fine arts schoolReport on Interlochen Center for the Arts details sexual allegations against 47 faculty and staff members since 1950sAssociated PressWed 29 Jul 2026 15.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 18.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo people who attended a prestigious Michigan fine arts school reported conduct of a sexual nature byJeffrey Epstein, a major donor, according to an investigation that also uncovered dozens of allegations spanning decades against nearly 50 other people.Interlochen Center for the Arts operates a summer camp and performing arts school that draws students from around the world. It hired a law firm in 2024 to investigatereports of sexual abuseby faculty and staff. Subsequently, it expanded the work to include information about Epstein, the 66-year-old financier who killed himself in jail in 2019.Interlochenremoved Epstein’s namefrom a lodge after he was convicted of sex offenses inFlorida in 2008. The building, renamed the Green Lake Lodge, was recently demolished after the US justice department released millions of pages about him that had been compiled over the years.Sanghavi law office says it collected 70 accounts from alumni alleging “physical conduct of a sexual nature” by 47 faculty and staff members affiliated with Interlochen from the 1950s through the 2010s, most before 2000.“The information gathered during this investigation is, simply, devastating,” the 97-page report says, noting that alumni reported grooming, flirting, sexual touching and sex.Blanche-led DoJ likely to derail Epstein survivors’ pursuit of justice, experts sayRead moreInterlochen said it has provided names of people accused of misconduct to Grand Traverse county authorities in northernMichiganto determine what steps, if any, might be taken. None are currently employed there and more than a third are dead.“We are deeply sorry for the harm experienced by members of our community and extend our apologies to those impacted by abuse at Interlochen,” president Trey Devey and board chair Barrett Rollins said in a letter to the community posted online.“While the vast majority of the incidents described in the investigation took place many decades ago, and reports of abuse at Interlochen have significantly decreased over the past 25 years, the passage of time does not diminish the experiences of our alumni,” they said. “Sexual abuse committed by an adult in a position of power or trust against a student is wrong, then and now.”Interlochen today “is fundamentally different from the institution described in this report”, Devey and Rollins wrote, with comprehensive safety policies and a changed culture.Epstein, who played the bassoon, was an Interlochen camper in 1967. He donated more than $400,000 to the school between 1990 and 2003.Two women told investigators that Epstein engaged in conduct of a sexual nature with them, one of them at the Interlochen lodge that bore his name.He brushed against her body “over her clothes, in a manner in which he indicated was accidental”, according to the report.Epstein also paid for her to visit him in New York while she was a student. She said “every time he was ‘handsy’ with her, she would freeze until he would stop”, the report states.The other woman said she gave Epstein a massage at his home, according to the report, and he may have asked her to remove her top. She never had any further contact with Epstein or his girlfriend,Ghislaine Maxwell.Outside of the school investigation, at least two Interlochen alumnae made allegations of grooming and abuse against Epstein and Maxwell, according to federal records and media reports. Their identities were not made public.One testified against Maxwell in 2021 when she was convicted of sex trafficking. It is unclear whether those women spoke to the law firm hired for the Interlochen investigation.Explore more on these topicsJeffrey EpsteinGhislaine MaxwellMichiganUS educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Prince Harry and co-claimants face huge legal bill due to insurance shortfall | Prince Harry | The Guardian
description: Claimants’ cover might not meet Associated Newspapers’ costs for defending phone-hacking case, high court hears
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Claimants’ cover might not meet Associated Newspapers’ costs for defending phone-hacking case, high court hears
Content: Prince Harry at the high court in London last January.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APView image in fullscreenPrince Harry at the high court in London last January.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APPrince HarryPrince Harry and co-claimants face huge legal bill due to insurance shortfallClaimants’ cover might not meet Associated Newspapers’ costs for defending phone-hacking case, high court hearsCaroline DaviesWed 29 Jul 2026 11.17 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Duke of Sussex and his co-claimants could be millions of pounds out of pocket afterlosing their privacy case against the publishers of the Daily Mail, the high court in London heard.The seven claimants, who include Prince Harry, Doreen Lawrence and Elton John, suedAssociated NewspapersLimited over allegations of unlawful information gathering.Their claims were dismissed in their entirety by Mr Justice Nicklin on 7 July and now their insurance may not cover the costs incurred by ANL in defending the case.In a two-day hearing beginning on Wednesday to determine how costs should be paid, the court heard there was a shortfall between the £16.2m insurance cover the claimants had, and ANL’s reported costs of £34.5m.Lawyers for ANL say the claimants should pay its costs on an indemnity basis, under which the losing party covers the other side’s costs without the need to show that those costs are proportionate.ANL is asking for an interim £9,950,624.37 payment. The claimants have offered an £8m interim payment.Antony White KC, for ANL, argued that the claimants’ conduct justified costs on an indemnity, rather than standard, basis, and said the allegations were “of the broadest scope and utmost seriousness”.They alleged misconduct including “serious wrongdoing amounting in many cases to criminal conduct” against no fewer than 77 journalists, editors and executives, although only 23 were involved in the claims. Some allegations were unceremoniously abandoned at trial “without any apology or even acknowledgment”.White said the legal action was part of a “campaign” to demonstrate ANL had “misled the Leveson inquiry”, using high-profile individuals to persuade the government to implement the second part of the inquiry.The allegations were pursued to the “bitter end”, with the proceedings seen as the “vanguard”, or first wave of cases, before a “banquet of litigation” in a strategy to swamp ANL with other potential claims, he said.The strategy was such that, even if the full panoply of allegations were not proved, any finding against ANL would be a “catastrophe” for theDaily Mailpublisher, White added.The claimants, who includedDavid Furnish, Sadie Frost, Liz Hurley and Simon Hughes, cast a “strikingly wide” net for their claim “in the hope of catching some fish”.White said he was sad to say that Lawrence, the mother of the murdered teenager Stephen Lawrence, was recruited to the case by Harry as a “national treasure” to garner public sympathy and give the claims the necessary degree of credibility. “That is a matter of regret for my client, but it is not to be shrunk from,” he said.White pointed to the statement, issued by Harry and Lawrence after the 11-week trial, which attacked the judge and called the 426-page ruling a “complete and obvious whitewash”.Nicholas Bacon KC, for the claimants, said in written submissions that the judge should not award ANL its costs on the stricter, indemnity basis, adding that the incurred costs as of this month were nearly £34.5m, which “exceed its approved budget” by more than £18.6m.It reflected “an astonishingly high legal spend” by ANL and an “entirely cavalier” and “no expense spared” approach, overriding the principle of proportionality that seeks to ensure parties are on an equal footing.The claimants had obtained insurance cover of a combined £16.2m. “At that level of cover, the claimants would reasonably expect to be insured for the total of Associated’s incurred costs and approved estimated costs.”He told the court ANL had increased its legal spend “without telling us”, and had previously told the court its spend would be £20m.He said that the group had “conducted themselves honestly and in good faith”. Referring to the post-trial statement by Harry and Lawrence, he said “The costs to be ordered at this hearing concern the action itself, not the reaction to it.”ANL argued the costs had been incurred during the four-year legal battle and 11-week trial.Bacon said ANL knew what adverse costs the claimants had insured themselves for, and there was no suggestion its costs were anything like what it was now seeking until it disclosed last Friday that its total spend was £34.5m. “They have left us in a world where we are uninsured,” he told the judge.All the claimants had entered the litigation in “good faith”, Bacon said. While the court dismissed their claims, it did not make any findings against them of “dishonesty or lack of sincerity in belief”.“They accept they have lost and costs should follow the event.” Bacon said. But ANL wished to take that further and had stated publicly that it intends to “go for the jugular” in the costs hearing, he added.The hearing continues.Explore more on these topicsPrince HarryDoreen LawrenceDaily MailAssociated NewspapersDaily Mail & General TrustNational newspapersNewspapersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Saltburn suspend fielder accused of cheating in ‘Clicky Ponting’ furore | Cricket | The Guardian
description: Saltburn have said the player from viral video ‘will not play again in foreseeable future’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Saltburn have said the player from viral video ‘will not play again in foreseeable future’
Content: Saltburn said they are cooperating with the League’s investigation.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSaltburn said they are cooperating with the League’s investigation.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianCricketSaltburn suspend fielder accused of cheating in ‘Clicky Ponting’ furore‘Will not play again in foreseeable future’Club concede Wednesday’s second-team cup fixturePA MediaWed 29 Jul 2026 14.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 17.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaltburn Cricket Club have said they are treating allegations of cheating very seriously and have suspended the player at the centre of the controversy for the “foreseeable future”. A Saltburn fielder was accused ofclicking his fingers to get a catch behindand footage of several incidents later went viral on social media.The first video, posted on Monday evening, was from Saltburn’s second XI victory over Norton in Division Two of North Yorkshire and South DurhamCricketLeague. It showed the fielder clicking his fingers as the ball passed the bat of the Norton batter, Noman Shabir, before being caught by the wicketkeeper, Josh Bowes, and the umpire gave him out.‘Saltburn are the Argentina of local cricket’: victims and neighbours on the ‘Clicky Ponting’ scandalRead moreSaltburn, who sit 17 points clear at the top of the table, won the match by 159 runs and announced they have conceded their second-team cup fixture against Marton on Wednesday.A statement on Saltburn’s social media channels read: “This is issued in response to the widely publicised complaint made against a Saltburn Cricket Club member and, as a consequence, against the club more generally.“We are treating this allegation with the utmost seriousness and, as a family-centric club, we are fully cooperating with the NYS League’s investigation.“We believe that the club acted decisively as soon as the complaint and investigation were made known to us. The player at the centre of the complaint has been suspended and will not play again for the club this season or in the foreseeable future, pending the outcome of this investigation.Cricket player seems to show fielder tricking umpire by clicking to imitate edges“Initial discussions have already taken place between club officials and the league.“This has been a very distressing and stressful experience for all those concerned, and we would ask that this reality is borne in mind and that personal boundaries are respected, as we are an amateur club entirely run by volunteers.”The video has now had more than 7.5m views on X, with several celebrities condemning the behaviour.Explore more on these topicsCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Organic eggs have worse impact on climate than eggs from caged chickens | Environment | The Guardian
description: Adopting organic free-range model in UK could lead to greenhouse emissions equivalent to 2,316,000 tonnes of CO2, study suggests
Author: Damien Gayle
Headline: Adopting organic free-range model in UK could lead to greenhouse emissions equivalent to 2,316,000 tonnes of CO2, study suggests
Content: Organic free-range production also scored worst in its potential for water eutrophication, acidification and land use.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOrganic free-range production also scored worst in its potential for water eutrophication, acidification and land use.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesEnvironmentOrganic eggs have worse impact on climate than eggs from caged chickensAdopting organic free-range model in UK could lead to greenhouse emissions equivalent to 2,316,000 tonnes of CO2, study suggestsDamien GayleWed 29 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOrganic eggs are twice as bad for the climate as eggs from chickens living in cages, research suggests.According to the study, switching the UK’s entire egg production to an organic free-range model would lead to greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to 2,316,000 tonnes of CO2 (tCO2e), while production through a fully caged system would emit 1,184,000 tCO2e.This is because organic free-range models need more chickens for the same number of eggs produced, as birds living in cages tend to be more efficient.Organic free-range production also scored worst in its potential for water eutrophication, acidification and land use. Chicken mortality was also highest in organic free range farming, the researchers said.However, the study used data from 2009-2010, which the researchers acknowledged as a limitation as it did not capture more recent developments in egg production. The research also did not take into account other environmental impacts such as pesticides or biodiversity.Laying hens are the largest group of animals kept in cages across the world, and global egg consumption is going up, making their treatment an important welfare consideration, said Dr Harriet Bartlett, one of the authors of the study.“I’d say perhaps it’s also a little bit of a blind spot when we talk about sustainability,” she added. “Meat and dairy get a bit more attention, talking about environmental sustainability, whereas [egg production] hasn’t been as researched.”Bartlett is the senior research associate at Oxford University’s Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment, and haspreviously studied factory farming methods.The latest study,publishedin Royal Society Open Science, involved Bartlett and colleagues examining data from UK poultry farms to calculate environmental impacts such as greenhouse gas emissions, land use and types of pollution. They also looked at welfare indicators such as mortality and the number of hens needed to produce a given number of eggs.“Then we did some some modelling to work out these environmental and welfare outcomes,” she said.“We found an important trade-off,” Bartlett added. “It’s that, the types of farms that are generally regarded as being better for animal welfare, like organic and free-range, can actually require more birds to produce the same amount of eggs because they’re less less efficient and they can have higher environmental impacts.”However, Bartlett said the research did not show the whole picture regarding factory farming. “Organic could come out better on pesticide toxicity, maybe biodiversity on farm as well,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLee Holdstock, the head of regulatory and trade affairs at Soil Association Certification, who was not involved in the study, said the research “highlights some important trade-offs” but gave an “incomplete picture of environmental impact”.“While intensive systems can have lower emissions per unit of output because birds use feed more efficiently, this reflects only one part of the picture,” Holdstock said. “A truly sustainable food system must also consider impacts on nature, soil health, water quality, the use of synthetic inputs, and animal welfare.”The researchers estimated that 1,439,000 tCO2e is emitted under the current regime, in which egg production is split between caged, barn-housed, free-range non-organic and free-range organic systems.One of the Soil Association’s standards for organic eggs is that chickens must have continuous and easy daytime access to an outdoor range covered with suitable vegetation.This article was amended on 29 July 2026 to add further detail about the Soil Association’s standards for organic eggs.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentAnimalsEggsFoodOrganicsEthical and green livingGreenhouse gas emissionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ships stuck in strait of Hormuz pose ‘super-spreader’ biodiversity threat, scientists warn | Strait of Hormuz | The Guardian
description: Biologists say cargo ships stranded in Gulf may carry highly potent invasive species around the world as trade resumes
Author: Matthew Pearce
Headline: Biologists say cargo ships stranded in Gulf may carry highly potent invasive species around the world as trade resumes
Content: Cargo vessels and crude oil tankers anchored in the Gulf of Oman, awaiting the reopening of the strait of Hormuz.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCargo vessels and crude oil tankers anchored in the Gulf of Oman, awaiting the reopening of the strait of Hormuz.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesThe age of extinctionStrait of HormuzShips stuck in strait of Hormuz pose ‘super-spreader’ biodiversity threat, scientists warnBiologists say cargo ships stranded in Gulf may carry highly potent invasive species around the world as trade resumesMiddle East crisis – live updatesThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentMatthew PearceWed 29 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe closure of the strait of Hormuz has created conditions for an extreme global biodiversity threat, with scientists warning that thousands of stranded ships could spread invasive marine species across the world’s oceans once they begin sailing again.More than 1,500 commercial vessels have been stuck in the Gulf since the strategic waterway closed on 28 February after the outbreak of theUS-Israel war on Iran. An international team of marine biologists said that with the stranded ships remaining motionless, their hulls were becoming encrusted with marine life – from microbes and algae to barnacles and other invertebrates – that could hitchhike to ports around the world when trade resumed.Prof Mario Tamburri, of the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science and the study’s lead author, said: “If you had to design the worst-case scenario, I don’t know if you could have done it differently. It is a perfect storm.”The researchdescribes the situation as a potential marine “bio-invasion super-spreader event”, arguing that no previous shipping disruption has involved so many vessels remaining idle for so long.According to the study, ships normally only remain at anchor in a harbour for one to three days, limiting the growth of organisms on their submerged surfaces. But many vessels trapped in the Gulf have remained stationary for months, allowing dense marine communities to establish themselves.If thousands of vessels leave carrying barnacles, algae, mussels and other organisms, they could introduce invasive species that outcompete with native wildlife, spread disease and permanently alter marine ecosystems.“When you move organisms around, they can reduce biodiversity in the regions they invade, cause local extinction of organisms that they displace,” Tamburri said.Invasive species can also devastate fisheries, clog the cooling systems of power plants and cost billions of dollars a year to manage, he added.View image in fullscreenBarnacles on the hull of a fishing boat awaiting repair in a dry dock.Photograph: N James/AlamyThe Gulf is already a hotspot for marine invasions, with previousstudies identifying dozens of non-native speciesintroduced largely by commercial shipping. Researchers said the region’s extreme heat and salinity may make the organisms especially resilient.“They’re pretty hardy. They’re used to extreme environments, high temperatures and high salinities,” Tamburri said. “Those hardy organisms that can often withstand those extreme environments make really good invaders.”Tamburri said regions with similarly warm, salty conditions were most under threat. “Ports that have very similar environments to the Gulf region are probably the highest risks,” Tamburri said, highlighting India and Singapore among the locations where authorities should be on alert.The study said individual ships may have already released millions of larvae into Gulf waters during the months-long lay-up. As shipping resumes, organisms in ballast water, as well as parasites and pathogens in “biofouling communities” that colonise ships’ hulls, could spread rapidly through the global shipping network.Tamburri urged governments and shipping companies to inspect and clean ships before they leave the Gulf wherever possible, while ports expecting arrivals should increase monitoring for invasive species and establish rapid-response plans.Drawing a comparison with public health, Tamburri said the response should mirror efforts to contain infectious diseases. “Early detection is really important – prevention before you move around is really important,” he said.“In a lot of ways, it is like tracking flu or Covid. You want to be prepared for it, detect it early. If you find something, manage it right away.”‘It’s an open invasion’: how millions of quagga mussels changed Lake Geneva for everRead moreA spokesperson from the International Maritime Organization said: “Biofouling can be a key vector for transfer of invasive aquatic species. There is a risk of transfer of species if ships are unable to remove fouling before moving out of an area, after a prolonged period of time in one area. The IMO recommends that ship operators follow theIMO biofouling guidelinesas far as possible.“The IMO is currently developing a standalone legally binding instrument for the control and management of ships’ biofouling to minimise the transfer of invasive aquatic species.”Referring to ecosystems such as coral reefs, seagrass meadows and oyster beds, Tamburri said: “If authorities fail to act, some of the world’s most valuable marine habitats could suffer lasting damage.“Some of those are likely to be impacted and perhaps damaged beyond repair,” he said, calling it a “super-spreader version” of the way ships already transported invasive species around the world.While human safety had to remain the priority, Tamburri asked governments not to lose sight of the environmental risks. “Conflicts like this are horrible,” he said. “There’s human suffering, but we can’t ignore the environmental consequences, either.”Explore more on these topicsStrait of HormuzThe age of extinctionShipping industryBiodiversityMarine lifeConservationWildlifeInvasive speciesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Caribbean bears brunt of £43bn climate-fuelled damage to developing islands | Caribbean | The Guardian
description: Findings can inform conversations about global climate reparations and financing for mitigations, researchers say
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: Findings can inform conversations about global climate reparations and financing for mitigations, researchers say
Content: Report also highlights devastating impact of Hurricane Melissa, which tore through Jamaica in October 2025.Photograph: Raquel Cunha/ReutersView image in fullscreenReport also highlights devastating impact of Hurricane Melissa, which tore through Jamaica in October 2025.Photograph: Raquel Cunha/ReutersCaribbeanCaribbean bears brunt of £43bn climate-fuelled damage to developing islandsFindings can inform conversations about global climate reparations and financing for mitigations, researchers sayNatricia Duncanin KingstonWed 29 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCaribbean nations suffered $53.2bn (£40bn) of damage from climate-fuelled disasters between 2000 and 2024, research into the cost of the climate crisis to developing small islands has found.The figure is more than 90% of the total $57bn in economic damage caused by floods, storms and drought across 39 developing island nations in the Caribbean, the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, according to astudy by development thinktank ODI Global.ODI Global also estimates the climate crisis caused more than 190 deaths a year over the 25-year period studied.The research is important for conversations about global climate reparations, the report’s author, Emily Wilkinson, said.The Caribbean has been pursuing climate justice after bearing the brunt of the crisis, which is primarily caused by high carbon emitters outside the region.Several Caribbean countries provided evidence to the international court of justice, the world’s top UN court, in a case thatended last year with a landmark advisory opinionthat could mean states are ordered to pay compensation if they fail to tackle fossil fuels and prevent harm to the climate system.Wilkinson said: “There have always been hurricanes, heavy rainfall, drought and temperature extremes, historically, but it’s really important to be able to say what percentage of that kind of strength or intensity is actually due to increasing global temperatures.“Climate scientists do theseattribution studiesand they’re really important for when we start to think about responsibilities for the impacts of climate change, compensation and climate reparation.“[They] tell you what kind of proportion of the intensity of the event is due to climate change. We’ve taken it a step further by doing an additional calculation, which is a fraction of attributable risk, to work out what percentage of the damage that’s been reported can be attributed to climate change.”View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of Hurricane Melissa, which hit Jamaica in October 2025 and which experts say was supercharged by global heating.Photograph: Ina Sotirova/The GuardianPublished on Wednesday, the report also highlights the devastating impact ofHurricane Melissa, which tore through Jamaica in October 2025 with winds of 185mph (298 km/h), the strongest ever recorded in the country.Experts say the storm was supercharged by global heating. The report attributes $9.7bn – about 80% of the $12.2bn of the government’s calculated damage and losses – directly to the climate crisis. This figure is almost half of the country’s total economy and far above commitments to the UN’s loss and damage fund to help climate vulnerable countries recover from disasters.For Jamaica, it was the second year in a row that brutal storms caused widespread damage, after 2024’sHurricane Beryl. Thousands of people were left without homes, livelihoods, communication services and basic utilities such as water and power.As climate losses escalate, ODI says that international financing for climate crisis mitigation and adaptation is moving in the wrong direction as some wealthy nations cut contributions.Government agencies and service providers in countries such as Jamaica have had to rethink their operations.In May,Jamaica’s government passedthe National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority Act to speed up post-disaster rebuilding and improve resilience, and last month its prime minister, Andrew Holness,promised to investin cleaner and cheaper renewable sources such as solar.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor Marcelo Cataldo, the chief executive of Digicel Group, one of the Caribbean’s leading internet and telecoms providers, the worsening climate shocks mean the company needs to rethink how it powers its network.View image in fullscreenA building destroyed by Hurricane Beryl, which swept through Jamaica in 2024. People were left without homes and basic utilities such as water and power.Photograph: Ina Sotirova/The GuardianDigicel has responded by accelerating a major shift to solar energy. The company has partnered with the American renewable energy companyCaban Energyto roll out solar‑powered telecom sites in Jamaica and Barbados, with plans to expand to 15 of its 25 markets.Digicel says their solar systems can generate 15,000MWh of clean energy a year, enough to power 10,000 Caribbean homes. They also avoid approximately 200,000 litres of diesel use annually and cut emissions by 16,457 tonnes of CO₂e – equivalent to removing 3,600 cars from the road.Solar, Cataldo says, is not just more environmentally friendly but also more resilient, allowing communication systems to remain online for longer if a storm knocks out power.“We know that in a big hurricane … the infrastructure of the electricity company will affect us and all the other industries. Having solar is an outstanding alternative to return the service faster to our customers,” Cataldo said.Wilkinson said switching to solar is one solution Caribbean nations could consider to improve resilience, but “they will need to overcome high upfront costs and address issues such as intermittency, storage and grid stability”.For Cataldo, the solution is partnerships with companies such as Caban Energy. “This is the kind of collaboration needed to accelerate the energy transition for our region,” he added.ODI Global’s findings suggest that such adaptations will become increasingly necessary. According to the report, under a 1.5C warming scenario, storms alone could cause a further $49bn in climate‑attributable losses across small island developing nations by 2050. At 2C, that rises to $51bn.Explore more on these topicsCaribbeanExtreme weatherClimate crisisHurricane MelissanewsShareReuse this content

title: Canada’s worst wildfire season fuels calls for national agency to tackle threat | Canada | The Guardian
description: More than 900 fires burning in only G7 country without national emergency agency to coordinate response
Author: Olivia Bowden
Headline: More than 900 fires burning in only G7 country without national emergency agency to coordinate response
Content: Smoke rises from the Bonanza Creek wildfire west of Cache Creek in Canada’s British Columbia on 22 July 2026.Photograph: BC Wildfire Service/ReutersView image in fullscreenSmoke rises from the Bonanza Creek wildfire west of Cache Creek in Canada’s British Columbia on 22 July 2026.Photograph: BC Wildfire Service/ReutersCanadaCanada’s worst wildfire season fuels calls for national agency to tackle threatMore than 900 fires burning in only G7 country without national emergency agency to coordinate responseOlivia Bowdenin TorontoWed 29 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 11.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs more than 900wildfiresburn acrossCanada, prompting evacuation orders and pushing Ontario into itsworst wildfire season on record, officials are renewing calls for the country to develop a national wildfire strategy through the creation of a federal agency.Canada is the only G7 country that does not have a national emergency agency that is mandated to respond to wildfires.After a disastrous July for wildfires thatrazed First Nations communitiesin north-eastern Ontario and sent poisonous smoke southward through the US, the provincial premier, Doug Ford, called for a countrywide response to the wildfire threat.“We need a large national fire strategy. We seem to be going through this every single year,” Ford told reporters.In 2023,Canada’s worst wildfire season on recordburned through a staggering 15m hectares (37m acres) of land, an area larger than England, according to the federal government. That catastrophe prompted the federal government, led then by Justin Trudeau, to consider the creation of a national disaster response agency.Yet such a body was never created. Summer 2024 was another destructive season, now the fourth worst on record. Then, 2025 ended up ranking only behind 2023 as the worst wildfire season in Canadian history, with 8.3m hectares burned.“Never in our modern record have we had three bad fire years,” said Mike Flannigan, a professor of wildland fire at Thompson Rivers University in Kamloops, British Columbia.Climate change, caused by the burning of fossil fuels, has led to warming that is fuelling calamitous fire seasons, he said. A national wildfire strategy through the creation of a federal emergency agency, he said, would help Canada be more prepared.“We definitely need one, and not just for fires, but for floods, earthquakes, hurricanes,” he said.In Canada, provinces and territories are responsible for managing wildfires and the federal government offers support as needed. That’s in contrast to the US which has the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) that organizes the national response to disasters through working with states.
