However, the Fema model is under threat as the Donald Trumpadministration has been accused of castigating the agency and politicizing disaster aid.But in principle, a group like Fema that could quickly alert provinces and territories to resources in advance would help Canada put out fires faster, said Flannigan.AJune reportfrom the Canadian senate also recommended Ottawa create a federal coordinating office for wildfires and emergency response.On Friday, the prime minister, Mark Carney, convened a cabinet-level emergency committee to organize the federal response to the wildfires, but fell short of creating a national wildfire strategy.However, Canada’s ministry of emergency management and community resilience told the Guardian it was considering “the potential creation of a federal emergency management agency”, as it reviews feedback from recent public engagement sessions.The costs of creating such an agency would be offset by the palpable savings that come with preventing community destruction and mitigating the negative health impacts of fires, said Flannigan.“We’re going to see more fire, more smoke and more impacts … that’s our new reality,” he said. “We’re going to have to adapt faster.”Explore more on these topicsCanadaWildfiresnewsShareReuse this content

title: Norwegian teenager guilty of travelling to UK to carry out contract killing | Organised crime | The Guardian
description: Johannes Kongsnes Natland was recruited to murder unknown person by international crime gang linked to Iran
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: Johannes Kongsnes Natland was recruited to murder unknown person by international crime gang linked to Iran
Content: Johannes Kongsnes Natland had agreed to shoot an unidentified victim for €25,000 but was arrested in Huddersfield by armed police.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PAView image in fullscreenJohannes Kongsnes Natland had agreed to shoot an unidentified victim for €25,000 but was arrested in Huddersfield by armed police.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PAOrganised crimeNorwegian teenager guilty of travelling to UK to carry out contract killingJohannes Kongsnes Natland was recruited to murder unknown person by international crime gang linked to IranPriya BharadiaWed 29 Jul 2026 13.02 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Norwegian teenager has been found guilty of travelling to England to carry out a killing ordered by an international crime gang linked to Iran.Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, from Stavanger, Norway, agreed to shoot an unknown person for €25,000 (£21,500) in March last year. Two days after he arrived in the UK armed police arrested him in a hotel room in Huddersfield,West Yorkshire, seizing two guns and ammunition.After deliberating for 17 hours and six minutes, a jury at the Old Bailey found him guilty of conspiracy to murder following a retrial.Photo issued by the Metropolitan police of Johannes Natland wearing gloves while handling a gun.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PANatland blinked but did not visibly react to the verdict. Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb remanded him into custody to be sentenced in October.Natland, who worked part-time in a pizza restaurant, was recruited by the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organised crime group with links to the Iranian government.Natland told jurors he agreed at first to the murder plot in exchange for money to pay for drugs, thinking it was just a “joke” or “scam”.Once he realised he was in a “pickle” with the Foxtrot Network, Natland said he planned to “shoot himself in the foot” to avoid carrying out the assassination.The potential victim of the foiled murder plot has never been identified. The Metropolitan police said their counter-terrorism officers “uncovered a significant amount of evidence demonstrating that Natland was fully aware he was being asked to kill someone in the UK”.“I’m going on crazy mission,” Natland had texted his girlfriend. “It will be a bit cool to kill someone. If I don’t get caught we have to celebrate.”When armed police banged on his hotel room door, Natland emerged from his room smiling, only wearing his boxer shorts, and mimed shooting one of the officers with his empty hands.In a search of his room, officers found a plastic bag under his bed containing a semi-automatic pistol, a revolver and 19 rounds of ammunition.View image in fullscreenNatland mimed shooting an armed officer during his arrest.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PAAt his trial, one of Natland’s friends recalled a conversation where the defendant bragged he was “going to get a lot of money and somebody is going to die”.Natland told jurors these statements were “bravado” and he was secretly “terrified”.“I wasn’t an international assassin,” he said. “I thought people had this impression and expected me to be this guy. I knew I wasn’t.”But jurors heard Natland lied after his arrest and had tried to persuade his girlfriend not to give evidence during his phone calls from prison.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe prosecutor Alistair Richardson said: “The reality is the defendant is a troubled but dangerous young man. A young man who agreed to kill in a foreign country for money.”The court heard that Natland, a talented young footballer, began taking drugs aged 13. He spent a short period of time in a care home, where he first met a teenage member of the Foxtrot Network and was passed on to a recruiter known as “Generalen”.On 17 March 2025, Natland took a flight from Stavanger to Manchester airport on a temporary passport. He was stopped by Border Force officials in Manchester, who bailed him to return to the airport and catch the next direct flight home.Instead, he took a taxi toHuddersfield, where he picked up £2,000 in cash, two guns and bullets, as well as a stolen Nissan with a fake number plate. He was arrested the following day at 5.15am.View image in fullscreenNatland was arrested at a hotel in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, where he had been caught on camera paying in cash.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PANatland was controlled by an English-speaking boss called “Agent 47” – an apparent reference to the Hitman game and movie series – whose identity and whereabouts remain unknown.Despite several high-ranking arrests in recent years, Foxtrot is stillthe dominant gang in Swedenand thought to be responsible for the majority of gang violence in the country including mass shootings and murders across the country.But with many of the gang’s key figures now believed to be fugitive abroad – including the leader, Rawa Majid, known as the Kurdish Fox, who is still at large and believed to be in Iran – the police operation to find them is global. Last year up to 30 of the wanted Swedes who were arrested outsideSwedenhad connections to Foxtrot, according to police.In June, Poya Shafie, described as the person who planned Foxtrot’s murders and who was one of the men closest to Majid, was sentenced to life imprisonment in a Swedish court after being arrested in Iraq.Explore more on these topicsOrganised crimeNorwayHuddersfieldCrimeEuropeWest YorkshireSwedennewsShareReuse this content

title: TfL brings case worth up to £1bn against carmakers over Ulez compliance | Low emission zones | The Guardian
description: Transport for London claims polluting diesel vehicles had been able to enter clean air zone without having to pay
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Transport for London claims polluting diesel vehicles had been able to enter clean air zone without having to pay
Content: TfL’s action had been paused while parallel ‘dieselgate’ ligitation took place.Photograph: Robert Evans/AlamyView image in fullscreenTfL’s action had been paused while parallel ‘dieselgate’ ligitation took place.Photograph: Robert Evans/AlamyLow emission zonesTfL brings case worth up to £1bn against carmakers over Ulez complianceTransport for London claims polluting diesel vehicles had been able to enter clean air zone without having to payGwyn TophamTransport correspondentWed 29 Jul 2026 13.03 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 13.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTransport forLondonis pursuing a potential £1bn legal action against car manufacturers over vehicles that it argues should not have been allowed to drive freely in the capital’s clean-air zone.The high court heard thatTfLwas making allegations of “fraud and negligence” against manufacturers including Stellantis, Jaguar Land Rover, BMW and Nissan over their vehicles’ levels of diesel emissions.The owners of the most polluting cars, largely diesels manufactured more than 11 years ago, have to pay a £12.50 daily charge to enter London’sultra-low emission zone(Ulez), which was launched in 2019 and expanded to cover every borough in the capital in 2024.Lawyers for TfL argue that vehicles, which should have paid a levy had entered the Ulez without charge, depriving TfL of revenue and undermining its attempts to improve air quality.Deaths linked to London air pollution have fallen 40%, study estimatesRead moreLegal action was launched in 2024 but stayed pending parallel “dieselgate” litigation, which sought to establish that car manufacturers deliberately designed cars to mask the true level of nitrogen oxide (NOx) pollution. The allegations were largelyrejected in a recent verdictfavouring car manufacturers but lawyers are considering an appeal.In a procedural hearing this week, first reported by the Financial Times, lawyers for TfL said manufacturers “expressly or impliedly represented” that certain diesel vehicles were compliant. Laurence Page, barrister for TfL, said: “The representations were false, made dishonestly or recklessly, alternatively negligently, and caused TfL loss,” and TfL would be seeking up to £1bn, the FT reported.Lawyers for carmakers said TfL was making serious allegations “with potentially far-reaching consequences” but had provided “no proper details or particulars whatsoever”, according to the FT.The details of TfL’s lawsuit have emerged after a rebuff for lawyers and clean air campaigners in the parallel“dieselgate” caseearlier this month. A high court ruling rejected most of the allegations that car manufacturers had knowingly installed so-called defeat devices to rig tests.TfL has been granted a stay until October, as lawyers in the dieselgate case consider an appeal over the verdict on which TfL’s suit would appear to depend. TfL was a signatory as a vehicle owner to the dieselgate case, brought by a number of law firms led by Leigh Day on behalf of 1.6 million drivers.A TfL spokesperson said: “This procedural hearing covers TfL’s claims against certain vehicle manufacturers relating to alleged losses of Ulez revenues. The Ulez is a key mechanism in TfL’s efforts to improve air quality in London.“The court indicated that it will stay these claims, while separate claims by vehicle owners against vehicle manufacturers proceed further.”Explore more on these topicsLow emission zonesTfLAutomotive emissionsLondonAutomotive industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: John Croft obituary | Second world war | The Guardian
description: Codebreaker at Bletchley Park who later worked at the Home Office and became a successful abstract artist
Author: Michael Smith
Headline: Codebreaker at Bletchley Park who later worked at the Home Office and became a successful abstract artist
Content: John Croft’s paintings were described by the art critic Brian Sewell as ‘exquisitely judged’View image in fullscreenJohn Croft’s paintings were described by the art critic Brian Sewell as ‘exquisitely judged’Second world warObituaryJohn Croft obituaryCodebreaker at Bletchley Park who later worked at the Home Office and became a successful abstract artistMichael SmithWed 29 Jul 2026 12.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 13.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Croft, who has died aged 103, was a codebreaker at Bletchley Park in Buckinghamshire during the second world war, and subsequently in London, where he worked on Soviet cipher systems used to send secret messages to European communist parties and sympathisers.Croft was studying history as an undergraduate at Christ Church, Oxford, in 1942 when his tutor asked if he might be interested in intelligence work. “The prospect, whatever that involved, seemed enticing and I gratefully accepted the opportunity,” he later recalled. He was subsequently interviewed in Oxford by Col John Tiltman, Bletchley Park’s chief codebreaker. “Tiltman himself appeared to me almost the parody of a regular army officer, with toothbrush moustache and rather clipped speech; as I was to discover later, he was a man of outstanding skill and experience.”A few months later, Croft was ordered to report to Bletchley for training in how to break basic codes and hand ciphers, along with a number of other recruits, including the future authorAngus Wilson, who was to become a lifelong friend.Croft was then put to work in the Testery, the section (run by Ralph Tester) which carried out the initial manual and linguistic process of breaking a recently intercepted German Lorenz enciphered teleprinter system. Tiltman managed to break into a single message as a result of a mistake by an operator, and the mathematicianBill Tutteworked out the internal cipher system. However, the settings changed daily and were different for each teleprinter link – Croft was one of the codebreakers brought in to break the cipher on a daily basis.The Lorenz ciphers, codenamed Fish by Bletchley, were used on the highest security links between Berlin and the various German fronts, and often carried personal orders from Adolf Hitler to his generals. The final breaking of individual messages was carried out in the Newmanry, run by Max Newman, where a number of different machines were used to decipher the messages, culminating in December 1943 in the creation of theColossus computer, the world’s first digital computer.View image in fullscreenCroft at work in the 1940sCroft recalled that one of the highlights of his time in the Testery was “the breaking of a personal message from Hitler demanding the apprehension of the Yugoslav partisan leader General Draza Mihailovic, for which the reward would be ‘a large quantity of gold’”.But the work was sometimes boring and Croft enlisted the help of an aunt, who had a close friend in MI6, to engineer a move to Bletchley’s diplomatic and commercial section, based in Mayfair. He was assigned to the section’s offices on the top floor of Aldford House, on Park Lane, where he briefly worked on Finnish diplomatic ciphers, before being transferred to a new section set up to read the messages between Moscow and communist parties and sympathisers across Europe.The section head was the mathematician Bernard Scott, who had managed to break into the messages, which used a substitution cipher, with the 36 letters of the Russian alphabet transposed as numbers.The indicators of each day’s keys were taken from an English edition of Shakespeare’s plays, and Scott and Croft spent a day searching through the editions on the British Library shelves looking for the one used to encipher the key, without success.“With the advance of the Russian armies in 1944, the traffic on the network began to increase rapidly,” Croft recalled. “It was mainly concentrated in the Balkans, although some but not extensive radio activity was identified as far afield as southern France and in other areas behind the allied lines.”The need for more hands led to three more codebreakers being brought in, including Ernst Fetterlein, who had been Tsar Nicholas II’s official codebreaker and had fled to Britain after the 1917 Bolshevik revolution.Kim Philby, who was now the head of a new counter-espionage section inside MI6 dealing with Soviet spies, was a recipient of the decoded messages and on one occasion he visited the section and was introduced to Croft.View image in fullscreenJune 2002, oil on canvas, by John Croft.Photograph: Courtesy of David Simon Contemporary“Fetterlein kept copies of his translations in a locked wooden cupboard,” Croft recalled. Shortly after Philby’s visit, “Fetterlein arrived to find that his cupboard had been forced open and his papers disturbed,” he said. Although nothing was taken, Croft made no secret of his belief that Philby, who was subsequently exposed as a Soviet double agent and part of the Cambridge spy ring, was responsible.John was born in Brondesbury, north London, to Doris (nee Phillips) and Oswald Cohen. The family was descended from Dutch Jewish immigrants and changed their name to Croft in the late 1930s. Oswald was an executive at the London offices of Paramount Pictures. His son was educated at the Hall preparatory school in Hampstead, and then Westminster school, before going to Christ Church.After the war, Croft returned to Oxford to finish his degree and then applied to join GCHQ (Government Communications Headquarters), the peacetime successor to Bletchley, based at Eastcote in west London, but he was refused and an appeal to the then foreign secretary, Ernest Bevin, failed.Croft then had a second encounter with a member of the Cambridge spy ring when he briefly considered taking a degree in the history of art at the Courtauld Institute in London, and was interviewed by its director, Anthony Blunt. When Blunt asked Croft what he had done during the war, he gave the official response that he had worked for “a department of the Foreign Office”. Croft recalled that Blunt, who would later be exposed as the “fourth man”, was “remote and chilly” for the rest of the interview.He studied for a master’s in sociology at LSE and graduated in 1953. After a spell as a teacher at North Hammersmith secondary school for boys, Croft joined theHome Office, eventually, in 1972, becoming head of the Home Office Research Unit, where one of his colleagues was the novelist PD James, another great friend. Croft retired in 1981 and was appointed CBE the following year.While working at the Home Office, he took up painting in oils and becamea highly regarded abstract artist, focusing on “non-figurative, minimalist work derived from landscape”. His paintings were included in group shows from the 1960s onwards, and were described by the art critic Brian Sewell as “exquisitely judged, hard-edged abstracts”. He had two solo exhibitions, at the Gardner Arts Centre (now the Attenborough Centre for the Creative Arts) at the University of Sussex in 1970, and at the University of Warwick in 1971.After a period living in the Isle of Man, Croft moved with his parter, Ray Kelly, a former employee of British Airways, to Bath. Kelly died in 1999.Ivor John Croft, codebreaker, civil servant and artist, born 6 January 1923; died 12 July 2026Explore more on these topicsSecond world warHome OfficeKim PhilbyArtPaintingobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Triple killer who dismembered bodies of two friends given whole-life jail sentence | Crime | The Guardian
description: James Desborough, who also strangled cellmate to death for snoring while awaiting trial, hid body fragments in Cornwall woods
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: James Desborough, who also strangled cellmate to death for snoring while awaiting trial, hid body fragments in Cornwall woods
Content: James Desborough used Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman’s money to buy drugs and alcohol after their deaths.Photograph: FacebookView image in fullscreenJames Desborough used Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman’s money to buy drugs and alcohol after their deaths.Photograph: FacebookCrimeTriple killer who dismembered bodies of two friends given whole-life jail sentenceJames Desborough, who also strangled cellmate to death for snoring while awaiting trial, hid body fragments in Cornwall woodsSteven MorrisWed 29 Jul 2026 10.12 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 09.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA triple killer who murdered and dismembered the bodies of two of his friends before strangling a third man to death in prison while awaiting trial has been told he will spent the rest of his life behind bars.Mr Justice Saini, who sentenced James Desborough, 40, at Winchester crown court, said the circumstances of the case were unique.Handing Desborough a rare whole-life order, he said the killer was a highly dangerous person who had considered his victims “worthless”.The judge said Desborough killed his two friends because they were vulnerable, homeless, physically slight individuals who he considered would not necessarily be missed given their chaotic personal lives.“I also find you did not consider them to be worthy of respect as humans,” the judge said. Saini added that a whole-life order was a “last resort”, used only when the seriousness of a case was “exceptionally high”.Devon andCornwallpolice have revealed they are reviewing the deaths of four people who were living in a homeless shelter at the same time as Desborough and his two victims.Det Supt Rachael Bentley, the head of the major crime investigation team, said at this stage the force did not believe Desborough had killed any of the four, “but it’s an ongoing investigation.”View image in fullscreenClaudio Aquilino.Photograph: Devon and Cornwall Police/PADesboroughkilled Claudio Aquilino, 57, and Daniel Coleman, 43,cut up their bodies and hid them in woodland close to a shack where he sometimes lived off-grid in south Cornwall.While in Exeter prison before his trial he murdered his cellmate, Steven Kempster, 65, apparently because his snoring annoyed him.View image in fullscreenJames Desborough’s cabin where he sometimes lived off-grid in south Cornwall.Photograph: Devon and Cornwall Police/PADuring the sentencing hearing, emotional victim statements were read out that made clear the men who were killed were loved and did have worthwhile lives.Coleman’s 14-year-old daughter said: “I love him. I was a daddy’s girl; now I can’t be. It hurts to see I’ll never see him smile again.” She said it terrified her to think her father would have been frightened when he was killed and told Desborough he was a “miscreant killer”.Aquilino’s family said he had been a talented artist and a good cook, although addiction problems had made his life very difficult.Sean Brunton KC, for Desborough, said he had been in trouble only once before, 20 years before the murders.The barrister said Desborough was “highly intelligent” and as a younger man had had great potential and found some success. In court he was polite and easy to deal with.Brunton said it was not possible to say if the “bleak events” had been brought on by drink and drugs or because Desborough had wrongly perceived the men he killed had nothing to live for.More than 700 officers and scientists were involved in the 175-day search of the woods, with Devon and Cornwall police drawing on resources from five other forces. The weather was very hot and the nature of the terrain jungle-like and boggy. Officers sometimes had to wade through water up to their chests as they searched.View image in fullscreenDaniel Coleman.Photograph: Devon and Cornwall Police/PAThe forcesaid they had even diverted a streamto enable the systematic sieving of 300 metres of its bed, which they said was a first. They discovered 1,900 burned bone fragments from the body of Aquilino and the remains of Coleman.Aquilino and Coleman, who suffered from long-term addictions, had previously lived with Desborough at a homeless hostel in the Cornish surfing hotspot of Newquay.Desborough used the men’s money to buy drugs and alcohol after their deaths.Desborough told a forensic biologist who was searching the woods that he had “particularly enjoyed the dismemberment scenes” in the television serial killer series Dexter.Explore more on these topicsCrimeCornwallEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Body found in suitcase in Athens is that of 38-year-old British woman | Greece | The Guardian
description: Greek authorities identify remains as those of Elizabeth Jane Ross after discovery in a derelict building 11 days ago
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Greek authorities identify remains as those of Elizabeth Jane Ross after discovery in a derelict building 11 days ago
Content: Elizabeth Jane Ross’s body was found in a suitcase in this abandoned building in Athens 11 days ago.Photograph: Danai Davlopoulou/EurokinissiView image in fullscreenElizabeth Jane Ross’s body was found in a suitcase in this abandoned building in Athens 11 days ago.Photograph: Danai Davlopoulou/EurokinissiGreeceBody found in suitcase in Athens is that of 38-year-old British womanGreek authorities identify remains as those of Elizabeth Jane Ross after discovery in a derelict building 11 days agoHelena Smithin AthensWed 29 Jul 2026 17.05 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 11.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA body found in a suitcase in an abandoned building in central Athens has been identified as that of a 38-year-old British woman.Eleven days after the find, and following an appeal to foreign law enforcement agencies, Greek police shed some light on the mystery of the body that until Wednesday had remained unidentified.“The remains, we can confirm, have been identified as belonging to a British woman,” one well-placed source said. “Her next of kin have been informed.” They added that it had been ascertained the victim had been born inScotlandin 1988.Late on Wednesday, Greek media named the victim as Elizabeth Jane Ross.She had been staying in the city with friends, who reported seeing her for the last time on 15 July.Adding to the mystery surrounding the circumstances of her death, it was revealed that her mobile phone had been fully operational until news of her identification was released.Police were alerted after a homeless man discovered the suitcase on 18 July in a derelict building in Kypseli, a district popular among foreign nationals in downtown Athens, according to the public broadcaster ERT.Ross had reportedly flown to the region from the US, arriving inGreece, on 29 June, from Cyprus.Greek homicide officers sent fingerprints toInterpolafter drawing a blank on local databases. US authorities had provided evidence on the basis of the DNA that police released on Wednesday.Detectives cordoned off the building on Evelpidon Street as they investigated the circumstances of Ross’s death.A police spokesperson, Konstantina Dimoglidou, had previously said CCTV was being examined to try to trace Ross’s movements before her death. Authorities were treating the incident “as a criminal act, given how the body was found”, she told Skai TV.Airlines are also believed to have been approached as investigators try to reconstruct Ross’s journey to Greece and determine whether she was travelling alone. Officials in Greece and Cyprus were scouring flight logs and hotel bookings.Local media, citing the results of a postmortem, said Ross had been dead for eight days before the discovery. There was “no evidence” of a struggle or signs of injury.Greek officials did not rule out UK investigators joining the inquiry.A British Foreign Office spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with Elizabeth’s family during this difficult time. We are providing consular support and are in contact with the local authorities.”Greece is no stranger to British tourists dying in what is a popular holiday destination – often by drowning or as a result of road accidents – “but incidents like this are very rare”, officials said.Explore more on these topicsGreeceScotlandEuropeInterpolnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fauci invokes fifth amendment and declines to testify in Senate Covid hearing | US Senate | The Guardian
description: Adviser to Trump and Biden for pandemic says Republican senator has ‘unhinged obsession’ with him
Author: Jessica Glenza
Headline: Adviser to Trump and Biden for pandemic says Republican senator has ‘unhinged obsession’ with him
Content: 2:35Fauci refuses to answer questions in Senate Covid hearing - videoUS SenateFauci invokes fifth amendment and declines to testify in Senate Covid hearingAdviser to Trump and Biden for pandemic says Republican senator has ‘unhinged obsession’ with himUS politics – live updatesJessica GlenzaWed 29 Jul 2026 15.03 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDrAnthony Faucirefused to answer questions at a high-profile Senate committee hearing on the origins of Covid-19 and accused the Republican senator leading questioning of having an “unhinged obsession” with him.Fauci, the veteran former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (Niaid), served as a key adviser to Donald Trump and Joe Biden during the Covid-19 pandemic. The hearing was called by Kentucky senator Rand Paul, who has investigated Fauci for years.Fauci said Paul’s goal was “embarrassing and intimidating me”, and ultimately landing him “behind bars”.“Therefore, although it pains me to do so, because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress, under the advice of my attorneys I will invoke my right under the fifth amendment of the constitution to refrain from answering your questions,” Fauci said in his opening statement.Fauci refuses to answer questions in Senate Covid hearing - videoRead morePaul, frustrated,later told reportersthat he would hold a vote to hold Fauci in contempt of US Congress next week, and described the question of whether the fifth amendment could shield him as “a question for the courts”.Fauci, 85, served under seven US presidents and through numerous health crises, including the HIV crisis, Ebola outbreaks and the first coronavirus outbreak, calledSars-CoV-1. He became a household name overnight when the Covid-19 pandemic halted social life in 2020.Quickly after opening statements, the hearing became a back-and-forth between Paul and Fauci. Paul grew visibly agitated as Fauci refused to answer, threatened the scientists with “repercussions”, and then tossed one of Fauci’s attorneys from the hearing room.“Did the [National Institutes of Health] ever fund gain-of-function [research] on monkeypox?” Paul asked, in reference to research that manipulates viruses to make them more effective to shed light on how outbreaks happen.“On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the fifth amendment of the constitution,” said Fauci.After another description of research Paul found unacceptable: “Dr Fauci, did the NIH ever conduct research for or in coordination with any element of the intelligence community, CIA, [Office of the Director of National Intelligence]?”Fauci responded: “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the fifth amendment of the constitution.”Paul pressed on: “Dr Fauci, would you at least like to answer this one question for us today, and let us know whether or not you have changed your mind on whether or not the benefits of gain-of-function [research] outweigh the risks?”Fauci replied: “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the fifth amendment of the constitution.”A visibly frustrated Paul soon scolded Fauci: “There will be repercussions to your refusal to testify today.”Soon, an attorney for Fauci attempted to join him at the table, and Paul demanded the attorney move.“This is not a game with his lawyers,” said Paul, to the attorney who was apparently trying to speak, but could not be heard for lack of a microphone. “The attorneys were not recognized.”“There’s a row behind you, sir,” said Paul. “This is the way Anthony Fauci wants to be remembered – for a lawyer not recognizing the rules … Security please remove him from the room,” Paul said. The attorney patted Fauci on the shoulder and voluntarily left, alongside a guard.Members of the audience, which conspicuously included rightwing media figure Laura Ingraham, applauded.Trump administration needs to stop ‘public harassment’ of Fauci and scientists, open letter saysRead moreIn part, Paul’s frustration at the hearing stemmed from a presidential pardon Fauci received from Biden, which in turn implicates the fifth amendment. There isdebateamong experts about how far the fifth amendment extends. Some argue that once a person accepts a presidential pardon, they cannot invoke the fifth amendment for federal crimes. Without that right, Congress could hold a witness in contempt, which can lead to fines or – in the extreme – jail time. Others have argued that the right extends as long as there is a valid threat of prosecution, particularly by states.“You don’t have any rights under the fifth amendment,” claimed Josh Hawley, a Republican senator of Missouri, in a line of accusatory questioning. “This is about contempt – contempt for this body, and contempt for the American people.”Democrats, meanwhile, defended Fauci. Paul is “single-mindedly fixated on seeing Dr Fauci prosecuted for imaginary crimes, and you are so invested in that outcome you have created a personal brand around it”, Fauci’s attorneys argued in a statement read aloud by the Democratic senator Richard Blumenthal, of Connecticut.Ahead of the hearing, Republicans characterized their work as investigating “the origins of Covid-19 and risky taxpayer-funded life science research”, while scientistshave characterizedthe investigation as “vilification and harassment” of Fauci, who led Niaid for 38 years before retiringin 2022.Indeed, Republican senator Bernie Moreno took the opportunity to demand Fauci apologize for a military policy that required service members to take the Covid-19 vaccine, to Americans who lost businesses during the pandemic and to a single Ohio mother who wasarrestedfor not wearing a mask during an outdoor football game early in the pandemic. The senator called Fauci a “total and complete disgrace”.Ron Johnson, a Republican senator of Wisconsin, used the hearing to call the Covid-19 vaccine, credited by scientists with savingmillions of lives, an “experimental gene therapy”. He also accused Fauci of “lying” to his own diary, which elicited a smirk from Fauci.The hearing was a continuation of Paul’s years-long support of the “lab leak” theory, or the idea that the Covid-19 pandemic began as a release from the Wuhan Institute of Virology, a theory many virologists contend is improbable.“For years, Americans were told a lab origin wasn’t just unlikely – it was dismissed outright by the very people funding and reviewing this research,” Paul, who chairs the Senate committee on homeland security and governmental affairs, where Fauci testified, said last week.Paul has argued that Fauci lied about the origins of the pandemic to shield his own culpability, because the NIH funded the lab in Wuhan through a sub-grant. Paul argued Fauci lied about the origins of the pandemic because, as Paul later hypothesized to reporters: “Holy you know what – if it came from the lab, If I funded the lab, I could be responsible for this entire pandemic.”Fauci expressed disillusionment with ‘rambling, crazy’ Trump in journalRead moreThe “lab leak” theory has gained significant traction in Republican circles since political opinion on the pandemic began to fracture. In just one example, the White House published atreatiseon the theory in April 2025 that served as a rationale for defunding the National Institutes of Health (NIH). The theory in part impugns gain-of-function research, in which scientists seek to develop better vaccines by working with potentially dangerous pathogens.A 2024 survey of virologists from theGlobal Catastrophic Risk Institutefound that most believed the pandemic began as a so-called spillover event, or a virus jumping from an infected animal to a human. Similarly, a group of virologists argued in theJournal of Virologythat the “preponderance” of evidence points to a natural origin, that the “lab leak” theory received outsized attentionand that, ultimately, the origin may never be known. Gain-of-function research, meanwhile,hassplitthe scientific community for years.The scheduled hearing comes just days after Paul released what he described as Fauci’s “diary”, a more than 1,100-page document characterized as revealing Fauci’s inner conflicts about the lab leak theory.Scientists have saidthis is a normal part of scientific debate.The diary also containedentries about Trump, who he advised closely during the early days of the pandemic. He described the president as “rambling”, “crazy”, “desperate”, “bumbling”, “incompetent”, “an idiot”, “a true embarrassment”, “totally nuts” and “truly an obnoxious adolescent”.Gary Peters, a Democratic senator of Michigan, described the hearing as damaging to science and ignoring ongoing public health threats, such as the outbreak of the food-borne parasitecyclosporaandmeasles, both at record highs.“It’s attempting to turn one person into a scapegoat for a crisis that hundreds of officials across the Biden and Trump administrations were responsible for handling,” said Peters, who did not ask Fauci any questions. “This is only going to deter other scientific experts from public service.”Explore more on these topicsUS SenateAnthony FauciUS politicsUS healthcareRepublicansCoronavirusnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump officials turned to AI and a mafia killer to bolster case, Comey lawyers allege | James Comey | The Guardian
description: James Comey’s lawyers say Secret Service illegally tracked him to develop case around his ‘8647’ seashell post
Author: Sam Levine
Headline: James Comey’s lawyers say Secret Service illegally tracked him to develop case around his ‘8647’ seashell post
Content: Former FBI director James Comey speaks during a Senate intelligence committee hearing on Capitol Hill in June 2017.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/APView image in fullscreenFormer FBI director James Comey speaks during a Senate intelligence committee hearing on Capitol Hill in June 2017.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/APJames ComeyTrump officials turned to AI and a mafia killer to bolster case, Comey lawyers allegeJames Comey’s lawyers say Secret Service illegally tracked him to develop case around his ‘8647’ seashell postSam Levinein New YorkWed 29 Jul 2026 12.35 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 14.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLawyers for former FBI directorJames Comeyalleged on Tuesday that US Secret Service agents illegally surveilled Comey, Donald Trump requested regular updates into the investigation, and law enforcement turned to ChatGPT and aknown mafia killeras they scrambled to find justification for criminally charging Comey for posting a picture of seashells that spelled out “8647”.The claims were laid out in amotionto dismiss a criminal case the US Department of Justice filed against Comey in April, in which it said the post by Comey – whom Trump fired in his first term – was a threat on the US president’s life.In the motion filed on Tuesday in federal court in North Carolina, Comey’s lawyers said the case should be dismissed for vindictive and selective prosecution.“The government had initially investigated Mr Comey’s seashells post, but that investigation appeared to be going nowhere until Mr [Todd] Blanche and US attorney Ellis Boyle reinvigorated it,” Comey’s lawyers wrote.“The ensuing indictment is not based on a good-faith application of the law to the facts; instead, it effectuates a years-long campaign by the president to use the criminal process to punish Mr Comey for his protected speech and because of the president’s deep-seated animosity.”Comey filed a separate motion earlier this week, seeking dismissal of the case on grounds that the post was protected speech andnot a “true threat”against the president.Trump has long fumed over the way Comey handled the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election while director of theFBI. Comey has also been an outspoken critic of Trump.The justice departmentindictedComey last year in a separate case, claiming he had lied to US Congress. Those charges, which were seen as thin,were tossed outafter a judge ruled the prosecutor handling them had been unlawfully appointed.Comey told investigators he came across the formation of shells while on vacation with his wife in eastern North Carolina in May 2025. The phrase “86” is often used as shorthand to get rid of something, while Trump is currently serving as the 47th US president, and Comey posted the photo to Instagram.Comey later deleted the photo, saying he didn’t know it could be interpreted as a violent threat. “It never occurred to me, but I oppose violence of any kind so I took the post down.”Comey and his wife, Patrice, voluntarily spoke with Secret Service investigators after the incident. Internal Secret Service documents show that Trump was requesting updates on the investigation as it was ongoing. Even though Comey agreed to a voluntary interview in Washington, a Secret Service supervisor was asked about the possibility of tracking Comey’s phone on his drive back from Washington to North Carolina through an “exigency” request without a warrant.The supervisor said it was a “bad idea”, accordingto their notesthat were attached to the motion.“To declare an exigency exemption, we needed to believe that there is an imminent threat to life or limb,” the supervisor wrote. “At that time we did not believe that anyone’s life was in immediate danger and legally it was a bad idea to ping the phone.”The supervisor wrote another agent agreed with him, but said the Secret Service might do it anyway. The next day, the supervisor wrote a note saying the “#3 guy at DOJ” wanted to ping the cellphone with an exigency request. The notes do not say the name of the official.Comey’s phone ultimately was tracked and the couple was also followed as they drove back from North Carolina, Patrick Fitzgerald, his attorney, said in asworn affidavit.Documents included in the filing also lay out how law enforcement officials were unable to confirm that the term “86” was one that implied violence.Secret Service agents interviewed an unidentified person who knew the Comeys, but said they had not talked to them in several years and hoped the former FBI director went to jail. After telling agents they initially believed the term “86” meant something on a menu, they came to believe it was a violent threat after hearing Rudy Giuliani claim Comey had worked on cases where the term “86” meant kill.The FBI searched records related to the federal case against mobster John Gambino, which Comey handled when he was a federal prosecutor for references to “86”, according to the motion. There were no references to it. The FBI also conducted a broader search of all of its records going back decades for the term and the results were inconclusive.After the indictment was filed against Comey in April, Comey’s lawyers said, law enforcement officials were still hunting for evidence that Comey would have understood the term “86” to be a violent one. They interviewed two former FBI agents who worked on mafia cases, who said they were familiar with the term, but could not say definitively that it would have been used violently by the mafia.Agents also turned to ChatGPT and Google AI to search for meanings of the term “86”. Neither returned definitive results.Officials also interviewed Salvatore“Sammy The Bull” Gravano, a one-time underboss in the Gambino crime family, who confessed to nearly 20 murders, to try to build a case against Comey, the filing says. Gravano was a cooperating witness in the Gambino case Comey prosecuted. He told agents that while he believed it meant “to get rid of someone” he did not recall ever discussing the term with Comey, Comey’s lawyers said.Gravano, a podcaster whohas praised Trump, told investigators that he interpreted Comey’s photo to mean “let’s kill Trump,” but he did not take it to mean Comey personally was going to kill Trump, Comey’s lawyers wrote.Explore more on these topicsJames ComeyUS politicsDonald TrumpFBInewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifa opens disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over Falklands banner and final chaos | Argentina | The Guardian
description: Fifa has begun disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over the Falkland Islands banner displayed after their World Cup semi-final win over England
Author: John Ashdown
Headline: Fifa has begun disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over the Falkland Islands banner displayed after their World Cup semi-final win over England
Content: Argentina’s Giovani Lo Celso holds a banner with the words ‘the Malvinas are Argentinian’ after their semi-final win over England.Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/APView image in fullscreenArgentina’s Giovani Lo Celso holds a banner with the words ‘the Malvinas are Argentinian’ after their semi-final win over England.Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/APArgentinaFifa opens disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over Falklands banner and final chaosPlayers held banner after semi-final against EnglandParedes and Molina investigated over brawl after finalJohn AshdownWed 29 Jul 2026 13.09 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 18.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifa has opened disciplinary ­proceedings against Argentina over the Falkland Islands banner ­displayed after theirWorld Cup semi‑final winagainst England in Atlanta.AsArgentinacelebrated ­reaching the final with their dramatic 2-1 ­victory, several players held a sign ­proclaiming “Las Malvinas son ­Argentinas” – the ­Malvinas are Argentinian – in ­reference to the ­British overseas territory in the south Atlantic.Uefa calls emergency meeting as opposition to Fifa plan hardensRead moreThe dispute over the islands, which have been ruled by Britain since 1833, is long running and led to a 74-day conflict in 1982, during which more than 900 people – 649 Argentinians and 255 Britons – lost their lives.Fifa’s disciplinary code ­prohibits “using a sports event for ­demonstrations of a non-sporting nature” and the banner prompted political debate on both sides of the ­Atlantic. A spokesperson for the then UK prime minister, Keir Starmer, said: “The World Cup might not be ours, but the Falkland Islands ­definitely are.”Andrew Giuliani, the head of the White House Fifa taskforce, defended Argentina’s players, saying the US believed in free speech.The incident was not the first time an Argentina team had expressed such sentiments. In 2014,Fifafined Argentina £20,000 for a far larger banner held ‌up by players before a friendly with Slovenia in La Plata.Fifa’s fullWorld Cupcharge sheet against the Argentinian Football Association also includes ­“discriminatory chants and gestures, late kick-offs, failure to comply with match and security protocols, the display of inappropriate messages by the team and spectators and the throwing of objects by spectators in relation to several matches”.0:18Ugly scenes as Argentina lose World Cup final – videoSeveral players are also under investigation in relation to the ­chaotic scenes that followed ­Argentina’s 1-0extra-time defeat by Spainin the final. As Spain attempted to celebrate, ­altercations broke out across the pitch at New York New Jersey Stadium.The Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes, who was seen wrestling Spain’s Eric García to the ground, faces three counts of assault under the Fifa disciplinary code, while the defender Nahuel Molina faces two counts of assault (one completed and one attempted) and one count of unsporting behaviour.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe assistant coach, Roberto Ayala, faces one count of assault, and Thiago Almada, an unused substitute in the final, one count of unsporting behaviour. Spain’s Gavi also faces an unsporting behaviour charge.“In accordance with the Fifa ­disciplinary code, the respondents have now been provided with the opportunity to present their position, following which a decision will be issued by the Fifa disciplinary committee in due course,” said Fifa.Explore more on these topicsArgentinaFifaWorld Cup 2026EnglandFootball politicsFalkland IslandsWorld CupnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fed holds interest rates steady despite Trump’s renewed calls to lower them | US economy | The Guardian
description: Rates remain unchanged for fifth time since December as tenuous Iran peace deal pushes energy prices up again
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Rates remain unchanged for fifth time since December as tenuous Iran peace deal pushes energy prices up again
Content: Kevin Warsh, the Fed chair, at a news conference on Wednesday.Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenKevin Warsh, the Fed chair, at a news conference on Wednesday.Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/UPI/ShutterstockUS economyFed holds interest rates steady despite Trump’s renewed calls to lower themRates remain unchanged for fifth time since December as tenuous Iran peace deal pushes energy prices up againGaya GuptaWed 29 Jul 2026 17.06 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 14.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe USFederal Reserveheld interest rates steady on Wednesday in a divided vote, indicating growing pressure on the central bank to address heightened inflation.The Fed’s federal open market committee voted 9-3 to maintain rates, with three dissenting members indicating a preference to raise the rate by a quarter-percentage point. It was the first time in a decade that three board members shared dissent over a policy decision.Coolerinflation datapublished earlier this month may have eased expectations for an imminent rate hike, but Kevin Warsh, the new Fed chair, said in a news conference that the committee was less interested in “any one piece of data” and was more focused on overall trends. The tenuous peace deal between the US and Iran has also sent energy prices creeping up again.Warsh has repeated that he wants policy decisions to emerge from a “good family fight” and said on Wednesday he “got one” during his second Fed meeting as chair.“Most of our discussion was on the big questions that matter to the conduct of monetary policy,” Warsh said. “We didn’t hide from them. We weren’t scared of them. There was a lot more interaction between my colleagues, it was a real family fight. My view, which you’ve long heard, is that’s the better way to get policy right.”Just two weeks ago, one of the dissenting bank presidents, Lorie Logan of Dallas, made the case for “modestly higher interest rates”, arguing in public remarks that they would better balance the “outlook and risks” for the Fed’s dual mandate of maximum employment and price stability.“Inflation has been too high, for too long, and does not appear to be on track all the way back to 2%,” she said. “And the inflation risks are to the upside. The labor market, meanwhile, is solid. Without any policy restraint, these conditions are likely to continue until there’s an unanticipated shock.”Logan joined Beth Hammack in Cleveland and Neel Kashkari in Minneapolis in the dissenting minority. The three bank presidents have formed a bloc before, most recently in April when they all disagreed with the committee’s decision to include a forward looking statement, or “easing bias”, in the Fed’s news release.Though Warsh was adamant about delivering price stability in Wednesday’s news conference, it was unclear exactly what tools he planned to use to achieve that goal. While he said that interest rates could be used as “part of that solution”, he added: “I wouldn’t say it’s in isolation.”Warsh has signaled he is ushering in a new era at the central bank, one that emphasizes a reservedness toward forward guidance. At his first meeting in June, he announced five new taskforces – comprising economics professors, business leaders and former central bank governors – that are meant to rethink how the Fed approaches its communications, data, balance sheet policy, inflation framework and the impact of artificial intelligence on its policy judgments.The US-Israel war with Iran, which has endured since the end of February, has pushed energy prices higher for American households and businesses.The Fed’s main tool to combat higher prices has traditionally been to hike interest rates, which raises borrowing costs and, in effect, cools the economy. But Trump has persistently and aggressively called for rate cuts since the start of his presidency, going so far as to attack the previous Fed chair, Jerome Powell – who is still on the Fed’s board – with verbal insults and target him with a Department of Justiceinvestigationfor failing to deliver.Fed governors periodically release forward-looking projections illustrating when they think further rate changes will occur. Last month, half of all Fed members projected at least one rate increase this year, in a U-turn in outlook from just months earlier, when a majority of Fed members called for at least one rate cut over the same time period.Wednesday’s decision is the fifth time rates have been left unchanged since December, despite Donald Trump’s renewed calls to lower rates.Trump on Monday repeated his push for lower interest rates, adding that the US “should have the lowest rates in the world”.Trump spared Warsh from any blame, calling him “fantastic” and implying Warsh would want to cut rates despite the opinions of his fellow board members, who Trump called “very political”.Explore more on these topicsUS economyFederal ReserveUS interest ratesUS politicsTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Meta misses earnings forecasts after Zuckerberg media push to promote AI | Meta | The Guardian
description: Stock tumbles nearly 8% after weaker-than-expected results, despite CEO’s blitz to tout positive effects of AI
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: Stock tumbles nearly 8% after weaker-than-expected results, despite CEO’s blitz to tout positive effects of AI
Content: Facebook headquarters in Menlo Park, California, on 28 October 2021.Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFacebook headquarters in Menlo Park, California, on 28 October 2021.Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesMetaMeta misses earnings forecasts after Zuckerberg media push to promote AIStock tumbles nearly 8% after weaker-than-expected results, despite CEO’s blitz to tout positive effects of AIJohana BhuiyanWed 29 Jul 2026 17.26 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 19.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark Zuckerberg’s media spree touting the positive effects of artificial intelligence did little to cushion the blow of Meta’s second-quarter earnings, which sent its stock tumbling on Wednesday.In aWall Street Journalop-ed published on Tuesday, the Meta chief executive expressed his optimism for a world where everyone has access to a super-intelligent machine.“As a thought experiment, imagine only one person had a super-intelligent lawyer,” Zuckerberg wrote. “He would have an unfair advantage in court. That would lead to a worse society. But now imagine everyone has a super-intelligent lawyer. Justice would be carried out much more fairly and efficiently than it is today.”But Zuckerberg’s message of AI optimism wasn’t enough to alleviate Wall Street’s initial reaction to Meta’s second-quarter earnings. The company’s stock slid nearly 8% after reporting weaker-than-expected results.Meta posted $6.18 in earnings per share, missingWall Street expectations of $7.14, according to Bloomberg consensus estimates. Revenue was $60.8bn, beating analyst predictions of $60.23bn.The company also raised the lower end of its expected expenses and spending for the year. Susan Li, Meta’s chief financial officer, said the company had $2.4bn in “charges related to legal proceedings” in the second quarter, raising total expenses to the range of $165bn to $169bn, up from $162bn to $169bn.And it expects 2026 capital expenditures to range from $130bn to $145bn, up from $125bn to $145bn. Meta has previously said a big portion of its capex is earmarked for its AI investments.Zuckerberg’s PR blitz comes as investors and analysts look for the company’s justification of its massive spending on AI infrastructure, a concern that has contributed to the10% drop in the company’s share price year over year.Big tech companies such as Meta, which have increasingly burned through free cash flow, need to sell consumers and Wall Street on the promise of AI to defend their spending. The stock market’s response to Zuckerberg’s remarks on the company’s earnings call, scheduled for later this evening, could reveal whether his messaging is enough to ease investor concerns.Meta has struggled to make an AI model to rival OpenAI or Anthropic, but it plans to start a cloud business to sell AI compute, monetizing some of its immense AI investments, Bloomberg reported this month. Thereportwas one of the few things to boost investor confidence this year, spurring a spike in the stock’s long decline.The day before earnings, Zuckerberg echoed his belief in decentralizing AI and creating an era of “personalized super-intelligence” where everyone has an AI assistant tailored to their needs and beliefs, in interviews with theNew York Timesand the Financial Times.Though he did not specify how Meta plans to approach this, based on the company’s history, personalization would likely require consumers to hand over even more of their data. Still, Zuckerberg said it was better than his competitors’ centralized models.“I think it is literally impossible to have a single benevolent super-intelligence that is simultaneously aligned with everyone at once,” Zuckerberg told the New York Times.Meta may be “trying to do too much at once”, Mike Proulx, vice-president and research director at advisory firm Forrester Research, said.“Every one of Meta’s major growth lanes now carries a trust toll,” Proulx said in a statement before listing Meta’s new projects. “AI-generated advertising raises new brand-control concerns, smart glasses create new privacy questions, youth safety remains under intense scrutiny and employee-tracking initiatives spark data-collection backlash.”Zuckerberg’s narrative speaks to Meta’s need to set itself apart from competitors – many of whom he said are sending messages filled with “doom” about the future of AI.“I don’t understand why anyone who believes that AI will eliminate most jobs and much of humanity’s relevance would rush to build that future,” Zuckerberg wrote in the WSJ.Still, Meta’s attempt to create a positive message around its AI systems may fall flat, said eMarketer senior analyst Minda Smiley.“It’s not surprising that Zuckerberg wants to come out with a more cohesive message around the company’s AI ambitions, especially as Meta tries to carve out its own lane,” Smiley said in a statement.“But the optimistic, positive tone he’s striking stands in stark contrast to the negative sentiment that’s building toward social media companies over claims that they’ve harmed and addicted kids. This juxtaposition could make it more difficult for Meta to build credibility in an area where it’s already a laggard.”While Zuckerberg makes an argument for Meta’s open-source approach to AI development, the company is being forced to answer for its previous practices developing its products and the effects they have had on users.Meta is facing about 3,000 lawsuits alleging that it deliberately creates addictive products leading to the harm of children. The suits have been brought by families, school districts and states’ attorneys general. Forty-two states have sued Meta in state courts, with Tennessee’s case currently at trial. A separate federal lawsuit brought by 29 attorneys general goes to trial in California next month.“The shifting regulatory environment is also a major Meta risk,” said Proulx. “Policymakers are more focused on youth wellbeing, addiction and platform safety … Youth restrictions will affect who Meta can reach. That’s a big problem for a company that depends on ad revenue.”The lawsuits not only call Meta’s corporate practices into question; they also come at a financial cost. The company has alreadysuffered damaging losses, with two separate juries finding Meta liable for harming children and awarding plaintiffs millions in damages. Lawyers for the families, schools and lawmakers say they will not stop seeking high-cost damages until Meta changes the design of its products.Dara Kerr and Nick Robins-Early contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsMetaAI (artificial intelligence)Mark ZuckerbergComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia accuses Telegram founder of aiding terrorism in its latest online crackdown | Telegram | The Guardian
description: FSB puts Pavel Durov on international wanted lists and says his messaging app is used for sabotage and murder
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: FSB puts Pavel Durov on international wanted lists and says his messaging app is used for sabotage and murder
Content: Pavel Durov, the founder of Telegram, says the Russian actions against him are an attempt to suppress privacy and free speech.Photograph: Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPavel Durov, the founder of Telegram, says the Russian actions against him are an attempt to suppress privacy and free speech.Photograph: Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty ImagesTelegramRussia accuses Telegram founder of aiding terrorism in its latest online crackdownFSB puts Pavel Durov on international wanted lists and says his messaging app is used for sabotage and murderAssociated PressWed 29 Jul 2026 12.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussian officials have chargedPavel Durov, the founder and chief executive of the messaging app Telegram, with aiding terrorism.The charges againstthe 41-year-old Russian-born billionaire, who lives in the Gulf, are the latest step by the Kremlin to bring the internet and digital communications under its control after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.The Federal Security Service said in a statement on Wednesday it had accusedTelegramof failing to remove “numerous channels, chats and bots” allegedly used by “Ukrainian intelligence agencies, terrorist and extremist organizations to prepare and coordinate acts of sabotage and terrorism, mass murder, and cyber fraud” in Russia.The FSB said Kyiv was using a dating chatbot on Telegram to lure and recruit Russians for “sabotage and terrorist activities” and it had detained 46 users, aged from 12 to 22, for assaulting law enforcement officers, arson and other acts over the past year.The agency said it was adding Durov’s name to international wanted lists.Durov said earlier this year that Russian officials hadopened a criminal investigation against himand he accused them of fabricating pretexts to restrict access to Telegram and “suppress the right to privacy and free speech”.If brought to trial and convicted, he could face life in prison.Telegram, which boasts more than 1 billion users worldwide, did not respond to a request for comment. Its official website links to an account on X that on Wednesday posted an image of Durov raising a middle finger to the camera.The website says the company is based inDubaiand that Durov, who holds dual citizenship of France and the United Arab Emirates, lives there too.View image in fullscreenPavel Durov speaks at the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona, Spain, in February 2016.Photograph: Manuel Blondeau/Corbis/Getty ImagesUnderVladimir Putin, Russian authorities have banned websites and platforms that do not comply with tight restrictions. They have also developed technology to monitor and manipulate online traffic.Facebook, Instagram and X have been banned in Russia and YouTube has been throttled. Popular messaging apps, such as Signal and Viber, have been blocked, and the most popular ones, WhatsApp and Telegram, have been restricted.VKontakte, a popular social media platform founded by Durov well before he launched Telegram, has come under the control of Kremlin-friendly companies. Russia tried to block Telegram between 2018 and 2020 but failed.It is possible to circumvent some Kremlin restrictions by using virtual private networks (VPNs) but many of these are now being blocked.Moscow is promoting what it calls a “national” messaging app known as Max, which critics say could be used for surveillance. The platform is touted as a one-stop shop for messaging, government services, payments and other activities. It openly says it will share user data with authorities upon request and experts say it does not use end-to-end encryption.Activists in multiple regions have tried to organise protests against the restrictions on Telegram but the authorities crushed nearly all their attempts.Military bloggers have also denounced the crackdown, arguing that Telegram is an indispensable communications tool for Russian troops inUkraineand for activists running crowdfunding campaigns to help Moscow’s forces.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe government initially promised not to restrict Telegram on the battlefield but a different message later emerged from the Kremlin. At a meeting with Putin for International Women’s Day, a servicewoman called Telegram an “adversarial tool” and agreed with the president when he said “the use of communications systems that are not ours, not under our control, poses a danger to personnel” in battle.Despite the restrictions, multiple Russian officials still use Telegram and regularly update their “channels” – its term for blogs – on the platform. The Kremlin’s Telegram page had more than 284,000 followers as of Wednesday.Durov was arrested in Paris in 2024 amid allegations that his platform was being used for illicit activity, including drug trafficking and the distribution of images of child sexual abuse. French authorities handed him preliminary charges for allegedly allowing criminal activity on the platform. In March last year, Durov said he had returned to Dubai after spending “several months” in France.View image in fullscreenThe chief culprit for a Russia-linked arson attack on this warehouse in London was recruited through Telegram.Photograph: London Fire Brigade/PAThe Kremlin criticised the French authorities for moving against Durov. Putin’s spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said at the time that “yes, indeed, terrorists use Telegram. But terrorists also use cars. Why aren’t they arresting the CEO of Renault or Citroën?”Peskov did not respond to a request for comment on what had made the Russian authorities change their position.Prosecutors in Paris told Associated Press on Wednesday that Durov remained under formal investigation, facing an array of potential charges for alleged criminal activities linked to Telegram. Investigators have questioned him repeatedly, most recently this month.Russia has faced accusations of using Telegram to coordinate and recruit people to carry out acts of arson and sabotage in Ukraine and across Europe. A British man was recruited on the platform, probably by Russian military intelligence, to organise a plot in 2024to set fire to a warehouse in Londoncontaining satellite equipment for Ukraine. He was also asked to kidnap a pro-Ukraine Russian billionaire living in London.Dutch teenagers were arrested in the Netherlands in September after being contacted by Russian hackers on Telegram who wanted them to map wifi networks in The Hague. The city is the location of many sensitive organisations, including the international criminal court, which has issued an arrest warrant for Putin, as well as the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons and Europol, which helps European countries fight international crime.Moscow has denied involvement in acts of sabotage in Europe.Explore more on these topicsTelegramPavel DurovRussiaSocial mediaUkraineVladimir PutinEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: BMW to cut ‘as many as 8,000 jobs’ under pressure from Chinese rivals | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Layoffs will come in admin and development divisions in Germany, with production operations unaffected
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Layoffs will come in admin and development divisions in Germany, with production operations unaffected
Content: BMW’s headquarters in Munich. The company has started a voluntary redundancy programme agreed with employee representatives, it said.Photograph: travelstock44/AlamyView image in fullscreenBMW’s headquarters in Munich. The company has started a voluntary redundancy programme agreed with employee representatives, it said.Photograph: travelstock44/AlamyAutomotive industryBMW to cut ‘as many as 8,000 jobs’ under pressure from Chinese rivalsLayoffs will come in admin and development divisions in Germany, with production operations unaffectedJasper Jollyand agenciesWed 29 Jul 2026 08.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBMW is planning to cut as many as 8,000 jobs inGermany, according to reports, in the latest sign of Europe’s largest carmakers reducing costs under pressure from Chinese rivals.The Munich-headquartered company has started a voluntary redundancy programme agreed with employee representatives, aBMWspokesperson said on Wednesday.The company and its ​works council had agreed a severance ⁠programme targeting the administration and development ​divisions, the spokesperson said. Production operations are excluded.BMW’s total workforce is about 160,000.Germany’s carmakers have come under intense pressure in recent years with the rise of Chinese competitors that havequickly come to dominate in the electric vehicle market. Chinese manufacturers have also launched a fierce price war in their home market, which had previously been a lucrative source of export earnings for European brands including BMW.Europe’s carmakers have also had to find cash for their own transition from petrol to electric, and cope with the impact ofUS tariffs. Several manufacturers – including Volkswagen, Stellantis and Ford – haveturned to partnerships with Chinese rivalsto help them build and sell in Europe.BMW’s cuts come after Milan Nedeljković, who was previously head of production, took over as chief executive in May.A spokesperson said: “The BMW Group is proactively shaping the profound changes taking place in its operating environment. These include the technological transformation of the automotive industry, geopolitical uncertainties, changing market conditions and developments inChina.”View image in fullscreenPorsche is also undergoing restructuring, with 9,000 redundancies – a fifth of its workforce – planned by 2035.Photograph: Ralph Orlowski/ReutersVolkswagen, Germany’s largest carmaker by volume, confirmed on Friday thatit would cut as many as 100,000 jobsfrom its total workforce of 650,000. The plans include closing four factories and halving the number of models produced.Porsche, the sports car brand part-owned by Volkswagen, is alsoundergoing a severe restructuring. Another 5,000 job cuts were agreed this week, taking total planned redundancies to 9,000 – a fifth of its workforce – by 2035. The Stuttgart-based company reported a €1.4bn (£1.2bn) profit before tax on Wednesday, up from €1.1bn a year earlier.Porsche’s sales in China slumped by 30% to 14,500 in the first half of 2026, faster than the 17% decline across the group as a whole. Donald Trump’s withdrawal of subsidies for electric cars such as Porsche’s Taycan also hit North American sales.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAston Martin reported a loss before tax of £89m in the second quarter of 2026.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAAston Martin has also struggled in China and the US. The Warwickshire-based company’s losses grew in the first half of the year despite it saying that its turnaround efforts had improved sales.Aston Martin reported a loss before tax of £89m in the second quarter of 2026, up from £61m in the same period a year earlier, in a statement to the stock market on Wednesday. That left the loss for the first six months at £154m.The FTSE 250 company’s share price rose by 3.5%, however, after it said its performance had “materially improved” during the half year with revenues up 38% to £629m.Famed as the maker of the sports cars featured in the James Bond films, Aston Martin has endured years of turmoil since itlisted on the London stock market in 2018.The fashion billionaireLawrence Stroll rescued the company in early 2020, only for the Covid pandemic and subsequent supply chain disruption to rock the global industry. The company has gone through years of new fundraisings and job cuts, most recentlymaking a fifth of its workers redundant in February.Get in touchContact the Guardian Business teamThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know.
