This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don't already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Scroll down and click onSecure Messaging.When asked who you wish to contact please select the ‘Business (UK & Global)’ team.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsAutomotive industryBMWManufacturing sectorGermanyEuropeJob lossesChinanewsShareReuse this content

title: Ronnie Le Drew obituary | Puppetry | The Guardian
description: Puppeteer best known for manipulating Zippy on the hit ITV series Rainbow and a stalwart of the Little Angel puppet theatre in London
Author: Duncan Barrett
Headline: Puppeteer best known for manipulating Zippy on the hit ITV series Rainbow and a stalwart of the Little Angel puppet theatre in London
Content: Rainbow, with, from left, Zippy, Bungle, host Geoffrey Hayes and George.Photograph: FremantleMedia Ltd/Rex FeaturesView image in fullscreenRainbow, with, from left, Zippy, Bungle, host Geoffrey Hayes and George.Photograph: FremantleMedia Ltd/Rex FeaturesPuppetryObituaryRonnie Le Drew obituaryPuppeteer best known for manipulating Zippy on the hit ITV series Rainbow and a stalwart of the Little Angel puppet theatre in LondonDuncan BarrettWed 29 Jul 2026 16.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 16.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe puppeteer Ronnie Le Drew, who has died aged 78, will be remembered for his long association with theirascible glove-puppet Zippyon ITV’s hit preschool series Rainbow. But to many in the British puppetry community, he was also an inspiring teacher, mentor and a generous on-stage colleague, as well as one of the country’s foremost marionettists.Rainbow launched in 1972 as ITV’s answer to Sesame Street, and the following year Ronnie was asked to take over operating Zippy. Working with the voice actorRoy Skelton(also known as the voice of the Daleks and Cybermen in Doctor Who), Ronnie helped turn Zippy into the show’s unlikely star. Zippy was a moody, garrulous creature – his exact species was never defined, although Ronnie referred to him as “a unique” – who could only be silenced by forciblyzipping his mouth shut.Ronnie developed a close connection with Skelton, who would deliver Zippy’s lines from a tiny booth at one side of the set, in between puffs on a cigar, while Ronnie operated the puppet from under a counter, with a tiny TV monitor wedged between his legs. Before long, they were so in sync that they could improvise together.As Rainbow’s popularity soared over the decades, its human stars – the hostGeoffrey Hayesand singers Rod Burton, Jane Tucker and Freddy Marks – became public figures, accosted by grown-up fans while out in the pub, and, in Hayes’s case, receiving propositions (and, apparently, knickers) in the post from enamoured mums. Ronnie, meanwhile, came to appreciate his own anonymity – Zippy might be famous, but he never would be, although the show ran continuously for two full decades, providing Ronnie with a reliable income – rare for a professional puppeteer.Ronnie caught the puppet bug early. He was born in Toronto, and his parents, Edna (nee Brooker), a shop assistant, and Leslie, a schoolteacher, brought the family over from Canada to London when he and his twin sister, Bonnie, were three years old, settling in a council flat in Stockwell. As their marriage deteriorated, Ronnie escaped to the world of make-believe, joining the Educational Puppetry Association in Holborn while still at school and attending meetings of theBritish Puppet and Model Theatre Guild. Back home, he performed on the concrete steps of the block of flats, where his father dismissed his efforts as “dolly-waggling”.When Ronnie was 14, a friend from the Guild took him to see a show at theLittle Angel puppet theatrein Islington – a formative experience that would launch him on his puppetry career. Ronnie was transfixed by a marionette performance of The Little Mermaid, begged the theatre’s owner, John Wright, for a job, and then persuaded his parents and headmaster to let him leave Priory Grove school to take it up.View image in fullscreenLe Drew at The Little Angel theatre in Islington, London, 2015.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianOver the next few years, Ronnie gradually worked his way up at the Little Angel, from sweeping the floor of the workshop to operating the lights, and eventually taking over as lead puppeteer. His role there also opened the door to TV and film work. In 1966 he worked with Wright on the BBC film A Touch of Don Juan, operating the arm of a moving statue, and two years later he provided the elaborate opening-credit sequence for the spy thriller A Dandy in Aspic. Then the regular TV gig of Rainbow beckoned.In 1983 he married Caroline Astell-Burt, and they had two children, John and Liz. They eventually separated.A workaholic by nature, Ronnie filled his summer breaks from Rainbow moonlighting as Sweep on The Sooty Show, and performing small roles in a range of projects for the Jim Henson company, includingLabyrinth,Little Shop of Horrors, andThe Muppet Christmas Carol. (He was impressed by Michael Caine, but truly starstruck in the presence ofDavid Bowie.)He also continued a lifelong association with the Little Angel, both as a performer and as director, and took part in productions at the Barbican Centre and the Royal Festival Hall in London.After Rainbow was cancelled in 1992, Ronnie was the only member of the cast to return for two short-lived revival series, which ran between 1994 and 1997, and saw him providing Zippy’s voice as well as operating the puppet. This earned the disapproval of Hayes, who, despite Ronnie’s insistence that he had been forced to audition for the role, felt he should have refused to participate on principle.They later patched things up before a gig at the Hammersmith Palais, part of the nostalgia-fuelled “Rainbow Revival” of the early 2000s, which saw members of the original cast touring the university circuit, performing the single It’s a Rainbow (by DJ George and MC Zippy) onTop of the Popsin 2002, and entertaining a 40,000-strong crowd at a retro music festival on Clapham Common.After Rainbow, Ronnie continued to work in TV and film, providing the giant hand for the National Lottery’s “It Could Be You” campaign, motion-capture for the candlestick Lumiere in Disney’s live-action remake of Beauty and the Beast, and in countless appearances as Zippy on shows such as Children in Need,The Weakest Linkand The X-Factor.He also fulfilled a childhood dream of performing in musical theatre, operatinga talking parrotin a national tour of Doctor Dolittle, to a voice track recorded by Julie Andrews.Ronnie maintained his close relationship with the Little Angel, where he performed across all seven decades of his career. In 1991, Wright told Ronnie he wanted him to succeed him – although, after Wright’s death, and much to Ronnie’s disappointment, the board went in a different direction.Ronniecontinued to perform at the Little Angel, and when his memoir,Zippy and Me, which I co-authored, was published in 2019 (Ronnie was a ghostwriter’s dream: as talkative as Zippy, but with none of the puppet’s famous snark), the launch party was held in the theatre foyer.In 2016, Ronnie was elected president of the British Puppet and ModelTheatreGuild, which had kindled his love of puppets as a boy, and was described by them as “possibly the most active and supportive president we have ever had or will have”.He is survived by his children, four grandchildren, Olive, Felix, Daisy and Theo, and a half-sister, Carol.Ronald Frederick Le Drew, puppeteer, born 23 October 1947; died 18 July 2026Explore more on these topicsPuppetryTheatreTelevisionLittle Angel theatreobituariesShareReuse this content

title: You can’t argue with 118 Brummies in their swimsuits: Attilio Fiumarella’s best photograph | Photography | The Guardian
description: ‘I was thinking about the Terracotta Army when I took this shot of Birmingham swimmers in their local pool, which faced closure. They had to stand there for an hour, waiting for the sun to come out’
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: ‘I was thinking about the Terracotta Army when I took this shot of Birmingham swimmers in their local pool, which faced closure. They had to stand there for an hour, waiting for the sun to come out’
Content: ‘We need to get together and take back power’ …swimmers in the empty Grade II listed Moseley Road Baths in Birmingham.Photograph: © Attilio Fiumarella. Courtesy of The Royal Photographic SocietyView image in fullscreen‘We need to get together and take back power’ …swimmers in the empty Grade II listed Moseley Road Baths in Birmingham.Photograph: © Attilio Fiumarella. Courtesy of The Royal Photographic SocietyMy best shotPhotographyYou can’t argue with 118 Brummies in their swimsuits: Attilio Fiumarella’s best photograph‘I was thinking about the Terracotta Army when I took this shot of Birmingham swimmers in their local pool, which faced closure. They had to stand there for an hour, waiting for the sun to come out’Interview byCharlotte JansenWed 29 Jul 2026 09.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 13.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleItook this image inBirminghamon 20 July 2014 – part of my first professional photography project. I had moved to the city in 2013 and I would pass this building every day on the bus on my way to the city centre. I remember looking at the facades and being impressed and intrigued by the three different entrances – what were once the first class, second class and women’s entrances.One day I decided to get off the bus and find out what the building was. The door was open, and a nice lady welcomed me in and started to explain its history. It is theMoseley Road Baths,an Edwardian-era community building. In 2014 the second pool was still operating but the gala pool, where I took this image, was already empty. The building was in need of restoration and, without funding, thecouncil planned to shut it downfor good. The woman I met there told me lots of stories about the place – people who had come to learn to swim, how it had served as a casualty station during the second world war, and how it had even been used as a dance hall. It was a very charming place with an incredible history: as soon as I saw the gala pool, I knew I had to fill the majestic empty space.double quotation markWe need to get together, show up and take back powerA few months later, I managed to get a local community bursary through Some Cities, run by Andrew Jackson and Dan Burwood, to make a portrait project about the pool community, and the relationship between them and the building. It was collaborative, we created the story together. And in July 2014, I organised this shot – the last picture of the project. The Friends of Moseley Road Baths helped recruit swimmers, and I also handed out flyers in the neighbourhood to encourage people to take part. What’s fantastic about the image is that it reflects how diverse the community there is, and how many different generations swim there.It still makes me smile that I decided to use a large format camera for the first time on a project like this. Looking back, it seems slightly crazy. It was an intense experience. We had 118 people in the pool, and everything depended on getting a single sheet of film right. There was a lot that could have gone wrong. Fortunately, many people helped make it possible. Ian Edwards from St Paul’s Community Trust coordinated everyone with a megaphone, while he and a team of volunteers helped people down into the empty pool using a temporary staircase they had built.Then I had a problem with the light. I knew that at 11am, it came in from the right to the left through the windows, giving me exactly the angle I wanted, but on the day it was overcast. After waiting for about an hour, people were starting to get nervous, but in the last five minutes, the sun finally appeared and I got the shot.In my work, I always reference architecture – that’s my background. In this image I was thinking of theTerracotta Army. What amazed me about the photograph was how it became an expression of solidarity and togetherness. In 2020 it won thePortrait of Humanity prize, and now it is getting new attention – I think because it reflects something about the time we’re living in. We need to get together, to show up and to take back power. I see this photograph as an act of resistance – these swimmers had never met me but they showed up to defend a place they cared deeply about.Recently, Moseley Road Bathssecured the final fundingneeded to complete its restoration, including a grant from the National Lottery Heritage Fund. The building is temporarily closed while the restoration works are completed, but it will soon reopen with renewed purpose and new public spaces. My contribution was only a very small part of that story, but I like to think it helped in some way. Looking back, I think it was a very generous thing for all those people to do. They stood together in their swimsuits, following the directions of a crazy Italian guy. To me, this photograph simply says: “We are here, together, standing up for something we believe in.”Attilio Fiumarella is one of the selected photographers in the Royal Photographic Society’s 167th annual international exhibition at theSaatchi Gallery, London, from 7 August to 11 SeptemberAttilio Fiumarella’s CVView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Attilio FiumarellaBorn:Naples, 1978High point:Seeing long-term projects find their audience over time, from winning Portrait of Humanity 2020 to being commissioned by institutions whose work and values I respectTop tip:Be persistent, and care deeply about the people you photograph. As photographers, we have a responsibility to help their stories reach a wider audienceExplore more on these topicsPhotographyMy best shotBirminghamSwimmingHeritageArchitecturefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Tinie Tempah’s popular house extension series returns  | Television | The Guardian
description: Great Gatsby glamour and a sailing theme guide two house-proud couples. Plus: Katie Price’s kids talk about their turbulent lives. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Great Gatsby glamour and a sailing theme guide two house-proud couples. Plus: Katie Price’s kids talk about their turbulent lives. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Transforming their Norfolk cottage … Jenny and James with Tinie Tempah (centre) in Extraordinary Extensions.Photograph: Channel 4View image in fullscreenTransforming their Norfolk cottage … Jenny and James with Tinie Tempah (centre) in Extraordinary Extensions.Photograph: Channel 4TV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Tinie Tempah’s popular house extension series returnsGreat Gatsby glamour and a sailing theme guide two house-proud couples. Plus: Katie Price’s kids talk about their turbulent lives. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil Harrison,Hannah J Davies,Ali Catterall,Priya ElanandSimon WardellWed 29 Jul 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExtraordinary Extensions8pm, Channel 4Tinie Tempah is back with his surprisingly popular series about house extensions. The first wealthy couple are “unleashing Great Gatsby glamour on to their Edwardian terrace”; the second are transforming their chocolate-box cottage in Norfolk with an eco-build inspired by their love of sailing. Just one concern is that they will finish the job, then wish they had never bothered.Hollie RichardsonHoratio’s Drive: America’s First Road Trip1.15pm, PBS AmericaIt’s Ken Burns Day on PBS America, as the titan of US documentary is celebrated. The pick is this funny, fascinating film about Dr Horatio Nelson Jackson (voiced by Tom Hanks) and his eccentric, pioneering 1903 car journey across America. The country had hardly any paved roads then, but to Jackson that was a mere detail.Phil HarrisonDeal Or No Deal: Banker’s Best Battles7.30pm, ITV1A compilation episode of the glorified gambling gameshow, now hosted by Stephen Mulhern but still imbued with hints of Noel Edmonds’ woo-woo antics. Self-confessed risk-taker Leon has overcome serious health challenges to make it to the show, but plays it surprisingly safe when it comes to his turn in the hot seat.Hannah J DaviesCasualty 24/7: Every Second Counts8pm, Channel 5A taxing day at an overcrowded casualty unit at Barnsley hospital, where 71-year-old Enid is struggling to breathe, Wayne has been shot in the foot, volunteer Jane’s mother arrives after a fall, and three-year-old Rory has something unusual stuck up his nose: “I’ve seen garden peas. I’ve seen little bits of Lego. But I’ve never seen a conker.”Ali CatterallMurder 24/79pm, BBC OneWhen Chris Hemming rings in to confess to police that he has stabbed his partner, Cheryl McKenna, to death, DCI Gareth Lougher has to establish if the murder was premeditated or if it was manslaughter. Shot using multiple screens and shaky real-time camerawork, this will have your adrenaline levels peaking.Priya ElanKatie Price: Nothing to Hide9pm, Sky DocumentariesIt might be the last in the series but Katie Price’s carousel of chaos just keeps spinning – she was engaged to Lee Andrews weeks after filming this. Before him, though, were husbands Alex (“walking weapon/perfect rebound”), Reid and Kieran Hayler. Her children Junior and Princess speak out about the turbulence of the last few years.HRFilmThe Devil Wears Prada 2 (David Frankel, 2026),Disney+View image in fullscreenConflict … Miranda Priestly (Meryl Streep) and Andy (Anne Hathaway) in The Devil Wears Prada 2.Photograph: Macall Polay/APMiranda Priestly is back – and the last 20 years haven’t diminished the fashion magazine editor’s hauteur one iota. But, in David Frankel’s couture-drenched comic sequel, her former callow assistant, Anne Hathaway’s Andy, is now an award-winning investigative journalist. Hired by the owner to improve Runway’s reputation, she can take all that Meryl Streep’s disdainful Priestly throws at her. This time round, the main conflict is with the internet, as declining print sales and clickbait competition threaten the publication’s future. It’s a jolly, aspirational outing, buoyed by scene-stealers Stanley Tucci and Emily Blunt, even if the gags are largely from the preloved rack.Simon WardellPrimate (Johannes Roberts, 2025),Paramount+A brutally efficient horror from Johannes Roberts that employs all your favourite slasher movie tropes – remote location, invincible foe, gut-wrenching dismemberings, final girl – but makes the serial killer a chimp. Ben was the test subject of a linguistics professor who has recently died, and can communicate using sign language. He now lives with her widower Adam (Troy Kotsur) and teenage daughters, Lucy (Johnny Sequoyah) and Erin (Gia Hunter). But a mongoose bite turns the cute ape into a rabid menace and the family’s Hawaiian clifftop home into a deathtrap.SWExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Billy Liar review – Tom Courtenay is superb in classic study of a young man and his quixotic dreams | Movies | The Guardian
description: Courtenay gives a beautiful performance as the undertaker’s clerk who nurses preposterous ambitions. But the film is too quick to surrender them
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Courtenay gives a beautiful performance as the undertaker’s clerk who nurses preposterous ambitions. But the film is too quick to surrender them
Content: Not that angry … Julie Christie and Tom Courtenay in Billy Liar.Photograph: RONALD GRANTView image in fullscreenNot that angry … Julie Christie and Tom Courtenay in Billy Liar.Photograph: RONALD GRANTMoviesReviewBilly Liar review – Tom Courtenay is superb in classic study of a young man and his quixotic dreamsCourtenay gives a beautiful performance as the undertaker’s clerk who nurses preposterous ambitions. But the film is too quick to surrender themPeter BradshawWed 29 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is John Schlesinger’s much-loved British comedy from 1963, based on the 1959 novel byKeith Waterhouse, itself part of the now almost forgotten Angry Young Man movement of which John Osborne’s Look Back in Anger and Kingsley Amis’s Lucky Jim were the other two classic texts – though perhaps it is really only Osborne’s hero who is actually angry.Tom Courtenay plays Billy, a cheeky, naughty young man who is as daft as a brush and lives semi-permanently inside his own Walter Mitty-ish fantasy world. (Amis’s Jim Dixon had his own propensity to indulge in micro-imagined situations to get him out of whatever mortifying little class-based humiliations he found himself in.) Billy lives at home in Yorkshire with his mum and dad and works as an undertaker’s clerk, of all the banal things; he takes refuge in his reveries, chiefly the fiction that he is the ruler of a bizarre Ruritanian land called Ambrosia (perhaps named after the brand of rice pudding). Billy wants to be a comedy writer, and he is, after all, the experienced comedy writer of preposterous situations that are happening inside his own head.But Billy has a complicated love life (though we can assume that as a nice young unmarried man he is still a virgin). He has recklessly proposed to two separate women: shy Barbara (Helen Fraser) and Rita (Gwendolyn Watts). But there is a third woman in his life: the gobsmackingly beautiful Liz, played byJulie Christie, and the sheer implausibility of this pairing means that the film almost has the air of science fiction. It is Liz who encourages him to try his luck in London – but Billy loses his nerve.And it is this final act of nerve-loss that has always soured me on Billy Liar, despite its massive reputation. I am heretically unenthused about the film,which I have written about before, as it appears to me finally to have a strange unfunny loyalty to unhappiness and defeat which is quite at odds with the aspiration of Billy’s comic fantasies. It is at odds also, as it happens, with the reality of Keith Waterhouse’s own experiences of getting out and getting on and, for what it is worth, Courtenay’s experiences too, as detailed in his superb autobiography Dear Tom: Letters from Home. On revisiting Billy Liar again, I’m prepared to concede that the ending, in its paralysis and shame, might relate specifically to Billy’s actual lying, not merely his fantasies: his silly and self-destructive fibbing to those two other women. But I still can’t bring myself to join in the chorus of praise. It is however a lovely performance from Courtenay, an enduringly amazing actor who is still doing outstanding work right now.Billy Liar is in UK cinemas from 31 July.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsFilm adaptationsKeith WaterhouseTom CourtenayJulie ChristiereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Personal Problems review – an exhilarating lo-fi epic of Black working-class life in 80s New York | Movies | The Guardian
description: The director of Ganja & Hess, Bill Gunn, turns analogue video and improvisation into a work of startling intimacy, humour and emotional force
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: The director of Ganja & Hess, Bill Gunn, turns analogue video and improvisation into a work of startling intimacy, humour and emotional force
Content: Quietly amazing … Mizan Kirby in Personal Problems.Photograph: Kino International/Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenQuietly amazing … Mizan Kirby in Personal Problems.Photograph: Kino International/Everett/ShutterstockMoviesReviewPersonal Problems review – an exhilarating lo-fi epic of Black working-class life in 80s New YorkThe director of Ganja & Hess, Bill Gunn, turns analogue video and improvisation into a work of startling intimacy, humour and emotional forcePeter BradshawWed 29 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1980, Bill Gunn, director ofcult 70s horror Ganja & Hess, took on this quietly amazing micro-budget video project with author Ishmael Reed. It is an improvised melodrama in two parts about Black lives in New York, originally intended for television, and shot on analogue video. It is rough and ready, and the sound mix is sometimes very muddy indeed, but it pops with energy and life.The film anticipates by decades the world of shooting movies on smartphones, even though they were presumably wielding camera equipment the size of a briefcase. Moreover, the opening titles to part one are so basic that they look like a modern intentionally VHS-fetishist gag by someone like Harmony Korine. You could also compare the boozy scenes and overlapping dialogue to Cassavetes or Altman. But for me, it all recalls Larry David’sCurb Your Enthusiasm; there is genuine comedy in one scene in which a stern-faced hospital administrator in the emergency room asks an endless series of form-filling questions of a young man who has arrived in mortal agony, but can’t be treated until the bureaucracy is complete.The story, though ramifying into all sorts of subplots and sidebars, revolves around a nurse at Harlem hospital called Johnnie-Mae (played by nonprofessionalVertamae Smart-Grosvenor, a poet and food writer). In the opening scene, she is interviewed about her life and family background and interest in writing poetry; in this sequence, she is calm, articulate and strong in a way that she is never permitted to be once the eventful drama kicks off.Johnnie-Mae is married to Charles, played by the film’s producer Walter Cotton, but is having an affair with jazz musician Raymon (played by Sam Waymon, brother of Nina Simone), a situation she reveals to two friends at a boozy, uproarious brunch. But idle, mopey Charles – whose main interest seems to be watching The Guns of Navarone on TV – is having an indiscretion of his own, something revealed so fleetingly that it seems like a dream someone is having. Johnnie-Mae is furious at having to share her cramped marital home with Charles’s rackety old dad, but then she also has to let her dodgy brother Bubba and his girlfriend Mary-Alice stay with them too; their criminal dealings mean they are dramatically arrested in the middle of the day while everyone else is out. Her relationship with Raymon deteriorates as he appears to become more famous and successful, and in the film’s second part, her father-in-law’s declining health means an explosive confrontation with Charles’s sister.Where is it heading? Everywhere and nowhere. It is a slice of life. Two slices in fact. The film’s second half quickly recapitulates the action of the first before moving things on, an indication of the way it was intended for TV, but Personal Problems has neither the extended storytelling sensibility of longform television nor the enclosed narrative shape of a feature film. It just rolls past for two and a half hours, an experiment in open-ended performance made with experimental, pioneering flair.Personal Problems is in UK cinemas from 31 July.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsNew YorkRaceTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: I thought Nolan’s Odyssey was an epic bore. If you want Greek myths brought to life, try the thrill of opera! | Music | The Guardian
description: Composers from Purcell to Birtwistle have created passionate dramas inspired by ancient Greek stories – and none of them require you to sit through three hours of solemn spectacle without an interval
Author: Tom Service
Headline: Composers from Purcell to Birtwistle have created passionate dramas inspired by ancient Greek stories – and none of them require you to sit through three hours of solemn spectacle without an interval
Content: Thrilling … Berlioz’s The Trojans at the Proms in 2023 with Alice Coote (centre) as Cassandra.Photograph: Andy ParadiseView image in fullscreenThrilling … Berlioz’s The Trojans at the Proms in 2023 with Alice Coote (centre) as Cassandra.Photograph: Andy ParadiseTom Service on musicMusicI thought Nolan’s Odyssey was an epic bore. If you want Greek myths brought to life, try the thrill of opera!Tom ServiceComposers from Purcell to Birtwistle have created passionate dramas inspired by ancient Greek stories – and none of them require you to sit through three hours of solemn spectacle without an intervalWed 29 Jul 2026 08.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 08.28 EDTShareFor me, the most astonishing thing aboutChristopher Nolan’s The Odysseyis its barnstorming popularity. I found this cinematic epic for the ages visually bloodless, expressively monotonous and very, very long. Mind you, it is good to know that Nolan thinks that war is, on balance, you know, once you really think about it, probably a bad idea.The music, too, was disappointing. If I were Nolan, I’d have askedMica Levito score The Odyssey. Ludwig Göransson could have surely done more to make a soundworld of genuine strangeness, but all he could manage is a falling tritone and then a descending fifth on the two reeds and pipes of a recreatedaulos, which he uses as a melancholy leitmotif in all-too-conventional Hollywood fashion. (The aulos is beautifully played by Callum Armstrong on the soundtrack, at least.) The best sounds in the film come inthe scene with Samantha Morton’s Circe, in which the crew’s gluttony is horrorshow ASMR: surround-sound mastication that threatens to devour the audience.View image in fullscreenEpically tedious? Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesMillions of people around the world are sitting through three hours of this monumental mythoverse, without so much as an interval to break up the monotony. And this gives me hope for another artform that thrives on its hubris and excessive self-importance: opera!There is no continuous sit in the entire operatic canon that’s as long or demanding as the three hours of The Odyssey (the most even Wagner asks in a single session is the two-and-a-half hours of Das Rheingold). I promise you, if you can make it throughRobert Pattinson’s one-note scowl for 180 minutes, you are well-prepared for the demands, longueurs and joys of opera.Opera, like film, has often turned to tales of ancient Greece for inspiration: here are a few highlights in which I guarantee the music’s better, the storytelling more compelling, and the emotional experience more involving than Nolan’s film. And when appropriate, there are intervals, too!Strauss: ElektraRichard Strauss’s savagely dramatic opera takes you by the throat from the start and doesn’t relent with its crimson orchestral dissonance and the bloodbath of the drama. Elektra embarks on a devastating journey of vengeance to appease her mother Klytämnestra’s murder of her father, Agamemnon, a journey that will consume everyone in the story – including herself, as she dances to oblivion before the curtain goes down.Mozart: IdomeneoElectra – as Mozart’s libretto spells her name – is another of the storm-tossed characters in his opera that broke all the conventions of so-calledopera seria(“serious opera”, often based on mythological subjects) in the early 1780s. Mozart’s music releases magical tempests and unholy monsters to tell the story of Idomeneo’s sacrifice of his son, Idamante, as well as Electra’s jealousy of Idamante’s lover, Ilia. It’s arguably Mozart’s single most adventurous score – Greek myth turned into contemporary parable.View image in fullscreenMusical myths: the Monteverdi Choir and English Baroque Soloists perform Purcell’s Dido and Aeneas at the Cutty Sark in London.Photograph: Paul Marc MitchellPurcell: Dido and AeneasVirgil’s Aeneid was the source for Purcell’s one-act opera that tells the story of the Queen of Carthage and her faithless lover. Her lament at the end of the opera is one of music’s most moving mandalas of mourning, a piece that’s become so powerful that it’s turned into its own musical myth.Berlioz: The TrojansBerlioz’s magnum opus, again on the Aeneid, has all the variety and character Nolan’s Odyssey lacks. There’s one of opera’s most shatteringly empathic characters in his portrayal of Dido; there are standout moments of thrilling orchestral imagination; and throughout, there’s the feeling that this is a drama in which all the characters are caught in a web of their own desires, set against the whims of the gods, and the ineluctable wheel of human history, as Carthage falls and Rome rises.View image in fullscreenJohn Tomlinson and Johan Reuter in The Minotaur by Harrison Birtwistle at the Royal Opera House in 2008.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianBirtwistle: The MinotaurSomething else thatThe Odysseyonly glimpses as a movie is the human connection at the heart of the supernatural phenomena of ancient Greek myths. Birtwistle makes his Minotaur the most fully dimensional creation on stage: his half-bull, half-human antihero is Asterios, the son of Pasiphaë and Poseidon, condemned to be caught between worlds, questioning his purpose as murderous labyrinthine horror – and as a character whose existential agonies are amplified by the callousness of the humans who visit him.The music in Nolan’s Odyssey is as well-crafted – and bloodlessly forgettable – as the film itselfRead moreAnd that’s just the start: what of Gluck’s Telemaco or Handel’s Teseo or Charpentier’s Medée or Tippett’s King Priam or Jacquet de la Guerre’s Céphale et Procris or Tom Smail’s forthcoming, er,The Odyssey? And then there’sOrfeo, or Orpheus in the Underworld and The Mask of Orpheus … There are hundreds more Greek-inspired operas out there to start your operatic odyssey and whichever you choose, I guarantee you Nolan-levels of ambition, and better music, better characters, and more fulfilling experiences, especially in the flesh of live performance. No need to tie yourself to the mast – just get to the opera house, where myths come to lifeThis week Tom has been listening to:Stravinsky’s poker-inspired balletJeu de cartes. This was one of the first pieces of his I ever heard – my mum had an LP of Colin Davisconducting it. I loved its fun, its wit and its surreal drama. And then read how it was one of Stravinsky’s supposedly less successful pieces. Never trust the judgments of biographers who should know better: enjoy this piece for how it sends up everyone from Rossini to Beethoven and even Stravinsky himself. title: ‘It sounds good next to almost anything’: how Choosin’ Texas became the biggest song of the year | Country | The Guardian
description: Ella Langley’s country single has spent 15 weeks as US number one thanks to its retro-modern sound, a viral misheard lyric – and a boost from the Ella Fellas
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ella Langley’s country single has spent 15 weeks as US number one thanks to its retro-modern sound, a viral misheard lyric – and a boost from the Ella Fellas
Content: Ella Langley performs at CMA Fest, Nashville, on 4 June 2026.Photograph: Taylor Hill/FilmMagicView image in fullscreenElla Langley performs at CMA Fest, Nashville, on 4 June 2026.Photograph: Taylor Hill/FilmMagicCountry‘It sounds good next to almost anything’: how Choosin’ Texas became the biggest song of the yearElla Langley’s country single has spent 15 weeks as US number one thanks to its retro-modern sound, a viral misheard lyric – and a boost from the Ella FellasWill GroffWed 29 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 17.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis week, Ella Langley beat a chart record held byWhitney HoustonandMariah Carey. The country singer’sChoosin’ Texashas now spent 15 weeks atop the BillboardHot 100, making it the longest-running US No 1 by a female solo artist for a non-holiday single. The previous record holders, Houston’s I Will Always Love You and Carey’s We Belong Together, were bombastic pop events, the sort of unassailable hits that make sense as Hot 100 chartbusters. Choosin’ Texas, meanwhile, is a midtempo two-step with a relaxed vocal delivery and decidedly retro sound.For Victoria Banks, a Nashville-based songwriter and instructor at Belmont University, the song’s breeziness is key to its success. “It’s a sleeper hit – it’s understated and unassuming,” she says. “Everything about the song throws back to a simpler time in country music that people are really craving.”‘A sublime, breezy confection’: writers on their 2026 songs of the summerRead moreThe lyrics to Choosin’ Texas tell the story of a Tennessee woman who accompanies her lover on a trip back to his home state of Texas – and discovers in real time that “his heart still belongs to the Lone Star state”. It’s heartbreak on a classic-country scale, which Langley expresses with lyrical homages to decades-old hits by Jerry Reed, Ronnie Millsap and George Strait. The danceable, guitar- and pedal steel-forward production evokes country hits from the late 70s and early 80s, albeit with a contemporary gloss.“There are a lot of throwback elements to the song, but it was obviously recorded in a very modern way,” Banks says. “It’s not so throwback that we don’t relate to it.”In a sign of country music’s continued dominance in the pop sphere, Choosin’ Texas is one of five country songs currently in the US top 10 on the all-genre Hot 100. Given country’sabysmal track recordwhen it comes to playing women, it’s not for nothing that each of these songs – includingTaylor Swift’s I Knew It, I Knew You, Stella Lefty’s Boston and Langley’s own Be Her and her Morgan Wallen duet I Can’t Love You Anymore – features a woman as the lead artist.Historically, during moments when country crosses over into the mainstream, tensions arise over just how far the music has strayed from its roots. “Someone killed country music, cut out its heart and soul,” George Strait famously declared onMurder on Music Row, a 2000 duet with Alan Jackson lamenting the state of the Nashville industry in the late 90s – when artists including Faith Hill and Lonestar ruled the airwaves with ultrasmooth, country-pop confections. In more recent history,Beyoncé’s Cowboy Carter provoked endlessdiscourseabout what constitutes country music and who gets to participate.Choosin’ Texas has largely dodged criticism of being “too pop”, in part due to the cleverness of the songwriting. Co-written with Miranda Lambert, Joybeth Taylor and Luke Dick, the song folds country signifiers – two-stepping, Texas and Tennessee, the interstate – into the emotional story in a way that feels organic. Even the requisite Jack Daniels mention serves a narrative purpose; it matters that it’s Tennessee whiskey she’s drinking all by herself.“All of these writers have been working in the Nashville market for years,” Banks explains. “So even though this is a song that they said they spat out in 30 minutes or whatever, it was coming through their instincts that have been developed for a long time about what is hooky and what pulls people in.”View image in fullscreenBeyoncé accepting the best country album award for Cowboy Carter at the 2025 Grammy awards.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for The Recording AcademyBrian Mansfield, managing editor of the trade publicationCountry Insider, says that the song’s twangy-but-smooth sound makes it appealing to program directors – whether in country, pop or adult contemporary – who tend to avoid songs that would sound jarringly rootsy next to fluffier pop fare. “It’s a song that sounds good next to almost anything you can play, and that is an underrated part of creating the music mix for any format,” he says.The song’s versatility also makes it well-suited to streaming playlists. According toLuminate, Choosin’ Texas racked up over half a billion streams in the first half of the year alone, making it the most-streamed song in the country by a wide margin.As well as co-signs from veteran singers such asSwiftandShania Twain, the song has also – as is now often a prerequisite for streaming success – been boosted by various viral social media moments. In October, shortly after Choosin’ Texas was released, TikTok user Lane Gorrell posted avideoof himself performing an interpretive dance to the song in front of some nonplussed-looking cows. The clip racked up millions of views, and Gorrell eventually took his dance all the way to theGrand Ole Opry.Then came the misheard lyric videos. Around January, in an echo of Taylor Swift’s famous “Starbucks lovers”sagafrom 2014, users started posting videos claiming they misheard the title phrase as “Jews in Texas” or even “Jews and Taxes”. Some also reported hearing the words “drinking Jack all by myself” as “drink and jack off by myself”. Langley laughed off the misheard lyrics in aninterviewwith podcaster Theo Von in April – which of course only drew more attention to the trend. A clip from the same interview of a clearly smitten Vonbutcheringthe word “tzatziki” in front of his crush also went viral.View image in fullscreenLangley photographed for her album Dandelion.Photograph: Courtesy Sony MusicEnter the Ella Fellas. Langley’s male fanbase has made itself known with all manner of viral content, fromuncomfortably earnestlip-syncing videosto clips of themselveslooking enrapturedat her concerts; there have even been Ella Fellabirthday parties. Langley’s team has nurtured this following, reposting popular videos and sending Ella Fellas T-shirts to some of her most ardent supporters. In comparison with many pop fandoms, whose obsessions can skewantisocial, the Ella Fellas seem like a remarkably sane and joyous bunch.How gen Z women are conquering country music: ‘Fans are speaking louder than gatekeepers’Read more“It’s one of those things that brings people together,” says Hunter Massey, a student at Georgia Southern University and TikToker whose videos of himselfgoing buck wildto country songs have earned him an audience of his own. “There can be people from different walks of life, different parts of the country, but we all seem to have this love for her music, and that’s what makes us Ella Fellas.”Massey is among the growing ranks of creators who get paid to post videos using artists’ songs on TikTok – including Langley’s. He says he sometimes turns down requests for songs that don’t speak to him, but he’s never had a problem promoting her music.For him and other Ella Fellas, the appeal is in how down-to-earth she seems. She’s bolstered this perception with songs includingDandelion, where she sings that she “wasn’t made for a fancy crystal vase” and Somethin’ Simple, which finds her musing about giving up stardom in exchange for “a house on a hill, horse in the yard”.“She’s not flashy, Hollywood, whatever,” Massey says. “It’s what we like about her.”Explore more on these topicsCountryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘No plan, no budget, no promotion’: how a genre-mashing masterpiece by a forgotten New York beatnik blew gen Z away | Culture | The Guardian
description: How did an album that began life in 1984 – fusing disco, folk, synth-pop and Chinese opera – end up as ‘one of 2026’s most thrilling releases’? And why does its creator call himself Nirosta Steel?
Author: Juan A Ramírez
Headline: How did an album that began life in 1984 – fusing disco, folk, synth-pop and Chinese opera – end up as ‘one of 2026’s most thrilling releases’? And why does its creator call himself Nirosta Steel?
Content: ‘They didn’t know what they were in for’ … Nirosta Steel, maker of My Skyscraper, at his home in Champaign, Illinois.Photograph: Claire Daly/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘They didn’t know what they were in for’ … Nirosta Steel, maker of My Skyscraper, at his home in Champaign, Illinois.Photograph: Claire Daly/The GuardianCulture‘No plan, no budget, no promotion’: how a genre-mashing masterpiece by a forgotten New York beatnik blew gen Z awayHow did an album that began life in 1984 – fusing disco, folk, synth-pop and Chinese opera – end up as ‘one of 2026’s most thrilling releases’? And why does its creator call himself Nirosta Steel?Juan A RamírezWed 29 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 10.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘It’s kind of mind-bending,” says 69-year old Steven Hall. For the last three years, the Scottish musician has been living with his lawyer husband a few hours south of Chicago, driving an Uber for some additional income. Now, suddenly, he is being lauded by critics for his double LP My Skyscraper, released last month under the name Nirosta Steel. Compiling material recorded between 1984 and 2025, it charts a sonic landscape through disco, folk and synth-pop with detours into Chinese opera and ecclesiastical a cappella. Pitchforkcalled it“an archival triumph and one of the year’s most thrilling new releases”.It all came about when a label head, impressed with Nirosta Steel’s 2014 album Cool Fire, asked Hall if he had any more music. “He didn’t know what he was in for,” says Hall. The couple of dozen unreleased songs he shared spanned four decades of eclectic musicianship, and revealed a globe-trotting life and career that intersects with experimental icons such as Arthur Russell and Allen Ginsberg. Now My Skyscraper seems poised to admit Hall into that rarified pantheon of historically salvaged artists whose time has belatedly arrived.double quotation mark‘I thought Bob Dylan coming over in his limo was normal’“I feel like Rip Van Winkle! Like I suddenly walked out of a cave and I’m blinking my eyes and there’s all this bright light shining on me,” says Hall. “Two weeks ago the label was maybe $2,000 in debt because we were going to do 200 copies. Now we have 1,000 orders and are looking to press 2,000.”View image in fullscreenPoets corner … Hall in 1977 photographed by Allen Ginsberg.Photograph: Courtesy of the estate of Allen GinsbergBorn in the Glasgow suburb of Milngavie to a middle-class optician father and a “tough as nails” mother from a family of 18, Hall grew up performing in the church choir and local theatre company. His parents sent him to a teacher to rid him of his accent, accounting for a rather unplaceable accent (“some people think I’m Swedish”), but they were much more lax as his sexuality developed, and the young Hall freely dated boys and girls throughout school. “There was never even the idea of coming out,” he says, “because I came from a very liberal background where my parents’ attitude was, ‘Whatever you want to do, it’s OK.’”After his father died, Hall’s mother posted a personal ad in the International Herald Tribune and consulted with her three children (Hall has a twin sister and a brother) as to which suitor she should pursue. A man in Delaware won out and the family relocated to the US, which had long dazzled Hall thanks to his fascination with American musicals (“especially the real fantasy, Judy Garland-Mickey Rooney, ‘let’s put on a show’ classics”) and the Chrysler Building, which was built from a stainless alloy called … Nirosta steel.View image in fullscreenHall today.Photograph: Claire Daly/The GuardianPoets – including Ginsberg – would visit his high school in Delaware, and Hall would join them on their return trips to New York City, which is how he found himself at the so-called Poets’ Building in the middle of the East Village’s then bustling arts scene. “I thought it was normal,” says Hall, “because it was the only thing I knew.‘Oh, Bob Dylan’s coming over, his limousine is parked downstairs.Richard Hellfrom Television has a show tonight.’ I thought I could be doing the same thing.”He briefly followed Ginsberg to Naropa University, where he studied dance and poetry under Douglas Dunn and William S Burroughs. But it was while visiting Ginsberg in the Poets’ Building that Hall met Arthur Russell, and the two developed a deep friendship and collaboration while playing backup for Ginsberg’s poetry sets. Russell, he says, was one of the few people who “just couldn’t help creating all the time, and it was hardly a conscious thing. His genius was totally organic and came from his Buddhist awakening. People credit Ginsberg with bringing Buddhism to the west, but Arthur was, in some ways, teaching Allen.”View image in fullscreen‘We didn’t stop and we didn’t go back’ … Hall in 1983 with friend, producer and cellist Arthur Russell.Photograph: Jonny FuHall and Russell collaborated on several projects, including the disco outfit Loose Joints with the DJ Steve D’Acquisto. One of only two songs they wrote together, the sweltering Go for the Night, appears on My Skyscraper, with production by members of Arthur’s Landing, a sort-of tribute band assembled by members of their circle after Russell’s death from Aids in 1992. Their other co-write, a lo-fi elegy titled Lost in Thought, was meant to feature on the album but was bumped in favour of the 22-minute diptych Fresh Feeling and Special Weakness – two of only three recordings of Russell, a gifted multi-instrumentalist, playing drums.Those last-minute additions survived somewhat miraculously, given Hall “had just had them transferred last year, after having them on two-track [tapes] for all those years. I was lucky they were still usable because they were never played, I think, since they were recorded.” More than that, the tracks were improvised one-takes: “Once we got going, the idea was we don’t stop, and we don’t go back and do it again. Everything I did, Arthur was right on top of it. That shows not only how talented he was, but also how close we were, because we could have that kind of interaction and it worked.”Beyond their collaborations, the two would find inspiration on joint journeys to now legendary nightclubs such as Danceteria and The Saint. One of their favourite pastimes, Hall says, was getting high and looking at guys in their diverse East Village, with a preference for its Ukrainian runners and Puerto Ricans “who didn’t like to wear underwear when they wore sweatpants”. With a naughty chuckle, he relates that, when a well-endowed man approached, “we would nudge each other and say, ‘entering binocular mode.’”Hall admits his relationship with Russell sometimes suffered from their clash of competitiveness, and what he viewed as his friend’s jealous streak. In the bookTravels Over Feeling, Hall reveals that he was seconds from signing to Russell’s Sleeping Bag Records label when Russell grabbed the pen from his hand, claiming he would become too famous and move on. “Arthur had a saying, ‘Sometimes paranoia is justified,’” Hall explains. “At that time, he thought some of the people at Sire Records, some of the sleazy people he was hanging out with and playing demos for, had taken some of his ideas, which is entirely possible.” Hall says Russell believed the Rolling Stones’ song Miss You, for example, was based on one of his drum tracks – though “there was not really any evidence of that, but that was the kind of thing”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markBoss Trix (Benny’s Song) is inspired by a Taiwanese lover with impressive bedroom skillsIn his 20s, Hall began spending substantial amounts of time in East Asia, initially staying with a wealthy boyfriend in Hong Kong. He began scoring performances and hosting movement workshops for Zuni Icosahedron, an experimental theatre company there, and later “made a really good living” recording location sound for film and television ads in Taiwan. Naturally, he picked up inspiration each step of the way. My Skyscraper track Lost in Music concludes with audio from a Cantonese funeral procession, and Boss Trix (Benny’s Song) is inspired by a Taiwanese lover with impressive bedroom skills.“I’ve been collecting all these songs for ever, basically, and it’s not just collecting,” he says. “A song that was written 30 years ago, or something I did with Arthur 40 years ago, I keep doing them in different ways so I don’t get bored, or it’s different versions of songs I’ve done with other people in other languages.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Claire Daly/The GuardianWith the album’s success, and with momentous live engagements on the horizon including his first performance at New York’s former Pyramid Club (now Nightclub 101) since he played there with Russell, Hall hopes to reignite his writing with new collaborators, and says he’d like to do a covers album that includes his take on Sade’s No Ordinary Love, originally intended for My Skyscraper.“It’s like surfing on a wave and just seeing where it goes,” he says. “There was no plan or budget for promotion, it was just the music we wanted to put out.”As for finding renewed success at such a late stage in his career, Hall remains unfazed. “I really admire older musicians, like Madonna, who’s two years younger than me, or Mick Jagger, who’s a lot older,” he says. “Certain musicians just keep finding ways to approach it. There’s an authenticity in terms of the process, because everyone was just doing it because they wanted to. And that’s what my music is like, too.”My Skyscraper by Nirosta Steel is out now on Ulyssa RecordsExplore more on these topicsCultureDiscoExperimental musicPop and rockElectronic musicFolk musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Petrol bombs, drugs and Bradley from S Club 7: inside the wild 00s hood movie that the police seized | Podcasts | The Guardian
description: Breakin’ the Cycle had celeb performers who hoped it would go to Cannes. Until they realised its creators were still running a drug gang while filming – and it all went very wrong
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: Breakin’ the Cycle had celeb performers who hoped it would go to Cannes. Until they realised its creators were still running a drug gang while filming – and it all went very wrong
Content: ‘Desperately trying to escape his clean tween pop image’ … Bradley McIntosh in Breakin’ the Cycle.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreen‘Desperately trying to escape his clean tween pop image’ … Bradley McIntosh in Breakin’ the Cycle.Photograph: BBCPodcastsPetrol bombs, drugs and Bradley from S Club 7: inside the wild 00s hood movie that the police seizedBreakin’ the Cycle had celeb performers who hoped it would go to Cannes. Until they realised its creators were still running a drug gang while filming – and it all went very wrongEmine SanerWed 29 Jul 2026 04.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 05.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe story of the making of the 2005 British film Breakin’ the Cycle is surely more compelling than the film itself. Nobody can say for sure, because a rough cut was confiscated by the Met police and the raw footage was considered lost. But the film’s origins and subsequent unravelling is extraordinary. Two of Hackney’s most notorious drug dealers try to go straight and become movie producers. It’s a strange combination of comedic chaos, an accidental stabbing, drug money and shootouts, big dreams of making a different life through art, and, ultimately, tragedy. The film-makers had to navigate real-life gang warfare, and an elitist, perhaps racist, film industry.The cast included the rapper Lethal Bizzle, and Bradley McIntosh from the pop group S Club 7. If McIntosh was desperately trying to escape his clean tween pop image, he wasn’t the only one trying to escape something, though the stakes were far higher for others. Colin Browne, the leader of the Hackney gang Love of Money, wrote the film while serving a prison sentence for cocaine smuggling, and directed it; he had plans to take it to the Cannes film festival. Browne would be killed shortly after filming had finished.The story is told in a new BBC Radio 4 podcast, Shadow World: Breakin’ the Cycle, by Lewis Albrow, the film’s editor. Over the last 20 years, he stayed in touch with D, Browne’s right-hand man who was also involved in the film, and who would go on to serve a prison sentence for drug dealing. “Occasionally, he would contact me and say: ‘One day we’ll finish this film, honour Colin’s legacy.’” After prison, says Albrow, “he came out a changed man. The time was right to go back and ask him questions – was he really truthful about wanting to get out of it? How does he feel about the damage he did? How did he pursue a new future? I think his answers to all of those questions are deep, truthful and fascinating. He really is the central voice in the podcast.”Now an established editor and director, back in 2005 Albrow was trying to break into film editing when he answered an online advert. Did it feel chaotic from the start? “Because I was so green, I didn’t quite know what to expect either,” says Albrow. “I knew it was low budget, so everything’s kind of scrappy. For instance, the sound was all over the place and some of it was unusable, but that got better as they got better.”Bradley McIntosh had been cast as a drug dealer. At the time, S Club 7 had come to an end and he was working on solo projects, “more R&B, trying to find a way to get out of that pop bubble and be taken a little bit more seriously. I thought [the film role] was a great opportunity for me to cross over.” He had acted in the S Club spin-off TV shows and film, but this was his first serious role (Albrow says “he delivers something amazing”).View image in fullscreenJ-Rock of Big Brovaz was one of the stars of Breakin’ the Cycle.Photograph: BBCMcIntosh was more familiar with Browne’s world than his teen pop image suggested. “Growing up around certain people, I was familiar with certain lifestyles. You see drug dealers and people that are gang members and stuff like that.” He didn’t know about Browne and D’s life at first, and thought the film was based on people who, like him, they had just seen around. “I don’t think it actually clicked until maybe halfway through filming that it was based on [their] true story,” he says.It was a fun set. “We became a family, lots of laughs every day. But there were some incidents that were kind of scary.” Filming on an estate in east London with his castmates J-Rock and Randy – from the south London hip-hop group Big Brovaz – some young men thought they were filming a music video on their patch. “They were like: ‘They can’t come round here. You got to move, otherwise we’re gonna start petrol bombing the cars.’” McIntosh smiles over Zoom. “I could see that Colin was pretty annoyed, but he did the right thing.” The cast and crew, he says, weren’t “affiliated with that lifestyle. I think in Colin’s world, he wouldn’t have wanted to show any sign of weakness, but he said, ‘Look, we’re gonna go, but we are gonna come back,’ and we did. But the next time, they had a bit of an entourage, backup.”Albrow’s job “was to deliver [Browne’s] vision. It was his voice, but I had to understand it. When you call a gangster film Breakin’ the Cycle, you are setting your stall out – this is a hopeful message. His central philosophy, I suppose, was about understanding that in his world it’s about everyone trying to escape. And that’s not my world.” He had long conversations with Browne about his life. “He’s like: ‘You’re a white middle-class man walking around [west London suburb] Hounslow, I’m a Black man who’s grown up in Hackney. We’ve had very different lives, and we see the world in a very different way.’ But he was on a trajectory. It was his first film. He comes out of prison and makes it. He went: ‘I want to do something. I’ve got to do something right.’”The transferable skills between drug-dealing and film-making are surely an entrepreneurial spirit and a refusal to be intimidated. “There’s an uncompromising thing going on,” says Albrow. “Colin was a businessman. His business was a bad business that hurt people and hurt the community, but [he had] film-making potential as a businessman and as a creative.” Many first-time film-makers plunge in without much fear, says Albrow, but Browne and D were also tough. “They were not scared of much. Their job in their criminal business was to scare others.” They both survived years in and out of prison, points out Albrow. “It’s a tough place to be. They’re going to go out and make a film, and they’re going to gangster the industry – whatever pushback they got from a fairly elitist, slightly closed group of the film and TV drama industry …” For instance, when they tried to hire an expensive camera to shoot on and were refused, they simply went out and bought one.Neither McIntosh nor Albrow knew that Browne and D continued to deal drugs while making the film. “They did a good job of keeping it from us. I think that’s called good professionalism,” says McIntosh. “I guess it’s a weird one, right, calling it professionalism?” Albrow says: “I believed they were ex-gangsters and they were out of that life. It’s not until now, 20 years later, going back and talking to D, that I understand what was going on. They were running two businesses at the same time, and getting out was not as easy as they thought. They were making a film about getting out of that life, at the same time as actively trying to get out of that life. That’s what makes this story so interesting and such a rollercoaster.”Both say the film doesn’t glorify gang violence, or the lifestyle. The original director had come from music videos, but he left a third of the way in and Browne took over. It changed, says Albrow, from being quite posturing to a “heartfelt, tender story about friendship and relationships. It’s about the connections between these people, their loyalties, betrayals.”Browne’s death at the age of 38 – he was shot and stabbed after intervening in a dispute – was shocking. Albrow and the rest of the crew tried to carry on, but then D was arrested and went to prison and the film fell apart. By then, says McIntosh: “It’s not about the film any more – someone’s lost their life. It’s about someone, a dad, a brother. But, in hindsight, it would have been nice if we had got that movie out.” It might have taken its place among London-set crime dramas, such asBullet Boyand Rollin’ with the Nines, that came out at a similar time.Albrow remembers D picked up the footage from him before he was sent to prison, and for years he thought a copy of it had died on an old hard drive. Not long ago, a specialist managed to resurrect the drive – “that was a wonderful day” – and now he has access to everything that was shot. For the past six months, Albrow has been editing it and hopes to put it out. The principal message of the film, says Albrow, is about “changing your life, and how to break out. You’ve got to have a reckoning, and you’ve got to make amends. I think Colin was ready.”Shadow World: Breakin’ the Cycle ison BBC SoundsnowExplore more on these topicsPodcastsGangsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Beginning Middle End by Valeria Luiselli review – a mother and daughter’s odyssey | Books | The Guardian
description: This journey of discovery from the US to Sicily tackles urgent themes, but is increasingly inward-looking
Author: Chris Power
Headline: This journey of discovery from the US to Sicily tackles urgent themes, but is increasingly inward-looking
Content: Valeria Luiselli.Photograph: Clayton CubittView image in fullscreenValeria Luiselli.Photograph: Clayton CubittBook of the dayBooksReviewBeginning Middle End by Valeria Luiselli review – a mother and daughter’s odysseyThis journey of discovery from the US to Sicily tackles urgent themes, but is increasingly inward-lookingChris PowerWed 29 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Grace Paley’s short story A Conversation With My Father, a request is made of the Paley-like narrator. “I would like you to write a simple story just once more,” her father says, “the kind Maupassant wrote, or Chekhov … Just recognisable people and then write down what happened to them next.” Her attempt, and its failure to impress him, is the action that powers the story. Valeria Luiselli’s fourth novel is propelled by a similar request, the daughter of the Luiselli-like narrator asking: “Will you finally write a novel with a beginning, a middle, and an end?” It’s a problem Luiselli has addressed before. In her 2017 book-length essay about undocumented migrant children, Tell Me How It Ends, she writes that the difficulty in telling their story “is that it has no beginning, no middle and no end”.Beginning Middle End charts the narrator’s efforts to corral life into a narrative. The father in Paley’s story would be similarly unimpressed. After a “slow, entangled” divorce, the narrator, a Mexican living in the United States, embarks on a European book tour with her 12-year-old daughter. She has a coil removed in Munich; her daughter loses a tooth in Prague; near Amsterdam they watch children learning to swim with their shoes on in case of floods. When summer comes, the pair fly to Catania in Sicily. The narrator’s grandmother grew up nearby. They stay in the apartment of a pianist who’s away on tour, with whom the narrator had a “brief and feverish encounter” the previous year.This book can be made to sound dense with plot: Etna is erupting. Wildfires rage. The narrator’s mother, in Baja California, might be developing dementia and is possibly planning an act of eco-terrorism. Before the narrator left for Europe her mother gave her a valuable heirloom, a Roman mosaic tile portraying the god Proteus; the narrator’s grandmother took it from an excavation site before leaving Sicily.Mother and daughter discuss Proteus’s appearance in the Odyssey, their explorations of myth and classical literature becoming a central strand. The narrator’s daughter grows obsessed with returning the mosaic to the ruined villa it came from.After a few weeks the pianist returns, the narrator’s attraction to him rapidly eroding as the sex gets rough, he fights with her daughter, and neglects to help when she gets stung by jellyfish. Yet despite all this, the novel has trouble gathering momentum – or perhaps isn’t interested in doing so. Paley’s narrator calls plot “the absolute line between two points which I’ve always despised”. Luiselli’s seems to feel the same way, breaking her narrative into discrete little segments like the tesserae from which Proteus’s face emerges.Throughout, the narrator questions what she is writing. “I don’t have a clear idea about what I am doing, or what will happen next, not yet,” she admits. “I get entangled in possible beginnings, intricate plots, improvised premises.” Later she wonders if this project isn’t a novel at all but an essay. “Perhaps the middle does not fit into the tighter architecture of a novel, the corset of plot. The middle feels more akin to the distracted, loose, meandering spirit of essaying. Maybe it will have to be an essay until it can be a novel again, an essay with a beginning, a middle, and an end.” This persistent identity crisis is only resolved when the daughter eventually seizes control of the narrative.Luiselli’s writing has always been essayistic and self-reflexive. In fact, she began in 2010 as an essayist with the lyrical, literary Sidewalks. Her first novel, Faces in the Crowd, blended autofiction and metafiction – the book portraying its own construction, just as Beginning Middle End does – with a fictionalised account of the life of a real Mexican poet. Her second, The Story of My Teeth, is also partly about its own construction: in an author’s note Luiselli explains how the book was created in tandem with a group of factory workers. In a Sebaldian touch, photographs accompany the text.In many ways Beginning Middle End mirrors Luiselli’s previous novel, 2019’sLost Children Archive, itself a fictional expansion of Tell Me How It Ends. Its narration is shared between an unnamed woman, whose marriage is collapsing, and her stepson, who addresses his part to his stepsister. In Beginning Middle End the unnamed narrator’s marriage has ended, and her daughter writes postcards to her stepbrother. In both books the text is divided into short, titled chapters that prefer essayistic thought to the construction of dramatic scenes. Both children come into possession of Polaroid cameras, their pictures providing wordless conclusions to each novel. There is another explicit link, one that paradoxically divides the books’ narrators, but revealing it would be a spoiler.The larger contradiction within Luiselli’s work is that although the subjects it returns to – the role and status of the mother, migration, the climate crisis – are universal and urgent, it is becoming ever more inward-looking. The most dramatic journey Beginning Middle End describes is whether it can succeed in becoming the book we hold in our hands. In a knowing moment, the narrator’s daughter studies the mosaic of Proteus – a shapeshifter, just like this novel – “as if she were looking into a mirror or a pool of water, like a little Narcissus peering at himself”. Since finishing the book, it’s the image that has persisted most strongly in my memory.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Alive by Melanie Challenger review – a maverick study of what it means to have a body | Books | The Guardian
description: In this disorienting book, a poet argues we have been looking at nature – and ourselves – the wrong way
Author: Edward Posnett
Headline: In this disorienting book, a poet argues we have been looking at nature – and ourselves – the wrong way
Content: A humboldt squid.Photograph: Brian Skerry/Minden/naturepl.comView image in fullscreenA humboldt squid.Photograph: Brian Skerry/Minden/naturepl.comBooksReviewAlive by Melanie Challenger review – a maverick study of what it means to have a bodyIn this disorienting book, a poet argues we have been looking at nature – and ourselves – the wrong wayEdward PosnettWed 29 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe eastern breakwater of Granton harbour is almost 1km long, and swimmers can follow its crooked finger, heading straight out into the Firth of Forth, while benefiting from its reassuring presence. One Thursday lunchtime, I thought: why not, let’s give it a go, and headed for its tip. I felt cold, but, as I progressed, I seemed to grow strangely warmer. I did not notice the complaints from my body: the creeping numbness which proceeded from my fingers to my elbow, nor the coldness of my pee. Only by the time I exited the water, club footed and claw handed, did it hit me that I was hypothermic.The irony of this reckless exercise was that in my swim bag there was a book by Melanie Challenger called Alive: The Hidden Intelligence of the Living World. It’s an ambitious examination of the wisdom of bodies, a rhizomatic guide not just to our own, but also all the living forms around us: from bacteria to chimps. Her case is that we have ignored or misread the agency and purpose of bodies to our detriment; in a way it is a plea to listen to them. I wish I had read it before my ill-advised swim.Challenger notes that her book was born out of “wild curiosity”, and a sense that the “stories we were telling ourselves … were both presumptuous and unconvincing”. For her, our focus on souls, genes or minds is a distortion of reality, and we should instead direct our attention to our bodies, which have been marginalised, perhaps because they remind us of our own vulnerability and mortality. It is not that Challenger denies the importance of genes; what she questions is the lens through which we read the world.double quotation markShe presents a range of different organisms, from slime to squid, exploring the ways in which they relate and respond to the world around themThroughout the book she vividly presents a range of different organisms, from slime to squid, exploring the ways in which they relate and respond to the world around them. Among other things, Challenger is a poet, and her descriptions are often beautiful. She describes glacial ice as “blue sheened like an eyeball” and a Humboldt squid as “a lozenge of silver”. By denigrating or ignoring bodies, she argues, we are blinded to the sophistication of other life forms, and do not afford them the respect that they deserve; we mistake machines for consciousness and our own consciousness for machines; we destroy habitats with little regard for the non-human life that resides there.Challenger cites an encyclopaedic range of scientists and philosophers, but her own intellectual guide is Aristotle (she thanks him in the acknowledgments). According to her, it was Aristotle who first grasped the intelligence of bodies, though he lacked the science to support his intuitions. She brings him to life at several points in the book, entering into his head, and turning the philosopher – this figure based on a collection of texts, translations, and commentaries – into flesh and bone.I struggle to think of a book for whose subject I have felt more sympathy and excitement: its turn to the body, its trenchant critique of scientific reductionism and misguided metaphors. But as a lay reader I often found myself disoriented, almost dizzied, by the text. I desperately wanted to follow my guide, but I kept on feeling lost, left behind, as the author charged into a dense thicket of ideas and scientific research. This is perhaps the risk run by any pioneer: you can cross a frontier, but can you bring others with you?When I got out of the water, corpse-grey and shaken, I was greeted by two concerned women, experienced swimmers in dry-robes, who kept an eye on me, and offered me a cup of tea and some sound guidance. I’m grateful to them and the way they could quietly read their own bodies, and mine, skilfully relating them to world around us. In a way this book is an invitation to the reader to do something similar; to abandon the harmful readings that we have inherited, and sidestep our own self-destruction.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: After 40 years, Aliens is still shaping the way video games are made | Games | The Guardian
description: James Cameron’s high-octane film sequel is a blueprint for modern action space slashers
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: James Cameron’s high-octane film sequel is a blueprint for modern action space slashers
Content: Take off and nuke the entire site from orbit … Ripley gets out the big guns in Aliens.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyView image in fullscreenTake off and nuke the entire site from orbit … Ripley gets out the big guns in Aliens.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyPushing Buttons newsletterGamesAfter 40 years, Aliens is still shaping the way video games are madeJames Cameron’s high-octane film sequel is a blueprint for modern action space slashersDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeith StuartWed 29 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 13.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is difficult to believe that James Cameron’s Aliens was released into cinemas 40 years ago. The seminal space shooter took the original Alien – a tense slasher film with a tiny cast and one monster – and transformed it into an intergalactic war movie crammed with wry one-liners, massive guns and an actual boss battle finale. As a 14-year-old, I stood in line at the Tatton Gatley cinema, unsure if I’d be allowed in – I came out three hours later a changed person, my head filled with esoteric military slang and a deep fear of beeping motion detectors. For days afterwards, I slept with my duvet covering my mouth so that no facehuggers could get me. (I was a highly impressionable teenager.)It’s little wonder that the film has had such a profound effect on video game design. Take the colonial marines, for example. Although the concept of the space soldier had been around in sci-fi novels since the 1930s, most notably in the works of EE “Doc” Smith and Robert Heinlein (the Starship Troopers), Hicks, Hudson, Vasquez and co, were the perfect 80s rendition, combining the witty banter of contemporary buddy cop flicks with awesome weaponry and hi-tech gadgets. Their influence is easy to spotin Doom, where the nameless marine fights ceaseless waves of hellish monsters using a mix of futuristic rifles and good old shotguns. It’s there too in theHalo series, the Spartan soldiers sporting the same armour and mega weapons, cruising about in very similar highly militarised starships and fighting recognisable hive-mind space beasts. Gears of War,KillzoneandMarathonall borrow from the same set of costumes and deadly accessories.Also important to future game designers was the way in which James Cameron opened up the world of Alien after Ridley Scott’s original locked-room mystery of a movie. He beefed up the Weyland-Yutani Corporation, giving us the stencil for dozens of evil video game mega corps; he brought in an array of weapons from handguns to M41A pulse rifles and the M56 smart guns, introducing the idea of a scaled armoury to discover and master; and he employed a structure based around the repeated rhythm of tense exploration followed by explosive encounters that countless games would follow.View image in fullscreenAlien: Isolation … in your living room, everyone can hear you scream.Photograph: SegaIt’s weird, then, how difficult it has proven to directly translate the movie into games. While the original Alien spawneda cult 8bit translationand thebrilliant Alien: Isolation, Cameron’s sequel is best known for the disastrously buggedAliens: Colonial Marines, which led to alawsuit for deceptive marketing. Elsewhere, third-person co-op blaster Aliens: Fireteam Elite drew mixed reviews but has at least birthed a forthcoming sequel, and the 2D Metroid-style game Aliens: Infestation has plenty of fans. My favourite, though, was one of the two official tie-ins from 1986. Aliens: the Computer Game from Electric Dreams Software was a thrilling proto-FPS, allowing you to control several of the movie’s characters as they stalked through an atmosphere processing plant getting attacked by xenomorphs and facehuggers. I’m not sure it’s ever been bettered.Watching the movie again this week, it’s impossible not to notice all the little scenic and narrative touches that have since shaped how sci-fi action games function. Even the sentry gun, which was cut from the cinematic release and only turned up in the special edition home release, has become a staple special weapon, present in everything fromCall of DutytoHelldivers. I wonder how many of today’s game creators were also stood in cinema lines in the summer of 1986, too young to be there, not quite ready to have their minds blown for ever?What to playView image in fullscreenDanger at every turn … Scarlet Deer Inn.Photograph: Attu GamesThose of us with an interest in the fibre arts are always delighted to see them crop up in other media. Here, embroidered character art helpsScarlet Deer Innto stand out in a crowded market. Once players are in, they’ll find the charming medieval village has some horrific secrets. Players guide mother-of-two Elise through danger-filled caverns on a quest to find her children and prevent them from meeting a gruesome end, a goal that gained additional meaning when the husband-and-wife developers had a baby of their own.
