Armed only with a torch, you must keep it lit or likely repeatedly succumb to the darkness.Jordan Erica WebberAvailable on:PCEstimated playtime:four hoursWhat to readView image in fullscreenRipe for the AI slop machine … Grand Theft Auto VI.Photograph: NintendoIn what is likely to become a familiar problem for the games industry, Rockstar’sGrand Theft Auto VImarketing schedule is being infiltrated by AI-generated trailers purporting to show scenes from the forthcoming game. Examples include asurfing videoand awoman enjoying champagne on a yacht. AsEurogamer points out, the videos are filling a vacuum left by Rockstar’s somewhat stingy approach to releasing in-game footage. The company does notseem to be impressed.Rather embarrassingly for console manufacturers seeking to go digital only,network outagesare back. On Friday,PlayStation Network went downfor several hours, leaving players with no access to their games. And on Monday, it wasthe turn of Xbox, a major outage making it impossible to sign in to user accounts, launch games or download content. While the PlayStation situation has now been resolved, the Xbox network was still having issues at time of press. All hail our disc-less future!When Valve announced its new Steam Machine PC, fans were intrigued by a custom front plate the company had attached to the machine, which appeared to bean e-ink screendisplaying performance data from inside the computer, such as memory and CPU performance. Now, Valve has released all the files and details for what it callsThe Inkterface, so owners can build one – and gaming site Aftermathhas done just that. Very nerdy, but very cool.And if you enjoyed reminiscing aboutAliens,you might want to check out forthcoming bookAliens: The Video Gamesby Mike Diver, a complete history of adaptations, including lots of developer interviews.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to clickSilent Hill Townfall: the series is coming to Scotland, but what fresh horrors will it bring?Glitched into empty space: why video games are obsessed with the BackroomsHaex – a wilder, weirder open-world adventure‘An anthem for the co-dependent’: Bad Magpie’s corvid carnage with a side of existential angstThere Are No Ghosts at the Grand – stripping back the physical and metaphorical layers of a haunted hotelThe best gaming chairs in the UK for comfort, support and serious play in 2026 – testedThe Mermaid Mask – the funniest underwater murder mystery you can play | ★★★★☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenThe gaming canon … a lot of top 100 lists.Photograph: Justin Towell/AlamyThis week’s question is fromBenvia email:“I want to learn more about the history of video games and I wondered if there are any canonical lists of the best titles– perhaps a gaming equivalent of the BFI’s250 Greatest Films of All Timeor the American Film Institute’s100 Years 100 Movies?”Many publications that write about video games have their own top 100 list, although these tends to be compiled by their own critics or readers rather than a broader spread of experts.GQ,GameRantandRolling Stoneall have versions, while IGN has a “mathematically derived” list of thetop 500, andwe’vedonethe best games of the 21st century(so far). For more formal attempts at developing a canon, the Strong Museum has aWorld Video Game Hall of Fame, MoMA hasa games collection(but for some reason its website does NOT want you to find a definitive list!), and for itsArt of Gamesexhibition in 2012, the Smithsonian compiled alist of 80 important titleswith the help of gamers and game makers. There have also been a few books on the subject: try Penguin’s 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die (full disclosure: I wrote some of this book), BFI’s 100 Video Games, or Game On!: From Pong to Oblivion – The Greatest Video Games of All Time, compiled by ex-Edge magazine writers.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterJames CameronAlienRidley ScottfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Silent Hill Townfall: the series is coming to Scotland, but what fresh horrors will it bring? | Games | The Guardian
description: An amnesiac loner arrives in a remote town for who knows what reason … this may sound familiar but this time we’re on a remote Scottish island and surprises lie in wait
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: An amnesiac loner arrives in a remote town for who knows what reason … this may sound familiar but this time we’re on a remote Scottish island and surprises lie in wait
Content: Foggy notions … Silent Hill: TownfallPhotograph: Konami, Annapurna Interactive, Screen Burn/PRView image in fullscreenFoggy notions … Silent Hill: TownfallPhotograph: Konami, Annapurna Interactive, Screen Burn/PRGamesSilent Hill Townfall: the series is coming to Scotland, but what fresh horrors will it bring?An amnesiac loner arrives in a remote town for who knows what reason … this may sound familiar but this time we’re on a remote Scottish island and surprises lie in waitKeith StuartWed 29 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAman washes up at the harbour of a small coastal village, his memories vague, an eerie sea fog rolling in all around him. As beginnings go, this couldn’t be more Silent Hill – an amnesiac loner drawn to a remote town for who knows what reason. But this time, we’re not in the Pacific Northwest of the original games or the Japan of last year’s excellentSilent Hill f. We’re on an island off the northern coast of Scotland, and it’s 1996. Lead character Simon Ordell knows this place, but isn’t sure how – and why does he have an IV cannula stuck in his hand?Announced back in 2022, Townfall is the work of Glasgow-based studio Screen Burn, previously responsible for tense horror adventure titles Stories Untold and Observation. LikeSilent Hillf, it moves the setting far out of Silent Hill itself: St Amelia is a fishing town, inspired by St Monans and dozens of other seafront towns the team visited and extensively photographed.Why make that geographical change? “We felt that players were starting to become a little fatigued,” says series producer Motoi Okamoto. “Silent Hill was becoming slightly repetitive, we were using similar locations, the gameplay felt the same. We wanted to refresh the series and create a new sort of experience by interpreting Silent Hill not as a physical location but as a phenomenon, a state of mind.”View image in fullscreenNo place for a holiday … Silent Hill: Townfall.Photograph: Konami, Annapurna Interactive, Screen BurnDuring a preview event at Konami in Tokyo, we played an almost finished version of the game for two hours, and it’s clear this is very much a Silent Hill experience, but with a deliciously gloomy British slant. The visual detail is incredible. As Simon, you walk along the harbourside with its stacks of lobster cages, and reach the town itself, a muddle of tiny houses, the grey stone walls worn by sea spray, little shops selling seaside tat, an old British Telecom phone box in the town square. It’s familiar but also uncanny because as soon as you arrive, you realise everything has been abandoned. Estate agent signs line every street, the homes are dark, streetlights flicker ominously. There’s a suggestion of local anger at a corporation named CEG – street protests have taken place. A note at the police station says there’s nothing they can do until help arrives.For the opening hour you’re free to explore, letting yourself into any home with an unlocked door, and finding old PCs, horrible bathroom suites and Formica-clad kitchens, and the ordinariness makes it even creepier. As you go, strange little details emerge – Simon was staying in the local hotel, but his room is filled with medical equipment. People have been getting ill, some have disappeared. A male voice on the telephone thanks you for coming back and begs you for help. A little later, you discover a video recording of a woman named Zoe telling Simon, “You can’t stay in this room for ever, you have to come back to me.” It’s got that slow burn feel of the best Silent Hill titles – clues are dredged out of the world in little snippets.View image in fullscreenAnalogue intrigue … Silent Hill: Townfall.Photograph: Konami, Annapurna Interactive, Screen Burn/PR IMAGEFrom the start, it’s clear both the period and the setting have been intricately built into the gameplay. For one early puzzle you have to use a PC in Zoe’s house to check her emails, but to do that, you must restore her electricity by fetching a pre-paid card from the local newsagent and putting it in the meter. It’s something a lot of UK gamers will recognise, especially if they were around in the 90s – although apparently, it’s confused American and Japanese journalists. Elsewhere, the portable radio from previous titles, which was used to sense incoming enemies, is now a small handheld television, expertly styled to look like one of those Casio mini TVs. In certain places you can tune it in to see hazy, static-filled images or video clips that act as puzzle clues; but when monsters are near, it can track their movements through walls.This interest in ageing tech is a familiar element of Screen Burn’s previous titles. “The tactility is the main reason behind it,” says Jon McKellan, director and writer of Townfall. “It’s kind of become our calling card and before Screen Burn I worked onAlien: Isolationand there was a lot of that VHS analogue aesthetic. I like marrying those visual concepts with narrative and UI design. Analogue tech is fragile, it’s imperfect, it feels like it could break at any minute – and all those things work really well with horror. You worry that the gadgets in front of you might not be able to save you from whatever’s out there. I think if Simon was walking around with a mobile phone and Google Maps it would be a very different experience.”As your search of the town takes you from houses and shops to the local medical centre, the evidence of some sort of massive cover-up mounts. And naturally, the monsters arrive – strange, tortured humans with axe heads for faces, their arms bound by leather straps. At first you have nothing but planks to defend yourself with and combat is demanding: you can block or strike, but the creatures are fast, deadly and difficult to take down. There’s no parry or dodge so if you commit, you need very good timing. The alternative is stealth – the CRTV shows you where enemies are, while a peeking system lets you look out from cover to study their patrol patterns, and the first-person perspective means you rely on these elements much more heavily.Our time with the game also took in a slightly later section set in a hellish, phantasmagorical underworld of sewers, wire cages and scary red lighting. It could be beneath the town or lodged in Simon’s brain, but it’s classic Silent Hill territory. This time, however, along with the psychological horror, there are also political undertones – the CEG corporation has exploited and destroyed the village, bringing to mind the plight of towns such as Grangemouth and Mossmoran at the hands of petrochemical giants. Simon’s personal story is set to feed into that.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenWill you take the high road? Silent Hill: TownfallPhotograph: Konami, Annapurna Interactive, Screen Burn/PR IMAGE“We wanted to look at the relationship between the character and the society around them,” says McKellan. “What does it mean for someone to be in a town like this and have an impact on it – what do you do with that? I’m hoping that by the end of the game, people are relating to the decisions, and some of the things Simon has been through. You begin to unravel and process that, and projecting your fears, your inner turmoil on to the world around you is obviously a major Silent Hill component.”There are questions that will need to be answered before acknowledging Townfall as another successful step in the rejuvenation of the series after Silent Hill f. Right now, the enemy figures we’ve seen are very familiar versions of Silent Hill archetypes and it’s difficult to judge how intuitive the new stealth/peek system will become. But the setting is beautifully realised, while the shadowing of the Silent Hill 2 narrative – a man searching for a woman he seems to have had a relationship with – is intriguing, and from what we’ve seen, highly likely to be subverted in some horrible way. This is promisingly bleak stuff.“There is a lot of personal trauma in there – things that have happened to me or members of the team,” says McKellan. “We try to pull reference from real life because usually that’s less bombastic and more grounded than Hollywood, and to me that’s where the best horror comes from. I’m just channelling all that trauma instead of getting a therapist!”Silent Hill: Townfall will be released on 24 SeptemberKeith Stuart attended a press event in Tokyo with other journalists. Transport and accommodation costs were paid for by Konami.Explore more on these topicsGamesSilent HillfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: BBCSO/Oramo review – Turnage’s satisfying and clever Festen Suite makes UK debut  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The festering atmosphere of Thomas Vinterberg’s film and its celebrated opera adaptation lingers in this vivid orchestration, a foil to Sibelius’s cathartic second symphony
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: The festering atmosphere of Thomas Vinterberg’s film and its celebrated opera adaptation lingers in this vivid orchestration, a foil to Sibelius’s cathartic second symphony
Content: ‘A hip-shimmy and wriggle’ … Sakari Oramo conducting the BBC Symphony Orchestra at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreen‘A hip-shimmy and wriggle’ … Sakari Oramo conducting the BBC Symphony Orchestra at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewBBCSO/Oramo review – Turnage’s satisfying and clever Festen Suite makes UK debutRoyal Albert Hall, LondonThe festering atmosphere of Thomas Vinterberg’s film and its celebrated opera adaptation lingers in this vivid orchestration, a foil to Sibelius’s cathartic second symphonyAlexandra CoghlanWed 29 Jul 2026 08.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 10.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSibelius’s second symphony is “a confession of the soul” – an outpouring, however ambiguous. But what happens when a confession never comes, and a secret festers instead in collective silence? That’s the starting point for Festen, Thomas Vinterberg’s 1998 film, which wasadapted into an award-winning operaby Mark-Anthony Turnage and librettist Lee Hall last year.There’s a fair bit of plot to a work in which incestuous child abuse is exposed during a patriarch’s 60th birthday party, but it’s the atmosphere that lingers, stylishly distilled in Turnage’s new Festen Suite – receiving its UK premiere here from theBBC Symphony Orchestraand Sakari Oramo.You can almost smell the stale wine and cigar smoke coming off the composer’s vividly orchestrated prelude, gurning with faux-jollity – literally beaten into it by percussion wallops that try to keep its lurching progress on track. Thereafter, the eight-movement suite ricochets between lyricism – the gentle melancholy of Blue or Green, pastoral tenderness in Grandma’s Song – and denial, slinky in the Conga with its rictus grin, sleazy in Interlude I. Then revelations break the surface in the jabbing thrusts of The Fight, string padding stripped away to allow brass and woodwind to land their punches cleanly. It’s cleverly made and musically satisfying on its own terms, without the dramatic scaffolding of the opera. I think we’ll be hearing it a lot in future.View image in fullscreenSensitively faithful to Britten’s conception: cellist Guy Johnston with Oramo and the BBCSOPhotograph: Mark AllanIf the Turnage brought a hip-shimmy and wriggle to Oramo’s conducting, the Sibelius – home turf for the Finn – found him straight as a Scots pine, guiding us through this patchwork of a symphony with clarity, that finale in sight from the off. Momentum rather than release was the order of the day, until at last he let the brass off the leash, romping us home with grandeur, certainly, but also an overflowing joy.It was the catharsis we needed after Britten’s inscrutable cello symphony. Soloist Guy Johnston stayed scrupulously, sensitively faithful to the composer’s conception: the orchestra’s equal, often a part of the texture rather than its focus. It’s a tough balance to pull off anywhere; in the Royal Albert Hall it risked disappearing entirely in a cerebral performance whose subtleties will have been captured on radio, but which were a little lost in the moment.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicProms 2026BBC Symphony OrchestraMark-Anthony TurnageJean SibeliusPromsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Staff at newest V&A site in London vote overwhelmingly for strike action | V&A | The Guardian
description: V&A Storehouse dispute centres on toilet and hydration breaks as employees across V&A in London also vote to strike in wider action
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: V&A Storehouse dispute centres on toilet and hydration breaks as employees across V&A in London also vote to strike in wider action
Content: The V&A Storehouse offers an ‘order an object’ service which requires staff members to retrieve items requested by members of the public from around the building.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe V&A Storehouse offers an ‘order an object’ service which requires staff members to retrieve items requested by members of the public from around the building.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianV&AStaff at newest V&A site in London vote overwhelmingly for strike actionV&A Storehouse dispute centres on toilet and hydration breaks as employees across V&A in London also vote to strike in wider actionNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentWed 29 Jul 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStaff at the V&A’s Storehouse site in eastLondonhave voted overwhelmingly to strike in a dispute over what they say are inadequate toilet and hydration breaks.They will join staff across V&A sites in London who on Wednesday also voted to strike in a wider dispute over pay, working conditions, andthe museum having declined to seek living wage accreditation.The trade union Prospect said members at V&A Storehouse, which opened in May 2025, are denied enough time during the day for toilet breaks or hydration.The dispute centres on collections access officers who facilitate the “order an object” service, a central part of the Storehouse’s offering of public access to its vast collection.The union is calling for two paid breaks a day, saying staff need time to use the toilet and hydrate during what it describes as a punishing schedule. It said a collective grievance failed to secure an “extremely reasonable request for customary paid breaks”, which workers elsewhere in the organisation receive.Prospect said many of the staff had been recruited from the local community, something the V&A had highlighted publicly, but they were treated worse than colleagues at other sites.One Prospect member told the Guardian: “We get just one unpaid lunch hour, even though we’re on our feet for long hours, interacting with the public and doing a lot of manual labour.“Breaks are a welfare issue. The Storehouse is purpose-built for storing objects, but they haven’t really thought about the human aspect – how far we have to travel around the building or where the bathrooms are.“We’ve experienced a lot of dehydration, and sometimes people don’t even go to the bathroom for the whole day.”They added: “We’ve tried every internal procedure possible. We’ve brought the issue up in one-to-one meetings, we did a petition, we went through a formal grievance, and we’ve never got proper answers.”V&A East Storehouse and Norwich Castle among finalists for museum of the yearRead moreAnother Prospect member said: “Every day we go into work, there’s someone who has a headache because they’re dehydrated. Management says we always have time to take breaks and drink water.“But we need someone to relieve us because we can’t leave trolleys of collection objects unattended. We need breaks scheduled fixed into our calendars.“We are the newest department at the V&A. We are the most diverse back-of-house department. It’s not lost on us that we were hired to represent the east London community, but our welfare is being neglected.”At V&A Storehouse, 100% of those voting backed strike action on a turnout of nearly 88%, while 92% supported action short of a strike.As part of the wider dispute, Prospect is seeking a minimum 4% pay rise for staff earning above the living wage, time-and-a-half for bank holiday working, accreditation as a London living wage employer within 12 months and improved food provision at V&A East sites.Across the V&A, 83% voted for strike action on an 82% turnout, and 95% voted for action short of a strike. The timing of any industrial action has yet to be decided.Mike Clancy, Prospect’s general secretary, said: “This incredible new way of showing off our heritage is being delivered by workers who are denied adequate break time to use the toilet or have a drink of water.“Visitors will be appalled to learn that the kinds of working practices unions campaign against in companies like Amazon also exist in an internationally renowned heritage institution.”He said the dispute reflected “a shocking lack of respect” for staff across the museum.The V&A has been approached for comment. Responding previously toa separate strike ballot by the Public and Commercial Services union, it said all staff had access to water, toilet facilities and regular breaks, and pointed to additional measures introduced during this summer’s heatwave, including extra rest breaks, staff rotations and temporary gallery closures.The London living wage is£14.80 an hour. While the V&A has said all its staff are paid at least this rate, some of the museum’s outsourced contractors are not in receipt of the living wage and V&A has not so far become an accredited living wage employer, although it says this will be reviewed this year. V&A Dundee is an accredited living wage employer.Explore more on these topicsV&ALondonEnglandIndustrial actionTrade unionsMuseumsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Dua Lipa to interview Zadie Smith at London Literature festival | Books | The Guardian
description: The pop star is curating the 2026 festival, which also features Patti Smith, Mustafa and Ta-Nehisi Coates, as part of the Southbank Centre’s anniversary year
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: The pop star is curating the 2026 festival, which also features Patti Smith, Mustafa and Ta-Nehisi Coates, as part of the Southbank Centre’s anniversary year
Content: Dua Lipa is curating this year’s London Literature festival.Photograph: Madison PhippsView image in fullscreenDua Lipa is curating this year’s London Literature festival.Photograph: Madison PhippsBooksDua Lipa to interview Zadie Smith at London Literature festivalThe pop star is curating the 2026 festival, which also features Patti Smith, Mustafa and Ta-Nehisi Coates, as part of the Southbank Centre’s anniversary yearEmma LoffhagenWed 29 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZadie Smith, Patti Smith and Mustafa are among the star names lined up to be interviewed by Dua Lipa, as the pop star reveals her curation of this year’s London Literature festival at theSouthbank Centre.The festival, now in its 19th year, will run from 21 October to 1 November, with the Brit award-winning singer shaping a programme of events in collaboration with her Service95 book club.Lipa said curating the programme had been “a true joy”, adding that she wanted to bring together “some of the most exciting writers, poets and thinkers from around the globe”, alongside more familiar names.Lipa will sit down withZadie Smithon 24 October to discuss her 2000 debut novel, White Teeth, published when Smith was just 24. The pair are expected to reflect on “learning to live with an artistic legacy earned at such a young age”, and how the novel’s characters might fare in Britain today.The night after, she will interviewPatti Smithabouther memoir Bread of Angels,which charts Smith’s life from childhood, through her marriage to Fred “Sonic” Smith, and her return to music after his death.View image in fullscreenZadie Smith will discuss her novel White Teeth.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamyThe programme will also feature appearances from the Sudanese Canadian poet and musicianMustafa,the Nobel peace laureate Nadia Murad discussing her memoir, I Choose My Beginning, and a conversation between Ta-Nehisi Coates and Tareq Baconi on Baconi’s new book about Palestine.Other events include a translated fiction showcase, a poetry and music night with Kae Tempest, and Censorship Live!, a collaboration with English PEN examining threats to free expression.Lipa has increasingly established herself as an advocate for reading. She launched her book club in 2023 as an extension of her wider cultural platform Service95, which sees monthly selections and long-form author interviews with writers including Margaret Atwood, George Saunders and Olga Tokarczuk. Last month, she opened a permanent collection of 100 banned, censored and challenged books inside the historic Livraria Lello bookshop in Porto, Portugal.Mark Ball, the Southbank Centre’s artistic director, said Lipa’s “deep curiosity about the world” made her a fitting curator for the venue’s 75th anniversary. “It’s a milestone year and she’s the perfect curator to help us celebrate it,” he added.The literature festival also includes free family events and a wider national programme, part of Southbank Centre’s efforts to reach a million people across the UK in 2026.Last year, the festival was curated by Self Esteem, and previous headliners include Ai Weiwei, Greta Thunberg, Malala Yousafzai, Margaret Atwood, Philip Pullman, Tom Hanks and Yulia Navalnaya.Tickets go on sale to Southbank Centre members on 3 August, Service95 members on 4 August, and the general public on 5 August.Explore more on these topicsBooksDua LipaSouthbank CentreZadie SmithPatti SmithFestivalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: French music producer Kavinsky, known for Drive soundtrack hit Nightcall, dies aged 50 | Electronic music | The Guardian
description: French authorities investigate death of musician who performed at Paris Olympics, but say ‘no suspicious elements’ at play
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: French authorities investigate death of musician who performed at Paris Olympics, but say ‘no suspicious elements’ at play
Content: Kavinsky performing at the 2024 Olympic Games closing ceremony in Paris.Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKavinsky performing at the 2024 Olympic Games closing ceremony in Paris.Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty ImagesElectronic musicFrench music producer Kavinsky, known for Drive soundtrack hit Nightcall, dies aged 50French authorities investigate death of musician who performed at Paris Olympics, but say ‘no suspicious elements’ at playBen Beaumont-ThomasWed 29 Jul 2026 07.55 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe French electronic musician Kavinsky, known for the song Nightcall which achieved iconic status after its inclusion in the Ryan Gosling filmDrive, has died aged 50.A police source speaking to French newspaper Le Figaro indicated that the suspected cause of death was a stroke. Kavinsky, real name Vincent Belorgey, had reportedly been complaining of headaches in recent days, and he was discovered at home after a concerned neighbour alerted emergency services.Parisian authorities are investigating his death but said “no suspicious elements” were found at his home.Emmanuel Macron was among those paying tribute to him, calling him “a source of French pride forever”.Part of the rich electronic music scene inFrancethat flourished in the wake of Daft Punk and others, Belorgey earned so much acclaim for Nightcall that he ended up performing it at the closing ceremony of the Olympic Games in Paris in 2024, backed by the French band Phoenix and Belgian pop singer Angèle on vocals.Born in Paris in 1975, Belorgey’s music career took off in the mid-00s. The high-energy electro of his debut singleTestarossa Autodrivemeant it dovetailed with the “blog house” scene that had also spawned French artists such as Justice and SebastiAn, and he was signed to the label Record Makers, with whom he released five EPs and two albums.With Brazilian singer Lovefoxxx on vocals, 2010’s Nightcall became his most successful and renowned track. Co-produced with Daft Punk member Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo, this prowling, nocturnal electronic reverie paired malevolence and romance in a way that made it a perfect choice for the opening credits of Nicolas Winding Refn’s 2011 thriller Drive. It has been streamed more than half a billion times onSpotifyalone, with another 350m YouTube plays. It reached the French Top 10 on release, with the version performed at the Olympics reaching No 3.His debut album Outrun sketched out the grand concept for Belorgey’s Kavinsky alter ego – a young man who crashes a Ferrari Testarossa in the 80s and returns zombie-like in the 00s – and it reached No 2 in the French album charts. He followed it with Reborn, in 2022.Along with the vintage Ferrari references and sunglasses-and-bomber-jacket fashion sense, his sound also harked back to 1980s and that decade’s cinematic synths. “Everyone says, that guy is stuck in the past!”, he said in a 2013 interview. “I don’t sit around missing things from older times – I’m just from the 80s, and so my influences come from that period. That is what is in my veins.”The Weeknd appeared on a version of Kavinsky’s songOdd Look, and in 2022 Kavinsky said the pair would potentially work on new music together.Also paying tribute was French culture minister Catherine Pégard, who said: “France loses one of its most singular voices. From the film Drive to the Paris Olympics, the entire world had pulsed to Nightcall. Both danceable and nostalgic, his music will continue to resonate across generations and borders.”Explore more on these topicsElectronic musicPop and rockParisFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Andrew Scott’s Oscar-tipped Ian Charleson biopic to open London film festival | London film festival | The Guardian
description: ‘Few films will leave a lasting imprint on audiences this year quite like Elsinore,’ LFF director says of movie about Chariots of Fire actor
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: ‘Few films will leave a lasting imprint on audiences this year quite like Elsinore,’ LFF director says of movie about Chariots of Fire actor
Content: Andrew Scott in Elsinore.Photograph: Anthony Dickenson/© Focus FeaturesView image in fullscreenAndrew Scott in Elsinore.Photograph: Anthony Dickenson/© Focus FeaturesLondon film festivalAndrew Scott’s Oscar-tipped Ian Charleson biopic to open London film festival‘Few films will leave a lasting imprint on audiences this year quite like Elsinore,’ LFF director says of movie about Chariots of Fire actorCatherine ShoardWed 29 Jul 2026 09.22 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 10.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElsinore, one of the most hotly anticipated dramas of the year, has been announced as the opening night film at this year’sLondon film festival. The drama, which stars Andrew Scott as actor Ian Charleson, will have its European premiere at the Southbank Centre – yards from the National Theatre, in which many of its scenes are set.Directed bySimon Stoneand written by Stephen Beresford (who reunites with Scott 12 years after Pride), the film depicts the final months in the life of the highly acclaimed actor, who reprised the role of Hamlet while terminally ill, aged 40.Diagnosed with Aids in 1986, the actor – who had come to international fame through his roles in Chariots of Fire and Gandhi – was drafted in by Richard Eyre to take over the role of Hamlet in a 1989 production after Daniel Day-Lewis abruptly left, having seen theghost of his fatheron stage.Charleson, who concentrated on classical theatre work both before and after his film success, persuaded Eyre to let him reprise the role he had first played 15 years before, despite the director’s misgivings over his health. Both fellow cast and crew, as well as the audience, were told that Charleson’s face was swollen following a sinus operation; in fact he was suffering from septicaemia.Charleson’s performance, which ran for six weeks until mid-November, was widely felt to be one of the finest ever seen on stage. The day after his final show, Ian McKellen refused the Evening Standard award for best actor and instead gave his statuette to Charleson.View image in fullscreenIan Charleson, centre, in Chariots of Fire.Photograph: Moviestore/Rex/ShutterstockCharleson died eight weeks later and was the first showbiz star in the UK to request that Aids be listed as the cause of death, leading to considerably more awareness about the condition.The film also starsOlivia Colmanas Charleson’s doctor, alongside Billie Piper, Johnny Flynn and Monica Dolan. Dickie Beau, who toured a one-man tribute to Charleson’s Hamlet for six years, also features, while David Dawson plays Derek Jarman. It is believed Juliet Stevenson and Peter Mullan play Charleson’s parents.Elsinore has also been selected as a gala screening at the Toronto film festival, with a world premiere a week beforehand at the Telluride film festival predicted.Kristy Matheson, BFI London film festival director, said: “Anchored by Andrew Scott’s astounding central performance, few films will leave a lasting imprint on audiences this year quite like Elsinore.” The actor’s role in the film has already attracted considerable awards buzz, with many anticipating voters will be keen to reward a popular actor whose role inAll of Us Strangerswas overlooked in both Oscar and Bafta nominations.Elsinore opens in the US on 20 November and in the UK on 29 January. The London film festival is on 7-18 October.Explore more on these topicsLondon film festivalAndrew ScottOlivia ColmanSimon StonenewsShareReuse this content

title: The 10 best running vests and hydration packs in the UK for men and women, tested by an ultra runner | Running | The Guardian
description: Here are our expert’s favourite running packs for everyday plods, all-out races and trail adventures
Author: Kieran Alger
Headline: Here are our expert’s favourite running packs for everyday plods, all-out races and trail adventures
Content: View image in fullscreenThe FilterRunningReviewThe 10 best running vests and hydration packs in the UK for men and women, tested by an ultra runnerHere are our expert’s favourite running packs for everyday plods, all-out races and trail adventuresThe best running shoes for every runnerKieran AlgerWed 29 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Runners can end up carrying a surprising amount of paraphernalia – phone, keys, jacket, maybe snacks (OK, definitely snacks) and water. If you dare to venture into the world of ultra marathons, that list grows even longer. While shorts and running tights have started packing in extra pockets to ease the burden, the best way to boost your mid-run storage is to invest in a running vest or hydration pack.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Likerunning backpacks, running vests range from minimal race-ready designs to big-volume options for trail-taming self-sufficiency. The best running vests give you the confidence to go further, knowing you’ve got everything you need to conquer your run. Over the years, I’ve relied on vests to help me through thousands of training miles, as well as dozens of marathons and ultras.I’ve also spent the past two months plodding UK roads and trails, covering hundreds of miles in models from brands such as Salomon, Osprey, Kiprun and Nathan to find the best running vests you can buy. Here are my top picks, all unisex unless men’s and women’s fits are specified below.At a glanceBest running vest overall:The North Face Summit run vest 5l£124.99 at Sports ShoesBestbudget running vest:Harrier Kinder 10l£29.99 at HarrierBest running vest for hydration:Nathan Pinnacle Series Vapor 12lFrom £100.94 at AmazonBest running vest for winter runs:OMM UltraFire 5From £72 at AmazonBest running vest for urban miles and longer runs:Stolt 4l vest£129 at Stolt RunningWhy you should trust meI test running gear to pay the mortgage. So when I’m not training for a race, I’m generally running around, sampling the latest shoes, clothing and other kinds of running kit. If I can get somewhere by running, I prefer to. I’ve also run close to 70 marathons, as well as lots of ultras and frequent solo marathons around the streets of London.Over the past decade, I’ve tested dozens of running vests and hydration packs while on a perpetual personal and professional mission to find the very best. Whether you’re racing 100 miles or just out for an easy 10k, it’s a piece of kit every runner should own.How I testedView image in fullscreenReady to run … each vest was tested for storage, hydration, comfort and durability.Photograph: Kieran Alger/The GuardianI strapped myself into 19 running vests from a wide selection of brands. I recently conducted a full test of biggerrunning packs, so this test focused on lighter, lower-capacity vests.First, I challenged each vest’s capacity by filling them with a typical run payload. This included awaterproof jacket, a litre of water and enough energy gels to cover a five-hour marathon, plus essentials such as gloves, ahead torch, abattery packand other bits and bobs to keep me self-sufficient, safe and warm on a solo long run.I then plodded my way through a series of test runs, first with a full load and then removing some of the kit to see how it performed.After many, many miles (and a lot of energy gels), I rated the running vests based on storage capacity and hydration options, plus practicality, fit, comfort and durability. I gave extra kudos for versatility and overall value for money. Here are my top picks.The best hydration vests for runningBest running vest overall:The North Face Summit run vest 5lThe North FaceSummit 5l run vestfrom£124.99£124.99 at Sports Shoes£130 at the North FaceWhat we loveLight body-hugging fit; easy soft flask accessWhat we don’t loveNo sweat or rain protectionView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kieran Alger/The Guardian£124.99 at Sports Shoes£130 at the North FaceDesigned for speedy trail racing but equally good for long Sunday runs, this Summit five-litre vest is light, breathable and packed full of clever details.Why we love itLightweight, airy and fast drying, this flexible vest takes top place in our best running vests test because it hits the sweet spot with a barely there, secure fit, good flexible storage, comfort and versatility.You’ll see elite trail runners using it to race Alpine ultras, but it’s also an excellent option for regular folk tackling trail adventures, long city runs or even just runs where you want to carry water and a few gels.I used it for a 22-hour Berlin Wall 100-mile race, and I liked the body-hugging, adjustable fit. It’s not completely bounce-free when it’s fully loaded, but the front straps and extra side compression straps work well for fine-tuning the fit.The five litres of storage is ample for most adventures. I love the two zippered bottle holsters that make it much easier to refill and replace your soft flasks. There are two stretch drop-in pockets upfront for easy access to gels, two more in the rear, and a trekking pole sleeve that can also double as a jacket stash.The zippered phone pocket happily swallows larger smartphones, but there’s no weatherproofing here. The fine fabric is incredibly light, and the back-panel mesh can leak sweat through to the main rear pocket, so any spare kit ideally needs to be in a dry bag.It’s a shame that …there’s no weatherproof pocket.Suitable for:lightweight racing and long runsCapacity:5lSizing available:XS, S, M, L, XLWeight (M):169gSoft flask compatible?Yes (included)The North FaceSummit 5l run vestfrom£124.99£124.99 at Sports Shoes£130 at the North FaceWhat we loveLight body-hugging fit; easy soft flask accessWhat we don’t loveNo sweat or rain protectionBest budget running vest:Harrier Kinder 10lHarrierKinder 10l£29.99£29.99 at HarrierWhat we loveLots for the price; plenty of sizes for a better fitWhat we don’t loveIt’s a bit heavy, and the phone pocket is too smallView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kieran Alger/The Guardian£29.99 at HarrierHarrier’s trail vest is a reliable yet affordable workhorse, pairing excellent comfort with loads of stash space.Why we love itThe Kinder 10-litre is on the heavier side for a trail vest. But you trade the extra weight for extra padding in the back and harness, and form-fitting fabric that moulds nicely to your lumps and bumps. This all adds up to boosted comfort and minimal bounce on longer-haul adventures.The wide shoulder harness prevents unwanted pressure points and cutting in, even with a heavy load. The mesh back panel also keeps things pretty airy, though I would have liked a better barrier between my dry kit in the large main compartment and my inevitably sweaty back.Storage is solid. There are nine easy-to-reach pockets upfront, including room for soft flasks (sold separately), two well-sized stretch pockets and two zippered pockets with nice big zips. You also get a zip pocket on the shoulder strap, but sadly it’s too small for even a smaller phone.Two height-adjustable sternum straps let you adjust the fit to how you like it. I enjoyed the smart details, such as little silicone grippers on the straps that make them easier to grip and pull, and a bungee cord that can securely cinch kit and/or hold a jacket. A great all-rounder that offers excellent value.It’s a shame that …the phone pocket is tiny.Suitable for:long runs, trail runs, hikes and run commutesCapacity:10lSizing available:XXS, XS, S, M, L, XLWeight (M):287gSoft flask compatible?Yes (not included)HarrierKinder 10l£29.99£29.99 at HarrierWhat we loveLots for the price; plenty of sizes for a better fitWhat we don’t loveIt’s a bit heavy, and the phone pocket is too smallBest running vest for hydration:Nathan Pinnacle Series Vapor 12lNathanPinnacle Series Vapor 12l£100.94From £100.94 at AmazonWhat we loveComes with a 1.6-litre hydration bladderWhat we don’t lovePhone pockets are a bit of a squeezeView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kieran Alger/The GuardianFrom £100.94 at AmazonWith a smart hydration bladder system and enough capacity to tackle big mileage on the road or trail, the Pinnacle quenches your thirst for adventure. I tested the unisex version, but there’s also awomen’s fitwith smaller sizes.Why we love itA close-fitting soft fabric vest with a second skin feel, the Nathan Pinnacle is wonderfully comfortable and surprisingly roomy. It’s light and compact enough for shorter runs, but the 12-litre capacity and impressive pocket array provide excellent storage and organisation for longer runs, too.The main large rear compartment has an easy-access diagonal zipper that makes it simple to stow and retrieve your stuff in a hurry. There are two Velcro stretch pockets within easy reach and two water-resistant, zippered harness pockets, including somewhere to store your phone (though it was a squeeze for a larger iPhone in a case). The front right zip pocket also has a headphone-case-friendly pill pocket and a safety whistle.The Pinnacle comes with a 1.6-litre insulated bladder, with handy magnets to fix your hydration tube in place on the harness: no flappy hose here. You can also carry soft flasks, though you’ll need to buy your own.The substantial, height-adjustable chest and sternum straps made it easy to find a fine-tuned fit, with large glove-friendly clips.It’s a shame that …there aren’t more muted colour options.Suitable for:ultra-running, long-distance or all-day adventuresCapacity:12lSizing available:XXS,XS, S, M, L, XLWeight (M):386g with empty bladderSoft flask compatible?Yes, not includedNathanPinnacle Series Vapor 12l£100.94From £100.94 at AmazonWhat we loveComes with a 1.6-litre hydration bladderWhat we don’t lovePhone pockets are a bit of a squeezeBest running vest for winter runs:OMM UltraFire 5OMMUltraFire 5from£72£74.95 at Cotswold OutdoorFrom £72 at AmazonWhat we loveThe zip pulls are nice and grabbable – even with glovesWhat we don’t loveSoft flasks aren’t includedView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kieran Alger/The Guardian£74.95 at Cotswold OutdoorFrom £72 at AmazonOMM makes great mountain-going gear, and this mid-capacity vest is ideal for battling tougher terrain and changeable weather.Why we love itThis OMM UltraFire vest is great for storage. It has loads of upfront space, and a big water-resistant rear roll-top compartment keeps spare kit dry, safe from the elements and your sweaty back.The seven easy-to-reach front pockets include two 500ml soft flask holders, two huge stretch-mesh front pockets, and two zippered pockets ideal for securing a smartphone and other mission-critical kit. There’s also a small mesh pocket I found great for storing gloves and a head torch.With loads of access to snacks, hats and all your other essentials, it’s great for runs where you don’t want to waste time stopping to dig around in the main compartment, such as wet winter runs.You also have the option to fix a two-litre bladder in the back, though sadly there’s no clip to attach the hose to the front harness. But other neat touches are included: bungees on the back for attaching extra kit; a strap to cinch everything down; a reinforced bottom in case you put your bag on a wet floor; and a built-in safety whistle.It’s a shame that …there are no soft flasks included and there’s no hydration hose clip.Suitable for:long runs and trail runsCapacity:5lSizing available:S, M, LWeight (M):228gSoft flask compatible?Yes (not included)OMMUltraFire 5from£72£74.95 at Cotswold OutdoorFrom £72 at AmazonWhat we loveThe zip pulls are nice and grabbable – even with glovesWhat we don’t loveSoft flasks aren’t includedBest running vest for urban miles and longer runs:Stolt 4l vestStolt4l vest£129£129 at Stolt RunningWhat we loveReally well built and durable with excellent comfortWhat we don’t loveLimited accessible storage and can run a bit hotView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kieran Alger/The Guardian£129 at Stolt RunningThe Stolt four-litre vest is built stronger than most, designed to handle everything from long Sunday runs to daylong ultras.Why we love itThis is a no-nonsense running vest that screams “solid durability”. While some vests are a bit flimsy, here everything from the harness to the back is built robustly, with a more padded feeling from the much thicker fabric. That makes it a touch heavier than many of the vests on test, but that’s the price for extra cushioned comfort and durability.I tested a medium/large and the fit was close. It hugged securely with virtually no movement, and two height-adjustable front straps made it easy to lock down. The vest sits high on your torso, keeping everything well out of the way of flailing arms.There are nine pockets: in the front there are two soft flask holsters, two slip pockets for gels and other essentials, and two water-resistant lined zipped pockets that can swallow a larger smartphone. There’s not much stretch and flex to those front storage slots, though, which limits what you can carry and makes it all feel somewhat squeezed. At the rear, the two-litre zipped pocket has enough room for a lightweight shell jacket, or there’s a couple of loops if you want to stash the jacket externally (or fit in a couple of trekking poles if you head for the hills).It also comes with two 500ml soft flasks and some reflective detailing. There’s no built-in whistle or key hook, though, which I’ve come to expect as standard.It’s a shame that …front storage is a bit cramped, and it can run a bit hot.Suitable for:everyday miles, longer runs and races carrying minimal kitCapacity:4lSizing available:XS/S, M/LWeight (M):205gSoft flask compatible?Yes (included)Stolt4l vest£129£129 at Stolt RunningWhat we loveReally well built and durable with excellent comfortWhat we don’t loveLimited accessible storage and can run a bit hotThe best of the restDecathlon Kiprun Race 900 3lDecathlonRace 900 3l£49.99£49.99 at DecathlonWhat we loveBrilliant barely there fit for running fast and lightWhat we don’t loveNo rear storage or weatherproof pocketsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kieran Alger/The Guardian£49.99 at DecathlonBest for:marathonsA great-value option that weighs just 90g, this super-minimal Decathlon Kiprun three-litre vest is perfect for runs and races where you only need the bare essentials. This racing hydration pack is set up for chasing PBs across any distance, but particularly ideal for marathons where you want to bring your own backup hydration. There’s room for two250ml soft flasks(sadly not included), two big front stretch pockets and front zippered stowage that held my 6.7inch iPhone 15 Pro Max.The thin fabric and mesh back aren’t as robust as on heavier vests, but it all stays cool even when you’re working hard. It also dries fast if you get wet or sweaty. Rear storage is limited to a mesh pouch that’s only really big enough for a lightweight jacket. But this vest is all about having water, gels, a phone and a few bits right where you can reach them. Oh, and a big thumbs up for the wide range of sizes from XXS to XL.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s not as versatile as a larger-capacity vest.Suitable for:everyday runs, fast training runs, races and marathons;capacity:3l;sizing available:XXS, XS, S, M, L, XL;weight (M):94g;soft flask compatible?Yes (not included)DecathlonRace 900 3l£49.99£49.99 at DecathlonWhat we loveBrilliant barely there fit for running fast and lightWhat we don’t loveNo rear storage or weatherproof pocketsSilva Strive 5SilvaStrive 5from£59£59 at RunningXpert£66.99 at Mountain WarehouseWhat we loveCompact and lightweight with a better fit for smaller framesWhat we don’t loveShoulder harness is prone to rolling upView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kieran Alger/The Guardian£59 at RunningXpert£66.99 at Mountain WarehouseBest for:petite runnersLighter and sleeker, Silva’s extra-small Strive 5 weighs in at just over 150g while the large is only 191g. The soft, flexible ripstop fabric and 3D mesh have a close-hugging fit and more compact cut, ideal for anyone who feels swamped by larger vests. The five-litre storage is spread across soft flask holders, two big stretch pockets on the front, a phone-friendly zippered pocket (sadly not water-protected), and a large rear compartment that accommodates a hydration bladder. The large stretch-mesh rear pouch is perfect for stashing jackets.The wide harness isn’t very padded and can sometimes roll up, and soft fabric vests like this are never entirely bounce-free when you’re packing full soft flasks. The hook clips on the bungee sternum straps were a bit fiddly with gloves, too, although they adjust easily for a fairly secure fit.It didn’t make the final cut because …it wasn’t entirely bounce-free when fully loaded.Suitable for:long-distance runs and races;capacity:5l;sizing available:XS, S, M, L;weight (M):170g;soft flask compatible?Yes (not included)SilvaStrive 5from£59£59 at RunningXpert£66.99 at Mountain WarehouseWhat we loveCompact and lightweight with a better fit for smaller framesWhat we don’t loveShoulder harness is prone to rolling upCamelBak Apex Pro 12lCamelBakApex Pro 12lfrom£139.38£169.99 at Tredz£139.38 at AmazonWhat we loveBucketloads of space in a low-bounce vestWhat we don’t loveA bit big for the day-to-dayView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kieran Alger/The Guardian£169.99 at Tredz£139.38 at AmazonBest for:big loads, run-hiking and fast-packingThe Apex Pro 12l is one of the best options when you need more capacity for longer runs, adventures and races but you still want a vest rather than a regular backpack.You can pack in an impressive amount. There are two front-holstered soft flasks and an optionaltwo-litre bladderthat you’ll have to buy separately, plus almost endless storage for all your other fuel and essentials, including a water-resistant zippered pocket, big enough to carry larger smartphones like my iPhone 15 Pro Max. For steeper, challenging terrain, there’s a handy detachable quiver (think of an archer’s arrow sleeve) for trekking poles, and it’s reliably comfortable for long runs, with a soft, comfortable, thicker fabric back and harness. Built-in Recco safety technology can also help rescue crews find you, should something go wrong.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s a bit too big for everyday use, unless you run-commute.Suitable for:long solo runs, ultra races and off-grid adventures;capacity:12l;sizing available:XS, S, M, L, XL;weight (M):345g;soft flask compatible?Yes (included)CamelBakApex Pro 12lfrom£139.38£169.99 at Tredz£139.38 at AmazonWhat we loveBucketloads of space in a low-bounce vestWhat we don’t loveA bit big for the day-to-daySaysky Flow Vest 12l packSayskyFlow Vest 12l pack£177£177 at SayskyWhat we loveBig capacity in a very light, comfy vestWhat we don’t loveIt’s a bit expensiveView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kieran Alger/The Guardian£177 at SayskyBest for:trail runningA 12-litre pack that feels like a five-litre on the move. This brilliantly versatile vest offers enough stash space for longer trail excursions and ultra races while staying lightweight. It doesn’t feel baggy when you’re just carrying water and a few gels on long training runs, either.The slightly padded, bounce-free harness has a great hugging fit; the adjustable hook-fastening system secures easily and doesn’t work loose. Storage is pretty practical, too, with two 500ml soft flasks, two big zippered front pockets, open drop-in pockets with toggles to secure important items, plus a large main compartment that’s big enough for a jacket and waterproof trousers. The rear well can also take a bladder, and there’s a built-in safety whistle.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s on the pricey side.Suitable for:long runs and trail adventures;capacity:12l;sizing available:XS, S, M, L;weight (M):233g without bottles;soft flask compatible?Yes (included)SayskyFlow Vest 12l pack£177£177 at SayskyWhat we loveBig capacity in a very light, comfy vestWhat we don’t loveIt’s a bit expensiveOsprey Duro/Dyna LTOspreyDuro/Dyna LTfrom£55.30Men’s, £65 at TredzWomen’s, £55.30 at AmazonWhat we loveComfortable with a close fit for long distancesWhat we don’t loveWorries about mission-critical kit bouncing outView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kieran Alger/The GuardianMen’s (Duro)£65 at Tredz£80 at OspreyWomen’s (Dyna)£80 at OspreyFrom £55.30 at AmazonBest for:marathon racing in comfortIt has more storage than a running belt, but Osprey’s 0.5-litre running hydration pack is another race-ready vest built for the bare essentials rather than a full-day’s backup kit. There’s more padding and plush comfort in the harness and back than the really minimal Kiprun, but you still benefit from a close fit that lets you run free.Everything’s just a touch more comfy and durable, and less floaty. The two adjustable bungee-style elasticated sternum straps with their hook-clip fastening are easily tweaked for a good fit. There’s easy access to soft flasks and a front phone pocket, though rear storage is limited. There’s a two-way entry mesh pouch that’ll take a jacket, but it’s not very secure, and I never felt completely confident that mission-critical kit wouldn’t bounce out. On the plus side, it comes with two 500ml soft flasks and easy-to-adjust elastic straps to hold them in place.It didn’t make the final cut because …I had worries about losing kit.Suitable for:short to medium runs;capacity:0.5l;sizing available:S, M, L;weight (men’s M):159g without bottles;soft flask compatible?Yes (included)OspreyDuro/Dyna LTfrom£55.30Men’s, £65 at TredzWomen’s, £55.30 at AmazonWhat we loveComfortable with a close fit for long distancesWhat we don’t loveWorries about mission-critical kit bouncing outWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenWhat should you look for in a running vest?Running vests tend to follow similar designs. A vest-style harness with holsters for water bottles, various combinations of zippered and mesh pockets on the shoulders and rib cage, and bigger compartments in the back for big kit, jackets and hydration bladders. Some also add bungee systems for extra storage.Capacity can vary. As a rough guide: for short runs up to an hour, you probably only need a two- or three-litre vest. These minimal hydration vests offer soft flask water stowage but prioritise a barely there fit and weight saving over carry space. They’re great for race day (such as a marathon), long training runs or any plods where you need to carry only a few vitals.At the other end, there are 15-litre monsters to swallow everything you need to be self-sufficient on multiday remote adventures in the mountains. Some may also double for lighter-load midweek run commutes.For maximum versatility, I find a five-litre vest to be the sweet spot. Unloaded, they’re light enough to handle hydration on shorter weekday runs, but they also have the capacity to carry backup kit for daylong ultras.How do I find the right fit?Fit is the top priority: the best running vests need to feel as if they’re part of you. They should be as lightweight as possible, breathable, secure and bounce-free – even when fully loaded.The sternum straps are key. Look for maximum adjustability, with easy and reliable fastenings that aren’t fussy or fiddly. If you have to lash it down so tight you can’t breathe, it’s not the one for you. Also look for a shoulder harness that’s wide and won’t cut in, ideally padded if you know you need more protection from heavy loads on longer runs.Many packs are unisex (the occasional pack, such as the Osprey Duro LT, offers men’s and women’s fits), some are one size, some offer a size range, so shop armed with your measurements. I also highly recommend filling a vest when you try it on for size before you commit. Everything changes once you’re bounding down the road with a fully laden vest. Watch out for how well your soft flasks stay put and how easy it is to get them in and out, too.Any other details to look out for?I always look for good front storage space for a few essentials such as your phone, fuel and headphone case. You’re less likely to eat that gel if it’s tucked away in the back of your pack. A running vest with a phone holder in the front is always useful, and I always miss it when it’s not there. If that pocket is waterproof, even better.If the vest has bladder compatibility, make sure you can route the hose and clip it somewhere it won’t flap in your face.I also geek out about zips. Fiddly little zips may save weight, but they’re not your friend when you’re frozen-finger cold or exhausted as you approach the final six miles of a marathon.Bonus points to running vests that come with a built-in safety whistle, key hooks, reflectivity and some weatherproofing and rain repellence.For more:The best running backpacksThe best running shoesThe best running watches to hit your fitness goalsKieran Alger is arunning, fitness and health journalist who splits his time between testing, training and tapping out reviews. You’ll regularly find him strapping on a running vest, racking up miles or chasing down a lofty challenge while wearing three watches, brand new running shoes and a whole host of kit that needs putting through its pacesExplore more on these topicsRunningThe FilterFitnessHealth & wellbeingHobbiesWalkingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: San Lorenzo: Rome’s rebel neighbourhood shaped by resistance, art and students | Rome holidays | The Guardian
description: This overlooked quarter swaps the grandeur of tourist-saturated central Rome for murals, graffiti, cheap eateries and a working-class rhythm
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This overlooked quarter swaps the grandeur of tourist-saturated central Rome for murals, graffiti, cheap eateries and a working-class rhythm
Content: San Lorenzo is a working class area of Rome, little frequented by tourists but full of cultural riches and great places to eat and drink.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSan Lorenzo is a working class area of Rome, little frequented by tourists but full of cultural riches and great places to eat and drink.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesZoning inRome holidaysSan Lorenzo: Rome’s rebel neighbourhood shaped by resistance, art and studentsThis overlooked quarter swaps the grandeur of tourist-saturated central Rome for murals, graffiti, cheap eateries and a working-class rhythmJessica LionnelWed 29 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhy go now?One of Europe’s hotspots, central Rome has increasingly come to resemble a tube station during rush hour: stifling, overpacked and claustrophobia-inducing. Last year, the Eternal City welcomed a record number of tourists, driven in part by the 2025 Vatican Jubilee -22.9 million arrivalsstayed in the city, almost 10 times the number of residents.There is no sign of the great tourist boom slowing down, either, with local sourcesindicatingthat 2026 could steal the crown from 2025.Yet while holidaymakers stream out of Rome’s main railway station, Termini, making a beeline towards the Colosseum, the Roman Forum and Piazza Venezia, few realise that a 20-minute walk in the opposite direction leads to one of Rome’s most overlooked quarters: San Lorenzo.View image in fullscreenLa Sapienza is one of the world’s oldest universities. It was founded in 1303.Photograph: Peter Spiro/Getty ImagesBuilt in the late 19th century for the working-class community, San Lorenzo carries more modern historical weight than many of its city-centre counterparts. During Benito Mussolini’s rise to power, both local residents (sanlorenzini) and theArditi del Popolo(AdP)–an anti-fascist military group – were involved in acts of resistance.double quotation markThe neighbourhood has retained much of the character that sets it apart from Rome’s increasingly crowded centreDuring the little-documented 1922 battle of San Lorenzo, members of the AdP resisted squadrist incursions into the neighbourhood, forcing them to retreat under gunfire. Five months later, during theMarch on Rome, barricades were erected to prevent the blackshirts from entering the area. Though13 people were killedin the unrest, fascist forces never fully controlled the neighbourhood. It became known as the red zone, symbolising its leftwing politics.Tragedy struck again towards the end of the second world war, when allied bombing destroyed swathes of the area and killed about 1,500sanlorenzini.Today, the living situation in this counterculture quarter is a lot less combative. Students from nearby La Sapienza University mingle with artists, creatives and longtime residents who have remained rooted in their working-class, leftwing identity. Although it has had acash injection, and clubhouse chainsSoho HouseandSocial Hubhave opened their doors, the neighbourhood has retained much of the character that sets it apart from Rome’s increasingly crowded centre.Where to eat and drinkView image in fullscreenSan Lorenzo is known for its non-touristy eating and drinking spots.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesSticky menus with photos of food on them are thankfully few and far between, as are plates of carbonara for more than €10. The district’sPizzeria Formula 1is a rite of passage for those living in the area. The no-frills spot has served up Roman-style thin-crust pizza since 1978, specialising in classic toppings such as margherita. Its interior matches what is served: a wood-lined room with white ceilings that looks like it hasn’t been touched since its opening. Both old and young come for meals that rarely stretch beyond €10 per head.A few minutes away isOsteria da Marcello, a family-run fixture since 1961. Before Marcello Santececca and his wife, Alessandrina, opened their doors, the premises catered largely tofagottari,diners who bought food from home and wine from the establishment. Typical Roman dishes, such as stewed tripe, deep-fried Jewish-style artichokes (carciofi alla giudia),cacio e pepepasta, and braised oxtail are served on plates placed on paper-covered tables in a dining room retaining its indoor picnic atmosphere.It’s not just inexpensive eateries that prevail.Nena Mercato e Cucina, run by Italian actorCristiano Caccamoand his business partner Lorenzo Biancolella, represents a newer side of San Lorenzo: trendy without pomp. Tiled tables and plates hung on the walls lend a Spanish feel, while the menu reworks old-school Italian staples with a sprinkle of modernity, from duck fettuccine with parmesan foam to carbonara with truffles.View image in fullscreenPizzeria Formula 1 is a rite of passage forsanlorenziniThose with a sweet tooth can cleanse their palates with a bona fide gelato from the aptly namedGelato San Lorenzo, which serves flavours ranging from the obscure (avocado, lemon and pepper) to classic (strawberry).Nearby, 103-year-old chocolate factorySAID dal 1923serves up desserts centred on chocolate. Display cabinets show off handmade pralines and truffles, and chocolate-making paraphernalia dangles from the walls, offering a reminder of the zone’s industrial past. Come autumn, the chocolatier’s rich hot chocolate is moreish enough for Augustus Gloop to want to wade in.As dusk falls, Piazza dell’Immacolata becomes the neighbourhood’s unofficial living room, where raucous university students spill out with beers and plastic cups of wine in hand.Wine bars are few, but it doesn’t mean they are non- existent. Hidden in plain sight is minusculeRamnes, a wine bar where patrons and newcomers revel in conversation between sips of local wine (such as the crisp Bellone) and beverages from slightly further afield (such as velvety reds from nearby Abruzzo).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCultural experiencesView image in fullscreenBasilica San Lorenzo fuori le mura (Basilica of St Lawrence Outside the Walls).Photograph: Reda/Getty ImagesMuch like central Rome, faith makes up a part of San Lorenzo’s sightseeing.The Basilica of St Lawrence Outside the Wallswas built around the tomb of the quarter’s namesake. The basilica is one of theSeven Pilgrim Churches of Romeand houses the relics of St Stephen. The original church was destroyed by allied bombings in 1943, with the latest facade rebuilt from the rubble.In keeping with the religious theme, tree-linedVerano Monumental cemetery(known asIl Veranoby locals) offers a place of reflection and tranquillity away from the hubbub of the area. The 83-hectare burial ground is divided into Jewish, Catholic and Protestant sections, with a monument to the victims of the first world war. The resting place of Italian acting iconsAlberto Sordi,Bud SpencerandGigi Proietti, it’s Rome’s answer to London’s Highgate cemetery.double quotation markWhere central Rome is defined by frescoes, San Lorenzo is defined by street artBeyond piety, San Lorenzo’s modern spin stands out. Where central Rome is defined by frescoes, San Lorenzo is defined by street art. As in any neighbourhood, there’s a fair amount of graffiti, but then there are standout pieces such as Marina Biagini andElisa Caracciolo’sMurale contro il Femminicidio(Mural Against Femicide, 2012-13), each of the 107 figures representing a victim of femicide from the year before. Rome-born street artist Alice Pasquini painted a block-long mural called “Welcome to San Lorenzo” along Via dei Sabelli. Street arttoursare frequent.View image in fullscreenElisa Caracciolo’sMurale contro il FemminicidioPhotograph: Andrea Sabbadini/AlamySan Lorenzo’s creative identity extends beyond the streets. It is also a key destination for contemporary art in Rome, anchored by theFondazione Pastificio Cerere, a former pasta factory transformed into a cultural centre in the 1970s, with frequent exhibitions. Independent galleries and creative spaces also contribute to the area’s broader artistic ecosystem, includingCollettivo noMadeandMonti8.Where to shop‘Year-round sunshine practically guaranteed’: Le Mourillon is Toulon’s cool, beachy quarterRead moreWith not a pristine Gucci bag or a sharp suit in sight, alternative, vintage clothing is high on the priority list forsanlorenzini. There are many secondhand clothes shops, such asLatini 34, where everything from boldly coloured preloved trench coats to shoes can be found. You can also find artisanal leather goods atLaboratorio Pellerossa, and handpicked garments from little-known designers across the globe atL’Anatra all’Arancia. Music-aficionados can pick up a range of vinyl fromUltrasuoni Records Roma.Don’t missIt’s pretty hard to missGiardino Veranoin the summer, an open-air space near Il Verano;noise and laughter can be heard throughout the quarter. The four-month-long summer festival hosts (every day until October) free concerts, an outdoor cinema and drinks and games until 2am.Where to stayView image in fullscreenThe Social Hub.Photograph: leonardoworldwide.comThere’s little in the way of plush hotels in San Lorenzo butAteneo Garden Palace(doubles from €188) is set with a sizable courtyard, and offers spacious, airy rooms. Down the road, the newly openedSocial Hub(doubles from €250) offers all the facilities from onsite restaurants to a rooftop pool with a bar.Explore more on these topicsRome holidaysZoning inItaly holidaysEurope holidaysCity breaksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I tested the best camping stoves for cooking like a pro in the wild – here are my favourites | Camping holidays | The Guardian
description: Forget soggy sandwiches! From pocket-size burners to charcoal cookers for a wonderfully smoky flavour, these stoves came top in our tests
Author: Sian Lewis
Headline: Forget soggy sandwiches! From pocket-size burners to charcoal cookers for a wonderfully smoky flavour, these stoves came top in our tests
Content: Alfresco feasting … from sizzling steaks to charred veg, the best camping stoves make outdoor cooking easy.Photograph: Jacob Little/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAlfresco feasting … from sizzling steaks to charred veg, the best camping stoves make outdoor cooking easy.Photograph: Jacob Little/The GuardianThe FilterCamping holidaysReviewI tested the best camping stoves for cooking like a pro in the wild – here are my favouritesForget soggy sandwiches! From pocket-size burners to charcoal cookers for a wonderfully smoky flavour, these stoves came top in our testsThe best camping mattresses and sleeping matsSian LewisWed 29 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Areliable camping stove makes all the difference to food alfresco, allowing you to cook a stew in the evening and then warm up in the morning with a hot cup of coffee. The great thing about these stoves is that they’re essentially portable hobs, meaning anything you can cook on the stove at home can be whipped up in the great outdoors by sticking a pot or frying pan on top.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.There’s a dizzying variety on offer, ranging from dinky ultralight burners that fit into your pocket to big stove-tops with multiple hobs, grills, wind protectors and a lid – the latter are like bringing along your cooker from home. Most run on gas, such as propane and butane, although I’ve also included charcoal options for traditional types. I’ve tested 20 of the best portable stoves, for everyone from ultralight wild campers to families who need to cook dinners for the masses.At a glanceBest camping stove overallCadac2 Cook 2 Pro Deluxe£125 at ArgosBest budget camping stoveRobensFire Beetle£40.99 at DecathlonBest portable BBQEverdureCube£109 at AmazonBest no-frills burnerCampingazCamp & Trek Twin CV Connect stove£104 at BlacksBest stove for backpackingPrimusLite Plus stove£69.95 at WildboundsBest stove for wild campersPetromaxAtago£229.95 at Mountain WarehouseBest grill for campingPrimusKuchoma portable grill£172.99 at Mountain WarehouseWhy you should trust meI’m a keen camper and spend many nights a year under canvas, either wild camping solo in the hills or on weekends away in my bell tent with friends and family. Wherever I pitch my tent, I also love making supper in the great outdoors – whether it’s a bowl of noodles in the wild, a hearty stew at a campsite or a spot of marshmallow toasting on a campfire. With my journalist hat on, I’ve been testing all kinds of outdoor kit for years, so I know what works – and what will last.Read our expert guide tothe best tentsfor more inspirationHow I testedView image in fullscreenEach stove was tasked with cooking camping staples.Photograph: Jacob Little/The GuardianI fired up 20 stoves across two testing periods, cooking camping staples such as porridge, pancakes and fried eggs, as well as checking how long it took to boil water on each. I looked for an easy setup without any complicated instructions to follow and tested to see if each stove cooked evenly and reliably, and that the components felt good quality and built to last.I hate cleaning stoves, but I took one for the team and gave each of my top-rated models a good scrub to see how easy they were to get spick and span after use. My selection of the 12 best camping stoves includes lightweight models and larger camping stoves, as well as portable barbecues and even a smoker you can take camping.The best camping stoves in 2026View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jacob Little/The GuardianBest camping stove overall:Cadac 2 Cook 2 Pro DeluxeCadac2 Cook 2 Pro Deluxefrom£125£125 at Argos£140 at Go OutdoorsWhat we loveGreat all-rounder; cooks it all; good valueWhat we don’t loveNo wind guardView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jacob Little/The Guardian£125 at Argos£140 at Go OutdoorsThis is a compact gas stove with two independent burners. It also has built-in ignition, and ceramic-coated flat and ribbed grill plates, allowing for simultaneous grilling, frying and boiling. It weighs 4.8kg and is compatible with butane and propane.Why we love itThere are camping stoves out there to suit everyone, from the hardiest mountaineer who wants to fit a stove in the palm of their hand to the van-lifers in need of a setup that would rival a kitchen. If pressed, I’d say this was the best camping stove I tested overall.It’s lightweight, at less than 5kg, and is portable, folding into its case for carrying and storage. Pop off the lid and there are two burners, each with its own built-in ignition, so you can have coffee going on one and bacon and eggs sizzling on the other. You can also stick two grill surfaces (a ceramic flat plate grill and a ribbed grill plate) on top and simply pop ingredients straight on to sizzle and sear. The case makes for fuss- and mess-free storage in your van or car boot (or cupboard back at home), and it sits sturdily on tabletops.This is ideal for campervans or on family camping trips, although it would benefit from the addition of a wind guard, as it doesn’t like anything stronger than a mild breeze. This is also a well-priced camping stove.It’s a shame that… it doesn’t like high winds.Weight:4.8kgBurners:twoFuel type:gasTime to boil water: six minutesCadac2 Cook 2 Pro Deluxefrom£125£125 at Argos£140 at Go OutdoorsWhat we loveGreat all-rounder; cooks it all; good valueWhat we don’t loveNo wind guardBest budget camping stove:Robens Fire BeetleRobensFire Beetlefrom£40.99£40.99 at Decathlon£40.99 at Mountain WarehouseWhat we lovePocket size and lightweight, with decent legsWhat we don’t loveThere are even dinkier stoves if you’re counting every gramView image in fullscreen£40.99 at Decathlon£40.99 at Mountain WarehouseRedefining what it means to be a “Beetles fan”, this compact stove may be small but it’s also mighty. It weighs 189g – not as featherweight as the teeny, less-than-50g stoves favoured by hardcore hikers, but it’s great for its price and will do just fine for most backpackers and trekkers.The Beetle folds out into a surprisingly sturdy pot stand, which I found steady even on uneven surfaces. I’d suggest adding a foil windscreen if you’re out in the wild, as it proved sensitive to any kind of wind, but it was easy to light and control the power of the flame, and it boiled water fast. Other reviewers report this stove doesn’t work well in winter conditions, but in spring it was an efficient cooking companion I barely noticed in my pack – and it’s well priced.It’s a shame that …there are lighter stoves out there if the weight is important to you.Weight:189gBurners:oneFuel type:gasTime to boil water: four minutesRobensFire Beetlefrom£40.99£40.99 at Decathlon£40.99 at Mountain WarehouseWhat we lovePocket size and lightweight, with decent legsWhat we don’t loveThere are even dinkier stoves if you’re counting every gramBest portable BBQ:Everdure CubeEverdureCubefrom£109£137 at Everdure£109 at AmazonWhat we loveCute, compact and easy to moveWhat we don’t loveLimited grill space; expensive for limited useView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sian Lewis/The Guardian£137 at Everdure£109 at AmazonDesigned with input from chef Heston Blumenthal, the Everdure Cube is a portable, reusable charcoal barbecue, all packed into a compact box. It’s easy to carry, with a simple grill design aimed at casual outdoor cooking rather than full-scale feasts.Why we love itThe rather cute Cube is thoughtfully designed, with heatproof handles that stay cool so you can move it mid-cook, plus a bamboo prep board built into the lid. The lid also doubles as storage for ingredients, but you can’t use it to cover the grill once it’s lit, which limits the Cube’s usefulness in wind or rain. Inside, a porcelain enamel firebox holds a grill – simply pop charcoal inside and light.On test I found the Cube a doddle to set up and cook on, and cleaning it afterwards is made easier because of the wipe-clean firebox. The Cube is quite cool, too – I like the citrus orange version I tested, and while good looks aren’t top of my list when recommending stoves, they don’t hurt.
