Space on the grill is limited: this is great for beach trips, solo suppers and couple cookouts, but you’ll need something bigger for family camps.It’s a shame that…it’s too dinky for a big family, and it’s pricey for something so simple.Weight:7kgBurners:oneFuel type:charcoalTime to boil water:not applicableEverdureCubefrom£109£137 at Everdure£109 at AmazonWhat we loveCute, compact and easy to moveWhat we don’t loveLimited grill space; expensive for limited useBest no-frills burner:Campingaz Camp & Trek Twin CV Connect stoveCampingazCamp & Trek Twin CV Connect stovefrom£104£104 at Blacks£110 at Go OutdoorsWhat we loveSimple to use; two burners; portableWhat we don’t loveNo bells and whistles – or wind protectionView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sian Lewis/The Guardian£104 at Blacks£110 at Go OutdoorsIts name is a bit of a mouthful, but the Campingaz Camp & Trek Twin CV Connect is otherwise a straightforward, no-fuss gas stove with two burners, designed to mimic the simplicity of using your hob at home. It connects to Campingaz gas cartridges using the Easy Clic system, so setup is quick and secure, with minimal faff.Why we love itI’m wary of overly complicated camping stoves – most campers just want something that works – so this simple, intuitive option was a welcome relief on test. The gas cartridge clicks neatly into place, the built-in ignition fires up instantly (even in breezy conditions), and the Camp & Trek boils water in minutes. With two burners, you can have a kettle going while cooking breakfast, which makes this stove ideal for family trips or campervan use.This design is lightweight, portable and it comes with a carry bag, although there are no fancy features such as wind guards or built-in prep space on this pared-back stove. Still, for the price, it’s a reliable, no-fuss option that covers all the basics well.It’s a shame that… it’s a bare-bones burner design – but then, that’s the point.Weight:1.4kgBurners:twoFuel type:gasTime to boil water:four minutesCampingazCamp & Trek Twin CV Connect stovefrom£104£104 at Blacks£110 at Go OutdoorsWhat we loveSimple to use; two burners; portableWhat we don’t loveNo bells and whistles – or wind protectionBest stove for backpacking:Primus Lite Plus stovePrimusLite Plus stovefrom£69.95£69.95 at Wildbounds£130 at Go OutdoorsWhat we loveSimple to use; fast to boil; integrated lighterWhat we don’t loveNot the lightest; only suitable for oneView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sian Lewis/The Guardian£69.95 at Wildbounds£130 at Go OutdoorsThe Primus Lite Plus stove system is a compact “personal stove system” designed for solo campers who want a reliable, all-in-one setup. Primus doesn’t reinvent the wheel here, but instead refines it into something good quality, efficient and easy to pack.Why we love itSummertime, and the wild camping is easy – if you’ve got this intuitive little stove packed in your rucksack. Just screw it on to a Primus gas canister, pop the pot on top, and you’re good to go. The Lite Plus was the speediest stove in my test, boiling water in around three minutes, which makes a big difference when you’re after a quick coffee or hot meal out-of-doors. The flame is easy to control, so you won’t scorch the bottom of the pot, and there’s a built-in igniter to save you from fumbling with matches.The integrated pot packs everything neatly into itself, and includes a cork cosy for insulation and grip. The included pot’s capacity is limited at 800ml for carrying and 500ml for boiling, making this best for solo backpackers, although you can use other pots and pans instead.It’s a shame that …it’s not ultralight, and it’s best for one.Weight:402gBurners:oneFuel type:gasTime to boil water:three minutesPrimusLite Plus stovefrom£69.95£69.95 at Wildbounds£130 at Go OutdoorsWhat we loveSimple to use; fast to boil; integrated lighterWhat we don’t loveNot the lightest; only suitable for oneBest stove for wild campers:Petromax AtagoPetromaxAtagofrom£229.95£229.95 at Mountain Warehouse£229.95 at B&QWhat we loveFun to cook on; works in the wild; converts to a fire bowlWhat we don’t lovePricey; accessories not included; a little bulkyView image in fullscreen£229.95 at Mountain Warehouse£229.95 at B&QThe Atago is a four-in-one charcoal cooking kit designed to function as a grill, stove, oven and firepit. It’s made from stainless steel, which makes it durable, and features a double-walled design for efficient heat retention, plus it has a one-step folding mechanism for portability. It’s also compatible with various iterations of Petromax cast-iron cookware.Why we love itThis might be the hardiest portable stove on the market. The stainless-steel unit uses charcoal or charcoal briquettes for fuel, so it’s ideal for wild campers, foragers and explorers who fancy cooking a feast when they’re far from the nearest plug socket or shop.The Atago is designed to be compatible with Petromax’sDutch ovens, woks, pans and even acamping coffee percolator, although you’ll have to buy these separately – and this cooking system is already expensive. You’ll also have to tend to a fire rather than just turn on the gas, though I found the Atago easy to light and use, plus grilling meat and fish on charcoal gave a wonderful smoky flavour.Gourmet chefs who want to produce Instagram-worthy eats even if they’re in the wild will love this setup, and I liked that it converts into a fire bowl – a great way to have a campfire without causing damage wherever you set up your tent. All in all, this is a fun mini mobile kitchen, and worth investing in if you’re serious about food even when you’re in the backcountry.It’s a shame that …it’s expensive – and you’ll have to buy the accessories.Weight:6.1kgBurners:oneFuel type:charcoal, charcoal briquettes and firewoodTime to boil water:five minutes (once the fire is hot)PetromaxAtagofrom£229.95£229.95 at Mountain Warehouse£229.95 at B&QWhat we loveFun to cook on; works in the wild; converts to a fire bowlWhat we don’t lovePricey; accessories not included; a little bulkyBest grill for camping:Primus Kuchoma portable grillPrimusKuchoma portable grillfrom£172.99£172.99 at Mountain Warehouse£213.59 at AmazonWhat we lovePortable; feels like great quality; easy to cleanWhat we don’t loveExpensive and there are limited ways to cook on itView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jacob Little/The Guardian£172.99 at Mountain Warehouse£213.59 at AmazonThe Swedish-designed Primus Kuchoma is a lightweight, portable gas-powered grill designed for outdoor cooking adventures. Weighing 4.6kg, it features a ceramic non-stick grill grate, a stainless-steel drip tray and foldable legs.Why we love itThe Kuchoma felt rather like the Cadac 2 Cook 2 Pro in terms of shape, size and portability, but it’s a dedicated grill rather than a two-burner. This was the most portable grill I could find to test, and if you love a proper barbecue but want to travel light, it’ll be your bestie, allowing you to sizzle a steak or brown toast wherever you pitch your tent (or simply on the beach, patio or in the garden).I liked the foldout legs, which protect the ground and make a solid base for the grill, and there’s room on the Kuchoma to cook supper for two people, with heat distributed well across one wide grill plate. The steel hood seals tight, too, so the burner stays lit in windy weather. It’s quick to remove the grill to wash it and wipe clean the grease tray.If you already own a stove, this will be a great addition to liven up your camping culinary adventures – but it won’t cover the basics such as boiling the kettle or making pasta.It’s a shame that…it’s expensive, especially for a one-trick pony.Weight:4.6kgBurners:oneFuel type:gasTime to boil water:not applicablePrimusKuchoma portable grillfrom£172.99£172.99 at Mountain Warehouse£213.59 at AmazonWhat we lovePortable; feels like great quality; easy to cleanWhat we don’t loveExpensive and there are limited ways to cook on itThe best of the restView image in fullscreen‘Good fun and affordable’: the Bar-Be-Quick smoker and grill barbecue.Photograph: Jacob Little/The GuardianMSR XGK EXMSRXGK EXfrom£225£225 at Base Camp Food£247.50 at DecathlonWhat we loveTakes any fuel; pocket-size; sturdy surfaceWhat we don’t loveFiddly to use; no simmer option; priceyView image in fullscreen£225 at Base Camp Food£247.50 at DecathlonBest for:a multi-fuel stoveMulti-fuel stoves do what they say on the tin, and by allowing you to swap between fuels they’re versatile for travel. MSR’s XGK EX is a popular choice with hardy outdoorsy types as it burns white gas, paraffin and diesel. It’s a hard-wearing stove that should last a long time; its stainless-steel, scorpion-like legs provide a wide, sturdy surface for your pot.All this little stove really does is boil liquids (albeit fast and reliably, and it will also melt snow in harsh weather conditions), so you can’t simmer your meal or make anything complicated. It’s pricey, too, so casual campers need not splash their cash here, though for international adventures – where you really need to rely on your kit – it’s worth the spend.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s expensive and has no temperature control.Weight:366gBurners:oneFuel type:gas, paraffin and dieselTime to boil water: three to five minutesMSRXGK EXfrom£225£225 at Base Camp Food£247.50 at DecathlonWhat we loveTakes any fuel; pocket-size; sturdy surfaceWhat we don’t loveFiddly to use; no simmer option; priceyBar-Be-Quick smoker and grill barbecueBar-Be-QuickSmoker and grill barbecuefrom£69.99£69.99 at Robert Dyas£85 at ArgosWhat we loveSmokes ingredients well; doubles as a grillWhat we don’t loveFiddly to assemble; feels less durable than othersView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jacob Little/The Guardian£69.99 at Robert Dyas£85 at ArgosBest for:a portablebarbecue and smokerA smoker you can take into the sticks? The Bar-Be-Quick’s multilayered design looks too hefty to be portable at first glance – but this smoker and grill (which weighs 8.3kg) will fit into larger cars if you fancy a gourmet camping feast. It can also be converted into a small portable barbecue by taking away the top section, making it ideal for shorter trips. You can then choose whether you fancy smoking, grilling, roasting or steaming ingredients.During testing, it took me a few goes to put the smoker-grill together and then to use it correctly, but once I got the hang of it cooking was simple – and more fun than your standard barbecue or camping stove. It works well as a simple charcoal grill, too. This grill perhaps isn’t as solid as some premium models, but it’s good fun and affordable.It didn’t make the final cut because…it’s flimsier than some models on test.Weight:8.3kg;burners:one;fuel type:charcoal;time to boil water:not applicableBar-Be-QuickSmoker and grill barbecuefrom£69.99£69.99 at Robert Dyas£85 at ArgosWhat we loveSmokes ingredients well; doubles as a grillWhat we don’t loveFiddly to assemble; feels less durable than othersChar-Broil Patio Bistro Cube EChar-BroilPatio Bistro Cube E£229£229 at Char-BroilWhat we loveEasy to use; heats up in a jiffyWhat we don’t loveNot lightweight; no charcoal taste or smellView image in fullscreen£229 at Char-BroilBest for:a portable electric barbecueIf nothing but a proper barbecue will do on your adventures, the Char-Broil Patio Bistro Cube E is a compact electric option that works well for camping and van trips – as long as you’ve got a power hook-up handy. Its cube design is easy to pack into a car boot or campervan cupboard, and it’s a doddle to cook on.Despite its size, this barbecue punches above its weight, reaching up to 320C and heating up quickly, so you can get cooking fast. There’s room on the grill to cater for a family of four, and the controls are simple to use. While you won’t get the barbecue flavour of charcoal, that also means no smoke, and the ease and reliability of cooking on the Patio Bistro Cube makes dinner stress-free, without any of the effort of heating coals to just the right temperature. This dinky grill is also easy to clean. A fuss-free option for electric-friendly sites (as well as for balconies, gardens and its namesake – your patio), all in a portable package.It didn’t make the final cut because …there are limited places you can use it.Weight:13.2kg;burners: one;fuel type: electric;time to boil water:not applicableChar-BroilPatio Bistro Cube E£229£229 at Char-BroilWhat we loveEasy to use; heats up in a jiffyWhat we don’t loveNot lightweight; no charcoal taste or smellGozney Tread pizza ovenGozneyTreadfrom£499£499.99 at Gozney£499 at AmazonWhat we loveWell made; makes posh pizza in minutes; portableWhat we don’t loveVery pricey; some accessories not includedView image in fullscreen£499.99 at Gozney£499 at AmazonBest for:a portable pizza oven for campingPizza ovensare having a moment in back gardens across Britain, but believe it or not, there’s also a model you can easily take camping with you if you fancy whipping up a margherita under the stars.Gozney’s Tread is pleasingly compact, and at 13.5kg, not too heavy or bulky to stick in the boot of a car or load into your campervan. It makes 12in pizzas in three minutes flat, a great way to quickly feed the masses, and you can also pop a cast-iron pan inside, so it can stand in as an oven. There’s also a stand, a pizza paddle and a carry bag available, although these are sold separately.The Tread isn’t cheap, at just shy of £500 – but I have to say, I’m a convert. If you love whipping up gourmet food alfresco all summer, it might be worth the investment – and it doubles up as a pizza oven you can use in the garden when you’re home, of course.It didn’t make the final cut because …do youreallyneed a pizza oven?Weight:13.5kgBurners:oneFuel type:propaneTime to make pizza:three to five minutesGozneyTreadfrom£499£499.99 at Gozney£499 at AmazonWhat we loveWell made; makes posh pizza in minutes; portableWhat we don’t loveVery pricey; some accessories not includedFor more, read our guide to thebest pizza ovensPetromax Rocket StovePetromaxRocket Stovefrom£144.95£144.95 at Rackhams£144.95 at Mountain WarehouseWhat we loveEasy to light and to cook on; good qualityWhat we don’t loveLimited use; one burnerView image in fullscreen£144.95 at Rackhams£144.95 at Mountain WarehouseBest for:a portable wood-burning stoveIf you love to camp in the back of beyond, and don’t want to rely on gas when it’s time to whip up supper, you may well get on with the Rocket Stove. Essentially a mini chimney you can light a fire in and then feed with wood, pine cones or other kindling, it has a cast-iron top to pop a pan or pot on, which cooks food evenly while you feed the fire. This wilderness-ready stove is basically a Swedish fire log you can use on repeat.The Rocket Stove is well made and good fun to use, too. It’s easy to get the fire going, as the chimney is well insulated from wind, and once the stove is hot, water will boil in less than 10 minutes. The stove will happily sit on a camping table, too. This design looks hefty but weighs just over 6kg, so it’s portable, and if you have a power failure at home, it could be a handy backup.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s a one-trick pony, suitable only if you’re keen to cook over fire.Weight:6.5kgBurners:oneFuel type:woodTime to boil water:five to 10 minutesPetromaxRocket Stovefrom£144.95£144.95 at Rackhams£144.95 at Mountain WarehouseWhat we loveEasy to light and to cook on; good qualityWhat we don’t loveLimited use; one burnerWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jacob Little/The GuardianKey features to look out forA lightweight canister stove is ideal for boiling water quickly for solo hikers and minimalists, but less suited to multi-pot gourmet meals. For groups or more elaborate campsite cooking, I’d opt for a dual-burner stove so you’ve got room for frying, simmering and brewing coffee all in one place. Ensure you buy the correct fuel canister for your stove.The most common models use gas or liquid fuel (paraffin etc), and different canisters are designed to clip or screw on to different stoves. This can be confusing to shop for. Most gas stoves run off propane, butane or a mixture of the two gases. First, check what fuel is recommended for use with your new stove – some are compatible only with branded gas canisters, while others allow multiple fuel options. If you’re camping in cold weather, it’s sensible to pick propane if you can, as it has a lower boiling point.‘The only thing that gets me out of my tent’: the camping essentials you need (and what you don’t)Read moreGas canisters come in different sizes – mini ones are great for wild campers, while big refillable bottles will suit family weekenders. Larger stoves may require a refillable gas bottle – these also usually need you to buy a separate regulator, but they are more eco-friendly, as they can be used again and again. Check if you need a clip-in or screw-in canister and have a go at setting up your new stove with the gas cylinder before you go camping, so you’re confident it works.Whatever stove you go for, look for features such as wind protection, simmer control and easy ignition (built-in igniters are handy in case you forget to bring matches). Weight, packability and setup time are also important – especially if you’re trekking rather than car camping.How to choose a camping stove that will lastIt’s worth investing in the best camping stove you can afford. Stainless steel and titanium offer durability and rust resistance. Canister stoves are perfect for lightweight trips, but make sure you look for sturdy pot supports and quality valves. Liquid fuel stoves often come with serviceable parts, a major plus for longevity.Fuel efficiency is just as important for the planet and your wallet, and a wind-resistant burner will save fuel – and frustration. Wood-burning stoves will appeal to the off-grid minimalist and should last for ever if they’re well constructed.How to use a camping stoveFind a stable, flat surface away from tents or dry brush. Wind is your enemy, so shield the stove. Attach the fuel canister or line securely and double-check for leaks before lighting. Most camping stoves require you to turn on the gas and then light it with a match or lighter, or click the built-in igniter. Some will burn with a bright blue flame; others are hard to see alight but make a roaring noise. If it’s windy, watch carefully to make sure the flame hasn’t gone out.We’ve included wood and charcoal stoves and grills in our roundup – these usually require you to light a fire with kindling and then add bigger pieces of wood until you have a fire hot enough to cook over. Never cook inside your tent: you could poison yourself with carbon monoxide fumes. It’s a sensible idea to have a go at setting up your stove at home first before you head off on holiday – there’s little more frustrating than realising you brought the wrong fuel when you’re desperate for a cuppa.For more:The best camping chairs for every budgetThe best camping mattresses and sleeping matsThe best tents for every camperSian Lewis is an award-winningoutdoors and travel journalist and author who loves putting adventure kit through its paces while hiking, swimming and wild camping. She also shares her adventures at@sianannalewisandthegirloutdoors.comThis article was originally published on 11 July 2025. title: How to turn mozzarella whey into delectable muffins – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: Don’t pour it down the sink. This subtly tangy liquid is naturally acidic, adding flavour and fluffiness to your baking
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Don’t pour it down the sink. This subtly tangy liquid is naturally acidic, adding flavour and fluffiness to your baking
Content: Tom Hunt’s mozzarella whey muffins with sundried tomatoes and olives.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s mozzarella whey muffins with sundried tomatoes and olives.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notFoodHow to turn mozzarella whey into delectable muffins – recipeDon’t pour it down the sink. This subtly tangy liquid is naturally acidic, adding flavour and fluffiness to your bakingTom HuntWed 29 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMozzarella comes in a bag or pot surrounded by whey or brine. This is known aslatticelloin Italy, and has all the flavour of the cheese and more – it’s lactic, sour and subtly sweet, with a powerful, salty, umami-rich depth of flavour. It’s delicious as a drink in it’s own right, but it’s also great to cook with. It can be used instead of buttermilk or yoghurt in marinades, even though it has less viscosity than both, and in baking. I’ve included the mozzarella itself in today’s recipe, but it is entirely optional and could easily be saved for another recipe.Mozzarella whey muffinsWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appMozzarella whey is my latest Waste Not discovery. While researchingmy buffalo mozzarella taste test for the Filterearlier this month, I tasted the whey of each cheese to gauge its quality, and found all of them pretty delicious. By the end, I had the whey from 10 pots to use up, so tried out a few recipes, including drinks, marinades and muffins. Mozzarella whey is naturally acidic, much like yoghurt or buttermilk, so it stands to reason that it would make an excellent muffin by activating the baking powder and helping the muffins to rise, while also adding flavour. Explore your own combinations of optional extras: I adapted this recipe from one of my early Guardian recipes forceleriac and blue cheese muffins, which is another lovely combination.Makes6150g spelt flour, or wholemeal flour1½ tsp baking powder1 egg, lightly beaten125ml mozzarella whey100goptional extras– olives, sun-dried tomatoes, roast red peppers, or whatever you fancy or have to hand125g ball mozzarella, torn (optional)3 sprigs fresh herbs(rosemary, thyme, oregano), leaves picked (optional)Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6, and grease and line a six-hole muffin tin. In a large bowl (or plastic tub for which you have a lid), combine the flour, baking powder, beaten egg and mozzarella whey. Add your chosen optional extras and herbs, if using; if you like, tear in some mozzarella, too, then beat to combine (if using a tub, simply pop on the lid and shake vigorously).Divide the batter between the lined muffin tray holes, top each one with more olives and mozzarella, if using, then bake for 15-18 minutes, until golden on top. Remove from the tray, transfer to a rack and enjoy warm, or leave to cool and store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to three days.Explore more on these topicsFoodWaste notFood wasteCheeseBakingSnacksVegetablesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cherry sundaes and banana splits: Helen Graves’ recipes for barbecued fruit | Food | The Guardian
description: These new spins on nostalgic desserts will elevate your summer barbecues, while their prep-ahead nature will keep the day stress free
Author: Helen Graves
Headline: These new spins on nostalgic desserts will elevate your summer barbecues, while their prep-ahead nature will keep the day stress free
Content: Helen Graves' barbecued banana splits with salted date cream and coconut crunch.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food styling: Aya Nishimura. Prop styling: Polly Webb-Wilson. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.View image in fullscreenHelen Graves' barbecued banana splits with salted date cream and coconut crunch.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food styling: Aya Nishimura. Prop styling: Polly Webb-Wilson. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.FoodCherry sundaes and banana splits: Helen Graves’ recipes for barbecued fruitThese new spins on nostalgic desserts will elevate your summer barbecues, while their prep-ahead nature will keep the day stress freeHelen GravesWed 29 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen it comes to barbecued desserts, a few squares of chocolate melted inside a banana will no longer cut it. Get ahead with some easy-to-prep elements, then add a final flourish of smoke-licked fruit to bring new energy to classic desserts, such as banana splits and layered fruit sundaes. They need not be complex, and will interest your guests far more than the same old stale ideas. I’ve had some fun with these nostalgic favourites, and hope you will, too.Barbecued banana splits with salted date cream and coconut crunch (pictured top)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appThe natural caramel sweetness of dates flavours salted whipped cream in this grownup take on an often kitsch dessert. The coconut crunch is so good you may wish to make double the quantity – sprinkle the excess over yoghurt, ice-cream or just eat a handful every time you go to the kitchen.Prep5 minCook20 minCool10 minServes6600ml double cream80ml date syrup1 pinch sea salt6 bananas, unpeeled and cut in half lengthways30g butter, meltedFor the coconut crunch1½tbsp maple syrup¼tsp light soy sauce1 pinch flaky sea salt30g flaked almonds30g coconut chipsFirst make the topping. Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5 and line an oven tray with greaseproof paper. Mix the maple syrup, light soy sauce and sea salt in a bowl, then stir in the almonds and coconut chips. Spread out in an even layer on the lined tray, bake for five minutes, then give everything a good stir and bake for another six to eight minutes, until lightly toasted. Remove and leave to cool – the mix will crisp up as it does so.When you’re ready to grill the bananas, in a medium bowl whip the cream, date syrup and salt to soft peaks. Brush the cut sides of the bananas with the melted butter, then grill cut side down directly over the coals for two to three minutes, until lightly charred.Serve the bananas topped with the date cream and garnished with a good sprinkling of coconut crunch.Smoky cherry baklava sundaeWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenHelen Graves’ smoky cherry baklava sundae.Skewering is the easiest way to handle cherries on a barbecue grill – you’ll need thin ones for this. Cherry juice varies enormously in sweetness, so taste it after adding the sugar and lemon juice, and adjust to your liking. I sometimes add clotted cream to this when I’m feeling mischievous.Prep5 minCook30 minChill1 hr+Serves4300ml cherry juice1 tbsp caster sugar1 tbsp lemon juice1 tbsp cornflour mixed with 1 tbsp cold water500g cherries, pitted4 scoops vanilla ice-cream8 piecesbaklava– a pistachio one works well here4 spoonfuls clotted cream(optional)1 small handful pistachios, shelled and finely choppedMix the cherry juice, caster sugar and lemon juice in a small saucepan, bring to a simmer, stirring to dissolve the sugar, then leave to bubble gently for 10 minutes. Whisk in the cornflour slurry to thicken the mix, then bring back to a simmer and cook for two minutes more. Take off the heat, leave to cool, then chill thoroughly.When you’re ready to serve, thread the pitted cherries on to small skewers and grill them directly over the coals for five minutes on each side, until lightly charred. Layer the grilled cherries in sundae glasses with the ice-cream, baklava, clotted cream, if using, and cherry syrup, garnish with the chopped pistachios and serve.Helen Graves is a cook, food writer and editor ofPit magazineExplore more on these topicsFoodBarbecueFruitDessertSummer food and drinkIce-cream and sorbetNuts and seedsrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Ask the right questions’: what you need to know before buying shares | Investments | The Guardian
description: Whether it is SpaceX or a bank, getting the right facts about a firm can offer vital insights before you invest in it
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Whether it is SpaceX or a bank, getting the right facts about a firm can offer vital insights before you invest in it
Content: Experts caution that a company’s past performance may not be a reliable indicator of future returns.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersView image in fullscreenExperts caution that a company’s past performance may not be a reliable indicator of future returns.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersInvestments‘Ask the right questions’: what you need to know before buying sharesWhether it is SpaceX or a bank, getting the right facts about a firm can offer vital insights before you invest in itLisa-Marie VoneshenWed 29 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenElon Musk’s SpaceX launched on to the stock market, tens of thousands of Britons clamoured to buy a stake, putting the spotlight on DIY investing.Going it alone and buying shares in individual companies can be rewarding, but also risky. Unless you have a huge amount of cash, you are likely to end up investing in far fewer companies than if you invested in a fund. This means you are more exposed to the ups and downs of those companies’ fortunes.Maybe you have been putting money into funds for a while and have decided to choose a few individual companies to invest in, or maybe you want to build your own portfolio with no help.High-profile initial public offerings (IPOs) can often be the catalyst for this: it has been reported that more than 100,000 individual UK investors applied for just under $1bn of SpaceX shares.But, whatever your background, before you dive in and start buying shares in individual companies, it is vital you do your research. This should include looking at facts and figures that reveal something about a business’s financial health, anticipated returns and profitability. This will help you discover any warning signs about a company’s long-term prospects.Jemma Slingo, a pensions and investment specialist at Fidelity International, says looking at data can helpinvestors “ask the right questions”, including if they are paying a reasonable price, and whether the returns shareholders are getting look sustainable.However, she says the numbers “cannot predict the future, and past performance is not a reliable indicator of future returns”.View image in fullscreenMore than 100,000 individual UK investors applied for SpaceX shares.Photograph: John Raoux/APListed companies must publish financial results. You can find them on sites such as Investegate, Yahoo Finance and investment platforms such as Fidelity. Yahoo Finance allows you to compare data for several stocks, and a company’s current and past investment data and that of its competitors.Here is a guide to some of the investment data that can offer vital insights before buying shares in a company.Price-to-earnings ratioThe P/E ratio measures a company’s share price relative to its earnings per share. It indicates how much investors are willing to pay for every £1 of profit a company makes. The ratio is calculated by dividing the current share price by earnings per share.There is not “an objectively ‘good’ or ‘bad’ number” when looking at the P/E ratio and it depends on what the company is being compared with, Slingo says.She says the average FTSE 100 company has a P/E of about 12. While a lower P/E could suggest a stock is cheaper, it does not necessarily represent better value, as it could also indicate weaker future growth is expected, she adds.“Equally, a higher P/E may be justified if a company is growing quickly and has strong prospects,” Slingo says.Victoria Scholar, the head of investment at the platform Interactive Investor, says some investors use a P/E of 15 as a rough guide, with anything below seen as relatively inexpensive, but adds that valuations vary by sector.Bank figures tableTo give you an example of what you might find, we looked at data from Fidelity for some of the UK’s biggest banks (see table). At the time of writing, it shows NatWest has a relatively low P/E ratio among UK banks at 9.52, while Metro Bank’s is much higher at 22.05.Price-to-book ratioThe P/B ratio compares a company’s stock market value to its assets minus liabilities, and can reveal whether its shares are fairly priced. You divide the share price by the book value per share, which you can find for a specific company under Statistics on Yahoo Finance. A number below one implies it is undervalued, while above one suggests the opposite.This data is helpful for analysing companies with cash and physical assets. Slingo says the P/B ratio is a crucial metric for investors, which could be used when looking at banks. She flags that investors have been wary of banking stocks owing to rising bad debts and weak loan demand after the 2008 financial crisis, which was reinforced by the pandemic. This was shown by them having low P/B numbers.View image in fullscreenSeveral big UK banks have a P/B ratio above one.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPABut the sector had a “dramatic rerating” in late 2023 and early 2024, Slingo says. Now several banks have a P/B ratio above one, and the share price of the big banks have recorded a sustained rise.Return on equityROE shows how effectively a company’s management uses shareholders’ investments to generate profits. It is calculated by dividing the company’s net income (income after business costs are deducted) by shareholders’ equity (total assets minus total liabilities).Lee Wild, the head of equity strategy at Interactive Investor, says many websites suggest a ratio of 15% to 20% is good, but adds that it depends on the industry, so comparing with companies in the same sector is the best approach.Tina Cook, a senior equity analyst at the investment company Raymond James,cites the example of the life-saving technology group Halma, which has had an average ROE of 17% over the past five years.Scholar says the debt-to-equity ratio (D/E) ratio should be considered, because when there is more debt, the ROE rises. The D/E ratio, which can be found on Yahoo Finance, measures how a company finances its operations by comparing total liabilities to shareholders’ equity.Dividend yieldThis reveals how much a company pays out in dividends (a portion of profits distributed to shareholders) as a percentage of its share price. To calculate it, you divide the annual dividend of a share by the current share price, then multiply by 100.The dividend yield is useful for investors seeking an income. Slingo says a high yield may reveal an attractive opportunity, but can be a warning sign if there is doubt over whether the dividend is sustainable.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMetro Bank is alone among the banks in out table in paying no dividend.Photograph: David Levenson/Alamy“Investors should therefore look at whether dividends are supported by earnings and cashflow, rather than focusing on the headline figure alone,” she says. This can be tricky, as investors must look at whether a company is consistently profitable, if it converts a good proportion of profits into cash, and if cashflow is stable.Cook says the household goods company Procter & Gamble is a “dividend king”, with a long track record of consistent and growing shareholder returns, and 70 consecutive years of payout increases.She says P&G returned more than $16bn (£11.9bn) to shareholders in the financial year 2025 – $9.9bn of which was in dividend payments and $6.5bn in share buybacks.Among the banks in our table, Metro is alone in paying no dividend.CashflowCashflow shows how much money goes in and out of a company over a specific period.Cook says strong cashflow is the “lifeboat of a business”, as it offers flexibility to invest for future growth while returning value to shareholders, regardless of the economic backdrop. She says P&G has made returns to shareholders while still investing in the business.Net debtNet debt offers investors some insight into how financially stable a company is.“Companies with strong cashflows and lower debt levels are typically seen as more resilient and better able to withstand financial challenges,” says Scholar, who adds that excessive debt “can be risky”.View image in fullscreenMarks & Spencer’s share price fell below 100p in 2022, but it is now about 390p.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPATo calculate net debt, subtract the firm’s cash and cash equivalents from the total debt.Scholar says Marks & Spencer was a good example of an attractive stock in 2022, as debt was falling and it traded at a cheap P/E ratio compared with its rivals. The share price fell below 100p. It is now about 390p, at the time of writing, thanks to strong growth in M&S’s grocery market share and improvements at the retailer’s clothing, home and beauty divisions.‘Done extremely well’: Aidan shares his tipsAidan says the quality of a firm’s management is key when investing.“I went out on my own looking at investments 13 years ago,” says Aidan, from Suffolk, who is retired and used to work for the NHS.He was disappointed by the returns and management of his investments, and switched to the AJ Bell platform owing to its fees and the range of companies available.Aidan started investing on behalf of his family, using various products, including Isas. He has invested in funds, exchange-traded funds, investment trusts and individual companies, and also holds some cash.An important motivation to invest was to support his sons with house deposits.Since 2015, he has invested in a range of companies. One is a sustainable infrastructure product and services provider called Hill & Smith, which has given him a total return of 217% over 10 years.Among his other investments are the international engineering business Avingtrans (since 2017) and the environmental and industrial services provider Hargreaves Services (since 2021), the latter of which he says has “done extremely well”.Avingtrans has given a total return of 287% over 10 years, while Hargreaves has made 124% over the past five years.“My key thing is the quality of management,” Aidan says.He looks at their previous employment and the quality and breadth of their experience, and its relevance to the company’s strategy.Aidan says things he has read in the Financial Times and Investors’ Chronicle are “often the trigger for investigating a particular share”.Explore more on these topicsInvestmentsSharesInvestingStock marketsFinancial sectorfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sali Hughes on beauty: the new crop of fig perfumes make perfect scents | Beauty | The Guardian
description: Fragrances with superior tones are cutting through the sugary, cheaper efforts that have been pervasive recently
Author: Sali Hughes
Headline: Fragrances with superior tones are cutting through the sugary, cheaper efforts that have been pervasive recently
Content: Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kellie French/The GuardianSali Hughes on beautyBeautySali Hughes on beauty: the new crop of fig perfumes make perfect scentsFragrances with superior tones are cutting through the sugary, cheaper efforts that have been pervasive recentlySali HughesWed 29 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 06.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.After a lengthy sabbatical, I’m ready to let fig fragrances back into my life. There were years when I couldn’t get enough of lush, green Philosykos by Diptyque – a bona fide masterpiece and the greatest of all fig scents. Then a million sugary, inferior dupes sullied the whole category, cynically transporting it from the fruit groves of Turkey to the air freshener aisle at Halfords. With familiarity, grew contempt. But a new crop of figs is emerging to restore reputation and none are attempting to pass off as Diptyque.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Tom Ford’s recentFigue Erotique(£188 for 30ml), takes fig at various stages of its life cycle (sharp, nutty, green and unripe; rich, juicy, warm and sun-drenched; and finally sugary, creamy and ready to burst) and isolates each in its own accord. Bigger and bolder than most figs, with a sultry, musky sexiness that reads almost as humid, it may not be your most worn in a heatwave (reach for Chloé’s vivid, sparkling fig,Plage duFiguier(£115 for 50ml) then) but do give it a sniff when next you’re next at the shops – it’s a glorious scent for all seasons.If you find the price egregious (I hear you) or the scent too punchy, try Prada’sInfusion de Figue(£152 for 100ml). I didn’t love it at first but truly, this is the just-poured Guinness of fragrances – you’re going to have to wait to get the best of it.double quotation markIt’s warm, woody and earthy, without weighing down what is an olfactory tonic. Imagine fig as a Starburst sweet and you get the ideaHere, we deal with unripened figs – woody, sappy and fresh. The sweetness is gentle; a touch of mandarin zest cuts through the jam. It’s decent on first spray and delightful an hour later. And worth the spend, since 100ml contains the equivalent of two or three regular bottles of perfume.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. The green notes keep things grownup and the cumin (“sweaty” in so many fragrances) appears here as I’d want it: warm, woody and earthy, without weighing down what is an olfactory tonic. title: ‘The shaking was terrifying’: stories of survival and loss emerge after Japan earthquake | Japan | The Guardian
description: Rescuers pulling people from the wreckage in southern Japan in a haunting repeat of disaster that struck 10 years ago
Author: Gavin Blair
Headline: Rescuers pulling people from the wreckage in southern Japan in a haunting repeat of disaster that struck 10 years ago
Content: Rescuers work at a collapsed house in Hikawa on Wednesday, a day after the earthquake.Photograph: Naoki Hiraoka/Kyodo News/APView image in fullscreenRescuers work at a collapsed house in Hikawa on Wednesday, a day after the earthquake.Photograph: Naoki Hiraoka/Kyodo News/APJapan‘The shaking was terrifying’: stories of survival and loss emerge after Japan earthquakeRescuers pulling people from the wreckage in southern Japan in a haunting repeat of disaster that struck 10 years ago‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missingGavin Blairin TokyoWed 29 Jul 2026 05.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“There was a voice coming from the collapsed house, and I could see a hand,” Tomohide Nagata, a volunteer firefighter, told the Kumamoto Nichinichi Shimbun. “One of our senior members crawled in and pulled him out. He was bleeding from the head, but I’m so glad he survived.”Nagata had heard a noise coming from one completely flattened home in the rural town of Hikawa, close to the epicentre of Tuesday’s6.8-magnitude earthquakein southern Japan. The town was one of the areas hardest hit, with numerous older houses collapsing. Terrified of the ongoing aftershocks, many residents spent Tuesday night in their cars outside Hikawa’s town hall, where staff distributed food and drinks.‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missingRead moreAt least 13 people were killed and hundreds injured when the earthquake struck the island of Kyushu. The prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said on Wednesday: “There are people who are still waiting to be rescued, and it’s a race against time. We will go all out to find and rescue as many people as we can.”Iwaoka Shigemi, 79, and his wife, Michiyo, 77, had escaped from their house and spent the night sleeping in their car in Hikawa, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. With temperatures expected to reach 35C on Wednesday, they were now worried about the risk of heatstroke.Suemi Nagata, 79, was unable to escape Hikawa by car because her garage had been destroyed but had made it to the town hall with her husband and older sister. “The lateral shaking was worse than the Kumamoto earthquake 10 years ago, and it was terrifying,” she told the town’s local newspaper. “Just to have survived with my life is something to be grateful for.”View image in fullscreenA damaged road in Hikawa.Photograph: Kyodo/ReutersIn April, the prefecture of Kumamoto commemorated the 10th anniversary of the 2016 earthquake that killed more than 275 people and caused widespread devastation. In that case, a 6.2-magnitude foreshock was followed two days later by the deadly 7-magnitude quake, something that will be on the mind of tens of thousands across Kumamoto in the week ahead.At the Kumamoto Aeon mall, which was severely damaged by what is understood to have been a gas explosion triggered by the earthquake, a number of employees had gone back inside after evacuating customers and were caught in the blast.A 16-year-old girl who got out with other shoppers moments before the explosion, told the Asahi Shimbun she “felt completely safe once she was outside”, only to be left struggling to breathe by dust and smoke.A 74-year-old man who often shopped at the malltold the Nikkei newspaperthat he had just learned that an acquaintance who worked there was hurt. “I could have been caught up in it myself,” he said.Up to 30 employees were initially reported trapped inside and four remain missing.View image in fullscreenA rescue worker walks in front of the Aeon mall, which was damaged by an explosion after the earthquake.Photograph: Hiro Komae/APIn nearby Uki City, which also experienced shaking ranked at the maximum 7 on the Japanese shindo scale, residents told of lucky escapes and heartbreaking unsuccessful rescue efforts.Earthquake rocks southern Japanese island of Kyushu – in picturesRead moreA woman in her 40s had managed to get to an evacuation shelter with three generations of her family after putting herself between falling furniture and her children. “I was pinned under a chest of drawers at home. I protected my children and then hurried to evacuate,” shetold the Kumamoto Nichinichi Shimbunfrom Toyono elementary school, which was being used as an evacuation shelter after the ceiling of the local disaster facility fell in.On Tuesday evening as neighbours and relatives attempted to check in on each other, residents in the Asakawa district of Uki found one house flattened, with roof tiles scattered on the ground around where it had once stood. As family members looked on, a handful of volunteer firefighters attempted to rescue an elderly man trapped inside.“The man is a childhood friend of mine,” the visibly shaken 70-year-old head of the local district told the Kumamoto newspaper. “We tried to pull him out, but the aftershocks came one after another, so we had no choice but to give up.”As in Hikawa, many Uki residents slept in their cars, and local government workers handed out water and food. Unable to use the damaged disaster facility, the city set up a makeshift response headquarters in a car park.In Yatsushiro, south of Hikawa, one man’s life may have been saved by his schedule when his workplace, a single-storey wooden structure, collapsed. “It was a day off and I wasn’t at work, so I escaped with my life,” said the self-employed man, 63, who spent the night in a tent pitched in his garden. “Though I have no idea what I’ll do starting tomorrow.”Explore more on these topicsJapanEarthquakesAsia PacificfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From 400 hives to 35: the Gaza beekeeper refusing to let war end his life’s work | Bees | The Guardian
description: Ibrahim al-Dabba continues to care for his colonies despite losing his home and most of his hives and equipment
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ibrahim al-Dabba continues to care for his colonies despite losing his home and most of his hives and equipment
Content: Photograph: Omar Ashtawy/The GuardianIbrahim al-Dabba continues to care for his colonies despite losing his home and most of his hives and equipmentByLina Abu Zayed; photographs by Omar AshtawyWed 29 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEach morning, Ibrahim Naji al-Dabba climbs to the roof of a damaged residential tower inGazaCity’s Tel al-Hawa neighbourhood, where rows of beehives sit surrounded by shattered concrete and the scars of war. The rooftop is far from an ideal place for beekeeping, but for the 49-year-old father of seven, it is the only place where he can continue the profession that has sustained his family for decades.Before the war, al-Dabba owned more than 400 beehives spread across eastern Gaza. His apiaries, equipment, storage facilities, and four-wheel-drive vehicle allowed him to manage a thriving beekeeping business that supported his family. Today, almost everything he built over years of work has disappeared.View image in fullscreenIbrahim Naji al-Dabba, 49, (in green) working with his sons. He was displaced from the Shuja’iyya area, east of Gaza City to Tel al- to the southView image in fullscreen“Beekeeping is not just a business,” he says. “It is my family’s only source of income. It is our life, our livelihood, and our future.”Al-Dabba, who also serves as president of the Gaza Beekeepers’ cooperative society, says beekeeping became a passion long before it became a profession. Over the years, he specialised in producing honey, breeding queen bees, and developing bee strains adapted to Gaza’s climate. Before the war, Gaza’s beekeeping sector had continued to grow despite years of blockade, with hundreds of beekeepers producing honey and supporting local agriculture through pollination.That changed after the war erupted.Unable to reach his apiaries because of bombardment and displacement, al-Dabba watched his life’s work vanish. He lost his home, more than 400 beehives, honey-processing equipment, storage facilities, and nearly all the tools required for his trade. He estimates his financial losses at more than $350,000 (£263,000).“The hardest moment was realising that everything I had spent years building was gone,” he says. “I lost not only my beehives but also my home, my equipment, and my only source of income.”double quotation markBeekeeping … is our life, our livelihood and our future.IbrahimView image in fullscreenIbrahim’s 18-year-old son, Musa, who helps with the beekeepingView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenLike hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza, al-Dabba was repeatedly displaced throughout the war, moving from one area to another with his family. When conditions became relatively calmer, he searched for other work but found none.Instead, he returned to the profession he knew best.With savings and determination, he bought just three beehives for more than $3,000 – a significant investment under Gaza’s current conditions. Because moving between agricultural areas had become dangerous and transporting hives was nearly impossible, he placed them on the roof of a heavily damaged residential tower.He knew the risks. The building itself had been damaged, and even the wooden hive boxes could be stolen by people desperate for firewood or building materials. Still, he believed the rooftop offered the best chance to protect what little remained.View image in fullscreen“I wanted the bees to adapt to these harsh conditions, just as we have had to adapt,” he says.double quotation markI wanted the bees to adapt to these harsh conditions, just as we have had to adaptIbrahimTogether with his sons, he gradually expanded those three colonies into 35 beehives. Although honey production remains limited, every successful harvest represents something far greater than income.“I don’t feel that I’m only taking care of bees,” al-Dabba says. “I’m trying to preserve a part of the life that I lost because of the war.”The challenges continue every day. Essential supplies such as medicines, wax foundation, supplemental feed, and beekeeping equipment have become scarce or prohibitively expensive. Rebuilding an apiary has become financially impossible for many beekeepers, while the high cost of packaging materials has made selling honey increasingly difficult.View image in fullscreenAl-Dabba: ‘I’m trying to preserve a part of the life that I lost because of the warDespite these obstacles, al-Dabba believes beekeeping remains essential not only for producing honey but also for sustaining agriculture itself.“There is no sustainable agriculture without bees,” he says. “Supporting beekeepers means supporting food production and the livelihoods of thousands of families.”Standing among the hives on the damaged rooftop, al-Dabba says the bees remind him of the people of Gaza.“The bees are like the people here,” he says. “They continue working despite the hardship. They always find their way back to the hive.”For him, every surviving colony carries a message that extends beyond honey production: “As long as there is even one beehive, and one beekeeper holding on to this profession, there is hope that life can begin again.”Explore more on these topicsThe Guardian picture essayBeesGazaInsectsMiddle East and north AfricaPalestinefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why US military prosecutes alleged rapes of women in UK as ‘sexual assaults’ | UK criminal justice | The Guardian
description: Experts say lower-severity charges for American service personnel are deepening traumatic impact on survivors
Author: Louisa Loveluck
Headline: Experts say lower-severity charges for American service personnel are deepening traumatic impact on survivors
Content: Tyrion Davis (left) and Jacob Wulfson, two servicemen whose cases were handed over to US military authorities by British police.Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenTyrion Davis (left) and Jacob Wulfson, two servicemen whose cases were handed over to US military authorities by British police.Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyBase justiceUK criminal justiceAnalysisWhy US military prosecutes alleged rapes of women in UK as ‘sexual assaults’Louisa LoveluckandHarry DaviesExperts say lower-severity charges for American service personnel are deepening traumatic impact on survivorsWed 29 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTShareAmerican service personnel accused of rape on British soil are being charged with lesser offences by their military courts, a discrepancy that experts say is deepening the traumatic impact on survivors long after verdicts are passed.There are more than 12,000 personnel stationed in US military bases across the UK, most of them in England. Although UK law enforcement has primary jurisdiction over crimes that occur when personnel are off duty, local police often choose tocede authority to the American military.When that happens, British victims are thrust into an unfamiliar world, where their alleged attackers are tried at courts martial, often by a panel of American military personnel stationed at the same base.‘They said: wear angelic white’: British women who accused US airman of rape tell of American military trialRead moreVictims of sexual attacks by military personnel that would meet a common definition of rape are also finding that their attackers are instead being prosecuted for lesser offences, which carry more lenient sentences.Under the set of laws that govern US forces, known as the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ), the crime of rape carries a narrower definition to that adopted by the British courts, meaning many cases are charged instead as sexual assault.British law defines rape as when someone puts their penis in another person’s vagina, anus or mouth without their consent and carries a maximum life sentence. Whether or not a victim was intoxicated is not relevant; the law centres on whether the alleged victim consented to the sexual act.In contrast, under article 120 of the UCMJ, a rape charge requires the prosecution to prove that the defendant, without consent, used force or administered an intoxicant. In cases where the victim was drinking alcohol voluntarily, or is not proven to have been overwhelmed by force, the case is charged as sexual assault, with a maximum penalty of 20 years.“It’s concerning if the occupation of the accused pulls a survivor into a justice system that she doesn’t know very much about, or understand, and isn’t one that she feels she has got a voice in,” said Kelly Johnson, a senior criminology lecturer at the University of Glasgow whose research examines policing responses to sexual violence.“A process might say it’s complying with its own formal rules, and still be experienced by survivors as alienating, degrading, and fundamentally unfair.”In the case of Capt Jacob Wulfson, an American fighter pilot,prosecutors accused him of drugging and strangling Sarah Steele, a British academic, during a date in his apartment in December 2023, before penetrating her vagina with his penis without her consent.The charge for the non-consensual penetration was sexual assault and “aggravated sexual contact” – a crime that does not even appear in UK statutes.An all-male panel of airmen found Wulfson not guilty of the sexual assault charge, but guilty of strangulation. They sentenced him to be confined to a corrections facility for six months.Steele said: “Words have power. Legal terminology isn’t just a technical exercise, it shapes how victims are understood. I respect that the law uses precise definitions, but the language carried a profound emotional weight for me.”She recalled “having to explain what the legal label meant and what it didn’t mean. Having to repeatedly explain that distinction has been exhausting and, frankly, retraumatising.”In another case, Tyrion Davis, an American airman, was tried in a court martial in June 2022 after two British women, including his wife,accused him of rape. The official charge sheet said that he was convicted on one charge of sexual assault – described as penetrating the victim’s vagina with his penis without consent – but acquitted of 10 further counts of sexual assault and abusive sexual contact, and two counts of assault.Experts working with survivors of sexual violence say that a perception that the crime on the charge sheet reflects their lived experience can be integral to how a victim is able to process their experience.Katrin Hohl, a professor of criminology and criminal justice at the University of London, said: “The way other people respond to what happened to you, the way other people label it and frame it and see it has profound consequences for your ability to move forward. If the criminal justice system treats you in a way that denies you validation, it doesn’t just not help you recover, it actually adds further trauma.”Get in touchContact our investigations teamThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailinvestigations.contact@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreAn earlier version of the UCMJ’s article 120 defined crimes of sexual violence more loosely, but a new definition adopted in 2007, and refined several times since then, instituted the narrower definition of rape.Critics of article 120 say it fails victims because it was not developed in consultation with victims’ rights groups and individuals specialising in the field of sexual assault.“I think the intention came from a good place,” said Don Christensen, who served as chief prosecutor for the US air force between 2010 and 2014. “They modelled some of these changes on some state laws, but they didn’t really, to my understanding, talk to many of us who were prosecuting cases to ask us what the problems were.”Rachel VanLandingham, a law professor and former US air force judge advocate involved in efforts to reform military law, said the broader problem with prosecuting sexual offences under the UCMJ was a structural one.“They pick the charges and then they get to pick the jury members, which is completely structurally unfair, but the system was never designed to be fair. It was designed to be a commander’s tool for strict discipline,” she said.For victims, the consequences of having their experiences funnelled through such an opaque and militarised process can be devastating. “When victims don’t feel like they’re taken seriously, they’re not treated with respect and dignity, they’re not heard, that causes retraumatisation or what’s known as a secondary victimisation,” said Johnson, of the University of Glasgow. “Some victims say this is more profoundly damaging and harmful than the initial experience.”Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 inScotland, or 0800 0246 991 inNorthern Ireland. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsUK criminal justiceBase justiceUS militaryPoliceRape and sexual assaultanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Kenya investigating unexpected deaths of 15 elephants in national park | Kenya | The Guardian
description: Potential toxic substance detected in several of 15 elephants found dead in Kenya’s Amboseli national park
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Potential toxic substance detected in several of 15 elephants found dead in Kenya’s Amboseli national park
Content: An elephant herd walking on the savannah in Amboseli national park, Kenya. An investigation has been opened into the unexplained death of 15 elephants in the park.Photograph: Ronald S Phillips/AlamyView image in fullscreenAn elephant herd walking on the savannah in Amboseli national park, Kenya. An investigation has been opened into the unexplained death of 15 elephants in the park.Photograph: Ronald S Phillips/AlamyKenyaKenya investigating unexpected deaths of 15 elephants in national parkPotential toxic substance detected in several of 15 elephants found dead in Kenya’s Amboseli national parkGuardian staff and agenciesTue 28 Jul 2026 20.48 EDTLast modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 23.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOfficials are investigating the deaths of 15 elephants over the past month in Kenya’s Amboseli national park.The KenyaWildlifeService (KWS) said 10 of the elephants showed signs of partial paralysis before dying within two days.The remaining five carcasses were too decomposed or had been scavenged, making it impossible to establish the cause of death, the wildlife authority said.Most of those affected were female elephants and their calves, with only one male among the dead. The deaths happened in the Kimana sanctuary and Kuku ranch areas surrounding the park, officials said.Ancient elephant migration routes are being blocked off – can anything stop the rising death toll?Read moreKenya has previously recorded incidents of elephants being poisoned as a result of poaching and human-wildlife conflict.Preliminary tests on samples collected from the elephants by a laboratory at the University of Nairobi detected a “potential toxic substance,” while separate analyses by a government laboratory were negative for the toxins tested. KWS said further tests are under way.“Environmental investigations are also being undertaken, including the analysis of water sources and other potential environmental contaminants within the affected areas, to establish whether the elephants were exposed to a common source,” the authority said in a statement.The authorities sought to reassure the public, saying there was no evidence the condition could be transmitted to humans.Amboseli is world-renowned for its herds of elephants and its savannah landscapes, with Kilimanjaro visible across the border in Tanzania.It is estimated there are about 2,000 elephants in the park.With Associated Press and Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsKenyaWildlifeAfricaConservationAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rescue teams face ‘race against time’ in search for trapped survivors as death toll in Japan rises to at least 13 – as it happened | Japan | The Guardian
description: Emergency workers are continuing their search for survivors in southern Japan after yesterday’s powerful earthquake
Author: Tom Ambrose
Headline: Emergency workers are continuing their search for survivors in southern Japan after yesterday’s powerful earthquake
Content: 03.15 EDTRescuers search for survivors in Japan after earthquake kills 13 peopleEmergency workers are continuing their search for survivors in southernJapanafter yesterday’s powerful earthquakeleft widespread devastation, with buildings collapsed, roads severely damaged and emergency teams digging through rubble.At least 13 people have been killedand many reported missing after the earthquake struck the Kumamoto area on the southern main island of Kyushu with a magnitude of 7.1, according to the Japan meteorological agency. The US Geological Survey measured it at magnitude 6.8.Collapsed buildings after an earthquake with a magnitude of 7.1 struck Japan’s southern Kumamoto district.Photograph: KYODO/ReutersThe Japanese prime minister,Sanae Takaichi,said rescue workers faced a“race against time”to reach more people still trapped in rubble. “We will go all out to find and rescue as many people as we can,” she said.Eight people ⁠were pulled from the rubble of a ​partially collapsed Aeon shopping centre near the city of Kumamotofollowing an apparent explosion that occurred around an hour after the earthquake,according to reports. Aeon said four workers at the shopping centre remained unaccounted for.“I thought a bomb had gone off,” Takateru Sonoda, 41, who runs a hair salon and cafe near the shopping centre, told the Japanese Jiji Press news agency.“There were people calling on others to evacuate and sirens were ringing out. Nearby ⁠roads were gridlocked, it was a state of panic.”Aeon shopping centre was damaged by an explosion following the earthquake.Photograph: Hiro Komae/APSeven people are also still missing at the Nippon Paper Industries factory where a chimney collapsed on to the site. Japan’s Mainichi newspaper reported that four people were rescued from the rubble at the paper mill, including two who were seriously injured.Nearly 37,000 homes were still without electricity, 9,500 homes were without gas and communication networks were not working in some areas, chief government spokespersonMinoru Kiharatold reporters. More than 9,000 people left their homes to stay in more than 500 shelters, Kihara added.Read our overnight report here:‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missingRead moreShareUpdated at03.17 EDT
