We will go all out to find and rescue as many people as we can.”Iwaoka Shigemi, 79, and his wife, Michiyo, 77, had escaped from their house and spent the night sleeping in their car in Hikawa, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. With temperatures expected to reach 35C on Wednesday, they were now worried about the risk of heatstroke.Suemi Nagata, 79, was unable to escape Hikawa by car because her garage had been destroyed but had made it to the town hall with her husband and older sister. “The lateral shaking was worse than the Kumamoto earthquake 10 years ago, and it was terrifying,” she told the town’s local newspaper. “Just to have survived with my life is something to be grateful for.”View image in fullscreenA damaged road in Hikawa.Photograph: Kyodo/ReutersIn April, the prefecture of Kumamoto commemorated the 10th anniversary of the 2016 earthquake that killed more than 275 people and caused widespread devastation. In that case, a 6.2-magnitude foreshock was followed two days later by the deadly 7-magnitude quake, something that will be on the mind of tens of thousands across Kumamoto in the week ahead.At the Kumamoto Aeon mall, which was severely damaged by what is understood to have been a gas explosion triggered by the earthquake, a number of employees had gone back inside after evacuating customers and were caught in the blast.A 16-year-old girl who got out with other shoppers moments before the explosion, told the Asahi Shimbun she “felt completely safe once she was outside”, only to be left struggling to breathe by dust and smoke.A 74-year-old man who often shopped at the malltold the Nikkei newspaperthat he had just learned that an acquaintance who worked there was hurt. “I could have been caught up in it myself,” he said.Up to 30 employees were initially reported trapped inside and four remain missing.View image in fullscreenA rescue worker walks in front of the Aeon mall, which was damaged by an explosion after the earthquake.Photograph: Hiro Komae/APIn nearby Uki City, which also experienced shaking ranked at the maximum 7 on the Japanese shindo scale, residents told of lucky escapes and heartbreaking unsuccessful rescue efforts.Earthquake rocks southern Japanese island of Kyushu – in picturesRead moreA woman in her 40s had managed to get to an evacuation shelter with three generations of her family after putting herself between falling furniture and her children. “I was pinned under a chest of drawers at home. I protected my children and then hurried to evacuate,” shetold the Kumamoto Nichinichi Shimbunfrom Toyono elementary school, which was being used as an evacuation shelter after the ceiling of the local disaster facility fell in.On Tuesday evening as neighbours and relatives attempted to check in on each other, residents in the Asakawa district of Uki found one house flattened, with roof tiles scattered on the ground around where it had once stood. As family members looked on, a handful of volunteer firefighters attempted to rescue an elderly man trapped inside.“The man is a childhood friend of mine,” the visibly shaken 70-year-old head of the local district told the Kumamoto newspaper. “We tried to pull him out, but the aftershocks came one after another, so we had no choice but to give up.”As in Hikawa, many Uki residents slept in their cars, and local government workers handed out water and food. Unable to use the damaged disaster facility, the city set up a makeshift response headquarters in a car park.In Yatsushiro, south of Hikawa, one man’s life may have been saved by his schedule when his workplace, a single-storey wooden structure, collapsed. “It was a day off and I wasn’t at work, so I escaped with my life,” said the self-employed man, 63, who spent the night in a tent pitched in his garden. “Though I have no idea what I’ll do starting tomorrow.”Explore more on these topicsJapanEarthquakesAsia PacificfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missing  | Japan | The Guardian
description: Military mobilises thousands of personnel after quake on southern Kyushu island that registered a maximum 7 on the Japanese shindo intensity scale
Author: Gavin Blair
Headline: Military mobilises thousands of personnel after quake on southern Kyushu island that registered a maximum 7 on the Japanese shindo intensity scale
Content: 1:09Aerial footage shows collapsed buildings after 6.8 magnitude Japan earthquake – videoJapan‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missingMilitary mobilises thousands of personnel after quake on southern Kyushu island that registered a maximum 7 on the Japanese shindo intensity scaleEarthquake rocks southern Japanese island of Kyushu – in picturesGavin Blairin Tokyo, andRachel HallTue 28 Jul 2026 22.40 EDTFirst published on Tue 28 Jul 2026 20.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 13 people were killed when a 6.8 magnitude earthquake struck southernJapanon Tuesday, injuring hundreds and knocking out power and water to tens of thousands.“There are people who are still waiting to be rescued, and it’s a race against time,” the prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said on Wednesday. “We will go all out to find and rescue as many people as we can.”The quake registered a maximum 7 on the Japaneseshindointensity scale when it struck Kumamoto prefecture on the southern island of Kyushu on Tuesday afternoon. The government has said more than 9,000 people were in evacuation centres across the country early Wednesday.“We have received reports of seven people with serious injuries and 29 with minor injuries. Furthermore, as of 7:00 am today (2200 GMT Tuesday), 9,186 people have sought refuge in 506 evacuation centres across five prefectures, including Kumamoto and Fukuoka,” government spokesman Minoru Kihara said a day after the quake that killed at least 13 people.1:09'People are waiting to be rescued': race under way to find Japan quake survivors – videoRescue crews were sifting through the wreckage at key sites, including that of a paper mill in Yatsushiro where a chimney collapsed. Two workers were found and taken to hospital in a state of cardiac arrest, with nine others missing.An explosion was reported in an Aeon shopping mall, which houses around 200 outlets, in the prefecture shortly after the earthquake and footage appeared to show the upper section of the main building torn away and partially collapsed. Two women in their 20s were confirmed dead, and another person reportedly suffered cardiac arrest.Japan earthquake injures at least 100 and kills two inside shopping mallRead moreShoppers flee Aeon mall in Japan after 6.8 magnitude earthquakeAn Aeon spokesperson said customers and employees were evacuated after the initial quake and the cause of the explosion remained unclear. A government official told reporters that Aeon Kumamoto reported a gas leak, though the cause had not yet been determined.The Japanese military mobilised 3,600 personnel for disaster relief operations and sent 20 aircraft to assess the damage from the air, the defence minister said. Hundreds of first responders from neighbouring prefectures arrived in the affected areas on Tuesday evening.The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) warned that areas with the biggest tremors would remain at risk of further strong quakes and landslides for about a week because the shallow earthquake was triggering seismic activity in the area.quake mapBy Wednesday morning more than 60 aftershocks had been recorded, ranging in magnitude from 1 to 4, the agency said. A tsunami warning was issued immediately after the quake, ​but was lifted within two hours.Nearly 50,000 households were without power late on Tuesday, along with 140,000 without water. Temperatures in the region were forecast to top 35C on Wednesday, with high humidity increasing the chance of heatstroke for those without access to air conditioning and water. Large numbers of people slept in their cars overnight out of fear of aftershocks.Despite the earthquake’s intensity, relatively few buildings collapsed, reducing the number of fatalities and injuries. Japan has strict construction standards and earthquake resistance requirements for new buildings have been raised multiple times over recent decades. Technology such as apartment blocks with foundations laid on rollers that can sway means newer structures are able to withstand intense shaking.View image in fullscreenAn aerial view shows a collapsed chimney at Nippon Paper Industries’ Yatsushiro paper mill after the earthquake.Photograph: KYODO/ReutersTakaichi said on Tuesday evening that authorities were still assessing the extent of the damage in the area, which was devastated by another deadly quake a decade ago.“We have already been informed that people have been injured. Power outages and fires have occurred in some areas, and there has also been damage to roads and bridges and the collapse of buildings,” Takaichi said. “I ask everyone to take action to protect themselves, including evacuating to a safe location.”By Wednesday morning, five houses had been confirmed collapsed. More than 350 people had been treated at local hospitals, many of which were affected by power and water outages and damage to medical equipment.“People are coming in with burns and fractures from being trapped under objects due to the earthquake, and ambulances are constantly bringing in injured people,” NHK quoted one hospital employee as saying. “Inside the hospital there are water leaks and electrical system failures.”About 300,000 people were instructed to go to evacuation centres, the disaster management agency said.​JR Kyushu, the regional railway company, suspended services on Tuesday, including its high-speed bullet trains. Kumamoto airport also shut its runway as airlines diverted and ​cancelled flights.View image in fullscreenAn ambulance passes by a collapsed building in Yatsushiro, Kumamoto prefecture, on Wednesday.Photograph: Juntaro Yokoyama/Kyodo News/APTelecoms operators KDDI and NTT Docomo ‌said there was disruption to their ​mobile phone services owing to power shortages ​and transmission-line failures. There were no irregularities reported at the nuclear power stations in the area, Japan’s nuclear regulation authority said.Footage from NHK on Tuesday showed multiple buildings on fire or partly collapsed, along with large fissures on ‌major roads, including an elevated highway. TSMC, the world’s largest contract chip maker, Sony and Fujifilm evacuated workers from their factories in the area.Chiharu Hara, a 35-year-old recruitment agent who was in Kumamoto, told AFP that she was “terrified” when the quake struck. “The office swayed violently side to side. I was afraid it would collapse. Everyone panicked,” Hara said.The quake’s epicentre was about 12 miles (20km) south of Kumamoto, central Kyushu island’s largest city, with a population of about 700,000. The US Geological Survey initially said the earthquake had a magnitude of 7.1, but revised it later to 6.8. The JMA said it had a magnitude of 7.1 but reached the highest level of 7 on Japan’s own shindo scale. A subsequent aftershock with a magnitude of 6.1 was registered at 5.08pm.The Geospatial Information Authority of Japan reported that the Earth’s crust had moved 84cm in Yatsushiro city, where the paper mill is located, and up to 40cm in Kumamoto city.Japan, which is located along the “ring of fire” of volcanoes and oceanic trenches in the Pacific basin, is one of the world’s most earthquake-prone countries, with a tremor occurring at least every five minutes. The country accounts for about 20% of the world’s earthquakes of magnitude 6 or higher.Anearthquake in Kumamoto10 years ago killed 275 people and injured a further 2,739. It damaged thousands of buildings including the city’s castle, a popular tourist site. Some of the castle’s stone walls were damaged in the latest quake. Two days before that earthquake, a powerful foreshock struck nearby.Japan is haunted by the memory of amassive 9.0-magnitude undersea quake in 2011,which triggered a tsunami that left around 18,500 people dead or missing and wrecked the Fukushima nuclear plant.Explore more on these topicsJapanEarthquakesAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Body found in suitcase in Athens is that of 38-year-old British woman | Greece | The Guardian
description: Greek authorities identify remains as those of Elizabeth Jane Ross after discovery in a derelict building 11 days ago
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Greek authorities identify remains as those of Elizabeth Jane Ross after discovery in a derelict building 11 days ago
Content: Elizabeth Jane Ross’s body was found in a suitcase in this abandoned building in Athens 11 days ago.Photograph: Danai Davlopoulou/EurokinissiView image in fullscreenElizabeth Jane Ross’s body was found in a suitcase in this abandoned building in Athens 11 days ago.Photograph: Danai Davlopoulou/EurokinissiGreeceBody found in suitcase in Athens is that of 38-year-old British womanGreek authorities identify remains as those of Elizabeth Jane Ross after discovery in a derelict building 11 days agoHelena Smithin AthensWed 29 Jul 2026 17.05 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 11.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA body found in a suitcase in an abandoned building in central Athens has been identified as that of a 38-year-old British woman.Eleven days after the find, and following an appeal to foreign law enforcement agencies, Greek police shed some light on the mystery of the body that until Wednesday had remained unidentified.“The remains, we can confirm, have been identified as belonging to a British woman,” one well-placed source said. “Her next of kin have been informed.” They added that it had been ascertained the victim had been born inScotlandin 1988.Late on Wednesday, Greek media named the victim as Elizabeth Jane Ross.She had been staying in the city with friends, who reported seeing her for the last time on 15 July.Adding to the mystery surrounding the circumstances of her death, it was revealed that her mobile phone had been fully operational until news of her identification was released.Police were alerted after a homeless man discovered the suitcase on 18 July in a derelict building in Kypseli, a district popular among foreign nationals in downtown Athens, according to the public broadcaster ERT.Ross had reportedly flown to the region from the US, arriving inGreece, on 29 June, from Cyprus.Greek homicide officers sent fingerprints toInterpolafter drawing a blank on local databases. US authorities had provided evidence on the basis of the DNA that police released on Wednesday.Detectives cordoned off the building on Evelpidon Street as they investigated the circumstances of Ross’s death.A police spokesperson, Konstantina Dimoglidou, had previously said CCTV was being examined to try to trace Ross’s movements before her death. Authorities were treating the incident “as a criminal act, given how the body was found”, she told Skai TV.Airlines are also believed to have been approached as investigators try to reconstruct Ross’s journey to Greece and determine whether she was travelling alone. Officials in Greece and Cyprus were scouring flight logs and hotel bookings.Local media, citing the results of a postmortem, said Ross had been dead for eight days before the discovery. There was “no evidence” of a struggle or signs of injury.Greek officials did not rule out UK investigators joining the inquiry.A British Foreign Office spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with Elizabeth’s family during this difficult time. We are providing consular support and are in contact with the local authorities.”Greece is no stranger to British tourists dying in what is a popular holiday destination – often by drowning or as a result of road accidents – “but incidents like this are very rare”, officials said.Explore more on these topicsGreeceScotlandEuropeInterpolnewsShareReuse this content

title: Three firefighters killed on Crete and in mainland Greece as Europe battles wildfires | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Repeated heatwaves and strong winds alarm experts, who warn blazes are becoming harder to quell
Author: Ajit Niranjan
Headline: Repeated heatwaves and strong winds alarm experts, who warn blazes are becoming harder to quell
Content: Low-lying vegetation ablaze in Krya Vrysi, Rethymno, Crete on Wednesday.Photograph: Nikos Chalkiadakis/EPAView image in fullscreenLow-lying vegetation ablaze in Krya Vrysi, Rethymno, Crete on Wednesday.Photograph: Nikos Chalkiadakis/EPAWildfiresThree firefighters killed on Crete and in mainland Greece as Europe battles wildfiresRepeated heatwaves and strong winds alarm experts, who warn blazes are becoming harder to quellAjit NiranjanandJennifer RankinWed 29 Jul 2026 14.30 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 10.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree Greek firefighters have died while tackling wildfires on the island of Crete and in the south of the mainland, the Greek fire department has said, as extreme heat hinders efforts to control blazes ravaging southernEurope.The arc of brutal fires, which runs from the Atlantic coast to the eastern Mediterranean, and from the Scottish Highlands to the south ofSpain, has alarmed experts because many of the fires have been out of control and burning close to towns and cities.Temperatures exacerbated by the climate crisis reached 38C on Wednesday in Bordeaux in France, where firefighters kept ahuge blazein nearby pine forests from reaching the suburbs, and 37C in Madrid, west of which Spain’s largest wildfire on recordhad been “technically stabilised”, according to the interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska.Dozens of ground crews had managed to contain the Madrid fire overnight, emergency services for the region said on Wednesday morning, but a separate fire near València, where temperatures will peak at a cooler 32C, is still out of control.View image in fullscreenMembers of the Emergency Military Unit utilise controlled burns to halt the spread of wildfires in the Madrid border region in Cebreros, Ávila province, on Tuesday night.Photograph: Pablo Blázquez Domínguez/Getty ImagesIn televised comments from the Navalcarnero command centre on Wednesday morning, the Spanish prime minister,Pedro Sánchez, said the situation near the capital was improving but stressed it was the first time in Spanish history that a wildfire had been raised to “operational level 3”, with the national government taking over the disaster response.“I believe the next 12 hours will be very important,” he said. “They are going to be decisive in consolidating the work done by the national civil protection system.”Accompanied by strong winds, the fourth heatwave of western Europe’s scorching summer hasalarmed firefighters, who warn it makes blazes harder to quell and raises the risk of fires restarting in areas that have been stabilised. New fires also prompted evacuations in Greece and Turkey.View image in fullscreenWildfires in Crete, where authorities say two firefighters ‘fell heroically in the line of duty’.Photograph: ERT GRView image in fullscreenThe remains of a firefighting vehicle seen south of Rethymno in Crete on Wednesday.Photograph: Costas Metaxakis/AFP/Getty ImagesFrench authorities benefited from a calm night on Tuesday that allowed flare-ups to be swiftly extinguished but warned of “unfavourable” developing weather conditions that could hamper progress. The prefecture of Gironde said 126 firefighters had been injured since the start of the fire but the total burned area remained stable at 42,000 hectares (104,000 acres) on Wednesday morning.Wildfires have burned a record-breaking area of France, data from the European Forest Fire Information System shows, while France and Spain have experienced record-breaking numbers of fires for this time of year. More than 330,000 people in southern Europe have been forced to flee their homes and hotels.Officials began to lift evacuation orders on Tuesday as fires were brought under control, allowing tens of thousands of people living in towns near Bordeaux, Madrid and València to go back to their homes.Some of them returnedto find burnt-out buildings and charred belongings.View image in fullscreenA house which remained untouched by wildfires despite nearby land being scorched, in La Vilavella, Castellón province, in Spain.Photograph: Nacho Doce/ReutersJosé Fernández, a 74-year-old pensioner, told AFP he had “no money, no documents, no home” after he came back to the remains of what used to be his house in Pelayos de la Presa, in the Community of Madrid. “This place has been reduced to a total ruin.”Europe’s wildfire season is growing hotter and longer as carbon pollution heats the continent twice as fast as the global average. Repeated heatwaves this year have dried vegetation and turned forests and shrubland into tinderboxes, alarming EU officials, who have said wildfires could still be burning in November.Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, thanked firefighters for their “courage and commitment” on Wednesday.“As the fires in France and Spain continue to ravage, European solidarity knows no limit,” she said in a social media post. “Romania andGreecehave decided to extend their missions, continuing their support to the affected regions. And from Saturday, Poland will join the fray.”View image in fullscreenA volunteer carries a water bucket to help battling the fire in Lanton, west of Bordeaux.Photograph: Romain Perrocheau/AFP/Getty ImagesEarlier this week, the European Commission said it had sentFranceseven planes and four helicopters from countries as far away as Sweden and Turkey, while in Spain, it said it had mobilised six planes from Greece, Italy and Turkey, along with 134 personnel and 41 vehicles from Portugal. A Super Puma helicopter from Serbia was expected to arrive in Madrid on Wednesday, according to Spain’s interior ministry, with 40 personnel and 18 vehicles to shortly follow.The European Union’s crisis management team said on Wednesday it expected difficult weeks ahead, fearing a further outbreak of wildfires in Italy and Greece later in the summer.View image in fullscreenA firefighting plane makes a drop amid efforts to battle a wildfire in Artana, Spain on Wednesday.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersMaria Zuber, a senior official at the EU’s emergency response coordination centre (ERCC) in Brussels, which coordinates the dispatch of firefighting planes, equipment and teams to countries that have asked for help, said the next few days would be “very difficult” for France and that “now we see it will go to Greece”.Moisés Galán Santano, a wildfire expert at the ERCC, said more needed to be done to prevent wildfires and that it would be a task for many years. “The [emergency] response is not only the answer. It’s the last answer. But it’s not all the answer. We need to focus on prevention.”mapEarlier this year, a policy paper from the European Commission set out how countries could better prevent and recover from wildfires that are expected to become bigger and more damaging across the continent. It promoted measures such as more extensive grazing, the restoration of wetlands, rivers and floodplains, better data on forest fires and raising public awareness of risky behaviour and safe evacuation.Scientists say western Europe’s scorching summer has been deadly, costly and exacerbated by fossil fuel pollution. Rapid analyses have found June’s heatwave would have been “virtually impossible”in a world without climate breakdown, while the recent level of soil dryness in western Europe – a driver of bigger blazes – was madefive times more likely. The heatwaves are estimated to have claimed at least 10,000 lives andcost grain farmers€2bn in lost crops.View image in fullscreenPeople try to extinguish a fire in the town of Plomari on the Greek island of Lesbos on Wednesday.Photograph: Manolis Lagoutaris/AFP/Getty ImagesVula Tsetsi, a co-chair of the European Green party, called on European institutions to take action on Wednesday and noted the European Commission had not yet published its heating and cooling plan, which was expected in April.“Climate-driven heatwaves and wildfires are already claiming lives, destroying homes and ravaging forests at a record pace,” she said. “There is a widening gap between the scale of Europe’s heatwaves – literally hitting every EU country – and the absence of decisive European action.”Explore more on these topicsWildfiresFranceSpainGreeceExtreme heatPedro SánchezEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Norwegian teenager guilty of travelling to UK to carry out contract killing | Organised crime | The Guardian
description: Johannes Kongsnes Natland was recruited to murder unknown person by international crime gang linked to Iran
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: Johannes Kongsnes Natland was recruited to murder unknown person by international crime gang linked to Iran
Content: Johannes Kongsnes Natland had agreed to shoot an unidentified victim for €25,000 but was arrested in Huddersfield by armed police.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PAView image in fullscreenJohannes Kongsnes Natland had agreed to shoot an unidentified victim for €25,000 but was arrested in Huddersfield by armed police.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PAOrganised crimeNorwegian teenager guilty of travelling to UK to carry out contract killingJohannes Kongsnes Natland was recruited to murder unknown person by international crime gang linked to IranPriya BharadiaWed 29 Jul 2026 13.02 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Norwegian teenager has been found guilty of travelling to England to carry out a killing ordered by an international crime gang linked to Iran.Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, from Stavanger, Norway, agreed to shoot an unknown person for €25,000 (£21,500) in March last year. Two days after he arrived in the UK armed police arrested him in a hotel room in Huddersfield,West Yorkshire, seizing two guns and ammunition.After deliberating for 17 hours and six minutes, a jury at the Old Bailey found him guilty of conspiracy to murder following a retrial.Photo issued by the Metropolitan police of Johannes Natland wearing gloves while handling a gun.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PANatland blinked but did not visibly react to the verdict. Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb remanded him into custody to be sentenced in October.Natland, who worked part-time in a pizza restaurant, was recruited by the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organised crime group with links to the Iranian government.Natland told jurors he agreed at first to the murder plot in exchange for money to pay for drugs, thinking it was just a “joke” or “scam”.Once he realised he was in a “pickle” with the Foxtrot Network, Natland said he planned to “shoot himself in the foot” to avoid carrying out the assassination.The potential victim of the foiled murder plot has never been identified. The Metropolitan police said their counter-terrorism officers “uncovered a significant amount of evidence demonstrating that Natland was fully aware he was being asked to kill someone in the UK”.“I’m going on crazy mission,” Natland had texted his girlfriend. “It will be a bit cool to kill someone. If I don’t get caught we have to celebrate.”When armed police banged on his hotel room door, Natland emerged from his room smiling, only wearing his boxer shorts, and mimed shooting one of the officers with his empty hands.In a search of his room, officers found a plastic bag under his bed containing a semi-automatic pistol, a revolver and 19 rounds of ammunition.View image in fullscreenNatland mimed shooting an armed officer during his arrest.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PAAt his trial, one of Natland’s friends recalled a conversation where the defendant bragged he was “going to get a lot of money and somebody is going to die”.Natland told jurors these statements were “bravado” and he was secretly “terrified”.“I wasn’t an international assassin,” he said. “I thought people had this impression and expected me to be this guy. I knew I wasn’t.”But jurors heard Natland lied after his arrest and had tried to persuade his girlfriend not to give evidence during his phone calls from prison.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe prosecutor Alistair Richardson said: “The reality is the defendant is a troubled but dangerous young man. A young man who agreed to kill in a foreign country for money.”The court heard that Natland, a talented young footballer, began taking drugs aged 13. He spent a short period of time in a care home, where he first met a teenage member of the Foxtrot Network and was passed on to a recruiter known as “Generalen”.On 17 March 2025, Natland took a flight from Stavanger to Manchester airport on a temporary passport. He was stopped by Border Force officials in Manchester, who bailed him to return to the airport and catch the next direct flight home.Instead, he took a taxi toHuddersfield, where he picked up £2,000 in cash, two guns and bullets, as well as a stolen Nissan with a fake number plate. He was arrested the following day at 5.15am.View image in fullscreenNatland was arrested at a hotel in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, where he had been caught on camera paying in cash.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PANatland was controlled by an English-speaking boss called “Agent 47” – an apparent reference to the Hitman game and movie series – whose identity and whereabouts remain unknown.Despite several high-ranking arrests in recent years, Foxtrot is stillthe dominant gang in Swedenand thought to be responsible for the majority of gang violence in the country including mass shootings and murders across the country.But with many of the gang’s key figures now believed to be fugitive abroad – including the leader, Rawa Majid, known as the Kurdish Fox, who is still at large and believed to be in Iran – the police operation to find them is global. Last year up to 30 of the wanted Swedes who were arrested outsideSwedenhad connections to Foxtrot, according to police.In June, Poya Shafie, described as the person who planned Foxtrot’s murders and who was one of the men closest to Majid, was sentenced to life imprisonment in a Swedish court after being arrested in Iraq.Explore more on these topicsOrganised crimeNorwayHuddersfieldCrimeEuropeWest YorkshireSwedennewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia accuses Telegram founder of aiding terrorism in its latest online crackdown | Telegram | The Guardian
description: FSB puts Pavel Durov on international wanted lists and says his messaging app is used for sabotage and murder
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: FSB puts Pavel Durov on international wanted lists and says his messaging app is used for sabotage and murder
Content: Pavel Durov, the founder of Telegram, says the Russian actions against him are an attempt to suppress privacy and free speech.Photograph: Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPavel Durov, the founder of Telegram, says the Russian actions against him are an attempt to suppress privacy and free speech.Photograph: Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty ImagesTelegramRussia accuses Telegram founder of aiding terrorism in its latest online crackdownFSB puts Pavel Durov on international wanted lists and says his messaging app is used for sabotage and murderAssociated PressWed 29 Jul 2026 12.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussian officials have chargedPavel Durov, the founder and chief executive of the messaging app Telegram, with aiding terrorism.The charges againstthe 41-year-old Russian-born billionaire, who lives in the Gulf, are the latest step by the Kremlin to bring the internet and digital communications under its control after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.The Federal Security Service said in a statement on Wednesday it had accusedTelegramof failing to remove “numerous channels, chats and bots” allegedly used by “Ukrainian intelligence agencies, terrorist and extremist organizations to prepare and coordinate acts of sabotage and terrorism, mass murder, and cyber fraud” in Russia.The FSB said Kyiv was using a dating chatbot on Telegram to lure and recruit Russians for “sabotage and terrorist activities” and it had detained 46 users, aged from 12 to 22, for assaulting law enforcement officers, arson and other acts over the past year.The agency said it was adding Durov’s name to international wanted lists.Durov said earlier this year that Russian officials hadopened a criminal investigation against himand he accused them of fabricating pretexts to restrict access to Telegram and “suppress the right to privacy and free speech”.If brought to trial and convicted, he could face life in prison.Telegram, which boasts more than 1 billion users worldwide, did not respond to a request for comment. Its official website links to an account on X that on Wednesday posted an image of Durov raising a middle finger to the camera.The website says the company is based inDubaiand that Durov, who holds dual citizenship of France and the United Arab Emirates, lives there too.View image in fullscreenPavel Durov speaks at the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona, Spain, in February 2016.Photograph: Manuel Blondeau/Corbis/Getty ImagesUnderVladimir Putin, Russian authorities have banned websites and platforms that do not comply with tight restrictions. They have also developed technology to monitor and manipulate online traffic.Facebook, Instagram and X have been banned in Russia and YouTube has been throttled. Popular messaging apps, such as Signal and Viber, have been blocked, and the most popular ones, WhatsApp and Telegram, have been restricted.VKontakte, a popular social media platform founded by Durov well before he launched Telegram, has come under the control of Kremlin-friendly companies. Russia tried to block Telegram between 2018 and 2020 but failed.It is possible to circumvent some Kremlin restrictions by using virtual private networks (VPNs) but many of these are now being blocked.Moscow is promoting what it calls a “national” messaging app known as Max, which critics say could be used for surveillance. The platform is touted as a one-stop shop for messaging, government services, payments and other activities. It openly says it will share user data with authorities upon request and experts say it does not use end-to-end encryption.Activists in multiple regions have tried to organise protests against the restrictions on Telegram but the authorities crushed nearly all their attempts.Military bloggers have also denounced the crackdown, arguing that Telegram is an indispensable communications tool for Russian troops inUkraineand for activists running crowdfunding campaigns to help Moscow’s forces.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe government initially promised not to restrict Telegram on the battlefield but a different message later emerged from the Kremlin. At a meeting with Putin for International Women’s Day, a servicewoman called Telegram an “adversarial tool” and agreed with the president when he said “the use of communications systems that are not ours, not under our control, poses a danger to personnel” in battle.Despite the restrictions, multiple Russian officials still use Telegram and regularly update their “channels” – its term for blogs – on the platform. The Kremlin’s Telegram page had more than 284,000 followers as of Wednesday.Durov was arrested in Paris in 2024 amid allegations that his platform was being used for illicit activity, including drug trafficking and the distribution of images of child sexual abuse. French authorities handed him preliminary charges for allegedly allowing criminal activity on the platform. In March last year, Durov said he had returned to Dubai after spending “several months” in France.View image in fullscreenThe chief culprit for a Russia-linked arson attack on this warehouse in London was recruited through Telegram.Photograph: London Fire Brigade/PAThe Kremlin criticised the French authorities for moving against Durov. Putin’s spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said at the time that “yes, indeed, terrorists use Telegram. But terrorists also use cars. Why aren’t they arresting the CEO of Renault or Citroën?”Peskov did not respond to a request for comment on what had made the Russian authorities change their position.Prosecutors in Paris told Associated Press on Wednesday that Durov remained under formal investigation, facing an array of potential charges for alleged criminal activities linked to Telegram. Investigators have questioned him repeatedly, most recently this month.Russia has faced accusations of using Telegram to coordinate and recruit people to carry out acts of arson and sabotage in Ukraine and across Europe. A British man was recruited on the platform, probably by Russian military intelligence, to organise a plot in 2024to set fire to a warehouse in Londoncontaining satellite equipment for Ukraine. He was also asked to kidnap a pro-Ukraine Russian billionaire living in London.Dutch teenagers were arrested in the Netherlands in September after being contacted by Russian hackers on Telegram who wanted them to map wifi networks in The Hague. The city is the location of many sensitive organisations, including the international criminal court, which has issued an arrest warrant for Putin, as well as the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons and Europol, which helps European countries fight international crime.Moscow has denied involvement in acts of sabotage in Europe.Explore more on these topicsTelegramPavel DurovRussiaSocial mediaUkraineVladimir PutinEuropenewsShareReuse this content
