title: US-Saudi strikes in Iraq push region into ‘uncharted territory’, analysts warn | Iraq | The Guardian
description: Riyadh’s decision to join US in strikes on Iran-backed militia further complicates widening and ‘unpredictable’ war
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Riyadh’s decision to join US in strikes on Iran-backed militia further complicates widening and ‘unpredictable’ war
Content: Mourners in Mosul, Iraq, carry coffins draped in Iranian and Iraqi flags during a group funeral for Popular Mobilisation Forces fighters killed in US-Saudi airstrikes on Wednesday.Photograph: Hadi Mizban/APView image in fullscreenMourners in Mosul, Iraq, carry coffins draped in Iranian and Iraqi flags during a group funeral for Popular Mobilisation Forces fighters killed in US-Saudi airstrikes on Wednesday.Photograph: Hadi Mizban/APIraqUS-Saudi strikes in Iraq push region into ‘uncharted territory’, analysts warnRiyadh’s decision to join US in strikes on Iran-backed militia further complicates widening and ‘unpredictable’ warMiddle East crisis – live updatesPeter BeaumontSenior international correspondentWed 29 Jul 2026 13.55 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 11.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS-Saudi strikes on Iran-backed militia in Iraq have pushed the region into “uncharted territory”, analysts have warned.Amid stark warnings of a widening and increasingly “unpredictable” conflict,Riyadh’s decision to publicly join the USin striking sites associated with Iraq’s Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), killing at least 20 fighters, has added another complicating dimension to the war.The strikes on Wednesday came after a brief lull in direct US attacks on targets in Iran, but Tehran’s allies in Yemen and beyond have become increasingly drawn in.Iran, meanwhile, launched missiles at US military installations in Jordan in its first attack in the region since the pause in fighting with the US.33:00Is Iran a ‘forever war’? – Stateside with Kai and CarterThose tit-for-tat strikes seemed to indicate the pause in fighting was at an end The US president,Donald Trump, said the US would be “be hitting [Iran] hard”, even as he claimed the strikes in Iraq were coordinated with the government, despite Baghdad’s condemnation.Also on Wednesday, explosions ⁠hit a natural gas loading port on the Mediterranean Sea in Damietta, Egypt, reportedly involving a drone strike, the first reported strike on Egypt in the war. The source of the drone was unclear.The British maritime security company Ambrey said a US-owned floating storage tanker there had been hit by a drone, in another potential spread of the Middle East war.View image in fullscreenThe group funeral for militia fighters killed in US-Saudi airstrikes.Photograph: Hadi Mizban/APIn Baghdad, the Iraqi presidency called the air raids on the PMF, also known as al-Hashd al-Shaabi – an armed alliance that includes powerful pro-Iran factions – “a blatant violation of Iraq’s sovereignty, targeting its official institutions”.The PMF is a network of Shia-majority factions that was established in 2014 to fight the Islamic State group. Their efforts were overseen by the Iranian general, Qassem Suleimani, the former head of the al-Quds force, the foreign operations arm of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Suleimaniwas killed by a US missile strike in Baghdadduring Trump’s first term.The Iraqi ⁠prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, who recently met Trump, ⁠called off ​a planned meeting ⁠with Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin ⁠Salman ​in ‌Jeddah on ‌Thursday in the wake of the strikes.Iraq’s Harakat ⁠Hezbollah ⁠al-Nujaba, ​an Iran-backed ⁠militia, added that ‌Washington’s and ‌Riyadh’s interests ‌and security would face ‌consequences. Mourners shouted Shia ⁠sectarian slogans and “Death to America!” as they carried the bodies of slain fighters in body bags out of a hospital in Mosul, northern Iraq.Iraq, heavily affected by the closure of the strait of Hormuz, through which most of its oil is exported, has struggled to prevent the war between the US and Iran spilling over its borders.Its governments have tried to maintain a delicate balance between the US, which invaded the Shia-majority country in 2003, and Iran, which has long sought to exert influence there and has backed powerful militias that played a leading role in the fight against IS.View image in fullscreenPeople carry bodies on Wednesday after members of Iraq’s Popular Mobilisation Forces were killed in strikes by the US.Photograph: Al Ahad/ReutersWhile Saudi Arabia has reportedly been involved in a handful of secretive strikes on Iran as part of the war, Riyadh’s overt involvement marks a new turning point in the conflict. Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels announced a blockade of Saudi ports and cargoes at the entrance to the Red Sea barely a week ago.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe latest serious flare-up in fighting follows days in which Tehran and its proxies have targeted bases and facilities of the US and its allies, including in Saudi Arabia, despite the brief US pause.The sense of growing chaos in the Middle East was summed up by Sanam Vakil, the director of theMiddle East and north Africaprogramme at the Chatham House thinktank.“Everyone is trying make sense of something that is increasingly senseless,” she said. “One view is that the informal [US] pause in direct strikes on Iran saw a shift from Tehran to its proxies to maintain pressure [on Washington]. But there is no longer any plausible deniability because everyone knows how the relationships are intertwined.”On the Iranian side, suggested Vakil, the unpredictability of Tehran’s tactics appeared to be a deliberate strategy to pressure Trump “either into confrontation or concession” with the aim of maintaining “a stranglehold on the strait of Hormuz”.View image in fullscreenThe site of an airstrike on a Popular Mobilisation Forces base in Mosul, Iraq, on Wednesday.Photograph: Farid Abdulwahed/APVakil also said countries in the region were interpreting the chaotic context of the conflict as a historic opportunity, including to weaken Iran. And on the Saudi side, she said there was a similar desire to be unpredictable. “No one wants to stay in the status quo.”“I think from the point of view of the Saudis,” said HA Hellyer, a senior associate fellow in Middle East studies at the Royal United Services Institute, “there is a feeling that the Iranians are doing what they are doing because they feel that the Gulf Arab states won’t move up the escalatory ladder. The Saudis want to make it clear that assessment is wrong and that if Tehran thinks the Gulf states are easy prey, they are wrong.”The problem, Hellyer said, was that while the Saudis may have rationalised the attack on the PMF as a precisely calculated act, it may be impossible to anticipate the response.“Because we don’t know that, we are in uncharted territory not just because of the context of the war this year, but the wider issues in the region,” he said. “And it is risky because Tehran sees itself as having been targeted by the US and Israel in a war of existential survival. They see everything through a prism that they have to reset the rules of the game in the region dramatically even if they are wrong and overplaying their hand.”Explore more on these topicsIraqIranStrait of HormuzSaudi ArabiaDonald TrumpMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: US joins forces with Saudis to strike Tehran-backed militias in Iraq | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Oil price spikes after flare-up of fighting and claimed Iranian attacks on three tankers in strait of Hormuz
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Oil price spikes after flare-up of fighting and claimed Iranian attacks on three tankers in strait of Hormuz
Content: A man inspects the damage at the site of a strike in the northern Iraqi Nineveh province. The US and Saudi Arabia said they had struck Iran-backed militants in IraqPhotograph: Zaid Al-Obeidi/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA man inspects the damage at the site of a strike in the northern Iraqi Nineveh province. The US and Saudi Arabia said they had struck Iran-backed militants in IraqPhotograph: Zaid Al-Obeidi/AFP/Getty ImagesUS-Israel war on IranUS joins forces with Saudis to strike Tehran-backed militias in IraqOil price spikes after flare-up of fighting and claimed Iranian attacks on three tankers in strait of HormuzGuardian staff and agenciesWed 29 Jul 2026 05.52 EDTFirst published on Tue 28 Jul 2026 20.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US military said it knocked down an Iranian missile barrage and worked withSaudi Arabiaforces to strike sites in Iraq that Tehran-backed militias have used to launch attacks in recent days. The strikes on Wednesday killed at least 20 members of a former paramilitary alliance that includes pro-Iran groups.In what Washington cast ⁠as “an attempted surprise ⁠attack” by Tehran,Iranhad launched multiple ballistic missiles at US forces in the Middle East, shattering a brief pause in fighting. Iran’s target was a US base in Jordan, Axios cited a US official as saying.US Central Command (Centcom) said all Iranian missiles launched on Tuesday were intercepted, and the US warned any further attacks on American troops or Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure would trigger retaliatory strikes.The joint US-Saudi strikes on targets in Iraq killed at least 20 members of Iraq’s Popular Mobilisation Forces and wounded others. The PMF is an Iraqi state security service that Iran has infiltrated.In a further sign that the lull in fighting could be over, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed on Wednesday to have struck and halted three “violating” oil tankers sailing an “illegal” route in the strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported. The price of Brent crude oil rose after news of the flare-up, hovering around $88 a barrel.Trump pausing Iran attacks shows US military power is not enough on its ownRead moreBoth sideshad held fire over the weekend, after nearly two weeks of nightly strikes by the US on Iran, and repeated missile and drone salvoes by Tehran targeting Washington’s allies around the Gulf.Oil prices had plummeted after the weekend lull and Donald Trump said there was a“good chance” of progress in negotiationsto end the war.View image in fullscreenA commercial vessel passes through an international shipping lane off Yemen’s Hanish Island in the Red Sea.Photograph: Khaled Ziad/AFP/Getty ImagesThe US and Saudi warplanes carried out strikes on Iran-backed militants in Iraq after accusing them of launching drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities in recent days.On Tuesday, the Iraqi prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, ordered security agencies to investigate the alleged attacks by militant groups, saying his country was committed to “preventing Iraqi territory from being used as a route or launching point for any attack targeting brotherly or friendly countries.”The Iraqi militias have denied any role in the drone attacks. The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed armed groups, called the Saudi claims “fabrications” and implied that Monday’s attacks were carried out by theHouthis, who had themselves claimed to have attacked Saudi oil facilities.The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen claimed to have forced a Saudi oil tanker to turn around as part of their self-styled blockade. Last week, they announced a blockade of Saudi shipping,putting another key Middle Eastern waterway– through the Bab el-Mandeb strait leading to the Red Sea – at risk.The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center said a tanker reported hearing explosions while travelling in the southern Red Sea. It did not name the tanker but said the crew and vessel were safe.The Houthis also fired onat least one Saudi tankerin the Red Sea last week.View image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu meets Donald Trump in the Oval Office on Tuesday.Photograph: GPO/AFP/Getty ImagesIran’s surprise attack came as the Israeli prime minister,Benjamin Netanyahu, visited Washington. Israel has been notably absent from the recent fighting with Iran.Netanyahu said he had an “excellent” meeting with Trump at the White House, their first sit-down since launching the war, which offered Netanyahu a chance to smooth out strains in their relationship.The closed-door meeting lasted nearly an hour and a half and was “positive and productive”, the White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, said.It comes as both leaders face growing pressures at home. Netanyahu is up for re-election and is embattled in part because of his deteriorating relationship with Trump. Trump is under pressure to end an unpopular war that has wreaked economic havoc and driven prices higher ahead of midterm elections this November.With the Associated Press and Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranIranUS foreign policyTrump administrationIsraelStrait of HormuzYemennewsShareReuse this content

title: Trident renewal central to defence spending, says Andy Burnham | Politics | The Guardian
description: Prime minister to highlight investment in communities as he launches next phase of nuclear submarine replacement
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Prime minister to highlight investment in communities as he launches next phase of nuclear submarine replacement
Content: Andy Burnham’s visit to Barrow-in-Furness shipyard, owned by BAE Systems, offers an opportunity to reinforce his pro-Trident credentials.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham’s visit to Barrow-in-Furness shipyard, owned by BAE Systems, offers an opportunity to reinforce his pro-Trident credentials.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianPoliticsTrident renewal central to defence spending, says Andy BurnhamPrime minister to highlight investment in communities as he launches next phase of nuclear submarine replacementDan SabbaghDefence and security editorWed 29 Jul 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will place the renewal of Trident at the heart of his vision of a reindustrialised Britain on Thursday when he travels to Barrow-in-Furness to launch the next phase of the nuclear submarine replacement programme.The new prime minister intends to emphasise that defence spending on projects such as the £31bn Dreadnought-class boats built in the Cumbrian town is a case study of taxpayer investment revitalising communities around the UK.“Keeping this country safe is the first responsibility of any government – but security is not only about what we build; it is about who builds it, and who benefits from it,” Burnham said ahead of his visit to England’s north-west.A new phase of contracts worth £8.4bn, part of the already agreed Dreadnought programme, will help support 18,000 extra jobs in nuclear defence by 2030 and 22,000 additional apprentices by 2035, Downing Street said.“To every young person across the country, I want you to know that there is a path for you into a reindustrialised Britain, and it starts with the apprenticeships we are funding through this investment today,” the prime minister added.The visit also presents an opportunity to reinforce Burnham’s pro-Trident credentials. The prime minister voted to build the new submarines in 2016, when theLabourparty split over the issue and its then leader, Jeremy Corbyn, voted against.Wes Streeting, the new defence secretary, and John Healey, the chancellor, were also among the MPs who voted in favour, though other another key figure in Burnham’s team, Louise Haigh, who runs the newoffice of the prime minister, voted no.View image in fullscreenLabour has previously been split over the issue of Trident, with Jeremy Corbyn voting against new submarines in 2016.Photograph: Anthony Devlin/PA Archive/PA ImagesThe UK’s military nuclear activities currently support 47,000 jobs, including 13,500 in the Barrow shipyard. Its surrounding constituency historically switched from Labour to Conservative, and was retaken by Labour at the last election in 2024.Burnham, who has had limited previous engagement with foreign and defence policy, entered office just over a week ago and immediately lent into a Nato commitment to increase defence spending by over £25bn a year to reach 3.5% of GDP by 2035.A row over whether his predecessor, Keir Starmer, was serious about the pledge led to the shock resignation of Healey as defence secretary last month. Starmer was so seriously undermined it precipitated his own departure.When Healey quit, he also called for military budgets to hit 3% of GDP by 2030 as an interim target to show the UK was committed to the Nato goal. Starmer had only been willing to offer an increase to 2.68% of GDP.But on Wednesday, at a press conference, Burnham declined to commit to hitting 3% by 2030. Instead he referred to the UK pledge to meet the Nato target to increase it to 3.5% of GDP by 2035, reiterating comments already made by Streeting and Healey.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“When it comes to defence, obviously those commitments … relate to the parliament after this one,” Burnham said. “In terms of our Nato commitments, I have been very clear that we will honour those commitments. It does mean being prepared to look at challenging issues,” he added.The new Dreadnought submarines are intended to replace the ageing Vanguard-class submarines, one of which is always at sea carrying Britain’s nuclear deterrent. Each of the existing submarines can carry 40 nuclear warheads, with enough destructive power to destroy Moscow and several other major Russian cities.The largest share of the latest phase of work in the Dreadnought programme is being awarded to BAE Systems, the owner of the Barrow shipyard. The British defence giant has been awarded a new £5.9bn contract to complete the build of the first four new boats, HMS Dreadnought, so it can be ready for service in early 2030s.The work is part of the overall £31bn Dreadnought programme, which is so complex it includes a £10bn contingency to cover overspends. Concern about the scale of the programme has meant it has already been placed on amber alert by government procurement monitors.Trident warheads are designed and built at AWE in Aldermaston and Burghfield in Berkshire, which employ 9,000, while a further 4,000 at Rolls-Royce in Derby help build the nuclear reactors that power the Dreadnought and other submarines used by the Royal Navy.Explore more on these topicsPoliticsDefence policyAndy BurnhamLabourCumbrianewsShareReuse this content

title: Police take no further action over Polanski sharing Farage guillotine image | Zack Polanski | The Guardian
description: Scotland Yard says threshold not met for criminal action against Green leader, who has refused to apologise to his Reform rival
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Scotland Yard says threshold not met for criminal action against Green leader, who has refused to apologise to his Reform rival
Content: Zack Polanski says sharing an image of a T-shirt showing a guillotine and the words ‘we’re only making plans for Nigel’ was an ‘inadvertent mistake’.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAView image in fullscreenZack Polanski says sharing an image of a T-shirt showing a guillotine and the words ‘we’re only making plans for Nigel’ was an ‘inadvertent mistake’.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAZack PolanskiPolice take no further action over Polanski sharing Farage guillotine imageScotland Yard says threshold not met for criminal action against Green leader, who has refused to apologise to his Reform rivalAletha AduPolitical correspondentWed 29 Jul 2026 15.56 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 02.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo further action will be taken by police afterZack Polanskishared a photo of a man with a T-shirt showing a guillotine and the phrase “we’re only making plans for Nigel”.The Metropolitan police’s decision comes after the Green party leader for England and Wales said he had made an “inadvertent mistake” and would not apologise toNigel Farage.Polanski told the BBC’s Newsnight programme he had accepted a request to collaborate with a photographer on Instagram, with the first photo in a set of 20 showing himself, and the fifth showing the T-shirt.The image was later removed from Polanski’s feed, with the Greens saying the T-shirt was “clearly in poor taste”. Polanski told Newsnight: “As soon as I was aware of what happened, I unaccepted it and took it down.”A Met spokesperson said: “We absolutely understand the reaction to this image being shared online, particularly in the context of increasing threats toward politicians.“While there will be people who will argue that those who shared the image in this Instagram post should be subject to criminal action, our review has concluded that on this occasion, the threshold is not met.”‘Terminally online’: why frustrated Greens want Polanski to hand over his social mediaRead morePolanski repeatedly ruled out apologising to Farage. “If I’d done it deliberately, I’d be apologising,” he said. “But because this was a mistake, I think the important thing is that I point out it’s a mistake, that I also make sure that I condemn political violence and also crucially make a commitment to be better on my social media.”Reform UK had reported Polanski to the Metropolitan police. Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, accused him of “inciting murder”. Farage called for Polanski to be arrested.But the Met said that after“conducting inquiries”it had concluded that it was unlikely that the sharing of the image online would constitute a criminal offence.However, it added that the wearing of the T-shirt should be recorded as a crime and had referred a crime report to Avon and Somerset police, which covers Bristol, where the photo was taken.Writing in the Daily Mail, Farage said Polanski must “face the consequences of his appalling decisions”, adding: “Political violence is real, it is serious, it needs dealing with.”Polanski stressed on Newsnight: “This was not my post, it was a collaboration from a photographer. It had 20 images and I just didn’t look carefully enough and I accepted it.“As soon as I was aware of what happened, I unaccepted it and took it down. I think it would be odd for the police to speak to me about that because I think it’s quite obvious that I’ve not done anything wrong other than making an inadvertent mistake. That being said, if the police do want to talk to me, of course I’m very happy to cooperate.”A Reform UK source told BBC Newsnight: “It’s truly astonishing and quite frankly sickening that Zack Polanski won’t apologise for inciting murder. He admits it was wrong. He admits it’s dangerous, but he still refuses to apologise. Mr Polanski is not fit to lead a national political party.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCriticising Farage’s messaging, Polanski said: “If Nigel Farage wants to apologise for all the times that he’s put other people in danger than I’ll be happy to make an apology.”The work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, when asked about the controversy, said all politicians had “a duty to be careful about what they post”. He said people could make mistakes and it was for the police to decide if any action was needed. “It’s not the first time Zack Polanski has done something like this,” McFadden added.In May,Polanski apologised for sharing a post on X critical of policeafter the Golders Green stabbings. Police were filmed detaining a suspect after two Jewish people were stabbed in the north-west London suburb. Footage of the arrest shared on social media showed two officers appearing to kick the man on or near his head.Polanski retweeted, without comment, a post on X alleging that officers were “repeatedly and violently kicking a mentally ill man in the head” when he was already incapacitated by a stun gun.When challenged on Newsnight over why he chose to appear on television to highlight his mistake but not apologise, Polanski replied: “They’re different mistakes. This time I’ve inadvertently accepted something and as soon as I’ve realised I’ve corrected it. They’re different things.”One national opinion poll this week showed the Greens’ score falling by three percentage points, while a second showed the party holding at 13%, well above the level before Polanski became leader last September.AGreen partyspokesperson said: “The police have examined the evidence and concluded that no crime was committed. This was obvious from the start, as was the fact that Reform were always using this as a political football for their own cynical purposes to distract from questions about their own dodgy donations.”Explore more on these topicsZack PolanskiGreen partyNigel FarageReform UKnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hackers steal sensitive data from UK Department for Education and police | Cybercrime | The Guardian
description: Details of parents and staff, including email addresses and phone numbers, are among data taken by cybercriminals
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Details of parents and staff, including email addresses and phone numbers, are among data taken by cybercriminals
Content: The police national legal database hack includes the theft of passwords used to access the site.Photograph: Dave Hunt/AAPView image in fullscreenThe police national legal database hack includes the theft of passwords used to access the site.Photograph: Dave Hunt/AAPCybercrimeHackers steal sensitive data from UK Department for Education and policeDetails of parents and staff, including email addresses and phone numbers, are among data taken by cybercriminalsDan MilmoandVikram DoddWed 29 Jul 2026 15.10 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 16.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheDepartment for Educationand a police database have been targeted by a cyber-attack, exposing more than 740,000 pieces of data.Details of government officials, senior school leaders, university staff, police officers and members of the public have been taken by hackers.Just over 600,000 lines of data have been stolen from the DfE’s help-desk portal. They show parent and staff contacts including full names, email addresses, phone numbers and job titles, according to a “leak” website set up by the hackers.A smaller package of similar data has been taken from the department’s Turing portal, which manages a scheme for students studying abroad.The hackers have also breached the police national legal database (PNLD), which provides legal assistance to UK police forces. The cybercriminals claimed to have taken 135,000 pieces of data.The PNLD said the details taken related to “police officers and those working in criminal justice including their name, the force or organisation they work for and their work email address”.Some names and addresses of members of the public who had previously submitted a question to the Ask thePoliceservice had also been taken. It said the database did not hold confidential victim, witness or offender information.While embarrassing, the breach of the police legal database is not thought to be serious.A previously unknown hacking gang calling itself ExfilSquad claimed it had carried out the attack and posted samples of the data on its leak site, a typical gambit for cybercriminals seeking money for the information they have stolen.The hackers are demanding a payment from the DfE and PNLD in exchange for not posting all the data, according to screen grabs seen by the Guardian.The message states that only a small sample of data has been posted for now but indicates that all of it will be uploaded if the DfE, PNLD and other hacking victims do not make an unspecified payment.“The payment we request of you is simply a rounding error compared to the litigation costs of your data leaking. Be smart and just pay,” said the gang.The message is apparently directed at 14 hacking victims including the DfE. The list of alleged victims includes a UK university that has been contacted by the Guardian.Sophos, a cybersecurity company that provided the screenshots, said the data samples appeared to be legitimate. It added that an account on the social media platform X apparently belonging to the group had been suspended but had been illustrated by a picture of a cybersecurity researcher who had been targeted before by members ofthe Com, a sprawling ecosystem of native English-speaking hackers.However, it is understood that the DfE has not seen evidence that ransomware – a type ofmalicious softwarethat locks up a victim’s IT systems – had been deployed in the hack.The Times, which first reported the DfE hack, said the data included details of government officials, senior school leaders and university staff. The DfE is responsible for early years, schools, higher and further education in England.The PNLD hack includes the theft of passwords used to access the site.One senior source briefed on the PNLD leak said: “The risk is low. The question is, if you use your password for the PNLD, do you use it for more sensitive systems?”The database is hosted by West Yorkshire police and is open for forces across England and Wales to view.The source added that it was “early days in our understanding of what has happened.”Any hack of two other police databases – the police national database and the police national computer – would have been deemed far more serious. It is not believed that any direct information about officers in sensitive postings could be gleaned from the data leaked.The government said it was working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and the NationalCrimeAgency on the DfE hack. The DfE and PNLD have also reported the incident to the Information Commissioner’s Office, the data watchdog.The DfE said “swift action” had been taken to contain the incident.“The information involved is limited to customer service contact details relating to individuals and organisations,” it said. “No other data has been accessed.”It is understood the help-desk data includes different sets of data that cannot be connected to each other easily.Explore more on these topicsCybercrimeDepartment for EducationData and computer securityData protectionPoliceCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Brave New World or Groundhog Day? Burnham revisits old ground in speech on social care | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Rightwing media hostility helped sink his reform plans in 2010, but the new PM’s passionate speech suggests there is now clear political will for change
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: Rightwing media hostility helped sink his reform plans in 2010, but the new PM’s passionate speech suggests there is now clear political will for change
Content: Andy Burnham meets residents and staff at a Jewish care home in north London after his speech on reforming England’s social care system.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham meets residents and staff at a Jewish care home in north London after his speech on reforming England’s social care system.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APAndy BurnhamAnalysisBrave New World or Groundhog Day? Burnham revisits old ground in speech on social carePatrick ButlerSocial policy editorRightwing media hostility helped sink his reform plans in 2010, but the new PM’s passionate speech suggests there is now clear political will for changeWed 29 Jul 2026 14.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 15.57 EDTShareFor campaigners perpetually disappointed by the failure of England’s political classes to fix England’s creaking adult social care system, the fear was that Andy Burnham’s long-trailed speech on Wednesday would be less Brave New World, more Groundhog Day.Burnham acknowledged he had been here before. Back in 2010, as health and social care secretary, he unveiled extensive proposals to overhaul social care, only for them to collapse amid rightwing media hostility and furious political rows about “death taxes”.The new PM might talk a good game about expending political capital on an issue close to his heart, but recent history suggests that social care reform invariably ends up in what the King’s Fund thinktank calls the “Westminster graveyard of good intentions” – 22 official reviews in the past 30 years, all which have come to nothingBurnham sketched out his broad ambitions for social care reformin a brisk, partly off-the-cuff speech at a Jewish care home in north London on Wednesday. There was, as expected, little policy detail, but enough to show a clear direction of travel.He would be acceleratingLouise Casey’s review of social care, which under Keir Starmer had been slated for 2028, effectively pushing it back into a putative Labour second term. Lady Casey’s recommendations for a National Care Service would be published within 12 months. He would back Casey “100%”, he promised.He was dropping no clues as to what it might look like. It could be “fully fledged or lesser options or something in between”, he said vaguely. Casey would come up with funding options. But it wasn’t just about money: the quality of social care had to improve, work more closely with theNHS, be built around the needs of care users.There would be investment and focus on the social care workforce, boosting pay and training. He wasn’t opposed to private providers (which currently provide most care in England) but he wouldn’t put up with “profiteering” by care firms. There needed to be more support for unpaid carers, too often broken by their sacrifices.The key message, however, was about politics. Blame for the dire state of English social care lay with his generation of politicians, he said. They had serially ducked the challenge of reform, put point-scoring before fixing injustices, fomented a political culture of risk aversion and inertia.“How have we got to a position where it’s too difficult to fix the basic care that we give to each other, that fellow human beings receive?” he asked.He arrived at No 10 promising he would do politics differently, but this was a challenge to the other main political parties to do the same. He wouldn’t be drawn on whether he’d raise tax to reform social care, but it felt like he was prepared to test the very idea that a government might raise taxes to fix a glaring social injustice.“If everybody, on the NHS principle, contributed a little, it would mean everyone could protect the majority of what they’d worked for,” he said at one point. “Now I know the Mail and probably the Telegraph doesn’t support that. But I don’t know – do people support that?”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe consensus in the social care world was that this was an impressive start. “There was a sense of excitement in the room,” one veteran campaigner said. “He had every opportunity to downplay expectations but he didn’t.”Burnham showed passion, humanity, and a grasp of detail. He framed the injustices simply. He strikingly compared the inequity of social care in England with the privatised US healthcare system: “The vulnerable pay with everything and it can completely leave them with nothing.”For once, some observers said, with a flicker of amazement, there was clear political will, from the very top, to break the entrenched consensus that fixing social care is impossible. It’s early days, but for now there is the rare whiff of hope and optimism.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamSocial careNHSHealthLabouranalysisShareReuse this content

title: Parliamentary watchdog decides against inquiry into £80,000 loan to Reform’s deputy leader | Party funding | The Guardian
description: Richard Tice had been referred to standards commissioner over undeclared sum from Farage aide George Cottrell
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Richard Tice had been referred to standards commissioner over undeclared sum from Farage aide George Cottrell
Content: Richard Tice with Nigel Farage. The investigation against the latter has been paused as he is not currently an MP.Photograph: Jacob King/PAView image in fullscreenRichard Tice with Nigel Farage. The investigation against the latter has been paused as he is not currently an MP.Photograph: Jacob King/PAParty fundingParliamentary watchdog decides against inquiry into £80,000 loan to Reform’s deputy leaderRichard Tice had been referred to standards commissioner over undeclared sum from Farage aide George CottrellBen QuinnPolitical correspondentWed 29 Jul 2026 13.57 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 08.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleParliament’s standards watchdog has declined to investigate a complaint made against Richard Tice over an undeclared loan of nearly £80,000 from Nigel Farage’s aideGeorge Cottrell.The Liberal Democrats had referred Reform’s deputy leader to the parliamentary standards commissioner, which was investigating Farage after the Guardian’s revelation that he receivedan undeclared £5m giftfrom the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.However, the commissioner told the Liberal Democrat MP, Lisa Smart, that he was proposing to take no further action on the basis that her complaint had not provided “sufficient evidence” to justify a investigation into a potential breach of the MPs’ code of conduct.Tice received the loan in late 2024, months after he was elected as the MP for Boston and Skegness, in a transaction that originally caused bankers to raise concerns with authorities.It was alleged that Tice may have breached the MPs’ code of conduct for failing to declare the loan on the basis that the money appears to have been given at a preferential rate, and that Cottrell’s tax residency in Montenegro made him an “impermissible donor”.Tice had said earlier on Wednesday that the loan was a corporate one, to one of his companies, which he said was not declarable.“I have a number of corporate loans in my companies. None of them are declarable, They are to do with my property business activities not to do with politics,” said the MP, who added that his shareholdings and directorships were fully declared.View image in fullscreenLisa Smart, the MP for Hazel Grove in Greater Manchester, said in her letter that an investigation into the matter was ‘essential for public trust’.Photograph: House of CommonsIn a letter sent this week to Daniel Greenberg, the commissioner, Smart wrote: “Mr Cottrell is not merely a private acquaintance of Mr Tice, he is an official adviser to Reform UK andNigel Farage(demonstrated by his use of Reform UK business cards).“It is highly implausible that the loan would have been negotiated without their party political connection, given this is the central basis of their relationship.”The sum of £78,100 was paid in December 2024 by Cottrell into the account of Tisun Investments Ltd, a British company of which Tice is a director. It manages many of his financial investments.The transaction from Cottrell, who was convicted of wire fraud in the US in 2017, was closely examined by bankers, given that the money was being received by a serving MP and came from a convicted criminal.It was one of a number flagged to the National Crime Agency under its suspicious activity report scheme, which requires banks to highlight large transactions, particularly international ones, under anti-money-laundering legislation.Around the same time as the loan from Cottrell, Tice is said to have sent approximately £92,000 to fund a property purchase in Dubai for a development called Peninsula Five.In January last year, Tice gave £613,000 to Reform via Tisun Investments in a relatively unusual case of an MP donating to their own party. A month later a sum of £655,000 was paid into Tisun’s account in what was described by Tice as an overpayment for the property purchase.Instead of paying cash for the property, he said he had got a mortgage, the Guardian understands.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenRichard Tice said the loans were ‘to do with my property business activities, not to do with politics’.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAAround the same time, Tice sent £80,000 from Tisun to Cottrell, seemingly repaying the loan.However, the £80,000 loan from Cottrell does not appear to have been disclosed either in Tisun Investments’ corporate filings to Companies House or the parliamentary authorities.Tice is understood to have paid back £1,900 more than he borrowed from Cottrell. This was a loan that appears to have been repaid on terms that were favourable to Tice, given commercial rates of interest, the difficulty in securing loans as large as £80,000 and the likely early repayment fees when paying back a loan so quickly.In her letter urging Greenberg to investigate, Smart wrote: “Transparency on these financial arrangements, and an investigation into Mr Tice, are essential for public trust. We cannot allow the rules that protect our democracy from corruption and sleaze to be disregarded by senior politicians – including those fromReform UK.”Greenberg replied on Wednesday to say he had read her letter, adding: “I am satisfied that it does not disclose sufficient evidence of a failure to register a registrable interest to justify an investigation into a potential breach of Rule 5 of the Code of Conduct, and accordingly I propose to take no further action.”The watchdog’s investigation into Farage is currently paused because he is no longer an MP after stepping down as the member for Clacton, where he is fighting a byelection that will take place on 13 August.Explore more on these topicsParty fundingRichard TiceReform UKNigel FaragenewsShareReuse this content

title: Meta misses earnings forecasts after Zuckerberg media push to promote AI | Meta | The Guardian
description: Stock tumbles nearly 8% after weaker-than-expected results, despite CEO’s blitz to tout positive effects of AI
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: Stock tumbles nearly 8% after weaker-than-expected results, despite CEO’s blitz to tout positive effects of AI
Content: Facebook headquarters in Menlo Park, California, on 28 October 2021.Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFacebook headquarters in Menlo Park, California, on 28 October 2021.Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesMetaMeta misses earnings forecasts after Zuckerberg media push to promote AIStock tumbles nearly 8% after weaker-than-expected results, despite CEO’s blitz to tout positive effects of AIJohana BhuiyanWed 29 Jul 2026 17.26 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 19.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark Zuckerberg’s media spree touting the positive effects of artificial intelligence did little to cushion the blow of Meta’s second-quarter earnings, which sent its stock tumbling on Wednesday.In aWall Street Journalop-ed published on Tuesday, the Meta chief executive expressed his optimism for a world where everyone has access to a super-intelligent machine.“As a thought experiment, imagine only one person had a super-intelligent lawyer,” Zuckerberg wrote. “He would have an unfair advantage in court. That would lead to a worse society. But now imagine everyone has a super-intelligent lawyer. Justice would be carried out much more fairly and efficiently than it is today.”But Zuckerberg’s message of AI optimism wasn’t enough to alleviate Wall Street’s initial reaction to Meta’s second-quarter earnings. The company’s stock slid nearly 8% after reporting weaker-than-expected results.Meta posted $6.18 in earnings per share, missingWall Street expectations of $7.14, according to Bloomberg consensus estimates. Revenue was $60.8bn, beating analyst predictions of $60.23bn.The company also raised the lower end of its expected expenses and spending for the year. Susan Li, Meta’s chief financial officer, said the company had $2.4bn in “charges related to legal proceedings” in the second quarter, raising total expenses to the range of $165bn to $169bn, up from $162bn to $169bn.And it expects 2026 capital expenditures to range from $130bn to $145bn, up from $125bn to $145bn. Meta has previously said a big portion of its capex is earmarked for its AI investments.Zuckerberg’s PR blitz comes as investors and analysts look for the company’s justification of its massive spending on AI infrastructure, a concern that has contributed to the10% drop in the company’s share price year over year.Big tech companies such as Meta, which have increasingly burned through free cash flow, need to sell consumers and Wall Street on the promise of AI to defend their spending. The stock market’s response to Zuckerberg’s remarks on the company’s earnings call, scheduled for later this evening, could reveal whether his messaging is enough to ease investor concerns.Meta has struggled to make an AI model to rival OpenAI or Anthropic, but it plans to start a cloud business to sell AI compute, monetizing some of its immense AI investments, Bloomberg reported this month. Thereportwas one of the few things to boost investor confidence this year, spurring a spike in the stock’s long decline.The day before earnings, Zuckerberg echoed his belief in decentralizing AI and creating an era of “personalized super-intelligence” where everyone has an AI assistant tailored to their needs and beliefs, in interviews with theNew York Timesand the Financial Times.Though he did not specify how Meta plans to approach this, based on the company’s history, personalization would likely require consumers to hand over even more of their data. Still, Zuckerberg said it was better than his competitors’ centralized models.“I think it is literally impossible to have a single benevolent super-intelligence that is simultaneously aligned with everyone at once,” Zuckerberg told the New York Times.Meta may be “trying to do too much at once”, Mike Proulx, vice-president and research director at advisory firm Forrester Research, said.“Every one of Meta’s major growth lanes now carries a trust toll,” Proulx said in a statement before listing Meta’s new projects. “AI-generated advertising raises new brand-control concerns, smart glasses create new privacy questions, youth safety remains under intense scrutiny and employee-tracking initiatives spark data-collection backlash.”Zuckerberg’s narrative speaks to Meta’s need to set itself apart from competitors – many of whom he said are sending messages filled with “doom” about the future of AI.“I don’t understand why anyone who believes that AI will eliminate most jobs and much of humanity’s relevance would rush to build that future,” Zuckerberg wrote in the WSJ.Still, Meta’s attempt to create a positive message around its AI systems may fall flat, said eMarketer senior analyst Minda Smiley.“It’s not surprising that Zuckerberg wants to come out with a more cohesive message around the company’s AI ambitions, especially as Meta tries to carve out its own lane,” Smiley said in a statement.“But the optimistic, positive tone he’s striking stands in stark contrast to the negative sentiment that’s building toward social media companies over claims that they’ve harmed and addicted kids. This juxtaposition could make it more difficult for Meta to build credibility in an area where it’s already a laggard.”While Zuckerberg makes an argument for Meta’s open-source approach to AI development, the company is being forced to answer for its previous practices developing its products and the effects they have had on users.Meta is facing about 3,000 lawsuits alleging that it deliberately creates addictive products leading to the harm of children. The suits have been brought by families, school districts and states’ attorneys general. Forty-two states have sued Meta in state courts, with Tennessee’s case currently at trial. A separate federal lawsuit brought by 29 attorneys general goes to trial in California next month.“The shifting regulatory environment is also a major Meta risk,” said Proulx. “Policymakers are more focused on youth wellbeing, addiction and platform safety … Youth restrictions will affect who Meta can reach. That’s a big problem for a company that depends on ad revenue.”The lawsuits not only call Meta’s corporate practices into question; they also come at a financial cost. The company has alreadysuffered damaging losses, with two separate juries finding Meta liable for harming children and awarding plaintiffs millions in damages. Lawyers for the families, schools and lawmakers say they will not stop seeking high-cost damages until Meta changes the design of its products.Dara Kerr and Nick Robins-Early contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsMetaAI (artificial intelligence)Mark ZuckerbergComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Uefa calls emergency meeting as opposition to Fifa plan hardens | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Uefa’s 55 members will meet on Thursday afternoon to discuss a coordinated response to Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Uefa’s 55 members will meet on Thursday afternoon to discuss a coordinated response to Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup
Content: Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors has drawn widespread criticism.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino’s plan to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors has drawn widespread criticism.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAFifaUefa calls emergency meeting as opposition to Fifa plan hardens55 members to meet on Thursday to coordinate response‘Uefa knows there is significant and growing opposition’Matt HughesandNick AmesWed 29 Jul 2026 15.07 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 18.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUefa has called an emergency ­meeting of its 55 members for Thursday afternoon to discuss a coordinated response to Gianni Infantino’splan to sell off stakes in the World Cupto private investors. A European boycott of Fifa tournaments is among the options under consideration.As the next major event in the Fifa calendar, a boycott of next year’s Women’sWorld Cuphas been ­mentioned in preliminary ­discussions, although there would be a reluctance in some quarters to make the women’s game suffer as a consequence of a protest against Fifa proposals that primarily revolve around ­monetising the men’s World Cup and Club World Cup.Infantino’s World Cup plan is part of a desire for expansion that was clear from the start | Paul MacInnesRead moreUefa’s initial condemnation of Fifa’s plan to “sell the soul” of ­football has received strong backing from Concacaf – the North, Central ­American and Caribbean ­confederation – and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC). If their members follow their leads there should be sufficient votes to block the proposal.Those three confederations make up 143 of the 211Fifamembers, but unanimity is not guaranteed, as was made clear when Czechia’s ­football association became the first in Europe to back the plan.Having received more than 200 ­letters of endorsement backing his re-election next year, Infantino is confident he has enough votes – although it is unclear whether the proposal requires a simple ­majority to be passed. Several sources have said that creating a new commercial entity – Fifa Forward Enterprise [FFE] – and selling a 20% stake to investors would necessitate a change of Fifa statutes, which requires a 75% majority that would be much harder to obtain.View image in fullscreenFifa’s branding was impossible to miss during the World Cup.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersOn Wednesday evening, Infantino released a video to address the ­backlash. “FFE is actually a ­proposal, an offer,” he said. “It’s part of a democratic process – a ­consultation process – and, above all, it is an opportunity but not an ­obligation. It is a golden opportunity to turbocharge the development of the game globally.”Earlier, Uefa redoubled its attack on Fifa by accusing the world ­governing body of “using our sport to enrich themselves and their friends” after it emerged that ­Infantino had ­presented members with a deadline of 19 September to decide whether to apply for an ­initial payment of $20m (£15m) from the proposed sell-off.A further $20m for each ­association would also be made available at a later date, although it is unclear whether accepting the money would equate to a formal ­endorsement and therefore remove the need for a vote.Uefa has to show backbone: concrete action can make Fifa’s World Cup plans untenable | Nick AmesRead more“Today we have learned of Fifa’s deadline to associations to support their proposals or have the one-off payout offer withdrawn,” Uefa said. “This says everything you need to know about this plan. But having held discussions with many stakeholders across the game, Uefa knows there is significant and growing opposition to Fifa’s scheme. Fifa cannot continue to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends. We can grow the game correctly. It’s time to prioritise associations, clubs, leagues, players and fans.”Uefa’s second statement of condemnation followed a similarly strong intervention from ­Concacaf, which is particularly ­significant given the confederation has just hosted the most ­lucrative World Cup and covers the region that has brought the proposed new investment from the New York-based Thrive Eternal.The Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, was instrumental in the success of the US, Mexican and Canadian bid for the tournament, but along with the seven other Fifa vice‑presidents and Fifa council members he was kept in the dark over the plans.“Concacaf was only made aware of this matter through media reports and, subsequently, via a media release,” Concacaf said. “We are deeply concerned by the lack of due process.“We share the ­disappointment of many within our region and the game that this level of detail has been designed and shared publicly before any discussion with the ­relevant governance bodies and stakeholders has taken place.“As leaders within football, we are the custodians of the game. Collectively, Fifa, the confederations and every member association have a responsibility to always act in the best interests of the sport. Every decision we make must be guided by good governance, robust processes and long-term stewardship.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino announces Saudi Arabia as the 2034 World Cup hosts. The AFC’s statement is understood to have the backing of the Saudi Arabian federation.Photograph: Fifa“This is the framework within which Concacaf operates. We trust that all within the Fifa family will act in the same manner.”The AFC issued a similar statement of disapproval, which significantly is understood to have the backing of the Saudi Arabian football federation, a close ally of Infantino and the host of the 2034 World Cup.“The AFC was not consulted on the proposal and is disappointed that a matter of such significance entered the public domain before the AFC family had been afforded the opportunity to examine and discuss it through the appropriate and established governance channels,” it said.“While the AFC recognises the importance of exploring innovative approaches that can strengthen the future of global football, initiatives of this scale and consequence must be founded upon the principles of good governance, transparency and meaningful consultation.“Decisions that may reshape the commercial and financial future of the game require comprehensive prior engagement with confederations, member associations and other relevant stakeholders before any proposal is made to the appropriate decision-making bodies.”Elite clubs also expressed their unhappiness, with the European Football Clubs organisation pointing out that Fifa had not consulted it despite the two bodies having signed a memorandum of understanding.“As an institution that represents over 850 football clubs – whose member clubs, their players and communities are fundamental participants in football worldwide, not least in Fifa’s competitions including all the international club competitions – it would be wholly appropriate for EFC to be fully consulted on a proposal of such magnitude,” it said.“EFC learned about this proposal in the same way as most global football stakeholders – without warning and through the media.”Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoWorld CupFootball politicsUefanewsShareReuse this content

title: Where all 20 Premier League clubs should strengthen before the season | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Manchester United and Arsenal need midfielders, Liverpool should sign a winger and Chelsea require a goalkeeper
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Manchester United and Arsenal need midfielders, Liverpool should sign a winger and Chelsea require a goalkeeper
Content: Carl Rushworth thrived on loan at Coventry (left); Aston Villa are interested in Pervis Estupiñán (centre); and Xabi Alonso has several problem positions at Chelsea.Composite: Guardian Design; Shutterstock; EPA; Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCarl Rushworth thrived on loan at Coventry (left); Aston Villa are interested in Pervis Estupiñán (centre); and Xabi Alonso has several problem positions at Chelsea.Composite: Guardian Design; Shutterstock; EPA; Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesGuardian Sport NetworkPremier LeagueWhere all 20 Premier League clubs should strengthen before the seasonManchester United and Arsenal need midfielders, Liverpool should sign a winger and Chelsea require a goalkeeperByOpta AnalystAli Tweedale, Ryan Benson and Aryan JollyWed 29 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 08.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal: central midfielderDeclan Rice was worked to the bone by Arsenal last season, playing 4,456 minutes in all competitions. This showed at points during the World Cup, when the midfielder’s body looked on the verge of breaking down. Arsenal need high-quality reinforcements in the centre of the pitch so Rice can occasionally have a rest. Christian Nørgaard struggled to get on to the park last season, with Mikel Arteta seemingly not trusting the former Brentford captain. An extra midfield option could prove crucial to Arsenal retaining their crown.Aston Villa: left-backAston Villa have finished in the top seven for the last four years andthey won the Europa League last season. They need more depth in the squad to establish themselves among the Premier League’s elite permanently, but may lose the left-back Lucas Digne to Paris Saint-Germain. Ian Maatsen is a fine player but he cannot play every week in a season that includes a Champions League campaign, hence Villa’s interest in signing Pervis Estupiñán from Milan.Bournemouth: right-backAdam Smith is a Bournemouth legend who has made more than 400 appearances for the club but he is 35. Max Aarons and Julián Araujo were signed to replace him but, for one reason or another, things have not worked out for them. And Álex Jiménez has gone out on loan to Fiorentina. Marco Rose needs to make a statement signing at right-back so Smith can finally rest.View image in fullscreenAdam Smith puts in some work in the gym during Bournemouth’s pre-season testing.Photograph: Robin Jones/AFC Bournemouth/Getty ImagesBrentford: left-backBrentford have already addressed their biggest weaknesses, but they could do with an upgrade at left-back. Rico Henry has struggled for fitness and form since suffering a horrific injury three years ago. He played 30 games in all competitions last season but made four errors leading to shots – the joint most of any Brentford player. Reinforcing the left flank would also free up Keane Lewis-Potter to play further forward if Keith Andrews wants to utilise him more on the wing.Brighton: central midfielderBrighton will have been planning for James Milner’s retirement and Pascal Gross’s ageing legs for a long time. Only six midfielders over the age of 34 played in thePremier Leaguelast season, and two of them did so for Brighton. They are thin in the middle of the park and there’s also the possibility of more departures. Carlos Baleba is frequently linked with a move and Yasin Ayari’s impressive performances at the World Cup may have caught someone’s eye. Nobody scored more goals from outside the penalty area at the tournament than the Sweden midfielder. Brighton could do with someone else in there even if Baleba and Ayari stay.Chelsea: goalkeeperChelsea have spent more than £200m this summer –£117m of it on Morgan Rogers– but still have several problem positions. They seem keen to sign a centre-back and should add depth in central midfield and on the left wing, but a goalkeeper is where the most urgent attention is needed. Robert Sánchez has never truly convinced. Since he joined in August 2023, he ranks second in the Premier League for errors leading to shots (17) and errors leading to goals (seven). Of the worst 10 culprits in both metrics, Sánchez has made the fewest appearances and played the fewest minutes. Mike Penders has arrived from Strasbourg but, at 20, he is one for the future. Xabi Alonso does not want to start his tenure worrying about the reliability of his first-choice goalkeeper.View image in fullscreenCoventry: goalkeeperThere are a lot of unknowns for Coventry as they return to the Premier League after 25 years, not least how well the centre-forwards Haji Wright and Ellis Simms will take to leading the line against the best defences in England. But the biggest unknown of all is who will be between the sticks, because Coventry do not have a first-choice goalkeeper. They want to make Carl Rushworth’s loan deal permanent, but have not been able to agree a fee with Brighton. Only Bristol City keeper Radek Vitek (+8.5) prevented more goals with his saves in the Championship last season than Rushworth (+8.2). Without him, there’s a big hole that needs filling.Crystal Palace: centre-backPierre Sage used a back three in all of Lens’ league games last season, so it’s likely that Crystal Palace will continue to employ the 3-4-2-1 formation that served them so well under Oliver Glasner. They will need more depth at centre-back, though. Having lost Marc Guéhi to Manchester City in January, their Premier League win rate last season dropped from 35% withthe England international starting to 22.2% withouthim. Jaydee Canvot is an adequate replacement, but Palace are still short on numbers at the back. If Maxence Lacroix also leaves the club, their need for another centre-back will become even starker.Everton: right-backSéamus Coleman’s 17-year stay at Everton has come to an end and Nathan Patterson is also expected to depart, meaning Jake O’Brien is likely to be their only remaining recognised right-back. Well, we say “recognised right-back”, but the consensus among Everton fans is that the hulking Republic of Ireland international is not dynamic or technical enough to be a full-back. James Garner has also filled in there from time to time. It has been a problem position for a while now.View image in fullscreenFulham: centre-forwardFulham need more players who can score goals. Raúl Jiménez (nine) and Harry Wilson (10) accounted for 19 of their 43 Premier League goals (excluding own goals) last season and they have both left on free transfers. No one else scored more than four league goals last season. More will be expected from Rodrigo Muniz (one goal), Samuel Chukwueze (three goals) and Kevin (one goal), but Fulham clearly need greater depth in attack. Álvaro Arbeloa, the new manager, is keen to sign Gonzalo García from Real Madrid but Fulham need at least two fresh faces.Hull: wide forwardHull City desperately need to add a few splashes of quality to their attack. Oli McBurnie has the physicality to lead the line, but the 30-year-old needs players to run off him to be effective. Hull have sold Kyle Joseph to Middlesbrough and have not tried to re-sign Joe Gelhardt after his loan, meaning they are light in attack.Ipswich: strikerMost promoted sides are let down by a lack of precision in both boxes. By signing Issa Diop, Ipswich have secured a proven defender to play alongside Dara O’Shea. But they need more firepower up front. George Hirst has reached double figures for goals in a season only twice and the £24m signing Emersonn has never scored more than six league goals in a single campaign (though he is only 22). Daizen Maeda is a much-needed addition from Celtic.View image in fullscreenThe signing of Daizen Maeda is a boost to Ipswich’s attack.Photograph: Steve Welsh/PALeeds: goalkeeperLeeds signed Lucas Perri from Lyon last summer for £15.6m in the hope he would solve what had become a problem position. He didn’t. Karl Darlow, originally acquired as backup to Illan Meslier in 2023, ended up playing more games in the league last season. But Darlow then left on a free transfer, ultimately joining Manchester United. Leeds also opted to let Meslier’s contract expire. Their remaining goalkeeper options are Perri, who underwhelmed in his first season, and the 33-year-old Alex Cairns, whose most recent competitive appearance was for Salford in the 2023-24 season. They need another keeper.Liverpool: right-wingerMohamed Salah’s final season at Liverpool was his most underwhelming, but he still had a hand in 22 goals across all competitions. In terms of what he achieved in nine years at Anfield, Salah is one of the greatest players in Liverpool’s history and close to irreplaceable. His output last season is not irreplaceable, though. A dynamic wide attacker who provides goals and creativity – such as Bradley Barcola – is on the agenda, and Andoni Iraola has a good track record developing such players.View image in fullscreenManchester City: wingerEnzo Maresca has addressed one hole in the Manchester City squad bysigning Elliot Anderson, but he could do with another option on the flanks to give City more attacking variety. At the end of last season, City lacked strength in depth on the wing. Antoine Semenyo struggled during the run-in and City did not have a quality replacement to turn to on the bench. Savinho regressed in his second season in England, starting only seven league games and scoring one goal, and Phil Foden and Rayan Cherki are better in the middle.Manchester United: central midfielderMichael Carrick’s central midfield options have beenenhanced by Andrey Santosand Youri Tielemans. It’s a pretty good start, but they need more. If we categorise Bruno Fernandes and Mason Mount as No 10s, Manchester United had only three senior central midfielders last season: Kobbie Mainoo, Casemiro and Manuel Ugarte.Casemiro has joined Inter Miamiand Ugarte would probably have left too had he not suffered an anterior cruciate ligament injury at the World Cup that will keep him out for most of the season. United still need an athletic, ball-winning midfielder.Newcastle: full-backWe could have picked a few positions for Newcastle but have chosen full-back as they need one for each flank or, failing that, someone who can play on both sides of the defence. Tino Livramento and Lewis Hall are two of the best full-backs in the Premier League, but they have had injury problems and Newcastle lack depth now that Kieran Trippier, Emil Krafth and Matt Targett have departed. Dan Burn can fill in at left-back but that is not ideal; they have Leo Shahar at right-back but he is an unproven teenager; and Alex Murphy can fill in at left-back but he is more of a central defender.View image in fullscreenNottingham Forest: centre-backLet’s assume replacing Elliot Anderson is a given for Nottingham Forest. The other area they need reinforcements is centre-back. Oliver Glasner, their new coach, swears by a back three; he lined up with three or five at the back in every game during his two seasons at Crystal Palace. Forest have several centre-backs already – Nikola Milenkovic, Murillo, Morato and Jair Cunha, plus a couple of prospects – but bringing in at least one more defender with experience of playing in a back three would not go amiss.Tottenham: wingerWhen Mohammed Kudus and Dejan Kulusevski are fit again, Tottenham will have a couple of good options on the right flank. However, they are not on the club’s pre-season tour to New Zealand and Australia, and may not be available for the start of the season. On the left, Spurs have only Mathys Tel and Wilson Odobert, neither of whom can be relied upon for consistent output. Between them, Tel and Odobert racked up just four goals and three assists in a combined 55 league appearances last season. Odobert is also recovering from a serious knee injury and will miss at least the first few months of the season. That leaves Tottenham with almost no options out wide. They need at least one winger.Sunderland: creative midfielderAfter a very busy transfer market last summer and an extremely successful first season back in the top flight, Sunderland have been quieter this time around. That is understandable but, with a first European campaign since 1973 coming up, they need more depth, and that could mean reinforcement across the pitch. They could really do with a little more creativity, having generated just 23.2 expected goals in open play in 38 league games last season – only relegated Burnley and Wolves fared worse.This is an article byOpta AnalystExplore more on these topicsPremier LeagueGuardian Sport NetworkTransfer windowfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Chiefs say Eric Bieniemy’s wife is out of ICU, ‘making progress’ after shooting | NFL | The Guardian
description: Chiefs coach Andy Reid said that Mia Bieniemy had been released from the intensive care unit, where she was being treated for multiple gunshot wounds
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Chiefs coach Andy Reid said that Mia Bieniemy had been released from the intensive care unit, where she was being treated for multiple gunshot wounds
Content: Kansas City Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy will be away from the team as his wife recovers from multiple gunshot wounds.Photograph: Matt Rourke/APView image in fullscreenKansas City Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy will be away from the team as his wife recovers from multiple gunshot wounds.Photograph: Matt Rourke/APNFLChiefs say Eric Bieniemy’s wife is out of ICU, ‘making progress’ after shootingMia Bieniemy is being treated for gunshot woundsSon Elijah Bieniemy was arrested and charged in incidentAssociated PressWed 29 Jul 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheKansas City Chiefsheld their first full-squad workout of training camp Wednesday without offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy, who remained with his family after the shooting of his wife – allegedly by their son – at their Virginia home last weekend.Chiefs coach Andy Reid said after the workout that Mia Bieniemy had been released from the intensive care unit, where she was being treated for multiple gunshot wounds. But there was no timetable for when Eric Bieniemy would be back with the team.“She’s making progress,” Reid said, “so we’re happy about that.”Son of Kansas City Chiefs assistant Eric Bieniemy charged in shooting of his motherRead moreElijah Zion Bieniemy, the 27-year-old son of the couple, was arrested in connection with the late-Sunday shooting. He was charged with malicious wounding, use of a firearm in commission of a felony and discharge of a firearm inside a dwelling, and was being held without bond Wednesday at the Loudoun County Adult Detention Center.Elijah Bieniemy has a court date to hear motions scheduled for Thursday. His preliminary hearing date is 31 August.Eric Bieniemy returned earlier this year to the Chiefs, where he experienced his greatest success as an assistant. He was instrumental in Kansas City reaching three Super Bowls and winning two of them before departing for the Washington Commanders in 2023, where he had wanted to build upon his resumé in the hopes of landing a head coaching job.Bieniemy was part of Ron Rivera’s staff that was let go after that season. He spent one season as offensive coordinator at UCLA before spending last season coaching the running backs with the Chicago Bears.However long he misses training camp is noteworthy, given Bieniemy is trying to get up to speed with any changes to Reid’s playbook over the past few years.Pass game coordinator Joe Bleymaier, who has been with the Chiefs for the past decade and is widely considered a rising star in the profession, has assumed many of Bieniemy’s responsibilities. Others have fallen upon veteran offensive line coach Andy Heck, who has held that job ever since Reid’s initial Kansas City coaching staff was put together after the 2012 season.Explore more on these topicsNFLKansas City ChiefsUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alexandrova collapses on court during defeat as Memphis heat takes toll | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Russia’s Ekaterina Alexandrova collapsed on court during her match against Kristina Liutova and left the arena in a wheelchair
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Russia’s Ekaterina Alexandrova collapsed on court during her match against Kristina Liutova and left the arena in a wheelchair
Content: Ekaterina Alexandrova leaves the court in a wheelchair after collapsing during her match.Photograph: Justin Ford/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEkaterina Alexandrova leaves the court in a wheelchair after collapsing during her match.Photograph: Justin Ford/Getty ImagesTennisAlexandrova collapses on court during defeat as Memphis heat takes tollRussian retires from match against Kristina LiutovaVenus Williams and Katie Boulter beaten in WashingtonReuters andGuardian sportWed 29 Jul 2026 08.35 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 09.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEkaterina Alexandrova collapsed on the court before retiring from her match against Kristina Liutova at the Memphis Classic due to heat-related illness.Alexandrova, the tournament’s No 1 seed, was two points away from defeat to the 16-year-old Liutova, who was making her WTA Tour debut. The temperature was around 97F (36C) in Tennessee as the two Russians played out a gruelling first-round match ​lasting more than three hours.Alexandra Eala is the giantkiller who lit up Wimbledon – but will she rise to the top?Read moreWith Liutova leading 7-6 (2), 4-6, 5-4, Alexandrova began to struggle on serve, and initially received a time violation. The world No 19 then fell to the ground during the next point, and received treatment on court. Alexandrova was able to stand briefly but left the arena in a wheelchair. Her young opponent was left in tears after being told her opponent could not play on.The tournament’s second seed, McCartney Kessler, also went out in the first round, suffering a 6-4, 6-1 loss to Mexico’s Renata Zarazua. The American, who is still seeking ⁠her first WTA title this year after winning two events in 2025, led ​4-2 in the first ​set but dropped four straight games and never recovered.Alexandrova’s withdrawal raises questions over the decision to add Memphis as a summer stop on the WTA Tour. The new WTA 250 event has replaced Cleveland on the schedule this year. It takes place across late July and early August, when average temperatures in Tennessee are around 83F (29C).Elsewhere,Venus Williamswas beaten in the first round of the Mubadala DC Open on Tuesday, suffering a 6-3, 6-3 ⁠loss to Austria’s Anastasia Potapova in Washington.The tournament’s fifth seed,Anna Kalinskayaof ⁠Russia, defeated Daria Kasatkina ​6-4, 6-1 by converting four of her ‌six break-point chances.Katie Boulterclaimed the first set against Ashlyn Kreuger but went on to lost 3-6, 6-2, 6-2.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPoland’sMagdalena Frechbeat Ann Li 6-4. 6-3 to set up a second-round match against Jessica Pegula.
