title: USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino, US Soccer in ‘final stages’ of agreeing on new contract | USA | The Guardian
description: A new deal, which multiple sources told the Guardian is close to being finalized, would extend the Argentinian through the 2030 World Cup
Author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Headline: A new deal, which multiple sources told the Guardian is close to being finalized, would extend the Argentinian through the 2030 World Cup
Content: Mauricio Pochettino and US Soccer are in negotiations about his future as the USMNT’s coach.Photograph: Christopher Torres/EPAView image in fullscreenMauricio Pochettino and US Soccer are in negotiations about his future as the USMNT’s coach.Photograph: Christopher Torres/EPAUSAUSMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino, US Soccer in ‘final stages’ of agreeing on new contractDeal would extend Argentinian through 2030 World CupCoach would stand to earn ‘significantly’ morePochettino’s tenure has been mixed bag of resultsPablo Iglesias MaurerWed 29 Jul 2026 11.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUSMNT head coachMauricio Pochettinoand US Soccer are “in the final stages” of finalizing an agreement for a new contract through the 2030 World Cup, multiple sources briefed on ongoing negotiations have told the Guardian. Those sources requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the matter.Pochettino was brought on as US head coach in September 2024, tapped to lead the team through the 2026 World Cup, where the Americans suffereda disappointing exitin the last 16. Both sides had expressed interest in potentiallyextendingthe deal in the run-up to the tournament, with US Soccer chief executive JT Batson saying the federation was “excited” about the potential of building on progress made during Pochettino’s initial spell as head coach.US Soccer coy on Mauricio Pochettino and future of sporting director positionRead moreTelemundo’s Andres Cantor was first to report progress on recent contract talks.Pochettino had told Spanish-language media on 17 July that a decision on his future was coming “next week”, but neither the federation nor Pochettino himself has spoken on the matter. Sources said on Tuesday that both sides were eager to get a deal over the line so focus could be turned towards the USMNT’s next slate of friendlies, due to be played in late September and early October.Pochettino’s tenure as US coach has been a mixed bag. Early results, including a fourth-place finish in the Nations League and losing to Mexico in a Gold Cup final were balanced by more respectable results, including the US’s best-ever group-stage finish at a World Cup. To some, Pochettino’s initial run as US coach will be remembered for one thing alone: the team’s 4-1 humiliation at the hands of Belgium in the last 16 of the World Cup.Financial details of Pochettino’s potential new deal have not yet surfaced, though one source close to the ongoing negotiations said that the Argentinian stands to earn “significantly” more than his previous deal. Pochettino earned roughly $6m per year as US coach, notwithstanding performance bonuses, with a $2.5m signing bonus. That number already made Pochettino the third-highest-earning international coach in global soccer. It was partially subsidized by philanthropic support, most notably from hedge fund billionaire Ken Griffin.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPochettino, who had never coached internationally prior to taking over the USMNT, continued to attractwidespread interestduring his tenure, most notably from Premier League side Tottenham Hotspur, where he’d previously enjoyed success. The Argentinian was also linked with Real Madrid, though both clubs have since filled their coaching vacancies.Explore more on these topicsUSAMauricio PochettinoUS sportsWorld Cup 2026newsShareReuse this content

title: Fifa opens disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over Falklands banner and final chaos | Argentina | The Guardian
description: Fifa has begun disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over the Falkland Islands banner displayed after their World Cup semi-final win over England
Author: John Ashdown
Headline: Fifa has begun disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over the Falkland Islands banner displayed after their World Cup semi-final win over England
Content: Argentina’s Giovani Lo Celso holds a banner with the words ‘the Malvinas are Argentinian’ after their semi-final win over England.Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/APView image in fullscreenArgentina’s Giovani Lo Celso holds a banner with the words ‘the Malvinas are Argentinian’ after their semi-final win over England.Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/APArgentinaFifa opens disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over Falklands banner and final chaosPlayers held banner after semi-final against EnglandParedes and Molina investigated over brawl after finalJohn AshdownWed 29 Jul 2026 13.09 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 18.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifa has opened disciplinary ­proceedings against Argentina over the Falkland Islands banner ­displayed after theirWorld Cup semi‑final winagainst England in Atlanta.AsArgentinacelebrated ­reaching the final with their dramatic 2-1 ­victory, several players held a sign ­proclaiming “Las Malvinas son ­Argentinas” – the ­Malvinas are Argentinian – in ­reference to the ­British overseas territory in the south Atlantic.Uefa calls emergency meeting as opposition to Fifa plan hardensRead moreThe dispute over the islands, which have been ruled by Britain since 1833, is long running and led to a 74-day conflict in 1982, during which more than 900 people – 649 Argentinians and 255 Britons – lost their lives.Fifa’s disciplinary code ­prohibits “using a sports event for ­demonstrations of a non-sporting nature” and the banner prompted political debate on both sides of the ­Atlantic. A spokesperson for the then UK prime minister, Keir Starmer, said: “The World Cup might not be ours, but the Falkland Islands ­definitely are.”Andrew Giuliani, the head of the White House Fifa taskforce, defended Argentina’s players, saying the US believed in free speech.The incident was not the first time an Argentina team had expressed such sentiments. In 2014,Fifafined Argentina £20,000 for a far larger banner held ‌up by players before a friendly with Slovenia in La Plata.Fifa’s fullWorld Cupcharge sheet against the Argentinian Football Association also includes ­“discriminatory chants and gestures, late kick-offs, failure to comply with match and security protocols, the display of inappropriate messages by the team and spectators and the throwing of objects by spectators in relation to several matches”.0:18Ugly scenes as Argentina lose World Cup final – videoSeveral players are also under investigation in relation to the ­chaotic scenes that followed ­Argentina’s 1-0extra-time defeat by Spainin the final. As Spain attempted to celebrate, ­altercations broke out across the pitch at New York New Jersey Stadium.The Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes, who was seen wrestling Spain’s Eric García to the ground, faces three counts of assault under the Fifa disciplinary code, while the defender Nahuel Molina faces two counts of assault (one completed and one attempted) and one count of unsporting behaviour.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe assistant coach, Roberto Ayala, faces one count of assault, and Thiago Almada, an unused substitute in the final, one count of unsporting behaviour. Spain’s Gavi also faces an unsporting behaviour charge.“In accordance with the Fifa ­disciplinary code, the respondents have now been provided with the opportunity to present their position, following which a decision will be issued by the Fifa disciplinary committee in due course,” said Fifa.Explore more on these topicsArgentinaFifaWorld Cup 2026EnglandFootball politicsFalkland IslandsWorld CupnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘People are loving it’: Formula One chief Domenicali hits back at critics of regulations | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Stefano Domenicali has issued a rebuttal to critics of Formula One’s current regulations, claiming most fans are enjoying the sport more than ever
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Stefano Domenicali has issued a rebuttal to critics of Formula One’s current regulations, claiming most fans are enjoying the sport more than ever
Content: The world champion Lando Norris of McLaren, who won the Hungarian Grand Prix on Sunday, is one of many critics of the current F1 regulations.Photograph: Darko Vojinović/APView image in fullscreenThe world champion Lando Norris of McLaren, who won the Hungarian Grand Prix on Sunday, is one of many critics of the current F1 regulations.Photograph: Darko Vojinović/APFormula One 2026‘People are loving it’: Formula One chief Domenicali hits back at critics of regulationsChief executive says fans don’t care about technologySeason may finish in Europe due to war in Middle EastGiles RichardsWed 29 Jul 2026 10.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStefano Domenicali has issued a stout rebuttal to critics of Formula One’s new regulations, claiming most fans are enjoying the sport more than ever and are unconcerned by driver complaints. TheFormula Onechief executive also confirmed that this season’s finale would be staged in Europe if the last two grands prix, in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, are called off due to the Middle East war.Lando Norris, the defending world champion,hit out at F1 in Hungarylast week for putting profit before the sport to attract engine manufacturers with the new regulations. The focus on electrical energy management has been roundly disliked by drivers.F1 summer report card: from top of the class Mercedes to the team that must do betterRead moreDomenicali, however, argued F1’s fanbase did not share the objections. “There is a lot of action on the track, people are loving it. They are focused on what is happening on the track,” he said. “They don’t understand our technology, ‘clipping’ or whatever it is, because it’s too technical.“I had an incredibly interesting discussion with George Lucas [the Star Wars creator] on Saturday. He was in Hungary and he was giving me an incredible view on how the new fans are watching Formula One.“For the vast majority of the people, trust me, they just want to see what is happening on the track. They’re not interested in the angle of throttle or the percentage of brake pressure in how you can take and overtake a driver.”Since Hungary Norris has acknowledged that the FIA and F1 are listening to the drivers and was more conciliatory toward Domenicali and F1, echoing the Italian’s take on the sport. “These regulations are a bit of a departure from what’s come before,” Norris said. “But what we are seeing is more intense racing, more overtaking and more battles. It’s important to find the right balance. I know everyone involved in the sport, me included, is passionate about making it even better still.”Domenicali was speaking asthe sport enters its summer breakafter 11 meetings and with its owners able to assess the first half of the season. According to F1’s figures, attendances have risen and there has been a growth in global TV audiences, although the broadcast numbers were not given. Most striking was the continued change in the demographics of F1’s audience, which have transformed since Liberty Media took over the sport and with the success of the Netflix series Drive to Survive. F1 says 42% of its audience is now female, with women making up three-quarters of new fans, while 43% of the total fanbase is under 35.This new audience had different demands from the sport than those of the traditional, older fanbase, said Domenicali. One focused on drivers and personalities, exemplified by Max Verstappen – who has also been a fervent critic of the new rules – when he made a superb pass on Lewis Hamilton in Hungary on Sunday.View image in fullscreen‘For the vast majority of the people, trust me, they just want to see what is happening on the track,’ said Stefano Domenicali of the current F1 regulations.Photograph: David Davies/PA“If you think, for example, of Max and Lewis at turn one in Hungary, this is a piece of art that these people just want to see and just connected to the quality of the drivers,” said Domenicali. “This is a skill that the driver can have on how you can maximise the performance of your car, no matter if it’s braking, accelerating, or power that is done by the electrification or not.”The 61-year-old said F1 would make a decision by mid-September on whether the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi would go ahead, depending on the region’s conflict. “If the situation will not be cleared the way that we believe it should be, before the middle of September we will take the decision,” he added. “If this will not be possible, the end of the season will be in Europe, because we cannot go in other places.” Imola in Italy is believed to be the favoured venue. He also confirmed that contingency plans for 2027 were being made should the war continue and any alternative calendar would run to the 24 meetings planned for next year.“The calendar that will be presented, let’s say in autumn, will be as a sort of normal plan,” he said. “But in case the situation in the Middle East will not be solved, we have options, a different plan and the trigger for that is at the end of the year.”Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: This week’s soccer questions: is this Fifa’s Super League moment and can Arsenal land Vinícius Júnior? | Fifa | The Guardian
description: We look at the controversy around the plan to sell stakes in the World Cup, what the Gunners need to get to the next level and Liverpool’s uncertain summer
Author: Graham Ruthven
Headline: We look at the controversy around the plan to sell stakes in the World Cup, what the Gunners need to get to the next level and Liverpool’s uncertain summer
Content: Fans rallied against the European Super League breakaway effort five years ago. The backlash to Fifa’s plans to sell stakes in the World Cup has been similarly widespread.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenFans rallied against the European Super League breakaway effort five years ago. The backlash to Fifa’s plans to sell stakes in the World Cup has been similarly widespread.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAFifaThis week’s soccer questions: is this Fifa’s Super League moment and can Arsenal land Vinícius Júnior?We look at the controversy around the plan to sell stakes in the World Cup, what the Gunners need to get to the next level and Liverpool’s uncertain summerGraham RuthvenWed 29 Jul 2026 10.23 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 10.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs Infantino’s World Cup investment plan Fifa’s Super League moment?So $15bn wasn’t enough. That’s therecord amountFifa is estimated to have made from the 2026 World Cup, but Gianni Infantino wants more. Approximately $20bn more throughan investment planthat would see soccer’s governing body sell the commercial rights to its tournaments, including the World Cup, to private investors.The backlash to Tuesday’s announcement was swift and widespread. Uefa accused Fifa of “attempting to sell the soul of football”. UK prime minister Andy Burnham reminded Infantino that the World Cup “was never anyone’s to sell”. Concacaf voiced its concerns and the FA revealed it had been“completely unaware”of the plans.Is the World Cup for sale? Here’s what Fifa’s plans mean and what happens next | Paul MacInnesRead moreInfantino attempted to get ahead of the news cycle on Monday by postinga 15-part messageon Instagram accusing his critics of spreading hate. More criticism will come his way if these plans to privatize the sport’s most prestigious competition come to pass. European nations are reportedly ready to boycott future World Cups after a summer that had already pushed many to the brink.This story is fast becoming Fifa’s European Super League moment. Fans begrudgingly tolerated the extortionate ticket prices and politicization of this summer’s World Cup, but Infantino may have gone too far in the same way many of Europe’s biggest clubs went too far inthreatening a breakaway divisionfive years ago.Back then, supporters took to the streets to oppose a move that threatened to rip up the club game as we know it. Soccer’s collective response to Fifa’s proposals could be just as forceful. The European Super League thankfully never happened and the World Cup will hopefully remain the property of the people, not Infantino and his private equity buddies.Would Vinícius Júnior’s signing take Arsenal to the next level?Arsenal need a left-winger and there aren’t many (any?) better than Vinícius Júnior. The Gunners’ recruitment department has done an excellent job in recent years, identifying the likes of Declan Rice, Martin Ødegaard and Kai Havertz as players for Mikel Arteta to build a title-winning team around. Theirscoutingof Vinícius, however, surely wasn’t so deep.Everyone knows how good Vinícius is. The Brazilian has racked up 228 goal contributions (128 goals, 100 assists) in 375 appearances for Real Madrid. The two-time Champions League winner is one of the most impactful attackers in the sport and would elevate Arsenal’s forward line to an entirely new level.Arsenal make shock approach to sign Vinícius Júnior from Real MadridRead moreAtlético Madrid’s Julián Álvarez, RB Leipzig’s Yan Diomande and Bradley Barcola of Paris Saint-Germain are also on Arsenal’s radar, but Vinícius – who is in the final year of his contract at Real Madrid – is the most tantalising prospect.Leandro Trossard’s departure to Besiktas left a hole in Arsenal’s squad. Even before Trossard left, the left-winger position was the most obvious area for the north London outfit to upgrade. Gabriel Martinelli and Trossard combined for just seven league goals last season. Vinícius, meanwhile, scored 22 goals in all competitions on his own.Arsenal have been methodical in the way they have bulked up their squad. When they needed an orthodox frontman last summer, they signed Viktor Gyökeres. When another midfield anchor was required to ease some of the load on Rice, they signed Martín Zubimendi. Now, it is clearly time for left-winger to be addressed. No player would do this more emphatically than Vinícius.View image in fullscreenDominik Szoboszlai celebrates after scoring in Liverpool’s preseason friendly against Sunderland.Photograph: George Walker IV/APIs Liverpool’s uncertain summer affecting Andoni Iraola’s rebuild?Andoni Iraola had already labelled Liverpool’s defensive depth as “very thin” when Joe Gomez went down injured after only eight minutes of Saturday’s preseason friendly against Sunderland. He surely would use the same terms to describe some other areas of his squad as his first season as Res manager gets closer and closer.Liverpool still haven’t replaced Mohamed Salah. Or Andy Robertson. There are lingering questions over their midfield unit and the right-back position where the Reds restlessly rotated between Conor Bradley, Jeremie Frimpong, Gomez and Dominik Szoboszlai last season. There has even been speculation over Alisson’s future.Iraola has been hired to remold Liverpool in his own image, but it’s not currently clear what he has to work with. Or who is aiding him in the front office following theexitof Michael Edwards as the head of Fenway Sports Group’s football department and reports that Liverpool sporting director Richard Hughes is also on his way out.Jeff Bezos could be on his way in as a new investor. The Amazon founder is in talks tojoin a consortiumled by the former Queens Park Rangers co‑owner Amit Bhatia seeking a 30% stake in Liverpool. There is so much happening at Anfield, and yet not nearly enough happening on the field or in the transfer market.Of course, 12 months ago Liverpool “won” the transfer window, signing Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz for club-record fees, and if anything their blockbuster business disrupted Arne Slot’s team. Big business isn’t always good business, but it’s fair to question if Liverpool’s uncertain summer off the field is affecting things on it.Explore more on these topicsFifaArsenalVinícius JúniorGianni InfantinoLiverpoolAndoni IraolafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: WSL brings back Sunday evening kick-offs after indifferent viewing figures | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: The move is part of an overhaul of its broadcast strategy after Sunday evening kick-offs were dropped last season after negative feedback from clubs and fans
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The move is part of an overhaul of its broadcast strategy after Sunday evening kick-offs were dropped last season after negative feedback from clubs and fans
Content: The WSL will offer six different TV slots to broadcasters after releasing its fixtures for the 2026-27 campaign.Photograph: Richard Pelham/WSL/The FA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe WSL will offer six different TV slots to broadcasters after releasing its fixtures for the 2026-27 campaign.Photograph: Richard Pelham/WSL/The FA/Getty ImagesWomen's Super LeagueWSL brings back Sunday evening kick-offs after indifferent viewing figuresMove part of an overhaul of its broadcast strategySunday evening games were dropped last seasonExclusive byMatt HughesWed 29 Jul 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 19.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Women’s Super League will bring back Sunday evening kick-offs this season as part of an overhaul of its broadcast strategy after indifferent viewing figures last season.The Guardian has learned that the WSL will offer six different TV slots to broadcasters after releasing its fixtures for the 2026-27 campaign later on Thursday in a significant change from last season, when the majority of televised games took place on Saturday and Sunday lunchtimes.Why Tottenham Women have provided distraction from the gloom of watching men’s team | Mark BurtonRead moreSky Sports, which has the live rights for 163 of the WSL’s 182 games, retains the Saturday 12.45pm slot and noon on Sundays, but has also been given new regular kick-off times of 7pm on Friday and 6pm on Sunday.The BBC will broadcast 19 matches live at 12.30pm on Saturdays and 2.30pm on Sundays.The WSL’s new strategy is to spread games across the weekend after scheduling most fixtures at noon on Sundays last season, with multiple televised matches kicking off at the same time in a move that diluted the audience.The change this seasonfollows a lengthy consultationwith broadcasters, clubs and fans, with the WSL seeking a schedule that maximises its TV audience and matchday attendances.The Sunday evening kick-off was dropped last season after negative feedback from clubs and fans, as attendances were generally poor, but it was popular with broadcasters and was Sky’s best performing slot in 2024-25 with an average audience of 144,000.In an attempt to balance these competing interests, the Sunday evening game will mostly be brought forward 45 minutes to 6pm – with some changes likely to avoid clashes with the 4.30pm Premier League games – while the WSL will attempt to schedule derbies for that slot and Friday evenings where possible.The Guardian revealed last December that the WSL was considering further changes to its kick-off times this season after concern from Sky in particular at some of their viewing figures for lunchtime games.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAn average audience of 59,000 watched Sky’s live coverage of Arsenal’s home win over Liverpool that month, even fewer than the 71,000 people who watched Arsenal v Chelsea on Sky in the same noon kick-off slot the previous month.As well as struggling to attract a casual audience the decision to schedule up to four of the six weekly matches at the same time proved unpopular with the most committed WSL fans, who were unable to watch multiple matches live.Sky are paying the vast majority of the joint £65m broadcast deal with the BBC, who are believed to contribute around £8m in rights fees, so have a significant say but the WSL has consulted widely.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m very sorry’: Mancini apologises after being reappointed as Italy head coach | Italy | The Guardian
description: Roberto Mancini, who quit the Italy job to take over Saudi Arabia in 2023, said: ‘I realise that some will be against me … maybe people will forgive’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Roberto Mancini, who quit the Italy job to take over Saudi Arabia in 2023, said: ‘I realise that some will be against me … maybe people will forgive’
Content: The Italy head coach, Roberto Mancini (right), will work alongside the new technical director, Claudio Ranieri.Photograph: Fabio Cimaglia/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Italy head coach, Roberto Mancini (right), will work alongside the new technical director, Claudio Ranieri.Photograph: Fabio Cimaglia/EPAItaly‘I’m very sorry’: Mancini apologises after being reappointed as Italy head coachMancini quit Italy job to take over Saudi Arabia in 2023‘Some will be against me … maybe people will forgive’Associated PressWed 29 Jul 2026 14.06 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 14.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRoberto Mancini issued an apology in his first public comments after beingreappointed as the Italy head coach, three years after he abandoned the same job for a lucrative contract with Saudi Arabia.Roberto Mancini returns as Italy head coach with Claudio Ranieri named technical directorRead more“I’m very sorry,” Mancini said. “It was like losing the woman of your life. And it means you did something that shouldn’t have been done. So I’m sorry, very sorry also for everything that happened over these last three years … I’m going to try to bring the national team back where it belongs.”Italy failed for a third straight time to qualify for the World Cup, prompting the resignations of Gabriele Gravina as federation president and Gennaro Gattuso as head coach in April, shortly after the playoff defeat to Bosnia and Herzegovina.The 61-year-old Mancini led theAzzurrito the European Championship title in 2021 but resigned as Italy coach in August 2023, taking over Saudi Arabia’s national team two weeks later. “It was completely my fault,” Mancini said, referring to a lack of communication with Gravina.Mancini’s first match back in charge will be against Belgium in the Nations League on 25 September at the Stadio Olimpico in Rome. He was asked about what type of reception fans might give him. “I realise some people will be against me,” Mancini said. “I’m hoping the squad plays well enough that maybe people will forgive me.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMancini wasfourth-choice optionfor the Italy job after Carlo Ancelotti and Pep Guardiola turned it down and Andrea Pirlo was dropped as a candidateamid political concernsover a sponsorship deal with a Russian betting firm.Explore more on these topicsItalyRoberto MancininewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester City leading opposition to Premier League’s £1.5bn EFL proposal | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Manchester City is leading the opposition to the Premier League’s plans to offer £1.5bn to the English Football League in a landmark financial settlement
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Manchester City is leading the opposition to the Premier League’s plans to offer £1.5bn to the English Football League in a landmark financial settlement
Content: Manchester City are understood to have come up with a counterproposal to the Premier League’s plans.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenManchester City are understood to have come up with a counterproposal to the Premier League’s plans.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersPremier LeagueManchester City leading opposition to Premier League’s £1.5bn EFL proposalMeeting on Thursday to discuss landmark settlementCity have concerns about how the package will be fundedExclusive byMatt HughesWed 29 Jul 2026 09.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester City are leading the opposition to the Premier League’s plans to offer £1.5bn to the EnglishFootball Leaguein a landmark financial settlement which will be discussed at a meeting of the 20 clubs on Thursday.ThePremier Leaguewants to put its proposed offer, which would be spread over 10 years, to a vote in the hope of getting the matter resolved before the start of the season, but City are understood to have come up with a counterproposal amid concerns about how the package will be funded.A number of City’s misgivings are shared by other members of the so-called big six, who will be asked to pay more than other Premier League clubs towards the New Deal for Football, but it is unclear how many of them are prepared to back their rivals.City remain short of allies within the top flight as they wait for the much-anticipated judgment of an independent tribunal after being charged with 115 breaches of financial fair play rules, despite settling a long-running legal dispute with the Premier League over its associated party transaction rules last year.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The Guardian has learned that City irritated several clubs by submitting a series of late amendments to proposed rule changes before the Premier League’s annual general meeting in June, which were defeated by 19 votes to one.City and other big clubs are understood to be unhappy with the Premier League’s proposal to fund the financial redistribution package by increasing the levy on transfer fees from 4% to 6%, which would leave the bigger spending clubs with a large bill. The Premier League will only ballot clubs on Thursday if it is confident of getting the 14 votes required for the proposal to pass, with sources describing executives as cautiously optimistic despite facing some opposition.At an average of £150m a year, the Premier League’s proposed contribution has not altered significantly since a similar offer of £750m over five years was put forward in September 2023, although it has doubled the length of the deal.If approved by the clubs and accepted by the EFL an initial payment of £100m would be made this season, with larger contributions to be made in subsequent years until the 2035-36 season.It is unclear whether the EFL would accept the Premier League’s first offer however, with its chair, Rick Parry, believed to be holding out for a bigger deal.If approved the EFL would allocate 80% of the New Deal to the Championship clubs, 12% to League One and 8% to League Two.City and the Premier League declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueManchester CityFootball LeagueFootball politicsFinancial fair playnewsShareReuse this content

title: Defence promises to be a central issue for Carrick and Manchester United | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Manager may have concerns over his group of five central defenders withstanding the demands of a long campaign
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Manager may have concerns over his group of five central defenders withstanding the demands of a long campaign
Content: (Clockwise from top left): Leny Yoro, Harry Maguire, Lisandro Martínez, Ayden Heaven and Matthijs De Ligt.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen(Clockwise from top left): Leny Yoro, Harry Maguire, Lisandro Martínez, Ayden Heaven and Matthijs De Ligt.Composite: Getty ImagesManchester UnitedDefence promises to be a central issue for Carrick and Manchester UnitedManager may have concerns over his group of five central defenders withstanding the demands of a long campaignJamie JacksonWed 29 Jul 2026 10.05 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester United’s central defender quintet of Leny Yoro, Ayden Heaven, Harry Maguire, Matthijs De Ligt and Lisandro Martínez: an ideal blend of youthful zest and experienced winners or a unit that may prove vulnerable and injury-prone across the long months of the campaign?In Yoro, Heaven, Maguire, De Ligt, and Martínez,Michael Carrickcan talk of high potential and seasoned operators who will patrol the manager’s backline safely. Except it would be understandable if the 44-year-old privately has any concerns about the five defenders, as a unit, especially as there is no plan to strengthen the position unless one (or more) departs.Carrick is after all entering a debut full season as manager and will be leading United on four fronts for a first time: in the Premier League, FA Cup, Carabao Cup and, after two years, the Champions League.Manchester City leading opposition to Premier League’s £1.5bn EFL proposalRead moreWhen taking temporary charge last January, following the sacking of Ruben Amorim, Carrick had only 17 league matches to negotiate, as United were out of all other competitions. The job he executed impressed. Carrick wiped away the angst and chaos left behind by Amorim. He lifted United from seventh with 32 points, nine behind Aston Villa in third place, where the team finished by the end of the season.The coming term, though, is the acid test that may expose a callowness at elite level that totals only 20 games piloting United, including the three of his previous temporary incumbency. So being difficult to beat is a fundamental requirement. In those 17 matches last year, United lost only twice - the 2-1 reverses to Newcastle and Leeds - and conceded 18 times.Yet closer scrutiny of the five whose task is to secure the rearguard’s middle - the fullbacks Noussair Mazraoui, Diogo Dalot and Luke Shaw can operate there, too - throws up uncomfortable questions regarding a zone that requires surety and confidence, as a vital foundation for the side’s success.Yoro, 20, and Heaven, 19, are young and yet to progress beyond the potential stage of their nascent careers. For each the answer to how soon they should mature into cast-iron performers has to be now.Yoro, with 66 appearances since joining in July 2024 from Lille for £52m, is the more senior but has been lightweight, at times, and prone to the occasional error. After two seasons, needing time to bed in can no longer be mitigation, so the hope is Yoro’s 6ft 3in frame, serious turn of pace, and calm style will elevate his game.Heaven, who signed in February 2025 from Arsenal for a nominal fee, made 11 league starts last season and is blessed with technique, recovery speed, and a more physical 6ft 2inch build. He says: “I’m young and I’ve got to be patient, especially in my position. You don’t see a lot of 19-year-olds playing week in, week out. I know it’s nothing personal. I’m waiting for my opportunity.”Maguire is at the opposite end of the career spectrum. A player who at 33 possesses guile and a defend-first ethos yet is one-paced and may soon creak. Left at home by Thomas Tuchel for England’s World Cup campaign, the former United captain offers leadership.Under Carrick, Maguire would expect to enter the season as first-choice, alongside Martínez. Except the 28-year-old, who is in his prime, remains plagued by injury, being forced off before halftime of Argentina’s 1-0 World Cup final loss to Spain with a muscle problem, so his fitness for the season-opener at Hull is in the balance.After a starring role in United’s 2-1 defeat of Manchester City in the 2024 FA Cup final, Pep Guardiola called him “a top-five centre-back in the world”. But however good “The Butcher” is, Carrick cannot rely on him if availability is a struggle.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDe Ligt’s physical robustness may be an even greater concern for the manager. The 26-year-old has not featured since the 2-1 win at Crystal Palace on 30 November due to a back injury that was finally operated on in May.Speaking after the procedure, he said: “Since November I have done everything, pushing myself in every session and exploring every option, to get back to doing what I love, playing football.” The aim is for De Ligt, who boasts league-winners medals from the Netherlands (with Ajax), Italy (Juventus) and Germany (Bayern Munich), to be back early in the season.Manchester United consider Camavinga and Berge as midfield overhaul continuesRead moreYet the uncertainty regarding De Ligt, Maguire, Martínez, Yoro and Heaven is mirrored by the club’s so far unconvincing summer window, particularly compared with their rivals.City, with Elliot Anderson for £116m and possibly also Ayyoub Bouaddi for £85m, Chelsea (Morgan Rogers, £117m), and Tottenham (Sandro Tonali, £100m with add-ons, Mateus Fernandes, £85m) have all splurged big, while Arsenal target Bruno Guimarães (circa £70-80m) and Vinícius Júnior (£140-50m). United’s major signings compass the triggering of a £35m release-clause for Aston Villa’s Youri Tielemans, a 29-year-old with 13 years in his legs and who they faced no competition for, plus the £48m plus £2m Andrey Santos, a 22-year-old with 11 league starts last season for Chelsea.There are still five weeks of the market left so the picture may have changed significantly by 1 September. But at the moment, making a case for a fit-for-purpose defence - as with the squad - is difficult.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedHarry MaguireMichael CarrickfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gianni Infantino’s big World Cup sale and Fifa’s race to the bottom line | Fifa | The Guardian
description: In today’s newsletter: Fifa and an investment idea so egregious, even Sepp Blatter is chiming in
Author: Rob Smyth
Headline: In today’s newsletter: Fifa and an investment idea so egregious, even Sepp Blatter is chiming in
Content: Gianni Infantino and Donald Trump are covered in gold confetti, in what could almost be a metaphor.Photograph: Mark J Rebilas/Imagn/ReutersView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino and Donald Trump are covered in gold confetti, in what could almost be a metaphor.Photograph: Mark J Rebilas/Imagn/ReutersFootball Daily newsletterFifaGianni Infantino’s big World Cup sale and Fifa’s race to the bottom lineSign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!Rob SmythWed 29 Jul 2026 12.14 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 11.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFIFA UNITES THE WORLDWe begin Football Daily’s 29 July 2026 edition with a trip back to 26 February 2016.Gianni Infantinohas been elected as the new Fifa president on a promise to clean up a disgraced organisation. “A good day for football,” says the FA director, David Gill. “A good day for the sport,” concurs the American Fifa executive committee member, Sunil Gulati. “Who’s that bald loser on the news?” says an unnamed Republican candidate.Uefa accuses Fifa of ‘enriching themselves and their friends’ over World Cup sell-offRead moreInfantino’s message is simple. “Fifa has gone through sad times, moments of crisis. But those times are over. We enter now a new era. We’ll restore the image ofFifaand make sure you will be happy with what we do.” Infantino, whose pitch included a boast that he had vastly increased Uefa’s revenues, promised to address Fifa’s $550m (£414m) financial black hole. “It’s your money, not the money of the Fifa president,” he said. “The money of Fifa has to be used to develop football … I’m a candidate of the whole world and football. We have to build bridges, not walls.”We’re tempted to leave it at that, as we’re quietly confident you get the message, but editorial norms dictate we should talk about the news that Fifa is seeking private investment in the World Cup and the rest of its competitions.Big Website has done an explainer and everything. The proposed investment is in excess of £7.5bn and, according to a Fifa statement, would be used to expand the net worth of Infantino and Joshua Kushn – we beg your pardon, we completely misread that. We forgot to meditate, pray and chill this morning, so our focus isn’t as good as it could be. The Fifa statement says the money will be used to “expand football development funding”. Fifa’s money does not belong to its president – Infantino said it himself in 2016.Look, we all know football is about the bottom line. Money doesn’t just talk; it never shuts up. In that context, it’s some achievement for Infantino and friends to come up with an idea so egregious that almost everyone in football has responded with: “Bit much, mate.” Uefa, Concacaf and the FA are among those who have strongly criticised the proposals. Uefa’s 55 members are to hold an emergency meeting, with a potential World Cup boycott on the table. Just 10 days ago, Ferran Torres scored the winning goal in the Geopolitics World Cup final, a moment of pure euphoria that would be worth gazillions if only you could bottle it. But you can’t. At its best, football revives the child in all of us. Whatever the linguists tell you, there’s no infant in Infantino.QUOTE OF THE DAY“Football belongs to no individual and to no ‌institution. It belongs to the people. If Fifa were transferred into a profit-oriented ⁠corporate structure, it ​would lose ​its soul” – former Fifa president and man of the people Sepp Blatter weighs in on plans to sell off the World Cup.FOOTBALL DAILY LETTERS“I note that, despite the fact that the GWC is over, Football Daily is still arriving in my inbox in the early afternoon. As someone used to it screeching in late like a Djed Spence sliding tackle, I find this disconcerting. Also, the realisation that it isn’t home time yet is almost as disappointing as the contents of the email” – Richard O’Hagan [normal service has resumed, for today at least – Football Daily Ed].“I think Readng/Readino (yesterday’s full email edition) should turn their grammatical errors into a rebranding opportunity that adds a little continental pizazz. Athletic Readino, Real Readino, Dynamo Readng, Sporting Readino. It’d see people flocking to this bustling, cosmopolitan destination town. Possibly” – Martin Clifford.“Cancel Football. Too much info” – Peter Craswell.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf you have any, please send letters tothe.boss@theguardian.com.Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Martin Clifford. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, arehere.RECOMMENDED FOLLOWINGBig Website: now onBlueSpace,TikBook,Instachat, you name it.This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. To get the full version,just visit this page and follow the instructions.Explore more on these topicsFifaFootball Daily newsletterGianni InfantinofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gina Rinehart lobbied for controversial plan to move 2032 Olympic rowing to crocodile-inhabited river | Rowing | The Guardian
description: Decision to host event on Fitzroy River at Rockhampton, 600km north of host city Brisbane, prompted significant backlash
Author: Ben Smee
Headline: Decision to host event on Fitzroy River at Rockhampton, 600km north of host city Brisbane, prompted significant backlash
Content: An undated letter from Gina Rinehart to Queensland’s deputy premier, Jarrod Bleijie, lobbied for the relocation of the Brisbane Olympic Games 2032 rowing events to the Fitzroy River, a natural habitat for saltwater crocodiles.Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAPView image in fullscreenAn undated letter from Gina Rinehart to Queensland’s deputy premier, Jarrod Bleijie, lobbied for the relocation of the Brisbane Olympic Games 2032 rowing events to the Fitzroy River, a natural habitat for saltwater crocodiles.Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAPRowingGina Rinehart lobbied for controversial plan to move 2032 Olympic rowing to crocodile-inhabited riverDecision to host event on Fitzroy River at Rockhampton, 600km north of host city Brisbane, prompted significant backlashFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastBen SmeeWed 29 Jul 2026 19.23 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 19.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia’s richest person,Gina Rinehart, lobbied for controversial plans to host 2032 Olympic rowing events on the Fitzroy River at Rockhampton, documents released by the Queensland government show.The plans to send rowers 600km north of host city Brisbane – to a river that isnatural habitat for saltwater crocodiles, and whichprompted significant backlashamong the rowing and broader Olympic communities – were announced by the Queensland government in March last year.The newly electedQueenslandgovernment conducted a venues review that was finalised in early 2025.Can crocodiles and canoeists coexist at Australia’s 2032 Olympic Games?Read moreIt used the review process to justify breaking election promises not to build a new stadium. But the decision to send rowing events to Rockhampton went against the review’s recommendations, which suggested rowing be relocated to Sydney and held at the existing facility near Penrith.Concerns about the Fitzroy River’s suitability go well beyond the most glaring reason – the saltwater crocodiles, which are occasionally found in the water at Rockhampton, which sits just above the Tropic of Capricorn.View image in fullscreenAndrew Miller paddles along the Fitzroy River, which will host 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games events despite concerns about crocodile numbers.Photograph: Sylvia Liber/The GuardianInternational and Australian rowing officials and competitors have raised various concerns, including that a rowing facility built in Rockhampton would become a“white elephant”. There are also concerns any potential course would not it meet the strict technical requirements for international racing regarding weeds, water quality and currents.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe situation has led to brinkmanship: the Queensland deputy premier, Jarrod Bleijie, has said publicly that rowing would be held in Rockhampton or cancelled altogether.Anundated letter from Rinehart to Bleijie obtained by Brisbane Times, but understood to have been sent prior to the government’s decision to move rowing to Rockhampton, lobbies for the relocation of rowing to central Queensland.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRinehart, a key financial backer of the rightwing One Nation party, and who has extensive mining and pastoral interests, says in the letter that hosting an Olympic event in the “beef capital” would “enable Queensland to tell the iconic Australian story of our pastoralists and farmers”.“As a supporter of Australian rowing for more than a decade, I am aware that the Australian team often trains on the Fitzroy River and that Rockhampton annually hosts the Queensland state school championships,” Rinehart said.“This rowing facility is world class and is already close to major infrastructure, so it offers the potential to save taxpayer money.“As you would know too, Rockhampton has also always been a major mining town, the nearby Mt Morgan mine was once the biggest gold mine in the world.“I am told that metals from this mine will produce the gold, silver, and bronze medals for the Olympics! To marry showing where the Olympic medals come from and having Olympic events nearby, sounds to me like a beautiful extra!”Explore more on these topicsRowingQueensland politicsGina RinehartQueenslandOlympic GamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Idi Amin’s grandson disqualified from Commonwealth Games boxing for head-butt | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: The Commonwealth Games debut of Idi Amin’s grandson ended in disgrace after Aziz Abdul was disqualified for head-butting Damar Thomas in the boxing
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The Commonwealth Games debut of Idi Amin’s grandson ended in disgrace after Aziz Abdul was disqualified for head-butting Damar Thomas in the boxing
Content: Aziz Abdul (left) was disqualified for head-butting Damar Thomas.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAziz Abdul (left) was disqualified for head-butting Damar Thomas.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026Idi Amin’s grandson disqualified from Commonwealth Games boxing for head-buttAziz Abdul disqualified for ‘Glasgow kiss’ in third roundUgandan boxer: ‘Why can’t they let this fight continue?’Sean Ingleat SEC CentreWed 29 Jul 2026 18.12 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 18.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheCommonwealth Gamesdebut of Idi Amin’s grandson ended in ignominy and disgrace as the boxer was disqualified in the third round for head-butting his English opponent – and then launched a bitter verbal assault on the referee.Things then took an even more bizarre turn as Aziz Abdul, a 25-year-old from Uganda, refused to speak to a journalist afterwards because of what he had writtenabout the tyrannical dictator.Madias Ngake’s real-life movie script ends with weightlifting silver for EnglandRead more“No, not you,” Abdul told the man from the Press Association. “I don’t like you.” A Ugandan team official quickly clarified: “It is because of the things you said about his grandad.”Amin is estimated to have killed half a million people in Uganda after coming to power in a coup d’état in 1971, and also forced the expulsion of 80,000 people of Asian descent.However, Abdul insisted before his super-heavyweight fight with the 21-year-old Damar Thomas from Kilburn that his grandfather’s achievements “had inspired me” and “I am so proud of him”.Abdul, who is alsoknown as Aziz Ringoafter his self-titled signature punch, also promised he would be “the new king of Scotland” – after his grandfather had offered to liberate the Scots from England. However, the most Scottish thing about Abdul proved to be the Glasgow kiss he planted on Thomas when he was 20-16 down on the scorecards. Afterwards he complained, without foundation, that the decision was unfair.Afterwards Abdul complained that the decision was unfair. “There were a lot of fouls,” he said. “Holding, elbowing, a lot of bullshit. The officials cannot judge them. When other countries do this they are disqualified. All I can say about this is the referee’s decision is not right and I am not happy.”View image in fullscreenAziz ‘Ringo’ was critical of the referee’s ruling in his contest.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianAbdul also criticised the referee for ruling that he had been knocked down in the first round, after taking a punch. “He took a light punch and they counted,” he said. “I landed a heavy punch on him and they deducted my points and warned me. I’m a black African, I know. It’s God’s plan. I don’t know why the officials are scared about this fight. Why can’t they let this fight continue?”He also insisted he had not deliberately head-butted his opponent. “He got me with the elbow,” he said. “It was not intentional because I was trying to come back. How can I head-butt someone? I would not head-butt someone.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“When I was still in Uganda, I said I must win by knockout. It’s an away match for me here. Next time I must end the fight in the first minute.”“Next time, I will get him,” he added. “Anytime in the future. Two years, five years, 10 years. I will show him that Aziz Ringo is a real warrior. It’s so painful.”Thomas, meanwhile, is now guaranteed a medal after a wild fight with plenty of haymakers and very little quality work. “I got the job done, not how I wanted to, but the job is done,” he said. “He was running at me with his head. There was a bit of ring rust from me but it is what it is.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026BoxingCommonwealth GamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ramsay-Peaty ends his Commonwealth Games with silver for England in medley relay | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Adam Ramsay-Peaty’s Commonwealth Games ended with a silver medal as England were beaten by Australia’s swimmers in the 4x100m medley relay
Author: Yara El-Shaboury
Headline: Adam Ramsay-Peaty’s Commonwealth Games ended with a silver medal as England were beaten by Australia’s swimmers in the 4x100m medley relay
Content: England’s (from left) Jacob Mills, Oliver Morgan, Adam Ramsay-Peaty and Edward Mildred celebrate winning silver in the medley relay.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/ReutersView image in fullscreenEngland’s (from left) Jacob Mills, Oliver Morgan, Adam Ramsay-Peaty and Edward Mildred celebrate winning silver in the medley relay.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/ReutersCommonwealth Games 2026Ramsay-Peaty ends his Commonwealth Games with silver for England in medley relayEngland second behind Australia in 4x100m medleyScotland win silver in women’s 4x100m medley relayYara El-Shabouryat Tollcross International Swimming CentreWed 29 Jul 2026 18.11 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 17.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter six days of Australian dominance in the pool, the swimming programme at Glasgow 2026 came to a close in familiar fashion as the green and gold claimed one final victory after finishing with an extraordinary 37 gold, 16 silver and 23 bronze medals in the water. The closing race also produced a slice ofCommonwealth Gameshistory as South Africa’s bronze in the men’s 4x100m medley relay earned Chad le Clos a record-breaking 21st Commonwealth Games medal, making him the most decorated athlete in the competition’s history.Adam Ramsay-Peaty, meanwhile, bowed out of the Games with a silver medal after England finished runners-up to Australia in the final swimming event. Australia surged through the second half of the race to secure gold in a Games record of 3min 28.71sec, while England’s quartet of Oliver Morgan, Ramsay-Peaty, Edward Mildred and Jacob Mills claimed silver in 3:30.68 after holding off South Africa.Madias Ngake’s live movie script ends with weightlifting silver for EnglandRead moreMorgan gave England a strong start with a 53.20 opening leg before Ramsay-Peaty kept them in second with a 58.74 split. Mildred slipped briefly to third on the third leg despite clocking 51.04, before Jacob Mills produced a 47.70 anchor to haul England back into second.“To come in with the boys and get a silver medal, I can’t complain whatsoever,” said Morgan. “It’s my fifth of the week. Some of us have had tough weeks but it shows the resilience we’ve had in the team. I’ve not had the best week individually, so to come away with some silverware is really impressive. It’s about building on that, moving into next season and into LA [2028 Olympics].”In the penultimate race, Scotland rounded off their memorable night with a silver medal in the women’s 4x100m medley relay after coming out in kilts as Australia stormed to gold in another record time.“It’s absolutely amazing,” said Katie Shanahan. “I’m sure I can speak for all of us when I say there’s no better way to finish off a home meet than by getting that silver medal. It’s just been such an amazing meet, and it’s a week I’ll definitely remember for the rest of my life.”“It’s something we save for the last night,” said Evelyn Davis on walking out with kilts on. “Katie’s falling off in the walkout actually calmed my nerves a bit before the crowd got going again, so it was good fun.”View image in fullscreenAdam Ramsay-Peaty finished the Commonwealth Games with a silver in the medley relay.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/ReutersRoared on by a vocal crowd, Shanahan, Angharad Evans and Keanna MacInnes battled for the lead throughout before Davis produced a composed anchor leg to hold off South Africa and Canada to secure second place. Australia, who had qualified more than four seconds faster than the field, lived up to their billing as favourites as Iona Anderson, Sienna Toohey, Alex Perkins and Meg Harris powered to gold, while South Africa snatched bronze ahead of Canada in the closing stages.Earlier Evans had delighted the home support by winning a second breaststroke gold of the Games. The 23-year-old followed up her 100m breaststroke triumph by winning the women’s 200m breaststroke, holding off a late charge from South Africa’s Kaylene Corbett to seal victory by 0.67. Northern Ireland’s Ellie McCartney completed the podium with bronze.“It’s been absolutely unreal,” Evans said. “With the 100m I put too much pressure on myself because that’s what I see as my main event. The 200m feels even more special because afterwards I had all these doubts: did I only win the 100m because it was a fluke? Did I just get lucky? As crazy as that sounds. To back it up with not just another medal but another gold is just so surreal.”The evening had begun with another statement performance from South Africa’s Pieter Coetze, who retained his men’s 100m backstroke crown in emphatic fashion. He clocked a Commonwealth Games record of 51.77 – just 0.17 outside the world record – to collect his third gold medal in Glasgow after winning the 50m and 200m backstroke titles. England’s Morgan claimed silver, while Coetze’s compatriot Ruard van Renen secured bronze.Australia also dominated the sprint events, with clean sweeps in the women’s 50m freestyle and men’s 50m butterfly. Harris led home her teammates Perkins and Shayna Jack, taking bronze in the final race of her career, in the women’s event. The Welsh teenager Theodora Taylor was fourth. In the men’s butterfly, Kyle Chalmers and Ben Armbruster shared gold after both broke the Games record with identical times of 22.7. Cameron McEvoy took bronze.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesSwimmingAdam Ramsay-PeatynewsShareReuse this content

title: Madias Ngake’s real-life movie script ends with weightlifting silver after sleeping rough | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Madias Nagake, who gave up elite sport for more than a decade after representing Cameroon, said: ‘I never believed that I would ever be here’
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Madias Nagake, who gave up elite sport for more than a decade after representing Cameroon, said: ‘I never believed that I would ever be here’
Content: Madias Ngake said ‘I never believed that I would ever be here’ after her silver medal in the women’s 87kg competition.Photograph: François Nel/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMadias Ngake said ‘I never believed that I would ever be here’ after her silver medal in the women’s 87kg competition.Photograph: François Nel/Getty ImagesCommonwealth Games 2026Madias Ngake’s real-life movie script ends with weightlifting silver after sleeping roughNgake left Cameroon due to homosexuality lawsShe fled from London 2012 village and slept on streetsSean Ingleat the SEC ArmadilloWed 29 Jul 2026 17.57 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 17.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirst Madias Ngake lifted the weight of an upright piano to her shoulders. Then, with another staggering act of power and defiance, she sent a 128kg barbell high above her head.And, just like that, the 34-year-old Team England weightlifter had won a silver medal and written one of the most remarkable stories of these Games.Fourteen years ago, Ngake fled the London 2012 Olympic village after finishing sixth in her competition and ended up sleeping rough for a month.Ramsay-Peaty ends Commonwealth Games career with silver for England in medley relayRead moreThe reason? She was competing for Cameroon, where homosexuality is illegal, and someone in the team had found out that she was a lesbian. And so began a journey that led to Ngake giving up elite sport for more than a decade, deciding to come back in 2023, and then transferring allegiances to Britain a year later.“When I left the Olympics in 2012 I got on a bus,” she explained. “After the last stop, they told me this is closed, so I can’t go anywhere. So I decided I will sleep outside at the bus stop. I slept rough for about a month. Nobody looked after me.“I had to leave because someone on the team knew about my situation, that I am a lesbian.”But having won a European medal earlier this year, Ngake showed her strength as she led the women’s 87kg competition after the first event, the snatch, with a powerful lift of 108kg.That put her 3kg clear of Australia’s Eileen Cikamatana. However in the clean and jerk, Cikamatana was able to thrust a barbell 140kg over her head like it was a rag doll to score a combined lift of 245kg – a new Games record – to take gold by 6kg.View image in fullscreenEileen Cikamatana with her gold medal, flanked by Madias Ngake (left) and the bronze medallist Rose Beaudoin of Canada.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPBut Ngake was not too disappointed afterwards. Asked if her life was like a movie, she replied: “Yes. And I never believed I would ever be here.”Ngake’s hair was dyed red, the colour of her home country. Afterwards she said that it had been the idea of Emily Campbell, Team GB’s double Olympic medallist, who competes on Thursday.Ngake also explained it was only after 2017 that she was legally able to work. She was an office cleaner in Leeds for nine years, earning about £2,000 a year. However she has recently moved to Nottingham to train as a full-time athlete and hopes to make the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.Amazingly, if she were to win an Olympic medal, it would be her second one. That’s because in 2019, she was awarded a bronze medal from London 2012 after three weightlifters who finished above her at the Games were disqualified for doping offences.However, as the medal was sent to Cameroon, Ngake has never seen it as she has not been back to her home country. “I would like to have it, yes,” she explained. “But I don’t think it’s going to be possible because the medal is in Cameroon and there is a situation and I don’t want to do politics.”But Ngake knows how to do medals. And her adopted country was certainly delighted on Wednesday night.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesWeightliftingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Stephen Fleming to be appointed England Test coach after impressing ECB | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: Stephen Fleming is to be England’s new Test coach, but he will probably not start until the South Africa tour in December
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: Stephen Fleming is to be England’s new Test coach, but he will probably not start until the South Africa tour in December
Content: Stephen Fleming is a compatriot, former teammate and friend of Brendon McCullum.Photograph: Prakash Singh/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStephen Fleming is a compatriot, former teammate and friend of Brendon McCullum.Photograph: Prakash Singh/Getty ImagesEngland cricket teamStephen Fleming to be appointed England Test coach after impressing ECBNew Zealander will succeed Brendon McCullumLikely to start on South Africa tour in DecemberSimon BurntonWed 29 Jul 2026 15.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 16.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStephen Fleming is expected to be named as England’s Test coach, after impressing the England and Wales Cricket Board in a series of interviews over the past two weeks. The 53-year-old would work alongside his predecessor, compatriot, former teammate and friendBrendon McCullum, who remains in charge of the white-ball teams.Fleming stood down as head coach of the Indian Premier League franchise Chennai Super Kings – as well as their subsidiaries Joburg Super Kings in South Africa’s SA20 and Texas Super Kings in America’s Major League Cricket – this month. That announcement was made after CSK finished eighth out of 10 teams in this year’s IPL, following on from a last-place finish in 2025, but also less than 24 hours afterMcCullum was sacked by the ECBas Test coach.Justin Langer has not heard from ECB about England job but could be temptedRead moreIt is expected Fleming will be in place for the tour of South Africa starting in December, but the three-Test series against Pakistan that begins at Headingley on 19 August may still be overseen by an interim, probably Marcus Trescothick.Fleming has extensive experience of English cricket, not just from playing 10 Tests and 17 ODIs in this country between 1994 and 2004, but also from spells at Middlesex, Yorkshire and Nottinghamshire. He also coached Southern Brave in the Hundred for two years, leaving in 2024.He was approached by England in 2009, shortly after he retired as a player, only to turn them down. “I was flattered to be offered,” he said. “It came down to the fact it wasn’t my time. If I get another couple of years [as a coach] I can see if it is what I want to do and if I would be any good at it.”England ended up turning to Andy Flower, who,having been the early frontrunnerto replace McCullum, has now returned the favour byrejecting the joband opening the door for Fleming’s appointment.Fleming’s relationship with McCullum gave him an advantage over his rivals for the England job, the Australian Tom Moody, the former England batter and Afghanistan coach Jonathan Trott and Richard Dawson, the head coach at Glamorgan.View image in fullscreenNew Zealand’s Brendon McCullum (left) and Stephen Fleming celebrate the wicket of England’s Andrew Strauss in the third Test at McLean Park in Napier in March 2008.Photograph: Ross Setford/APBeyond their friendship, the pair have been business associates at two companies, the software company CricHQ and the export business Quality New Zealand. Daniel Vettori, another former New Zealand captain coaching in England, at Sunrisers Leeds, described the pair as “very good friends” with “a lot of similar traits”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMcCullum made 126 of his 432 international appearances under Fleming’s captaincy before taking over from him and has described him as a major influence. “The way Stephen Fleming led the team tactically was something that really resonated with me,” he said in 2019.“He’s one of my great mates as well now, and what I loved about Stephen Fleming is whilst on the field it looked quite instinctive there was always scores and scores of detail in behind.“The other thing I loved about him was his man management as a leader. It’s very hard to ask players to implement the plans that you have if you don’t understand those players.”Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamBrendon McCullumECBCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Saltburn suspend fielder accused of cheating in ‘Clicky Ponting’ furore | Cricket | The Guardian
description: Saltburn have said the player from viral video ‘will not play again in foreseeable future’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Saltburn have said the player from viral video ‘will not play again in foreseeable future’
Content: Saltburn said they are cooperating with the League’s investigation.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSaltburn said they are cooperating with the League’s investigation.Photograph: Gary Calton/The GuardianCricketSaltburn suspend fielder accused of cheating in ‘Clicky Ponting’ furore‘Will not play again in foreseeable future’Club concede Wednesday’s second-team cup fixturePA MediaWed 29 Jul 2026 14.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 17.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaltburn Cricket Club have said they are treating allegations of cheating very seriously and have suspended the player at the centre of the controversy for the “foreseeable future”. A Saltburn fielder was accused ofclicking his fingers to get a catch behindand footage of several incidents later went viral on social media.The first video, posted on Monday evening, was from Saltburn’s second XI victory over Norton in Division Two of North Yorkshire and South DurhamCricketLeague. It showed the fielder clicking his fingers as the ball passed the bat of the Norton batter, Noman Shabir, before being caught by the wicketkeeper, Josh Bowes, and the umpire gave him out.‘Saltburn are the Argentina of local cricket’: victims and neighbours on the ‘Clicky Ponting’ scandalRead moreSaltburn, who sit 17 points clear at the top of the table, won the match by 159 runs and announced they have conceded their second-team cup fixture against Marton on Wednesday.A statement on Saltburn’s social media channels read: “This is issued in response to the widely publicised complaint made against a Saltburn Cricket Club member and, as a consequence, against the club more generally.“We are treating this allegation with the utmost seriousness and, as a family-centric club, we are fully cooperating with the NYS League’s investigation.“We believe that the club acted decisively as soon as the complaint and investigation were made known to us. The player at the centre of the complaint has been suspended and will not play again for the club this season or in the foreseeable future, pending the outcome of this investigation.Cricket player seems to show fielder tricking umpire by clicking to imitate edges“Initial discussions have already taken place between club officials and the league.“This has been a very distressing and stressful experience for all those concerned, and we would ask that this reality is borne in mind and that personal boundaries are respected, as we are an amateur club entirely run by volunteers.”The video has now had more than 7.5m views on X, with several celebrities condemning the behaviour.Explore more on these topicsCricketnewsShareReuse this content
