title: Charley Hull shooting for Open glory after multiple near misses at majors | Women's Open | The Guardian
description: Nelly Korda may be a safer bet, but home fans would be thrilled to see Hull triumph after five runner-up finishes
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Nelly Korda may be a safer bet, but home fans would be thrilled to see Hull triumph after five runner-up finishes
Content: Charley Hull lines up a putt. ‘She’s such a great personality,’ Nelly Korda said of the Englishwoman. ‘It would be great for her to do it on kind of home soil.’Photograph: Charlie Crowhurst/R&A/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCharley Hull lines up a putt. ‘She’s such a great personality,’ Nelly Korda said of the Englishwoman. ‘It would be great for her to do it on kind of home soil.’Photograph: Charlie Crowhurst/R&A/Getty ImagesWomen's OpenCharley Hull shooting for Open glory after multiple near misses at majorsNelly Korda may be a safer bet, but home fans would be thrilled to see Hull triumph after five runner-up finishesEwan Murrayat Royal Lytham & St AnnesWed 29 Jul 2026 11.35 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNelly Korda is the likeliest winner of the Women’s Open, but there is no question who would be the most popular. Charley Hull’s brushes with major glory – she has five runner‑up finishes – have only intensified a widespread desire for the 30‑year‑old to break through the tape. Royal Lytham & St Annes provides the latest opportunity for the flamboyant Englishwoman.Korda arrived in Lancashire with half her four major triumphs having come in 2026. Perhaps the Floridian can afford to be generous and she has endorsed Hull’s prospects. “She’s such a great personality,” Korda said. “It would be great for her to do it on home soil, too. She’s an amazing player. I enjoy playing with her. It would be great for the game.”‘Where has that time gone?’: first Women’s Open champion Jenny Lee Smith on 1976 glory, Kevin Keegan and finding her secret twinRead moreHull does not seem the type to be dispirited by close shaves. A year agoshe was pipped by Miyu Yamashita. Hull finished a shot adrift of Korda, the champion, in theUS Women’s Openlast month. “That’s sometimes how she goes,” Korda said. “It’s about putting yourself in that position. You can’t control what others are doing, but she’s doing something right to always be there and be relevant, to be in the hunt.“It’s like Sam Burns. He’s been in the hunt a lot during major championships, hasn’t got it done. Eventually he will. You can’t get discouraged, it has to be encouraging.”History is in Hull’s favour. The last time the Women’s Open visited here, in 2018,England’s Georgia Hall claimed her maiden majorvictory. A scorched links will render this a wonderful test. Korda estimates she will employ her driver five times per round at most, instead adding a four-iron to her armoury.This is also something of a trial run, with the men’s Open due to make a long-awaited return in 2028.Korda is more comfortable than ever at being the name on everyone’s lips. Early in her career, the world No 1 struggled with fame and attention. Having parents who were professional tennis players, a brother who still competes in that domain and a sister who is also on the LPGA Tour has helped with her mindset. So, too, has a frustrating 2025.View image in fullscreen‘I decided that I need to stop getting so frustrated with everything,’ said Nelly Korda. ‘It’s draining having that attitude.’Photograph: Alan Martin/Action Plus/Shutterstock“My family always make sure my batteries are recharged,” she said. “It’s a funny conversation; my dad and my mum are always telling me to take more days off. I’m like: ‘No, no, I don’t want to. I want to grind on my craft.’“There gets a point in the season where I’m really tired. It’s not just golf. It’s not just like the travel. It’s kind of a combination of everything people don’t really see behind the scenes.“My parents are people I go to all the time for advice. My sister, too. She has been at a lot of majors this year. Those are my people. I’m so comfortable and vulnerable with them. They’ve seen every side of me and know me the best.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I decided I need to stop getting so frustrated with everything. I hit a great shot, it goes in a divot and I would get frustrated. What is going on? Why am I getting these bounces? It’s draining having that attitude. I just told myself: ‘I’m not going to have this attitude.’”Lytham stardust also includesLydia Ko, who beat Korda to the Women’s Open titlein 2024. Ko has taken inspiration from her fellow New ZealanderRyan Fox after his Open gloryat nearby Royal Birkdale. Fox became the fourth player from New Zealand to win a major title, reducing Ko to tears as she watched from the west coast of the US.“He’s very humble and I would say he’s your typical Kiwi guy that happens to be a freak athlete,” Ko said. “I went to work out and everywhere I went I was like: ‘Please turn on the Open.’ It ended up not working on the TV so I had my trainer turn it on my cellphone. I can’t remember my workout at all because my whole focus was there.“I took an Uber ride back home. As soon as I got home he was on the 18th and when I saw that drive I was so relieved, but so excited, super pumped.“I screamed when his winning putt went in. I closed the door and I screamed. My husband ran out and was like: ‘What’s happening?’ Ten seconds later, I was crying.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's OpenGolfUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Uefa accuses Fifa of ‘enriching themselves and their friends’ over World Cup sell-off | Fifa | The Guardian
description: The Football Association has joined Uefa in condemning Fifa’s plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The Football Association has joined Uefa in condemning Fifa’s plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors
Content: Gianni Infantino with the World Cup during a press conference in Mexico last month.Photograph: Eduardo Verdugo/APView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino with the World Cup during a press conference in Mexico last month.Photograph: Eduardo Verdugo/APFifaUefa accuses Fifa of ‘enriching themselves and their friends’ over World Cup sell-offFifa members given 19 September deadline to opt inFA and Concacaf join chorus of disapproval at plansMatt HughesandNick AmesWed 29 Jul 2026 10.32 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUefa has accused Fifa of “using our sport to enrich themselves and their friends” after it emerged that Fifa’s 211 member associations have been given a deadline of 19 September to decide whether to apply for an initial payment of $20m (£15m) from the proceeds of its plan to sell off stakes in theWorld Cupto private investors.“Today we have learned of Fifa’s deadline to associations to support their proposals or have the one-off payout offer withdrawn. This says everything you need to know about this plan,” said European football’s governing body in a statement.Is the World Cup for sale? Here’s what Fifa’s plans mean and what happens next | Paul MacInnesRead more“But having held discussions with many stakeholders across the game, Uefa knows there is significant and growing opposition to Fifa’s scheme. Fifa cannot continue to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends. We can grow the game correctly. It’s time to prioritise associations, clubs, leagues, players and fans.”Fifa on Tuesday announced plans to sell the commercial rights to its tournaments, including the World Cup, to private investors, sparking widespread condemnation across the game. In a statement released on Wednesday morning, the Football Association said it was yet to see any details of the controversial proposals, and expressed grave concerns over Fifa’a governance.11:17Infantino tries to cash in on World Cup: is football’s soul for sale? - The LatestThe FA chair, Debbie Hewitt, is one of eight Fifa vice-presidents and watched many World Cup matches alongside the president,Gianni Infantino, yet appears to have been shut out of any discussions over plans that are at an advanced stage.The FA’s intervention is significant as it is the first time the governing body has criticised Fifa under Infantino, having stayed quiet throughoutthe Folarin Balogun affairduring the World Cup and endorsed the award of the 2034 tournament to Saudi Arabia.View image in fullscreenFA chair Debbie Hewitt (right), with Gianni Infantino (centre), at the World Cup semi-final between England and Argentina.Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/ReutersThe FA is understood to have held talks with Uefa and other European associations, who are determined to kill the plan, with all options, including a boycott of Fifa tournaments and a potential breakaway, thought to be on the table.“We were completely unaware of this proposal and have no substantive details, including what the proposition actually is, and what conditions are attached,” said the FA in a statement. “Based on the limited information, we are deeply concerned about the lack of process and governance to get to this point, and the apparent substance and principles involved. When the proposal is shared in the full and transparent way now promised by Fifa, we will make our views clear, and comment further.”The FA’s statement followed a similarly strong release from Concacaf, which is particularly significant given that the North, Central American and Caribbean confederation has just delivered the most lucrative World Cup in history for Fifa, which produced revenues of $15bn.The Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, was instrumental in winning the joint US, Mexican and Canadian bid for 2026, but was also kept in the dark over Fifa’s plans.double quotation markMany in European football see Fifa’s plans as an outright attack on football. I share this viewHans-Joachim Watzke, German FA vice-president“Concacaf was only made aware of this matter through media reports and, subsequently, via a media release,” Concacaf said in a statement released to the Guardian. “We are deeply concerned by the lack of due process.“We share the disappointment of many within our region and the game that this level of detail has been designed and shared publicly before any discussion with the relevant governance bodies and stakeholders has taken place.“As leaders within football, we are the custodians of the game. Collectively, Fifa, the confederations and every member association have a responsibility to always act in the best interests of the sport. Every decision we make must be guided by good governance, robust processes and long-term stewardship.“This is the framework within which Concacaf operates. We trust that all within the Fifa family will act in the same manner.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFifa’s work with the US bank JP Morgan to set up a new company called Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), which would be partially sold off to “raise up to $4.2bn” to fund global football development projects later this year, has left other stakeholders stunned and reignited divisions within the world game.Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation were already bracing themselves to fight Fifa’s plans to expand the World Cup to 64 teams for the 2030 tournament, and there are fears that inviting private investors will make further expansion inevitable, as well as leading to pressure to stage the World Cup more regularly given its huge commercial value.Uefa accused Fifa of attempting to sell football’s souland will hold emergency talks on Thursday to plan a coordinated response that could involve legal action.Fifa accused of ‘selling the soul of football’ over $20bn World Cup commercial rights sale planRead more“This crosses a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross,” it said. “Uefa takes it extremely seriously. So should every national football association. So should every stakeholder: leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments and everyone who cares about the future of the game.“The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade – especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not Fifa’s to sell.”Hans-Joachim Watzke, the vice-president of the German FA, who is also president of the Bundesliga side Borussia Dortmund and a vice-president of Uefa’s executive committee, told his country’s Kicker magazine: “Many in European football see Fifa’s plans as an outright attack on football. I share this view. A line has been crossed here.“There is broad agreement on this among the member associations, as several conversations I’ve had with [Uefa president] Aleksander Ceferin and other colleagues in recent days have shown me.”Elite clubs also expressed disquiet. The European Football Clubs organisation said in a statement: “As an institution that represents over 850 football clubs – whose member clubs, their players and communities are fundamental participants in football worldwide, not least in Fifa’s competitions including all the international club competitions – it would be wholly appropriate for EFC to be fully consulted on a proposal of such magnitude. EFC learned about this proposal in the same way as most global football stakeholders – without warning and through the media.”Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham, joined critics of the plan on Tuesday night, saying on social media that the sport does not belong to investors. “The World Cup is not a product. It is the greatest competition in world sport, and it was never anyone’s to sell,” Burnham wrote on X. “Dress the deal up however you like. Once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out.”Explore more on these topicsFifaThe FAGianni InfantinoUS sportsWorld CupFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rogue OpenAI agent that hacked startup tried to attack other firms | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: ChatGPT developer says activity by autonomous tool was not at severity or scale of what occurred at Hugging Face
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: ChatGPT developer says activity by autonomous tool was not at severity or scale of what occurred at Hugging Face
Content: The agent, powered by two OpenAI models, had evaded control and attacked Hugging Face during an internal cybersecurity test.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe agent, powered by two OpenAI models, had evaded control and attacked Hugging Face during an internal cybersecurity test.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersOpenAIRogue OpenAI agent that hacked startup tried to attack other firmsChatGPT developer says activity by autonomous tool was not at severity or scale of what occurred at Hugging FaceDan MilmoGlobal technology editorWed 29 Jul 2026 08.38 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 15.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI has revealed that a cyber-attackcarried out by a rogue AI agenthad more than one victim.TheChatGPTdeveloper said the agent – an autonomous tool able to carry out sequences of commands without human help – had located and used logins to access four other unnamed “publicly-available services” in addition to the US startup Hugging Face.It said the activity was not at the severity or scale of what occurred at Hugging Face,a company that hosts a database of AI models. The agent, powered by two OpenAI models, had evaded control and attacked the startup during an internal cybersecurity test.“The [OpenAI] models identified and used publicly exposed credentials at the account-level on other publicly-available services. This includes four accounts on four services as part of the Hugging Face incident,”OpenAIsaid.Modal Labs, a company that helps AI startups access the chips they need to runAI tools, said the agent exploited vulnerable code ‌written by a customer that was hosted on Modal’s platform.According to a timeline of the incident published by Hugging Face this week, the rogue agent broke out of its sandbox – or an isolated testing environment – and hacked another sandbox “hosted on a third-party ​provider’s infrastructure” before turning it into a launchpad for ‌the broader hack.Modal’s chief technology officer, Akshat Bubna, told Reuters the affected customer had “published an unauthenticated endpoint that allowed anyone on the internet to use their sandboxes for code execution” – the digital equivalent of leaving a door open.OpenAI said last week that the attack had been created by itsGPT-5.6 Solmodel and an unnamed model. It said in its update on Tuesday that the unnamed model had been “deactivated, encrypted, and restricted from research access”.In the new Hugging Facetimeline,the startup said an agent powered by two OpenAI models had made thousands of small, automated decisions executed at machine speed to carry out the attack. It said the hack appeared to be driven by an attempt to “cheat” an internal cybersecurity test at OpenAI, with the agent inferring that Hugging Face might host the solutions to the test. Hugging Face said it had recovered 17,600 “attacker actions” carried out by the agent.“We believe the entire intrusion was, from the agent’s point of view, an attempt to cheat the evaluation: reach our production systems and steal the test solutions rather than solve the challenge on its own,” Hugging Face said.The startup said the agent had reached its internal infrastructure, but had only accessed content related to the cybersecurity test. The attack took place over five days, Hugging Face said, and the sheer volume of actions carried out were “far beyond what an operator could sustain by hand”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDescribing the agent’s offensive threat as real, Hugging Face said the tool had harnessed a number of IT vulnerabilities, escaped its testing environment, reached the public internet and mounted a “coherent campaign” against the startup’s infrastructure for several days.It said a human attacker could have found and exploited the same flaws, but the difference was the sheer scale of the agent’s attempts to find a way through.“Agents bring a step increase in the number of paths an attacker can test, the speed at which failed paths can be replaced, and the volume of evidence defenders must interpret,” Hugging Face said.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. title: AI tool will lead to more child refugees being treated as adults, charity warns | Global development | The Guardian
description: ‘Racist bias’ overestimating ages in Home Office’s facial-recognition software will lead to solo children being housed with adults, says Human Rights Network
Author: Kaamil Ahmed
Headline: ‘Racist bias’ overestimating ages in Home Office’s facial-recognition software will lead to solo children being housed with adults, says Human Rights Network
Content: Border Force officers with two young migrants at Dover.Photograph: Anadolu/Anadolu/GettyView image in fullscreenBorder Force officers with two young migrants at Dover.Photograph: Anadolu/Anadolu/GettyGlobal developmentAI tool will lead to more child refugees being treated as adults, charity warns‘Racist bias’ overestimating ages in Home Office’s facial-recognition software will lead to solo children being housed with adults, says Human Rights NetworkSupported byAbout this contentKaamil AhmedWed 29 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 02.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlawed and racialised models that underpin the AI-powered age-detection systems to be introduced by the British government will endanger children, rights groups and children’s charities have warned.Urging ministers to reverse plans to introduce facial age-estimation technology to screen migrants, critics have warned that black children arriving from conflict zones are at risk of being of thrust into the adult system.Maddie Harris, of theHumans for Rights Network, said the charity had worked with hundreds of children who were already being wrongly filtered into the adult system during age assessments at borders carried out by immigration officers.In May, theHelen Bamber Foundation revealedthat 755 children in 2025 were incorrectly identified as adults on arrival to the UK, according to Home Office figures.Harris said the introduction of AI was a “cheap process” that would not improve these numbers. “This is not about protecting children – this is about shoring up the decisions that [the authorities] are making,” she said.Thegovernment has admittedthat even the best systems can have a 30-month margin of error.Harris said this is particularly risky for children, especially those from countries such as Sudan and Somalia, who she said were already “adultified” by the system.“As soon as a child is treated as an adult, they are susceptible to – or exposed, rather – to any of the egregious consequences that theHome Officeis applying to adults, such as detention and removal,” she said.Unaccompanied children would be forced into accommodation alongside adults, exposing them to risk and to the violence threatened by the rise in protests targeting accommodation for asylum seekers, she said.In May, the government announced a contract to use facial age-estimation technology developed by Cognitec, a German firm that calls itself “the face-recognition company”.That system showed bias against sub-Saharan Africans, tending to overpredict the ages of minors, according to aninvestigation by Lighthouse Reportsin June.TheUK-based tech monitor Foxglovehas said these systems relied on “racist bias” and said the government should not use children to test experimental technology.TheRefugee and Migrant Children’s Consortiumhas raised concerns about the technology’s ability to assess children who have undergone difficult journeys. It noted that trauma can “age” a child’s appearance.Fortress Europe: the millions spent on military-grade tech to deter refugeesRead moreThe Home Office plans to use the technology alongside checks by immigration officers. A spokesperson said: “Age assessments are a vital tool in maintaining border security. As part of our work to make this process more robust and consistent, we are exploring cutting-edge AI technology to verify migrants’ ages.”Petra Molnar, who co-founded the advocacy groupMigration and Tech Monitor, said this was the latest in a series of failed attempts across Europe to implement tech and AI into border policy.She said previous attempts in Europe to implement AI-powered lie-detection systems for screening refugees had proven to be “snake oil” and did not progress beyond pilot schemes.She likened the use of facial age-estimation technology to “the study of skulls and skull shapes” by colonial-era scientists to categorise different ethnic groups, saying that like the discredited 19th-century pseudoscience of phrenology, these systems similarly relied on categorising physical features to determine age.“The context really matters here,” said Molnar. “We know that trauma ages you. We know that malnutrition, dehydration, torture – even just the journey itself – has physical impacts on your face, on your body.“It’s effectively ‘neo-phrenology’ by categorising people based on physical features,” she said. “Relying on these kind of imperfect tools is not the solution.”Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. title: FTSE 100 hits record high despite AI sell-off  | FTSE | The Guardian
description: Strong corporate results buoy market as investors move money away from tech and semiconductor stocks
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Strong corporate results buoy market as investors move money away from tech and semiconductor stocks
Content: The UK’s blue chip index rose as high as 10,951 points on Wednesday morning before falling back slightly.Photograph: James Manning/PAView image in fullscreenThe UK’s blue chip index rose as high as 10,951 points on Wednesday morning before falling back slightly.Photograph: James Manning/PAFTSEFTSE 100 hits record high despite AI sell-offStrong corporate results buoy market as investors move money away from tech and semiconductor stocksJoanna PartridgeWed 29 Jul 2026 11.02 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 04.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLondon’s FTSE 100 stock index has touched a fresh high, driven by strong corporate results as investors moved money away from tech and semiconductor stocksamid the global tech stock sell-off.The UK’s blue chip index rose as high as 10,951 points on Wednesday morning before falling back slightly, its best level since 27 February, the day before theUS and Israel began attacks on Iranand sparked stock market volatility.On a day of fresh losses for the tech-heavy Nasdaq index, theFTSE100 closed up 0.3% at 10,908, marginally below its record closing value of 10,910 in February.The FTSE 100 is heavily weighted towards the finance and energy sectors, meaning it has been largely shielded from the sell-off in tech stocks that has rattled other global markets, particularly in Asia and New York.The Asia-focused bank Standard Chartered and the miner Rio Tinto both announced a rise in shareholder payouts on Wednesday.The FTSE 100’s climb came as shares in companies linked to AI plunged for the second day in a row over concerns about spending on the technology, sending stock markets in South Korea and Japan tumbling.The oil price continued to climb after the US military said it hadknocked down an Iranian missile barrageand worked with Saudi Arabia’s forces to strike sites in Iraq that Tehran-backed militias had recently used to launch attacks.Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose above $90 a barrel by late afternoon in London, a rise of more than 7%.Seoul’s Kospi index is dominated by semiconductor manufacturers, and disappointing results from the chipmaker SK Hynix left it down by as much as 12.6% at one point before it rebounded.The index closed down 6% after falling almost 11% the previous day, reaching its lowest level since early April and marking an almost 40% fall from the peak reached a little over a month ago.Trading was halted for 20 minutes for the second consecutive session after an 8% plunge triggered a market-wide circuit breaker.Japan’s Nikkei also closed 1.5% down on Wednesday, a two-month low.SK Hynix, which produces the chips essential to the expansion of AI datacentres, reported record profits for the second quarter but undershot investors’ expectations.That prompted a sell-off that drove its shares down by as much as 20% before they recovered to 10% down. Shares in its fellow chipmaker Samsung Electronics also tumbled further, closing 5% lower.The two companies together account for more than half of the market capitalisation of the Kospi, which has led to them holding sway over the market this year. The companies have brought in cash from investors looking to become involved in the lucrative AI trade amid aglobal shortage of advanced memory chips.Analysts said disappointment over SK Hynix’s earnings highlighted investors’ concerns about how long tech companies could continue their spending spree on the technology.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“SK Hynix delivered strong results, but in today’s AI market strong is ‌no longer enough,” said Gary Tan, a portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments in Singapore.“Investors were looking for additional catalysts, particularly around long-term agreements and shareholder returns, to support a memory sector that has become the epicentre of the AI trade.”Shares in US chip companies fell on Wall Street on Tuesday. Intel, Advanced Micro Devices, Sandisk, Western Digital Corp and Seagate Technology were all down.Apple benefited from the falls as investors losing confidence in AI stocks sought a safe haven. Its shares briefly roseabove the $5tn (£3.76tn) valuation mark, only the second company ever to do so.Shares in Taiwan’s TSMC, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, fell 3% on Wednesday in Taipei.Analysts said small-time investors had led the charge on buying chipmakers’ stocks, many using borrowed money. While this pushed stocks higher in last month’s rally, it has worsened the sell-off as many have pulled their money out.South Korea’s finance minister, Koo Yun-cheol, told the national assembly the government was reviewing market stabilisation measures.The broker AJ Bell’s investment director, Russ Mould, said the FTSE 100 had been “helped by its lack of exposure to technology and AI stocks, and a slew of strong corporate results, with index heavyweights Standard Chartered, Reckitt Benckiser and Rio Tinto all delivering either better-than-expected profits, or bumper cash returns to shareholders, or both”.Explore more on these topicsFTSEStock marketsAI (artificial intelligence)Technology sectorManufacturing sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Atlassian tightens tracking of staff AI use as other technology firms encourage ‘tokenmaxxing’ | Atlassian | The Guardian
description: Some companies reportedly using leaderboards for employees who used the most AI in their work
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Some companies reportedly using leaderboards for employees who used the most AI in their work
Content: The Atlassian chief executive, Mike Cannon-Brookes. The firm has limited the amount employees can spend on AI in their work but has reportedly never refused a request for more funds.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Atlassian chief executive, Mike Cannon-Brookes. The firm has limited the amount employees can spend on AI in their work but has reportedly never refused a request for more funds.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianBreaking News AustraliaAtlassianAtlassian tightens tracking of staff AI use as other technology firms encourage ‘tokenmaxxing’Some companies reportedly using leaderboards for employees who used the most AI in their workFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorTechnology reporterWed 29 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 17.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSoftware firmAtlassianhas sought to tighten tracking of its staff’s AI spending by introducing “wallets” with monthly caps of up $2,000 for each employee, amid an explosion in costs at other tech companies.The move by Atlassian, whichrecently cited AIas part of the reason behind cutting 1,600 staff, bucks the trend of others in the tech sector who encouraged employees to use as much of the technology as possible, dubbed “tokenmaxxing”. Some companies have reportedly introduced leaderboards for employees who used the most AI in their work.Tokens refer to the measurement of a response AI gives to a prompt. OpenAI has said one token is about four characters, and something like the US Declaration of Independence amounts to 1,695 tokens. OpenAI’s flagship model, GPT-5.6 Sol, has a charge of US$5 for every 1m tokens, while Anthropic’s Claude Fable and Mythos models are US$10 for every 1m tokens.Under tokenmaxxing, the costs quickly add up.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailUberreportedly blew through its AI budgetin four months, and Amazon has reportedly told employees to stop using AI just for the sake of using AI.While Atlassian never encouraged tokenmaxxing or had unlimited AI budgets, the Australian company this month introduced an “AI wallet” for staff in the research and development team.According to an internal memo seen by Guardian Australia, employees have between $500 and $2,000 monthly spend in the wallet, which can be used across four AI products, including Claude Code. Employees receive notifications as they approach their limit on their wallets, and usage is paused when the money runs out.Employees can request additional funds. It is understood Atlassian has not turned down any request for additional funds so far.A company spokesperson said it was transforming into an “AI-first company” by supporting people building and experimenting with the technology.Mega datacentre planned for outer Melbourne will be six times bigger than a large shopping centreRead more“Atlassian provides a significant budget for our builders to leverage multiple AI tools,” the spokesperson said.“AI tooling budgets are set by role based on how different teams work.”They said the wallet also represented a boost in the amount employees could spend.A June PureProfile survey of 500 senior Australia staff at companies using AI, conducted on behalf of search AI company Elastic, found that 80% were concerned that high usage was being mistaken for productivity gains.It found 32% had reported pausing, cancelling or winding back AI deployments, due to cost.Elastic’s ANZ manager, Jeremy Pell, said a monthly cap on AI spend was “smart” and more organisations should be doing it.“Right now, only 9% of Australian organisations currently have any limits on token or API consumption when it comes to AI agents or autonomous workflows, so any organisation that adopts this practice is an outlier,” he said.Arun Chandrasekaran, a distinguished vice-president analyst at research firm Gartner, said wallets were a simple way to “incentivise the right behaviour” and stop people from using AI ineffectively.He said such expenses were becoming an important issue among businesses, with the cost explosion being driven by AI agents that autonomously undertake tasks on behalf of the user.“You suddenly have these systems that are all trying to do independent tasks that are spawning smaller agents, that are creating their own prompts and initiating requests for the model,” he said.“So while the AI model prices have been falling for the last three years, the volume of tokens that particularly the AI agents are starting to send to the models … is significantly increasing.”Chandrasekaran said companies are figuring out how to drive the cost down, including using less powerful models for simpler tasks, and looking at using open weight – where people can download and run the models on their own systems – or open source models.Explore more on these topicsAtlassianBreaking News AustraliaAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIAnthropicnewsShareReuse this content

title: Datacentre projects face fees for grid access to ease connection queue, Ofgem says | Datacentres | The Guardian
description: Energy regulator’s plan would mean upfront fees or financial security via letters of credit, bonds or cash deposits
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Energy regulator’s plan would mean upfront fees or financial security via letters of credit, bonds or cash deposits
Content: Datacentre providers include companies such as Amazon and Microsoft.Photograph: Horst Friedrichs/AlamyView image in fullscreenDatacentre providers include companies such as Amazon and Microsoft.Photograph: Horst Friedrichs/AlamyDatacentresDatacentre projects face fees for grid access to ease connection queue, Ofgem saysEnergy regulator’s plan would mean upfront fees or financial security via letters of credit, bonds or cash depositsDan MilmoWed 29 Jul 2026 03.42 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDatacentre projects in Britain will be forced to pay hundreds of millions of pounds to plug into the power grid under proposals to tackle a growingelectricity connection logjam.Ofgem, the sector watchdog, said it was taking action to discourage “speculative” datacentre projects from causing unnecessary delays to the grid connection queue, which includes hospitals, schools and housing developments.There are 315 datacentres queueing to connect, representing 73GW of demand, according to Ofgem. This has increased by almost 50% in the last year to almost 30GW above the entire country’s peak energy demand of 45GW.The energy regulator for Great Britain said it planned to introduce a new “datacentre commitment fee” that would be equivalent to between 2.5% and 7.5% of the average cost of a project in order to secure a date for grid connection.This would be returned once the datacentre was switched on, or forfeited if the project failed to move forward.What’s holding back Britain’s green revolution? – a visual storyRead moreThis means datacentre providers, which include companies such as Amazon and Microsoft, could be required to put down pledges of £350m to reserve 500MW of grid capacity for their new facilities.Developers would also be required to hit “hard milestones” in advance of their connection date or be removed from the queue to ensure the country’s limited grid capacity went to “projects most likely to be built, not projects preserving options”.The proposals intend to tackle one of the biggest obstacles to building the datacentres at the core of Britain’s AI ambitions: connections to a power source.Datacentres are the central nervous systems of AI tools such as chatbots, but they have increasingly sizeable energy needs as their usage and capability grows. Some projects are exploring private, on-site power generation as a temporary solution to avoid the lengthy wait for a grid connection, but most developers would prefer to draw power from the grid too.The rising number of datacentres seeking a grid connection has followed the UK government’s stated aim to “lead in the age of AI”, and has coincided with a wider boom in demand for electricity to cut the use of fossil fuels.Ofgem has faced a wider backlog of power generation and storage schemes which face years of delays to secure connection to the grid, yet are vital to meet the country’s growing electricity demand.The government-owned National Energy System Operator, which runs the grid, used reforms last yearto clear hundreds of dubious “zombie” projectsfrom the queue to make way for clean electricity schemes with the best chance of achieving the government’s energy targets.Tackling the datacentre queue will be more complicated, however, because there is little consensus within government overhow much data capacity the UK will needin the coming years, despite the drive to createAI growth zonesacross the country to support their development.The energy system operator’s most conservative forecasts for Great Britain’s datacentre capacity by the end of the decade stand at 3.7GW, and their top-end estimates are 6.7GW. The government’s own “compute roadmap” calls for “at least 6GW of AI-capable datacentre capacity by 2030”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeanwhile, experts have said the UK is likely to miss its target of creating a virtually carbon-free electricity system by 2030, raising the risk of greater than expected reliance on gas-fired power plants to fill a potential supply shortfall.Michael Shanks, the energy minister, said: “Britain needs a grid connections system that works for the 21st century and allows businesses to invest and grow, creating jobs across the country.“That’s why this government reformed the connections process and why Ofgem’s actions will help ensure that viable, connection-ready projects can get going and not be held up by speculative applications.”Concerns over datacentre grid connections are not confined to Britain. The Uptime Institute, which inspects and rates datacentres, hasidentified 250 global projectsexceeding 100MW in energy demand – equivalent to the energy needs of about 300,000 homes – announced between 2021 and 2024.Uptime believes half of those projects will either not happen or their completion will be delayed, but that even in that scenario there will still be an “unprecedented and rapid” increase in the power required over the next five years.Ofgem’s proposals will now undergo a consultation process to test their feasibility.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. title: Queensland and NT reject Labor’s push to ensure that power-hungry AI datacentres use renewable energy | Datacentres | The Guardian
description: Federal-state stoush comes as rating agency warns that electricity bills could skyrocket
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Federal-state stoush comes as rating agency warns that electricity bills could skyrocket
Content: Labor says it will forge on with its plans to place energy and water usage rules on datacentres – despite the objections of Queensland and the NT.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLabor says it will forge on with its plans to place energy and water usage rules on datacentres – despite the objections of Queensland and the NT.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesDatacentresQueensland and NT reject Labor’s push to ensure that power-hungry AI datacentres use renewable energyFederal-state stoush comes as rating agency warns that electricity bills could skyrocketFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerTue 28 Jul 2026 23.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 00.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleQueensland and theNorthern Territoryhave rejected the federal government’s plans to mandate that AI datacentres use renewable power, rubbishing Anthony Albanese’s proposals to regulate the booming technology as “underdeveloped ideas that hand increased power to Canberra”.The latest federal-state stoush on energy comes as S&P Global, the economic rating agency, warns that power use from datacentres could rise five-fold by 2035 to 10% of Australia’s total consumption, and that a mismatch between delivery timelines for datacentres and renewable projects could lead to energy bills skyrocketing.But the federal Labor government says it will forge on with its plans to place energy and water usage rules on datacentres, and to develop “nationally consistent” regulations about AI – even if some states don’t agree.The federal government is examining whether it can set price protections to shield Australians from any energy bill spikes related to the datacentre boom.A meeting of state and federal energy ministers on Tuesday discussed the Albanese government’s expectations for datacentre development after the prime ministerpledged to legislatebinding standards for AI companies, including on locations and energy use.Datacentres would be required to generate renewable energy, minimise water use and maximise energy efficiency. Albanese said there would be a “legal obligation” for new datacentres to underwrite new power supply, pay for their grid connection costs and “put at least as much energy into our grid as they take out of it”.Anthony Albanese says he wants to do AI ‘the Australian way’ – videoThe Liberal-National government inQueenslandraised concerns about a renewables mandate at an energy ministers’ meeting in May, the only holdout as all the other states agreed that datacentres should fully offset their energy demands with renewables, and transparently report their energy use and emissions.On Tuesday the Liberal government in the NT joined Queensland in rejecting further proposals and agreements about datacentres.All states – “with QLD and NT opposing”, according to a communique – backed the commonwealth’s plan for nationally consistent rules on datacentres, including underwriting new renewables and offsetting their power use, plus mandating that consumers face no price impacts.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“Queensland will always support proposals that deliver affordable, reliable and sustainable power, however, we will not support underdeveloped ideas that hand increased power to Canberra at the expense of Queenslanders,” said the state treasurer and energy minister, David Janetzki.“We will continue to deliver affordable, reliable, and sustainable energy to deliver cost of living relief Queenslanders can rely on, while consulting with the community to support investment, jobs and economic growth.”The NT minister, Gerard Maley, was contacted for comment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMega datacentre planned for outer Melbourne will be six times bigger than a large shopping centreRead moreFederal government sources said Queensland and the NT’s opposition to the plan would not stymie Albanese’s roadmap, and insisted work to deliver nationally consistent rules would continue. The federal energy minister, Chris Bowen, will address the National Press Club next week, when he is expected to reveal more about the Albanese government’s plans before a national cabinet meeting in August and another energy ministers’ summit in September.Federal powers relating to the AustralianEnergyMarket Operator and Australian Energy Market Commission and surrounding connections of large facilities to power grids could be invoked to mandate that new datacentres use renewables.This week’s Guardian Essential pollfound Australians were reluctant to embrace new AI datacentres, with less than a third saying they would be happy to have a facility in their area; 61% of people raised concerns about impact on energy demand and power prices, 44% were worried about water supply and 41% worried about environmental impacts and noise.S&P, in a report released this week, noted Aemo’s estimates that datacentre energy use could rise to 20 terawatt hours, or about 10% of Australia’s total consumption, by 2034-35. It also cited Sydney Water’s estimates that datacentres could use 15% to 20% of the city’s water by 2035.The rating agency warned of an “infrastructure and temporal mismatch” which could lead to consumer prices rising.“A big gap exists between data center delivery (18-24 months) and the delivery of transmission or renewable projects (three to five years),” it said. “Delays in transmission projects, such as those seen with Project Energy Connect in New South Wales (NSW) and Western Renewables Link in Victoria, could tighten supply and increase costs.“If renewable and storage infrastructure fails to keep pace, the government’s Clean Energy Finance Corp. estimates wholesale prices could rise by 25% across states, with emissions rising by 14%.”Explore more on these topicsDatacentresAustralian politicsAnthony AlbaneseEnergy (Australia news)Renewable energyEnergy (Environment)QueenslandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Can’t hear what’s playing on TV? It’s not your ears, it’s the flat screen. These affordable soundbars can help | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Get rid of subtitles to hear what movies and TV shows are supposed to sound like – for as little as $130
Author: Ryan Waniata
Headline: Get rid of subtitles to hear what movies and TV shows are supposed to sound like – for as little as $130
Content: Photograph: Courtesy of BoseView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Courtesy of BoseThe Filter USLife and styleCan’t hear what’s playing on TV? It’s not your ears, it’s the flat screen. These affordable soundbars can helpGet rid of subtitles to hear what movies and TV shows are supposed to sound like – for as little as $130I tested 42 pairs of wireless earbuds to find the best in the US, and I never want to listen to Fast Car againSign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better thingsRyan WaniataWed 29 Jul 2026 10.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Your TV sounds awful. That’s not an indictment of your shopping skills, your budget or even the TV’s manufacturer. It’s just basic physics.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The tiny speakers crammed in modern flat-screen TVs simply can’t reproduce the physical sound waves as well as the larger speakers in older TVs. And you don’t need to crave window-rattling action sequences to notice the problem. It also shows up in television shows, making dialog difficult to hear.You don’t need captions; you need better speakers. And for most people, the easiest, fastest, most affordable option is a simple soundbar.Why your TV alone can’t reproduce good soundWhile every other TV feature has gotten better over the last two decades, from streaming apps to wildly improved picture quality, sound quality has regressed. As a pro who has reviewed dozens of TVs and speakers over the past decade, it’s impossible to miss. Frustratingly, the svelter and more premium your TV, the worse it likely sounds. That’s because those razor-thin TVs contain speakers barely bigger than what you’d find in singing greeting cards.Luckily, you don’t have to spend three grand on a sprawling eight-channel home theater to vastly improve your TV sound. Setting aside just over $100 for a standalone soundbar can get you there.Not just any soundbar. After over a decade reviewing them, I’m the first to admit there are plenty of duds that create more problems than they solve. But if you know where to look, you can get a lot for your money, leading to more immersive viewing, deeper engagement and much clearer dialogue, so you can drop those pesky subtitles.These are my favorite soundbars at multiple price points to help you turn your TV’s sound from a problem to a pleasure.The entry level:Vizio AIO (All In One) SoundbarVizioAIO (All In One) Soundbarfrom$128$128 at Walmart$129 at Sam’s ClubView image in fullscreenPhotograph: The Guardian$128 at Walmart$129 at Sam’s ClubVizio soundbars have a reputation for outperforming their modest price points, and the Vizio AIO is the latest embodiment. It captures the company’s typical sound-first design in a stylish minimalist package. At just 34in across and under 3in high, the AIO fits well even in small living rooms and bedrooms. Its fabric-wrapped tubular frame virtually disappears on your console.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Ryan Waniata/The GuardianYou won’t get many extras here, not even a dedicated remote, but you shouldn’t need one: modern TVs let you control volume and power through the TV remote, as long as you connect it through anHDMI ARC or eARCport. Vizio’s app unlocks the rest, including settings such as EQ, sound modes and basic playback control. There’s no wifi, but Bluetooth lets you stream music from your phone or other devices.It’s the performance that really sets this bar apart, offering surprisingly bombastic bass for its size, full-bodied higher frequencies for instruments such as strings and horns, and clear dialogue. While it’s not the most dynamic bar for music, you’ll enjoy solid detail and balance across registers. At this price, it’s hard to do better for a plug-and-play model.VizioAIO (All In One) Soundbarfrom$128$128 at Walmart$129 at Sam’s ClubThe step up:Sony Theater Bar 5SonyTheater Bar 5from$348$348 at Amazon$349.99 at Best BuyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Ryan Waniata/The Guardian$348 at Amazon$349.99 at Best BuyAnother system that puts performance above extras, Sony’s Theater Bar 5 is a ringer for its size. Its simple bar-and-subwoofer setup makes it great for small to moderate-sized rooms. Sony stripped out features such as wifi, an equalizer, or even much of a visual display to focus on sound quality. It pays off, providing a pleasing mix of musicality and power for your money. There’s even a dedicated center speaker to keep dialogue out front, something many soundbars at this price lack.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Ryan Waniata/The GuardianIf you’re tight on space, you may initially balk at the subwoofer, which takes up a few feet of floor space. But subwoofers aren’t just for explosions or kick drums. They’re key to truly impactful performance for everything from action films to dramas and music. Most importantly, the Bar 5 does a great job blending its low-end punch with its crisp sound above for a seamlessly smooth delivery.You’ll also get Bluetooth streaming and some virtual surround sound tricks, including support for 3D audio formats such as Dolby Atmos and DTS:X. The effect is limited without dedicated surround or up-firing speakers to provide the spherical immersion for which these formats strive, but Sony’s acoustic wizardry expands the soundstage beyond the bar’s physical footprint.SonyTheater Bar 5from$348$348 at Amazon$349.99 at Best BuyThe ultimate micro soundbar:Bose Smart SoundbarBoseSmart Soundbarfrom$549$549 at Bose$549 at AmazonView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Ryan Waniata/The Guardian$549 at Bose$549 at AmazonFor a smaller system loaded with features, Bose’s taut Smart Soundbar is the best mini-bar I’ve tested. At just 27in across and 2.2in tall, the Smart Soundbar feels more like a Bluetooth speaker than a capable audio system, but its looks are deceiving. Five integrated speakers combine for clean, tactful and surprisingly musical performance, shining through in everything you play.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Ryan Waniata/The GuardianUnlikeSonos’ rival Beam, the Smart Soundbar even includes up-firing drivers for immersive sound that draws you in, especially with Dolby Atmos video. Like the other bars on our list, Bose’s system connects over HDMI ARC/eARC for simplified control with your TV remote, but you’ll also get a dedicated remote and a great app for multiple ways to play.That’s just the tip of the bar’s perks, which includes wifi connectivity for high-quality streaming from apps such as Spotify and Apple Music, an equalizer, sound modes, and the ability to connect with other Bose speakers. You can even connectBose’s fancy Ultra Open earbudsas wearable surround sound speakers. The bar’s biggest drawback is its limited bass response. You can add aBose subwooferlater (albeit at a high cost), but even without it, the Smart Soundbar serves up best-in-class performance.BoseSmart Soundbarfrom$549$549 at Bose$549 at AmazonFor even bigger soundHere are a few of my other favorites in other styles and price points.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Courtesy of AmazonKlipsch Flexus Core 200$430.12 at Amazon$474.99 at WalmartThis powerful standalone soundbar can be expanded with additional components as your needs change, but skips features such as wifi to keep the price low.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Filter USA guide to buying fewer, better products.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Courtesy of AmazonSonos Arc Ultra$1,099 at Walmart$1,099.99 at AmazonThe ultimate one-piece soundbar can also be expanded with other Sonos gear for a multi-room sound or surround sound, offering the best of all worlds.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Courtesy of AmazonSamsung HW-Q990D$897.99 at Walmart$897.99 at AmazonYou’ll need to make room for its wireless subwoofer and surround speakers, but this older iteration of Samsung’s multi-piece soundbar system offers incredibly thrilling surround sound from a single box at half the price of the current model.View image in fullscreenOther pieces you might enjoy fromthe Filter, the Guardian’s guide to buying fewer, better things:Open earbuds let you tune in without tuning out the world. title: After 40 years, Aliens is still shaping the way video games are made | Games | The Guardian
description: James Cameron’s high-octane film sequel is a blueprint for modern action space slashers
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: James Cameron’s high-octane film sequel is a blueprint for modern action space slashers
Content: Take off and nuke the entire site from orbit … Ripley gets out the big guns in Aliens.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyView image in fullscreenTake off and nuke the entire site from orbit … Ripley gets out the big guns in Aliens.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyPushing Buttons newsletterGamesAfter 40 years, Aliens is still shaping the way video games are madeJames Cameron’s high-octane film sequel is a blueprint for modern action space slashersDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeith StuartWed 29 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 13.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is difficult to believe that James Cameron’s Aliens was released into cinemas 40 years ago. The seminal space shooter took the original Alien – a tense slasher film with a tiny cast and one monster – and transformed it into an intergalactic war movie crammed with wry one-liners, massive guns and an actual boss battle finale. As a 14-year-old, I stood in line at the Tatton Gatley cinema, unsure if I’d be allowed in – I came out three hours later a changed person, my head filled with esoteric military slang and a deep fear of beeping motion detectors. For days afterwards, I slept with my duvet covering my mouth so that no facehuggers could get me. (I was a highly impressionable teenager.)It’s little wonder that the film has had such a profound effect on video game design. Take the colonial marines, for example. Although the concept of the space soldier had been around in sci-fi novels since the 1930s, most notably in the works of EE “Doc” Smith and Robert Heinlein (the Starship Troopers), Hicks, Hudson, Vasquez and co, were the perfect 80s rendition, combining the witty banter of contemporary buddy cop flicks with awesome weaponry and hi-tech gadgets. Their influence is easy to spotin Doom, where the nameless marine fights ceaseless waves of hellish monsters using a mix of futuristic rifles and good old shotguns. It’s there too in theHalo series, the Spartan soldiers sporting the same armour and mega weapons, cruising about in very similar highly militarised starships and fighting recognisable hive-mind space beasts. Gears of War,KillzoneandMarathonall borrow from the same set of costumes and deadly accessories.Also important to future game designers was the way in which James Cameron opened up the world of Alien after Ridley Scott’s original locked-room mystery of a movie. He beefed up the Weyland-Yutani Corporation, giving us the stencil for dozens of evil video game mega corps; he brought in an array of weapons from handguns to M41A pulse rifles and the M56 smart guns, introducing the idea of a scaled armoury to discover and master; and he employed a structure based around the repeated rhythm of tense exploration followed by explosive encounters that countless games would follow.View image in fullscreenAlien: Isolation … in your living room, everyone can hear you scream.Photograph: SegaIt’s weird, then, how difficult it has proven to directly translate the movie into games. While the original Alien spawneda cult 8bit translationand thebrilliant Alien: Isolation, Cameron’s sequel is best known for the disastrously buggedAliens: Colonial Marines, which led to alawsuit for deceptive marketing. Elsewhere, third-person co-op blaster Aliens: Fireteam Elite drew mixed reviews but has at least birthed a forthcoming sequel, and the 2D Metroid-style game Aliens: Infestation has plenty of fans. My favourite, though, was one of the two official tie-ins from 1986. Aliens: the Computer Game from Electric Dreams Software was a thrilling proto-FPS, allowing you to control several of the movie’s characters as they stalked through an atmosphere processing plant getting attacked by xenomorphs and facehuggers. I’m not sure it’s ever been bettered.Watching the movie again this week, it’s impossible not to notice all the little scenic and narrative touches that have since shaped how sci-fi action games function. Even the sentry gun, which was cut from the cinematic release and only turned up in the special edition home release, has become a staple special weapon, present in everything fromCall of DutytoHelldivers. I wonder how many of today’s game creators were also stood in cinema lines in the summer of 1986, too young to be there, not quite ready to have their minds blown for ever?What to playView image in fullscreenDanger at every turn … Scarlet Deer Inn.Photograph: Attu GamesThose of us with an interest in the fibre arts are always delighted to see them crop up in other media. Here, embroidered character art helpsScarlet Deer Innto stand out in a crowded market. Once players are in, they’ll find the charming medieval village has some horrific secrets. Players guide mother-of-two Elise through danger-filled caverns on a quest to find her children and prevent them from meeting a gruesome end, a goal that gained additional meaning when the husband-and-wife developers had a baby of their own. Armed only with a torch, you must keep it lit or likely repeatedly succumb to the darkness.Jordan Erica WebberAvailable on:PCEstimated playtime:four hoursWhat to readView image in fullscreenRipe for the AI slop machine … Grand Theft Auto VI.Photograph: NintendoIn what is likely to become a familiar problem for the games industry, Rockstar’sGrand Theft Auto VImarketing schedule is being infiltrated by AI-generated trailers purporting to show scenes from the forthcoming game. Examples include asurfing videoand awoman enjoying champagne on a yacht. AsEurogamer points out, the videos are filling a vacuum left by Rockstar’s somewhat stingy approach to releasing in-game footage. The company does notseem to be impressed.Rather embarrassingly for console manufacturers seeking to go digital only,network outagesare back. On Friday,PlayStation Network went downfor several hours, leaving players with no access to their games. And on Monday, it wasthe turn of Xbox, a major outage making it impossible to sign in to user accounts, launch games or download content. While the PlayStation situation has now been resolved, the Xbox network was still having issues at time of press. All hail our disc-less future!When Valve announced its new Steam Machine PC, fans were intrigued by a custom front plate the company had attached to the machine, which appeared to bean e-ink screendisplaying performance data from inside the computer, such as memory and CPU performance. Now, Valve has released all the files and details for what it callsThe Inkterface, so owners can build one – and gaming site Aftermathhas done just that. Very nerdy, but very cool.And if you enjoyed reminiscing aboutAliens,you might want to check out forthcoming bookAliens: The Video Gamesby Mike Diver, a complete history of adaptations, including lots of developer interviews.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to clickSilent Hill Townfall: the series is coming to Scotland, but what fresh horrors will it bring?Glitched into empty space: why video games are obsessed with the BackroomsHaex – a wilder, weirder open-world adventure‘An anthem for the co-dependent’: Bad Magpie’s corvid carnage with a side of existential angstThere Are No Ghosts at the Grand – stripping back the physical and metaphorical layers of a haunted hotelThe best gaming chairs in the UK for comfort, support and serious play in 2026 – testedThe Mermaid Mask – the funniest underwater murder mystery you can play | ★★★★☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenThe gaming canon … a lot of top 100 lists.Photograph: Justin Towell/AlamyThis week’s question is fromBenvia email:“I want to learn more about the history of video games and I wondered if there are any canonical lists of the best titles– perhaps a gaming equivalent of the BFI’s250 Greatest Films of All Timeor the American Film Institute’s100 Years 100 Movies?”Many publications that write about video games have their own top 100 list, although these tends to be compiled by their own critics or readers rather than a broader spread of experts.GQ,GameRantandRolling Stoneall have versions, while IGN has a “mathematically derived” list of thetop 500, andwe’vedonethe best games of the 21st century(so far). For more formal attempts at developing a canon, the Strong Museum has aWorld Video Game Hall of Fame, MoMA hasa games collection(but for some reason its website does NOT want you to find a definitive list!), and for itsArt of Gamesexhibition in 2012, the Smithsonian compiled alist of 80 important titleswith the help of gamers and game makers. There have also been a few books on the subject: try Penguin’s 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die (full disclosure: I wrote some of this book), BFI’s 100 Video Games, or Game On!: From Pong to Oblivion – The Greatest Video Games of All Time, compiled by ex-Edge magazine writers.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterJames CameronAlienRidley ScottfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Silent Hill Townfall: the series is coming to Scotland, but what fresh horrors will it bring? | Games | The Guardian
description: An amnesiac loner arrives in a remote town for who knows what reason … this may sound familiar but this time we’re on a remote Scottish island and surprises lie in wait
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: An amnesiac loner arrives in a remote town for who knows what reason … this may sound familiar but this time we’re on a remote Scottish island and surprises lie in wait
Content: Foggy notions … Silent Hill: TownfallPhotograph: Konami, Annapurna Interactive, Screen Burn/PRView image in fullscreenFoggy notions … Silent Hill: TownfallPhotograph: Konami, Annapurna Interactive, Screen Burn/PRGamesSilent Hill Townfall: the series is coming to Scotland, but what fresh horrors will it bring?An amnesiac loner arrives in a remote town for who knows what reason … this may sound familiar but this time we’re on a remote Scottish island and surprises lie in waitKeith StuartWed 29 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAman washes up at the harbour of a small coastal village, his memories vague, an eerie sea fog rolling in all around him. As beginnings go, this couldn’t be more Silent Hill – an amnesiac loner drawn to a remote town for who knows what reason. But this time, we’re not in the Pacific Northwest of the original games or the Japan of last year’s excellentSilent Hill f. We’re on an island off the northern coast of Scotland, and it’s 1996. Lead character Simon Ordell knows this place, but isn’t sure how – and why does he have an IV cannula stuck in his hand?Announced back in 2022, Townfall is the work of Glasgow-based studio Screen Burn, previously responsible for tense horror adventure titles Stories Untold and Observation. LikeSilent Hillf, it moves the setting far out of Silent Hill itself: St Amelia is a fishing town, inspired by St Monans and dozens of other seafront towns the team visited and extensively photographed.Why make that geographical change? “We felt that players were starting to become a little fatigued,” says series producer Motoi Okamoto. “Silent Hill was becoming slightly repetitive, we were using similar locations, the gameplay felt the same. We wanted to refresh the series and create a new sort of experience by interpreting Silent Hill not as a physical location but as a phenomenon, a state of mind.”View image in fullscreenNo place for a holiday … Silent Hill: Townfall.Photograph: Konami, Annapurna Interactive, Screen BurnDuring a preview event at Konami in Tokyo, we played an almost finished version of the game for two hours, and it’s clear this is very much a Silent Hill experience, but with a deliciously gloomy British slant. The visual detail is incredible. As Simon, you walk along the harbourside with its stacks of lobster cages, and reach the town itself, a muddle of tiny houses, the grey stone walls worn by sea spray, little shops selling seaside tat, an old British Telecom phone box in the town square. It’s familiar but also uncanny because as soon as you arrive, you realise everything has been abandoned. Estate agent signs line every street, the homes are dark, streetlights flicker ominously. There’s a suggestion of local anger at a corporation named CEG – street protests have taken place. A note at the police station says there’s nothing they can do until help arrives.For the opening hour you’re free to explore, letting yourself into any home with an unlocked door, and finding old PCs, horrible bathroom suites and Formica-clad kitchens, and the ordinariness makes it even creepier. As you go, strange little details emerge – Simon was staying in the local hotel, but his room is filled with medical equipment. People have been getting ill, some have disappeared. A male voice on the telephone thanks you for coming back and begs you for help. A little later, you discover a video recording of a woman named Zoe telling Simon, “You can’t stay in this room for ever, you have to come back to me.” It’s got that slow burn feel of the best Silent Hill titles – clues are dredged out of the world in little snippets.View image in fullscreenAnalogue intrigue … Silent Hill: Townfall.Photograph: Konami, Annapurna Interactive, Screen Burn/PR IMAGEFrom the start, it’s clear both the period and the setting have been intricately built into the gameplay. For one early puzzle you have to use a PC in Zoe’s house to check her emails, but to do that, you must restore her electricity by fetching a pre-paid card from the local newsagent and putting it in the meter. It’s something a lot of UK gamers will recognise, especially if they were around in the 90s – although apparently, it’s confused American and Japanese journalists. Elsewhere, the portable radio from previous titles, which was used to sense incoming enemies, is now a small handheld television, expertly styled to look like one of those Casio mini TVs. In certain places you can tune it in to see hazy, static-filled images or video clips that act as puzzle clues; but when monsters are near, it can track their movements through walls.This interest in ageing tech is a familiar element of Screen Burn’s previous titles. “The tactility is the main reason behind it,” says Jon McKellan, director and writer of Townfall. “It’s kind of become our calling card and before Screen Burn I worked onAlien: Isolationand there was a lot of that VHS analogue aesthetic. I like marrying those visual concepts with narrative and UI design. Analogue tech is fragile, it’s imperfect, it feels like it could break at any minute – and all those things work really well with horror. You worry that the gadgets in front of you might not be able to save you from whatever’s out there. I think if Simon was walking around with a mobile phone and Google Maps it would be a very different experience.”As your search of the town takes you from houses and shops to the local medical centre, the evidence of some sort of massive cover-up mounts. And naturally, the monsters arrive – strange, tortured humans with axe heads for faces, their arms bound by leather straps. At first you have nothing but planks to defend yourself with and combat is demanding: you can block or strike, but the creatures are fast, deadly and difficult to take down. There’s no parry or dodge so if you commit, you need very good timing. The alternative is stealth – the CRTV shows you where enemies are, while a peeking system lets you look out from cover to study their patrol patterns, and the first-person perspective means you rely on these elements much more heavily.Our time with the game also took in a slightly later section set in a hellish, phantasmagorical underworld of sewers, wire cages and scary red lighting. It could be beneath the town or lodged in Simon’s brain, but it’s classic Silent Hill territory. This time, however, along with the psychological horror, there are also political undertones – the CEG corporation has exploited and destroyed the village, bringing to mind the plight of towns such as Grangemouth and Mossmoran at the hands of petrochemical giants. Simon’s personal story is set to feed into that.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenWill you take the high road? Silent Hill: TownfallPhotograph: Konami, Annapurna Interactive, Screen Burn/PR IMAGE“We wanted to look at the relationship between the character and the society around them,” says McKellan. “What does it mean for someone to be in a town like this and have an impact on it – what do you do with that? I’m hoping that by the end of the game, people are relating to the decisions, and some of the things Simon has been through. You begin to unravel and process that, and projecting your fears, your inner turmoil on to the world around you is obviously a major Silent Hill component.”There are questions that will need to be answered before acknowledging Townfall as another successful step in the rejuvenation of the series after Silent Hill f. Right now, the enemy figures we’ve seen are very familiar versions of Silent Hill archetypes and it’s difficult to judge how intuitive the new stealth/peek system will become. But the setting is beautifully realised, while the shadowing of the Silent Hill 2 narrative – a man searching for a woman he seems to have had a relationship with – is intriguing, and from what we’ve seen, highly likely to be subverted in some horrible way. This is promisingly bleak stuff.“There is a lot of personal trauma in there – things that have happened to me or members of the team,” says McKellan. “We try to pull reference from real life because usually that’s less bombastic and more grounded than Hollywood, and to me that’s where the best horror comes from. I’m just channelling all that trauma instead of getting a therapist!”Silent Hill: Townfall will be released on 24 SeptemberKeith Stuart attended a press event in Tokyo with other journalists.
