title: The Guardian view on selling off the World Cup: a red-card offence by Gianni Infantino | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Fifa’s president hopes to sell stakes in the planet’s most watched sporting event. In the wider interests of football, he must be resisted
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Fifa’s president hopes to sell stakes in the planet’s most watched sporting event. In the wider interests of football, he must be resisted
Content: Gianni Infantino and Donald Trump with the World Cup trophy after the final match between Spain and Argentina.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino and Donald Trump with the World Cup trophy after the final match between Spain and Argentina.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoOpinionGianni InfantinoThe Guardian view on selling off the World Cup: a red-card offence by Gianni InfantinoEditorialFifa’s president hopes to sell stakes in the planet’s most watched sporting event. In the wider interests of football, he must be resistedWed 29 Jul 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 14.30 EDTShareLike a sporting Dr Pangloss, Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, would like to persuade football followers that they are living in the best of all possible worlds. Maddeningly for him, many disagree. On Monday, Mr Infantinopublisheda 15-page Instagram rant in which he bemoaned the “hate and false rumours” in circulation during the recent men’s World Cup. White Houseinterferenceover a crucial refereeing decision, prohibitive ticketprices, unnecessary but lucrativehydration breaks; it was all, as his best friend in politics, Donald Trump, would say, “fake news”.But where the president of world football’s governing body sees haters, others see lovers of the game rightly concerned over where he is taking it. On Tuesday, Fifaconfirmedthat it hopes to sell stakes in the World Cup and other tournaments to private investors who may include Joshua Kushner, the brother of Mr Trump’s son-in-law Jared. The investors would buy into a new$20bn company, Fifa Forward Enterprise, which would sell all of Fifa’s commercial rights, including ticketing, and take charge of “operational delivery” of World Cups.View image in fullscreenJoshua Kushner.Photograph: Edward Berthelot/Getty ImagesMembers of the extended Trump family do not generally contemplate business ventures out of a desire to spread “joy and happiness” in the world (which the egregious Mr Infantino presents as hismission). If the plans go ahead – sweetened by offers of a $30m windfall for national associations – investors’ desires to maximise revenues would undoubtedly accelerate the hyper-monetisation of the World Cup that is already taking place.Almost certainly there would be pressure for more frequent and bigger tournaments at both club and national level, distorting the international game’s calendar to the detriment of domestic leagues. Mr Infantino has already indicated that he would look favourably on such an expansion, despiteobjectionsfrom bodies such as Uefa, European football’s governing body. Innovations such as the widely loathed hydration breaks – which by breaking games up into four quarters, US-style, allowed extra advertising slots – would no doubt proliferate.The prospect revives fears generated by the failed European Super Leagueproposals, which were furiously opposed by football supporters in 2021. During this summer’s World Cup in the US, Mr Kushner and others will haveseenat first-hand the vast commercial possibilities of an event that unites a global audience in an age of fragmented media. As the highest-level steward of the game, Fifa’s primary job is to protect football from forces that might be interested in exploiting its appeal by selling its soul; instead, under Mr Infantino, it appears happy to do their job for them.Angry opposition to the plans from Uefa and Concacaf (the equivalent body for North and Central America) suggests that the governance of the game may be at a crossroads. Mr Infantino’s tireless self-promotion, and shameless efforts to curryfavourwith the Trump administration, have long grated. But placing the planet’s most-watched sporting competition at risk from predation by private capital is of a somewhat different order of magnitude.The visionary creator of the World Cup, Jules Rimet,hopedthat it would help foster unity and solidarity between nations. Mr Infantino routinely pays lip service to such ideals, and did so again in his Instagram screed. In reality, though, he is dragging the world’s favourite sport further and further away from its roots, as he relentlessly follows the money wherever it leads.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Trump has singled out us Canadians for special treatment in his tariff war – there is no choice but to get nasty | Matt Gurney | The Guardian
description: The White House fails to understand that Mark Carney and Canada’s regional leaders can’t cave in to the US president: it’s too toxic to voters, says Toronto-based journalist Matt Gurney
Author: Matt Gurney
Headline: The White House fails to understand that Mark Carney and Canada’s regional leaders can’t cave in to the US president: it’s too toxic to voters, says Toronto-based journalist Matt Gurney
Content: Donald Trump and Mark Carney at a working lunch with G7 and Middle East leaders in Évian-les-Bains, France, 16 June 2026.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Pool Reuters/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Mark Carney at a working lunch with G7 and Middle East leaders in Évian-les-Bains, France, 16 June 2026.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Pool Reuters/APOpinionCanadaTrump has singled out us Canadians for special treatment in his tariff war – there is no choice but to get nastyMatt GurneyThe White House fails to understand that Mark Carney and Canada’s regional leaders can’t cave in to the US president: it’s too toxic to votersMatt Gurney is a journalist based in TorontoWed 29 Jul 2026 07.01 EDTShareThough many hate to admit it, Canadians have long wished for more attention from the US. Well, we’re getting it now. And it turns out that President Trump and some of his top supporters in the Maga movement don’t much like us.The first big hint was when he startedtalking about annexing us, saying we couldn’t survive without American support. But the most recent example of Trump’s dislike for Canada can be seen in his latest tariff policies. Canada was largely spared the impact of his“Liberation Day” tariffsin April 2025 by its pre-existing free trade deal with the US (and Mexico), but earlier this month, as expected, the USdeclined to extendthat deal for another 16-year term. It’s now subject to annual renegotiations. Then, last week, the White House announcedtariffs as high as 50%on a selection of Canadian products including, for the first time, items previously protected by the trade agreement. The US called it retaliation for Canadian trade practices.It’s true that the US announced tariffs against dozens more countries just days later, but there has been something odd about the lopsided attention paid to Canada, which most US presidents tend to politely ignore. Most of the tariffsTrump recently announcedwere in the range of about 10%, but Canada was hit by 50% tariffs (albeit on a narrower range of exports). The president, it seems, wanted to send a message to Canada, but without hurting US consumers too much.The tariffs also land differently here, given Trump’s stateddesire to annexCanada as a 51st state. The president has ruled out using military force to accomplish that, saying instead thathe would use “economic force”. Tariffs would meet that definition.There may have been little sign that the talk of annexation is anything more than typical Trumpian bluster, but even the suggestion, along with the tariffs, has been a shock for a Canadian political class that has long taken a friendly America as a law of nature – and has letCanadagrow shockingly dependent on the US for defence and trade. An unfriendly, potentially even hostile US is a staggeringly consequential change. It’s hard to overestimate how huge a shock this has been.And it’s having a massive effect on our domestic politics, thus far to the benefit of the Liberal party and the prime minister, Mark Carney. The return of Trump to the White Houseupset an election last yearthat the Liberals had been set to lose decisively. Canada’s Conservatives were cruising to an easy win with a campaign focused on public safety and the cost of living, but once Trump began musing about annexation, the Liberals dumped Justin Trudeau, replaced him with Carney, wrapped themselves in the flag, and won decisively. Carney remains popular, largely because Canadians see him as the right choice to deal with Trump.US pressure is complicating Canada’s increasingly fraught internal politics in other ways. Canada does not have a true national economy, but a series of regional ones. Ontario and Quebec, the most populous provinces, are heavily dependent on manufacturing. In western Canada, particularly the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, the economies depend more on exporting natural resources, including oil. Most of this goes to the US, as Canada lacks the transportation infrastructure to readily export it elsewhere (there’s that dependency).The response has therefore been more fragmented than unified. Ontario has pursued astrategy of confrontation; the western provinces havepreferred to appealto shared interestswith the US. These are obvious fissures that the US could choose to exploit. It was strange to see, when the most recent round of tariffs was announced, that most of the economic damage landed on Ontario and Quebec and the province of British Columbia – three jurisdictions that have taken stronger anti-Trump positions. The economies of Alberta and Saskatchewan were relatively spared.Trump’s administration was probably hoping to mete out some punishment to provincial leaders it finds irritating. But it would have given Canada a much more challenging problem had it targeted instead the western provinces, where scepticism of rule by “eastern elites” and separatist movements are intensely divisive issues (Albertans will vote in areferendum this fallon whether to pursue independence). Carney must consider domestic blowback from any possible retaliation, such as an export tax on oil, lest he further inflame existing regional tensions.Trump’s new tariffs aren’t due to take effect for several weeks, and Canada has not yet given any signal of how it will respond. To date, though, it has generally retaliated against US levies – Carney, whose political success rests on public belief that he will stand up to Trump, would find it very difficult not to retaliate this time.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis, more than anything else, is what the White House has failed to understand about Canada. The US has some legitimate gripes with us, including trade barriers and Canada’s chronic underinvestment in defence. It’s reasonable to be angry about those things. But the nature of Trump’s actions has made resistance the only plausible Canadian response: caving in to the US president is toxic for Canadian voters. Some provincial resistance is likely due to unpopular regional leaders seeing salvation in battling Trump – and although Carney has made some concessions since becoming prime minister, includingscrapping a planned digital taxthat angered US tech companies, he dare only go so far.Trump has often complained that dealing with Canadians is unpleasant and nasty. He should expect us to get nastier still. Whether he knows it or not, he’s left us little choice.Matt Gurney is a journalist based in Toronto, and co-editor of The Line, an online magazineExplore more on these topicsCanadaOpinionMark CarneyTariffsDonald TrumpRepublicansAmericasTrump administrationcommentShareReuse this content

title: What should replace the American-led world order? | Aslı Bâli and Samuel Moyn | The Guardian
description: The task now is to stop mourning the old order and build the foundations of the new multipolar world
Author: Samuel Moyn
Headline: The task now is to stop mourning the old order and build the foundations of the new multipolar world
Content: ‘The current moment calls for an anti-war agenda suited to an inevitably plural and rivalrous world.’Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The current moment calls for an anti-war agenda suited to an inevitably plural and rivalrous world.’Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersOpinionUS foreign policyWhat should replace the American-led world order?Aslı Bâli andSamuel MoynThe task now is to stop mourning the old order and build the foundations of the new multipolar worldWed 29 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 10.21 EDTShareAmerica is in decline. And so is Pax America: the American-led world order. While there are many genuine dangers of American decline, there has never been a better chance to say clearly how much the unipolar order always left to be desired, and to imagine a multipolar world that might secure peace better than the old order ever did.Idealizing the American peace since 1945 and its “rules-based international order” – a phrase that came into common use only decades later, but never mind – is a misguided response to our current situation.The dominant response has been a futile effort to get the good old days back: liberal commentators mourn the fact that Atlanticism is under threat, and issue sentimental defenses of lost multilateralism, and, often enough, a hankering for morally uplifting wars to wage.When charged with idealizing the past, these nostalgists retreat to a defense of useful illusions: yes, the old order lied, but at least it lied in the name of ideals.The speech by the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, at Davos in 2026 was greeted in some quarters as daringly honest for saying aloud that, at least for great powers, the old talk of ideals and rules had always rested on a pleasant myth. But that was hardly news.America is destroying itself. It’s no surprise | Stephen MarcheRead moreAnd Carney was wrong to suggest that the lie had once made the world better. Few outside the Atlantic core ever mistook Pax Americana for the best of all possible worlds. Carney soon exposed the limits of his own candor when, only weeks later, he publicly supported Trump’s war of choice against Iran.The old order of high-minded hypocrisy was never good enough for the global south; it was not simply ruined by a president offering too raw a deal.More important, the conventional responses to our moment are not only unconvincing and undesirable; they are also unavailable. That is a good thing.Instead of trying to revive a flawed and morally bankrupt former world order, the current moment calls for an antiwar agenda suited to an inevitably plural and rivalrous world.An antiwar agenda for this world should begin with four commitments.First, states should reaffirm and strengthen limits on the right of self-defense they can claim under article 51 of the UN Charter.Second, states should recommit to the inadmissibility of annexation or territorial acquisition by force (including de facto annexation, as in Israel/Palestine today).Third, great and middle powers should commit not to instigate, enable or intensify proxy wars against one another.Fourth, states should neither furnish military assistance nor allow arms sales that predictably abet gross violations of rules against aggression or atrocity.The virtue of such a bargain lies in its thinness. It does not ask states to agree on the whole architecture of world order, or to share a moral vocabulary.It asks those who join to accept one clear, narrow and urgent proposition: no state is safer in a world in which coercion is unconstrained because every exception claimed by one power becomes available to its rivals.This bargain also answers the most obvious danger of the emerging order. Trump’s foreign policy shows how an American hegemon in decline may help produce an even more violent order than the one that has prevailed since the end of the cold war.But that danger should not lead internationalists to pine for restored unipolarity under better liberal management (let alone the same crew of liberal internationalists). Multipolarity also creates an opening.If no single power can plausibly claim to enforce rules for everyone else, then an order based on mutual restraint may prove more stable than one built on a hierarchy that no longer commands belief.Reviving the antiwar norm requires more than a restoration of the mid-century compact, though it should begin from some of the insights that were clear to the original architects of the postwar order.Reciprocity need not entail moral equivalence between aggressor and victim, nor does it require indifference to atrocities.But it does require enlightened self-restraint, meaning that states must be asked to accept rules they would also want applied to their rivals, their allies and themselves.A restraint bargain framed in this way has advantages. It addresses the charge of hypocrisy more directly than appeals to an older order whose enforcement was systematically uneven.He’s commander-in-chief of chaos. Now we’re all victims of Trump’s wars | Nesrine MalikRead moreIt also gives rival powers a reason to comply even when they do not share a common political project.Every major and middle power is less secure in a world where preventive war, annexation, proxy conflict and coercive strangulation are normalized tools of statecraft.The last quarter century has vividly demonstrated this reality through the global costs of the so-called war on terror, as well as Russia’s war againstUkraineand the US-Israeli war on Iran.These costly wars of choice illustrate an argument for restraint grounded in self-interest, rather than virtue.Our four points provide the details of a newer world order.First, states should reaffirm and strengthen limits on the right of self-defense they can claim under the UN charter. The right of self-defense was never meant to be a general license to attack on the basis of speculative future threats, degraded deterrence, or broad claims of regional danger.The distinction between defense against an imminent attack and preventive war is essential. Once that distinction collapses, every rivalry can be redescribed as a security emergency and every powerful state can claim the right to strike first.Likewise, states must oppose other interpretations of self-defense, such as the noxious doctrine that self-defense permits attacks on the territory of states “unwilling or unable” to control non-state actors on their territory.Second, states should recommit to the inadmissibility of annexation or territorial acquisition by force, including de facto annexation accomplished through occupation, settlement, demographic engineering, or the creation of irreversible facts on the ground. This principle is one of the clearest tests of whether multipolarity will be governed by mutual restraint or by regional domination.A world of spheres of influence is, almost by definition, a world in which weaker states’ territorial integrity becomes negotiable, as US threats against Venezuela, Cuba, Greenland and even Canada have made clear.The implications for any prospective resolution to Russia’s war against Ukraine are obvious.Third, great and middle powers should commit not to instigate, enable or intensify proxy wars against one another. Defensive support to a state resisting aggression is one thing; measures designed to prolong war or turn a local conflict into a means of bleeding a rival are quite another.Proxy conflict is one of the main ways in which formal adherence to the charter coexists with escalating violence. It allows states to deny direct responsibility while sustaining conflicts that devastate civilian populations, destabilize regions and increase the risk of wider war.Fourth, states should not furnish military assistance or permit or sponsor arms sales that predictably abet gross violations of rules against aggression or atrocity. When outside powers arm and shield partners engaged in aggressive war or mass civilian harm, they help convert local or regional wars into tests of global alignment, as the wars in Gaza and Ukraine have illustrated.The limits of nostalgia are nowhere clearer than in the old “rules-based” order’s failure to interdict or regulate the trade in conventional weapons. World military expenditure reached nearly $2.9tn in 2025.From the strait of Hormuz to the North Sea, a global maritime war rages around us – and more than the price of oil is at stake | Simon TisdallRead moreThe international market in major arms is also highly concentrated: in 2021–25, the United States accounted for 42% of global exports, and the five permanent members of theUnited Nationssecurity council together accounted for nearly 68%.A robust agenda on this front could build on the Arms Trade Treaty, which prohibits transfers where a state knows that the arms would be used to commit genocide, crimes against humanity, grave breaches, attacks on civilians, or other war crimes, and requires denial where there is an overriding risk of specified serious violations.That framework should be extended to arms transfers foreseeably facilitating aggression, annexation or other non-defensive force.The point of this agenda is not to settle the entire future of international order in advance. It is to begin where agreement is most necessary and where evasion is most dangerous: no preventive war dressed up as self-defense, no annexation by force, no proxy war conducted through other people’s countries, and no arms transfers that knowingly feed aggression or atrocity.Far from being utopian demands, these are the minimum conditions for a world in which rival powers can compete without making war the normal instrument of politics.Multipolarity must be understood as more than a fall from the American order into disorder. It could become a scramble for domination if the strongest states are left to carve up regions, arm clients and rename coercion as security.But it also creates a chance to build an order less dependent on one power’s virtue, less compromised by selective enforcement, and less vulnerable to the nostalgia that mistakes yesterday’s hypocrisies for lost law. The task now is to stop mourning the old order, refuse the new lawlessness, and make restraint the thin, hard core of whatever comes next.Aslı Bâli and Samuel Moyn are law professors at Yale UniversityExplore more on these topicsUS foreign policyOpinionUnited NationsUS-Israel war on IranUkrainecommentShareReuse this content

title: Even Maga is falling out of love with JD Vance. If only his rivals weren’t even worse … | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The US vice-president is facing a barrage of allegations and complaints from inside and outside the Republican ranks. Good news for Marco Rubio – but not for the rest of the world, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The US vice-president is facing a barrage of allegations and complaints from inside and outside the Republican ranks. Good news for Marco Rubio – but not for the rest of the world, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: ‘The president is loving Vance’s svelte new figure’ … the vice-president in Winconsin earlier this month.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The president is loving Vance’s svelte new figure’ … the vice-president in Winconsin earlier this month.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/ReutersOpinionJD VanceEven Maga is falling out of love with JD Vance. If only his rivals weren’t even worse …Arwa MahdawiThe US vice-president is facing a barrage of allegations and complaints from inside and outside the Republican ranks. Good news for Marco Rubio – but not for the rest of the worldWed 29 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTShareThere’s something a bit off about JD Vance. And I mean that literally: the vice-president has been snacking on sauerkraut and other fermented foods as part of a weight-loss regime. Health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr got a number of Trump officials, including Vance, on to the diet, and isthrilled with the results. “Within 20 days I lost 20 pounds,” Kennedy said at an event in Michigan last month. “JD Vance is also on the diet and you can see how different he looks.” Dunno about that: still looks like a naked opportunist to me.If you want to get into Donald Trump’s good books, improving your looks is a surefire way to do so.According to MS Now, the president is loving Vance’s svelte new figure; it’s helped propel him back into Trump’s good graces. Which is lucky for him because he doesn’t have many other fans. They may be full of beneficial bacteria, but everyone around Vance seems to hate his guts.That includes a member of his protective detail, who is now under investigation for revealing to the media the Vance family’s lavishtravel requests. The Hillbilly Elegy authorreportedly askedfor one of his sons to be dropped off at a golf lesson via helicopter, and demanded last-minute chopper trips to Virginia to go house-hunting. With help like that you can understand why Vance is so pronatalist. I’d be popping out kids too, if I could get the taxpayer to fund helicopter trips to their extracurriculars.It’s not just the help he has angered. On Fridaythe Washington Postreported that Vance has faced a barrage of attacks from within his party “unlike that faced by other vice-presidents in decades”. Vance’s allies told the Post that the attacks, which seem largely driven by his mild criticism of Israel and the Iran war, are a “coordinated” attempt to poison his 2028 presidential chances. Over the weekend aFox News panelcriticised Vance for a recent appearance on Joe Rogan’s podcast where (in a brief moment of good judgment) he questioned putting troops on the ground in Iran. “[Vance] seems to be going off base a lot, and contradicting the president a lot in public lately, and it’s not helpful,” Fox News contributor Marc Thiessen said.I can’t say it’s not fun to watch Maga infighting. Nevertheless, it’s hard to take too much satisfaction from Vance’s troubles considering they only really benefit his rival for the 2028 Republican nomination: the odious war hawk Marco Rubio, who is nownarrowing the gapwith Vance in the polls. A setback for one awful politician always seems to spell a career boost for someone even worse. It’s really quite the pickle.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Welcome to America, where you’re never quite sure if your senator is dead or not | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Is it normal for a sitting senator to have to routinely submit proofs of life to a public who suspect he might be braindead? Just asking for 340 million friends
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Is it normal for a sitting senator to have to routinely submit proofs of life to a public who suspect he might be braindead? Just asking for 340 million friends
Content: ‘US lawmakers seem determined to cling to power until they die at their desks.’Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPAView image in fullscreen‘US lawmakers seem determined to cling to power until they die at their desks.’Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPAOpinionUS politicsWelcome to America, where you’re never quite sure if your senator is dead or notArwa MahdawiIs it normal for a sitting senator to have to routinely submit proofs of life to a public who suspect he might be braindead? Just asking for 340 million friendsWed 29 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 10.10 EDTShareIs it normal for a sitting senator to have to routinely submit proofs of life to a public who suspect he might be braindead? Just asking for 340 million friends in the US.Mitch McConnellwas hospitalized for a medical event on 14 June and we are now in week six of What on Earth Is Going on With Mitch? – a mystery that has riveted the nation.According to McConnell’s team there isn’t actually a mystery at all. The 84-year-old is doing great, they want us to know. So great that they have now released two photos to prove it.The firstwas madepublic on Sunday 12 July, almost a month after McConnell’s hospitalization and appears to have been prompted in part by Trump ally and far-right agent of chaos Laura Loomer’sclaimthat Mitch was “officially brain dead”.Kentucky’s Democratic governor, Andy Beshear, had also just sent a letter to McConnellasking himto be transparent and put an end to the speculation about his health. Funnily enough, the day before that photo came out, I’d published a columnwith the headline“Is Mitch McConnell secretly deceased?”Rarely is a question answered so quickly. Perhaps, as my next offering to the mischievous headline gods, I’ll put out a piece titled: “Is Benjamin Netanyahu going to escape accountability forever?”The Mitch McConnell mystery is solved. But it doesn’t look good for America | Moira DoneganRead moreBut back to that photo, which we’ll call Proof of Life One (POL1). Mitch, I’ll be honest, looked pretty good. He was wearing a nice pink shirt and his wife was standing next to him with her mouth stretched into something resembling a human smile.I wouldn’t say she was caressing him exactly, but she had a hand under his arm. Mitch was also holding a copy of the day’s Washington Post Sports section so we could all see that he was not secretly deceased. Very normal stuff!Our tech overlords have ushered in a world where no one can be ever sure that visual evidence is real and POL1 immediately set off rabid speculation that the photo was AI.There is, I should note, no evidence whatsoever that the photo was AI. But there is also no evidence that McConnell had any idea what was going on in that photo, or that he is in a fit state to continue serving his constituents. His office put out a statement saying he’d had a fall in his home and had subsequently been treated for pneumonia, but we still haven’t actually heard directly from the senator.All of which is why POL1 did not put an end to the speculation that McConnell’s office is hiding details about the senator’s condition from the public. So, on Monday, to try and quell a new round of speculation, his officereleased a new photodated 26 July, which we’ll call Proof of Life Two (POL2).This photo is pretty similar to the first one, except the senator is in a blue shirt. His office also put out a statement saying the senator is out of hospital, but still having “intense physical therapy” and wouldn’t be able to travel to the annual Fancy Farm picnic in western Kentucky. The statement did not say when he might be expected back in the Senate, which is scheduled to break for a month on 7 August. He has already missed 38 votes.Once again, this photo of an apparently living, breathing Mitch has not put an end to the questions around McConnell’s health. If the issue is his mobility rather than his mental capacity, why can’t McConnell come into the Senate in a wheelchair to do his job?That’s what happened last year, after all, after he suffered a fall and then wasseen using a wheelchairat the Capitol. Demanding more transparency from a public servant who is collecting a taxpayer-funded salary to represent his constituents is not unreasonable.Indeed, if McConnell were in perfect health and a Democratic senator were in this position, McConnell would be leading the charge to ensure they resigned. The man has never been interested in empathy or civility, just power.It looks like Kentucky’s governor hasn’t been reassured by POL2 either. On Monday, Beshear renewed his calls for transparency, asking the senator to directly address Kentuckians about his health or resign.“As Governor of the state you serve, I am calling on you to directly and verbally address the people of Kentucky and provide proof of your capacity to serve, or resign,” Beshearwrote in a letter. “If you are unwilling to voluntarily show that you still have the capacity to serve, I will insist Leader Thune fully investigate your condition, report to the American people, and begin the process [to fill your Senate seat] if warranted.”Is this letter finally going to lead to answers? I don’t know. But I do know that it’s highly likely that a situation like this is going to happen again. Regardless of where they are on the political spectrum, US lawmakers seem determined to cling to power until they die at their desks.Earlier this month, Senator Lindsey Graham became the fourth member of the US Senate since 2013to have diedwhile in office and the sixth member of Congress to have died while serving in the 119th Congress. Because the US is the greatest democracy in the world, Graham has now been replaced in the Senateby his sister Darline.Lindsey Graham’s hawkish ideology leaves a legacy of destruction | Moustafa BayoumiRead moreAnd if lawmakers aren’t dying in office, then they’re vanishing from their responsibilities without feeling the need to be transparent with their constituents.In 2024, for example, a reporter discovered that Kay Granger, a Republican congresswoman from Texas, who hadn’t cast a vote in months, was dealing with “dementia issues”at a senior living facility. Her office hadn’t felt the need todisclosethis to the public.There was also somespeculationthat House Republican leaders had been aware of the situation and deliberately chose to keep the information quiet to maintain their majority.And earlier this year Tom Kean Jr, a Republican, went off the radar foralmost four months. He missed more than100 votesbut continued to collect his salary. Eventually he resurfaced and said he’d been to inpatient treatment for depression and hadn’t wanted to explain because he was a private person. Which is fair enough. But then may I suggest that a job in public office isn’t for you?It’s funny, isn’t it? There are millions of Americans who are never going to have the funds to retire. Who are going to be forced to work for minimum wage until they keel over on the job. Our lawmakers, however, have excellent salaries and an array of taxpayer-funded health benefits. They can retire early if they choose to do so. It’s a tragedy for our democracy that more of them don’t.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist and the author of Strong Female LeadExplore more on these topicsUS politicsOpinionMitch McConnellUS CongressUS SenateRepublicanscommentShareReuse this content

title: Battles loom over social care, but this fight must be won. At last, we have a PM who believes that | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Burnham seems ready to use his power and influence. He understands the depth of this crisis: the task is persuading all those still in denial, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Burnham seems ready to use his power and influence. He understands the depth of this crisis: the task is persuading all those still in denial, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Illustration: Bill Bragg/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Bill Bragg/The GuardianOpinionSocial careBattles loom over social care, but this fight must be won. At last, we have a PM who believes thatPolly ToynbeeBurnham seems ready to use his power and influence. He understands the depth of this crisis: the task is persuading all those still in denialWed 29 Jul 2026 13.48 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 14.30 EDTShare“People pleaser!” That’s the insult Andy Burnham’s enemies sneer at him. And yes, he will need all his mightiest people-pleasing talents to win over voters to contribute to a new national care service. Choosing this forever failed policy (22 major reviews over three decades) as his first great challenge is a remarkable act of bravery. No mere people pleaser would dare step on this political live rail.It will use up vast amounts of political capital to get a national care service off the ground. He hardly neededTuesday’s Mail front page(“Burnham’s £18bn ‘death tax’ nightmare”) to remind him. But he has already fought on the battleground that is social care reform. “I do have some of the scars,”he said. How good to also hear him take a firm swipe at media attackers, who will now redouble their efforts. “You can’t create scare stories when people are already scared by what they’re seeing anyway through their own eyes in their own homes or in care homes,” he said. This is no grasp at low-hanging fruit, no search for a quick win. It’s a cause of deep conviction.In his speech from a north London care home, the prime minister told of his father with dementia, and of the struggle for families to get any help, the poor quality of much of it, the astronomical costs for some and the profiteering of private equity firms buying up care homes. That will have resonated with many, but his challenge now is to win the attention, hearts and minds of those who know nothing of social care. Making people care about care is the first vital step.Asurvey last yearfound 33% of people in England believed care was generally free at the point of need, like the NHS, and another 18% didn’t know whether it was. Many get a nasty shock when they need it for their family and find they must pay if they have savings above £23,250. Only 4% listed social care as a top priority for the country; its political salience is low because at any one time, few people are using it – and they put it out their minds afterwards. In England, this unseen serviceuses up a phenomenal 78% of local council funds: no wonder people think they get bad value for their council tax, as visible services keep shrinking to pay for it. Everything about it is broken.People need to wake up to what confronts us. They need to know that the roulette wheel of fate decides which families are stricken by dementia:one in three people alive today will get this most dreaded of diseases. Some may live for years in a nursing home:one in seven will pay over £100,000and some will have to sell the family home.But still, this nation of gamblers shrugs. People bet that it will never happen to them; that when their time comes, they will just drop dead. Burnham rightly described the UK’s social care system as equally unfair as the US health system: it bankrupts some. Would people rather pay a defined amount or risk losing everything? It’s an insurance offer to protect against the risk of catastrophic loss.Researchby the Health Foundation has found public support for funding reform, but – here’s the catch – “once people understand the current system”. As Louise Casey embarks on herBig Conversationon care, educating people about the system will be her primary task: only then can we discuss which other payment options are least unacceptable.This is about better care, too. For-profit care is lower quality than voluntary, non-profit or local authority-run care services,the Blavatnik School of Governmenthas found. This chaotic system includes16,500 care homes: 85% for profit, many small family-run businesses and some private equity big chains that will not be part of the new care service.Why do we endure this barely regulated, barely inspected patchwork of confusion? This was another disastrous Margaret Thatcher privatisation, of the kind Burnham intents to repair. After a 1988 report by the supermarket executive Roy Griffiths, Thatcher effectively ordered councils to close their own homes and services, outsourcing them to the private sector, and closedNHSgeriatric care wards. Crafting a new national care service out of all this would be the hardest of all in-sourcing tasks.This week, the prime minister warned the NHS could collapse unless social care is repaired. Last month, about 13,600 beds were occupied by people who were there only for lack of social care elsewhere, and delayed dischargescost the NHS £2.7bn last year. Burnham talks of integrating NHS and social care, with a workforce eventually on the same pay and with the same career progression. Currently, a starter NHS healthcare assistant is paid more than a care assistant.Will people agree to pay up? There are signs they will: when Boris Johnsonproposed a care levy, it was surprisingly popular. But it wasabolished by Kwasi Kwartengbefore it could be implemented. Which was just as well, because the plan added 1.25 percentage points to employee and employer national insurance. That meant workers, not pensioners, would pay. No extra tax would fall on dividends or other unearned income that doesn’t attract NI contributions. What’s more, the highest paid pay the lowest marginal NI rates.Whatever system emerges from these consultations, one principle must be that not a penny more is paid by the young for the old. Pensioners in the UK are theleast likely group to be in poverty(though, of course, some are). They generally have the most wealth and property, alongside final salary and triple-locked pensions. They are the overwhelming beneficiaries of the NHS. It’s no cliche to say the young are the future, so they must come first, in better early-years education, holiday childcare and schools with a wider technical, arts, drama, sports and design curriculum, while further education gets the funding and status it needs. The old must pay for the old, in one way or another.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis is a minefield. The politics of social care are fraught beyond all the other great problems Burnham could have chosen at the start. But the tone of his speech suggests the new prime minister really may lift this as a national priority. The wreckers in the Tory and Reform parties may find themselves wrong-footed; the Mail, yet again, out of tune with the public mood.When Burnham says we need “a different kind of politics: problem-solving, not point-scoring”, some old hands sigh and say: “Good luck with that!” But Burnham may strike a chord. A public grown hostile to politics may see through Kemi Badenoch’s deliberately impossible conditions for consensus agreement, asshe cynically and childishly demandsno borrowing, no taxes and no taking from “those who have made provisions and saved up over the course of their lives”. They know someone must pay, and that includes those lucky enough to have “made provisions”.It has never been the right time to brave social care reform. But it may be now, with a leader driven by personal belief, in his early stages, when he still has substantial amounts of political capital. He has grasped the nettle: will society, politics and the media? If not now, when?Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
