title: I’m running against the prime minister to stand up to a system that has facilitated the success of Pauline Hanson | Hannah Ferguson | The Guardian
description: I refuse to allow a cynical outlook of politics to infect our country, which is why I’m standing as an independent in Anthony Albanese’s seat of Grayndler
Author: Hannah Ferguson
Headline: I refuse to allow a cynical outlook of politics to infect our country, which is why I’m standing as an independent in Anthony Albanese’s seat of Grayndler
Content: Hannah Ferguson, who will run against Anthony Albanese in the next federal election and is the CEO of Cheek Media, writes that ‘Australians are fed up with the political establishment’.Photograph: Bec Lorrimer/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHannah Ferguson, who will run against Anthony Albanese in the next federal election and is the CEO of Cheek Media, writes that ‘Australians are fed up with the political establishment’.Photograph: Bec Lorrimer/The GuardianOpinionAustralian politicsI’m running against the prime minister to stand up to a system that has facilitated the success of Pauline HansonHannah FergusonI refuse to allow a cynical outlook of politics to infect our country, which is why I’m standing as an independent in Anthony Albanese’s seat of GrayndlerFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastWed 29 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 20.41 EDTShareThis week, I announced my intention to run as an independent candidate for my home seat of Grayndler. The seat is currently represented by the prime minister,Anthony Albanese.The response has been overwhelming and largely positive. Much of the criticism has been made in good faith and is crucial for me to hear and respond to. A lot of it has also been men calling me an attention-seeking influencer – but hey, that’s democracy baby.A consistent question is appearing in comment sections: why would I stand against the current leader of themore progressiveof the major parties? Instead, they suggest, I should be focusing on the rise of Pauline Hanson’s One Nation.Pressure is growing inside Labor to properly tax gas exports. Here’s what a 25% tax could pay for | Greg JerichoRead moreI understand the mindset behind this criticism, because I previously held a similar perspective. For a long time, I only permitted myself to focus on responding to the most extreme view on display. The loudest threat often feels like the biggest one. Many of us have been taught to bunker down and defend against “the worse option” rather than exploring how those in power have created the material conditions for this extremism to thrive. The 2024 US presidential election is the blueprint for this mistake.In order to have this conversation, we need to remember thatpolling analysts are findingOne Nation’s recent surge in popularity is not, in many cases, an endorsement of the party’s full platform. Instead, it’s a clear communication that Australians are fed up with the political establishment. They want something different and see Hanson as a vehicle for protest. As a nation, we deserve a better contest than this race to the bottom.For me, the defining word of Albanese’s prime ministership has been disappointment.Australians feel betrayed by a party who claim to fight for the average punter, and a leader who refuses to do more than the bare minimum to improve our standing.I have spoken with locals in my area who feel disappointed by our elected representative cutting160,000 people from the NDISwhile refusing to raise an estimated $17bn for Australians every year bytaxing our gas exports.I know the community around me are frustrated that after three years of pressure, the Albanese government announced weak gambling reforms that protect the betting industry and ignore the evidence.I remain disgusted that our prime minister invited President Isaac Herzog to our country earlier this year, as Israel continues to perpetrate a genocide against Palestinians.During Labor’s national conference last week we saw the machinery of party politics on full display. Open debate was stifled, because dissent is a dirty word in the era of Albanese’s Labor. Separately, we’ve witnessedprivate dinners with billionaire donorsandcash-for-access events. Most Australians don’t realise how rampant these “pay for play” functions are, with the Financial Review reporting that tickets priced at up to $12,000 allowed lobbyists to “speed date” with 36 Labor ministers.While many Australians face abject poverty, donors are buying potential influence for corporations. Secrecy is rampant within the Labor andCoalition“uniparty”.For most of Australia’s history, the two-party system entrenched the belief that “the lesser evil” was all we could aspire to at the ballot box. The major parties had flanked us, narrowing the Overton window to ensure we say thank you for the crumbs – while the banquet is served behind locked doors.Albanese is fond of saying people underestimate him. He should be careful not to do the same with Pauline HansonRead moreI refuse to allow this cynical outlook of politics to infect our country. I am truly patriotic about the opportunity we have in front of us. We have a powerful system of preferential voting, which distinguishes us from the binary trap of other nations. It has allowed us to socialise a new idea of what a strong Australian democracy can look like, where communities are represented directly – outside of rigid party lines.Grayndler is my home, my community. We are not a “one size fits all”.It is not radical to say we are entitled to better than this. It is not a threat to progress to stand up to a system that has facilitated Hanson’s success. We need more voices offering evidence-based, community-informed policies. Australian democracy will be better for it.Hannah Ferguson is the chief executive officer of Cheek Media Co and is running as an independent candidate in the federal seat of GrayndlerExplore more on these topicsAustralian politicsOpinionIndependentsAnthony AlbaneseOne NationLabor partyCoalitionPauline HansoncommentShareReuse this content

title: The likelihood of the RBA raising interest rates has fallen. Have we finally come to our senses? | Greg Jericho | The Guardian
description: The latest inflation figures have put off the expectation of another rate rise until early next year – unless we look for an excuse for the RBA to move earlier
Author: Greg Jericho
Headline: The latest inflation figures have put off the expectation of another rate rise until early next year – unless we look for an excuse for the RBA to move earlier
Content: ‘All the talk from the RBA has been how carefully they are looking for any signs that will require them to act to lower inflation.’Photograph: Mark Baker/APView image in fullscreen‘All the talk from the RBA has been how carefully they are looking for any signs that will require them to act to lower inflation.’Photograph: Mark Baker/APGrogonomicsReserve Bank of AustraliaThe likelihood of the RBA raising interest rates has fallen. Have we finally come to our senses?Greg JerichoThe latest inflation figures have put off the expectation of another rate rise until early next year – unless we look for an excuse for the RBA to move earlierFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastWed 29 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 21.34 EDTShareThe Juneinflation rate of 3.8%ended any real prospect of a rate rise next month, despite investors assuming the Reserve Bank would rather raise rates than not.There is a certain ghoulishness when it comes to economics and especially inflation. A “good” number will inevitably be dull news, whereas a bad number – one that is higher than expected or just higher – can lead to all manner of gnashing of teeth and wailing as the topic quickly shifts to interest rates.The linking of things to interest rates is not limited to inflation.Last weekthe June unemployment figuresnotionally showed unemployment had remained steady at 4.4% but when you scrapped back some of the rounding, it actually rose from 3.37% to 3.43%:The underemployment rate rose from 6.3% to 6.5%, which meant that the underutilisation rate – the total percentage of people in the labour force looking for a job or for more hours – rose rather steeply from 10.7% to 10.9%If the graph does not display click hereLike a naive fool I suspected this would mean the likelihood of an interest rate rise would perhaps fade. After all, only a very silly person would want to raise rates and thus slow the economy even more when unemployment and underemployment were both rising. Why seek to make things worse?Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailAnd then investors went from betting that the odds of a rate rise next month were a 19% chance to a 37% chance and then the following day to a 47% one.What the hell?This was all based on people noting that June employment grew solidly.Well, great, but so did unemployment and underemployment.Seriously what are we doing here?It was a reflection that we know the RBA is pretty desperate to raise rates again. All the talk from the RBA has been how carefully they are looking for any signs that will require them to act to lower inflation.Australia’s life dissatisfaction levels double as ‘wellbeing poverty’ reaches new highsRead moreAnd if that means raising them just because employment grew, well so be it, because heck those workers might want a higher wage and surely the wage-price spiral is due to come any day now!Thankfully, it seemed people regained some sense of reality and the likelihood of a rate rise had fallen to 19% by Tuesday.And now that inflation in the year to June has come in at 3.8% – lower than expected and down from 4.0% in May – the expectations of a rate rise have crashed to just 3%:If the graph does not display click hereAll that talk of a rate rise in August because Trump was being insane in Iran and raising oil prices and too many people had jobs rather dissipated as the reality of the economy not overheating and prices not being driven by excess demand withered.If the graph does not display click hereSo what happened in June?The biggest fall was petrol prices.Oil prices had fallen in the month as the Iran conflict seemed to be working towards some sort of conclusion:If the graph does not display click hereAs a result, petrol prices fell nearly 11% in the month:If the graph does not display click hereBut in the July figures petrol prices will have increased about 5%-6% due to higher oil prices and the reduction in the government’s cut to the fuel excise.The biggest cause of inflation over the past year was electricity prices.But this is purely due to the federal and stateenergy subsidiesstill being in place a year ago. The impact of these will largely exit the figures in next month’s numbers, which should lead to a lower overall inflation figure – especially as a full half of a per cent of the 3.8% is due to that electricity price jump:If the graph does not display click hereThe numbers also highlight how people’s experience of the cost-of-living crisis probably does not match the official inflation numbers.For example, in the past year the cost of lamb rose 15%, beef was up 12% and tea and coffee prices rose 5.1%.Telling someone whose most regular interaction with prices (namely groceries) that inflation is slowing and was just 3.8% would probably trigger a puzzled look (if not a hollow laugh):If the graph does not display click hereThat doesn’t mean the figures are wrong, just that while the CPI is weighted to get an average of how much Australian households spend on each item every week, people are less likely to weight the fact that over the past year the price of motor vehicles was less than 3.8% or that the price of eggs fell 5.4%:If the graph does not display click hereMore likely they remember that while eggs might be cheaper than they were 12 months ago, they are still more expensive than they were 18 months ago.Also remember that the inflation figures don’t count the cost of home loan repayments, which have risen in the past few months. Those repayments are included in the cost-of-living figures that will be out next week.For now, the market sees no rate rise next month but the prospect of one to come later remains:If the graph does not display click hereMostly what these inflation figures have done is put off the expectation of another rate rise till early next year, rather than in November.But that rise continues to loom as we return to the ghoulish practice of looking for any excuse the RBA might find in order to raise the cash rate.Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia InstituteExplore more on these topicsReserve Bank of AustraliaGrogonomicsAustralian economyCost-of-living crisisInterest ratesOilInflationcommentShareReuse this content

title: Wildfires are raging – and the world has junked 45 climate pledges. Disaster looms, and little wonder | Bill McGuire | The Guardian
description: Five years ago, I wrote an open letter asking climate scientists to speak out. Now governments are in retreat, it is surely time to act, says climate professor Bill McGuire
Author: Bill McGuire
Headline: Five years ago, I wrote an open letter asking climate scientists to speak out. Now governments are in retreat, it is surely time to act, says climate professor Bill McGuire
Content: 0:57Spain wildfire burns 'out of extinguishing capacity' as fires engulf parts of Europe – videoOpinionClimate crisisWildfires are raging – and the world has junked 45 climate pledges. Disaster looms, and little wonderBill McGuireFive years ago, I wrote an open letter asking climate scientists to speak out against fossil fuels. Now governments are in retreat, it is surely time to actFrance and Spain race to contain huge wildfires before fresh heatwave beginsWed 29 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 13.53 EDTShareSuch is the astonishing scale of the wildfires burning at the gates ofBordeauxandMadrid, that if they had happened 20 – even 10 – years back, they may well have shocked the world into taking action on the climate crisis. But like the proverbial frog in a pot of slowly heating water, we have become inured; not only to the ever more devastating impacts of climate breakdown, but increasingly to the actions needed to bring global heating to heel.Even as more than35,000 wildfiresrage across the surface of our world, and as we continue to rewind our planet’s climate so itresembles hotter episodes from its distant past, governments and trading blocs are very deliberately turning away from climate action.The latest evidence that we are not only doing too little but actually doing less as time goes by isprovided by the climate action media platform, We Don’t Have Time. It reported last week that the 12 months to July this year saw the reversal across the world of 45 climate policies. The retreat on climate action is global, but Europe – previously seen as a leader in emissions reductions – is in the vanguard, weakening measures across the board, including in the areas of carbon pricing, methane emissions and the phasing out of petrol and diesel vehicles.This isn’t yet an apocalyptic reversal of the majority of climate commitments, as the continuity of countless other climate policies testifies. We are, however, at an especially critical period: if we don’t want backsliding on climate action to continue, we have to act now.Croatian firefighting pilots help battle wildfire in France – loopWe Don’t Have Time lays the blame squarely at the foot of lobbying by the fossil fuel sector, and other industries antagonistic to climate action, making the point that as long as the usual suspects continue to make the most noise in the meetings where decisions are made, they will get what they want. What we have to do, then, is to make even more noise – on the streets, via the ballot box and in the media – putting pressure on politicians and governments so that they don’t cave in to vested business interests.We must force those in power to join the dots between the fires raging across Europe and theEl Niño building in the Pacific, and the activities of the fossil fuel corporations and others who choose not to do so.But we need our own lobbyists too – those qualified and in positions to speak truth to power about the dire straits we are already in, who can add credence to the noisy debate. Cue the world’s climate scientists. At this critical moment, the science has a duty to out-shout and out-shine corporate weasel words and government irresponsibility. The problem is that even now, at a time when the rate of global heating has doubled, this is just not happening.Sure, there are climate scientists out there telling it like it is, making a lot of noise and often putting their livelihoods and career prospects on the line, but they remain the exception rather than the rule. Far too many individuals, for one reason or another, still keep silent, heads below the parapet, fears and frets internalised.In 2021, Iwrote an open letterto all climate scientists, reminding them that they had a duty to speak out, to come down off the fence and to force those who need to know to listen to the truth. Sadly, five years on, little has changed. For far too many, fears about funding, academic advancement, prestige, and the contempt or ridicule of colleagues, still trump speaking out.As the heat continues to ratchet up, this cannot go on. If we want to have any possibility of drowning out the bogus claptrap of those determined to prevent serious climate action, then climate scientists – all scientists for that matter – need to wake up now and make themselves heard.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionClimate science is a vast tent that incorporates aspects of geology, chemistry, physics, oceanography, meteorology, economics, social science and many other fields, so that one source putting the number of climate scientists at18,000 worldwideis almost certainly an underestimate. When it comes to scientists of every ilk, the global figurecomes out at not far short of 10 million. Just imagine how much racket the scientific community could make if it spoke with the same voice – demanding the reinstatement of climate-friendly policies, arguing for more rapid emissions cuts, and at the same time overwhelming the perfidious calls for inertia from those lobbying for business as usual.This may well be our last chance to turn things around; to help politicians grow the backbones they need to stand up to vested interests. At this crucial time every scientist needs to examine their conscience, take on board the reality that there will be no research grants on a dead planet – and act accordingly.Bill McGuire is professor emeritus of geophysical and climate hazards at University College London and author ofThe Fate of the World: a History and Future of the Climate CrisisThe Guardian’s climate forum 2026On Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington and our panel of experts – including Professor Andy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman – for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening.Book ticketshereExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionWildfiresExtreme heatFranceSpainGreenhouse gas emissionsFossil fuelscommentShareReuse this content

title: What makes a good wedding these days? I say flirting and chaos, but not three days in a French castle | Rachel Connolly | The Guardian
description: Modern weddings seem to have become all about the spectacle – although, if you do take the opulent route, I still want to come, says writer Rachel Connolly
Author: Rachel Connolly
Headline: Modern weddings seem to have become all about the spectacle – although, if you do take the opulent route, I still want to come, says writer Rachel Connolly
Content: ‘These days – even for non-celebrities – weddings are often big, flashy affairs, perhaps in exotic destinations, sometimes over several days.’Photograph: wundervisuals/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘These days – even for non-celebrities – weddings are often big, flashy affairs, perhaps in exotic destinations, sometimes over several days.’Photograph: wundervisuals/Getty ImagesOpinionWeddingsWhat makes a good wedding these days? I say flirting and chaos, but not three days in a French castleRachel ConnollyModern weddings seem to have become all about the spectacle – although, if you do take the opulent route, I still want to comeWed 29 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 13.05 EDTShareAm I allowed to start a column about weddings by saying I don’t know exactly what I think about weddings and marriage in general? Well let’s see.One thing I do know: I really like attending weddings. I love to go as a valued guest, to see close friends in love and watch dads I have known for many years gruffly and fearfully breach the dancefloor. But I also love to go as a totally minor guest (the better for people-watching) and collect anecdotes about who, from the various overlapping families, hates who. People will just tell you these things, especially if your presence is quite random. I like to see the freshly single sporting their revenge dresses and haircuts and physiques. I like to witness and partake in the abundance of flirting. I don’t think I’ve ever had a bad time at a wedding.I asked friends their views on weddings while writing this. One of them said: “In general, I feel like weddings bring out behaviour we could use more of. For example flirting, dancing, and making plans, getting dressed up etc.” I agree completely. In fact, I have always dreaded getting the call to write about weddings precisely because I don’t want to compromise my cherished status as a frequent guest. But the truth is, I do feel some ambivalence about the contemporary execution, and I do consider my generation’s approach to weddings, and even marriage, a little odd.I started thinking about this after former rugby player Danny Cipriani and his fiancee, the actor Annalynne McCord, launched a “tacky and distasteful” (asone source had it) crowdfunding page asking guests to help pay for their wedding. The total amount they are asking for is £10,660. It seems fair to say that their combined earnings considerably outstrip those of your average newlyweds.And yet, unexpectedly, I find myself feeling sorry for them. I feel wary of the spectacle that weddings have become. I don’t think it was always like this. Talk to older people and you’ll hear stories of a family dinner and then a dance in the local pub. These days – even for non-celebrities – they are often big, flashy affairs, perhaps in exotic destinations, sometimes over several days. I hear so much about arguments when people don’t get invited, even though we all know space is usually limited. I wonder why people feel it has to be like this. I wonder, too, if the opulence makes the whole thing even more emotionally charged.Admittedly my own views on weddings and marriage, as these things might apply to me, make no sense at all. On the one hand, I’m an Irish Catholic who has been in a heterosexual relationship for a while. On the other hand, the institution of marriage feels odd to me. I wouldn’t argue my own lifestyle is radical, but I am sometimes surprised that big white weddings are still such a widespread norm.I never imagined my own wedding as a child. And when I try to picture a wedding for myself now, it would have to be in a Catholic church. The version of Catholicism I subscribe to could absolutely be described as “one I just invented in my head”. I stop into churches all the time to light candles and pray, meanwhile I pay attention to basically nothing the church has to say. Some would say that a humanist wedding might allay my discomfort with the institution of marriage, and I would agree. Still, the idea of being married in a humanist service by someone wearing, say, skinny jeans and a black T-shirt gives me willies. Why is this? Logically, it makes no sense. But that’s how I feel.And actually, I think that’s the core of it.Weddingsseem governed not by logic but by random yet passionately held whims. Maybe that is what causes people to have their names monogrammed on to hundreds of napkins, or to demand hundreds of people traipse to a country that even the two people getting married have never visited. It is precisely this sense of heightened and crazed emotions that makes weddings fun.So much deranged behaviour occurs. I myself have been asked out several times over the years, at weddings I have attended with my boyfriend. Once, memorably, a man with swept-back hair (a doctor no less) sort of charged up to me and said: “Look how are things going with your boyfriend? It seems like they’re going well. But if not …”. Then he gestured at himself, to present the alternative option. You have to admire it.I’m not deluded enough to interpret this as proof of my startling beauty or charm. Instead, I see it as evidence that the sentiment and nostalgia that suffuse every wedding does something strange to us all. Picture the kind of man who’s spent a decade or so juggling situationships arriving on the dancefloor as the music of his misspent boyhood floods the room (a Calvin Harris song orMr Brightside, say). He thinks: “God, I’m tired!” And then, casting frantically around: “Look, just pick somebody, anybody! Well she would do, would she?” Time comes for us all.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAll the money in the world wouldn’t make up for this kind of experience. The atmosphere at weddings exists all by itself. There’s no need to book a French castle for a memorable day. Having said that, if you have cash to burn, why not? I wouldn’t turn down the invitation. Which is all to say: please continue to invite me to your weddings.Rachel Connolly is a writer and the author of the novel Lazy CityExplore more on these topicsWeddingsOpinionRelationshipsMarriageFamilycommentShareReuse this content

title: Suddenly the British right feels a political chill. It’s getting cold in Andy Burnham’s shadow | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: The Tories and Reform had it easy when Keir Starmer was self-destructing – but a new PM with ideas exposes how vacant the opposition has become, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: The Tories and Reform had it easy when Keir Starmer was self-destructing – but a new PM with ideas exposes how vacant the opposition has become, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/GettyOpinionAndy BurnhamSuddenly the British right feels a political chill. It’s getting cold in Andy Burnham’s shadowRafael BehrThe Tories and Reform had it easy when Keir Starmer was self-destructing – but a new PM with ideas exposes how vacant the opposition has becomeWed 29 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 11.13 EDTShareAndy Burnham’s recollections of Britain in the 1970s must be pretty hazy. He was nine when the decade ended. Kemi Badenoch, born in 1980, can remember nothing. Lacking first-hand experience, the Conservative leader evokes the turmoil of a bygone era with cautionary zeal borrowed from an older generation. In a speech last week, sheaccused the new prime ministerof pining for “endless strikes, rubbish not being collected, bodies not being buried, inflation at 25% and a chancellor going cap-in-hand to the IMF”.This is more incantation than argument, a ritual fondling of beads on the Tory rosary. It is a symptom of a leader under stress, affirming her faith in Our Lady Margaret Thatcher and warding off socialist devils. Burnham has done nothing to support the claim that his government is a 70s tribute act, unless you count the appointment of aman named Healeyaschancellorand the imposition of price controls on buses.What the prime minister has done is trace Britain’s present malaise to choices made in the Thatcher era. From thethreshold of No 10he delivered the verdict on that legacy: “Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, large parts of the country de-industrialised, and they still haven’t recovered.” That statement has become the foundation stone for an edifice of neuralgic conservative commentary, bemoaning Britain’s capture by anti-market, pro-state fanatics.The right of British politics seems to be disoriented by the appearance of a Labour prime minister whose message isn’t crafted as a preemptive flinch at the accusation that he might come from the left, believe some leftish things and gamble on them being popular. Nigel Farage is playing it safe with the predictable but flimsy complaint that Burnham lacks a mandate. The Reform UK leader knows that isn’t how British politics works and, given that his personal ratings areon a downward drift, he doesn’t want a general election anyway.Badenoch’s reach back to the Seventies is a default setting in the absence of better ideas. It isn’t totally irrational, given the hint of nostalgia in Burnham’s tone. His ascendancy to No 10 relied on him being acceptable to a coalition of disputatiousLabourfactions. Lamentation over the death of a proletarian way of life, killed by Thatcher’s hand, is a hymn the party can sing in harmony. The new leader is a skilled choirmaster – in contrast to his predecessor, who knew the words but couldn’t carry a tune.But Burnham has also just spent nine years as mayor of Manchester, leaving it an enterprising capitalist city. He argues that its success is a function of pragmatic partnership between government and business, and that this model can be replicated on a national scale. It is hardly wild dogma to suggest that a strategically minded state can guide the hand of the market. The prime minister believes devolving power will give that hand a defter feel for local needs.Conservatives might disagree, but it takes wilful denial, or maybe intellectual laziness, to pretend that Burnham’s Manchester blueprint is retro-socialism, plain and simple. The prime minister could hardly be more explicit in rejecting the 20th-century central planner’s adage that “the gentleman in Whitehall knows best”.It is normal for oppositions to take time to get the measure of a new prime minister, and vice versa. Leaders need to make a few mistakes before their weaknesses form a pattern that can be woven into an effective political attack. Keir Starmer was a slippery target in opposition. But in government he made life easy for his enemies by shedding what modest popularity he had accrued almost immediately. Badenoch didn’t have to develop an argument against a prime minister who struggled to explain what he was trying to do and waseasily bulliedinto doing something else.The Tories were bystanders while Starmer’s government self-immolated, mostly to the benefit of Reform UK and the Greens. Badenoch’s personal ratings have picked up over the past year, reflecting perhaps growing squeamishness on the right about Farage as a prospective prime minister. But the Conservative vote share hasyet to climb as highas the giddy depths it fell to in July 2024, when the party suffered itsworst ever general election defeat.Disillusionment with Labour rule has done nothing to revive public interest in a Conservative alternative. Badenoch has done nothing to make her party interesting. She wasted her first year fretting perversely that the Tories had been too leftwing in office, thereby endorsing the case for defection toReform UK.She then switched to a focus on fiscal parsimony, hoping to occupy electoral terrain between public wariness of Labour’s tax-and-spend instincts and suspicion that Farage was a bit spivvy where money is concerned. But having scoped out a desirable patch of political real estate, Badenoch isn’t building anything. She has no theory of public service reform. Toread her speechesis to inhabit a parallel universe where the obvious causes of dissatisfaction with the state are chronic overfunding and infestation by militant leftwing civil servants.It is a vacuous analysis, coloured by excessive consumption of radical US conservative content online. British politics has always been shaped by trends across the Atlantic, but the radicalisation of the British right throughexposure to Maga influence(both cultural and financial) in recent years amounts to cognitive surrender. Political fandom has usurped judgment; craving validation from a foreign power takes precedence over loyalty to the national interest.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA Labour prime minister has the excuse of realpolitik, being obliged to show deference to a despotic US president who despises democratic allies but remains indispensable when it comes to their defence needs. Even then, Starmer found the courage to distance himself from Donald Trump’s disastrous military adventure in Iran. Not so, Badenoch. She turned squeamish only when she realised how far her initial gung-ho instincts had carried her from British mainstream opinion.What British conservatives either fail to observe or refuse to acknowledge in their mindless orbit around Planet Trump is that Maga politics contains more heresies against the sacred Thatcherite creed than anything Burnham proposes. The US president hates free trade. He admires single-party regimes where a supreme ruler directs economic activity. He imposes arbitrary tariffs. He uses his office to extort money from private companies or coerce them into givingequity stakesto his government. And he acquired the power to do all of this by skilfully manipulating economic and social grievances caused by deindustrialisation – the alienation and dislocation felt by working-class communities that felt their security and dignity washed away by cold global market tides.It is the same trend that Burnham identifies as a cause of British discontent and economic stagnation. The difference is that the UK prime minister talks about healing wounds, while Trump keeps them salted with partisan spite. It should be obvious to anyone who cares about democracy and the rule of law which model is preferable. Maybe the new prime minister’s methods will not work. Perhaps his prescriptions are flawed. At least his diagnosis belongs in 2026. It is the leader of the opposition, craving reenactment of a battle that was won before she was born, who is stuck in the wrong century.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionKemi BadenochNigel FarageLabourConservativesReform UKDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Germany’s leaders say the Berlin Pride attack targeted ‘all of us’. What utter hypocrisy | Fatma Aydemir | The Guardian
description: The queer community has lost resources and protection due to decisions made by the people now mouthing solidarity in public, says Guardian Europe columnist Fatma Aydemir
Author: Fatma Aydemir
Headline: The queer community has lost resources and protection due to decisions made by the people now mouthing solidarity in public, says Guardian Europe columnist Fatma Aydemir
Content: People at the Brandenburg Gate, which is illuminated with the message ‘Berlin, city of freedom’, 26 July 2026.Photograph: Ebrahim Noroozi/APView image in fullscreenPeople at the Brandenburg Gate, which is illuminated with the message ‘Berlin, city of freedom’, 26 July 2026.Photograph: Ebrahim Noroozi/APOpinionGermanyGermany’s leaders say the Berlin Pride attack targeted ‘all of us’. What utter hypocrisyFatma AydemirThe queer community has lost resources and protection due to decisions made by the people now mouthing solidarity in publicWed 29 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 00.01 EDTShareIt feels like a well-rehearsedscript. First come the flowers, then the pious statements. One after another, mainstream German politicians have lined up to claim that the attack onBerlin Pridelast weekend was an attack on “all of us”, “our values” and “our society”.Except it was not. This atrocity in which a van was rammed into the crowdwas, first and foremost, an attack on queer people. A vulnerable community that has been fighting for its rights for many decades; that, in recent years and all over the world, has increasingly been targeted by conservative forces.But, of course, the script is comfortable, because it requires nothing, least of all memory. InGermany, under the centre-right coalition led by the conservative chancellor, Friedrich Merz, the queer community has lost more and more resources, spaces and protection, due to decisions made by the very same people who are now expressing solidarity in public.When Merz made the statement on Sunday that Pride-goersshould not be intimidated, and that this attack was intended to divide our society, many queer people and allies wondered: is this the same Friedrich Merz who rejected the suggestion to flya rainbow flag from the Bundestag during last year’s Pride,with the remark, “The Bundestag is not a circus tent”?Then there is Karin Prien, the federal minister for education and family affairs, who sees the brutal assault as an attack on diversity and therefore, on “the heart of our democracy”. Is this the sameKarin Prienwho as education ministerbanned gender-inclusive languagefrom her ministry and cancelled “diversity” as a funding criterion for democracy projects, only a few months ago?The list of Christian-Democrat hypocrites goes on and on. Their opportunism is so obvious that you might in fact mistake the Bundestag for a circus, if the occasion wasn’t so horrendous. The victims (one person was killed and 29 injured, some in life-threatening ways) had simply gathered with their community on a warm day to celebrate visibly and joyfully in the centre of Berlin. This is what should drive the national conversation, before the grief of those directly affected is drowned out by the din of competing political narratives.View image in fullscreenFriedrich Merz speaking at a memorial service for the victims of the Berlin Pride attack, St-Marien-Kirche, Berlin, 26 July 2026.Photograph: Christian Mang/ReutersThe most urgent question should be: what do queer people need now?Do they need more policing? I doubt it, and I’m a long way from being the only one who thinks that. “Given the amount of police we already have, adding more won’t increase security,”says Mohamed Amjahid, a journalist who has extensively researched police violence. Amjahid’s plea that authorities reexamine the concept of security as they investigate the Pride attack, rather than hand police more access to citizens’ personal data, resonates with me.How about also restoring funding for projects such as Lambda, a queer youth organisation that, after 36 years, has had itsgovernment fundingcut due to austerity measures? Organisations that can answer crisis hotlines, offer counselling, accompany traumatised young people and provide safe spaces, in rural areas too, are badly needed.Does the community need the government to ramp up deportations and enact more restrictive immigration laws? My answer to that would be: what about the countless asylum seekers who have had to flee their homes and families simply for being queer?TheBerlin attacker, later shot dead by police, was an Islamist extremist. Islamist extremism is a real threat and this attack is not, unfortunately, the first in Germany to prove it. To pretend otherwise is not only dishonest, it’s a different form of hypocrisy against queer people who have to survive every day in autocratic Islamic regimes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor outraged Germans, the Jens Spahn scandal is about more than his surrogate baby | Tania RoettgerRead moreWhat is too easily forgotten, however, is that Christian conservativesand Islamists are quite similar when it comes to their stance on queerness. They may differ in their methods, projects and theological language. But not in their hostility. Both are rooted in rigid ideas about gender, sexuality and family.The far-right AfD is already exploiting this Pride attack to campaign for September elections in three federal states, accusing the government of “catastrophic migration politics”.But reducing this to a discussion about migration clearly misses the point. The attacker, who was later shot dead by the police, was a German citizen: a 21-year-old man, born and raised and radicalised in Germany. According to reports, he had recently participated in a deradicalisation programme. The more urgent question is why young men become susceptible to violent extremist ideologies in the first place, and how the government can justify cutting funding forextremism prevention.At the same time, Germany’s commitment to democratic values is questionable if those values become nothing more than rhetorical tools. The state’s commitment needs to be measured instead by the consistency of policy, domestic and foreign. But a government that courts authoritarians and Islamistssuch as the Syrian president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, must face difficult questions about the principles it now claims to defend.Fatma Aydemir is a Berlin-based author, novelist, playwright and a GuardianEuropecolumnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
