title: Jared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret review – the tales of abuse are utterly disturbing | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Four women speak out about their underage experiences with the movie star and musician. Are the floodgates finally about to open?
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: Four women speak out about their underage experiences with the movie star and musician. Are the floodgates finally about to open?
Content: ‘No longer a box office draw’ … Jared Leto: Hollywood's Dark Secret.Photograph: BBC/Pete DaddsView image in fullscreen‘No longer a box office draw’ … Jared Leto: Hollywood's Dark Secret.Photograph: BBC/Pete DaddsTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewJared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret review – the tales of abuse are utterly disturbingFour women speak out about their underage experiences with the movie star and musician. Are the floodgates finally about to open?Stuart HeritageWed 29 Jul 2026 08.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 13.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJared Leto has long been a person with something of a reputational issue. The public-facing side of this was bad enough – while playing The Joker in 2016’s Suicide Squad, he reportedly sent rats, dead pigs and used condoms to his cast mates – but for years there have been upsetting rumours about what he does in private. After a lengthy investigation, the BBC documentary Jared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret has finally brought at least some of them to light.This is, as you might imagine, not a fun thing to watch. The film documents allegations of what are said to be decades of systematic criminal misconduct against teenage girls. The women interviewed here allege sexual assault, threatened sexual assault, sexualised grooming and statutory rape. They are backed up by anonymous male former co-workers who claim to have witnessed the machinery that Leto set up to procure underage girls from concerts.What is particularly galling about Hollywood’s Dark Secret is that this is not the first time someone has tried to investigate these claims. As far back as 2005, the New York Post was runninggossip columnsthat claimed he was “aggressively pursuing” what were described as “underage objects of desire” at a New York hotel. By 2018, actor Dylan Sprouse and director James Gunn weretrading jokesabout Leto’s interest in teenage girls online. Last year,Air Mail’s Elena Clavarino spoke to nine womenwho variously claimed that Leto pursued them, engaged in sexually explicit telephone conversations with them, exposed himself to them and masturbated in front of them – all while they were underage.View image in fullscreenLet the testimonies speak for themselves … Alex on Jared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret.Photograph: BBC Studios/Theo TennantWhen that report was published, Leto’s representatives issued a denial. It seemed that everything continued as normal. He promoted his movie. He toured with his band. For a while it seemed that the world had blinked and moved on.However, something with the heft of Hollywood’s Dark Secret will be harder to ignore. Released on YouTube as well as the BBC to ensure maximum impact, it is a disturbing look at what is alleged to be a skin-crawling pattern of behaviour. Jessica Sartenaer and her team have put together a case that bears the unmistakable smell of shoe leather. Clearly, it often takes a long time for allegations like this to see the light because of a culture of silence. People are often scared to go public for fear of shame or reprisal, and it is in the financial interests of many people to keep the Jared Leto machine running as long as possible.That Sartenaer was able to find four women, and allay their concerns enough to let them show their faces onscreen, speaks volumes. We should let their testimonies speak for themselves (this really is a documentary that deserves to be seen, rather than simply read about), but their bravery deserves to be commended.View image in fullscreenIncredible bravery … Isabel on Jared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret.Photograph: BBC Studios/Theo TennantAlthough historical – these women are now all in their 20s, 30s and 40s – it is difficult to watch them recount what they experienced while they were underage. Some of their stories are straight from the Hollywood predator playbook, with them being procured by Leto’s team and led to dingy hotel rooms. Others are more baffling, like the woman who found herself receiving sexually explicit calls from Leto as a 16-year-old girl, only to then receive further calls of a similar nature from a man she believes was Leto in character as somebody else.Cumulatively, when these stories have been added to archive footage of concerts where Leto has his arms draped around young girls, and talkshow appearances where he brags about sleeping with fans, and one particularly unnerving clip where he quotes the old Dazed and Confused line about high school girls – “I keep getting older but they stay the same age” – the effect is completely disturbing.So far, Leto has been bulletproof against allegations like these, but you can’t help feeling that this film will land a blow. Of course, it should be noted that the timing of the documentary might help. Leto is no longer the box office draw he once was. Last year’s Tron: Ares reportedly lost somewhere in the region of $130m, and his latest film – Masters of the Universe – is among the biggest flops of the year so far. It isn’t the best reflection of Hollywood that it will only choose to round on alleged sexual predators once the bottom line has been weakened, but better late than never.Leto declined to comment to Sartenaer and her team, unlike the robust denial he gave after the Air Mail investigation. Maybe it’s a sign that the floodgates will finally open?Jared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret is on BBC iPlayer and YouTube nowSupport for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 inScotland, or 0800 0246 991 inNorthern Ireland. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionJared LetoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: You can’t argue with 118 Brummies in their swimsuits: Attilio Fiumarella’s best photograph | Photography | The Guardian
description: ‘I was thinking about the Terracotta Army when I took this shot of Birmingham swimmers in their local pool, which faced closure. They had to stand there for an hour, waiting for the sun to come out’
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: ‘I was thinking about the Terracotta Army when I took this shot of Birmingham swimmers in their local pool, which faced closure. They had to stand there for an hour, waiting for the sun to come out’
Content: ‘We need to get together and take back power’ …swimmers in the empty Grade II listed Moseley Road Baths in Birmingham.Photograph: © Attilio Fiumarella. Courtesy of The Royal Photographic SocietyView image in fullscreen‘We need to get together and take back power’ …swimmers in the empty Grade II listed Moseley Road Baths in Birmingham.Photograph: © Attilio Fiumarella. Courtesy of The Royal Photographic SocietyMy best shotPhotographyYou can’t argue with 118 Brummies in their swimsuits: Attilio Fiumarella’s best photograph‘I was thinking about the Terracotta Army when I took this shot of Birmingham swimmers in their local pool, which faced closure. They had to stand there for an hour, waiting for the sun to come out’Interview byCharlotte JansenWed 29 Jul 2026 09.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 13.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleItook this image inBirminghamon 20 July 2014 – part of my first professional photography project. I had moved to the city in 2013 and I would pass this building every day on the bus on my way to the city centre. I remember looking at the facades and being impressed and intrigued by the three different entrances – what were once the first class, second class and women’s entrances.One day I decided to get off the bus and find out what the building was. The door was open, and a nice lady welcomed me in and started to explain its history. It is theMoseley Road Baths,an Edwardian-era community building. In 2014 the second pool was still operating but the gala pool, where I took this image, was already empty. The building was in need of restoration and, without funding, thecouncil planned to shut it downfor good. The woman I met there told me lots of stories about the place – people who had come to learn to swim, how it had served as a casualty station during the second world war, and how it had even been used as a dance hall. It was a very charming place with an incredible history: as soon as I saw the gala pool, I knew I had to fill the majestic empty space.double quotation markWe need to get together, show up and take back powerA few months later, I managed to get a local community bursary through Some Cities, run by Andrew Jackson and Dan Burwood, to make a portrait project about the pool community, and the relationship between them and the building. It was collaborative, we created the story together. And in July 2014, I organised this shot – the last picture of the project. The Friends of Moseley Road Baths helped recruit swimmers, and I also handed out flyers in the neighbourhood to encourage people to take part. What’s fantastic about the image is that it reflects how diverse the community there is, and how many different generations swim there.It still makes me smile that I decided to use a large format camera for the first time on a project like this. Looking back, it seems slightly crazy. It was an intense experience. We had 118 people in the pool, and everything depended on getting a single sheet of film right. There was a lot that could have gone wrong. Fortunately, many people helped make it possible. Ian Edwards from St Paul’s Community Trust coordinated everyone with a megaphone, while he and a team of volunteers helped people down into the empty pool using a temporary staircase they had built.Then I had a problem with the light. I knew that at 11am, it came in from the right to the left through the windows, giving me exactly the angle I wanted, but on the day it was overcast. After waiting for about an hour, people were starting to get nervous, but in the last five minutes, the sun finally appeared and I got the shot.In my work, I always reference architecture – that’s my background. In this image I was thinking of theTerracotta Army. What amazed me about the photograph was how it became an expression of solidarity and togetherness. In 2020 it won thePortrait of Humanity prize, and now it is getting new attention – I think because it reflects something about the time we’re living in. We need to get together, to show up and to take back power. I see this photograph as an act of resistance – these swimmers had never met me but they showed up to defend a place they cared deeply about.Recently, Moseley Road Bathssecured the final fundingneeded to complete its restoration, including a grant from the National Lottery Heritage Fund. The building is temporarily closed while the restoration works are completed, but it will soon reopen with renewed purpose and new public spaces. My contribution was only a very small part of that story, but I like to think it helped in some way. Looking back, I think it was a very generous thing for all those people to do. They stood together in their swimsuits, following the directions of a crazy Italian guy. To me, this photograph simply says: “We are here, together, standing up for something we believe in.”Attilio Fiumarella is one of the selected photographers in the Royal Photographic Society’s 167th annual international exhibition at theSaatchi Gallery, London, from 7 August to 11 SeptemberAttilio Fiumarella’s CVView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Attilio FiumarellaBorn:Naples, 1978High point:Seeing long-term projects find their audience over time, from winning Portrait of Humanity 2020 to being commissioned by institutions whose work and values I respectTop tip:Be persistent, and care deeply about the people you photograph. As photographers, we have a responsibility to help their stories reach a wider audienceExplore more on these topicsPhotographyMy best shotBirminghamSwimmingHeritageArchitecturefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tony review – knives out in tasty reheat of Anthony Bourdain’s memoir | Movies | The Guardian
description: Dominic Sessa stars as a conceited yet vulnerable young chef alongside Antonio Banderas – but the feelgood factor is compromised by what we know of the author
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Dominic Sessa stars as a conceited yet vulnerable young chef alongside Antonio Banderas – but the feelgood factor is compromised by what we know of the author
Content: Kitchen confidential … Antonio Banderas and Dominic Sessa in Tony.Photograph: A24View image in fullscreenKitchen confidential … Antonio Banderas and Dominic Sessa in Tony.Photograph: A24MoviesReviewTony review – knives out in tasty reheat of Anthony Bourdain’s memoirDominic Sessa stars as a conceited yet vulnerable young chef alongside Antonio Banderas – but the feelgood factor is compromised by what we know of the authorPeter BradshawWed 29 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor all the drugs and punch-ups, this is an unexpectedly sentimental coming-of-age story – or maybe origin myth – about the formative youthful kitchen experiences of legendary badass chefAnthony Bourdain. It is taken from the opening chapters in his bestselling memoir Kitchen Confidential; Canadian film-maker Matt Johnson directs and Dominic Sessa (the callow kid from Alexander Payne’s The Holdovers) plays the conceited, smug yet lonely and vulnerable young college student Tony. “Anthony” is in the future.It is the mid-1970s and Tony effectively runs away from home after failing to get a residential summer writing scholarship that he had assured everyone was in the bag. He shows up nearly penniless in the seaside vacation resort of Provincetown, Massachusetts – a place that is pretty similar to Amity Island in Jaws, which is showing at every drive-in. The reason is that he has a desperate crush on Nancy (Emilia Jones) who is there for the summer too and whom he desperately wants to impress with his smouldering intellectualism.Then, having got drunkenly thrown out of a bar serving seafood, pathetic Tony gets hired there as a humble dishwasher by its kindly-stern chef (Antonio Banderas). He finds he kinda likes the heat in the kitchen, and gets to know louche, coke-addled womanising chef Sal (Leo Woodall) who shows Tony the ropes of being a tough guy and a player, but who is, in the time-honoured manner of films like this, Tony’s sacrificial mentor: inspirational figure and awful warning.This is a strange film in some ways. It is watchable and entertaining, but its feelgood trajectory is compromised by what we know of the author. In 2000, when the book came out and Bourdain was approaching the height of his celebrity, these anecdotes would have felt simply warm, wry and funny. If he was still alive now, Bourdain would assuredly have an ironic cameo, perhaps as one of the greybeard authority figures that obstruct the rake’s progress. But we are watching the film in the knowledge thatBourdain took his own life in 2018after a painful breakup, having suffered from instability and depression. All the sadness, all the emotional danger that this film gestures at, all the crises that the drama suggests are just obstacles to be surmounted … they are all very real.How exactly, for example, do we take the moment in this movie when Banderas’s character tells Tony aboutFrançois Vatel, chef to Louis XIV, who killed himself in shame when the key ingredients didn’t arrive for a banquet? (It’s not in the book, though Bourdain spoke about it in interviews as an example of extreme perfectionism.) The scene is presumably there tacitly to acknowledge Bourdain’s heartbreaking fate. It sits oddly.As for Sessa himself, Johnson gives him plenty of shots looking silently stricken, or hungover, often sporting a black eye. In a way, Tony is the author, the narrator who just bleakly sees it all, but for a writer he sometimes doesn’t have much to say about the situation in which he finds himself. There’s some nice support from Rich Sommer and Dagmara Dominczyk as Pierre and Gladys, Tony’s parents, and Banderas always has gentleness and charm. A bittersweet dish.Tony is out on 7 August in the US, 14 August in the UK, and 20 August in Australia.Explore more on these topicsFilmBiopicsAnthony BourdainFoodreviewsShareReuse this content

title: After 40 years, Aliens is still shaping the way video games are made | Games | The Guardian
description: James Cameron’s high-octane film sequel is a blueprint for modern action space slashers
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: James Cameron’s high-octane film sequel is a blueprint for modern action space slashers
Content: Take off and nuke the entire site from orbit … Ripley gets out the big guns in Aliens.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyView image in fullscreenTake off and nuke the entire site from orbit … Ripley gets out the big guns in Aliens.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyPushing Buttons newsletterGamesAfter 40 years, Aliens is still shaping the way video games are madeJames Cameron’s high-octane film sequel is a blueprint for modern action space slashersDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeith StuartWed 29 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 13.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is difficult to believe that James Cameron’s Aliens was released into cinemas 40 years ago. The seminal space shooter took the original Alien – a tense slasher film with a tiny cast and one monster – and transformed it into an intergalactic war movie crammed with wry one-liners, massive guns and an actual boss battle finale. As a 14-year-old, I stood in line at the Tatton Gatley cinema, unsure if I’d be allowed in – I came out three hours later a changed person, my head filled with esoteric military slang and a deep fear of beeping motion detectors. For days afterwards, I slept with my duvet covering my mouth so that no facehuggers could get me. (I was a highly impressionable teenager.)It’s little wonder that the film has had such a profound effect on video game design. Take the colonial marines, for example. Although the concept of the space soldier had been around in sci-fi novels since the 1930s, most notably in the works of EE “Doc” Smith and Robert Heinlein (the Starship Troopers), Hicks, Hudson, Vasquez and co, were the perfect 80s rendition, combining the witty banter of contemporary buddy cop flicks with awesome weaponry and hi-tech gadgets. Their influence is easy to spotin Doom, where the nameless marine fights ceaseless waves of hellish monsters using a mix of futuristic rifles and good old shotguns. It’s there too in theHalo series, the Spartan soldiers sporting the same armour and mega weapons, cruising about in very similar highly militarised starships and fighting recognisable hive-mind space beasts. Gears of War,KillzoneandMarathonall borrow from the same set of costumes and deadly accessories.Also important to future game designers was the way in which James Cameron opened up the world of Alien after Ridley Scott’s original locked-room mystery of a movie. He beefed up the Weyland-Yutani Corporation, giving us the stencil for dozens of evil video game mega corps; he brought in an array of weapons from handguns to M41A pulse rifles and the M56 smart guns, introducing the idea of a scaled armoury to discover and master; and he employed a structure based around the repeated rhythm of tense exploration followed by explosive encounters that countless games would follow.View image in fullscreenAlien: Isolation … in your living room, everyone can hear you scream.Photograph: SegaIt’s weird, then, how difficult it has proven to directly translate the movie into games. While the original Alien spawneda cult 8bit translationand thebrilliant Alien: Isolation, Cameron’s sequel is best known for the disastrously buggedAliens: Colonial Marines, which led to alawsuit for deceptive marketing. Elsewhere, third-person co-op blaster Aliens: Fireteam Elite drew mixed reviews but has at least birthed a forthcoming sequel, and the 2D Metroid-style game Aliens: Infestation has plenty of fans. My favourite, though, was one of the two official tie-ins from 1986. Aliens: the Computer Game from Electric Dreams Software was a thrilling proto-FPS, allowing you to control several of the movie’s characters as they stalked through an atmosphere processing plant getting attacked by xenomorphs and facehuggers. I’m not sure it’s ever been bettered.Watching the movie again this week, it’s impossible not to notice all the little scenic and narrative touches that have since shaped how sci-fi action games function. Even the sentry gun, which was cut from the cinematic release and only turned up in the special edition home release, has become a staple special weapon, present in everything fromCall of DutytoHelldivers. I wonder how many of today’s game creators were also stood in cinema lines in the summer of 1986, too young to be there, not quite ready to have their minds blown for ever?What to playView image in fullscreenDanger at every turn … Scarlet Deer Inn.Photograph: Attu GamesThose of us with an interest in the fibre arts are always delighted to see them crop up in other media. Here, embroidered character art helpsScarlet Deer Innto stand out in a crowded market. Once players are in, they’ll find the charming medieval village has some horrific secrets. Players guide mother-of-two Elise through danger-filled caverns on a quest to find her children and prevent them from meeting a gruesome end, a goal that gained additional meaning when the husband-and-wife developers had a baby of their own. Armed only with a torch, you must keep it lit or likely repeatedly succumb to the darkness.Jordan Erica WebberAvailable on:PCEstimated playtime:four hoursWhat to readView image in fullscreenRipe for the AI slop machine … Grand Theft Auto VI.Photograph: NintendoIn what is likely to become a familiar problem for the games industry, Rockstar’sGrand Theft Auto VImarketing schedule is being infiltrated by AI-generated trailers purporting to show scenes from the forthcoming game. Examples include asurfing videoand awoman enjoying champagne on a yacht. AsEurogamer points out, the videos are filling a vacuum left by Rockstar’s somewhat stingy approach to releasing in-game footage. The company does notseem to be impressed.Rather embarrassingly for console manufacturers seeking to go digital only,network outagesare back. On Friday,PlayStation Network went downfor several hours, leaving players with no access to their games. And on Monday, it wasthe turn of Xbox, a major outage making it impossible to sign in to user accounts, launch games or download content. While the PlayStation situation has now been resolved, the Xbox network was still having issues at time of press. All hail our disc-less future!When Valve announced its new Steam Machine PC, fans were intrigued by a custom front plate the company had attached to the machine, which appeared to bean e-ink screendisplaying performance data from inside the computer, such as memory and CPU performance. Now, Valve has released all the files and details for what it callsThe Inkterface, so owners can build one – and gaming site Aftermathhas done just that. Very nerdy, but very cool.And if you enjoyed reminiscing aboutAliens,you might want to check out forthcoming bookAliens: The Video Gamesby Mike Diver, a complete history of adaptations, including lots of developer interviews.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to clickSilent Hill Townfall: the series is coming to Scotland, but what fresh horrors will it bring?Glitched into empty space: why video games are obsessed with the BackroomsHaex – a wilder, weirder open-world adventure‘An anthem for the co-dependent’: Bad Magpie’s corvid carnage with a side of existential angstThere Are No Ghosts at the Grand – stripping back the physical and metaphorical layers of a haunted hotelThe best gaming chairs in the UK for comfort, support and serious play in 2026 – testedThe Mermaid Mask – the funniest underwater murder mystery you can play | ★★★★☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenThe gaming canon … a lot of top 100 lists.Photograph: Justin Towell/AlamyThis week’s question is fromBenvia email:“I want to learn more about the history of video games and I wondered if there are any canonical lists of the best titles– perhaps a gaming equivalent of the BFI’s250 Greatest Films of All Timeor the American Film Institute’s100 Years 100 Movies?”Many publications that write about video games have their own top 100 list, although these tends to be compiled by their own critics or readers rather than a broader spread of experts.GQ,GameRantandRolling Stoneall have versions, while IGN has a “mathematically derived” list of thetop 500, andwe’vedonethe best games of the 21st century(so far). For more formal attempts at developing a canon, the Strong Museum has aWorld Video Game Hall of Fame, MoMA hasa games collection(but for some reason its website does NOT want you to find a definitive list!), and for itsArt of Gamesexhibition in 2012, the Smithsonian compiled alist of 80 important titleswith the help of gamers and game makers. There have also been a few books on the subject: try Penguin’s 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die (full disclosure: I wrote some of this book), BFI’s 100 Video Games, or Game On!: From Pong to Oblivion – The Greatest Video Games of All Time, compiled by ex-Edge magazine writers.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterJames CameronAlienRidley ScottfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘No plan, no budget, no promotion’: how a genre-mashing masterpiece by a forgotten New York beatnik blew gen Z away | Culture | The Guardian
description: How did an album that began life in 1984 – fusing disco, folk, synth-pop and Chinese opera – end up as ‘one of 2026’s most thrilling releases’? And why does its creator call himself Nirosta Steel?
Author: Juan A Ramírez
Headline: How did an album that began life in 1984 – fusing disco, folk, synth-pop and Chinese opera – end up as ‘one of 2026’s most thrilling releases’? And why does its creator call himself Nirosta Steel?
Content: ‘They didn’t know what they were in for’ … Nirosta Steel, maker of My Skyscraper, at his home in Champaign, Illinois.Photograph: Claire Daly/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘They didn’t know what they were in for’ … Nirosta Steel, maker of My Skyscraper, at his home in Champaign, Illinois.Photograph: Claire Daly/The GuardianCulture‘No plan, no budget, no promotion’: how a genre-mashing masterpiece by a forgotten New York beatnik blew gen Z awayHow did an album that began life in 1984 – fusing disco, folk, synth-pop and Chinese opera – end up as ‘one of 2026’s most thrilling releases’? And why does its creator call himself Nirosta Steel?Juan A RamírezWed 29 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 10.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘It’s kind of mind-bending,” says 69-year old Steven Hall. For the last three years, the Scottish musician has been living with his lawyer husband a few hours south of Chicago, driving an Uber for some additional income. Now, suddenly, he is being lauded by critics for his double LP My Skyscraper, released last month under the name Nirosta Steel. Compiling material recorded between 1984 and 2025, it charts a sonic landscape through disco, folk and synth-pop with detours into Chinese opera and ecclesiastical a cappella. Pitchforkcalled it“an archival triumph and one of the year’s most thrilling new releases”.It all came about when a label head, impressed with Nirosta Steel’s 2014 album Cool Fire, asked Hall if he had any more music. “He didn’t know what he was in for,” says Hall. The couple of dozen unreleased songs he shared spanned four decades of eclectic musicianship, and revealed a globe-trotting life and career that intersects with experimental icons such as Arthur Russell and Allen Ginsberg. Now My Skyscraper seems poised to admit Hall into that rarified pantheon of historically salvaged artists whose time has belatedly arrived.double quotation mark‘I thought Bob Dylan coming over in his limo was normal’“I feel like Rip Van Winkle! Like I suddenly walked out of a cave and I’m blinking my eyes and there’s all this bright light shining on me,” says Hall. “Two weeks ago the label was maybe $2,000 in debt because we were going to do 200 copies. Now we have 1,000 orders and are looking to press 2,000.”View image in fullscreenPoets corner … Hall in 1977 photographed by Allen Ginsberg.Photograph: Courtesy of the estate of Allen GinsbergBorn in the Glasgow suburb of Milngavie to a middle-class optician father and a “tough as nails” mother from a family of 18, Hall grew up performing in the church choir and local theatre company. His parents sent him to a teacher to rid him of his accent, accounting for a rather unplaceable accent (“some people think I’m Swedish”), but they were much more lax as his sexuality developed, and the young Hall freely dated boys and girls throughout school. “There was never even the idea of coming out,” he says, “because I came from a very liberal background where my parents’ attitude was, ‘Whatever you want to do, it’s OK.’”After his father died, Hall’s mother posted a personal ad in the International Herald Tribune and consulted with her three children (Hall has a twin sister and a brother) as to which suitor she should pursue. A man in Delaware won out and the family relocated to the US, which had long dazzled Hall thanks to his fascination with American musicals (“especially the real fantasy, Judy Garland-Mickey Rooney, ‘let’s put on a show’ classics”) and the Chrysler Building, which was built from a stainless alloy called … Nirosta steel.View image in fullscreenHall today.Photograph: Claire Daly/The GuardianPoets – including Ginsberg – would visit his high school in Delaware, and Hall would join them on their return trips to New York City, which is how he found himself at the so-called Poets’ Building in the middle of the East Village’s then bustling arts scene. “I thought it was normal,” says Hall, “because it was the only thing I knew.‘Oh, Bob Dylan’s coming over, his limousine is parked downstairs.Richard Hellfrom Television has a show tonight.’ I thought I could be doing the same thing.”He briefly followed Ginsberg to Naropa University, where he studied dance and poetry under Douglas Dunn and William S Burroughs. But it was while visiting Ginsberg in the Poets’ Building that Hall met Arthur Russell, and the two developed a deep friendship and collaboration while playing backup for Ginsberg’s poetry sets. Russell, he says, was one of the few people who “just couldn’t help creating all the time, and it was hardly a conscious thing. His genius was totally organic and came from his Buddhist awakening. People credit Ginsberg with bringing Buddhism to the west, but Arthur was, in some ways, teaching Allen.”View image in fullscreen‘We didn’t stop and we didn’t go back’ … Hall in 1983 with friend, producer and cellist Arthur Russell.Photograph: Jonny FuHall and Russell collaborated on several projects, including the disco outfit Loose Joints with the DJ Steve D’Acquisto. One of only two songs they wrote together, the sweltering Go for the Night, appears on My Skyscraper, with production by members of Arthur’s Landing, a sort-of tribute band assembled by members of their circle after Russell’s death from Aids in 1992. Their other co-write, a lo-fi elegy titled Lost in Thought, was meant to feature on the album but was bumped in favour of the 22-minute diptych Fresh Feeling and Special Weakness – two of only three recordings of Russell, a gifted multi-instrumentalist, playing drums.Those last-minute additions survived somewhat miraculously, given Hall “had just had them transferred last year, after having them on two-track [tapes] for all those years. I was lucky they were still usable because they were never played, I think, since they were recorded.” More than that, the tracks were improvised one-takes: “Once we got going, the idea was we don’t stop, and we don’t go back and do it again. Everything I did, Arthur was right on top of it. That shows not only how talented he was, but also how close we were, because we could have that kind of interaction and it worked.”Beyond their collaborations, the two would find inspiration on joint journeys to now legendary nightclubs such as Danceteria and The Saint. One of their favourite pastimes, Hall says, was getting high and looking at guys in their diverse East Village, with a preference for its Ukrainian runners and Puerto Ricans “who didn’t like to wear underwear when they wore sweatpants”. With a naughty chuckle, he relates that, when a well-endowed man approached, “we would nudge each other and say, ‘entering binocular mode.’”Hall admits his relationship with Russell sometimes suffered from their clash of competitiveness, and what he viewed as his friend’s jealous streak. In the bookTravels Over Feeling, Hall reveals that he was seconds from signing to Russell’s Sleeping Bag Records label when Russell grabbed the pen from his hand, claiming he would become too famous and move on. “Arthur had a saying, ‘Sometimes paranoia is justified,’” Hall explains. “At that time, he thought some of the people at Sire Records, some of the sleazy people he was hanging out with and playing demos for, had taken some of his ideas, which is entirely possible.” Hall says Russell believed the Rolling Stones’ song Miss You, for example, was based on one of his drum tracks – though “there was not really any evidence of that, but that was the kind of thing”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markBoss Trix (Benny’s Song) is inspired by a Taiwanese lover with impressive bedroom skillsIn his 20s, Hall began spending substantial amounts of time in East Asia, initially staying with a wealthy boyfriend in Hong Kong. He began scoring performances and hosting movement workshops for Zuni Icosahedron, an experimental theatre company there, and later “made a really good living” recording location sound for film and television ads in Taiwan. Naturally, he picked up inspiration each step of the way. My Skyscraper track Lost in Music concludes with audio from a Cantonese funeral procession, and Boss Trix (Benny’s Song) is inspired by a Taiwanese lover with impressive bedroom skills.“I’ve been collecting all these songs for ever, basically, and it’s not just collecting,” he says. “A song that was written 30 years ago, or something I did with Arthur 40 years ago, I keep doing them in different ways so I don’t get bored, or it’s different versions of songs I’ve done with other people in other languages.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Claire Daly/The GuardianWith the album’s success, and with momentous live engagements on the horizon including his first performance at New York’s former Pyramid Club (now Nightclub 101) since he played there with Russell, Hall hopes to reignite his writing with new collaborators, and says he’d like to do a covers album that includes his take on Sade’s No Ordinary Love, originally intended for My Skyscraper.“It’s like surfing on a wave and just seeing where it goes,” he says. “There was no plan or budget for promotion, it was just the music we wanted to put out.”As for finding renewed success at such a late stage in his career, Hall remains unfazed. “I really admire older musicians, like Madonna, who’s two years younger than me, or Mick Jagger, who’s a lot older,” he says. “Certain musicians just keep finding ways to approach it. There’s an authenticity in terms of the process, because everyone was just doing it because they wanted to. And that’s what my music is like, too.”My Skyscraper by Nirosta Steel is out now on Ulyssa RecordsExplore more on these topicsCultureDiscoExperimental musicPop and rockElectronic musicFolk musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Petrol bombs, drugs and Bradley from S Club 7: inside the wild 00s hood movie that the police seized | Podcasts | The Guardian
description: Breakin’ the Cycle had celeb performers who hoped it would go to Cannes. Until they realised its creators were still running a drug gang while filming – and it all went very wrong
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: Breakin’ the Cycle had celeb performers who hoped it would go to Cannes. Until they realised its creators were still running a drug gang while filming – and it all went very wrong
Content: ‘Desperately trying to escape his clean tween pop image’ … Bradley McIntosh in Breakin’ the Cycle.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreen‘Desperately trying to escape his clean tween pop image’ … Bradley McIntosh in Breakin’ the Cycle.Photograph: BBCPodcastsPetrol bombs, drugs and Bradley from S Club 7: inside the wild 00s hood movie that the police seizedBreakin’ the Cycle had celeb performers who hoped it would go to Cannes. Until they realised its creators were still running a drug gang while filming – and it all went very wrongEmine SanerWed 29 Jul 2026 04.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 05.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe story of the making of the 2005 British film Breakin’ the Cycle is surely more compelling than the film itself. Nobody can say for sure, because a rough cut was confiscated by the Met police and the raw footage was considered lost. But the film’s origins and subsequent unravelling is extraordinary. Two of Hackney’s most notorious drug dealers try to go straight and become movie producers. It’s a strange combination of comedic chaos, an accidental stabbing, drug money and shootouts, big dreams of making a different life through art, and, ultimately, tragedy. The film-makers had to navigate real-life gang warfare, and an elitist, perhaps racist, film industry.The cast included the rapper Lethal Bizzle, and Bradley McIntosh from the pop group S Club 7. If McIntosh was desperately trying to escape his clean tween pop image, he wasn’t the only one trying to escape something, though the stakes were far higher for others. Colin Browne, the leader of the Hackney gang Love of Money, wrote the film while serving a prison sentence for cocaine smuggling, and directed it; he had plans to take it to the Cannes film festival. Browne would be killed shortly after filming had finished.The story is told in a new BBC Radio 4 podcast, Shadow World: Breakin’ the Cycle, by Lewis Albrow, the film’s editor. Over the last 20 years, he stayed in touch with D, Browne’s right-hand man who was also involved in the film, and who would go on to serve a prison sentence for drug dealing. “Occasionally, he would contact me and say: ‘One day we’ll finish this film, honour Colin’s legacy.’” After prison, says Albrow, “he came out a changed man. The time was right to go back and ask him questions – was he really truthful about wanting to get out of it? How does he feel about the damage he did? How did he pursue a new future? I think his answers to all of those questions are deep, truthful and fascinating. He really is the central voice in the podcast.”Now an established editor and director, back in 2005 Albrow was trying to break into film editing when he answered an online advert. Did it feel chaotic from the start? “Because I was so green, I didn’t quite know what to expect either,” says Albrow. “I knew it was low budget, so everything’s kind of scrappy. For instance, the sound was all over the place and some of it was unusable, but that got better as they got better.”Bradley McIntosh had been cast as a drug dealer. At the time, S Club 7 had come to an end and he was working on solo projects, “more R&B, trying to find a way to get out of that pop bubble and be taken a little bit more seriously. I thought [the film role] was a great opportunity for me to cross over.” He had acted in the S Club spin-off TV shows and film, but this was his first serious role (Albrow says “he delivers something amazing”).View image in fullscreenJ-Rock of Big Brovaz was one of the stars of Breakin’ the Cycle.Photograph: BBCMcIntosh was more familiar with Browne’s world than his teen pop image suggested. “Growing up around certain people, I was familiar with certain lifestyles. You see drug dealers and people that are gang members and stuff like that.” He didn’t know about Browne and D’s life at first, and thought the film was based on people who, like him, they had just seen around. “I don’t think it actually clicked until maybe halfway through filming that it was based on [their] true story,” he says.It was a fun set. “We became a family, lots of laughs every day. But there were some incidents that were kind of scary.” Filming on an estate in east London with his castmates J-Rock and Randy – from the south London hip-hop group Big Brovaz – some young men thought they were filming a music video on their patch. “They were like: ‘They can’t come round here. You got to move, otherwise we’re gonna start petrol bombing the cars.’” McIntosh smiles over Zoom. “I could see that Colin was pretty annoyed, but he did the right thing.” The cast and crew, he says, weren’t “affiliated with that lifestyle. I think in Colin’s world, he wouldn’t have wanted to show any sign of weakness, but he said, ‘Look, we’re gonna go, but we are gonna come back,’ and we did. But the next time, they had a bit of an entourage, backup.”Albrow’s job “was to deliver [Browne’s] vision. It was his voice, but I had to understand it. When you call a gangster film Breakin’ the Cycle, you are setting your stall out – this is a hopeful message. His central philosophy, I suppose, was about understanding that in his world it’s about everyone trying to escape. And that’s not my world.” He had long conversations with Browne about his life. “He’s like: ‘You’re a white middle-class man walking around [west London suburb] Hounslow, I’m a Black man who’s grown up in Hackney. We’ve had very different lives, and we see the world in a very different way.’ But he was on a trajectory. It was his first film. He comes out of prison and makes it. He went: ‘I want to do something. I’ve got to do something right.’”The transferable skills between drug-dealing and film-making are surely an entrepreneurial spirit and a refusal to be intimidated. “There’s an uncompromising thing going on,” says Albrow. “Colin was a businessman. His business was a bad business that hurt people and hurt the community, but [he had] film-making potential as a businessman and as a creative.” Many first-time film-makers plunge in without much fear, says Albrow, but Browne and D were also tough. “They were not scared of much. Their job in their criminal business was to scare others.” They both survived years in and out of prison, points out Albrow. “It’s a tough place to be. They’re going to go out and make a film, and they’re going to gangster the industry – whatever pushback they got from a fairly elitist, slightly closed group of the film and TV drama industry …” For instance, when they tried to hire an expensive camera to shoot on and were refused, they simply went out and bought one.Neither McIntosh nor Albrow knew that Browne and D continued to deal drugs while making the film. “They did a good job of keeping it from us. I think that’s called good professionalism,” says McIntosh. “I guess it’s a weird one, right, calling it professionalism?” Albrow says: “I believed they were ex-gangsters and they were out of that life. It’s not until now, 20 years later, going back and talking to D, that I understand what was going on. They were running two businesses at the same time, and getting out was not as easy as they thought. They were making a film about getting out of that life, at the same time as actively trying to get out of that life. That’s what makes this story so interesting and such a rollercoaster.”Both say the film doesn’t glorify gang violence, or the lifestyle. The original director had come from music videos, but he left a third of the way in and Browne took over. It changed, says Albrow, from being quite posturing to a “heartfelt, tender story about friendship and relationships. It’s about the connections between these people, their loyalties, betrayals.”Browne’s death at the age of 38 – he was shot and stabbed after intervening in a dispute – was shocking. Albrow and the rest of the crew tried to carry on, but then D was arrested and went to prison and the film fell apart. By then, says McIntosh: “It’s not about the film any more – someone’s lost their life. It’s about someone, a dad, a brother. But, in hindsight, it would have been nice if we had got that movie out.” It might have taken its place among London-set crime dramas, such asBullet Boyand Rollin’ with the Nines, that came out at a similar time.Albrow remembers D picked up the footage from him before he was sent to prison, and for years he thought a copy of it had died on an old hard drive. Not long ago, a specialist managed to resurrect the drive – “that was a wonderful day” – and now he has access to everything that was shot. For the past six months, Albrow has been editing it and hopes to put it out. The principal message of the film, says Albrow, is about “changing your life, and how to break out. You’ve got to have a reckoning, and you’ve got to make amends. I think Colin was ready.”Shadow World: Breakin’ the Cycle ison BBC SoundsnowExplore more on these topicsPodcastsGangsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I thought Nolan’s Odyssey was an epic bore. If you want Greek myths brought to life, try the thrill of opera! | Music | The Guardian
description: Composers from Purcell to Birtwistle have created passionate dramas inspired by ancient Greek stories – and none of them require you to sit through three hours of solemn spectacle without an interval
Author: Tom Service
Headline: Composers from Purcell to Birtwistle have created passionate dramas inspired by ancient Greek stories – and none of them require you to sit through three hours of solemn spectacle without an interval
Content: Thrilling … Berlioz’s The Trojans at the Proms in 2023 with Alice Coote (centre) as Cassandra.Photograph: Andy ParadiseView image in fullscreenThrilling … Berlioz’s The Trojans at the Proms in 2023 with Alice Coote (centre) as Cassandra.Photograph: Andy ParadiseTom Service on musicMusicI thought Nolan’s Odyssey was an epic bore. If you want Greek myths brought to life, try the thrill of opera!Tom ServiceComposers from Purcell to Birtwistle have created passionate dramas inspired by ancient Greek stories – and none of them require you to sit through three hours of solemn spectacle without an intervalWed 29 Jul 2026 08.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 08.28 EDTShareFor me, the most astonishing thing aboutChristopher Nolan’s The Odysseyis its barnstorming popularity. I found this cinematic epic for the ages visually bloodless, expressively monotonous and very, very long. Mind you, it is good to know that Nolan thinks that war is, on balance, you know, once you really think about it, probably a bad idea.The music, too, was disappointing. If I were Nolan, I’d have askedMica Levito score The Odyssey. Ludwig Göransson could have surely done more to make a soundworld of genuine strangeness, but all he could manage is a falling tritone and then a descending fifth on the two reeds and pipes of a recreatedaulos, which he uses as a melancholy leitmotif in all-too-conventional Hollywood fashion. (The aulos is beautifully played by Callum Armstrong on the soundtrack, at least.) The best sounds in the film come inthe scene with Samantha Morton’s Circe, in which the crew’s gluttony is horrorshow ASMR: surround-sound mastication that threatens to devour the audience.View image in fullscreenEpically tedious? Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesMillions of people around the world are sitting through three hours of this monumental mythoverse, without so much as an interval to break up the monotony. And this gives me hope for another artform that thrives on its hubris and excessive self-importance: opera!There is no continuous sit in the entire operatic canon that’s as long or demanding as the three hours of The Odyssey (the most even Wagner asks in a single session is the two-and-a-half hours of Das Rheingold). I promise you, if you can make it throughRobert Pattinson’s one-note scowl for 180 minutes, you are well-prepared for the demands, longueurs and joys of opera.Opera, like film, has often turned to tales of ancient Greece for inspiration: here are a few highlights in which I guarantee the music’s better, the storytelling more compelling, and the emotional experience more involving than Nolan’s film. And when appropriate, there are intervals, too!Strauss: ElektraRichard Strauss’s savagely dramatic opera takes you by the throat from the start and doesn’t relent with its crimson orchestral dissonance and the bloodbath of the drama. Elektra embarks on a devastating journey of vengeance to appease her mother Klytämnestra’s murder of her father, Agamemnon, a journey that will consume everyone in the story – including herself, as she dances to oblivion before the curtain goes down.Mozart: IdomeneoElectra – as Mozart’s libretto spells her name – is another of the storm-tossed characters in his opera that broke all the conventions of so-calledopera seria(“serious opera”, often based on mythological subjects) in the early 1780s. Mozart’s music releases magical tempests and unholy monsters to tell the story of Idomeneo’s sacrifice of his son, Idamante, as well as Electra’s jealousy of Idamante’s lover, Ilia. It’s arguably Mozart’s single most adventurous score – Greek myth turned into contemporary parable.View image in fullscreenMusical myths: the Monteverdi Choir and English Baroque Soloists perform Purcell’s Dido and Aeneas at the Cutty Sark in London.Photograph: Paul Marc MitchellPurcell: Dido and AeneasVirgil’s Aeneid was the source for Purcell’s one-act opera that tells the story of the Queen of Carthage and her faithless lover. Her lament at the end of the opera is one of music’s most moving mandalas of mourning, a piece that’s become so powerful that it’s turned into its own musical myth.Berlioz: The TrojansBerlioz’s magnum opus, again on the Aeneid, has all the variety and character Nolan’s Odyssey lacks. There’s one of opera’s most shatteringly empathic characters in his portrayal of Dido; there are standout moments of thrilling orchestral imagination; and throughout, there’s the feeling that this is a drama in which all the characters are caught in a web of their own desires, set against the whims of the gods, and the ineluctable wheel of human history, as Carthage falls and Rome rises.View image in fullscreenJohn Tomlinson and Johan Reuter in The Minotaur by Harrison Birtwistle at the Royal Opera House in 2008.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianBirtwistle: The MinotaurSomething else thatThe Odysseyonly glimpses as a movie is the human connection at the heart of the supernatural phenomena of ancient Greek myths. Birtwistle makes his Minotaur the most fully dimensional creation on stage: his half-bull, half-human antihero is Asterios, the son of Pasiphaë and Poseidon, condemned to be caught between worlds, questioning his purpose as murderous labyrinthine horror – and as a character whose existential agonies are amplified by the callousness of the humans who visit him.The music in Nolan’s Odyssey is as well-crafted – and bloodlessly forgettable – as the film itselfRead moreAnd that’s just the start: what of Gluck’s Telemaco or Handel’s Teseo or Charpentier’s Medée or Tippett’s King Priam or Jacquet de la Guerre’s Céphale et Procris or Tom Smail’s forthcoming, er,The Odyssey? And then there’sOrfeo, or Orpheus in the Underworld and The Mask of Orpheus … There are hundreds more Greek-inspired operas out there to start your operatic odyssey and whichever you choose, I guarantee you Nolan-levels of ambition, and better music, better characters, and more fulfilling experiences, especially in the flesh of live performance. No need to tie yourself to the mast – just get to the opera house, where myths come to lifeThis week Tom has been listening to:Stravinsky’s poker-inspired balletJeu de cartes. This was one of the first pieces of his I ever heard – my mum had an LP of Colin Davisconducting it. I loved its fun, its wit and its surreal drama. And then read how it was one of Stravinsky’s supposedly less successful pieces. Never trust the judgments of biographers who should know better: enjoy this piece for how it sends up everyone from Rossini to Beethoven and even Stravinsky himself.
