title: ‘It sounds good next to almost anything’: how Choosin’ Texas became the biggest song of the year | Country | The Guardian
description: Ella Langley’s country single has spent 15 weeks as US number one thanks to its retro-modern sound, a viral misheard lyric – and a boost from the Ella Fellas
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ella Langley’s country single has spent 15 weeks as US number one thanks to its retro-modern sound, a viral misheard lyric – and a boost from the Ella Fellas
Content: Ella Langley performs at CMA Fest, Nashville, on 4 June 2026.Photograph: Taylor Hill/FilmMagicView image in fullscreenElla Langley performs at CMA Fest, Nashville, on 4 June 2026.Photograph: Taylor Hill/FilmMagicCountry‘It sounds good next to almost anything’: how Choosin’ Texas became the biggest song of the yearElla Langley’s country single has spent 15 weeks as US number one thanks to its retro-modern sound, a viral misheard lyric – and a boost from the Ella FellasWill GroffWed 29 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 17.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis week, Ella Langley beat a chart record held byWhitney HoustonandMariah Carey. The country singer’sChoosin’ Texashas now spent 15 weeks atop the BillboardHot 100, making it the longest-running US No 1 by a female solo artist for a non-holiday single. The previous record holders, Houston’s I Will Always Love You and Carey’s We Belong Together, were bombastic pop events, the sort of unassailable hits that make sense as Hot 100 chartbusters. Choosin’ Texas, meanwhile, is a midtempo two-step with a relaxed vocal delivery and decidedly retro sound.For Victoria Banks, a Nashville-based songwriter and instructor at Belmont University, the song’s breeziness is key to its success. “It’s a sleeper hit – it’s understated and unassuming,” she says. “Everything about the song throws back to a simpler time in country music that people are really craving.”‘A sublime, breezy confection’: writers on their 2026 songs of the summerRead moreThe lyrics to Choosin’ Texas tell the story of a Tennessee woman who accompanies her lover on a trip back to his home state of Texas – and discovers in real time that “his heart still belongs to the Lone Star state”. It’s heartbreak on a classic-country scale, which Langley expresses with lyrical homages to decades-old hits by Jerry Reed, Ronnie Millsap and George Strait. The danceable, guitar- and pedal steel-forward production evokes country hits from the late 70s and early 80s, albeit with a contemporary gloss.“There are a lot of throwback elements to the song, but it was obviously recorded in a very modern way,” Banks says. “It’s not so throwback that we don’t relate to it.”In a sign of country music’s continued dominance in the pop sphere, Choosin’ Texas is one of five country songs currently in the US top 10 on the all-genre Hot 100. Given country’sabysmal track recordwhen it comes to playing women, it’s not for nothing that each of these songs – includingTaylor Swift’s I Knew It, I Knew You, Stella Lefty’s Boston and Langley’s own Be Her and her Morgan Wallen duet I Can’t Love You Anymore – features a woman as the lead artist.Historically, during moments when country crosses over into the mainstream, tensions arise over just how far the music has strayed from its roots. “Someone killed country music, cut out its heart and soul,” George Strait famously declared onMurder on Music Row, a 2000 duet with Alan Jackson lamenting the state of the Nashville industry in the late 90s – when artists including Faith Hill and Lonestar ruled the airwaves with ultrasmooth, country-pop confections. In more recent history,Beyoncé’s Cowboy Carter provoked endlessdiscourseabout what constitutes country music and who gets to participate.Choosin’ Texas has largely dodged criticism of being “too pop”, in part due to the cleverness of the songwriting. Co-written with Miranda Lambert, Joybeth Taylor and Luke Dick, the song folds country signifiers – two-stepping, Texas and Tennessee, the interstate – into the emotional story in a way that feels organic. Even the requisite Jack Daniels mention serves a narrative purpose; it matters that it’s Tennessee whiskey she’s drinking all by herself.“All of these writers have been working in the Nashville market for years,” Banks explains. “So even though this is a song that they said they spat out in 30 minutes or whatever, it was coming through their instincts that have been developed for a long time about what is hooky and what pulls people in.”View image in fullscreenBeyoncé accepting the best country album award for Cowboy Carter at the 2025 Grammy awards.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for The Recording AcademyBrian Mansfield, managing editor of the trade publicationCountry Insider, says that the song’s twangy-but-smooth sound makes it appealing to program directors – whether in country, pop or adult contemporary – who tend to avoid songs that would sound jarringly rootsy next to fluffier pop fare. “It’s a song that sounds good next to almost anything you can play, and that is an underrated part of creating the music mix for any format,” he says.The song’s versatility also makes it well-suited to streaming playlists. According toLuminate, Choosin’ Texas racked up over half a billion streams in the first half of the year alone, making it the most-streamed song in the country by a wide margin.As well as co-signs from veteran singers such asSwiftandShania Twain, the song has also – as is now often a prerequisite for streaming success – been boosted by various viral social media moments. In October, shortly after Choosin’ Texas was released, TikTok user Lane Gorrell posted avideoof himself performing an interpretive dance to the song in front of some nonplussed-looking cows. The clip racked up millions of views, and Gorrell eventually took his dance all the way to theGrand Ole Opry.Then came the misheard lyric videos. Around January, in an echo of Taylor Swift’s famous “Starbucks lovers”sagafrom 2014, users started posting videos claiming they misheard the title phrase as “Jews in Texas” or even “Jews and Taxes”. Some also reported hearing the words “drinking Jack all by myself” as “drink and jack off by myself”. Langley laughed off the misheard lyrics in aninterviewwith podcaster Theo Von in April – which of course only drew more attention to the trend. A clip from the same interview of a clearly smitten Vonbutcheringthe word “tzatziki” in front of his crush also went viral.View image in fullscreenLangley photographed for her album Dandelion.Photograph: Courtesy Sony MusicEnter the Ella Fellas. Langley’s male fanbase has made itself known with all manner of viral content, fromuncomfortably earnestlip-syncing videosto clips of themselveslooking enrapturedat her concerts; there have even been Ella Fellabirthday parties. Langley’s team has nurtured this following, reposting popular videos and sending Ella Fellas T-shirts to some of her most ardent supporters. In comparison with many pop fandoms, whose obsessions can skewantisocial, the Ella Fellas seem like a remarkably sane and joyous bunch.How gen Z women are conquering country music: ‘Fans are speaking louder than gatekeepers’Read more“It’s one of those things that brings people together,” says Hunter Massey, a student at Georgia Southern University and TikToker whose videos of himselfgoing buck wildto country songs have earned him an audience of his own. “There can be people from different walks of life, different parts of the country, but we all seem to have this love for her music, and that’s what makes us Ella Fellas.”Massey is among the growing ranks of creators who get paid to post videos using artists’ songs on TikTok – including Langley’s. He says he sometimes turns down requests for songs that don’t speak to him, but he’s never had a problem promoting her music.For him and other Ella Fellas, the appeal is in how down-to-earth she seems. She’s bolstered this perception with songs includingDandelion, where she sings that she “wasn’t made for a fancy crystal vase” and Somethin’ Simple, which finds her musing about giving up stardom in exchange for “a house on a hill, horse in the yard”.“She’s not flashy, Hollywood, whatever,” Massey says. “It’s what we like about her.”Explore more on these topicsCountryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Staff at newest V&A site in London vote overwhelmingly for strike action | V&A | The Guardian
description: V&A Storehouse dispute centres on toilet and hydration breaks as employees across V&A in London also vote to strike in wider action
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: V&A Storehouse dispute centres on toilet and hydration breaks as employees across V&A in London also vote to strike in wider action
Content: The V&A Storehouse offers an ‘order an object’ service which requires staff members to retrieve items requested by members of the public from around the building.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe V&A Storehouse offers an ‘order an object’ service which requires staff members to retrieve items requested by members of the public from around the building.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianV&AStaff at newest V&A site in London vote overwhelmingly for strike actionV&A Storehouse dispute centres on toilet and hydration breaks as employees across V&A in London also vote to strike in wider actionNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentWed 29 Jul 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStaff at the V&A’s Storehouse site in eastLondonhave voted overwhelmingly to strike in a dispute over what they say are inadequate toilet and hydration breaks.They will join staff across V&A sites in London who on Wednesday also voted to strike in a wider dispute over pay, working conditions, andthe museum having declined to seek living wage accreditation.The trade union Prospect said members at V&A Storehouse, which opened in May 2025, are denied enough time during the day for toilet breaks or hydration.The dispute centres on collections access officers who facilitate the “order an object” service, a central part of the Storehouse’s offering of public access to its vast collection.The union is calling for two paid breaks a day, saying staff need time to use the toilet and hydrate during what it describes as a punishing schedule. It said a collective grievance failed to secure an “extremely reasonable request for customary paid breaks”, which workers elsewhere in the organisation receive.Prospect said many of the staff had been recruited from the local community, something the V&A had highlighted publicly, but they were treated worse than colleagues at other sites.One Prospect member told the Guardian: “We get just one unpaid lunch hour, even though we’re on our feet for long hours, interacting with the public and doing a lot of manual labour.“Breaks are a welfare issue. The Storehouse is purpose-built for storing objects, but they haven’t really thought about the human aspect – how far we have to travel around the building or where the bathrooms are.“We’ve experienced a lot of dehydration, and sometimes people don’t even go to the bathroom for the whole day.”They added: “We’ve tried every internal procedure possible. We’ve brought the issue up in one-to-one meetings, we did a petition, we went through a formal grievance, and we’ve never got proper answers.”V&A East Storehouse and Norwich Castle among finalists for museum of the yearRead moreAnother Prospect member said: “Every day we go into work, there’s someone who has a headache because they’re dehydrated. Management says we always have time to take breaks and drink water.“But we need someone to relieve us because we can’t leave trolleys of collection objects unattended. We need breaks scheduled fixed into our calendars.“We are the newest department at the V&A. We are the most diverse back-of-house department. It’s not lost on us that we were hired to represent the east London community, but our welfare is being neglected.”At V&A Storehouse, 100% of those voting backed strike action on a turnout of nearly 88%, while 92% supported action short of a strike.As part of the wider dispute, Prospect is seeking a minimum 4% pay rise for staff earning above the living wage, time-and-a-half for bank holiday working, accreditation as a London living wage employer within 12 months and improved food provision at V&A East sites.Across the V&A, 83% voted for strike action on an 82% turnout, and 95% voted for action short of a strike. The timing of any industrial action has yet to be decided.Mike Clancy, Prospect’s general secretary, said: “This incredible new way of showing off our heritage is being delivered by workers who are denied adequate break time to use the toilet or have a drink of water.“Visitors will be appalled to learn that the kinds of working practices unions campaign against in companies like Amazon also exist in an internationally renowned heritage institution.”He said the dispute reflected “a shocking lack of respect” for staff across the museum.The V&A has been approached for comment. Responding previously toa separate strike ballot by the Public and Commercial Services union, it said all staff had access to water, toilet facilities and regular breaks, and pointed to additional measures introduced during this summer’s heatwave, including extra rest breaks, staff rotations and temporary gallery closures.The London living wage is£14.80 an hour. While the V&A has said all its staff are paid at least this rate, some of the museum’s outsourced contractors are not in receipt of the living wage and V&A has not so far become an accredited living wage employer, although it says this will be reviewed this year. V&A Dundee is an accredited living wage employer.Explore more on these topicsV&ALondonEnglandIndustrial actionTrade unionsMuseumsnewsShareReuse this content

title: BTS boycott Grammys after introduction of new Asian pop prize | BTS | The Guardian
description: K-pop superstars will not submit Arirang album or its songs for 2027 ceremony
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: K-pop superstars will not submit Arirang album or its songs for 2027 ceremony
Content: BTS in March.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenBTS in March.Photograph: ReutersBTSBTS boycott Grammys after introduction of new Asian pop prizeK-pop superstars will not submit Arirang album or its songs for 2027 ceremonyBen Beaumont-ThomasWed 29 Jul 2026 12.47 EDTFirst published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBTS, the biggest pop act in east Asia, have withdrawn themselves from the 2027 Grammy awards, intimating that their decision is due to the addition of a new award for best Asian pop music performance.Writing on Instagram, each of the South Korean group’s seven members said: “We have decided not to enter theGrammysthis year. I hope that music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language.”The comments are a striking – if gently worded – rebuke of the Recording Academy’s new category announced last month.The decision to add the category was due to “our music community sharing with us that they felt they needed to have more opportunities to celebrate different and new genres of music,” Academy president Harvey Mason Jr said when announcing the Asian pop award, along with another regionally specific award, best Latin song.BTS: Arirang review – the world’s biggest pop band return with dumb fun and downright weirdnessRead moreThat was perhaps unfortunate wording, given Asian and Latin pop markets are far from “new”: each command vast revenues and audiences, including in the US, after decades of maturity. There have therefore been fears in the Asian pop sphere that the category could end up ringfencing Asian pop artists away from contention in the top categories.The Recording Academy has not commented on BTS’s decision. The Guardian has requested comment.Asian pop artists have traditionally been ignored by the US-centric awards show – noK-popact was even nominated until BTS in 2021 – but they had a good showing at this year’s ceremony. Golden, from hit film KPop Demon Hunters, won best song written for visual media, the first win for a K-pop act. Golden was also up for one of the “big four” prizes, song of the year, alongside another K-pop artist, Rosé, for her Bruno Mars duet APT. The latter was also nominated for record of the year and best pop duo/group performance but lost in all three categories to US or British artists.View image in fullscreenRosé, who was nominated for three Grammys at this year’s ceremony.Photograph: Jill Connelly/EPAThe majority of lyrics in Golden and APT are in English, so they may not have qualified for the new Asian pop category, which requires “meaningful use” of an Asian language. But BTS’s recent material on their hugely successful albumArirangis overwhelmingly in Korean, making them a near-certainty for inclusion in the new category.This year’s Grammys also marked the first time a Spanish language album has won album of the year, with Bad Bunny winning for Debí Tirar Más Fotos.Other new categories being added for 2027 are best R&B collaboration or duo/group performance, best traditional pop vocal performance and best traditional folk album.The ceremony will take place on 7 February in Los Angeles.Explore more on these topicsBTSGrammysK-popPop and rocknewsShareReuse this content

title: Glen Hansard, Oscar-winning Irish singer-songwriter, dies aged 56 in motorcycle crash | Music | The Guardian
description: Frontman of chart-topping band the Frames had huge success as the star of 2007 romantic drama Once
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Frontman of chart-topping band the Frames had huge success as the star of 2007 romantic drama Once
Content: Glen Hansard pictured in 2017.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAView image in fullscreenGlen Hansard pictured in 2017.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAMusicGlen Hansard, Oscar-winning Irish singer-songwriter, dies aged 56 in motorcycle crashFrontman of chart-topping band the Frames had huge success as the star of 2007 romantic drama OnceBen Beaumont-ThomasWed 29 Jul 2026 07.55 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 19.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGlen Hansard, the Irish folk-rock musician and actor who fronted the band the Frames and had Oscar-winning success with the2007 film Once, has died aged 56.He died in a motorcycle crash in Lucan on the outskirts of Dublin, early on Wednesday morning. Without naming him, Irish police said he was treated at the scene for his injuries but died a short time later.Hansard won the Oscar for best original song for Falling Slowly, the centrepiece of Once, which starred Hansard opposite another real-life musician, Markéta Irglová, playing two struggling musicians in Dublin who embark on a tentative romance; Irglová co-wrote the song and shared the Oscar with Hansard. Once was then successfully adapted into astage musical in 2011.Hansard was also the frontman of the Frames, who released six studio albums, including 2004 Irish chart-topper Burn the Maps.A statement from Hansard’s representatives reads: “Glen’s family is deeply shocked and heartbroken by this tragic loss and respectfully requests privacy at this extremely difficult time. The family is grateful for the support they have received and wishes to thank the emergency services who attended the scene. As this matter remains the subject of an active Garda investigation, no further comment will be made at this time.”Among those paying tribute was Ireland’s culture minister, Patrick O’Donovan, who said: “Few artists made as big an impact on modern Irish storytelling … Hansard consistently poured passion and vulnerability into every note. His impact will last generations in Irish music, even as his life has ended far too soon.”Bruce Springsteen recalled meeting Hansard in Ireland “many years ago.”“He was always nothing but a great musician, a good friend and a generous and gracious man,” hewrote on social media. “Always positive, smiling and ready to sing.”Bonowrote a lengthy tribute, remembering Hansard as an “angelic presence” and “a smiling rascal if you needed him to be”.“For me, he will always be everywhere I see a coin spinning into an open guitar case,” he wrote.Warren Elliscalledhim “a good man and loyal friend” while band the Mountain Goatsposted, “His love of music was palpable, infectious, radiant.”Hansard had genuinely lived Once’s story of a busker down on his luck: he had started out performing on the streets of Dublin, having dropped out of school early.He formed the Frames in his late teens, named for his hobby of fixing up bicycle frames which populated his back garden. His mother secured a bank loan for their earliest recordings: “She went to the bank manager and asked could she get the house done up,” Hansard later said.Buoyed by being signed to Island Records, he recruited a range of local musicians and they released their debut Another Love Song in 1991. Island dropped them, without foreseeing the band’s growing potential: subsequent albums became more and more popular, and they caught the ear of legendary recording engineer Steve Albini who oversaw their first Irish Top 10 release, 2001’s For the Birds. Its followup Burn the Maps hit No 1 and their final studio album The Cost reached No 2.View image in fullscreenHansard performing in 2002.Photograph: mct/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockThe Cost featured the Hansard-Irglová duet Falling Slowly, which the pair also recorded in their duo the Swell Season, who had formed away from the Frames. Irglová met Hansard when she was in her mid-teens, after her father promoted Frames concerts in her native Czechia, and she was invited to contribute backing vocals.The film Once was written and directed by John Carney, who had once played bass in the Frames, and who signed up Irglová as one of the leads, with Cillian Murphy being courted for the male lead. Murphy turned down the role, leading Carney to cast an initially reluctant Hansard, who had only acted once before with a role in 1991’s The Commitments.“I don’t remember having any real connection with the creative process during The Commitments other than showing up on set at the right time and speaking my lines,” Hansard reflected in 2009. “The emotional investment was much higher in Once. It’s just you and your mates and if anyone’s in bad form it’s not going to work, so it was a case of throwing yourself into it completely.”Despite its small crew and a low budget, Once went on to gross more than $20m worldwide, and Falling Slowly was Grammy-nominated in addition to its Oscar win.The on-screen romance was mirrored in real life, despite the age gap between Hansard and Irglová, who were 37 and 19 at the time of filming. “I had been falling in love with her for a long time, but I kept telling myself she’s just a kid,” Hansard said, with Irglová saying: “The friendship and connection that you’re watching on screen between Glen and I exists, and it did grow into a deeper love afterwards.”They split in 2009, the year they released second Swell Season album Strict Joy, though a documentary was made about the pair in 2011 and they reunited as musicians for a third album, 2025’s Forward. They also recorded a song in 2022, Take Heart, with Ukrainian refugees.The Frames became less of a focus for Hansard after his Once success – though new songs were recorded for the 2015 compilation album Longitude – and beginning with 2012’s Rhythm and Repose, he released five solo albums.He did not pursue acting further, but did appear as a voice actor on an episode of The Simpsons, and recorded a song for the soundtrack of The Hunger Games.In 2023 he had the honour of performing the Pogues’ Fairytale of New York at the funeral of that band’s frontman, Shane MacGowan.Hansard is survived by his wife, Finnish poet Maire Saaritsa, and their three-year-old son Christy. He spoke of fatherhood in a 2023 interview: “For 52 years I was the most important person in my own life, and then suddenly I got a complete perspective shift, and I’m absolutely loving it.”Each year, he returned to busking on Dublin’s Grafton Street to raise money for the city’s homeless.Once went on to have a remarkable second life thanks to its stage adaptation, written by Enda Walsh and directed by John Tiffany. It opened on Broadway in 2012 and was nominated for 11 Tony awards that year, winning eight. It then ran in Dublin and London’s West End, and has since been revived numerous times in globe-spanning productions.Explore more on these topicsMusicFolk musicPop and rockIrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: French music producer Kavinsky, known for Drive soundtrack hit Nightcall, dies aged 50 | Electronic music | The Guardian
description: French authorities investigate death of musician who performed at Paris Olympics, but say ‘no suspicious elements’ at play
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: French authorities investigate death of musician who performed at Paris Olympics, but say ‘no suspicious elements’ at play
Content: Kavinsky performing at the 2024 Olympic Games closing ceremony in Paris.Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKavinsky performing at the 2024 Olympic Games closing ceremony in Paris.Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty ImagesElectronic musicFrench music producer Kavinsky, known for Drive soundtrack hit Nightcall, dies aged 50French authorities investigate death of musician who performed at Paris Olympics, but say ‘no suspicious elements’ at playBen Beaumont-ThomasWed 29 Jul 2026 07.55 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe French electronic musician Kavinsky, known for the song Nightcall which achieved iconic status after its inclusion in the Ryan Gosling filmDrive, has died aged 50.A police source speaking to French newspaper Le Figaro indicated that the suspected cause of death was a stroke. Kavinsky, real name Vincent Belorgey, had reportedly been complaining of headaches in recent days, and he was discovered at home after a concerned neighbour alerted emergency services.Parisian authorities are investigating his death but said “no suspicious elements” were found at his home.Emmanuel Macron was among those paying tribute to him, calling him “a source of French pride forever”.Part of the rich electronic music scene inFrancethat flourished in the wake of Daft Punk and others, Belorgey earned so much acclaim for Nightcall that he ended up performing it at the closing ceremony of the Olympic Games in Paris in 2024, backed by the French band Phoenix and Belgian pop singer Angèle on vocals.Born in Paris in 1975, Belorgey’s music career took off in the mid-00s. The high-energy electro of his debut singleTestarossa Autodrivemeant it dovetailed with the “blog house” scene that had also spawned French artists such as Justice and SebastiAn, and he was signed to the label Record Makers, with whom he released five EPs and two albums.With Brazilian singer Lovefoxxx on vocals, 2010’s Nightcall became his most successful and renowned track. Co-produced with Daft Punk member Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo, this prowling, nocturnal electronic reverie paired malevolence and romance in a way that made it a perfect choice for the opening credits of Nicolas Winding Refn’s 2011 thriller Drive. It has been streamed more than half a billion times onSpotifyalone, with another 350m YouTube plays. It reached the French Top 10 on release, with the version performed at the Olympics reaching No 3.His debut album Outrun sketched out the grand concept for Belorgey’s Kavinsky alter ego – a young man who crashes a Ferrari Testarossa in the 80s and returns zombie-like in the 00s – and it reached No 2 in the French album charts. He followed it with Reborn, in 2022.Along with the vintage Ferrari references and sunglasses-and-bomber-jacket fashion sense, his sound also harked back to 1980s and that decade’s cinematic synths. “Everyone says, that guy is stuck in the past!”, he said in a 2013 interview. “I don’t sit around missing things from older times – I’m just from the 80s, and so my influences come from that period. That is what is in my veins.”The Weeknd appeared on a version of Kavinsky’s songOdd Look, and in 2022 Kavinsky said the pair would potentially work on new music together.Also paying tribute was French culture minister Catherine Pégard, who said: “France loses one of its most singular voices. From the film Drive to the Paris Olympics, the entire world had pulsed to Nightcall. Both danceable and nostalgic, his music will continue to resonate across generations and borders.”Explore more on these topicsElectronic musicPop and rockParisFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Andrew Scott’s Oscar-tipped Ian Charleson biopic to open London film festival | London film festival | The Guardian
description: ‘Few films will leave a lasting imprint on audiences this year quite like Elsinore,’ LFF director says of movie about Chariots of Fire actor
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: ‘Few films will leave a lasting imprint on audiences this year quite like Elsinore,’ LFF director says of movie about Chariots of Fire actor
Content: Andrew Scott in Elsinore.Photograph: Anthony Dickenson/© Focus FeaturesView image in fullscreenAndrew Scott in Elsinore.Photograph: Anthony Dickenson/© Focus FeaturesLondon film festivalAndrew Scott’s Oscar-tipped Ian Charleson biopic to open London film festival‘Few films will leave a lasting imprint on audiences this year quite like Elsinore,’ LFF director says of movie about Chariots of Fire actorCatherine ShoardWed 29 Jul 2026 09.22 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 10.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElsinore, one of the most hotly anticipated dramas of the year, has been announced as the opening night film at this year’sLondon film festival. The drama, which stars Andrew Scott as actor Ian Charleson, will have its European premiere at the Southbank Centre – yards from the National Theatre, in which many of its scenes are set.Directed bySimon Stoneand written by Stephen Beresford (who reunites with Scott 12 years after Pride), the film depicts the final months in the life of the highly acclaimed actor, who reprised the role of Hamlet while terminally ill, aged 40.Diagnosed with Aids in 1986, the actor – who had come to international fame through his roles in Chariots of Fire and Gandhi – was drafted in by Richard Eyre to take over the role of Hamlet in a 1989 production after Daniel Day-Lewis abruptly left, having seen theghost of his fatheron stage.Charleson, who concentrated on classical theatre work both before and after his film success, persuaded Eyre to let him reprise the role he had first played 15 years before, despite the director’s misgivings over his health. Both fellow cast and crew, as well as the audience, were told that Charleson’s face was swollen following a sinus operation; in fact he was suffering from septicaemia.Charleson’s performance, which ran for six weeks until mid-November, was widely felt to be one of the finest ever seen on stage. The day after his final show, Ian McKellen refused the Evening Standard award for best actor and instead gave his statuette to Charleson.View image in fullscreenIan Charleson, centre, in Chariots of Fire.Photograph: Moviestore/Rex/ShutterstockCharleson died eight weeks later and was the first showbiz star in the UK to request that Aids be listed as the cause of death, leading to considerably more awareness about the condition.The film also starsOlivia Colmanas Charleson’s doctor, alongside Billie Piper, Johnny Flynn and Monica Dolan. Dickie Beau, who toured a one-man tribute to Charleson’s Hamlet for six years, also features, while David Dawson plays Derek Jarman. It is believed Juliet Stevenson and Peter Mullan play Charleson’s parents.Elsinore has also been selected as a gala screening at the Toronto film festival, with a world premiere a week beforehand at the Telluride film festival predicted.Kristy Matheson, BFI London film festival director, said: “Anchored by Andrew Scott’s astounding central performance, few films will leave a lasting imprint on audiences this year quite like Elsinore.” The actor’s role in the film has already attracted considerable awards buzz, with many anticipating voters will be keen to reward a popular actor whose role inAll of Us Strangerswas overlooked in both Oscar and Bafta nominations.Elsinore opens in the US on 20 November and in the UK on 29 January. The London film festival is on 7-18 October.Explore more on these topicsLondon film festivalAndrew ScottOlivia ColmanSimon StonenewsShareReuse this content

title: Dua Lipa to interview Zadie Smith at London Literature festival | Books | The Guardian
description: The pop star is curating the 2026 festival, which also features Patti Smith, Mustafa and Ta-Nehisi Coates, as part of the Southbank Centre’s anniversary year
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: The pop star is curating the 2026 festival, which also features Patti Smith, Mustafa and Ta-Nehisi Coates, as part of the Southbank Centre’s anniversary year
Content: Dua Lipa is curating this year’s London Literature festival.Photograph: Madison PhippsView image in fullscreenDua Lipa is curating this year’s London Literature festival.Photograph: Madison PhippsBooksDua Lipa to interview Zadie Smith at London Literature festivalThe pop star is curating the 2026 festival, which also features Patti Smith, Mustafa and Ta-Nehisi Coates, as part of the Southbank Centre’s anniversary yearEmma LoffhagenWed 29 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZadie Smith, Patti Smith and Mustafa are among the star names lined up to be interviewed by Dua Lipa, as the pop star reveals her curation of this year’s London Literature festival at theSouthbank Centre.The festival, now in its 19th year, will run from 21 October to 1 November, with the Brit award-winning singer shaping a programme of events in collaboration with her Service95 book club.Lipa said curating the programme had been “a true joy”, adding that she wanted to bring together “some of the most exciting writers, poets and thinkers from around the globe”, alongside more familiar names.Lipa will sit down withZadie Smithon 24 October to discuss her 2000 debut novel, White Teeth, published when Smith was just 24. The pair are expected to reflect on “learning to live with an artistic legacy earned at such a young age”, and how the novel’s characters might fare in Britain today.The night after, she will interviewPatti Smithabouther memoir Bread of Angels,which charts Smith’s life from childhood, through her marriage to Fred “Sonic” Smith, and her return to music after his death.View image in fullscreenZadie Smith will discuss her novel White Teeth.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamyThe programme will also feature appearances from the Sudanese Canadian poet and musicianMustafa,the Nobel peace laureate Nadia Murad discussing her memoir, I Choose My Beginning, and a conversation between Ta-Nehisi Coates and Tareq Baconi on Baconi’s new book about Palestine.Other events include a translated fiction showcase, a poetry and music night with Kae Tempest, and Censorship Live!, a collaboration with English PEN examining threats to free expression.Lipa has increasingly established herself as an advocate for reading. She launched her book club in 2023 as an extension of her wider cultural platform Service95, which sees monthly selections and long-form author interviews with writers including Margaret Atwood, George Saunders and Olga Tokarczuk. Last month, she opened a permanent collection of 100 banned, censored and challenged books inside the historic Livraria Lello bookshop in Porto, Portugal.Mark Ball, the Southbank Centre’s artistic director, said Lipa’s “deep curiosity about the world” made her a fitting curator for the venue’s 75th anniversary. “It’s a milestone year and she’s the perfect curator to help us celebrate it,” he added.The literature festival also includes free family events and a wider national programme, part of Southbank Centre’s efforts to reach a million people across the UK in 2026.Last year, the festival was curated by Self Esteem, and previous headliners include Ai Weiwei, Greta Thunberg, Malala Yousafzai, Margaret Atwood, Philip Pullman, Tom Hanks and Yulia Navalnaya.Tickets go on sale to Southbank Centre members on 3 August, Service95 members on 4 August, and the general public on 5 August.Explore more on these topicsBooksDua LipaSouthbank CentreZadie SmithPatti SmithFestivalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: BBCSO/Oramo review – Turnage’s satisfying and clever Festen Suite makes UK debut  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The festering atmosphere of Thomas Vinterberg’s film and its celebrated opera adaptation lingers in this vivid orchestration, a foil to Sibelius’s cathartic second symphony
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: The festering atmosphere of Thomas Vinterberg’s film and its celebrated opera adaptation lingers in this vivid orchestration, a foil to Sibelius’s cathartic second symphony
Content: ‘A hip-shimmy and wriggle’ … Sakari Oramo conducting the BBC Symphony Orchestra at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreen‘A hip-shimmy and wriggle’ … Sakari Oramo conducting the BBC Symphony Orchestra at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewBBCSO/Oramo review – Turnage’s satisfying and clever Festen Suite makes UK debutRoyal Albert Hall, LondonThe festering atmosphere of Thomas Vinterberg’s film and its celebrated opera adaptation lingers in this vivid orchestration, a foil to Sibelius’s cathartic second symphonyAlexandra CoghlanWed 29 Jul 2026 08.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 10.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSibelius’s second symphony is “a confession of the soul” – an outpouring, however ambiguous. But what happens when a confession never comes, and a secret festers instead in collective silence? That’s the starting point for Festen, Thomas Vinterberg’s 1998 film, which wasadapted into an award-winning operaby Mark-Anthony Turnage and librettist Lee Hall last year.There’s a fair bit of plot to a work in which incestuous child abuse is exposed during a patriarch’s 60th birthday party, but it’s the atmosphere that lingers, stylishly distilled in Turnage’s new Festen Suite – receiving its UK premiere here from theBBC Symphony Orchestraand Sakari Oramo.You can almost smell the stale wine and cigar smoke coming off the composer’s vividly orchestrated prelude, gurning with faux-jollity – literally beaten into it by percussion wallops that try to keep its lurching progress on track. Thereafter, the eight-movement suite ricochets between lyricism – the gentle melancholy of Blue or Green, pastoral tenderness in Grandma’s Song – and denial, slinky in the Conga with its rictus grin, sleazy in Interlude I. Then revelations break the surface in the jabbing thrusts of The Fight, string padding stripped away to allow brass and woodwind to land their punches cleanly. It’s cleverly made and musically satisfying on its own terms, without the dramatic scaffolding of the opera. I think we’ll be hearing it a lot in future.View image in fullscreenSensitively faithful to Britten’s conception: cellist Guy Johnston with Oramo and the BBCSOPhotograph: Mark AllanIf the Turnage brought a hip-shimmy and wriggle to Oramo’s conducting, the Sibelius – home turf for the Finn – found him straight as a Scots pine, guiding us through this patchwork of a symphony with clarity, that finale in sight from the off. Momentum rather than release was the order of the day, until at last he let the brass off the leash, romping us home with grandeur, certainly, but also an overflowing joy.It was the catharsis we needed after Britten’s inscrutable cello symphony. Soloist Guy Johnston stayed scrupulously, sensitively faithful to the composer’s conception: the orchestra’s equal, often a part of the texture rather than its focus. It’s a tough balance to pull off anywhere; in the Royal Albert Hall it risked disappearing entirely in a cerebral performance whose subtleties will have been captured on radio, but which were a little lost in the moment.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicProms 2026BBC Symphony OrchestraMark-Anthony TurnageJean SibeliusPromsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Tinie Tempah’s popular house extension series returns  | Television | The Guardian
description: Great Gatsby glamour and a sailing theme guide two house-proud couples. Plus: Katie Price’s kids talk about their turbulent lives. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Great Gatsby glamour and a sailing theme guide two house-proud couples. Plus: Katie Price’s kids talk about their turbulent lives. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Transforming their Norfolk cottage … Jenny and James with Tinie Tempah (centre) in Extraordinary Extensions.Photograph: Channel 4View image in fullscreenTransforming their Norfolk cottage … Jenny and James with Tinie Tempah (centre) in Extraordinary Extensions.Photograph: Channel 4TV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Tinie Tempah’s popular house extension series returnsGreat Gatsby glamour and a sailing theme guide two house-proud couples. Plus: Katie Price’s kids talk about their turbulent lives. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil Harrison,Hannah J Davies,Ali Catterall,Priya ElanandSimon WardellWed 29 Jul 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExtraordinary Extensions8pm, Channel 4Tinie Tempah is back with his surprisingly popular series about house extensions. The first wealthy couple are “unleashing Great Gatsby glamour on to their Edwardian terrace”; the second are transforming their chocolate-box cottage in Norfolk with an eco-build inspired by their love of sailing. Just one concern is that they will finish the job, then wish they had never bothered.Hollie RichardsonHoratio’s Drive: America’s First Road Trip1.15pm, PBS AmericaIt’s Ken Burns Day on PBS America, as the titan of US documentary is celebrated. The pick is this funny, fascinating film about Dr Horatio Nelson Jackson (voiced by Tom Hanks) and his eccentric, pioneering 1903 car journey across America. The country had hardly any paved roads then, but to Jackson that was a mere detail.Phil HarrisonDeal Or No Deal: Banker’s Best Battles7.30pm, ITV1A compilation episode of the glorified gambling gameshow, now hosted by Stephen Mulhern but still imbued with hints of Noel Edmonds’ woo-woo antics. Self-confessed risk-taker Leon has overcome serious health challenges to make it to the show, but plays it surprisingly safe when it comes to his turn in the hot seat.Hannah J DaviesCasualty 24/7: Every Second Counts8pm, Channel 5A taxing day at an overcrowded casualty unit at Barnsley hospital, where 71-year-old Enid is struggling to breathe, Wayne has been shot in the foot, volunteer Jane’s mother arrives after a fall, and three-year-old Rory has something unusual stuck up his nose: “I’ve seen garden peas. I’ve seen little bits of Lego. But I’ve never seen a conker.”Ali CatterallMurder 24/79pm, BBC OneWhen Chris Hemming rings in to confess to police that he has stabbed his partner, Cheryl McKenna, to death, DCI Gareth Lougher has to establish if the murder was premeditated or if it was manslaughter. Shot using multiple screens and shaky real-time camerawork, this will have your adrenaline levels peaking.Priya ElanKatie Price: Nothing to Hide9pm, Sky DocumentariesIt might be the last in the series but Katie Price’s carousel of chaos just keeps spinning – she was engaged to Lee Andrews weeks after filming this. Before him, though, were husbands Alex (“walking weapon/perfect rebound”), Reid and Kieran Hayler. Her children Junior and Princess speak out about the turbulence of the last few years.HRFilmThe Devil Wears Prada 2 (David Frankel, 2026),Disney+View image in fullscreenConflict … Miranda Priestly (Meryl Streep) and Andy (Anne Hathaway) in The Devil Wears Prada 2.Photograph: Macall Polay/APMiranda Priestly is back – and the last 20 years haven’t diminished the fashion magazine editor’s hauteur one iota. But, in David Frankel’s couture-drenched comic sequel, her former callow assistant, Anne Hathaway’s Andy, is now an award-winning investigative journalist. Hired by the owner to improve Runway’s reputation, she can take all that Meryl Streep’s disdainful Priestly throws at her. This time round, the main conflict is with the internet, as declining print sales and clickbait competition threaten the publication’s future. It’s a jolly, aspirational outing, buoyed by scene-stealers Stanley Tucci and Emily Blunt, even if the gags are largely from the preloved rack.Simon WardellPrimate (Johannes Roberts, 2025),Paramount+A brutally efficient horror from Johannes Roberts that employs all your favourite slasher movie tropes – remote location, invincible foe, gut-wrenching dismemberings, final girl – but makes the serial killer a chimp. Ben was the test subject of a linguistics professor who has recently died, and can communicate using sign language. He now lives with her widower Adam (Troy Kotsur) and teenage daughters, Lucy (Johnny Sequoyah) and Erin (Gia Hunter). But a mongoose bite turns the cute ape into a rabid menace and the family’s Hawaiian clifftop home into a deathtrap.SWExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Beginning Middle End by Valeria Luiselli review – a mother and daughter’s odyssey | Books | The Guardian
description: This journey of discovery from the US to Sicily tackles urgent themes, but is increasingly inward-looking
Author: Chris Power
Headline: This journey of discovery from the US to Sicily tackles urgent themes, but is increasingly inward-looking
Content: Valeria Luiselli.Photograph: Clayton CubittView image in fullscreenValeria Luiselli.Photograph: Clayton CubittBook of the dayBooksReviewBeginning Middle End by Valeria Luiselli review – a mother and daughter’s odysseyThis journey of discovery from the US to Sicily tackles urgent themes, but is increasingly inward-lookingChris PowerWed 29 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Grace Paley’s short story A Conversation With My Father, a request is made of the Paley-like narrator. “I would like you to write a simple story just once more,” her father says, “the kind Maupassant wrote, or Chekhov … Just recognisable people and then write down what happened to them next.” Her attempt, and its failure to impress him, is the action that powers the story. Valeria Luiselli’s fourth novel is propelled by a similar request, the daughter of the Luiselli-like narrator asking: “Will you finally write a novel with a beginning, a middle, and an end?” It’s a problem Luiselli has addressed before. In her 2017 book-length essay about undocumented migrant children, Tell Me How It Ends, she writes that the difficulty in telling their story “is that it has no beginning, no middle and no end”.Beginning Middle End charts the narrator’s efforts to corral life into a narrative. The father in Paley’s story would be similarly unimpressed. After a “slow, entangled” divorce, the narrator, a Mexican living in the United States, embarks on a European book tour with her 12-year-old daughter. She has a coil removed in Munich; her daughter loses a tooth in Prague; near Amsterdam they watch children learning to swim with their shoes on in case of floods. When summer comes, the pair fly to Catania in Sicily. The narrator’s grandmother grew up nearby. They stay in the apartment of a pianist who’s away on tour, with whom the narrator had a “brief and feverish encounter” the previous year.This book can be made to sound dense with plot: Etna is erupting. Wildfires rage. The narrator’s mother, in Baja California, might be developing dementia and is possibly planning an act of eco-terrorism. Before the narrator left for Europe her mother gave her a valuable heirloom, a Roman mosaic tile portraying the god Proteus; the narrator’s grandmother took it from an excavation site before leaving Sicily.Mother and daughter discuss Proteus’s appearance in the Odyssey, their explorations of myth and classical literature becoming a central strand. The narrator’s daughter grows obsessed with returning the mosaic to the ruined villa it came from.After a few weeks the pianist returns, the narrator’s attraction to him rapidly eroding as the sex gets rough, he fights with her daughter, and neglects to help when she gets stung by jellyfish. Yet despite all this, the novel has trouble gathering momentum – or perhaps isn’t interested in doing so. Paley’s narrator calls plot “the absolute line between two points which I’ve always despised”. Luiselli’s seems to feel the same way, breaking her narrative into discrete little segments like the tesserae from which Proteus’s face emerges.Throughout, the narrator questions what she is writing. “I don’t have a clear idea about what I am doing, or what will happen next, not yet,” she admits. “I get entangled in possible beginnings, intricate plots, improvised premises.” Later she wonders if this project isn’t a novel at all but an essay. “Perhaps the middle does not fit into the tighter architecture of a novel, the corset of plot. The middle feels more akin to the distracted, loose, meandering spirit of essaying. Maybe it will have to be an essay until it can be a novel again, an essay with a beginning, a middle, and an end.” This persistent identity crisis is only resolved when the daughter eventually seizes control of the narrative.Luiselli’s writing has always been essayistic and self-reflexive. In fact, she began in 2010 as an essayist with the lyrical, literary Sidewalks. Her first novel, Faces in the Crowd, blended autofiction and metafiction – the book portraying its own construction, just as Beginning Middle End does – with a fictionalised account of the life of a real Mexican poet. Her second, The Story of My Teeth, is also partly about its own construction: in an author’s note Luiselli explains how the book was created in tandem with a group of factory workers. In a Sebaldian touch, photographs accompany the text.In many ways Beginning Middle End mirrors Luiselli’s previous novel, 2019’sLost Children Archive, itself a fictional expansion of Tell Me How It Ends. Its narration is shared between an unnamed woman, whose marriage is collapsing, and her stepson, who addresses his part to his stepsister. In Beginning Middle End the unnamed narrator’s marriage has ended, and her daughter writes postcards to her stepbrother. In both books the text is divided into short, titled chapters that prefer essayistic thought to the construction of dramatic scenes. Both children come into possession of Polaroid cameras, their pictures providing wordless conclusions to each novel. There is another explicit link, one that paradoxically divides the books’ narrators, but revealing it would be a spoiler.The larger contradiction within Luiselli’s work is that although the subjects it returns to – the role and status of the mother, migration, the climate crisis – are universal and urgent, it is becoming ever more inward-looking. The most dramatic journey Beginning Middle End describes is whether it can succeed in becoming the book we hold in our hands. In a knowing moment, the narrator’s daughter studies the mosaic of Proteus – a shapeshifter, just like this novel – “as if she were looking into a mirror or a pool of water, like a little Narcissus peering at himself”. Since finishing the book, it’s the image that has persisted most strongly in my memory.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Alive by Melanie Challenger review – a maverick study of what it means to have a body | Books | The Guardian
description: In this disorienting book, a poet argues we have been looking at nature – and ourselves – the wrong way
Author: Edward Posnett
Headline: In this disorienting book, a poet argues we have been looking at nature – and ourselves – the wrong way
Content: A humboldt squid.Photograph: Brian Skerry/Minden/naturepl.comView image in fullscreenA humboldt squid.Photograph: Brian Skerry/Minden/naturepl.comBooksReviewAlive by Melanie Challenger review – a maverick study of what it means to have a bodyIn this disorienting book, a poet argues we have been looking at nature – and ourselves – the wrong wayEdward PosnettWed 29 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe eastern breakwater of Granton harbour is almost 1km long, and swimmers can follow its crooked finger, heading straight out into the Firth of Forth, while benefiting from its reassuring presence. One Thursday lunchtime, I thought: why not, let’s give it a go, and headed for its tip. I felt cold, but, as I progressed, I seemed to grow strangely warmer. I did not notice the complaints from my body: the creeping numbness which proceeded from my fingers to my elbow, nor the coldness of my pee. Only by the time I exited the water, club footed and claw handed, did it hit me that I was hypothermic.The irony of this reckless exercise was that in my swim bag there was a book by Melanie Challenger called Alive: The Hidden Intelligence of the Living World. It’s an ambitious examination of the wisdom of bodies, a rhizomatic guide not just to our own, but also all the living forms around us: from bacteria to chimps. Her case is that we have ignored or misread the agency and purpose of bodies to our detriment; in a way it is a plea to listen to them. I wish I had read it before my ill-advised swim.Challenger notes that her book was born out of “wild curiosity”, and a sense that the “stories we were telling ourselves … were both presumptuous and unconvincing”. For her, our focus on souls, genes or minds is a distortion of reality, and we should instead direct our attention to our bodies, which have been marginalised, perhaps because they remind us of our own vulnerability and mortality. It is not that Challenger denies the importance of genes; what she questions is the lens through which we read the world.double quotation markShe presents a range of different organisms, from slime to squid, exploring the ways in which they relate and respond to the world around themThroughout the book she vividly presents a range of different organisms, from slime to squid, exploring the ways in which they relate and respond to the world around them. Among other things, Challenger is a poet, and her descriptions are often beautiful. She describes glacial ice as “blue sheened like an eyeball” and a Humboldt squid as “a lozenge of silver”. By denigrating or ignoring bodies, she argues, we are blinded to the sophistication of other life forms, and do not afford them the respect that they deserve; we mistake machines for consciousness and our own consciousness for machines; we destroy habitats with little regard for the non-human life that resides there.Challenger cites an encyclopaedic range of scientists and philosophers, but her own intellectual guide is Aristotle (she thanks him in the acknowledgments). According to her, it was Aristotle who first grasped the intelligence of bodies, though he lacked the science to support his intuitions. She brings him to life at several points in the book, entering into his head, and turning the philosopher – this figure based on a collection of texts, translations, and commentaries – into flesh and bone.I struggle to think of a book for whose subject I have felt more sympathy and excitement: its turn to the body, its trenchant critique of scientific reductionism and misguided metaphors. But as a lay reader I often found myself disoriented, almost dizzied, by the text. I desperately wanted to follow my guide, but I kept on feeling lost, left behind, as the author charged into a dense thicket of ideas and scientific research. This is perhaps the risk run by any pioneer: you can cross a frontier, but can you bring others with you?When I got out of the water, corpse-grey and shaken, I was greeted by two concerned women, experienced swimmers in dry-robes, who kept an eye on me, and offered me a cup of tea and some sound guidance. I’m grateful to them and the way they could quietly read their own bodies, and mine, skilfully relating them to world around us. In a way this book is an invitation to the reader to do something similar; to abandon the harmful readings that we have inherited, and sidestep our own self-destruction.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
