title: Billy Liar review – Tom Courtenay is superb in classic study of a young man and his quixotic dreams | Movies | The Guardian
description: Courtenay gives a beautiful performance as the undertaker’s clerk who nurses preposterous ambitions. But the film is too quick to surrender them
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Courtenay gives a beautiful performance as the undertaker’s clerk who nurses preposterous ambitions. But the film is too quick to surrender them
Content: Not that angry … Julie Christie and Tom Courtenay in Billy Liar.Photograph: RONALD GRANTView image in fullscreenNot that angry … Julie Christie and Tom Courtenay in Billy Liar.Photograph: RONALD GRANTMoviesReviewBilly Liar review – Tom Courtenay is superb in classic study of a young man and his quixotic dreamsCourtenay gives a beautiful performance as the undertaker’s clerk who nurses preposterous ambitions. But the film is too quick to surrender themPeter BradshawWed 29 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is John Schlesinger’s much-loved British comedy from 1963, based on the 1959 novel byKeith Waterhouse, itself part of the now almost forgotten Angry Young Man movement of which John Osborne’s Look Back in Anger and Kingsley Amis’s Lucky Jim were the other two classic texts – though perhaps it is really only Osborne’s hero who is actually angry.Tom Courtenay plays Billy, a cheeky, naughty young man who is as daft as a brush and lives semi-permanently inside his own Walter Mitty-ish fantasy world. (Amis’s Jim Dixon had his own propensity to indulge in micro-imagined situations to get him out of whatever mortifying little class-based humiliations he found himself in.) Billy lives at home in Yorkshire with his mum and dad and works as an undertaker’s clerk, of all the banal things; he takes refuge in his reveries, chiefly the fiction that he is the ruler of a bizarre Ruritanian land called Ambrosia (perhaps named after the brand of rice pudding). Billy wants to be a comedy writer, and he is, after all, the experienced comedy writer of preposterous situations that are happening inside his own head.But Billy has a complicated love life (though we can assume that as a nice young unmarried man he is still a virgin). He has recklessly proposed to two separate women: shy Barbara (Helen Fraser) and Rita (Gwendolyn Watts). But there is a third woman in his life: the gobsmackingly beautiful Liz, played byJulie Christie, and the sheer implausibility of this pairing means that the film almost has the air of science fiction. It is Liz who encourages him to try his luck in London – but Billy loses his nerve.And it is this final act of nerve-loss that has always soured me on Billy Liar, despite its massive reputation. I am heretically unenthused about the film,which I have written about before, as it appears to me finally to have a strange unfunny loyalty to unhappiness and defeat which is quite at odds with the aspiration of Billy’s comic fantasies. It is at odds also, as it happens, with the reality of Keith Waterhouse’s own experiences of getting out and getting on and, for what it is worth, Courtenay’s experiences too, as detailed in his superb autobiography Dear Tom: Letters from Home. On revisiting Billy Liar again, I’m prepared to concede that the ending, in its paralysis and shame, might relate specifically to Billy’s actual lying, not merely his fantasies: his silly and self-destructive fibbing to those two other women. But I still can’t bring myself to join in the chorus of praise. It is however a lovely performance from Courtenay, an enduringly amazing actor who is still doing outstanding work right now.Billy Liar is in UK cinemas from 31 July.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsFilm adaptationsKeith WaterhouseTom CourtenayJulie ChristiereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Solo Sunny review – a rueful East German gem of ambition, loneliness and faded dreams | Movies | The Guardian
description: Konrad Wolf’s 1980 drama follows a singer trying to escape the drab compromises of GDR life, capturing the melancholy of thwarted ambition with warmth and wit
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Konrad Wolf’s 1980 drama follows a singer trying to escape the drab compromises of GDR life, capturing the melancholy of thwarted ambition with warmth and wit
Content: No Liza Minnelli … Renate Krößner in Solo Sunny.Photograph: Société Parisienne de ProductionNo Liza Minnelli … Renate Krößner in Solo Sunny.Photograph: Société Parisienne de ProductionMoviesReviewSolo Sunny review – a rueful East German gem of ambition, loneliness and faded dreamsKonrad Wolf’s 1980 drama follows a singer trying to escape the drab compromises of GDR life, capturing the melancholy of thwarted ambition with warmth and witPeter BradshawWed 29 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe terrible sadness, tattiness and poisoned idealism of the old GDR is preserved as if in a time capsule in this East German film from 1980; it could be a kind of B-side to Bob Fosse’s Cabaret. The heroine, would-be solo pop singer Sunny, is told by her ungallant MC that she is no Liza Minnelli; Cabaret fans might well incidentally recognise here the brusque German word “bumsen”.Solo Sunny is the work of Konrad “Koni” Wolf, a director with an impressive and strange pedigree: he was a garlanded state-sanctioned artist in East Germany, much admired at the Berlin film festival, whose older brother Markus happened to be one of the highest-ranking officials in the Stasi. It makes Wolf the second most politically compromised German film-maker in history. (The disillusioned communist East German character inJenny Erpenbeck’s novel Kairosis a big fan of Wolf.)Ingrid “Sunny” Sommer, played by Renate Krößner, is a former factory worker who tours the GDR with a hideously cheesy kind of gang show that plays clubs and community centres, headed by a tired, sub-jazz-funk band called the Tornadoes; she is one of the guest singers and they also have a kind of acrobat turn and a ghastly MC-slash-comedian. Sexy Sunny falls for Ralph (Alexander Lang), their stand-in sax player who is also a brooding intellectual; Ralph composes the English lyrics for a kind of James Bond theme-type torch song that Sunny has written for herself. Their brief relationship emboldens Sunny to try for a solo career, to break free from all these grotesque losers, the terrible band composed of slobbish guys with bad comb-overs who keep hitting on her.In striving for a glamorous solo career, is Sunny rejecting the collectivist ideals of the GDR in favour of the specious glamour of the capitalist west? The question is never asked explicitly, but – perhaps without really intending it – Wolf allows us to see the poignant ambition in every frame. “Do you think a non-celebrity can have personality?” Sunny asks sadly at one stage. “It’s worth aspiring to …” replies one band member. There is something very melancholy in the shots of the gaunt tenements, uncool denims and boxy Trabants on the gritty streets ofBerlin’s Prenzlauer Berg.Solo Sunny is onMubifrom 1 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsGermanyEuropeMubireviewsShareReuse this content

title: Personal Problems review – an exhilarating lo-fi epic of Black working-class life in 80s New York | Movies | The Guardian
description: The director of Ganja & Hess, Bill Gunn, turns analogue video and improvisation into a work of startling intimacy, humour and emotional force
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: The director of Ganja & Hess, Bill Gunn, turns analogue video and improvisation into a work of startling intimacy, humour and emotional force
Content: Quietly amazing … Mizan Kirby in Personal Problems.Photograph: Kino International/Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenQuietly amazing … Mizan Kirby in Personal Problems.Photograph: Kino International/Everett/ShutterstockMoviesReviewPersonal Problems review – an exhilarating lo-fi epic of Black working-class life in 80s New YorkThe director of Ganja & Hess, Bill Gunn, turns analogue video and improvisation into a work of startling intimacy, humour and emotional forcePeter BradshawWed 29 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1980, Bill Gunn, director ofcult 70s horror Ganja & Hess, took on this quietly amazing micro-budget video project with author Ishmael Reed. It is an improvised melodrama in two parts about Black lives in New York, originally intended for television, and shot on analogue video. It is rough and ready, and the sound mix is sometimes very muddy indeed, but it pops with energy and life.The film anticipates by decades the world of shooting movies on smartphones, even though they were presumably wielding camera equipment the size of a briefcase. Moreover, the opening titles to part one are so basic that they look like a modern intentionally VHS-fetishist gag by someone like Harmony Korine. You could also compare the boozy scenes and overlapping dialogue to Cassavetes or Altman. But for me, it all recalls Larry David’sCurb Your Enthusiasm; there is genuine comedy in one scene in which a stern-faced hospital administrator in the emergency room asks an endless series of form-filling questions of a young man who has arrived in mortal agony, but can’t be treated until the bureaucracy is complete.The story, though ramifying into all sorts of subplots and sidebars, revolves around a nurse at Harlem hospital called Johnnie-Mae (played by nonprofessionalVertamae Smart-Grosvenor, a poet and food writer). In the opening scene, she is interviewed about her life and family background and interest in writing poetry; in this sequence, she is calm, articulate and strong in a way that she is never permitted to be once the eventful drama kicks off.Johnnie-Mae is married to Charles, played by the film’s producer Walter Cotton, but is having an affair with jazz musician Raymon (played by Sam Waymon, brother of Nina Simone), a situation she reveals to two friends at a boozy, uproarious brunch. But idle, mopey Charles – whose main interest seems to be watching The Guns of Navarone on TV – is having an indiscretion of his own, something revealed so fleetingly that it seems like a dream someone is having. Johnnie-Mae is furious at having to share her cramped marital home with Charles’s rackety old dad, but then she also has to let her dodgy brother Bubba and his girlfriend Mary-Alice stay with them too; their criminal dealings mean they are dramatically arrested in the middle of the day while everyone else is out. Her relationship with Raymon deteriorates as he appears to become more famous and successful, and in the film’s second part, her father-in-law’s declining health means an explosive confrontation with Charles’s sister.Where is it heading? Everywhere and nowhere. It is a slice of life. Two slices in fact. The film’s second half quickly recapitulates the action of the first before moving things on, an indication of the way it was intended for TV, but Personal Problems has neither the extended storytelling sensibility of longform television nor the enclosed narrative shape of a feature film. It just rolls past for two and a half hours, an experiment in open-ended performance made with experimental, pioneering flair.Personal Problems is in UK cinemas from 31 July.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsNew YorkRaceTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: San Lorenzo: Rome’s rebel neighbourhood shaped by resistance, art and students | Rome holidays | The Guardian
description: This overlooked quarter swaps the grandeur of tourist-saturated central Rome for murals, graffiti, cheap eateries and a working-class rhythm
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This overlooked quarter swaps the grandeur of tourist-saturated central Rome for murals, graffiti, cheap eateries and a working-class rhythm
Content: San Lorenzo is a working class area of Rome, little frequented by tourists but full of cultural riches and great places to eat and drink.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSan Lorenzo is a working class area of Rome, little frequented by tourists but full of cultural riches and great places to eat and drink.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesZoning inRome holidaysSan Lorenzo: Rome’s rebel neighbourhood shaped by resistance, art and studentsThis overlooked quarter swaps the grandeur of tourist-saturated central Rome for murals, graffiti, cheap eateries and a working-class rhythmJessica LionnelWed 29 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhy go now?One of Europe’s hotspots, central Rome has increasingly come to resemble a tube station during rush hour: stifling, overpacked and claustrophobia-inducing. Last year, the Eternal City welcomed a record number of tourists, driven in part by the 2025 Vatican Jubilee -22.9 million arrivalsstayed in the city, almost 10 times the number of residents.There is no sign of the great tourist boom slowing down, either, with local sourcesindicatingthat 2026 could steal the crown from 2025.Yet while holidaymakers stream out of Rome’s main railway station, Termini, making a beeline towards the Colosseum, the Roman Forum and Piazza Venezia, few realise that a 20-minute walk in the opposite direction leads to one of Rome’s most overlooked quarters: San Lorenzo.View image in fullscreenLa Sapienza is one of the world’s oldest universities. It was founded in 1303.Photograph: Peter Spiro/Getty ImagesBuilt in the late 19th century for the working-class community, San Lorenzo carries more modern historical weight than many of its city-centre counterparts. During Benito Mussolini’s rise to power, both local residents (sanlorenzini) and theArditi del Popolo(AdP)–an anti-fascist military group – were involved in acts of resistance.double quotation markThe neighbourhood has retained much of the character that sets it apart from Rome’s increasingly crowded centreDuring the little-documented 1922 battle of San Lorenzo, members of the AdP resisted squadrist incursions into the neighbourhood, forcing them to retreat under gunfire. Five months later, during theMarch on Rome, barricades were erected to prevent the blackshirts from entering the area. Though13 people were killedin the unrest, fascist forces never fully controlled the neighbourhood. It became known as the red zone, symbolising its leftwing politics.Tragedy struck again towards the end of the second world war, when allied bombing destroyed swathes of the area and killed about 1,500sanlorenzini.Today, the living situation in this counterculture quarter is a lot less combative. Students from nearby La Sapienza University mingle with artists, creatives and longtime residents who have remained rooted in their working-class, leftwing identity. Although it has had acash injection, and clubhouse chainsSoho HouseandSocial Hubhave opened their doors, the neighbourhood has retained much of the character that sets it apart from Rome’s increasingly crowded centre.Where to eat and drinkView image in fullscreenSan Lorenzo is known for its non-touristy eating and drinking spots.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesSticky menus with photos of food on them are thankfully few and far between, as are plates of carbonara for more than €10. The district’sPizzeria Formula 1is a rite of passage for those living in the area. The no-frills spot has served up Roman-style thin-crust pizza since 1978, specialising in classic toppings such as margherita. Its interior matches what is served: a wood-lined room with white ceilings that looks like it hasn’t been touched since its opening. Both old and young come for meals that rarely stretch beyond €10 per head.A few minutes away isOsteria da Marcello, a family-run fixture since 1961. Before Marcello Santececca and his wife, Alessandrina, opened their doors, the premises catered largely tofagottari,diners who bought food from home and wine from the establishment. Typical Roman dishes, such as stewed tripe, deep-fried Jewish-style artichokes (carciofi alla giudia),cacio e pepepasta, and braised oxtail are served on plates placed on paper-covered tables in a dining room retaining its indoor picnic atmosphere.It’s not just inexpensive eateries that prevail.Nena Mercato e Cucina, run by Italian actorCristiano Caccamoand his business partner Lorenzo Biancolella, represents a newer side of San Lorenzo: trendy without pomp. Tiled tables and plates hung on the walls lend a Spanish feel, while the menu reworks old-school Italian staples with a sprinkle of modernity, from duck fettuccine with parmesan foam to carbonara with truffles.View image in fullscreenPizzeria Formula 1 is a rite of passage forsanlorenziniThose with a sweet tooth can cleanse their palates with a bona fide gelato from the aptly namedGelato San Lorenzo, which serves flavours ranging from the obscure (avocado, lemon and pepper) to classic (strawberry).Nearby, 103-year-old chocolate factorySAID dal 1923serves up desserts centred on chocolate. Display cabinets show off handmade pralines and truffles, and chocolate-making paraphernalia dangles from the walls, offering a reminder of the zone’s industrial past. Come autumn, the chocolatier’s rich hot chocolate is moreish enough for Augustus Gloop to want to wade in.As dusk falls, Piazza dell’Immacolata becomes the neighbourhood’s unofficial living room, where raucous university students spill out with beers and plastic cups of wine in hand.Wine bars are few, but it doesn’t mean they are non- existent. Hidden in plain sight is minusculeRamnes, a wine bar where patrons and newcomers revel in conversation between sips of local wine (such as the crisp Bellone) and beverages from slightly further afield (such as velvety reds from nearby Abruzzo).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCultural experiencesView image in fullscreenBasilica San Lorenzo fuori le mura (Basilica of St Lawrence Outside the Walls).Photograph: Reda/Getty ImagesMuch like central Rome, faith makes up a part of San Lorenzo’s sightseeing.The Basilica of St Lawrence Outside the Wallswas built around the tomb of the quarter’s namesake. The basilica is one of theSeven Pilgrim Churches of Romeand houses the relics of St Stephen. The original church was destroyed by allied bombings in 1943, with the latest facade rebuilt from the rubble.In keeping with the religious theme, tree-linedVerano Monumental cemetery(known asIl Veranoby locals) offers a place of reflection and tranquillity away from the hubbub of the area. The 83-hectare burial ground is divided into Jewish, Catholic and Protestant sections, with a monument to the victims of the first world war. The resting place of Italian acting iconsAlberto Sordi,Bud SpencerandGigi Proietti, it’s Rome’s answer to London’s Highgate cemetery.double quotation markWhere central Rome is defined by frescoes, San Lorenzo is defined by street artBeyond piety, San Lorenzo’s modern spin stands out. Where central Rome is defined by frescoes, San Lorenzo is defined by street art. As in any neighbourhood, there’s a fair amount of graffiti, but then there are standout pieces such as Marina Biagini andElisa Caracciolo’sMurale contro il Femminicidio(Mural Against Femicide, 2012-13), each of the 107 figures representing a victim of femicide from the year before. Rome-born street artist Alice Pasquini painted a block-long mural called “Welcome to San Lorenzo” along Via dei Sabelli. Street arttoursare frequent.View image in fullscreenElisa Caracciolo’sMurale contro il FemminicidioPhotograph: Andrea Sabbadini/AlamySan Lorenzo’s creative identity extends beyond the streets. It is also a key destination for contemporary art in Rome, anchored by theFondazione Pastificio Cerere, a former pasta factory transformed into a cultural centre in the 1970s, with frequent exhibitions. Independent galleries and creative spaces also contribute to the area’s broader artistic ecosystem, includingCollettivo noMadeandMonti8.Where to shop‘Year-round sunshine practically guaranteed’: Le Mourillon is Toulon’s cool, beachy quarterRead moreWith not a pristine Gucci bag or a sharp suit in sight, alternative, vintage clothing is high on the priority list forsanlorenzini. There are many secondhand clothes shops, such asLatini 34, where everything from boldly coloured preloved trench coats to shoes can be found. You can also find artisanal leather goods atLaboratorio Pellerossa, and handpicked garments from little-known designers across the globe atL’Anatra all’Arancia. Music-aficionados can pick up a range of vinyl fromUltrasuoni Records Roma.Don’t missIt’s pretty hard to missGiardino Veranoin the summer, an open-air space near Il Verano;noise and laughter can be heard throughout the quarter. The four-month-long summer festival hosts (every day until October) free concerts, an outdoor cinema and drinks and games until 2am.Where to stayView image in fullscreenThe Social Hub.Photograph: leonardoworldwide.comThere’s little in the way of plush hotels in San Lorenzo butAteneo Garden Palace(doubles from €188) is set with a sizable courtyard, and offers spacious, airy rooms. Down the road, the newly openedSocial Hub(doubles from €250) offers all the facilities from onsite restaurants to a rooftop pool with a bar.Explore more on these topicsRome holidaysZoning inItaly holidaysEurope holidaysCity breaksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to turn mozzarella whey into delectable muffins – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: Don’t pour it down the sink. This subtly tangy liquid is naturally acidic, adding flavour and fluffiness to your baking
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Don’t pour it down the sink. This subtly tangy liquid is naturally acidic, adding flavour and fluffiness to your baking
Content: Tom Hunt’s mozzarella whey muffins with sundried tomatoes and olives.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s mozzarella whey muffins with sundried tomatoes and olives.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notFoodHow to turn mozzarella whey into delectable muffins – recipeDon’t pour it down the sink. This subtly tangy liquid is naturally acidic, adding flavour and fluffiness to your bakingTom HuntWed 29 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMozzarella comes in a bag or pot surrounded by whey or brine. This is known aslatticelloin Italy, and has all the flavour of the cheese and more – it’s lactic, sour and subtly sweet, with a powerful, salty, umami-rich depth of flavour. It’s delicious as a drink in it’s own right, but it’s also great to cook with. It can be used instead of buttermilk or yoghurt in marinades, even though it has less viscosity than both, and in baking. I’ve included the mozzarella itself in today’s recipe, but it is entirely optional and could easily be saved for another recipe.Mozzarella whey muffinsWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appMozzarella whey is my latest Waste Not discovery. While researchingmy buffalo mozzarella taste test for the Filterearlier this month, I tasted the whey of each cheese to gauge its quality, and found all of them pretty delicious. By the end, I had the whey from 10 pots to use up, so tried out a few recipes, including drinks, marinades and muffins. Mozzarella whey is naturally acidic, much like yoghurt or buttermilk, so it stands to reason that it would make an excellent muffin by activating the baking powder and helping the muffins to rise, while also adding flavour. Explore your own combinations of optional extras: I adapted this recipe from one of my early Guardian recipes forceleriac and blue cheese muffins, which is another lovely combination.Makes6150g spelt flour, or wholemeal flour1½ tsp baking powder1 egg, lightly beaten125ml mozzarella whey100goptional extras– olives, sun-dried tomatoes, roast red peppers, or whatever you fancy or have to hand125g ball mozzarella, torn (optional)3 sprigs fresh herbs(rosemary, thyme, oregano), leaves picked (optional)Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6, and grease and line a six-hole muffin tin. In a large bowl (or plastic tub for which you have a lid), combine the flour, baking powder, beaten egg and mozzarella whey. Add your chosen optional extras and herbs, if using; if you like, tear in some mozzarella, too, then beat to combine (if using a tub, simply pop on the lid and shake vigorously).Divide the batter between the lined muffin tray holes, top each one with more olives and mozzarella, if using, then bake for 15-18 minutes, until golden on top. Remove from the tray, transfer to a rack and enjoy warm, or leave to cool and store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to three days.Explore more on these topicsFoodWaste notFood wasteCheeseBakingSnacksVegetablesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cherry sundaes and banana splits: Helen Graves’ recipes for barbecued fruit | Food | The Guardian
description: These new spins on nostalgic desserts will elevate your summer barbecues, while their prep-ahead nature will keep the day stress free
Author: Helen Graves
Headline: These new spins on nostalgic desserts will elevate your summer barbecues, while their prep-ahead nature will keep the day stress free
Content: Helen Graves' barbecued banana splits with salted date cream and coconut crunch.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food styling: Aya Nishimura. Prop styling: Polly Webb-Wilson. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.View image in fullscreenHelen Graves' barbecued banana splits with salted date cream and coconut crunch.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food styling: Aya Nishimura. Prop styling: Polly Webb-Wilson. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.FoodCherry sundaes and banana splits: Helen Graves’ recipes for barbecued fruitThese new spins on nostalgic desserts will elevate your summer barbecues, while their prep-ahead nature will keep the day stress freeHelen GravesWed 29 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen it comes to barbecued desserts, a few squares of chocolate melted inside a banana will no longer cut it. Get ahead with some easy-to-prep elements, then add a final flourish of smoke-licked fruit to bring new energy to classic desserts, such as banana splits and layered fruit sundaes. They need not be complex, and will interest your guests far more than the same old stale ideas. I’ve had some fun with these nostalgic favourites, and hope you will, too.Barbecued banana splits with salted date cream and coconut crunch (pictured top)Want to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appThe natural caramel sweetness of dates flavours salted whipped cream in this grownup take on an often kitsch dessert. The coconut crunch is so good you may wish to make double the quantity – sprinkle the excess over yoghurt, ice-cream or just eat a handful every time you go to the kitchen.Prep5 minCook20 minCool10 minServes6600ml double cream80ml date syrup1 pinch sea salt6 bananas, unpeeled and cut in half lengthways30g butter, meltedFor the coconut crunch1½tbsp maple syrup¼tsp light soy sauce1 pinch flaky sea salt30g flaked almonds30g coconut chipsFirst make the topping. Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5 and line an oven tray with greaseproof paper. Mix the maple syrup, light soy sauce and sea salt in a bowl, then stir in the almonds and coconut chips. Spread out in an even layer on the lined tray, bake for five minutes, then give everything a good stir and bake for another six to eight minutes, until lightly toasted. Remove and leave to cool – the mix will crisp up as it does so.When you’re ready to grill the bananas, in a medium bowl whip the cream, date syrup and salt to soft peaks. Brush the cut sides of the bananas with the melted butter, then grill cut side down directly over the coals for two to three minutes, until lightly charred.Serve the bananas topped with the date cream and garnished with a good sprinkling of coconut crunch.Smoky cherry baklava sundaeWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenHelen Graves’ smoky cherry baklava sundae.Skewering is the easiest way to handle cherries on a barbecue grill – you’ll need thin ones for this. Cherry juice varies enormously in sweetness, so taste it after adding the sugar and lemon juice, and adjust to your liking. I sometimes add clotted cream to this when I’m feeling mischievous.Prep5 minCook30 minChill1 hr+Serves4300ml cherry juice1 tbsp caster sugar1 tbsp lemon juice1 tbsp cornflour mixed with 1 tbsp cold water500g cherries, pitted4 scoops vanilla ice-cream8 piecesbaklava– a pistachio one works well here4 spoonfuls clotted cream(optional)1 small handful pistachios, shelled and finely choppedMix the cherry juice, caster sugar and lemon juice in a small saucepan, bring to a simmer, stirring to dissolve the sugar, then leave to bubble gently for 10 minutes. Whisk in the cornflour slurry to thicken the mix, then bring back to a simmer and cook for two minutes more. Take off the heat, leave to cool, then chill thoroughly.When you’re ready to serve, thread the pitted cherries on to small skewers and grill them directly over the coals for five minutes on each side, until lightly charred. Layer the grilled cherries in sundae glasses with the ice-cream, baklava, clotted cream, if using, and cherry syrup, garnish with the chopped pistachios and serve.Helen Graves is a cook, food writer and editor ofPit magazineExplore more on these topicsFoodBarbecueFruitDessertSummer food and drinkIce-cream and sorbetNuts and seedsrecipesShareReuse this content
